articles.title: Critical PwnEscape Linux Kernel Vulnerability Lets Guest VMs Read Host Memory
articles.text:
A newly disclosed critical flaw in the Linux kernel allows code inside a virtual machine to read memory on the host computer it runs on. A researcher demonstrated the leak against Vercel's live cloud sandboxes, and Vercel confirmed it.
The flaw, now tracked as CVE-2026-99999 and nicknamed PwnEscape, is in the Linux kernel's networking code, not in any one cloud's setup, so it reaches the shared layer that cloud providers use to keep customers' workloads apart.
It was found in a Vercel security challenge and reported privately before any public release, and there is no sign it has been used in a real attack.
What the Researcher Showed
Paulos Yibelo of the security firm pwn.ai found that specially made network packets sent from inside a virtual machine could do three things, he explained in a technical write-up: read the host's memory, crash the host, and run code on it. All three come from the same kernel flaw.
Vercel said in its report on the challenge that the memory leak was demonstrated against its production sandboxes. Each packet the guest sent out could carry back about 32 bytes of the host's memory, and the guest could keep going as long as it kept sending packets.
The crash and code execution were observed only on the researcher's own machines, which were set up to match Vercel's. Two specially crafted packets were enough to crash a host and take down every sandbox running on it.
Using the same flaw, the researcher then reached administrator control of a host, breaking out of the virtual machine. He stressed this was a lab result, "not a claim of root command execution in any vendor's production environment."
"Our research ran through Omega-Pwn, an internal harness combining our own security research tooling with elements of SingularityNET's OmegaClaw architecture. It let us carry hypotheses, code traces, failed attempts, and experimental results across long-running research sessions. GPT-5.6 Sol was the primary reasoning engine. We directed the investigation, challenged its findings, and validated the interesting ones against actual kernel behavior on systems we controlled," Paulos Yibelo told The Hacker News.
Vercel said no report in the challenge showed anyone reading a customer's files, secrets, or application data.
How Severe It Is, and Who Can Set It Off
The kernel's maintainers assigned the flaw CVE-2026-99999 and, in the published record, rated it 9.3 out of 10, or Critical. The U.S. National Vulnerability Database had received that entry but had not yet finished its own review.
The same record lists the attack vector as local. In plain terms, the attacker has to already be running code inside a guest, as the researcher was. This is not a flaw that an outsider can exploit by sending packets across the open internet.
It is not in CISA's catalog of actively exploited vulnerabilities, and no real-world use has been reported.
Why It Reaches Beyond Vercel
Vercel Sandbox runs each customer's code in its own Firecracker microVM, a small virtual machine with its own copy of the Linux kernel, on bare-metal Amazon EC2 hosts. That microVM is the wall between one customer and the host, and between one customer and another.
The flaw is not in that wall. It is in the Linux kernel's networking code, which the host runs. pwn.ai said Vercel's sandbox was already hardened beyond normal industry standards, with no misconfiguration it could find.
Because almost every large cloud separates customer workloads on the same layer of the Linux kernel, Vercel said that a flaw there poses a risk to shared infrastructure rather than to any one provider.
The Fix and the Fixed Versions
The fix is a single Linux kernel change, commit 6785011f8b16, written by Red Hat's Michael S. Tsirkin and merged into the mainline kernel. It adds a check that a packet's checksum data cannot point into the IPv4 header before the kernel acts on it, and applies that check at five places in the networking code.
The change is deliberately partial. Its author calls it "a defence in depth measure" and notes that a fuller check on the way packets enter the kernel still needs work.
The maintainers backported the fix to the stable kernel branches. According to the CVE record, these are the first fixed versions in each supported branch:
| Stable branch | First fixed version | 
|---|---|
| 5.10 | 5.10.272 | 
| 5.15 | 5.15.223 | 
| 6.1 | 6.1.190 | 
| 6.6 | 6.6.159 | 
| 6.12 | 6.12.113 | 
| 6.18 | 6.18.57 | 
| 7.2 | 7.2.11 | 
Linux distributions ship their own kernels and often add this kind of fix without changing the version number, so check your distribution's advisory and whether the fix is in the kernel the host is actually running, not only the number from uname.
What to Do
Update the host kernel to one of the fixed versions above, or to the vendor build that includes the fix, and reboot into it. Updating only a guest's kernel does not fix the host. The sources give no separate workaround for this flaw if you cannot update yet.
Where patching has to wait, the usual step is to limit what a break-in could reach. Vercel said it keeps host kernels up to date, disables nested virtualization, and runs each microVM under Firecracker's jailer, which grants the microVM process only the permissions it needs. That does not fix the flaw, but it narrows what an attacker who used it could do.
Found in a $1 Million Challenge
The flaw was found in a two-week challenge Vercel ran in August that offered up to $1 million in total to anyone who could break out of its sandbox. No single payout reached that figure. The top reward per report was $50,000; Vercel paid $242,000 across 1,285 reports, and this flaw was the one Critical finding.
pwn.ai said it found the flaw in three days using its own AI-assisted research system, with the model doing the source-code analysis and human researchers directing the work. The firm put the cost at under $700 in API tokens. It was the latest case of researchers using a large language model to help find and chain real flaws, after a separate team used one earlier this year to reach internal systems at OpenAI.

articles.title: Forget the iPhone Duo — the M4 iPad Air is a lot cheaper even at full price but it's now 21% off
articles.text:
Forget the iPhone Duo — the M4 iPad Air is a lot cheaper even at full price but it's now 21% off
Desktop-level performance for just under AU$1,000
Pre-orders for the much-anticipated iPhone Duo are set to start later tonight (11pm AEDT, October 16), but with the base 256GB model costing an eye-watering AU$3,499, it’s a big ask even for the most loyal of Apple fans.
Given the fact the iPhone Duo can feasibly be compared to an iPad when unfolded, in my mind, the better value alternative is to get an actual iPad and pair it with your current iPhone. And a great example is the 2026 model iPad Air, especially now it’s been given a rare 21% discount on Amazon Australia. That drops the price of the 128GB model to AU$987 and that's excellent value for a tablet that we called the “pro model tablet for most people”.
Having just been released this year, this 21% discount on the 11-inch iPad Air with the Apple M4 chipset is the biggest we’ve seen since the recent price hike in July. Purple and Starlight are available for this price, while Space Grey and Blue costs AU$1 more. The 256GB model is AU$200 more, while the 13-inch starts at AU$1,287, also 20% off.
While our iPad Air review noted that there were no real design changes from the previous model, getting the M4 chip, extra RAM and improved connectivity make the 2026 release a much more powerful tablet than previous generations.
These upgrades should make photo and video editing, gaming, multitasking or general computing tasks a breeze, although the display’s frame rate is still, annoyingly, capped at 60Hz (compared to the iPad Pro’s 120Hz ProMotion display).
Admittedly, the 11-inch screen means this iPad is much less portable than the iPhone Duo, even when it’s unfolded, but the extra screen real estate provides the added benefit of a large, vibrant canvas for entertainment, and Apple Pencil note-taking.
While this iPad Air isn’t going to be a must-have upgrade if you already own the M3 or M2 versions from recent years, you’ll see a massive performance boost over an older iPad Air, base model iPads, and even some older iPad Pros.
And let's also do some maths, shall we? With this discount on the latest iPad Air and purchasing the 256GB iPhone 18 Pro Max for AU$2,297 is a total of AU$3,287 — that's cheaper than the starting price of the iPhone Duo! 'Nuff said!
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Nico is an experienced writer and journalist, having previously written for business titles across Australia. He mainly focuses on evergreen content like buying guides and reviews, as well as finding deals and coupon codes at TechRadar Australia. Outside of work, Nico is a keen cyclist and occasionally goes on runs and hikes.

articles.title: ThreatsDay: Adobe RCE, DNS Wallet Theft, NVIDIA Container Escape, Self-Healing Backdoor + 23 More
articles.text:
Someone built a tool to steal data, then decided it should scare the victim for fun. Yes, that’s an actual feature. And somehow, it fits right in with this week's security stories.
The rest gets interesting in different ways. A small permission can lead to a big theft. A trusted login can hide the wrong person. Old bugs are finding new victims, familiar tools are being put to strange uses, and some flaws are so simple you wonder how nobody spotted them sooner.
There's a lot more hiding in the details, including a few twists you probably wouldn't expect. Here's what made the list this week.
The threats change every week. Subscribe, and we’ll alert you when each new ThreatsDay Bulletin is out.
- 
  
  Active ransomware exploitation Qilin and Settra ransomware groups are actively exploiting CVE-2026-0257, an authentication bypass vulnerability in PAN-OS GlobalProtect and Prisma Access. The vulnerability, disclosed in May 2026, has since come under active exploitation. "Because this access originates through an organization’s own VPN, malicious activity can resemble legitimate remote work and may go undetected until credential theft, lateral movement, data theft, or ransomware deployment is underway," ReliaQuest said. "Organizations should immediately upgrade affected deployments, disable authentication override cookies where they are not required, terminate all active GlobalProtect sessions after patching, and investigate unexpected connections, including sessions using hostnames such as 'kali.' Patching alone may not remove access established before remediation."
- 
  
  Hybrid warfare escalates across Europe Russia is assessed to have escalated its use of hybrid, asymmetric warfare across Europe following its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. "They do not involve troops moving across a country’s border or a state’s military dropping bombs on an adversary’s capital city," Recorded Future said. "Instead, they are a complex kit of psychological, cyber, and physical tactics meant to achieve several key aims: (1) Test the enemy’s defensive capabilities, as Russia evaluates whether to escalate aggression into a formal, kinetic conflict, (2) Degrade the enemy’s critical infrastructure, and (3) Sow an environment of fear in the enemy’s government and population to degrade the enemy’s ability to respond."
- 
  
  DNS-powered wallet theft Infoblox has analyzed a cryptocurrency wallet-drainer kit, self-branded as Noir, that makes use of DNS TXT records to locate its hosted pool, which currently runs on Cloudflare Pages. It's delivered by means of a loader that queries the TXT record through public DoH services to learn which backend pool is active. "The drainer does not need a seed phrase, password, or private key," Infoblox said. "It tailors content to the user after receiving initial read permissions, developing a plan for the specific wallet. Then it obtains spending permissions that can look less alarming than a direct transfer and performs the theft from attacker-controlled infrastructure." It's suspected that the malware was created and maintained with AI assistance.
- 
  
  Discord-based remote access threat A Rust-based remote access trojan dubbed CikaBika Bot has been observed being delivered via a document-themed lure containing a malicious LNK file and a PDF with an embedded payload. "The malware uses a Nim loader, PowerShell UAC bypass, and DLL search-order hijacking before leveraging Discord for C2, reconnaissance, remote execution, and data exfiltration through ngrok in observed malicious activity," Darktrace said. The malware also supports screenshot capture and file transfers.
- 
  
  RAT combines theft and intimidation A Windows remote access trojan (RAT) called KGB RAT is being marketed on underground forums since late 2025 as being fully undetectable. It features a built-in crypter, HVNC, credential theft, ransomware, and an unusual set of psychological harassment capabilities, per Group-IB. "KGB RAT is, in practice, a full-featured malware package that gives attackers silent and persistent control over infected Windows machines," it said. "What sets it apart from comparable RAT families is not only its technical breadth — combining credential theft, keylogging, hidden desktop takeover, and ransomware in a single builder — but also a dedicated set of psychological harassment features, including screamer functions, jump scares, and forced blue screens of death. These 'fun settings,' as the developers themselves describe them, signal a threat actor profile comfortable weaponizing victim anxiety alongside data theft." A public disclosure referencing a KGB RAT server at version 0.1 dates to late January 2022, indicating the developer had been building and testing the malware for years before bringing it to market.
- 
  
  Stealthy live-screen surveillance A multi-stage infection chain on Windows has been observed deriving a previously undocumented .NET RAT with live screen surveillance capability. It's been codenamed BotHelper RAT. "The first stage is a native x64 stager that fingerprints the host computer name, logged-on user, processor configuration, and installed memory, then connects to easyllms.xyz over HTTPS and retrieves a file named payload.bin from a path guarded by a long hexadecimal identifier, disabling TLS certificate validation beforehand," Point Wild said. "The second stage is BotHelper RAT. It copies itself to a hidden location, registers a scheduled task to relaunch every 30 minutes, patches the Antimalware Scan Interface, and registers with the same host that delivered it before polling a set of PHP endpoints for tasking."
- 
  
  New Android anti-scam defenses Google said it's rolling out multi-layered protections across Google Messages and third-party messaging apps to protect Android users against mobile scams. This includes enhanced Scam Detection with Private AI Compute, link safety checks with Gemini Nano, and redesigned warnings before tapping unfamiliar links. Google also said it's bringing Scam Detection in chat notifications to warn users about suspicious messages directly from their notification shade to other Android devices in partnership with device makers. Other security improvements include automatic screen-share privacy to hide sensitive information in native apps, Chrome, and Android WebView, blocking apps from quietly enabling call forwarding in the background, and real-time verification for bank calls in collaboration with Banco do Brasil, Itaú Unibanco, and other leading banks. "Android checks incoming calls in real time to verify whether the bank actually initiated the call," Google said. "If an incoming caller claiming to represent a bank fails this verification check, Android hangs up the call and immediately alerts you." Since launching this feature in June 2026, Android has blocked more than 3 million spoofed calls from Banco do Brasil and Itaú Unibanco alone.
- 
  
  AI model theft defenses strengthened Anthropic has disclosed that new measures like preserved thinking, two-stage classifiers, and charging for requests that are blocked by our safeguards before Claude responds in its Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5 models have reduced data harvesting through distillation attacks by about 90% to 99%.
- 
  
  Enterprise browser security controls Mozilla has launched Firefox Enterprise, a browser iteration "built for organizations with strict security, governance, and compliance requirements." Mozilla added, "IT and security teams get more control over their data, IT infrastructure and browser environment — helping strengthen technological independence and operational resilience."
- 
  
  Self-healing WordPress backdoor Wordfence has detailed an unusual malware that's installed as a must-use WordPress plugin and makes use of "several self-healing mechanisms in place in order to survive removal. It also makes use of EtherHiding, a technique that hides the location of the attacker's servers behind a smart contract on the Ethereum blockchain, making the command channel resilient to takedown." The malware is capable of establishing administrator access, hiding the rogue administrator account, harvesting administrator passwords, remote site modification, data exfiltration, and spreading to other WordPress installations on the file system.
- 
  
  Stolen credentials expose GitHub data Meta said it's notifying about 1,500 people, most of them its own employees in the U.S., after unknown threat actors broke into some of the company's GitHub repositories. The intrusion, detected a few weeks ago, involved the use of an employee's stolen credentials. The access has since been shut down, according to SecurityWeek.
- 
  
  XWorm expands surveillance capabilities The malware known as XWorm has transitioned from an infostealer to a full-blown surveillance platform. The malware's plugin count has expanded from 35 to 46. The latest versions detected since July 2025 are V6.4, V6.5 "XWorm Reborn," V7.2, and V7.4. "The Maps plugin provides victims' GPS location without triggering a user prompt," Netskope said. "The Microphone plugin streams live audio from the victim’s device. HBrowser gives operators interactive control of authenticated browser sessions without touching credentials, bypassing MFA entirely. Webcam capture is also available on demand."
- 
  
  Higher rewards for memory-safety bugs Google has announced that it's raising bug bounty rewards for some Chrome vulnerabilities, with a focus on memory safety issues. While the company lowered standard payout amounts for some vulnerabilities in April, such as a base reward of $500 for memory safety issues, it has now quadrupled base rates for memory safety flaws to $2,000. Vulnerabilities in Chrome's browser, GPU, and network processes can now earn researchers up to $20,000.
- 
  
  Post-quantum readiness warning Microsoft is urging organizations to prepare their certificate systems for post-quantum authentication, stating that public key infrastructure (PKI), hardware security modules (HSMs), and security appliances need testing before deployment. "Organizations should begin now by inventorying certificate dependencies, assessing vendor roadmaps, identifying long-lived infrastructure, and creating non-production test environments," Microsoft said. "Early testing can surface compatibility and process gaps before post-quantum authentication is required at scale."
- 
  
  AI tool credentials at risk A new malware-as-a-service (MaaS) infostealer written in Rust comes with its own loader and a built-in cryptocurrency clipper. "Warden Stealer is one of the first infostealers targeting configuration files and local data belonging to AI assistants and agentic coding tools," Gen Digital said. "Its builds are heavily obfuscated, morphed, and regularly updated to evade detection."
- 
  
  Advanced browser data theft Newer versions of CastleStealer can "bypass app-bound encryption in Chromium-based browsers, execute commands remotely, and exfiltrate stolen information in small encrypted transmissions rather than a single large archive," according to Flashpoint. The C#-based stealer was first discovered in April 2026.
- 
  
  AI developer credentials targeted The infostealer known as Aoki (aka Aokigahara) is targeting credential and session files used by AI coding assistants, including Claude, OpenAI's Codex, Cursor, Codeium, and Gemini. The stealer was first seen earlier this year. "API keys and Open Authorization (OAuth) or session tokens allow malicious activity to be carried out under a legitimate developer's identity and API quota," the Symantec Threat Hunter team said. "They can also expose connected repositories, cloud services and CI/CD pipelines linked to that account, and may bypass safeguards that assume requests originate from a trusted user." In a report published last month, Google-owned Wiz said AI service provider API keys are a hot commodity. "These AI credentials are highly lucrative; allowing attackers to freely run their own workloads or resell the access as part of the illicit LLM resale market," it said. "In addition, these keys can potentially grant access to historical chat logs that may contain sensitive corporate data, but we’re not aware of public occurrences of this scenario."
- 
  
  Customizable MaaS infostealer K7 Labs has detailed a Python-based builder that is sold under a MaaS model and is used to embed an infostealer payload. "Rather than operating as a standalone stealer script, the builder follows a MaaS-style model," it said. "It allows operators to generate customized Windows executables using Nuitka or PyInstaller, with webhook configuration integrated into the build process." The stealer capabilities include anti-analysis techniques, persistence, credential harvesting, and data exfiltration.
- 
  
  Cloud credential theft risk An SSRF vulnerability (GHSA-2phj-cp9f-qq6w, CVSS score: 8.5) in Harbor, the CNCF open-source container registry, can be abused by a registered user to steal cloud credentials. "Any registered user who can create a project can point a webhook at the cloud metadata endpoint and walk away with the server’s IAM credentials," OX Security said.
- 
  
  Unauthenticated RCE chain A set of high-impact vulnerabilities in Adobe Experience Manager (AEM) can be abused to achieve unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE). The chain combines four flaws: Unauthenticated DAM bulk import, stored cross-site scripting (XSS), unsafe XML parsing, and Groovy execution via /bin/asynccommand. The flaws affect only the cloud version of AEM and have been patched.
- 
  
  Critical unauthenticated RCE Samsung has patched a critical security flaw (CVE-2026-110392, CVSS score: 9.8) in QA-Board that allows unauthenticated RCE. Samsung's QA-Board is an experiment-tracking tool that's used to organize, visualize, compare, and share research runs, specifically for algorithm and performance tuning. The problem stems from a case of improper neutralization of user-controlled data that could result in shell command injection. The vulnerability was flagged by Claude Opus 5.5.
- 
  
  Linux root and container escape Security researcher Ziyi Guo has disclosed details of a critical Linux security vulnerability in NVIDIA's GPU Display Driver for Linux (CVE-2026-47595, CVSS score: 7.5, aka Bad UVM) that could allow an unprivileged user can write to read-only memory by taking advantage of the fact that the memory's permissions are not preserved. The vulnerability could be exploited to achieve code execution, escalation of privileges, denial-of-service, information disclosure, data tampering, and even a container escape. "By injecting our exploit code into nvidia-persistenced, we first force the hijacked process to execute a UVM-based local privilege escalation (LPE)," the researcher said. "Once the privilege barrier is crossed, we trigger the subsequent operations, ultimately granting us the ability to execute commands on the host with full root access."
- 
  
  Active command injection attacks A command injection vulnerability in EG Secure Solutions SiteGuard Server Edition (CVE-2026-106931, CVSS score: 8.5) has come under active exploitation in the wild. The flaw affects customers using version 2.20 or later with statistics enabled, which is turned on by default. Successful exploitation could allow an attacker to execute arbitrary OS commands with root or SYSTEM privileges on affected systems. It's currently not known how the flaw is being exploited, by whom, and who is being targeted.
- 
  
  Critical unpatched SQL injection Rapid7 has disclosed details of a critical SQL Injection vulnerability in Channel Software WebAlliance eCommerce (CVE-2026-108065, CVSS score: 9.8). "The exploit allows a malicious actor to read sensitive data from the database, or, if the database user has high privileges, run system commands on the database server," Rapid7 said. "The SQL Injection exploit can be leveraged to view sensitive information in the database, such as user PII and passwords. If logged in with DB admin privileges, the vulnerability can be exploited to run system commands on the server running the database."
- 
  
  Four code execution flaws patched NSD has released patches for four security flaws (CVE-2026-101341, CVE-2026-101339, CVE-2026-101338, and CVE-2026-101337) that could be exploited to achieve execution of arbitrary commands. The vulnerabilities, credited to Qifan Zhang from Palo Alto Networks and Gaurang Maheta, have been patched in NSD 4.15.3 or newer.
- 
  
  Potential VM-to-host escape The Xen project has published details of CVE-2026-79610, a race condition in Xen's grant-table mechanism that could be abused to compromise the security of a virtual machine host and allow an unprivileged guest to elevate its privileges to that of the host. All Xen versions from 4.0 onwards are vulnerable. The issue has been addressed in xsa517.patch. As mitigation, it's advised to use the "gnttab=max-ver:1" hypervisor command line option or the "max_grant_version=1" guest configuration option for guests. The project maintainers credited Anthropic's Claude Opus with the discovery and Teddy Astie of Vates for diagnosing it as a security issue.
- 
  
  SYSTEM-level remote code execution A Windows security vulnerability in MyReport Updater 2.1.1 can permit an attacker to seize control of a machine, including remotely, without authentication. "An attacker with standard user privileges can set an arbitrary reference server," Quarkslab said. "If MyReportUpdaterService can contact this server over gRPC on TCP port 9095, the attacker can write files into a chosen directory with NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM privileges. The attacker can use this file-write access to place a DLL that will be loaded by a privileged process. The DLL code is then executed with high privileges. This vulnerability gives full control of the Citrix server. It can also affect other machines where the vulnerable MyReport solution is installed."
If there's one thing this week's stories make clear, it's that attackers don't always need a clever trick. Sometimes a stolen login, a forgotten setting, or one small mistake is enough. And even when the bug gets fixed, the trouble it caused might still be sitting there.
The lesson is pretty simple: don't just check what's broken. Check who got in, what they touched, and whether they can come back. Keep an eye on the things everyone assumes are safe. Those are often the ones nobody looks at until something goes wrong. That's it for this edition. See you next week, hopefully with fewer surprises.

articles.title: The Mova V70 Ultra Complete is one of the most expensive robot vacuums I've tested — and it proves you don't always get what you pay for
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
The Mova V70 Ultra Complete has everything you expect from a flagship robot vacuum, including some industry firsts: high suction of up to 42,000Pa and yet it's the quietest bot I've tested to date, extendable side brush and mop arms reaching up to 12cm and 17cm respectively for edge cleaning, even a bagless dust tank that reduces ongoing costs. However, vacuuming isn't as good as I've seen from other flagship models with lower suction and the extending side brush doesn't quite work as well as I expected. These flagship features just don't come together to make a complete package, especially given its high price.
Reasons to buy
- + Good mopping around furniture legs
- + Eliminates dust bags
- + Very quiet even at highest suction
- + Comes with plenty of extras in the box
Reasons to avoid
- - Side brush doesn't remain extended along room edges
- - Edge cleaning and carpet vacuuming could be better
- - App can be slow to respond
- - Rotating mop pads not as good as rollers
- - Investment pricing
Why you can trust TechRadar
We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.
Mova V70 Ultra Complete: Two-minute review
If you've never heard of Mova as a brand, you're not alone as it was initially only available in select European and South-East Asian countries. The brand, which is owned by Dreame Technology, is now expanding and is supposed to be value-focused side of the company — although you'd be hard pressed to believe that when its latest flagship robot vacuum costs upwards $1,000 / £1,000 / AU$3,000.
However, the Mova V70 Ultra Complete brings everything you expect from such an expensive robovac, including some industry-first features that are now being adopted by other brands. This includes suction that's a whopping 42,000Pa at its maximum, as well as the impressively long reach of the side brush and mopping arm (12cm and 17cm respectively). I even love the fact that it eliminates the need for dust bags by using a tank you can clean out every now and then while still remaining as hands-free as possible.
It's also arguably the quietest robot vacuum I've tested, even at maximum suction — so quiet, in fact, that I had to check it was actually cleaning during my testing. Yes, it was.
It's vacuuming prowess, however, isn't a good reflection of its listed suction power, particularly on carpets. Case in point: it failed to pick up a mix of oats, tea and chia seeds from a mid-pile carpet even after two passes on its Max (or second-highest) suction setting. Hair pickup at the same setting is also not that great, but bump it up to Max+ (which significantly impacts battery life) and I found my carpets looking a lot better, with even bits of thread cleaned up. The mixture of pantry essentials, however, still remained and I needed to use my Dyson V15 Detect to clean up the leftovers.
Moreover, the extra reach the side brush promises isn't consistent. For example, I expected it to remain extended as long as the V70 was traversing along a room edge, but it repeatedly retracts, leaving dirt along some sections of a room edge. The timing of the extension while cleaning around furniture legs is also off, with the side brush opening up either just before or just after it gets to a chair leg.
The extending mop arm, however, performs better, but even it retracts along some sections of a room edge, but the bot is close enough for edges and areas around furniture to be mopped, if not vacuumed.
The Mova V70 Ultra Complete uses dual rotating mop pads that, in my opinion, aren't as good as rollers. It made a bigger mess of some spilled soy sauce in my kitchen, which a roller mop doesn't as these are constantly washed with fresh water while the robot vacuum is cleaning. I also found that for hard floors to even seem damp, waterflow rate needs to be set to high.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
It's also disappointing that, for an expensive robot vacuum, the docking sequence takes a few tries. In the four weeks of testing, I had to replace the bot in the dock manually twice, but at all other times, it took 2-3 attempts to correctly roll itself back in for self-cleaning and charging.
The companion app is near identical to the Dreame one, but can be slow to load and respond (at least on iOS, which is what I use). And, like its counterpart, some settings are tucked away in submenus, so you need to spend some time going through it all.
While there are features to love here, it's disappointing that they don't really come together well enough to make a complete package, especially when it has to the potential to be one and blow the competition out of the water. For its high asking price, it's a hard one to recommend.
Mova V70 Ultra Complete review: Price & availability
- First unveiled in May 2026 in Europe, followed by an August launch in the US
- Available in bigger markets, like the US, UK, Europe and Australia
- Investment pricing of $1,299 / £1,219 / AU$3,299
The very high $1,299 / £1,219 / AU$3,299 retail price of the Mova V70 Ultra Complete might make you balk but, given its feature set, it shouldn't be all that surprising.
Then again, it's a competitive price when you take into account other flagships recently released, including the $1,699 Roborock Saros 20 Flow (which is unavailable in the UK at the time of writing, but is a lot cheaper at AU$2,499 in Australia) and the Dreame Aqua20 Ultra Roller going for £1,299 / AU$3,299 (unavailable in the US at the time of publication).
All the aforementioned new flagships have different feature sets to justify their high asking prices, but we're yet to try the last two competitors ourselves. Given the results of my testing in this review, however, the Mova V70 Ultra Complete doesn't deliver on its promises as it should, making it a tough sell at its very high price point.
Instead, opting for slightly older models like the Roborock Saros 10 or Saros 20, even the Dreame Aqua10 Ultra, would be the better buy, especially if you can get them at a discounted price.
However, I should note that the Mova V70 Ultra Complete doesn't use dust bags, minimizing your ongoing costs. Plus there's a complete set of replacement brushes and three additional pairs of mop pads in the box, meaning you can go a very long while without needing to buy any replacement parts, adding some additional value to the initial cost.
The only ongoing purchase, if you wish, would be a mopping detergent and/or wood floor-care solution. Only the former is supplied, but Mova recommends you only purchase its proprietary detergents to avoid damaging the appliance and voiding warranty.
• Value score: 3 / 5
Mova V70 Ultra Complete review: Specs
| Max suction: | 42,000Pa | 
| Robot size: | 13.8 x 13.8 inches (35 × 35 × 8.8 cm) | 
| Robot height: | 3.4 inches (8.8cm) | 
| Dock dimensions (W x D x H): | 16.5 × 18.0 × 18.5 inches (42 × 45.8 × 47 cm) | 
| Mop type: | Dual spinning discs | 
| Max threshold clearance: | Double layer thresholds up to 3.5 inches (9cm) | 
| Dust bin volume (base): | 2L | 
| Water tank volume: | 4L (clean), 3.5L (dirty) | 
| Base functions: | Charge, empty dust, wash mop pads, dry mop pads, self-clean | 
Mova V70 Ultra Complete review: Design
- Clean, modern design with no dust bag
- Retractable LiDAR turret
- Extending side brush and mop arm with industry-leading reach
These days, if you've seen one premium robot vacuum, you've essentially seen them all. The Mova V70 Ultra Complete isn't, at least at first glance, very different from nearly every other set-and-forget alternative on the market, although there are some design elements you won't find elsewhere just yet.
Robot design
The first, and arguably the Mova V70 Ultra Complete's headline act, is on the bot itself — the MaxiReachX mechanism for the side brush and a mop arm. What this means is that for both vacuuming and mopping, the bot has quite the reach, extending 12cm and 17cm respectively. This is not only good for edge cleaning and sweeping into room corners, but it also allows the bot to clean around furniture legs that most other robovacs don't necessarily do well.
The efficacy of the cleaning, however, is a different story, with the side brush extension not quite timing itself right when around furniture and not remaining fully extended when traveling along a wall (or room edge). As you can see from the video clip below, the side brush opens just before it actually gets to the chair leg — when the bot 'sees' the furniture' — then retracts.
I do worry about the longevity of the side brush arm, though, as I found it often scraps against a wall or skirting board, which means it could suffer from wear and tear with constant use, potentially cracking or breaking. While it could still be usable, any jagged edges of the broken plastic could scratch walls. In the four weeks of almost daily use I put the Mova V70 Ultra Complete to, there has been no issues, but the sound the extended side brush makes while scraping has often made my jaw clench.
The mop arm, however, does often stay extended longer but, again, not as consistently as I had expected, retracting when the bot gets close enough to a skirting board to not need the extension.
Mova promises that the dual circular mop pads can apply 15N of downward pressure and, in combination with their spinning, should apply a little elbow grease when mopping but, in reality, that's asking for too much from any robot vacuum cleaner.
What I do appreciate is that the mop pads attach magnetically and they're left behind automatically in the dock whenever the V70 needs to vacuum, so there's no fear of dirty dampness transferring on carpets. That said, you can set the bot to vacuum carpets first anyway, so it really doesn't matter either way.
Most of its other features are similar to what you'll get with other premium bots, including its retractible navigation turret that allows it to roll under low-lying furniture. However, I should note that I often found the turret elevated when it was knocking against the underside of cabinets, and the bot itself isn't the thinnest on the market — at 8.8cm, it doesn't have as good a clearance as, say, the 7.98cm of the Roborock Saros 10R.
The Mova V70 Ultra Complete also features robotic legs that allow it to climb up to 9cm in two shallow steps, plus dual anti-tangle bar brushes that definitely don't require manual intervention to keep clean. I should mention, though, that during my testing, hair got badly entangled with the large wheels and the side brush, which were difficult to cut away.
One small point of difference on the bot compared to others is that along with lit buttons on the turret, the Mova V70 features a thin bar of blue light when it's powered on. It gives the otherwise white bot a slightly ethereal look in my opinion.
Dock design
The white and silver dock is quite standard on the outside but, instead of housing a dust bag inside, there's a 2L box with a filter that holds up to 100 days' worth of dirt. This means there are no ongoing costs for replacing bags and you're also reducing waste in the bargain. The dust tank, as Mova calls it, is washable, but it also gets dried out after every use, thus reducing the build up of odors and a bacterial or fungal ecosystem within.
Like the Dreame Aqua10 Ultra, the dock also houses a detergent dispenser with two compartments — one for a standard mopping soap, the other for either a pet odor neutralizer or a wood floor-care solution. You will need to use the app to enable the use of these as they're not set to flow into the clean water by default.
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
Both water tanks are under a lid, keeping them out of sight. Moreover, the lids on each tank clip on tightly, so odors from the dirty mop water don't escape in case you forget to clean it out regularly.
• Design score: 4.5 / 5
Mova V70 Ultra Complete review: Performance
- Hard floor cleaning is good, but carpet vacuuming is disappointing
- Excellent navigation and obstacle avoidance
- Auto docking requires multiple attempts
Say what you will about the Mova V70 Ultra Complete — and I do have a lot to say about its performance — but the one thing I love about it is how quietly it goes about its work. When vacuuming, even at its Max+ (its highest suction setting), the V70 did not hit more than 66dB on the Decibel X app, when others can average around the 80dB mark at similar settings. Understandably this isn't a very scientific method of measuring sound, but it's a good way to compare.
Even the dock isn't as loud as similar models, with auto-emptying of the onboard bin being easily be missed if you aren't paying attention.
How does it actually clean, though? Let's get into the crux of the matter.
Vacuuming
With up to 42,000Pa on tap, the expectation that the Mova V70 Ultra Complete would be able to ace my tests was high. And while it does vacuum well, especially hard floors, its edge cleaning isn't as good as I hoped it would be. That's due to the fact that, during use, the automatically extending side brush doesn't remain stretched as the bot is rolling along a room edge but, instead, retracts after a few seconds.
In fact, at one point in my tests, the bot moved away from a room edge, leaving behind dirt — a mixture of oats, tea from a tea bag, chia seeds and freeze-dried raspberries to emulate different debris sizes — that most other premium robovacs I've previously tested have successfully cleaned up (see video below).
Otherwise, it tackles regular daily vacuuming well enough on hard floors even at mid-suction settings, but it's a different story on carpets.
While I don't expect side brushes on any robovac to be as effective on carpet as on hard floors, I had hoped that on Max suction, the same mixture of oats, tea, chia seeds and bits of fruit would be easily tackled but, as you can see from the photos below, the V70 left behind a lot even after two passes. Bumping up to Max+ helped only marginally, but debris still remained on the carpet and I had to use my cordless vacuum to clean up the rest.
Hair pickup on carpets in the Max setting also wasn't as impressive as I had hoped — around 80% — but it was about 98% when bumped up to Max+. Given this performance, I found leaving the vacuum setting at Max worked best for regular jobs, but occasionally used the Max+ setting when a carpet needed a little extra work. And that's disappointing from such a premium flagship that boasts high suction.
Mopping
The Mova V70 Ultra Complete, however, is slightly better at mopping room edges as I found the extending mop pads stayed open for longer periods of the bot sensed room edges, corners and furniture legs.
Mova says it applies a downward pressure of 15N but, in real-world use, that doesn't translate for any robovac as there's never enough vibrations to emulate 'scrubbing'. So I can't blame the V70 for not being able to clean up a drop of dried up curry on my kitchen floor.
The same downward force also doesn't work along room edges, which I tested by sprinkling a few crystals of charcoal-infused sea salt under my kitchen cabinets and moistening by adding a few drops of water. The tiny black spots remained where they were even after two mopping sessions at high waterflow rates.
Where other premium robovacs have been able to successfully clean up small spills of liquid, like soy sauce, I found that the V70 made more of a mess, spreading the dark liquid across a larger section of floor until I ended its task to prevent the stain from expanding further (see video below).
That said, I was impressed by how well the bot identified furniture legs while mopping and the extending mop pad was able to clean a full 360º around each leg in both my dining and living rooms.
It doesn't, sadly, negate the overall performance of the mopping which, like the vacuuming is disappointing. If you don't have a messy household, though, what the V70 does do will leave you with clean floors — something a far less expensive robovac will also give you.
Navigation and obstacle avoidance
Here's the good news: the Mova V70 Ultra Complete has impeccable navigation skills with very good obstacle avoidance. Throughout the four-week testing period, not once did the Mova V70 Ultra Complete deviate from its prescribed path, whether that was a quick clean with wider zig-zags or a tighter grid for deeper cleaning.
It also never got lost when told to do a room or zone cleaning, finding the path of least resistance wherever it needed to go, even if there were obstacles in its path.
Speaking of which, the Mova V70 Ultra Complete promises to recognize up to 300 different obstacles, and that includes cables and your pets. For the most part, it gets them correct, although there were instances when it didn't quite recognize some items. For example, a large charging brick on the floor was picked up as a shoe, and that's OK.
All obstacles, even smaller pieces of furniture that you may not have added to the map get picked up and they're marked in the app. Just tap on any of these grey icons and a small diagram and name of the item is shown, along with accuracy of recognition.
The one thing it definitely struggles with is docking on its own — every single time, it took the bot two to three attempts to automatically engage docking. In the four weeks of testing, I was asked to manually replace the bot back in the dock for charging and self-cleaning.
Self-cleaning
Dock performance itself isn't bad, with self-emptying of the onboard bin into the dust tank quite good, leaving only the barest layer of very fine dust sticking to the plastic sides of the smaller box inside the bot. And, as I've previously mentioned, this self-emptying isn't as loud as I've experienced with other robovacs, and I appreciate that.
Like the Dreame Aqua10 Ultra where the dust bag is dried with warm air, the Mova V70 Ultra Complete also dries out the dust tank. However, it takes 5 hours to do so compared to just 3 hours on the Dreame. It's also a lot longer than the V70 takes to dry out the mop pads, which is 3 hours as well. I'm not entirely sure why the dust tank requires more time, and while the additional power consumption is unlikely to make a significant dent in your energy bills, it could become inconvenient if you run the robovac daily.
Mop pad washing is impressive as well, with even dark soy stains being 95% scrubbed away. The good thing is the circular pads can be removed and washed in the machine or soaked in a stain-removing solution to return them to pristine condition.
The wear and tear on the pads, however, is a little more than on other robovacs that use spinning pads. I've spotted bits of fiber stuck on the textured wash tray after only five mopping runs, so it's a good thing that Mova supplies three additional pairs in the box.
Dock maintenance is very easy as well, with the dust tank easy to empty and wash, and access to the tanks is minimal effort.
Battery life
The Mova V70 Ultra Complete uses a 6,400mAh battery pack like many premium robot vacuums and its runtime is quite standard, depending on the suction setting, of course.
For example, when doing a full-home clean on the Max (penultimate) setting in an area approximately 45sqm / 484sq ft, it drops from 100% to 44% when vacuuming only, and 100% to 32% when vacuuming and mopping at the same time. In both cases, dynamic suction was engaged when it detected carpets (which automatically boosts suction slightly).
When I ran it on Max+ (its highest suction) for approximately 20 minutes, battery life dropped from 100% to 82%, but that was nonstop cleaning with no dynamic suction engaged and no need to return to the dock for self-emptying.
This is, of course, based on a smaller test space, so bigger homes might not get a full clean on a single charge, and the one time in my testing when battery dropped off entirely with a task incomplete, the bot didn't pick up where it left off once there was sufficient battery even though I made sure it was toggled on in the app.
• Performance score: 2.5 / 5
Mova V70 Ultra Complete: App support
- Almost identical to the Dreamehome app with similar navigation and setup
- Mostly easy to understand, but some settings need a little digging
- App can be slow to load and respond
Given that Dreame Technology owns Mova, I suppose I shouldn't have been surprised to see that the MOVAHome app is identical to Dreamehome, with only minor differences, like the color scheme on the home page.
And I do mean identical as the entire bot setup and the settings, plus all the navigation, is the same. Since I've previously used a Dreame robovac, the learning curve needed for me to get around the MOVAHome app was small, but first-time users will need to spend a little time going through every setting to ensure they've got the V70 set up to how they want it, including toggling carpet-first for a 'global clean' and selecting detergent use if necessary.
However, the MOVAHome app is a little slower compared to the Dreame one, and that includes editing the map as well which, on iOS, was a little tedious to do. So much so, that I decided to not divide the study from the entry hallway in mine. Adding the rug to my living room was a heck of a lot fiddlier than on the Dreamehome app, while it took three attempts to add wall-to-wall carpet to the bedroom on the Mova app.
Once everything is set up just the way you like, though, the MOVAHome app becomes easy to use, and you'll only likely need to select the cleaning type and the space. Setting up scheduled runs isn't hard either, as is creating custom cleaning routines. All in all, it's a clean app, just one that might require some initial time investment to wrap your head around.
• App support score: 4 / 5
Mova V70 Ultra Complete review: Score card
| Attribute | Notes | Score | 
|---|---|---|
| Value | As one of the most expensive models in the market, and given its performance issues, it's hard to recommend. | 3 / 5 | 
| Design | It's a good-looking appliance with an easy-to-maintain design. | 4.5 / 5 | 
| Performance | It can handle daily hard floor cleaning, but the tougher jobs are, well, tough for it. | 2.5 / 5 | 
| App support | It's not a bad app, but it will require a little time investment up front to find all the right settings. | 4 / 5 | 
Should I buy the Mova V70 Ultra Complete?
Buy it if...
You don't like the idea of replacement dust bags
While there are some self-emptying cordless vacuums that don't need dust bags, there aren't many robovacs that have adopted the same ethos. So, if you're keen on reducing waste and save on ongoing costs, the V70 can help you do that.
You have high thresholds
The Mova V70 Ultra Complete can climb two shallow steps of approximately 4cm each, with a total clearance of 9cm. So if you have high room thresholds for a robovac to get past, the V70s robotic legs will get over them.
Don't buy it if...
You want value for money
While you get plenty of replacement parts in the box and don't need to buy dust bags, the V70 Ultra Complete is still expensive and its subpar performance means you'll be better off considering a cheaper flagship.
You have mixed flooring
The V70 Ultra Complete will handle daily cleaning easily on hard floors, but tougher jobs, especially on carpets, aren't up to expectations.
Mova V70 Ultra Complete review: Alternatives
I like that the Mova V70 Ultra Complete brings some good features to the market but, given its performance during my testing, there are other models I would consider instead.
Roborock Saros 20
If you're after a flagship released in 2026, then this one scored well in our tests and we called it "formidable". From being able to handle uneven floors to thick carpets, this is one to consider if money is no object.
Read our full Roborock Saros 20 review for more information
Dreame Aqua10 Ultra
It's now been succeeded by the Dreame Aqua20 Ultra, but that means this model can be had at a discount, making it excellent value. It's what I use in my own home and it's been reliable and excellent at cleaning for nearly two years.
Read my in-depth Dreame Aqua10 Ultra review to learn more
How I tested the Mova V70 Ultra Complete
I used the Mova V70 Ultra Complete three times a week for four weeks in my one-bedroom apartment that has mixed flooring and an internal cleaning area of approximately 45sqm (484sq ft). The mixed flooring includes wall-to-wall mid-pile carpet in the bedroom, tiles everywhere else, plus a mid-pile rug in the living room.
While many of the cleaning runs were for regular upkeep of the floors, I put the Mova V70 Ultra Complete through some of TechRadar's standard tests. For vacuuming, this included sprinkling oats, tea from a tea bag, chia seeds and pieces of freeze-dried berries on carpets and hard floors to emulate different debris sizes.
Since I don't have a pet, I collected strands of my long hair and spread them on the bedroom carpet, walked over them for a couple of days to ensure they were embedded in fibers, then ran the V70 on two different high suction settings to test results. I even used pieces of thread on carpets to enhance visibility of pickup.
For mopping tests, I poured a little soy sauce and dropped a dollop of mustard on my kitchen floor, but kept the waterflow rate high.
I regularly checked the onboard dustbin to ensure self-empty was good, while also washing the dust tank once. I tested the wash-board cleaning feature once during this time.
I also ensured I went through everything the app had to offer, comparing it to the Dreame alternative which I use regularly anyway.
I've tested several robot vacuums in the last 10 years and, having witnessed their rapid evolution, I've built a solid knowledge base to help me compare different models.
Read more about how we test vacuums
[First reviewed October 2026]
While she's happiest with a camera in her hand, Sharmishta's main priority is being TechRadar's APAC Managing Editor, looking after the day-to-day functioning of the Australian, New Zealand and Singapore editions of the site, steering everything from news and reviews to ecommerce content like deals and coupon codes. While she loves reviewing cameras and lenses when she can, she's also an avid reader and has become quite the expert on ereaders and E Ink writing tablets, having appeared on Singaporean radio to talk about these underrated devices. Other than her duties at TechRadar, she's also the Managing Editor of the Australian edition of Digital Camera World, and writes for Tom's Guide and T3.

articles.title: Citizen Lab Traces Zero-Click Candiru Spyware Infections at Al Jazeera to Targeted Online Ads
articles.text:
Candiru, an Israeli maker of spyware sold to governments, infected devices at the news network Al Jazeera through ordinary online ads, in attacks that needed no click or other action from the user, researchers at the Citizen Lab said Thursday.
The hidden attack code ran the moment an ad loaded on the screen, and in some cases the ad loaded out of sight, in the background.
The Citizen Lab, a research group at the University of Toronto, said this is the first public, technical confirmation that mercenary spyware, meaning hacking tools sold to governments, has reached real devices through targeted ads. The method had been described before from leaked company documents, but not shown in a live attack.
The researchers recovered the spyware itself from one device, but not the exploit that breaks into the browser or app to install it. That first break-in step is described from how the attack was set up, not from captured code.
How the Attack Worked
The ads were placed by Discover-Tech, an Israeli company that presents itself as a normal digital advertising firm. Each ad carried a small piece of code that, when the ad loaded, quietly sent the device's advertising ID and internet address back to a Discover-Tech server, the researchers found.
That server decided whether the device belonged to a target. If it did, the server sent back attack code for the browser or app to run. If it did not, the server sent nothing. Because the ad itself carried no attack code, the ad networks that delivered it had nothing harmful to detect.
At Al Jazeera, at least 45 devices were targeted in 2024 and 2025, the Citizen Lab said, and it linked the attacks to Candiru with high confidence. The researchers did not say which government was behind the operation.
The network gave the researchers its traffic logs. On infected devices, the logs showed the same order each time: first contact with a Discover-Tech ad server, then a Candiru server that screens the device, then a command-and-control server that runs the spyware.
Al Jazeera also pulled one Windows program file off a compromised device. Its code used the same distinctive techniques as a Candiru tool the Citizen Lab took apart in 2021, which is the basis for the high-confidence link.
Al Jazeera staff were targeted once before. In 2020, dozens of its journalists' iPhones were hacked with NSO Group's Pegasus spyware, in a different operation that used a different method.
Who Discover-Tech and Candiru Are
Google and the advertising trade group IAB Europe had both listed Discover-Tech as an approved ad vendor from 2020 until this month. The company was registered in Israel in 2020 and is led by its chief executive, Dekel Boni.
Candiru is one of the better-known names in the spyware trade. The United States put it on a trade blacklist in 2021 over spyware used to target government officials, journalists, and activists. In 2025, its assets were bought by a U.S. investment firm, Integrity Partners, and moved into a new company, reported to be Integrity Labs, that the sanctions do not cover.
What the Platforms Did
After the researchers shared their findings, Google and IAB Europe removed Discover-Tech from their vendor lists in early October, the Citizen Lab said. Google cut off the company's access to its ad exchanges, Beeswax removed it, Vungle paused its access for a review, and Eskimi blocked its accounts.
Google told Reuters it had worked with the researchers and removed Discover-Tech "for systematically violating our policies." IAB Europe said it suspended the company after an audit found policy violations. Comcast, which owns Beeswax, said it acted "following recent activity."
Discover-Tech, Candiru's owners, Al Jazeera, and the Russian ad network Yandex did not respond to Reuters. Discover-Tech's website was still online on Thursday and said nothing about the findings.
How Far the Ads Reached
Discover-Tech's reach went far beyond Al Jazeera. On one of its platforms, the company placed nearly four billion ad bids between March and June 2026, the Citizen Lab said, and the ads carrying the hidden callback code appeared in about 75,000 phone apps and 120,000 websites.
Confiant, a U.S. ad-security firm that investigated alongside the Citizen Lab, put Discover-Tech's traffic at roughly 10 million ads a day.
The ads turned up on the networks of governments and large institutions, the Citizen Lab said, including NATO, the United Nations, European Union bodies, government offices in about two dozen countries, chipmakers, and news organizations. An ad appearing on a network is not proof that anyone there was infected. It shows only how widely the system could reach.
Confiant found that the small number of ads it could tie directly to Candiru were low-volume and mostly reached home and mobile internet connections, rather than the sensitive networks themselves.
What Defenders Can Check
Both groups published the web addresses and files associated with the operation, so defenders can block them and search their own records. Organizations whose staff may have seen the ads, especially on the networks named in the report, can look for the attack's order of connections: a device reaching a Discover-Tech ad server, then a Candiru screening server, then a command-and-control server.
Among the published indicators:
- SHA-256 (recovered spyware sample): 255869de85e2a171993fc5eb8a556d873a1b8966e040f6f55926f2fa2d595cc8
- Domain (Discover-Tech ad server): mtrtb[.]com
- Full list: the indicators in Confiant's report, including the command-and-control servers.
Security researchers have warned for years that the ad-buying system could be turned to this use. In December, leaked documents tied the spyware maker Intellexa to a similar ad-based tool called Aladdin, though no live infection through it had been shown.

articles.title: Six évaluateurs indépendants s’installent chez Anthropic, et l’entreprise ne pourra pas les faire taire
articles.text:
Anthropic a annoncé, jeudi, avoir ouvert ses locaux à six évaluateurs indépendants de l’organisation METR, dotés d’un accès comparable à celui d’un salarié. Ils pourront publier leurs conclusions sur la sécurité de l’IA Claude sans que l’entreprise puisse y opposer son veto.
L'entreprise Anthropic a annoncé, jeudi 15 octobre, l’arrivée d’évaluateurs indépendants au sein de ses équipes, une étape concrète de sa stratégie de sécurité de l’intelligence artificielle. La société derrière le robot conversationnel Claude a accordé à une équipe de METR, une organisation à but non lucratif, un accès quasi équivalent à celui de ses propres salariés, et détaille un système à trois niveaux pour ses autres partenaires, dont SecureBio et Accenture. Ce dispositif soulève cependant une question autour de l’indépendance réelle de ces contrôleurs.
Des évaluateurs indépendants à la table d'Anthropic, prête à leur laisser une certaine liberté
Six employés de METR ont posé leurs affaires chez Anthropic. Ils disposent d'un bureau, de matériel de l'entreprise et d'un accès aux outils internes à peu près équivalent à celui des équipes maison chargées d'évaluer les risques posés par ses modèles d'IA. Les salariés sont même encouragés à partager l'information avec eux comme avec un collègue travaillant sur les risques d'alignement. Seules quelques catégories bien délimitées leur échappent, comme les données clients, les échanges protégés avec les avocats ou l'architecture des modèles. Pour cette dernière, Anthropic redoute les fuites, puisque ces évaluateurs peuvent aussi travailler pour d'autres entreprises. Elle dit toutefois chercher, en général, à la partager après validation interne quand l'enjeu le justifie vraiment.
Le plus important tient pourtant à ce que ces évaluateurs auront le droit de dire. METR pourra publier ses analyses sur le niveau de risque, les incidents ou les pratiques de l'entreprise, et Anthropic n'aura aucun droit de veto. La firme pourra seulement exiger le caviardage de passages relevant de catégories étroites, fixées à l'avance. Si METR juge les coupes excessives, il pourra le faire savoir publiquement, sans en dévoiler le contenu. En échange, l'équipe est tenue par des accords contraignants. Elle travaille aussi en vase clos, car même les chercheurs de METR qui collaborent avec Anthropic sur d'autres projets n'ont pas accès à ses travaux.
Pourquoi Anthropic s'impose-t-elle cette surveillance ? L'entreprise explique vouloir rendre des comptes, sans pour autant tout déballer en place publique. Certaines informations feraient le bonheur d'acteurs malveillants, et d'autres, comme les détails sur l'entraînement ou la puissance de calcul, relèvent du secret commercial. Le but est de réduire l'écart entre ce que l'entreprise sait de ses modèles et ce qu'en savent ses contrôleurs.
D'où quatre exigences. La première est une expertise pointue, qui inclut la capacité de comprendre comment une évaluation peut dérailler, par exemple face à un modèle qui simule l'alignement. Viennent ensuite une indépendance réelle, sans parts dans l'entreprise ni dépendance financière ou opérationnelle, un accès qui va jusqu'à l'entraînement et aux garde-fous, et enfin la liberté de publier.
Pour défendre son approche, Anthropic emprunte une comparaison au monde de la finance. Une grande banque connaît mieux ses propres risques que n'importe quel observateur extérieur, c'est pourquoi les régulateurs installent des examinateurs directement dans ses murs, afin de repérer à temps les prises de risque qui pourraient menacer le public. L'entreprise admet elle-même que le parallèle n'est pas parfait. Ce dispositif concrétise surtout l'engagement pris le 12 septembre dernier par son PDG, Dario Amodei. Ce jour-là, il appelait le secteur à ralentir le rythme auquel progressent les modèles d'IA, et faisait de ces évaluateurs intégrés la première étape de son plan. Anthropic a par ailleurs signé l'Accord de la Maison-Blanche sur la superintelligence, par lequel les entreprises s'engagent à travailler avec des auditeurs ou des évaluateurs externes indépendants, ce qui nourrit bien sûr la thèse « contrainte et forcée » de la démarche.
Trois niveaux d’accès, et une indépendance qui fait débat
Dans la grille d'évaluation imaginée par Anthropic, METR occupe pour l'instant seul le palier le plus élevé. L'organisation connaît déjà la maison, car elle a examiné plusieurs de ses rapports de risques au cours de l'année écoulée. Au premier niveau, l'évaluateur mène des enquêtes ciblées, avec l'accès que l'entreprise veut bien lui donner, et ne publie qu'avec son accord. Au deuxième, il voit davantage et publie librement, sous réserve des mêmes caviardages. Le troisième y ajoute l'accès quasi salarié. Les partenariats plus récents démarrent avec un accès et une liberté de publication plus restreints, le temps de vérifier que les évaluateurs savent garder un secret et disposent des moyens et compétences nécessaires.
SecureBio, une organisation spécialisée dans la biosécurité, se trouve au premier niveau. Après avoir publié une revue pilote d'un précédent rapport d'Anthropic, elle examine désormais le chapitre consacré aux armes chimiques et biologiques du rapport de risques d'août. Une fois cette revue terminée, un accès et des droits de publication élargis pourront être envisagés.
En parallèle, Anthropic avance sur un partenariat annoncé en septembre avec Accenture et Faculty, la filiale IA rachetée cette année par le cabinet de conseil. Au menu, il y a du red teaming (des attaques simulées pour débusquer les failles), l'évaluation de l'alignement des modèles, et le test de leurs garde-fous. Chacun des deux groupes prévoit d'investir au moins un milliard de dollars sur cinq ans dans ce domaine. Des discussions ont également commencé avec plusieurs autres organisations, dont Hugging Face, pas épargnée par les déboires malgré son rachat par NVIDIA.
Tout le monde s'interroge sur l'indépendance réelle de la démarche entamée par Anthropic. La firme américaine exige de ses évaluateurs qu'ils ne dépendent pas d'elle financièrement, mais c'est elle qui paie directement Accenture pour cette première phase. Elle estime d'ailleurs qu'à terme, ce travail devrait être financé par l'État ou un fonds dédié.
Et METR n'échappe pas non plus aux soupçons. Plusieurs critiques, dont celle de David Sacks, ancien conseiller de la Maison-Blanche sur l'IA, jugent que l'organisme n'est pas vraiment indépendant d'Anthropic. Ils pointent les liens qui unissent l'entreprise à la mouvance de la sécurité de l'IA dont METR est lui-même issu. L'organisation assure ne recevoir aucun financement des grands laboratoires, tout en admettant bénéficier gratuitement d'accès à leurs modèles. Anthropic, qui agit ici de son plein gré, invite tous les laboratoires de pointe à suivre son exemple. Les premiers rapports diront si ce chien de garde a des crocs.

articles.title: My favourite manual espresso machine of 2026 is now available with a huge 43% discount — there’s just one minor catch
articles.text:
My favourite manual espresso machine of 2026 is now available with a huge 43% discount — there’s just one minor catch
The KitchenAid Semi Automatic Espresso Machine is a worthy kitchen addition — provided you're happy with black
I love a good coffee machine, and appreciate the benefits of fully automatic and manual styles. I use the former type at home myself since it makes the morning orders for my partner and me as easy as possible. If I really had my way though, I’d choose manual, as it opens the door to a lot more experimentation, and the KitchenAid Semi Automatic Espresso Machine would be right at the top of my wishlist.
If you’re considering a manual espresso machine for your home (especially now that some cafés and coffee shops are charging more to reconcile the loss of card surcharges), I think it should be top of your wishlist too. The good news is that it’s now received a 43% discount on Amazon, which beats its October Prime Day price. The only slight caveat is that this huge discount only applies to the black model.
It’s a great-looking machine, don’t get me wrong, it just might understandably be a little tricker to match with kitchen decor compared to the porcelain white model, for example.
Beating its AU$699 Prime Day price by some margin, this is a great opportunity to nab a highly capable bean-to-cup espresso machine. It brews a delicious coffee — just as soon as you’ve experimented and dialled in the best settings for your beans. It also has a steam wand for frothing all types of milk.
I gave this espresso machine five stars in my KitchenAid Semi-Automatic Espresso Machine review. One of the standout features for me is its flat-bottom portafilter, which makes tamping the ground coffee beans an absolute breeze. The portafilters that come supplied with most other machines feature a couple of spouts, so you need to rest them on the edge of your counter, which can be cumbersome and messy.
Not so here. You can place the whole portafilter down on a flat surface, allowing you to apply a good amount of pressure to tamp the coffee down.
Another benefit is its ability to quickly heat up, so you could be drinking your coffee in a matter of minutes, while smart dosage control ensures the same amount of coffee is delivered each time — you will just likely need to experiment for a bit with your beans. There’s a line in the portafilter basket to indicate the ideal level once the coffee is tamped, giving you some assistance if you’re new to the whole process.
And if you take milk with your coffee or you want to try your hand at some latte art, the steam wand works wonders. Plus, it has the inherent ability to play nicely with dairy and non-dairy milks, as you can shut it off whenever you want.
This is a fantastic price for a fantastic machine, and given I can’t guarantee how long it will last, I encourage you to consider it if your home is crying out for a top-performing model.
