articles.title: Une seule enceinte pour remplacer tout un home cinéma ? Focal et Naim tente le pari à 5 000 €
articles.text:
Quinze haut-parleurs, du Dolby Atmos et 720 W de puissance cumulée : avec la Mu-so Utopia, Naim et Focal veulent réunir musique et cinéma dans un seul appareil. Une proposition ambitieuse, affichée à 5 000 €.
Une seule enceinte pour écouter de la musique et profiter d'un son immersif devant son téléviseur : voilà le pari de Naim avec sa nouvelle Mu-so Utopia. Développée avec le fabricant français Focal, elle emprunte plusieurs technologies à ses enceintes hi-fi les plus prestigieuses.
L'appareil reste imposant, avec son châssis en aluminium d'un mètre de large et ses 15,5 kg. Mais derrière ce format se cache une conception particulièrement ambitieuse.
Quinze haut-parleurs pour recréer une scène sonore immersive
La Mu-so Utopia réunit quinze haut-parleurs, dont plusieurs spécialement développés par Focal. Les tweeters, chargés de reproduire les aigus, bénéficient d'une amplification distincte de celle utilisée pour les autres haut-parleurs. L'ensemble totalise 720 W, une puissance qui ne garantit toutefois pas, à elle seule, une meilleure qualité sonore.
Compatible Dolby Atmos, l'enceinte utilise des haut-parleurs orientés dans différentes directions et des traitements numériques pour créer une impression de son surround. Une approche qui ne remplace pas nécessairement de véritables enceintes arrière.
Son système ADAPT adapte la restitution à la pièce à partir des distances renseignées dans l'application, sans mesure automatique par microphone. L'enceinte dispose aussi d'un port HDMI pour le téléviseur, d'une entrée optique et d'une sortie pour caisson de basses. Spotify Connect, Tidal Connect, Qobuz Connect et AirPlay 2 complètent les possibilités de streaming musical.
Une installation simplifiée, mais à quel prix ?
La Mu-so Utopia se positionne notamment au-dessus de la Focal Mu-so Hekla, qui propose déjà quinze haut-parleurs et du Dolby Atmos pour 3 300 €. Naim mise principalement sur des composants acoustiques plus sophistiqués pour justifier les 1 700 € supplémentaires.
À ce niveau de prix, il devient également possible de constituer une installation hi-fi ou home cinéma avec plusieurs enceintes, offrant davantage de liberté pour les disposer dans la pièce ou faire évoluer son équipement. Un point à considérer pour un système tout-en-un dont les fonctions connectées pourraient vieillir plus rapidement que les haut-parleurs.
La Mu-so Utopia s'adresse donc avant tout à ceux qui recherchent un système audio haut de gamme, compact dans son principe, simple à installer.

articles.title: Feds eyes $1.5 billion data centre in Ottawa
articles.text:
The Government of Canada is looking to build a data centre in Ottawa.
According to a notice from Defence Construction Canada, the facility would be used by Canada’s cyber spy agency, Communications Security Establishment Commission (CSE), on “mid- to long-term objectives” in government operations. The project is expected to cost between $1.5 billion and $1.8 billion, although it’s unclear how long it would take to build once plans are finalized.
In a statement to CTV News Ottawa, CSE said the data centre comes as part of the government’s “broader defence investments” that are being made to “modernize the secure infrastructure and capabilities needed to respond to evolving threats and support Canada’s national security and defence priorities.”
Outside of that, the spokesperson said it doesn’t disclose “specific operational or technical requirements beyond what is publicly available” to “protect national security and the integrity of its operations.”
Notably, news of this Ottawa project coincides with the feds’ announcement of $500 million in additional AI funding. It also comes just one month after the government outlined a framework for companies creating data centres in Canada. Per the guidelines, these facilities:
- Must create lasting local benefits
- Must not shift electricity costs to Canadians
- Must minimize water use and environmental impacts
- Must be transparent about local impacts
- Must bring strategic value to Canada
It’s important to stress, however, that the word “must” is misleading since the government hasn’t actually made this framework legally binding. Therefore, it doesn’t actually mean anything for big companies like Google, Meta, Microsoft, Bell and Telus to say they support the framework since they’re under no obligation to actually adhere to them.
This speaks to the larger issue regarding data centres and AI use in general: there’s simply little to no regulation. Even Brad Smith, the president of the notoriously AI-pilled Microsoft, recently admitted that milk and washing machines are more regulated than AI, leading him to call for greater global restrictions to be placed on the tech. Some of the measures he called for are requirements for companies to notify victims when AI agents go rogue and “killswitches” should they indeed go rampant.
Naturally, there are many other concerns associated with AI, too, especially when it comes to their steep energy costs, heavy water consumption, and major carbon emissions. This has led to many protests across Canada, with municipalities like Mississauga agreeing to data centre moratoriums to deliberate their numerous potential impacts.
It remains to be seen what public pushback might come about in response to this Ottawa data centre.

Via: CTV News

articles.title: Por primera vez en mucho tiempo, Marvel recupera el beneplácito de los espectadores: su nueva serie tiene puntuaciones estupendas
articles.text:
'VisionQuest' ha llegado a Disney+ el 14 de octubre con dos episodios y un sello que Marvel hace tiempo que no tiene garantizado solo presumiendo de franquicia y legado: el de Certified Fresh en Rotten Tomatoes, con más un 81% de críticas favorables de los profesionales y un 86% del público. Parece que tenemos entre manos la mejor serie Marvel en años, y podemos esperar los seis capítulos restantes con cadencia semanal hasta el 11 de noviembre.
Hace tres años, el estudio abría 'Invasión secreta' con una cabecera generada con inteligencia artificial, Bob Iger admitía que tanta serie había diluido el foco de Marvel y para solventarlo prometían rodar pilotos y fichar showrunners de verdad, una figura que sus series nunca habían tenido. 'VisionQuest' es la primera prueba de que aquella decisión funciona, porque hay alguien al volante: Terry Matalas, uno de los creadores de '12 Monos' y responsable de la tercera temporada de 'Star Trek: Picard'.
'VisionQuest' cierra la trilogía de 'Bruja Escarlata y Visión' y 'Agatha, ¿quién si no?’ con la mejor idea de las tres. La Visión blanca que salía volando al final de la primera serie vive escondido y con la cabeza llena de inquilinos: J.A.R.V.I.S., F.R.I.D.A.Y., E.D.I.T.H. y Ultrón, las inteligencias artificiales que fabricó Tony Stark, que conversan con él con cara y cuerpos. James Spader se lleva la mejor parte, porque once años después de ‘Vengadores: La era de Ultrón' interpreta por primera vez a Ultrón con su propio rostro.
Paul Bettany ha contado que la serie va de padres e hijos y del trauma que pasa de una generación a otra, y algo hay para desenterradores de lore oculto: un chaval llamado Tommy, con todas las papeletas para ser aquel gemelo de 'Wandavision', le acompaña en la huida cuando alguien pone precio a su cabeza. Marvel ha tardado más de cinco años en devolver a la Visión blanca a la pantalla, y lo hace con una historia sobre una máquina que intenta averiguar quién es realmente. Veremos si aparte de la redención del héroe artificial tenemos la de alguien más.

articles.title: Nvidia expands Nemotron LLM family with hyper-efficient models for agentic systems - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Nvidia expands Nemotron LLM family with hyper-efficient models for agentic systems
Nvidia Corp. today announced the launch of customizable Nemotron 3.5 Super LV large language models for always-on artificial intelligence agents and edge-focused 3.5 Bolt for local systems.
The company said the three new models will cover the full range of agent deployments, from large enterprise servers to edge devices and local hardware.
Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is an open 120-billion-parameter model, built in collaboration with the Nemotron Coalition, a group of model builders and AI labs advancing open frontier-level models, designed for high-accuracy multimodal agentic tasks. It is capable of instruction following, tool use, multistep business workflows and visual understanding. Nvidia said it has comparable power to the company’s largest reasoning models at one-fifth the size.
That size, plus a new architecture, lets Super VL produce outputs nearly five times faster than other models in the same class.
Unlike closed frontier models, Nvidia provides the Super VL weights in the open, meaning organizations can post-train it on their own data and deploy it on their own infrastructure. This means they can bring it behind their firewall and keep it inside their domain, maintaining sovereignty, privacy and safety.
To build Super VL, Nvidia trained the model with open data and open methods using about 26 trillion tokens across pretraining and continued pretraining. This also included 3.8 million post-training samples and reinforcement learning across 100 open environments to fine-tune the model.
Nvidia also said it’s releasing open datasets on Hugging Face spanning agentic tool use, finance, instruction following, long context, safety, fairness and vision-language understanding.
Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB is a smaller model designed to run agentic tasks locally and is based on Super VL. It uses a hybrid mixture-of-experts model that activates 9 billion of its 74 billion parameters at a time and uses two-bit quantization to fit within 24 gigabytes of memory. This lets it run comfortably on an enterprise workstation or PC graphics processing units, so users can delegate everyday projects, including writing and debugging code, without sending workloads to the cloud.
Later this month, Nvidia is also launching an even smaller model: Bolt E4B 4GB. This tiny model is built for edge deployment on GeForce RTX, Jetson and RTX/GTX Spark. This will allow physical AI and conversational agents to work within devices such as wearables, household devices, point-of-service, car dashboards, device assistants and other embedded interfaces.
Nvidia noted that it could be used to power interactive characters, conversational interfaces and smart user interfaces that localize or personalize.

articles.title: Local Matter control for Philips Hue lights in Google Home is the upgrade I've been waiting for — here's how it will improve your smart home
articles.text:
Philips Hue gets local Matter upgrade in Google Home — and I'm looking forward to the faster responses and offline boost
This is the upgrade I've been waiting for
- Google Home is adding local Matter support for Philips Hue lights
- It should mean faster response times and offline access
- There are other improvements in the latest app update as well
There's a new upgrade rolling out for Google Home and Philips Hue lights that might not sound all that significant at first, but will actually make a notable difference to functionality — and I'm keen to get it installed on my own system as soon as possible.
The upgrade in question is local Matter support. And as per a Google (via 9to5Google) report, it means there should be faster response times if you're controlling your Philips Hue lights via the Google Home app. It should also mean the connection works even if your internet goes down, as long as the local network is still operational.
Even better, the update should be applied smoothly and seamlessly in the background, so you don't even need to repair your lights. Just look out for an update to Google Home appearing in the Android or iOS app store.
While the Philips Hue app offers more in the way of features, I like controlling my Hue lights through the Google Home app, because all my other smart stuff is in there too — so faster responses and offline support are very welcome.
More upgrades and fixes
There are a bunch of other minor improvements coming to Google Home as well, including updates for the Gemini for Home early access program. Conversations will now end more naturally, Google says, and weather temperature units will be more consistent.
Gemini is also getting better at understanding when "stop" actually means stop — as in, you're trying to stop media playback or an alarm, rather than just bringing a conversation to a close. Plus, requests for "relaxing music" or similar will now open up a proper media player app, rather than switching to ambient sounds (like rain or white noise).
The Google Home app gets a few tweaks in terms of drag-and-drop stability and more prominent smoke and CO alarm messages, while third-party controls for lights, plugs, and switches have been revamped. Various camera fixes have been added too.

articles.title: New Steam Update Puts Startup Times Back Ahead of Epic's Vibe-Coded Launcher
articles.text:
Thursday, October 15th 2026
New Steam Update Puts Startup Times Back Ahead of Epic's Vibe-Coded Launcher
Epic Games released a preview of its rebuilt, "vibe coded" Epic Games Launcher on October 14, and took a direct shot at Steam while at it. Epic's own chart shows the new launcher cold starting in 5.47 seconds against 10.07 seconds for Steam, which the company bills as 46% faster. That lead apparently didn't last long, as a clip posted by user girlglock_ on X shows the current Steam client starting in 5.23 seconds. Although it might seem like it at first, this isn't a rushed reply from Valve. The stable Steam Client Update that lists "Improved Steam Client startup performance" is dated October 13, a day before Epic's announcement, and Steam's beta client was already getting startup improvements back in September. Valve hasn't shared any numbers for it, though.
Epic's figures, on the other hand, come from testing it commissioned from Keywords Studios earlier this month, averaging five runs on 13 machines with the three lowest-end systems left out, so they were probably taken on an older Steam build. Results will vary from one PC to the next, of course. Epic's launcher is also light on features for now, and the company advises competitive Fortnite and Rocket League players to stay on the current launcher during the preview. It does run natively on Linux, with Fortnite set to follow once Epic finishes rebuilding its anti-cheat, and the vibe coding part fits Epic's recent shift to AI-first development. Readers are advised to treat both sets of startup numbers as rough guides.Startup time is only one line in what is a fairly massive Steam update. The October 13 release moves a lot of what Valve has been testing in beta over to the stable channel, starting with Big Art Mode, which can be enabled from the Home settings and fills the background with the highlighted game's artwork. Big Picture Mode also gets screensavers, with the default one cycling through art from recently played games and your own in-game screenshots, alongside a retro-style bouncing logo. Custom screensavers are supported as well, and there's now a setting to keep them off while in game.
A Personal Calendar has also been added to the Recommended tab on the Home screen. Elsewhere, Remote Play gets an experimental video codec called Pyrowave, aimed at high-bandwidth, low-latency streaming, and download speeds on high-latency connections should be better. On Linux, Windows programs added as non-Steam games now run through Proton by default. The Steam Controller firmware adds a second Bluetooth pairing slot, and pressing the controller's system button can now switch a TV over to the Steam Machine, provided the TV supports HDMI CEC. The full changelog runs much longer, with plenty of Steam Input, overlay and game recording fixes on top.
Sources:
				Steam Client Update, October 13, 				girlglock on X			
	
	
	
		
	
		
8 Comments on New Steam Update Puts Startup Times Back Ahead of Epic's Vibe-Coded Launcher
I've been using EPIC since the alpha or whatever version of Unreal Torunament 4 and then picked it up again when Borderlands 3 was launched and the startup speed of the launcher honestly never bothered me nor Steam's ever since the launch day of Half Life 2 so I'm more than familiar with both.
I mean sure any progress is progress and its fine but to me these are more like a pissing contest and there would be more important things to focus on imo.
I mean... sure, I love a well optimized graphics engine. I understand some common instructions must be coded in assembly on an emulator to ensure best possible performance. But for something that is basically a bloated internet browser in disguise... I just cannot care less. My only concern would be about security, but with human coders things get even worse, specially with big companies bringing the funds.
Most of all I don't want my $3000 computer looking like a $500 kiddie konsole ......

articles.title: 5 Kristin Hannah lessons on the complexities of womanhood
articles.text:
5 Kristin Hannah lessons on the complexities of womanhood
Explore five powerful Kristin Hannah lessons that capture the complexities of womanhood, from love & sacrifice to resilience and the strength of women.
Being a woman often means carrying emotions that the world does not always see. It means learning to be strong when life feels overwhelming, making difficult choices for the people you love, and finding your identity in a world that constantly tells you who you should be. Sometimes, the most complicated feelings are also the hardest to put into words.
Few contemporary novelists explore these experiences as deeply as Kristin Hannah. Through stories of friendship, motherhood, love, loss and survival, Hannah captures the emotional realities of women's lives with remarkable sensitivity.
Her novels, including The Nightingale, The Four Winds and Firefly Lane, explore the sacrifices women make, the expectations they navigate and the quiet courage that often goes unnoticed.
For readers who have ever struggled to explain what womanhood means to them, literature can offer a sense of recognition.
5 Kristin Hannah lessons on the complexities of womanhood
1. The strength women discover in difficult times
Women are often expected to be strong for everyone around them. They become the dependable daughters, supportive partners, caring mothers and friends who hold others together, even when they are struggling themselves. Yet strength does not mean never feeling afraid, exhausted or uncertain.
Kristin Hannah's fiction frequently explores how ordinary women discover extraordinary courage when circumstances leave them with little choice.
In The Nightingale, for instance, women face the dangers and moral complexities of surviving during the Second World War. Their courage is not always loud or immediately visible; sometimes, it appears in the decision to keep going when giving up seems easier.
This is one of the most important realities of womanhood: strength can coexist with vulnerability. A woman can feel overwhelmed and still take another step forward. She can question herself and still make a courageous decision. Her strength does not depend on having all the answers but on finding the courage to face life as it unfolds.
2. The complicated relationship between love and sacrifice
Love can be one of the most beautiful parts of a woman's life, but it can also bring difficult choices. Women may find themselves balancing their ambitions with family responsibilities, their personal needs with those of others, and their desire for independence with their commitment to people they love.
In novels such as The Four Winds, Hannah examines the sacrifices women make in the face of hardship. Her characters reveal how love can become a source of determination, helping people endure circumstances they might otherwise find impossible.
However, sacrifice also raises an important question: how much of yourself should you give to others? Women are frequently praised for putting everyone else first, sometimes at the expense of their own happiness. But love does not have to mean disappearing into someone else's needs.
Healthy love makes room for individuality, dreams and boundaries. A woman's ability to care for others should never be measured by how much of herself she is willing to abandon.
3. The importance of female friendship
Some experiences are difficult to explain to people who have never lived through them. This is where female friendship can become especially meaningful. A close friend may understand the pressures, insecurities and unspoken expectations that accompany different stages of a woman's life.
Hannah explores the enduring power of these relationships in Firefly Lane, which follows the friendship between Tully Hart and Kate Mularkey across decades. Their relationship is not presented as perfect. It experiences jealousy, disagreements, distance and emotional pain, reflecting the reality that even the closest friendships require effort and understanding.
Yet female friendship can offer something that romantic relationships and family connections do not always provide: the reassurance that someone sees you beyond your responsibilities and achievements.
A good friend remembers who you were before the world began making demands of you. She can celebrate your success without competing with you and offer honesty without making you feel small. In a world that often encourages women to compare themselves with one another, friendship can become a powerful reminder that another woman's success does not diminish your own.
4. The search for identity beyond expectations
Who are you when you are no longer defined by what others need from you? It is a question many women encounter as they grow older, change careers, enter relationships, become mothers or begin questioning the paths they once believed they had to follow.
Society often presents women with conflicting expectations. They are encouraged to be ambitious but not intimidating, independent but always available, confident but never too outspoken. Trying to satisfy everyone can make it difficult to recognise what they genuinely want.
Hannah's characters frequently confront the tension between the lives they are expected to lead and the lives they wish to create. Their journeys suggest that identity is not something a woman must discover once and preserve forever. It can evolve through heartbreak, changing circumstances, mistakes and unexpected opportunities.
Choosing yourself does not necessarily mean rejecting the people you love. Sometimes, it simply means acknowledging that your own hopes and feelings deserve consideration, too.
5. Finding hope after loss and heartbreak
Womanhood is not a single experience, and neither is resilience. For some women, it means rebuilding after a relationship ends. For others, it means grieving someone they love, recovering from disappointment or learning to live with a future that looks different from the one they imagined.
In The Nightingale and The Great Alone, Hannah explores how women navigate devastating circumstances and find ways to continue living. Her stories do not suggest that courage makes suffering disappear. Instead, they examine how people carry their experiences while gradually discovering the possibility of a different future.
There is something deeply reassuring about this perspective. Healing does not always happen quickly, and moving forward does not mean forgetting what happened. Sometimes, progress looks like making a small decision for yourself, allowing yourself to feel joy again or accepting that you can be changed by an experience without being defined by it forever.
The complexities of being a woman include both the moments that break your heart and the moments that remind you of your capacity to begin again.
Final thoughts
Kristin Hannah's novels explore the experiences that shape women's lives, from friendship and sacrifice to identity and survival.
Women can be strong yet uncertain, independent yet connected to others, and vulnerable yet resilient. These qualities reflect the diversity of women's experiences.
Hannah's stories remind us that women need not fit a single definition of strength. Their choices, emotions and experiences deserve to be understood in all their complexity.

articles.title: Pour un bon objectif à prix abordable, privilégiez...
articles.text:
Pour un bon objectif à prix abordable, privilégiez...
L'objectif Canon EF-S 24 mm f/2,8 STM s'affiche aujourd'hui à 143,99 € chez Boulanger.com. C'est actuellement le meilleur objectif à prix abordable de notre comparatif, selon les 175 modèles testés dans notre laboratoire.
Le petit pancake Canon 24 mm EF-S 24 mm f/2,8 STM, en monture EF-S (pour capteur APS-C uniquement, donc) de 24 mm f/2,8, équivalent à un 38 mm, dispose d'une motorisation pas à pas STM (très efficace pour la mise au point en vidéo). L'objectif pèse environ 125 g pour une épaisseur d'à peine plus de 2 cm.
Canon EF-S 24 mm f/2,8 STM
- 
                            Ergonomie
                            
            
- 
                            En pratique
                            
            
- 
                            Performances optiques
                            
            
Points forts
- Conception pancake
- Poids et encombrement
- Ouverture maximale de f/2,8
- Prise en main et confort d'usage
- Qualité de construction et finitions
- Vignetage et distorsions contenus
- Motorisation STM
Points faibles
- Pas de stabilisation optique
- Piqué non homogène aux plus grandes ouvertures
- Présence d'aberrations chromatiques aux plus grandes ouvertures
Au final, difficile de ne pas être séduit par ce pancake ultra compact. Associé à un reflex APS-C, il permet d'obtenir une configuration discrète et relativement légère. Équivalent à un 40 mm, c'est un objectif idéal pour la photo de tous les jours. Son ouverture maximale de f/2,8 lui offre une bonne polyvalence dans de faibles conditions lumineuses et lui permet de produire des images avec une petite profondeur de champ. Sa motorisation STM lui assure un bon comportement lors de la prise de vidéo (autofocus sans à-coups).
La qualité optique, en revanche, est un peu décevante. Les plus grandes ouvertures sont marquées par un manque d'homogénéité ainsi que quelques aberrations chromatiques sur les bords aux plus grandes ouvertures. Malgré cela, les distorsions et le vignetage sont contenus. C'est cette qualité optique en demi-teinte qui lui coûte sa recommandation, mais ce pancake Canon 24 mm EF-S 24 mm f/2,8 STM reste malgré tout un excellent choix pour ceux qui veulent photographier simple, léger et discret.

articles.title: 500 € pour installer une borne de recharge chez soi : l’aide revient en 2027, avec de nouvelles conditions
articles.text:
Les propriétaires de voitures électriques qui avaient raté le coche du crédit d’impôt vont avoir une seconde chance. Supprimé au 1er janvier 2026, ce coup de pouce, qui remboursait 75 % de l’achat et de la pose d’une borne dans la limite de 500 euros, va être remplacé par une nouvelle aide du même montant dès le 1er janvier 2027. Elle figure parmi les mesures de la deuxième phase du plan d’électrification, présentée par la ministre déléguée à l’Énergie, Maud Bregeon. En revanche, elle ne concernera pas tout le monde.
Une borne pilotable, en maison individuelle
Dans la présentation de la deuxième phase du plan d’électrification, Bercy mentionne une aide de 500 euros visera l’installation d’une borne « pilotable » en maison individuelle. Concrètement, une borne connectée capable de décaler la recharge vers les heures où l’électricité est la moins chère, la nuit ou en milieu de journée, quand la production solaire est abondante. Cette condition n’a rien de nouveau : en 2025, le crédit d’impôt était déjà réservé aux bornes pilotables. Le changement porte plutôt sur le logement. L’ancien dispositif couvrait aussi les résidences secondaires et la quote-part des équipements communs en copropriété, et un couple pouvait cumuler jusqu’à 2 000 euros de crédit d’impôt. Le gouvernement ne mentionne, lui, que la maison individuelle, les immeubles collectifs relevant du programme Advenir. La prime sera intégrée à celle des certificats d’économies d’énergie (CEE) pour les véhicules électriques. Comme le leasing social ou la prime à l’achat, elle sera donc financée par les fournisseurs d’énergie, et non par le budget de l’État.
Surtout, l’aide ne sera pas ouverte à tous les propriétaires d’une voiture électrique. Dans sa feuille de route pour l’industrie automobile, dévoilée à l’occasion du Mondial de l’Auto, le gouvernement précise qu’elle sera « attribuée lors d’un achat d’un véhicule électrique d’occasion ». Les acheteurs d’un modèle neuf en seront donc exclus. Ils bénéficient toutefois déjà du coup de pouce CEE à l’achat, qui peut atteindre 7 700 euros pour un ménage précaire achetant une voiture assemblée en Europe avec une batterie européenne. Les conducteurs qui roulent déjà en électrique et voudraient simplement s’équiper restent, eux, sans aide. Le détail des modalités, et notamment l’articulation avec la prime CEE existante pour les voitures électriques d’occasion, reste à publier.
Jusqu’à 150 euros d’économies par an
Pour le conducteur, une borne pilotable permet surtout de payer sa recharge moins cher. D’après le gouvernement, un conducteur type ferait passer son budget annuel de recharge de 420 à 270 euros, soit environ 150 euros d’économies par an. Avec une borne bidirectionnelle, capable de réinjecter l’électricité de la batterie sur le réseau quand les prix sont élevés, le gain pourrait atteindre 300 euros. Pour le réseau électrique, l’intérêt est de voir les voitures se recharger la nuit ou en milieu de journée, quand l’électricité est la moins chère.
Reste que l’aide ne couvrira qu’une partie de la facture : pose comprise par un installateur qualifié, obligatoire au-delà de 3,7 kW, une borne de recharge à domicile revient généralement entre 1 500 et 2 500 euros, selon IZI by EDF.
Le gouvernement veut aller plus loin et faire du pilotage le mode « par défaut » de toutes les nouvelles bornes, par exemple via un raccordement au compteur Linky. La filière, réunie au sein de l’Avere-France, s’est engagée à faire passer la part des conducteurs qui pilotent leur recharge de 35 à 70 % d’ici 2030.

articles.title: Memtest86+
articles.text:
Memtest86+ is a free, open-source, stand-alone memory tester for x86, x86-64, ARM64, and LoongArch64 architecture computers. It provides a much more thorough memory check than that provided by BIOS memory tests.
It is also able to access almost all the computer's memory, not being restricted by the memory used by the operating system and not depending on any underlying software like UEFI libraries.
Memtest86+ can be loaded and run either directly by a PC BIOS (legacy or UEFI) or via an intermediate bootloader that supports the Linux 16-bit, 32-bit, 64-bit, or EFI handover boot protocol. It should work on any Pentium class or later 32-bit or 64-bit CPU.
What's New
ARM64 (AArch64) Now Supported!
Memtest86+ now runs on ARM64 platforms supporting UEFI and ACPI! Aarch64 support has currently been tested on Qualcommm Snapdragon X laptop, Raspberry Pi 4 & 5 (with community UEFI firmware) and QEMU.
Save Report to USB Drive
Writing reports to USB drive was probably the most wanted feature. Press F6 to save a full-text report with system information, memory modules and testing results to a FAT32-formatted USB drive. Each saved report will have its own number, so previous reports won't be overwritten.
Redesigned Test Algorithms
Memtest86+ tests have been reworked to detect errors faster, and optimized to find more complex failures.
SIMD Tests on 64-bit CPUs
Along with the new Bus stress test (see below), the old random-sequence moving test has been converted to SIMD to benefit from larger vectors instructions. Both use non-temporal stores that bypass the CPU caches and write to the main memory directly, resulting in significantly higher memory access/traffic than scalar tests.
Bus Stress Test
This new test targets common bus interface weaknesses on modern era plaform (DDR5+) while still being demanding on older architecture. The sequence keeps switching between write-bursts and read-checks while also inserting idle periods to create load transitions on the PMIC of the module (which can't be corrected by on-die ECC). This can uncover interface-related faults like signal integrity failures due to electrical noise or voltage drops, or XMP/EXPO training issues. This is exactly what an unstable overclocked DDR5 kit (or high density server motherboards) may show in real-world.
Improved Bit Fade Test
In addition to the previous 0s and 1s bit fills, the final test on a pass includes a new random sequence. Every DRAM cell is now filled with random date while its adjacent neighbor carry the opposite charge. All CPU Cores now charge and verify the memory cells simultaneously.
Rowhammer
Target Row Refresh (tRR) is a feature in modern DIMMs that defeats the classic double sided hammer . This test uses Blacksmith-style patterns from recent 2022 research with non-uniform, many-sided, and synchronized with DRAM refresh. It infers memory row layout from access timing ('DRAMA-lite' approach). Errors are reported but not included in BadRAM patterns.
Serial Log for Automation
The log= boot parameter allows for one line of machine-parsable output to be produced for each event during the test: start, system information, pass and progress through the tests, and errors. These lines are easy to parse but still human-readable. In addition to the new maxpasses= option (restart after N passes), Memtest86+ can now be run headlessly in test lab environments and CI build systems.
SPD Integrity Check
Checksum/CRC of the SPD of each memory module (DDR5, DDR4, and older) is now verified, and bad memory modules are marked as BAD CRC!. A corrupted SPD could lead to hanging of some motherboards during POST, but most utilities don't pay attention to that. Memtest86+ detects it. It can be turned off by the nospdcrc boot parameter.
Memory Info from DMI When SPD Is Unavailable
On some platforms (eg: laptops, desktops from big OEMs, ARM boards), reading the SPD data is unavailable due to SMBus being locked or inaccessible. Memtest86+ now uses SMBIOS data as a fallback to display infos about the memory module (size, type, speed, and model number).
Misc. Improvements & Bug Fixes
- 100+ new DRAM brands detected
- Support for new platforms (eg: Intel Wildcat Lake)
- Fixed random hangs in x2APIC SMP mode
- Better CPU Temperature reporting on Server platforms (eg: EPYC)
- Various bug fixes (cache detection, USB and keyboard handling, etc.)

articles.title: Mensajes falsos, cursos fraudulentos y malware: los riesgos de estudiar en línea en América Latina
articles.text:
El 43% de las personas que estudiaron de forma online o híbrida en América Latina durante el último año sufrió al menos un incidente digital relacionado con su educación.
El dato surge de una investigación de Kaspersky, que advierte sobre un fenómeno que crece al mismo ritmo que la adopción de plataformas virtuales de enseñanza en la región.
La cifra adquiere relevancia en un contexto donde el estudio a distancia ya forma parte de la rutina de millones de personas. Según el relevamiento, el 76% de los latinoamericanos encuestados realizó algún tipo de estudio en los últimos 12 meses. De ese grupo, el 38% lo hizo completamente en línea, mientras que otro 27% combinó actividades virtuales y presenciales.
Los incidentes más comunes durante el aprendizaje digital
El estudio identificó que los riesgos aparecen en distintos momentos de la experiencia educativa, no solo al ingresar a una plataforma. Entre los problemas más frecuentes se encuentran:
- Mensajes o enlaces sospechosos vinculados al aprendizaje, reportados por el 23% de los encuestados, el incidente más común detectado.
- Aplicaciones o sitios web falsos, que afectaron al 16% de los usuarios.
- Estafas difundidas en comunidades y grupos de mensajería.
- Cursos falsos ofrecidos a través de distintos canales.
- Malware oculto en archivos educativos.
- Casos de exposición de información personal.
Estos resultados muestran que los riesgos también se concentran en la descarga de materiales, la interacción en grupos de estudio y el registro en nuevos servicios, además del acceso directo a plataformas académicas.
Un problema que también afecta el bolsillo
Las consecuencias de estos incidentes no se limitan a una molestia puntual. La pérdida de tiempo fue el impacto más frecuente entre los afectados, con un 44%, seguida por la recepción de publicidad no deseada.
El componente económico resultó particularmente significativo: el 22% de quienes sufrieron un incidente perdió dinero como consecuencia directa. Otros usuarios reportaron pérdida de acceso a plataformas educativas, afectaciones en su progreso académico y fallas en sus dispositivos. En paralelo, varios encuestados señalaron haber perdido confianza en plataformas, proveedores o profesores tras enfrentar este tipo de situaciones.
Campañas que explotan el interés por la educación virtual
Los investigadores de la compañía de seguridad digital identificaron distintas campañas de spam diseñadas para aprovechar el auge de la enseñanza en línea. Algunas se dirigen a padres de familia y promocionan supuestas alternativas educativas mediante mensajes que cuestionan la enseñanza tradicional y buscan que los destinatarios reenvíen el contenido.
Otras campañas apuntan a adultos que trabajan y les ofrecen la posibilidad de retomar sus estudios sin dejar el empleo. En estos casos, los especialistas detectaron imágenes que no correspondían a la oferta real y enlaces que redirigían a sitios de terceros sin relación con el supuesto servicio. También se identificaron correos que promocionaban falsos préstamos estudiantiles.
Fabiano Tricarico, director de Productos para el Consumidor para las Américas en Kaspersky, advirtió sobre la magnitud del problema: “Perder una tesis porque un ransomware bloqueó un computador, pagar por un curso falso o comprometer una cuenta después de abrir un enlace malicioso son riesgos reales para cualquier persona que estudie online”.
Más dispositivos, más puntos de exposición
La investigación también detectó que las formas de estudiar en línea se diversificaron. Los usuarios combinan clases virtuales grupales, cursos, aplicaciones y sesiones privadas con profesores, lo que multiplica las plataformas, cuentas y servicios digitales que forman parte de su rutina académica.
En una misma jornada, un estudiante puede interactuar con videollamadas, plataformas académicas, aplicaciones, servicios en la nube y grupos de mensajería.
Frente a este panorama, Kaspersky amplía su portafolio de seguridad a computadores Windows basados en ARM, incluidos equipos con procesadores Qualcomm Snapdragon X, Snapdragon X Plus y Snapdragon X Elite, con el objetivo de extender sus tecnologías de protección contra estafas y malware impulsadas por inteligencia artificial a más plataformas.
Recomendaciones para reducir los riesgos
Los especialistas de la compañía sugieren una serie de medidas básicas de protección:
- Usar contraseñas diferentes para cada plataforma educativa y apoyarse en un administrador de contraseñas.
- Activar la autenticación multifactor siempre que esté disponible.
- Verificar la legitimidad de cursos, plataformas y enlaces antes de compartir datos o realizar pagos.
- Evitar redes Wi-Fi públicas para actividades sensibles o complementarlas con una VPN confiable.
- Mantener copias de seguridad de tesis, investigaciones y proyectos en servicios en la nube o unidades externas protegidas.

articles.title: Googlebooks from Dell, Lenovo, and HP tested: Nice hardware, but the OS isn't ready yet
articles.text:
Googlebooks from Dell, Lenovo, and HP tested: Nice hardware, but the OS isn't ready yet
Nice hardware, but it feels like Google rushed its OS.
Chromebooks have gotten a bad rap. The systems have often been seen as glorified web browsers designed only for schools. But with Googlebooks, Google is making a renewed push to show its laptops are designed to be full-on PCs, running a new operating system that feels more like Android than anything else.
Googlebook OS is also designed to merge your Android phone and your laptop in a way that has never been seen outside of Apple’s macOS and iOS devices.
And of course, Google has packed Googlebook OS full of AI features. Some of these are unique to the new laptops, while others, like Rambler, have been introduced on Android phones before.
The new undertaking currently has five hardware partners: Dell, Lenovo, HP, Acer, and Asus. The hardware that we tested is generally sound, though I wouldn't mind a bit more battery life.It's the OS itself that needs some more time in the oven. It largely feels like Android, with some features nailed on to fit a desktop OS. Despite the expansive Google Play Store, the platform is still limited and largely centered around the web browser.
In some ways, Googlebooks are more powerful than Chromebooks could ever be. In other ways, they feel like they haven't yet grown into a full PC operating system.
Googlebook Hardware
I've spent the last few days using the Lenovo Googlebook 15, HP Googlebook 14, and Dell’s XPS Googlebook. In general, if you've seen some recent Windows laptops, you've seen this hardware. The HP Googlebook 14 is clearly based off around the HP OmniBook Ultra, while the Dell XPS Googlebook is a carbon copy of the Dell XPS 13 — although there is a haptic touchpad in this version. I have few complaints there — both of those are solid machines, though I still wish HP would move away from the keyboards without spaces around the keys.
Of the systems, the HP feels the most premium, but I've come to appreciate Lenovo's airy design with the all-white Lenovo Googlebook 15. Despite the 15.3-inch OLED screen, the mix of carbon fiber with aluminum and magnesium doesn't feel as high-end, but is light at approximately 2.84 pounds.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
HP and Lenovo both include beautiful 2880 x 1800 OLED screens, while Dell opted for a 2560 x 1600 LCD panel instead.
While ports, materials, and screens might differ, all of the Googlebooks share a few things in common. The first is the Glowbar, which originated on the Chromebook Pixel and Pixel C tablet. Here, it serves as the sole unifying element that tells anyone looking at you that yes, you're using a Googlebook. When you turn the system on or put it to sleep, it has a nice rainbow pattern, but otherwise it largely glows white. It dances around when you speak to Gemini, and when you plug or unplug the device, it indicates battery life with colors (green, yellow, red) and flashing when the battery is low or there’s a charging problem.
Other than turning the Glowbar off, there's not much customization. Or rather, there isn’t unless you find the hidden Glowbar Disco app, which Google is positioning as an easter egg. (SPOILER ALERT: Go to Settings > Apps and click "See all [Number] apps." Click on the three dots in the corner and click "Show System." Click "Glowbar Disco" and press the External arrow button. This launches Glowbar Disco.)Glowbar Disco lets you choose a custom color, preset gradient, or a series of animations like a Knight Rider-style scanner, a rainbow, or my favorite "vibe code," which looks like the letters from The Matrix dropping. You can also set it to sync to music, which is set as "experimental." That's funny, given how hidden this app is. Effects aren't persistent when you close the app, and you can't even pin the app to the taskbar to easily reset it.
The other major similarity across all of the hardware is the keyboards. Google has a shared layout across all of the devices, including a G key that opens the app launcher and works with shortcuts, a Caps Lock key that doubles as Quick Insert, and, on F1 through F3, are the Back, Show Homescreen, and Overview buttons (The latter shows all open apps). These feel like throwbacks to Android phones before they largely went gesture-based, though they can still be found in Settings on Android phones today.
Performance: Intel vs. Qualcomm
There are two chips in the first crop of Googlebooks. The HP Googlebook 14 and Dell XPS Googlebook are powered by the Qualcomm Snapdragon X Elite X1-80-100, while the rest are using Intel's Core Series 3 "Panther Lake" processors, specifically the Core Ultra 5 325 in the Lenovo Googlebook 15.Since launch, there have been questions about app compatibility on the Intel models, as most Android apps are designed to run on Arm chips in phones. Google and Intel are in a bit of a back-and-forth over how many Android apps simply work on Intel right now. I've also found a few glitches in the Android based-version of Googlebook OS, like popping icons on the taskbar. Perhaps most notably, when trying browsers that weren't Chrome, the Arm-based Googlebooks were able to run Microsoft Edge, while the Intel-based Lenovo had issues. That app is marked as being "compatible with desktop" in the Play Store.
In benchmarks, we found that the Snapdragon X1 Elite models outperformed the singular Intel option we had to test. Notably, though, that's Qualcomm's high-end Oryon chip (albeit from its first generation) compared to an Intel Core Ultra 5. We didn't have a system with an Intel Core Ultra 7.
In Geekbench 7, the Snapdragon-based systems edged out the Lenovo Googlebook with Intel, particularly in multi-core. But on WebXPRT4, the Lenovo system won. Google claims people spend 70% of their time in the browser.
On 3DMark's Steel Nomad Light, the Snapdragon systems won out again, though not by a ton. If you're doing a lot of Android gaming, it's worth noting.
On our battery test, the Intel-based Lenovo won out at 11:52, while the HP hit 10:25 and the XPS reached 10:04. None of these are amazing times. Our Googlebook battery test browses a list of 30 live websites on a loop at 150 nits of brightness.
It's also notable that while Googlebooks as a class have at least 16GB of RAM, they appear, according to their task managers, to always have at least 7-8GB in use, likely housing local AI models to be ready at any moment.
Googlebook OS
If you use an Android phone, specifically one of Google's Pixels, you'll feel right at home with a Googlebook. For all the talk of merging ChromeOS and Android, Googlebook OS really feels like an Android phone, just on a laptop.
There's a taskbar on the bottom (there's no way to move that yet — shades of Windows 11 there), and the systems come with some precreated folders for Google apps on the desktop. There's also a dedicated My Googlebook app on the desktop to teach you the ropes.
Along the very top, there's a status bar with the time, date, a button to turn on the Magic Cursor, and some quick settings that can be accessed by clicking the Wi-Fi and battery icons (think macOS' Control Center).
Apps are in the G Menu, and, if you have a phone paired, it appears next to it with a separate drawer of apps you can cast to your phone.
It's quite simple — especially if your primary app is Google Chrome. If you use the rest of Google's ecosystem, like Photos, Calendar, and Messages, you'll almost be set up out of the box (they all wanted me to confirm my Google account, which was a bit annoying). In fact, if you don't use all of those services, I question the value of buying a Googlebook at all.
But the simplicity and elasticity of Android only goes so far. While it's clearly flexible enough to become a desktop OS, there are some areas where you can just tell the team needed more time.
For starters, a lot of the spacing feels meant for touch. When I right clicked on the desktop for context menus, there would be a significant amount of space to move my mouse. But when I touched the screen, that spacing felt natural for my finger.
You see more of that in the Files app. It's lacking features that make some sense on a phone but don't on a computer. For example, there are no forward and back buttons. Instead, you have to navigate through folders or the path at the bottom of the screen. Additionally, the Files app doesn't let you pin or re-order the folders in the sidebar.
Perhaps the most damning, given how flexible ChromeOS is with profiles, is that the version of Google Chrome on Googlebook OS doesn't, as of this writing, support multiple profiles. That breaks plenty of people's workflows, especially those who have separate accounts for work and personal use.
The best thought-out desktop feature is Quick Insert. Having a key that serves as a go-to place for your clipboard history, suggested emojis, recent browsing, and links to tools is a real time saver when you don't want to click around looking for them all.
All the apps you want, as long as you like the Play Store
The only way to install apps on a Googlebook is through the Play Store. That is where the system is most locked down. Unlike Windows, macOS, and Linux, you can't install software from the web browser.
In the Play Store, Google has five "desktop ratings" that lets you get an idea of how an app works on a Googlebook. Made for Desktop is the gold standard, which means it's a desktop-first app with features and controls designed for a mouse and keyboard. Optimized for Desktop is a close second, in which an app has been adjusted for the bigger screen.
Compatible with Desktop means a keyboard and mouse will work. After that, you get Better on the Website. Slack gave me this, as did Duolingo. Lastly, Built for Mobile means you'll get the app, but it will be formatted for a smartphone.
Compatible with Desktop doesn't always mean great. One of my go-to mobile games, Marvel Snap, is compatible, but it stretches out and leaves black bars on the sides. It did, however, support Google's ability to map touch to keyboard controls, though that's not really appropriate for this game. Given this game has a widescreen version on Steam, I'd hope Google could get developer Second Dinner to make it work on Google Play just as well.
Designed for Mobile should be a last resort. I downloaded my bank app, and I regretted not just going to the website.
Google's own apps are a mixed bag. Gmail and Calendar are just web apps in a nice wrapper. At least Messages feels like a proper Android app.
One issue I had is that when I connected a phone at setup, it offered to transfer my apps. It auto-selected some, like Apple Music (Optimized for Desktop), but left a bunch off. But I thought I'd want some, so I picked them. At that time, it didn't tell me why they left them off, though I'm guessing it's the lack of optimization many of them later displayed.
In many ways, that lack of optimization means that Googlebooks still feel like Chromebooks, with web apps as a major fallback. There are some major apps, like Photoshop, Netflix, Fantastical (leaving the Apple ecosystem!), Obsidian, Notability, Zoom, and Microsoft Office all optimized or straight up designed for desktop. But it's not enough just yet. Google really needs developers on board.
The other option is installing apps through a Linux virtual machine, but I don't recommend it (see below).
Cross-device use
The other trick up these Googlebooks' sleeve is to pair your laptop and phone together more closely than has ever been done before. In many ways, it's impressive. You can share notifications and drag files to and from devices wirelessly in the Files app.
Perhaps the biggest issue was finding a phone that worked. Google keeps it in the fine print that you need a phone with Android 17 to get the best cross-device features, like app casting, Continue On, and Quick Access in the Files app. If you have a phone that doesn't have Android 17 yet, like the Samsung Galaxy S23 I had set up ahead of this review, you'll only be able to use the phone to set up the computer and transfer apps. This is surely a technical hurdle, but one that leaves out the vast majority of people with Android phones right now.
Google loaned us a Pixel 10 Pro XL to test these features, and it's important they did. Even Samsung's Android phones, the most popular in the United States, don't all work with Googlebooks yet. On Reddit, one Google staffer wrote that support "will be rolling out across all Android 17-supported Samsung devices over the coming weeks. Sorry for the inconvenience!" News broke just days ago that support was rolling out for Samsung phones running Android 17 and Samsung’s One UI 9, but we still had issues connecting a Samsung S25 Ultra after initial setup with Dell’s XPS Googlebook.
Otherwise, perhaps my biggest issue was that you have to turn on a bunch of settings that you may not have turned on yet. Even Google's reviewer's guide had a bunch of steps to enable cross-device settings, and, if that didn't work, on its own, a series of restarts or QR code scans. When it works, though, it takes, and the experience is far better than what you get on Windows.
The key word being "when." I didn't always get notifications. I couldn't drag some small files from my Googlebook to the phone, and I still don't know why.
Casting Apps was my favorite use case, especially apps I wouldn't really install on my laptop. Unfortunately, there was some lag and hiccups with connections, both at work and at home, which occasionally made the whole thing unusable. It's impressive, however, that you can have your Android phone running other apps while you have one open only on your Googlebook; Apple's casting method mirrors the whole phone, so it can only be on a Mac or on the phone itself.
Continue On is also appreciated. Like Apple's continuity, I could be browsing the web on my phone and pick it back up on the laptop. I just wish it worked with more apps, as it mostly works with Google's work suite and Chrome.
So many ways to use Gemini
Googlebooks are smothered in AI. For the most part, you never have to use it, but the system is all about teaching you at first. For example, there are early prompts to learn about the Magic Cursor, which lets you click on something and share it with Gemini immediately.
It's quicker than copy and paste, but I never found myself using it as often as I expected. Maybe the next time I see a shirt I like, I’ll try it.
The idea of making your own widget is really neat, but I wish it was more flexible. Sure, countdowns and motivational quotes are fun, but when I asked the AI to create a widget showing me CPU usage, it denied me, expressly telling me that system telemetry wasn't allowed.
The most impressive thing, which Google should talk about even more, is Rambler. This isn't new to Googlebooks — it's already on Android phones. It lets you talk, make mistakes, and still correct your statements into what you ultimately meant. For people who talk to their computers and use dictation, this is powerful to have on the computer alongside the phone.
The one I worry the most about is Antigravity. This comes preinstalled, without a care if you are a developer. In theory, this is empowering Googlebook users to make their own apps. On the other hand, there's a reason AI models keep asking for human intervention and approval. The agentic-first IDE may let anyone make prompts, but given that your agents can execute shell commands, it's far safer if you understand what they're doing. I expect many people to just hit "yes" without knowing what they're talking about, but hey, it's just bringing vibe coding to more people.
Gemini is also sprinkled throughout Google's apps, and you can also talk to it with a simple "Hey Google" command. I would argue these systems are best if you are a Gemini user, if only because you'll get so many features.
The Debian Linux Terminal
Each Googlebook comes with a Debian Linux terminal and virtual machine preinstalled. I was able to install apps, like the photo editor GIMP and Steam for gaming, but I don't find these Linux apps decent replacements for most people.
For starters, the apps in the VM live there, and only there. You can't put them in the app drawer and run them separately later.
The VM is also laggy. Even lightweight games like Dead Cells didn't always run fluidly, and I had some issues with the sound making popping and groaning noises.
Resizing windows and using some tools in GIMP resulting in its own lag. This might work for basic development testing, but for applications, you're better off sticking with the Play Store or web apps.
Too early to tell, but already on sale
It's too early to render judgment on the ultimate fate of Googlebooks. If you like using Android on your phone and do everything on the web or Android apps, you can make this work.
Google clearly has some work to do to make Googlebook OS feel truly at home with a keyboard and mouse. And it needs a ton of developers to optimize their apps to feel like you're not using them on a phone when you put them on a big screen. With enough of them, the Googlebook platform will feel far more friendly.
At the moment, I think people should wait and see how the Googlebook platform evolves. If you buy now, you're getting the early adopter experience. There's too much that doesn't work as it should for you to spend your hard-earned money on these. The hardware is there, but Google's software doesn't feel done.
Google should ensure users’ favorite apps work no matter which silicon platform they use, and they should be darn sure their phone will work with the system they have. And prospective buyers should definitely wait and see if Google delivers on its promises that developers will improve their apps.
Andrew E. Freedman is a senior editor at Tom's Hardware focusing on laptops, desktops and gaming. He also keeps up with the latest news. A lover of all things gaming and tech, his previous work has shown up in Tom's Guide, Laptop Mag, Kotaku, PCMag and Complex, among others. Follow him on Threads @FreedmanAE and BlueSky @andrewfreedman.net. You can send him tips on Signal: andrewfreedman.01

articles.title: KDE turns 30 with Plasma 6.8, remote upgrades, and an X11 farewell
articles.text:
Marking the 30th anniversary of software developer KDE on October 14, the company released Plasma 6.8, debuted a movie, and retired Plasma’s native X11 session support. The announcement from KDE dubs the new Plasma 6.8 as the “30th Anniversary Edition” and describes the update as preparing Plasma for the future. Legacy X11 applications will still function via the XWayland compatibility layer, and KDE applications will also continue supporting X11 under other desktop environments.
After 42 years in service, the X11 protocol is losing another major desktop environment. Plasma will fully adopt the Wayland system and put support for starting new X11 sessions in Plasma to bed. Users opting to stay on Plasma 6.7 will keep their existing sessions for now. The move was expected, with GNOME officially dropping X11 sessions by default in 2025.
The new Plasma 6.8 brings many improvements, including increased support for adding window decorations (like shadows and rounded corners) to third-party apps, and a more streamlined Union theming system. Other notable additions include Nvidia triple buffering being enabled by default, Kup backup integration (KDE’s backup utility—now integrated into Plasma), and kscreenctl, a command-line utility that allows power users to adjust display configurations.

articles.title: Startup nFox to open-source its 'sandbox' for open AI models - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Startup nFox to open-source its ‘sandbox’ for open AI models
Artificial intelligence governance startup nFOX Lab today launched a platform for managing owned large language models and announced plans to open-source Blockhouse, a security sandbox designed to restrict what AI workloads can access and do.
The firm, which emerged from stealth mode this week, aims to help enterprises adopt open models safely on infrastructure they control while limiting the damage a compromised or misbehaving workload could cause. Blockhouse removes privileges by default and lets administrators restore access deliberately through policies enforced at the Linux kernel level.
The company’s approach borrows from zero-trust security principles by sharply limiting access and letting administrators restore privileges selectively. “Every model has the potential to be hostile,” said Gordon Allott, nFOX’s founder and chief executive. “We just presume hostility.”
That addresses a dilemma for companies that want AI capabilities but hesitate to send sensitive information to external providers. Running models internally gives enterprises control over their data, but it also makes them responsible for securing the software and infrastructure that support those models.
Blockhouse operates beneath the application layer, using Linux security mechanisms to restrict model workloads. Rather than relying on instructions telling a model what it should avoid, the system removes capabilities that could enable unauthorized activity, according to Allott.
“You’re basically removing the ability to do it in the first place,” he said.
Communications pass through Porthole, a monitored channel that allows requests to be reviewed before they are fulfilled. Runtime credentials and audit controls remain outside the model process. Administrators can restrict access to files and approve the destinations workloads may contact using a whitelist.
Although the approach is comprehensive, it doesn’t preclude the risk of human error. Allott acknowledged that an administrator could mistakenly authorize a malicious destination.
Blockhouse also checks model integrity. Approved files are sealed with SHA-256 hashes before serving, and built-in checks halt serving if those files change. The software records containment events and reports when a host can’t provide the expected protection.
The sandbox supports the vLLM, SGLang and llama.cpp inference engines. The accompanying nFOX Platform provides a console for evaluating, deploying and monitoring models across cloud virtual machines, rented graphics processing unit hosts and on-premises Linux servers equipped with Nvidia Corp. GPUs.
Teams can check model configurations, verify files and test models with adversarial prompts before deployment. Production workloads receive OpenAI Group PLC-compatible endpoints, while operational evidence can feed existing endpoint detection and security information management systems. Audit records use JavaScript Object Notation and Parquet formats.
Allott said nFOX plans to release Blockhouse under the Apache 2.0 license, while charging an annual license for its fleet management platform. He said open-sourcing the sandbox invites the public scrutiny that security software needs.
“The best security comes from many, many eyes and smart people working on it,” he said.
Allott pointed to Nvidia’s OpenShell as a similar technology that’s focused on securing agents and said nFOX intends to incorporate it. The startup’s roadmap has it expanding into agent protection over time.
The startup company is self-funded but intends to raise venture capital. Allott said nFox has paying beta pilot customers, though it is not yet profitable.
The nFOX Platform is available now. Blockhouse is available in beta test for qualified enterprise evaluations. The commercial platform adds deployment and oversight to the open-source sandbox, with both components focused on keeping privately operated AI under enterprise control.

Como ganhar diamantes de graça no Free Fire
Tenha cuidado com geradores, APKs modificados e páginas que prometem diamantes de graça no FF, utilize somente os canais e sites oficiais para obter as moedas do jogo
Os diamantes do Free Fire atuam como a moeda virtual do jogo, permitindo que os jogadores comprem skins, personagens exclusivos e passes de elite. Esse recurso é essencial para quem deseja personalizar o visual do avatar e aproveitar ao máximo todas as novidades lançadas pela Garena.
Para conseguir diamantes grátis, os jogadores podem participar de eventos oficiais, campeonatos da comunidade e resgatar códigos promocionais válidos. Outra opção bastante popular é utilizar o aplicativo oficial de recompensas do Google para acumular saldo na loja virtual.
A seguir, o Tecnoblog te mostra cinco formas de ganhar diamantes no Free Fire.
Os meios mais seguros de obter diamantes no Free Fire são por meio de eventos oficiais dentro do jogo, recompensas de partidas ranqueadas ou créditos da Google Play Store. Entenda como funciona:
Você pode ganhar diamantes de graça no Free Fire ao cumprir metas no próprio game. Para isso, basta completar tarefas diárias, desafios semanais e missões especiais para receber as recompensas.
Fique de olho também na aba de “Eventos”, em que campanhas temporárias costumam distribuir vouchers de diamantes e itens exclusivos aos jogadores. Assim, você aumenta o seu inventário de forma rápida e diminui a necessidade de gastar dinheiro real.
Subir de patente e alcançar marcos mais altos nas temporadas do Free Fire é um dos meios para conseguir diamantes grátis. Ao evoluir nos ranks (classificações), o jogador acumula baús e cupons de recompensa diretamente em seu perfil.
Embora a distribuição de diamantes mude a cada temporada, disputar partidas ranqueadas rende prêmios sazonais valiosos. Essas conquistas abastecem o inventário com itens importantes e ajudam a economizar os diamantes.
Outro caminho para conseguir diamantes no Free Fire de graça é participar de torneios promovidos pela Garena ou por streamers parceiros. Os jogadores com melhor desempenho nas disputas recebem premiações diretas e codiguins (códigos de resgate) na conta.
Além das competições, acompanhar as redes sociais oficiais permite participar de sorteios verificados e distribuições gratuitas. Essa é uma alternativa segura para reforçar seu saldo no jogo e evitar golpes na internet.
Responder a pesquisas no aplicativo Google Recompensa Sua Opinião acumula créditos na sua conta. Essa carteira digital armazena o saldo obtido na loja Google Play de forma simples e totalmente segura.
Esse saldo acumulado pode ser usado em microtransações de recarga no próprio aplicativo. Essa é uma estratégia inteligente para ganhar diamantes de graça no Free Fire sem mexer no seu bolso.
A Garena disponibiliza periodicamente o famoso codiguin do Free Fire, códigos promocionais com combinações de caracteres. Essas sequências concedem recompensas oficiais e cupons válidos para resgatar diamantes FF grátis ou itens cosméticos.
Para inserir os códigos, acesse o reward.ff.garena.com e faça login com sua conta. Em seguida, cole os dígitos na página oficial para validar os prêmios e recebê-los direto no cofre do jogo.
Não existe nenhum método oficial para conseguir diamante de graça e infinito no Free Fire, pois o saldo fica salvo nos servidores da Garena. Essa centralização de dados impede alterações externas e invalida qualquer promessa de moedas virtuais ilimitadas.
Aplicativos e geradores com nomes de “Free Fire diamante infinito” praticam clonagem de sites legítimos (phishing) e causam banimento. A melhor alternativa para ganhar diamante de graça continua sendo participar de missões, eventos e promoções oficiais do jogo.

articles.title: Avant l'hiver, le chauffage connecté Philips 5000 descend à 79,99€
articles.text:
Philips associe sur ce chauffage soufflant céramique un thermostat de 1 à 37 °C, une programmation par application et un mode Auto Plus qui apprend vos habitudes. Reste à savoir ce que valent vraiment les économies annoncées, et pour quelles pièces il est pensé.
Le Philips 5000 (CX5120/11) est un chauffage soufflant à élément céramique PTC de 2 000 W, conçu pour des pièces jusqu’à 20 m². Sa particularité tient moins à sa puissance qu’à sa régulation : thermostat réglable, minuterie, oscillation sur 60° et pilotage par l’application Philips Air+ en Wi-Fi.
Chez Amazon, le chauffage connecté Philips 5000 passe à 79,99 € contre 99,99 € de prix conseillé, soit 20 % de remise. L’offre parle surtout à ceux qui veulent compléter un chauffage principal dans une pièce précise, sans le laisser tourner pour rien.
Le chauffage électrique connecté Philips 5000 (CX5120/11) est proposé à 79,99 € au lieu de 99,99 € chez Amazon.
Pourquoi choisir le Philips 5000 (CX5120/11) ?
- Une chaleur programmée : L’application Air+ permet d’allumer l’appareil à distance et de planifier les plages de chauffe jour par jour. La pièce est chaude à votre arrivée sans que le chauffage tourne toute la journée.
- Deux niveaux et un mode auto : L’appareil alterne entre 1 200 et 2 000 W, ou laisse un algorithme réguler la chauffe autour de la température visée. Un mode ventilation seule, à 8 W, sert aussi en demi-saison.
- Cinq sécurités : Coupure au-delà de 30° d’inclinaison, arrêt à 85 °C, prise certifiée VDE, matériaux ignifugés V0 et extinction après 24 heures d’inactivité. Des garde-fous rassurants pour un appareil qu’on déplace souvent.
Une chambre, un bureau, une pièce qu’on chauffe à la demande
Avec 58 cm de haut, 21 cm de large et 2,4 kg, cette tour se glisse dans un angle et se déplace d’une pièce à l’autre grâce à sa poignée intégrée. Philips annonce une montée en chauffe en 2 secondes, ce qui correspond bien à un usage ponctuel : un bureau à domicile le matin, une chambre avant le coucher. L’oscillation sur 60° répartit l’air chaud au lieu de le concentrer sur un point. La minuterie de 1 à 12 heures évite de devoir penser à l’éteindre.
Le profil idéal est celui d’un logement dont le chauffage central peine dans une pièce, ou d’un télétravailleur qui préfère chauffer son seul bureau plutôt que tout l’appartement. Les 40,5 dB(A) annoncés au réglage le plus bas restent compatibles avec une chambre, Philips ne communique pas de chiffre pour le niveau de 2 000 W. Au-delà de 20 m², l’appareil n’est en revanche plus dans son domaine. Ce n’est pas non plus un chauffage principal.
Ce que la connexion change face à un soufflant classique
Un chauffage soufflant céramique d’entrée de gamme consomme autant à puissance égale : la différence se joue sur le temps de fonctionnement. C’est là que le Philips 5000 se distingue, avec son mode Auto Plus qui adapte la chauffe à la pièce et à vos habitudes. Philips chiffre le gain jusqu’à 50 % de kWh, mais par rapport au même appareil réglé à la main, et jusqu’à 25 % avec le seul thermostat. Face à un modèle sans thermostat, l’écart tient donc surtout à la discipline qu’il impose.
✅ Les points forts
- Programmation hebdomadaire et commande à distance via Air+
- Thermostat réglable de 1 à 37 °C
- Oscillation sur 60° pour mieux répartir la chaleur
- Cinq protections, dont l’arrêt en cas de basculement
- Format compact de 2,4 kg, facile à déplacer
❌ Les limites
- Le mode Auto Plus passe obligatoirement par l’application
- La température affichée est celle mesurée autour de l’appareil, pas celle de toute la pièce
- Limité aux pièces de 20 m²
- À 2 000 W, un appoint qui pèse sur la facture s’il tourne longtemps
Si votre bureau ou votre chambre reste froid en ce début d’automne, le Philips 5000 connecté affiche 79,99 € chez Amazon, soit 20 € sous son prix conseillé.
À 79,99 €, ce Philips 5000 se défend surtout par ce qui entoure sa résistance : thermostat, programmation, mode automatique et sécurités sérieuses. Il conviendra à ceux qui veulent chauffer une pièce précise à des horaires précis, sans avoir à y penser. Son application est la clé de ses arguments d’économie, et c’est aussi sa contrainte. Si vous n’avez pas l’intention de l’utiliser, un soufflant plus simple fera le même travail de chauffe.
Le chiffre de 50 % d’économie mérite d’être lu avec sa note de bas de page : il compare l’appareil à lui-même, utilisé sans régulation. Cela reste un argument réel pour qui laisse habituellement tourner son radiateur d’appoint plus que nécessaire. Pour une pièce de plus de 20 m² ou un chauffage de base, mieux vaut viser plus gros. Pour un bureau, une chambre ou une cuisine, l’équation est cohérente à ce prix.

articles.title: Advantech Expands Server Chassis Portfolio With Liquid Cooling and Compact Desktop Solutions
articles.text:
Thursday, October 15th 2026
Advantech Expands Server Chassis Portfolio With Liquid Cooling and Compact Desktop Solutions
Advantech, a leading provider of industrial edge AI and high-performance computing solutions, today introduces two new tower server chassis—the HPC-7046 Closed-Loop Liquid-Cooling Tower Chassis and HPC-5422 Desktop Workstation Chassis—designed to tackle the growing demands of enterprise AI, machine vision, robotics, and edge computing. From advanced liquid cooling for high-performance, thermally demanding AI workloads to compact desktop workstation with high-power PSU support for power-hungry GPU computing, the new chassis portfolio delivers scalable performance, expansion capabilities, and deployment flexibility, enabling modern AI computing in a compact footprint across industrial and enterprise edge, including small and medium-sized businesses (SMB) offices and server rooms, development laboratories, factory automation, and embedded industrial equipment.
HPC-7046: High-Performance Liquid Cooling for Next Generation AI Computing
Modern AI and compute-intensive workloads are driving the adoption of higher-performance CPUs with increasing thermal design power (TDP), making thermal management and acoustic critical for high-performance tower systems.The HPC-7046 supports a closed-loop liquid-cooling solution for EATX/ATX server boards, integrating the liquid-cooling module, liquid cooler, and system fan options into the chassis to efficiently manage demanding single- and dual-processor configurations based on Intel and AMD platforms, while simplifying thermal integration without requiring external cooling equipment. Under full CPU and GPU load, with the fans operating at 100% duty, the HPC-7046 achieves an acoustic level of approximately 58 dBA, comparable to a moderate open office environment.
Unlike traditional 7-slot chassis designs, the HPC-7046 features an optimized 9-slot expansion that supports a triple-width GPU while retaining system flexibility for additional add-in cards, making it ideal for AI, visualization, and edge computing. With 1350 W / 1650 W PSU options and support for up to 8 SATA/SAS drives, it provides a scalable foundation for GPU-accelerated AI, HPC, and other compute- and data-intensive workloads.The HPC-7046 also enables multiple platform configurations across server and workstation applications. Supported configurations include HPC-7046 + ASMB-928 EATX board with dual Intel Xeon 6, HPC-7046 + ASMB-808 CEB board with single Intel Xeon 600, and HPC-7046 + ASMB-831 ATX board with AMD EPYC Embedded 9004/9005, enabling scalable solutions across AI, HPC, workstation, storage, and edge applications.
HPC-5422: Compact Desktop Workstation with High-Power PSU Support for Flexible Edge Computing
As AI computing moves closer to the point of data generation, edge and workstation systems increasingly require higher computing performance within space-constrained environments. 
Compared with conventional IPC and workstation platforms, the HPC-5422 combines a compact desktop form factor with support for higher-power 850 W and 1200 W PSU, enabling the integration of more power-hungry GPUs in a space-efficient system. Supporting microATX and ATX motherboards as well as desktop and wall mount configurations, the HPC-5422 provides flexible deployment options for a wide range of edge and workstation applications.With up to five FHFL expansion slots, support for two 3.5" HDDs, and optional NVMe HDD backplane, the HPC-5422 provides flexible storage and expansion capabilities in a compact desktop form factor for GPU-accelerated edge computing, AI inference, industrial automation, and workstation applications.
The chassis supports multiple industrial platform solutions, including HPC-5422 + ASMB-808 CEB board with Intel Xeon 600 for high-end AI workstation computing, HPC-5422 + ASMB-589 microATX board with Intel Core Ultra 9/7/5 for desktop workstation, and HPC-5422 + ASMB-831 ATX board with AMD EPYC Embedded 9004/9005 for right-sized server applications, providing flexible platform options for different performance and deployment requirements.
Product Highlights:
