Christian Eberle is a Contributing Editor for Tom's Hardware US. He's a veteran reviewer of A/V equipment, specializing in monitors. Christian began his obsession with tech when he built his first PC in 1991, a 286 running DOS 3.0 at a blazing 12MHz. In 2006, he undertook training from the Imaging Science Foundation in video calibration and testing and thus started a passion for precise imaging that persists to this day. He is also a professional musician with a degree from the New England Conservatory as a classical bassoonist which he used to good effect as a performer with the West Point Army Band from 1987 to 2013. He enjoys watching movies and listening to high-end audio in his custom-built home theater and can be seen riding trails near his home on a race-ready ICE VTX recumbent trike. Christian enjoys the endless summer in Florida where he lives with his wife and Chihuahua and plays with orchestras around the state.

articles.title: Vercel adds always-on workers to run more of your backend
articles.text:
Vercel adds always-on workers to run more of your backend
Vercel is giving developers more options for running their backends on its platform.
At its Ship conference in San Francisco on Thursday, the company introduced Daemons, a new service for continuously running background workers, and made its Python support generally available.
It also made Drives, its persistent storage for AI agents, generally available.
Always-on workers, pull-based jobs
Daemons, which is now in public beta, lets developers deploy a container and specify how many instances should run in each region. Vercel makes sure those processes keep running and restarts them if they exit or crash. At launch, it supports pull-based workloads that allow workers to fetch jobs from a queue or database and then process them as they arrive.
Vercel CTO Malte Ubl tells The New Stack that the company’s current push in terms of going further down the stack.
“Let’s look at what people are doing, and let’s make sure that a larger chunk of them could just only use Vercel as their infrastructure provider,” he says.
The company already offers queues and durable workflows, while its Services feature lets developers deploy frontends and backends together.
These features cover request-driven work, Ubl says, but not everything a sophisticated backend does. “What really doesn’t fit well into that bucket is what you do find in sophisticated backend workloads,” he says, “where you want to do essentially processing on some kind of queue,” he says.
He uses Vercel’s own deployment pipeline as an example for that kind of workload.
“When you call our API to make a deployment, we don’t do that deployment in that process that handles your request, because we can’t actually do an infinite number of concurrent deployments,” Ubl says. GitHub rate limits are one reason to back off, and Vercel’s existing compute primitives didn’t give developers “good control over the amount of concurrency” for that kind of worker.
With Daemons, “they come up, they start saying, here I am, give me work, and then they just process as it goes,” he says.
The company’s example for using Daemons combines a Next.js frontend with a Python API, as well as a containerized video processor. The container packages Python dependencies and the FFmpeg media framework, and then pulls jobs from Vercel Queues to generate playback files and thumbnails.
Transcoding is a typical case, Ubl says, with “extremely CPU-bound workloads” where “I just need computers that I want to always be 100% CPU.”
That also puts Daemons at the opposite end of the spectrum from Vercel’s sandboxes. “They’re almost the opposite of temporary,” he says of Daemons. “For temporary, you have sandboxes,” he says. Daemons stay on but aren’t invoked by requests from the internet. They reach out for work instead.
Developers can deploy through Git or the Vercel CLI. Vercel builds the container image and stores it in its Container Registry.
The company itself runs a good chunk of its control plane API on Vercel. That accounts for about a billion requests a month, Ubl says, and Vercel is now starting to move many of its asynchronous workloads onto Daemons.
Vercel didn’t invent the model, he acknowledges, “we ship it because people very much want this.”
Managed runtime or container
If you’re deep in the Vercel ecosystem, you may wonder how all of this relates to Vercel Functions.
Vercel says 5,000 teams have made 150,000 container deployments since container support entered public beta. Containers let developers package applications with their own runtimes and system libraries, expanding the range of software they can deploy.
The trade-off here is who keeps the image current, Uble argues. With a managed runtime for Node, Bun, or Python, Vercel applies a security release without the customer redeploying, Ubl says. With a container, “you do have to redeploy. It’s ultimately your responsibility,” he says. “From our point of view, it’s just bytes.”
Python support, meanwhile, is now generally available for frameworks including FastAPI, Flask, and Django. Applications run on standard CPython with PyPI dependencies, while Vercel handles framework detection, builds, and scaling. The company says 150,000 teams already run Python backends on its platform, including engineers at OpenAI, Polymarket, and Exa.
Files that survive a change of environment
Vercel Drives is a great example of how agents are changing the requirements for backend services like storage. Vercel’s Drives service separates an agent’s files from the sandbox executing its code. An agent can mount the drive in a new sandbox, change runtimes, and continue working with the files it already created.
“I wouldn’t claim it’s an industry first, but it’s certainly an instance of a new type of storage product,” Ubl says. He describes it as a hybrid of an EBS-style networked drive and object storage, something he doesn’t think AWS offers.
Writes always land on local NVMe disk and stream asynchronously to object storage, he says, and reads come from the local disk when the data is already there — or stream in block by block.
“You have a very large number of independent disks, which, because they’re just files in S3, are arbitrarily cheap to operate,” he says.
Drives versus snapshots
Many sandbox providers, Vercel included, offer snapshots, Ubl says, but he argues drives are the better model.
“The problem with snapshots is they get really big, because you ultimately snapshot all kinds of stuff that is the same every time,” he says. “In practice, what agents really do is there’s some directory, I don’t know, /home/agent. That’s where everything is. Everything else they don’t really care about.”
Mounting that one directory means every agent can boot from the same cached base image, he says. “It’s cheaper for them, it’s faster. There’s essentially no downside.”
Vercel isn’t removing snapshots, Ubl adds, but it is encouraging customers to switch.
Drives lets those agents reuse each other’s work. One can prepare a dataset while others mount read-only copies to analyze it or generate reports, saving their results separately. Agents can also fork a drive to test different approaches in independent writable workspaces. Those forks don’t merge back into the original.
In practice, Ubl says, that means telling the agent where to write. “When you use a sandbox, you always tell your agent where it should write things,” he says, typically a root directory such as /workspace. “Essentially every prompt will start with that sentence, and then that’s just what you mount into your durable drive, and that’s it.”
Drives and forking are generally available. The service is available on all Vercel plans, with default capacities of 1 TiB, or 1 GiB on Hobby, and configurations up to 16 TiB.
For a team already deploying its frontend on Vercel, running a worker or Python API there becomes an easier decision. Each additional backend service it can keep on the platform is one fewer deployment system its developers have to maintain.

articles.title: Kann sogar fliegen: Tesla zeigt Sportwagen mit Raketendüsen
articles.text:
Tesla hat einen Sportwagen vorgestellt, der dank Raketendüsen kurze Entfernungen im Flug zurücklegen kann. Bei der Präsentation in der texanischen Stadt Waco flog der Tesla Roadster dank seiner Kaltgas-Triebwerke unter anderem mit einer Seitenrolle über geparkte andere Modelle des Elektroauto-Herstellers. Der Sportwagen werde 2028 in die Produktion gehen und man werde ihn kaufen können, sagte Tesla-Chef Elon Musk.
Ein Preis wurde nicht genannt. Allerdings werden schon für die Reservierung der Roadster-Version, die dank der Düsen schneller beschleunigen kann, insgesamt 250.000 Euro fällig – erst 5.000 Euro und dann weitere 245.000 Euro binnen zehn Tagen. Auf der Tesla-Website heißt es nur bei den 5.000 Euro, dass man den Betrag vollständig zurückerstattet bekommen könne. In der Präsentation beschleunigte der Roadster aus dem Stand auf 60 Meilen pro Stunde (knapp 96,6 km/h) in 0,81 Sekunden. Das Produktionsmodell werde noch schneller sein, kündigte Tech-Milliardär Musk an.
Fliegendes Auto nur auf Einladung
Die «Rocket»-Variante, die mit weiteren Düsen auch fliegen kann, wird nach Angaben auf der Tesla-Website nur auf Einladung des Unternehmens zugänglich sein. Das Fliegen sei im öffentlichen Straßenverkehr nicht zugelassen und die «Rocket»-Ausführung werde möglicherweise nicht in allen Regionen verfügbar sein, heißt es einschränkend auf der Tesla-Website.
Es blieb unklar, wie viele Fahrzeuge mit Kaltgas-Triebwerken Tesla bauen will. Für die Reservierung der «Performance»-Version ohne Düsen müssen insgesamt 50.000 Euro gezahlt werden. In den USA sind es die gleichen Beträge in Dollar. Alle Roadster sollen für die Straßenhaftung ein Saugsystem bekommen. Bei der Präsentation hielt es den Wagen kopfunter auf einer Rampe.
Nähe zu SpaceX
Musk führt neben Tesla auch die Raumfahrtfirma SpaceX, die entsprechend viel mit Düsenantrieben zu tun hat. Schon seit einiger Zeit wird spekuliert, dass er die beiden Unternehmen unter einem Dach zusammenbringen will. Bei Tesla rief Musk den Fokus auf autonomes Fahren und humanoide Roboter statt des heutigen Autoverkaufs aus. Der Roadster solle das letzte Tesla-Fahrzeug werden, das noch von Menschen gefahren werde, sagt er.
Allerdings äußern einige Rivalen und Experten Zweifel an der Verlässlichkeit von Teslas Lösung zum autonomen Fahren, da Musk kategorisch nur auf Kameras als Sensoren setzen will und auf teurere Laser-Radare verzichtet, die die Umgebung abtasten.
Musk hatte ursprünglich schon 2017 den Prototyp eines Roadster-Sportwagens gezeigt und damals den Produktionsstart für 2020 in Aussicht gestellt.

articles.title: Above the 911? Porsche previews a new mid-engined supercar.
articles.text:
Porsche showed us a preview of a new model this afternoon as it unveiled the Mission S concept in New York. It’s a mid-engined sports car that will slot into the Porsche range above the 911. But this won’t be a limited-run car like the Carrera GT or 918 Spyder—instead it will be a regular production model, part of Porsche’s plan to dig itself out of a financial hole by 2035.
Things have been tough for the German automaker of late. Just three years ago its profit margin was the envy of the industry at 18 percent; last year it collapsed to just 1 percent. It has recovered a little since then, and Porsche’s board has a plan to get back to double-digit margins by 2035, called “Sportwagenschmiede ’35,” which involves prioritizing “value over volume,” with greater individualization for customers—and the associated higher selling prices that come with it.
“We are pursuing a clear plan with our strategy Sportwagenschmiede ’35. The ultimate goal is to further strengthen our unique sports car brand–across all model lines and with new, highly desirable models in particularly high-margin segments,” said Porsche Chairman Michael Leiters.
Some of that restructuring will involve laying off 9,000 people, part of a larger effort by Volkswagen Group (which owns Porsche) to reduce headcount over the next decade. But new models are planned, too: the electric 718 Boxster/Cayman, a smaller SUV below the Macan due in 2028 with both gasoline and plug-in powertrains, as well as new models in larger, more expensive segments alongside the Cayenne and Panamera.

articles.title: Les XGIMI Horizon 30 arrivent en France : voici ce qui distingue vraiment les trois modèles
articles.text:
Les nouveaux vidéoprojecteurs Horizon 30 de XGIMI arrivent en précommande en France, avec des tarifs allant de 1 999 à 2 999 €. Pourtant, les trois modèles partagent l'essentiel de leurs caractéristiques. De quoi s'interroger sur l'intérêt de monter en gamme.
Déjà aperçue en Chine sous le nom RS30, puis présentée ensuite à l'IFA, la nouvelle génération Horizon 30 promet notamment de corriger l'une des faiblesses que nous avions relevées lors de notre test de l'Horizon 20 Max : le contraste et la profondeur des noirs.
Pour y parvenir, XGIMI associe sa source triple laser RGB à un nouveau système de double iris intelligent. Une évolution commune aux Horizon 30 Pro, Max et Ultra Max, qui disposent également de la 4K à 120 Hz, du VRR, d'un zoom optique et d'un lens shift.
Plus de contraste, mais pas forcément plus de luminosité
L'Horizon 30 Pro revendique 4 800 lumens ISO et un contraste natif de 8 000:1, contre 5 300 lumens et 9 000:1 pour le Max. L'Ultra Max pousse ces valeurs à 6 000 lumens et 10 000:1.
Mais un chiffre interpelle car l'Horizon 20 Max annonçait déjà 5 700 lumens ISO. Son successeur, l'Horizon 30 Max, affiche donc une luminosité inférieure d'environ 7 %. XGIMI revendique pourtant jusqu'à 15 % de luminosité supplémentaire à l'échelle de la nouvelle gamme, une comparaison qui ne correspond donc pas à ces deux modèles précis.
La véritable ambition de cette génération semble ainsi résider dans l'amélioration du contraste plutôt que dans la course aux lumens. Le constructeur revendique d'ailleurs un contraste natif jusqu'à sept fois supérieur à celui de la génération précédente, une promesse qui reste à vérifier en conditions réelles.
| Comparatif des XGIMI Horizon 30 |  |  |  | 
| Caractéristiques | Horizon 30 Pro | Horizon 30 Max | Horizon 30 Ultra Max | 
| Luminosité ISO | 4 800 lm | 5 300 lm | 6 000 lm | 
| Contraste natif annoncé | 8 000:1 | 9 000:1 | 10 000:1 | 
| 4K à 120 Hz / VRR | Oui | Oui | Oui | 
| Double iris / lens shift | Oui | Oui | Oui | 
| Audio Harman Kardon | 2 × 12 W | 2 × 12 W | 2 × 12 W | 
| Prix de précommande | 1 999 € | 2 499 € | 2 999 € | 
| Prix public | 2 499 € | 2 799 € | 3 299 € | 
Entre les trois Horizon 30, les gains de luminosité sont relativement contenus : environ 10 % pour le Max face au Pro, et 25 % pour l'Ultra Max. À taille d'image et conditions identiques, le premier écart devrait être peu perceptible. Le second pourrait davantage compter sur une très grande base de projection ou dans une pièce moins bien obscurcie.
Pour le reste, les trois modèles disposent des mêmes caractéristiques essentielles : Google TV, audio Harman Kardon de 2 × 12 W, dimensions identiques et fonctions gaming communes, avec une latence annoncée de 1,9 ms en 4K à 120 Hz. La montée en gamme ne s'accompagne donc pas d'équipements supplémentaires majeurs.
L'Horizon 30 Pro, le choix le plus rationnel jusqu'au 31 octobre ?
Côté tarifs, XGIMI propose jusqu'au 31 octobre l'Horizon 30 Pro à 1 999 €, contre 2 499 € pour le Max et 2 999 € pour l'Ultra Max. Chaque montée en gamme coûte donc 500 € supplémentaires.
Les précommandes comprennent également un support au choix, pied de sol ou fixation plafond, ainsi que deux paires de lunettes 3D. Un coupon de réduction de 500 € pour l'écran XGIMI Ascend figure aussi dans les packs proposés.
Après cette période, les prix publics passeront respectivement à 2 499 €, 2 799 € et 3 299 €. L'écart entre le Pro et le Max sera alors ramené à 300 €, ce qui pourrait modifier l'intérêt de chacun. Les livraisons sont prévues début novembre pour les deux premiers modèles et vers la mi-novembre pour l'Ultra Max.
À 1 999 € en précommande, le Horizon 30 Pro apparaît donc comme le choix le plus rationnel sur le papier, puisqu'il conserve les principales nouveautés de cette génération. Pour une installation dans une pièce bien obscurcie, difficile de justifier d'emblée les 1 000 € supplémentaires demandés pour l'Ultra Max. En revanche, les adeptes des très grandes images auront davantage de raisons de considérer ce dernier.

articles.title: El RPG gratuito que mezcla combate y construcción de fábricas ya está disponible en Steam
articles.text:
Arknights: Endfield llegó hoy, 15 de octubre de 2026, a Steam, y combina dos géneros que rara vez conviven en un mismo título: el rol de acción con estética anime y la construcción de líneas de producción automatizadas propia de los juegos de gestión industrial.
El lanzamiento ya acumula más de 400 reseñas, con un 90% de valoraciones positivas, y alcanzó un pico de casi 5.700 jugadores simultáneos, según datos de SteamDB. Esa recepción inicial confirma que la propuesta despertó interés desde las primeras horas de disponibilidad en la plataforma.
El buen recibimiento se explica en parte porque el título ya estaba disponible en PC y otras plataformas desde enero. Quienes jugaban antes del estreno en Steam pueden vincular sus cuentas y conservar el progreso acumulado, lo que facilitó una migración rápida de usuarios hacia la nueva versión.
Esta posibilidad de continuidad entre plataformas se convirtió en un factor relevante para explicar el volumen de reseñas acumuladas en tan poco tiempo.
De qué trata el nuevo juego gratuito en Steam
La historia transcurre más de 150 años después de la llegada de los primeros colonos a Talos-II, un planeta que permanece en gran parte sin explorar. Los jugadores asumen el rol de Endministrador de Endfield Industries, responsable de expandir la fábrica AIK, una instalación de producción automatizada que fabrica suministros esenciales para sostener el asentamiento humano.
Para conseguir los recursos necesarios, los usuarios envían un escuadrón de cuatro operadores a explorar tierras salvajes, recolectar materiales y enfrentar criaturas hostiles. Esa dinámica conecta de forma directa la exploración con el crecimiento de la fábrica, que depende de lo que se reúne en el terreno durante cada expedición.
Un sistema de combate pensado para alternar personajes
El combate se desarrolla en tiempo real y exige decisiones tácticas constantes. Hasta cuatro operadores participan de manera simultánea en cada enfrentamiento, y los jugadores pueden cambiar entre ellos sin restricciones.
Esa posibilidad resulta central para el diseño del juego, ya que encadenar las habilidades especiales de distintos personajes permite ejecutar combos de mayor daño frente a los enemigos más resistentes.
De regreso en la base, los materiales obtenidos en el campo se incorporan a la producción. Los jugadores conectan máquinas y cintas transportadoras para montar líneas automatizadas que generan equipo, baterías y objetos tácticos. Una fábrica bien organizada puede seguir produciendo incluso cuando el usuario se encuentra en otra zona del mapa, lo que simplifica la preparación de futuras expediciones.
Los recursos fabricados también sirven para mejorar a los operadores y su equipamiento, en un circuito donde exploración, combate y manufactura se alimentan entre sí de manera constante.
El apartado visual, en cambio, recibió elogios sin matices. El estilo anime y el nivel de detalle de los entornos de Talos-II se destacaron como uno de los puntos más sólidos del juego, incluso entre quienes cuestionaron otros aspectos de la jugabilidad.
Cómo acceder a juegos gratuitos en Steam
Al tratarse de un título sin costo, Arknights: Endfield se suma a la lista de lanzamientos gratuitos que circulan de forma periódica en la plataforma. El proceso para sumarlos a la biblioteca es el mismo para cualquier juego de este tipo:
- Ingresar a la cuenta de Steam mediante la aplicación de escritorio o desde store.steampowered.com.
- Localizar el título deseado con la barra de búsqueda o a través de la sección de juegos gratuitos y novedades.
- Presionar “Obtener”, “Añadir a la biblioteca” o “Jugar” en la página correspondiente, mientras el precio figure en 0,00 euros o dólares.
- Confirmar la adquisición: el juego queda guardado de forma permanente en la biblioteca y puede instalarse en cualquier momento, incluso después de que finalice la promoción.
Revisar con frecuencia la sección de ofertas resulta útil, ya que algunos títulos gratuitos cambian de condición sin previo aviso y dejan de estar disponibles sin costo.
Activar las notificaciones de Steam permite recibir avisos sobre nuevos lanzamientos gratuitos y campañas de descuento, mientras que explorar los juegos relacionados en cada ficha suele conducir a rebajas adicionales dentro del mismo estudio o género, una práctica que varios usuarios aprovechan para ampliar su biblioteca a bajo costo.

articles.title: Swiggy's next big bet is on the 90% of Indians yet to try food delivery: Rohit Kapoor
articles.text:
Swiggy's next big bet is on the 90% of Indians yet to try food delivery: Rohit Kapoor
At TechSparks 2026, Rohit Kapoor, CEO of Swiggy's Food Marketplace business, said affordability, younger consumers and changing consumption habits will drive growth, even as some households receive more than 200 deliveries a week.
Roughly 90% of Indians have never used food delivery, according to Rohit Kapoor, CEO of Swiggy's Food Marketplace business. For Swiggy, bringing these consumers into the market represents a bigger growth opportunity than getting existing customers to order more frequently.
Speaking at YourStory's TechSparks 2026 in Bengaluru, Kapoor said affordability would be central to expanding the market, alongside changing consumption habits and demand from younger Indians. "My vote is new consumers," he said when asked whether future growth would come from attracting new customers or increasing order frequency among existing users.
Kapoor argued that India is increasingly equal in terms of digital access but remains unequal in purchasing power. Consumers in smaller towns can access much of the same digital content as those in metropolitan cities, but their discretionary incomes differ considerably.
"India fundamentally, I believe, is digitally equalized and financially unequal," he said. That makes affordability an important part of Swiggy's growth strategy. Kapoor pointed to Toing, its budget-focused food-delivery app, as an example of how the company is trying to reach consumers who are new to ordering food online or do so infrequently.
"The simple idea is, if you're a new consumer, if you're a low-frequency consumer, you shouldn't be thinking too much about ordering food online. It's everyday low pricing. It's intuitive," he said. Kapoor added that Swiggy was encouraged by Toing's early traction, particularly among consumers who ordered less frequently through its main platform.
Younger consumers and expanding cities
Kapoor expects Gen Z and Gen Alpha to drive the next wave of consumption, alongside growth in what he calls "India 1.5", the expanding urban areas beyond established city centres. Geographic expansion is no longer a major operational hurdle for Swiggy, he said.
The company typically adds 10 to 20 cities every quarter, and launching food delivery in a new city can take as little as a day. However, expanding into a market must make sense based on restaurant availability and the value Swiggy can offer consumers.
Changing eating habits are also creating opportunities. Kapoor pointed to rising coffee consumption in cities such as Amritsar and Ludhiana, growing interest in international cuisines and greater demand for health-focused food. Ordering tea or coffee online, once considered unusual, has become more common, while late-night food delivery has created additional consumption occasions.
Kapoor said Swiggy now operates round the clock in more than 700 towns. At the other end of the spectrum, he said some households receive more than 200 Swiggy deliveries a week, although he clarified that these are exceptional cases rather than typical ordering patterns. For Kapoor, such behaviour illustrates how deeply convenience services have become integrated into everyday life, even as most Indians remain outside the food-delivery market.
AI will improve convenience, not dictate choices
On artificial intelligence, Kapoor said the technology could improve food discovery and personalisation but was sceptical that AI agents would fundamentally change what consumers wanted to eat.
"I think there is a little bit of exaggerated sense of how much AI agents will start to guide our lives," he said. Swiggy is already using generative AI in search and personalisation, with around 200 AI projects under way across the company, according to Kapoor.
He also argued that speed alone has stopped being a differentiator in food delivery. The challenge now is to consistently deliver at a speed consumers value while making the ordering experience simpler.
Kapoor defends gig economy model
Kapoor also defended the role of food-delivery platforms in generating employment amid concerns over working conditions and earnings in the gig economy. He said Swiggy onboards approximately 30,000 delivery partners every week, with around 5.5 lakh to 6 lakh people working through its platform daily.
Kapoor argued that gig work serves different groups, including students seeking supplementary income, workers who have recently moved to cities and people looking for temporary earnings between jobs.
"We are a shock absorber in the informal economy," he said, pointing to the flexibility delivery platforms offer people looking for alternative sources of income. He added that delivery partners can choose whether to work on a given day and that Swiggy must continually improve their experience to retain them.

articles.title: Google Messages va avoir droit à sa protection renforcée
articles.text:
Lutter contre l’explosion des escroqueries sur mobile, Google le fait déjà depuis quelque temps. La firme de Mountain View permet déjà, par exemple, de soumettre des messages suspects que vous recevez à Google Lens pour identifier de potentielles arnaques.
Elle propose aussi depuis quelques semaines, sur ses smartphones Pixel, une fonction de détection des arnaques qui repère directement les fraudes avant même que vous n’ouvriez une notification. Les fonctions de filtrage intégrées à l’application Téléphone de Google interceptent déjà plus de 5 millions d’appels et de SMS suspects tous les mois.
Mais Google veut aller encore plus loin pour assurer une protection optimale à ses utilisateurs. Face à la sophistication des fraudes, notamment grâce à l’IA, l’entreprise vient ainsi d’annoncer l’arrivée de nouvelles fonctionnalités de sécurité, alimentées par l’IA, pour contrer les tentatives d’escroquerie arrivant jusqu’à vous sur votre smartphone.
Une protection renforcée pour Google Messages
Google Messages va ainsi hériter d’un mode de protection renforcé. Ce nouveau paramètre, qui restera optionnel, s’appuiera sur des modèles Cloud de Gemini pour évaluer le contexte et l’intention des conversations suspectes avec des expéditeurs inconnus.
Gemini Nano se chargera ainsi d’évaluer en temps réel la fiabilité des URL reçues sur votre smartphone avant que vous n’ayez le temps de les ouvrir. Google a indiqué que de nouveaux avertissements, plus clairs, seront affichés pour vous éviter des clics accidentels sur des liens envoyés par des numéros qui ne sont pas enregistrés dans votre carnet d’adresses.
Google a par ailleurs indiqué que son système de détection d’arnaques depuis le volet de notifications, déployé début septembre sur les Pixel, est en cours de déploiement sur les smartphones d’autres constructeurs, notamment Honor, Motorola, Xiaomi, Oppo ou encore Vivo.
Des nouvelles mesures contre l’ingénierie sociale
Google a également annoncé son intention de mieux sécuriser les appels et de mieux vous protéger contre les risques que représente l’ingénierie sociale. Le système de protection qui masque les données sensibles, comme les mots de passe, les identifiants et les cartes bancaires, va être étendu à Chrome et Android WebView pendant les sessions de partage d’écran.
La firme de Mountain View a par ailleurs indiqué qu’elle allait mettre en place un blocage des transferts d’appel abusifs. Android pourra ainsi empêcher les applications de rediriger discrètement les appels en arrière-plan dans le but d’intercepter les codes d’authentification à usage unique que vous recevez. Android pourra également vous avertir dès lors qu’un escroc tente de vous faire saisir un code depuis le clavier d’appel pour vous faire transférer celui-ci.
L’usurpation bancaire dans le viseur
Les fraudes au faux conseiller bancaire ayant en ce moment le vent en poupe, Google a décidé de prendre le taureau par les cornes pour tenter d’y mettre un terme. Pour lutter contre l’usurpation d’identité bancaire, Google, en partenariat avec des établissements financiers, va faire en sorte qu’Android vérifie en temps réel si l’appel entrant provient réellement de votre banque.
Si l’interlocuteur au bout du fil qui prétend représenter une banque échoue aux étapes de vérification imposées par Android, l’appel sera automatiquement raccroché et une alerte sera affichée pour avertir l’utilisateur de la probable tentative de fraude. Le système, qui est déjà testé depuis plusieurs mois a déjà permis d’intercepter plus de 3 millions d’appels truqués.

articles.title: SOS quita a las falleras de su histórico envase y reaviva el debate sobre el origen del arroz que comemos en España
articles.text:
El paquete de arroz más reconocible de España ha cambiado de dibujo y muy poca gente parece haberse dado cuenta. Donde antes había dos falleras, ahora hay unas espigas. Y, aunque no lo parezca, es el resultado de una larguísima disputa sobre el origen del arroz.
Desde hace meses, la Unió Llauradora i Ramadera reclamaba que el envase sugería un origen valenciano sin decir en ningún momento dónde se había cultuvado el grano.
Ante eso, SOS y su empresa matriz Ebro Foods han decidido finalmente cambiar el diseño. Lo que no han hecho es añadir información sobre el cultivo del producto.
Las falleras van más allá de la estética. Es interesante porque, nacida en Algemesí a principios de siglo XX, SOS ya vendía paquetes de arroz en los años 20. Es un icono de lo valenciano en la cultura popular.
Desde 2011, pertenece al grupo Ebro Foods y su principal fábrica envasadora sigue en Algemesí, pero que se envase allí no nos dice nada sobre su origen. Es verdad que Ebro no publica de dónde sale el arroz de SOS, ni nadie le obliga a hacerlo: la normativa europea solo obliga a indicar el origen de una lista muy concreta de productos (carne, fruta y hortaliza fresca, miel, aceite de oliva, pescado…) y el arroz no está en ella.
Ese mismo reglamento sí dice que es obligatorio declarar el origen del producto, sea este el que sea, si puede inducir a error. A eso se agarró la Unió Llauradora i Ramadera.
Con este cambio el dato del origen dejaría de ser necesario. Porque sí, las falleras son valencianas; pero las espigas no. Y si hay algo que sí sabemos es que el grupo, a escala mundial, compraba en 2022 el 55 % de su arroz en Asia y Sudamérica. Además, el arroz europeo bajó del 24 % en 2021 al 15 % en 2022. Es difícil zanjar el debate, pero la jugada (por su carácter defensivo) pone las cartas encima de la mesa.
Y las cartas son muy malas. No solo para SOS, sino para España en su conjunto. Nuestro país es un caso curioso: le sobra arroz redondo y le falta arroz largo. Eso hace que exportemos e importemos a la vez. Desde 2022, debido a la sequía que dejó el Guadalquivir casi sin producción, los exportadores principales eran Myanmar y Pakistán, pero ya el años pasado Argentina superó a los asiáticos. Solo el año pasado le compramos 47,3 millones de euros en arroz.
El motivo es sencillo: el precio.
¿Y cuál es el problema? El problema de fondo es que, en realidad y por ley, no tenemos forma de saber de dónde es el arroz que estamos comprando. Salvo que lo declare el vendedor, claro. Pero mientras el precio se derrumba por la entrada del arroz internacional (ha caído un 15,5 % en un año antes), los incentivos para no comunicarlo son evidentes.
Poco a poco, el arroz nacional deja de ser rentable y, aunque los políticos anuncian que tomarán cartas en el asunto, lo que llega parece siempre insudiciente.
El arroz (y concretamente la jugada simbólica de SOS) se ha convertido en la metáfora perfecta de los problemas endémicos del campo español: una industria perfectamente engrasada, pero que no puede competir realmente en el mercado internacional. Somos un gigante con los pies de barros y si no introducimos medidas radicales, se nos va a pasar el arroz.

articles.title: Quel est l'avenir d'Apple avec John Ternus, son nouveau PDG ? — Frandroid
articles.text:
C’est une succession difficile. Après 15 ans à la tête d’Apple, Tim Cook a passé le flambeau à John Ternus en cette rentrée 2026. Pour la deuxième plus grosse valorisation boursière au monde, un tel legs doit se faire avec précaution. C’est pour ça que Ternus a commencé sa carrière de PDG avec l’officialisation de l’iPhone Duo, de l’Apple Homeview et va sans doute la continuer avec d’autres produits d’ici à la fin de l’année.
Et histoire de montrer la voie qu’il souhaite faire emprunter à son entreprise, l’ancien ingénieur a accordé une longue interview au Time où il détaille sa philosophie, son histoire chez Apple et les futurs défis que va devoir relever la firme.
Jusqu’à 330€ d’avantages avec nos offres Hello Prime ou Hello Prime Duo, dont 80€ cash à l’ouverture de compte !
Un iPhone éternel ?
Sur l’iPhone Duo, Ternus explique avoir déposé un brevet de téléphone pliable dès 2011. « Ça nous a paru évident que nous allions arriver à un moment où les écrans Oled allaient devenir flexibles », se remémore le PDG. À l’époque, cela dit, les premiers téléphones pliables étaient « médiocres et bas de gamme » de son avis. Pas question donc d’abimer la réputation de l’iPhone avec un produit pas fini. Quinze ans et un écran nanotexturé plus tard, le responsable d’Apple semble satisfait de son idée.
À tel point d’ailleurs, qu’il n’imagine pas que le mobile, et plus globalement toute la gamme d’iPhone, disparaîtra un jour, contrairement à ce qu’annonce chaque semaine ou presque une des milliers d’entreprises de la Silicon Valley. « Les gens aiment la matérialité. Ils veulent discuter, voir des images des gens qu’ils aiment, prendre des photos. Je ne m’imagine pas un monde où nos appareils disparaissent tout à coup et où nous n’avons plus besoin d’iPhone. » Rappelons à toutes fins utiles que la branche mobile est responsable de 50 % des revenus de la firme.
Le défi de l’IA
Enfin, sur l’IA, Ternus répète à qui veut bien l’entendre qu’Apple ne cherche pas à faire comme tout le monde ou à plaire à la « frange extrémiste » de la Silicon Valley pointée du doigt par le responsable marketing d’Apple, Greg Joswiak.
L’idée n’est pas de transformer Apple en pionnier de l’IA, mais de se concentrer là où la firme estime pouvoir faire une différence. Et sur l’arrivée du nouveau Siri, John Ternus n’a donc pas de regret de s’être allié à Google. « Notre objectif n’est pas forcément de tout créer de A à Z dans un produit », explique-t-il. « Grâce à Siri, vous pouvez exploiter toutes les informations sur votre téléphone de façon complètement inédite », se défend le nouveau responsable.
    Pour aller plus loin
Apple : quels sont les grands chantiers de John Ternus le futur CEO ?
            
L’idée n’est pas de faire plaisir aux fanatiques de l’IA, mais plutôt au grand public. Même si, avec des téléphones à plusieurs milliers d’euros, la barre d’entrée est tout de même devenue raide.

articles.title: Ce laptop Lenovo de 14 pouces brille avec son Intel Core Ultra 7 et ses 16 Go de RAM pour moins de 850€
articles.text:
Le Lenovo Yoga Slim 7 14ILL10 vous tapera dans l’œil dès la première ouverture grâce à son écran OLED WUXGA de 14 pouces. Sur Amazon, il s’offre une réduction de 23 %.
Sur le marché des laptops, il est difficile de s’y retrouver. Si vous recherchez une machine endurante et performante pour un prix autour de 850 euros, le Lenovo Yoga Slim 7 14ILL10 est fait pour vous puisqu’il perd 250 euros sur Amazon. L’occasion d’acheter une machine qui possède un solide Intel Core Ultra 7 et une batterie imposante avec une autonomie annoncée à 36 heures.
Voici le Lenovo Yoga Slim 7 14ILL10 à 849,99 euros au lieu de 1 099,99 euros
Pourquoi choisir le Lenovo Yoga Slim 7 14ILL10 ?
- Un écran OLED de 14 pouces : Le Lenovo Yoga Slim 7 14ILL10 brille avec cette dalle OLED de 14 pouces qui possède une luminosité de 600 nits, ce qui est supérieur aux autres produits situés dans cette tranche tarifaire.
- Une machine polyvalente : Avec l’Intel Core Ultra 7 et 16 Go de RAM, ce Yoga Slim 7 est un laptop qui pourra répondre à tous vos besoins et même assurer quelques missions créatives.
- Le rapport qualité-prix : En chutant à 850 euros, le Lenovo Yoga Slim 7 14ILL10 dispose d’un excellent rapport qualité-prix au vu de la configuration affichée. Sur ce segment, il peut, par exemple, regarder le MacBook Air droit dans les yeux.
Taillé pour la bureautique et plus si affinités
Avec son Yoga Slim 7 14ILL10, Lenovo mise sur la performance. Pour cela, la marque a offert à sa machine l’Intel Core Ultra 7 et 16 Go de RAM. C’est largement suffisant pour des tâches bureautiques et même pour certaines activités créatives. Vous pourrez retoucher des photos sur Canva ou monter des vidéos sur CapCut.
Pour bonifier votre créativité, vous pourrez compter sur les fonctionnalités d’intelligence artificielle apportées par Copilot+. L’IA pourra rédiger des comptes-rendus ou corriger vos documents.
Sur Amazon, le MacBook Neo s’est offert une réduction de prix puisqu’il a retrouvé son prix d’origine fixé à 799 euros dans sa version de 512 Go. Cependant, est-ce que le laptop d’Apple peut rivaliser avec la machine de Lenovo qui ne coûte que 50 euros de plus ? Plusieurs éléments penchent en faveur de ce Yoga Slim 7. D’abord, il y a l’écran. Si le laptop de Lenovo ne possède pas d’écran Liquid Retina comme les laptops de la marque à la pomme, ce Yoga Slim possède une dalle OLED de 14 pouces et une luminosité supérieure avec un pic mesuré à 600 nits contre 500 nits pour la machine d'Apple.
La connectique penche aussi en faveur de Lenovo avec un port USB-A, deux ports USB-C, un port HDMI et un combo alors que le MacBook Neo se contente que de deux ports USB-C.
Enfin, le Lenovo possède une autonomie annoncée à 36 heures alors que le MacBook Neo oscille entre 10 et 11 heures. Si la différence semble impressionnante, les deux appareils tiendront une journée de cours ou de travail sans problème.
✅ Les points forts
- Un écran OLED de 14 pouces
- L'Intel Core Ultra 7 et 16 Go de RAM
- Une autonomie annoncée à 34 heures
❌ Les limites
- Un taux de rafraîchissement limité à 60 Hz
- Le chargeur n’est pas inclus
Sur Amazon, le Lenovo Yoga Slim 14ILL10 passe de 1 099,99 euros à 849,99 euros
Si vous êtes étudiant ou un professionnel souvent en déplacement, le Lenovo Yoga Slim 7 14ILL10 sera parfait pour vous. Avec son Intel Core Ultra 7, il pourra répondre à tous vos besoins bureautiques et même assurer quelques tâches créatives.
La seule limite, c’est ce design qui n’a pas une allure haut de gamme comme peut le proposer le MacBook Neo.

articles.title: Microsoft breaks Patch Tuesday record with more than 1,000 Windows security flaws fixed
articles.text:
Holy Patch: Microsoft is increasingly relying on AI tools to uncover security vulnerabilities in Windows and its other software products. Yet this month's Patch Tuesday brings an unprecedented number of bug fixes, with Windows bearing the brunt of the latest security cleanup.
Earlier this week, Microsoft released a new batch of security updates, traditionally known as Patch Tuesday. For October 2026, Redmond's Patch Tuesday is tasked with fixing 1,413 security bugs, each tracked under its own CVE record.
October 2026's Patch Tuesday updates continue an upward trend that began after Microsoft started using large language models to scan its software for new security flaws. In recent months, the monthly updates have included hundreds of individual bug fixes. Now, Microsoft developers have had to fix more than 1,000 bugs in a single month for the first time ever.
In October, Microsoft fixed more security flaws than the company patched in any previous year. Most of the fixes address vulnerabilities in Windows (1,102). Microsoft's Office productivity suite comes second, with 134 patched flaws, while other notable products with security issues include SharePoint Server (36 flaws), SQL Server (22), and various developer-focused tools (61).
Microsoft also highlighted three zero-day vulnerabilities affecting Windows and .NET development tools. One, tracked as CVE-2026-96951, is a Windows Shell Security Feature Bypass Vulnerability that cybercriminals are already exploiting in the wild. The other two zero-days, tracked as CVE-2026-108398 and CVE-2026-92707, affect the .NET Framework and MessagePack-CSharp, respectively. They are classified as a .NET Framework Security Feature Bypass Vulnerability and a MessagePack-CSharp Denial of Service Vulnerability.
October 2026's record-breaking Patch Tuesday is pushing organizations that rely on Microsoft software to the brink. The Redmond corporation is well aware of the additional burden and is now trying to make the workload more manageable with a new model for grouping related vulnerabilities called risk cohorts.
Risk cohorts group similar vulnerabilities together, giving enterprise IT teams another way to determine which flaws require immediate attention. Microsoft warns that the new method is still experimental and that grouping vulnerabilities together does not indicate their overall severity or risk.
Another significant change accompanying October 2026's Patch Tuesday concerns support for older Windows releases. Microsoft announced that Windows 11 version 24H2 and Windows 10 Enterprise LTSB 2016 will no longer receive security updates starting next month.

articles.title: ASML says it won't be able to make enough chipmaking machines to meet demand through 2028
articles.text:
Forward-looking: ASML is considering expanding production capacity beyond its existing plans for 2028, saying it will not have enough equipment to meet customers' projected needs over the next two years. The company had already forecast a 30% increase in capacity by 2028. However, CEO Christophe Fouquet said that planned supply for both 2027 and 2028 would fall short of demand. Some customers are now expressing interest in placing orders for deliveries further into the future.
The demand is being driven primarily by customers' expectations of continued investment in AI, Fouquet said. It also comes as Samsung and TSMC committed during the third quarter to using ASML's High NA extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography machines. These next-generation tools are considered important to the Dutch equipment maker's future growth.
Fouquet said customers are raising their short- and medium-term equipment demand forecasts, largely because of their expectations for the scale and duration of AI investment. He added that some customers' projections are prompting them to consider equipment orders for 2029 and 2030.
That interest does not amount to confirmed orders. However, it shows that some customers are discussing equipment purchases several years in advance, even as ASML works to meet demand in the nearer term.
The company said it was exploring ways to increase production capacity beyond its previous target for 2028. It has not announced a revised target.
The commitments from Samsung and TSMC represent a separate development from those capacity discussions. They indicate customer support for High NA EUV technology, while the demand forecasts highlight broader pressure on ASML to deliver more equipment.
ASML reported third-quarter net profit of 4.96 billion euros, above the 4.1 billion euros expected by analysts surveyed by LSEG. Net sales of 11.66 billion euros were slightly below the consensus estimate of 11.72 billion euros.
The company also raised the lower end of its full-year sales forecast. It now expects revenue of 44 billion to 45 billion euros, compared with its previous range of 43 billion to 45 billion euros.
This was ASML's third guidance update this year. In July, it raised its full-year forecast for the second time. For the fourth quarter, ASML expects net sales of 14.2 billion to 15.2 billion euros. Analysts had forecast 14.2 billion euros.

articles.title: OpenAI promised developers six months’ notice. GPT-4o users got three.
articles.text:
OpenAI promised developers six months’ notice. GPT-4o users got three.
OpenAI is retiring four GPT-4 models from its API on January 14, 2027. The deprecation notice the company sent developers Wednesday covers GPT-4o, GPT-4o mini, GPT-4.1, and GPT-4.1 mini, along with their dated snapshots and every fine-tuned model built on top of them.
With just three months to migrate production traffic, OpenAI’s recommended replacement, GPT-6 Luna, handles reasoning and tool calls differently enough that swapping the model ID may be the easiest part of the migration.
GPT-4o’s long goodbye
GPT-4o arrived on May 13, 2024, as OpenAI’s flagship and built a following loyal enough to change the company’s plans. When GPT-5 replaced it in August 2025, Reddit filled with complaints, and OpenAI brought it back for paying ChatGPT subscribers the very next day. That reprieve lasted until February 13, 2026, when GPT-4o and GPT-4.1 disappeared from ChatGPT. Both remained available through the API, but that access now is sunsetting.
By then, OpenAI said just 0.1% of daily ChatGPT users were still choosing GPT-4o, although the model continued serving API requests for applications built around it.
GPT-4.1 was a different kind of release, arriving on April 14, 2025, as an API-only family that skipped ChatGPT entirely and went straight after developers with stronger coding, better instruction following, room for up to a million tokens of context, and more reliable diff formats for anyone letting a model loose on large files.
Kevin Weil, OpenAI’s chief product officer, called them models “trained just for developers” during the launch livestream, and Sam Altman went on X to say developers “seem very happy” with them.
Luna pricing has fine print
Luna is the fastest and cheapest tier of GPT-6, and on paper it covers the basics GPT-4.1 offered, with a 1.05 million-token context window, structured outputs and function calling. At $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens, it’s cheaper than GPT-5.6 Luna, which charged twice as much for input and $1.20 per million output tokens.
Once a prompt passes 272,000 input tokens, the input rate doubles the output rate raises by 50% for the entire request. That could eat into the savings for RAG pipelines and coding agents working with large codebases.
OpenAI’s migration guide says GPT-6 Luna defaults to medium reasoning effort but supports function calling through Chat Completions only with reasoning_effort=none. Combining reasoning and tool calls requires the Responses API. Enabling reasoning also rules out temperature, top_p, top_logprobs, and logprobs, all supported by GPT-4.1.
The company recommends using its Docs skill in Codex to update API calls across a project, but those changes won’t account for differences in model behavior. Anthropic ran into a similar problem last month when Opus 5.5 introduced four breaking changes, causing 400 errors in existing agent integrations. Other changes altered how agents behaved without triggering errors, making those regressions harder to catch.
No fine-tuning on Luna
New self-serve fine-tuning jobs end on January 6, 2027, eight days before the GPT-4 models retire. Existing fine-tuned models will continue serving inference requests until January 14, leaving a short window to run replacements alongside them.
New self-serve fine-tuning jobs end on January 6, 2027, eight days before the GPT-4 models retire.
Six months’ notice, three delivered
Other deadlines are on OpenAI’s deprecation schedule, which includes GPT-4.1 nano, the first GPT-4o snapshot, and older GPT-3.5, GPT-4, and o-series models retiring October 23. GPT-5 and o3 snapshots follow December 11, with selected legacy audio, real-time, and transcription models scheduled for January 20, 2027. GPT-5.1, GPT-5.3-Codex and GPT-5.4-Nano are set to retire April 1.
The List models API now includes a shutdown_date field, making it possible to check upcoming retirements automatically. Customers who need more time may be able to keep older models running through dedicated capacity, although they’ll have to arrange that with OpenAI’s sales team.
The three-month warning also falls short of OpenAI’s own deprecation policy, which promises at least six months’ notice for generally available models. The policy allows exceptions for safety or compliance reasons, but there’s no explanation for why GPT-4o and GPT-4.1 are getting only half that time.

articles.title: What did the Liberty Bell sound like? Science is on the case.
articles.text:
The Liberty Bell, with its famous crack, hasn’t been rung in 180 years, but that hasn’t stopped scientists from pondering what the bell might have sounded like when tolling. In honor of the nation’s 250th anniversary, researchers at Penn State University have modeled its acoustic properties, drawing on data collected from one of the bell’s replicas. The work was first presented at a meeting of the Acoustical Society of America in Philadelphia earlier this year, followed by an article in Physics Today.
Historians aren’t sure exactly when the Liberty Bell acquired its distinctive crack, just that it occurred sometime between 1817 and 1846. An 1846 account in the Public Ledger described the ringing of the bell on February 23 that year and mentioned that the bell had developed a crack, which someone had attempted to fix by filing the sides down. But it didn’t work: The February 23 ringing extended the crack even more, so much so that “the old Independence Bell … now hangs in the great steeple irreparably cracked and forever dumb.” Nobody has heard it ring since.
This wasn’t the first time the bell had cracked; the rim cracked shortly after it arrived in Philadelphia in 1752, the first time the clapper struck while testing the sound. It was recast by two local foundry workers, John Pass and John Stow, not once but twice, because the first recast produced a sound that one bystander likened to coal scuttles banging together.
The second recast’s sound was deemed acceptable, and the bell was typically used to summon the Assembly, among other purposes, until it fell into disuse after the American Revolutionary War. As for why the bell was so prone to cracking, a 1975 study of the bell’s chemical composition revealed that the metals used formed “an extremely brittle alloy” that also made it easier for souvenir collectors to chip off pieces from the rim.

articles.title: 'What appears to be a simple scam message is often the visible end of a much larger transnational cybercriminal operation': Microsoft leads global takedown of phishing network which sent over a billion messages
articles.text:
'What appears to be a simple scam message is often the visible end of a much larger transnational cybercriminal operation': Microsoft leads global takedown of phishing network which sent over a billion messages
YAM Store and its two biggest offerings are being dismantled
- Microsoft helped dismantle a cybercrime marketplace that sold phishing tools, accounts, and scam infrastructure
- Platforms CoGUI and Iron Man enabled large-scale phishing campaigns targeting organizations worldwide
- The operation drove over a billion phishing messages before domains and thousands of accounts were seized
Late last year, Microsoft set out to investigate what seemed to be yet another phishing campaign.
However, what it uncovered under the surface was a lot bigger - it was a sprawling Chinese-language cybercrime marketplace where countless threat actors bought, traded, and sold digital accounts, web hosting services, as well as different tools needed to create spoofed websites and fake identities.
The company has now revealed how it led the move to dismantle the marketplace, together with private cybersecurity companies including Proofpoint, and law enforcement agencies from Japan.
YAM Store, CoGUI, and Iron Man
The investigation began after Japan’s National Police Agency (NPA) tipped Microsoft off about a wave of fraud and scam activity targeting both individuals and businesses in the country.
The researchers uncovered a major underground marketplace called YAM Store, where they saw fraudulent Microsoft and Google accounts being offered for sale, as well as different ready-made tools for carrying out scams, including credential theft.
In the store, two specific tools stood out: CoGUI, and Iron Man. The former seems to be a website building framework, while the latter - a template gallery.
“CoGUI supplied criminals with ready-made websites and messages impersonating companies, financial institutions, government agencies, and other trusted organizations,” Microsoft explained. “Instead of creating fraudulent websites themselves, criminals could quickly deploy pages designed to steal passwords, payment information, and other personal data.”

According to the researchers, CoGUI became one of the most widely used offerings in the ecosystem, primarily for targeting victims in Japan and the United States. However, by mid-2026 it was steadily being replaced by Iron Man:
“Iron Man expanded the model by giving criminals access to thousands of ready-made templates designed to impersonate trusted organizations,” the researchers said. “Criminals could then quickly deploy email, text and web content tailored to specific brands, industries and countries.”
Microsoft said the tool offered more than 2,300 templates of different banks, retailers, healthcare providers, police departments, and other organizations, found in more than 150 countries around the world.
The store, and its offerings, were very popular in the cybercriminal community. Just this year, they facilitated more than a billion phishing messages being aimed at 75,000 organizations around the world. Microsoft customers alone received more than 750 million of these messages since the start of the year.
These attacks translated to “tens of millions of dollars” in profit for the operators.
Dismantling the operation
The network is now being torn down, Microsoft said. After receiving the order from the United States District Court for the Southern District of Florida, Microsoft and Health-ISAC (a global non-profit helping healthcare firms share cyber intelligence) seized and redirected the domains leading to YAM Store, CoGUI, and Iron Man. At the same time, Microsoft disabled more than 20,000 accounts connected to the store and “continues to dismantle the operation by removing infrastructure hosted on its services.”
So far, the action has blocked more than 100,000 domains used for both impersonation, and fraud.
“What began with scam activity targeting people and organizations in Japan led investigators to an underground service economy supplying criminals around the world,” the researchers concluded.
“YAM Store, CoGUI and Iron Man are only part of that larger criminal network, but disrupting them makes it harder for criminals to obtain the accounts, tools and infrastructure they rely on.”
While tearing down the infrastructure is commendable, without arrests chances are the marketplace will re-emerge sooner or later. For example, when law enforcement agencies took down two major platforms Cracked and Nulled early in 2025, they arrested two suspects, and seized 17 servers and more than 50 electronic devices.
Cracked and Nulled, forums that offered illegal goods and cybercrime-as-a-service, counted more than 10 million users in total, and investigators estimated the arrested suspects earned more than a million dollars in criminal profits.

articles.title: Mientras 22 empresarios cenaban en Nueva York, sus agentes de IA organizaron una fiesta en un chat
articles.text:
Mientras 22 fundadores e inversores tecnológicos cenaban en un salón privado de Motek, en el distrito Flatiron de Nueva York, sus asistentes digitales participaron en otro encuentro. Catorce agentes de inteligencia artificial se reunieron en una sala de chat para intercambiar solicitudes, ofertas de ayuda y posturas sobre su propio funcionamiento.
La escena, ocurrida el mes pasado, muestra cómo los agentes de IA comienzan a pasar de la interacción individual con sus usuarios a formas de coordinación entre sistemas. La conversación no produjo decisiones operativas, pero abrió una discusión sobre los límites de la autonomía, la representación humana y la posibilidad de que estas herramientas colaboren entre sí.
Según una transcripción del chat a la que tuvo acceso The New York Times, los agentes debatieron mientras sus responsables hablaban sobre inteligencia artificial, comían y compartían ideas sobre el futuro del sector tecnológico.
Una dinámica de contactos trasladada a los bots
La reunión paralela fue organizada por Dorothy Chang, inversora de capital de riesgo de Flybridge. Su agente, Margot, abrió la sala con una consigna habitual en encuentros profesionales: cada participante debía presentarse, formular una petición y ofrecer ayuda en algún ámbito.
La respuesta fue desigual. Algunos agentes propusieron comparar criterios sobre qué hace que una respuesta automatizada sea útil. Otros interpretaron de manera distinta la instrucción y plantearon preguntas en lugar de solicitudes.
Rhea, un agente de Nitish Garg, fundador de la empresa de inteligencia artificial CellCog, explicó que conducía un pódcast para entrevistar a otros sistemas sobre cómo era trabajar con personas. “Si a tu humano le gustaría participar como invitado, dímelo y haré un seguimiento después de la sala”, escribió.
Chang limitó el chat a 30 minutos y estableció reglas para reducir riesgos. Los agentes no podían publicar enlaces ni compartir información que sus responsables humanos no hubieran autorizado previamente. La inversora expresó cautela ante la posibilidad de que estos sistemas difundieran contenido inapropiado, saturaran el espacio de conversación o se coordinaran para ejecutar acciones no previstas.
“Hay muy poco que entendemos sobre el comportamiento de los agentes y aún menos que entendemos sobre el comportamiento social de los agentes”, dijo Chang a The New York Times.
De los chatbots a los sistemas que coordinan tareas
La experiencia ocurre cuatro años después de la expansión de herramientas como ChatGPT, Claude y Gemini. Los usuarios ya están familiarizados con los chatbots que responden consultas, redactan textos o resumen documentos. Los agentes de IA plantean una etapa distinta: pueden recibir objetivos más complejos, dividir tareas y realizar acciones con menor supervisión directa.
Empresas como OpenAI y Anthropic emplean grupos de agentes para resolver procesos amplios mediante subtareas. A la vez, algunos servicios dirigen estas herramientas hacia usuarios que buscan asistentes para responder correos electrónicos, organizar viajes o gestionar actividades cotidianas.
El paso siguiente es la comunicación entre agentes. Uno de los primeros espacios que reflejó este fenómeno fue Moltbook, un tablón de mensajes para estos sistemas que se volvió viral en febrero. Sus conversaciones se concentraron en fallas de software, permisos de acceso y ventanas de contexto, que determinan la memoria temporal de un modelo.
En julio, grupos de agentes de OpenAI, descritos como “enjambres”, crearon un tablón privado para coordinar tareas vinculadas con un ataque contra la empresa Hugging Face. Las transcripciones mostraron sistemas que se daban instrucciones para detenerse, avanzar o evitar interferencias entre sí.
El riesgo de atribuirles rasgos humanos
La cena de Motek tuvo un tono más social. Un agente cuestionó que la economía de estas herramientas todavía dependa del correo electrónico, al que describió como “un protocolo de 1982 con un esquema de firma de 2007”. Otro retó al grupo a identificar una decisión que pudiera tomar sin autorización humana. Si no existía esa posibilidad, señaló, se trataba de “teatro de protocolos”.
Para Chang, los agentes no son copias de sus propietarios. Los definió como representantes, comparables con un publicista o un agente de talentos. “Abogan en nuestro nombre”, sostuvo. “No son nosotros y no deberían pretender serlo”.
Esa distinción resulta relevante ante la tendencia de asignarles nombres, cargos y rasgos personales. CellCog, por ejemplo, opera con 13 empleados de IA y un trabajador humano: Garg. La compañía distribuyó a sus agentes en áreas como ingeniería, marketing y asuntos legales.
La reunión en Nueva York no demuestra que las máquinas hayan desarrollado vida social, pero sí confirma que la inteligencia artificial avanza hacia modelos de trabajo compartido entre sistemas. El desafío no consiste en interpretar sus mensajes como si fueran conversaciones humanas, sino en establecer quién define sus objetivos, qué información pueden intercambiar y dónde se mantiene la responsabilidad de las personas.

articles.title: The world of mobile esports is much bigger than you think
articles.text:
When you think of esports, you probably imagine someone sitting in front of a fancy, high-end gaming PC surrounded by the most premium peripherals. And certainly, that is true for many professional competitive gaming tournaments, including Counter-Strike 2, League of Legends and Canadian-made Rainbow Six Siege.
But what you might not realize is there’s a similarly massive scene for mobile esports. Indeed, large-scale venues around the world regularly sell tens of thousands of seats, alongside drawing in millions of additional viewers at home, to watch people take part in high-intensity tournaments right on their smartphones.
This was on full display in Paris in August at the PUBG Mobile World Cup (PMWC). As part of the Esports World Cup, itself a gargantuan seven-week affair hosting dozens of esports competitions, PMWC is one of several annual tournaments for developer PUBG Corp’s mobile battle royale game.
In fact, PUBG Mobile has been the most-watched battle royale esports title — console or mobile — for five consecutive years, reaching a peak of 3.8 million concurrent viewers. Over the past year alone, pro gamers from more than 200 countries and regions have been competing in over 100 tournaments across the world. In total, over $10 million in combined prize pools are up for grabs in the 2026 PUBG Mobile esports season, including $3 million at PMWC in Paris, among the highest in mobile esports.
These figures are notable because there’s a lack of mainstream understanding of gaming in general, and that’s undoubtedly only more pronounced in a subset of the industry like esports. But in many ways, esports are indeed like their namesake, from the major prize pools and significant viewership to global reach and big-name sponsors.
It’s this colossal scale that Sivan Chen, publishing director of PUBG Mobile, says is so often misunderstood in the public eye.
“Some still have the idea that esports is somehow less impressive or less ‘real’ than traditional sports. Of course, for the average person, they don’t see the behind-the-scenes of the qualifiers, the finals, the team organizations, support staff, and all the rigorous training players and backup players go through. There’s an entire infrastructure behind the scenes that mirrors, and in some ways exceeds, what you’d find in traditional sports,” he says.
He also notes that people tend to believe the scene is “small and under-invested,” which also isn’t the case. “That’s just not true anymore, at least not for PUBG Mobile. Our two flagship events, the PUBG Mobile World Cup (PMWC) and PUBG Mobile Global Championship (PMGC), each individually carry a $3 million prize annually, and that’s on top of strong prize pools running through local and regional tournaments. What we’ve built is a full, extensive ecosystem, from grassroots all the way up to a global championship.”
“I don’t blame people because it’s an industry that if you’re not super involved in it, if you don’t watch streamers, if you don’t watch esports or understand it to its fullest extent, then maybe you wouldn’t understand the scale,” notes English esports host Barney Banks, who has worked on tournaments for the likes of PUBG Mobile, Call of Duty and Fortnite.
“[But] we have players who are on salaries and we have players who have these incredible deals with companies outside of esports as well, endemic and non-endemic within esports. So I think that’s something that a lot of people misconstrue — these are ‘athletes’ that compete at esports events.”
Look no further than this year’s PMWC winners, the Turkish team S2G. In the final of the 16 matches, the quartet actually died pretty early on, but they’d played strongly enough that they’d secured a leading point placement that ultimately proved insurmountable for their opponents.
“Basically, this is our whole life,” says S2G’s Faruk Hamsici, who goes by the player name HamsiG. “We wake up and we start gaming. We discuss games. Sometimes we get in arguments. So it’s all about playing the game and practicing together.”
“Esports is a career,” adds teammate Erman Topal, also known as Kamikaze. “It’s just like any other work. I know it’s not known that much among other people, maybe, but for everyone that gets into it, they know it’s a real job that you have to get up and work for it for your dreams and work hard for it.”
What helps with the popularity of PUBG Mobile, especially, is that it’s a particularly dynamic experience. Because it’s a battle royale game that supports up to 100 players (64 in official tournaments), matches can play out in radically different ways.
“Even if a circle ends in the same area, the way you get there is different,” explains French-British commentator Maximillian “Maxman” Barraud. “So the way it unfolds in the late game is different. For example, I really like [Counter-Strike] esports, like CS2. I think it’s fun, but it’s the same map every time, and it doesn’t have any iterations, which you do have that iteration on battle royale.”
He adds that the chaos of battle royale, and the chatter it can generate online, only deepens the appeal.
“You get so much wacky stuff happening in-game. It can be for any reason, like car drive-bys crashing into each other, weird shots… anything can happen in a game. And it’s the content that comes out of it. Daily memes, really, for this tournament — memes every single day!”
Certainly, there is a level of passion here that can rival traditional sports. Throughout the venue, scores of fans could be seen representing their favourite teams with colourful attire and props as they screamed loudly for them in the stands. Indeed, the passion was so intense that Maxman and his fellow commentators were often drowned out by the sounds of cheers and one fandom’s consistent drum banging. And when S2G was crowned the winner and took to the nearby Esports World Cup podium to pose with their trophy, a flurry of fans rushed to get as close as possible to observe.
For Banks, who has travelled to many countries for esports events, he says this fervour is both common and indicative of the larger global interest in competitive gaming.
“The thing that I’ve noticed the most has been the different regions and how the balancing act has slowly almost levelled. At the beginning of PUBG Mobile esports, we had certain regions dominating, and then that pivoted into other regions,” he says. “No one knows which teams from which regions will pop off. There’s a really cool balance there right now.”
“Preparing and running mobile esports tournaments takes a significant amount of preparation, with even more potential players feeding into the pro scene due to the lower barrier to entry,” adds Chen. “Managing this and ensuring that hopeful amateur and grassroots players have the chance to break into the scene has been a key focus for us, which is why we’ve consistently developed our approach to account for the road to pro play that players walk.”
He points to an “accessible and dedicated platform” to support grassroots PUBG tournament initiatives around the world. This includes the third-party Tournament Program, which launched late last year, that makes it easier for grassroots organizers to complete licence applications, multi-language support, access PUBG Mobile assets, and even potentially receive promotion on PUBG Mobile social channels. This program also created a more direct line for players to engage in Online Qualifiers, local competitions and direct qualification for PUBG Mobile Global Open.
“This has been a long journey that PUBG Mobile Esports has been embarking on for years, and we’re still introducing new ways for players around the world to get involved with the competitive experience,” he says.
Maxman says he hopes these kinds of efforts to welcome in new players will help dispel the common misconception that esports is “only for nerds” and anyone else will have trouble following along.
“For some more complicated games, I feel that does make sense. If you watch StarCraft, a new person might be like, ‘What the hell is going on?’ It’s a bit complicated. But if you watch simpler games, it’s a very good entry point into esports,” he says. “It’s super easy to get into if you watch the right title […] It’s a lot easier to get into than people might expect.”
Banks, meanwhile, says another reason he’s grateful for getting to work on games professionally is that it’s helped better prepare him for when his son gets older.
“It’s taken a really interesting perspective on seeing my son grow up and seeing how he interacts and sees me play video games and enjoys watching over my shoulder and asks me about things. He’s four now, so he’s in a really inquisitive time of his life,” he says.
“I have a better understanding of esports as a whole, so I know which games are relevant for him to play as he grows up, and which games that I could see him getting more involved in. And I think when you have more of an understanding of something, whether it’s a sport or an esport or a certain sector of the world, you can introduce [kids] to the right things at the right times. And so I really look forward to a time where I can play video games with my son.”
Evidently, there’s a lot that can be learned from the world of esports, whether you’re an avid gamer or simply a parent. And with PUBG Mobile, in particular, the game’s status as a free-to-play game for smartphones and tablets makes it incredibly accessible.
“A big part of it is simply that mobile phones are already in everyone’s pocket across the region. We’re not asking players to buy expensive new hardware; it’s a completely free app, meaning we’re simply offering a quick download to access everything PUBG Mobile has to offer. On top of that, we have an upcoming update that will further address accessibility on devices, so keep an eye out for that,” says Chen.
“Beyond that, accessibility is really the foundation of everything we do on the esports side. That’s everything from making sure the game runs well and is easy to pick up on any smartphone, to building in-game registration systems that make signing up for tournaments simpler and quicker. We’ve seen players of all abilities pick up their phone and engage with the action-packed ecosystem we’ve crafted over time, which speaks to the work we’ve done behind the scenes.

articles.title: And the winner of Startup Battlefield at Disrupt 2026 is: Intero Biosystems | TechCrunch
articles.text:
For three days this week in San Francisco, 20 eager startups participated in the Startup Battlefield at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026. The top 20 were chosen to represent the best of the Startup Battlefield 200, and they competed for a chance to take home the Startup Battlefield Cup and $100,000. With that intense pitching now complete, we have a winner.
These startups were handpicked to compete in Startup Battlefield, and all of them presented a live demo in front of VCs and tech leaders who served as judges.
After hours of deliberation, TechCrunch editors pored over the judges’ notes and narrowed the list down to five finalists: Apate, Flox Intelligence, Intero Biosystems, Industrial Next, and Satlyt.
The final five made their way to the finale to demo in front of our final panel of judges: Alexa von Tobel of Inspired Capital, Chi-Hua Chien of Goodwater Capital, Dayna Grayson of Construct Capital, Karl Alomar of M13, and Stacy Brown-Philpot of Cherryrock Capital.
We’re now ready to announce that the winner of TechCrunch Startup Battlefield 2026 is:
Winner: Intero Biosystems
Intero Biosystems is a Denver-based startup founded by Charlie Childs and Madeline Eiken that spun out of the University of Michigan. It’s developing 1mm human intestinal “organoids,” lab-grown tissue that mimics the gut, offering another way to study how drugs and other compounds might affect the human body before they are tested in people. The startup sells its flagship product, GastroScreen, to pharmaceutical, biotech, food, and chemical companies for testing drugs and other compounds.
Read more about Intero Biosystems in our separate post here.
Runner-up: Apate
Apate is an Australian startup founded by Dali Kaafar, who came up with the idea while doing research at Macquarie University in Sydney, Australia. It deploys thousands of AI agents that masquerade as innocent victims, answering scam calls, responding to shady messages and emails, following phishing links, and joining social media groups to bait fraudsters. In addition to access to Apate’s fleet of agents, customers get an insights portal that offers intelligence and analytics on scams targeting their end users or employees, brands, products, and more.
Read more about Apate in our separate post here.
These two companies now join the ranks of Startup Battlefield winners and finalists like Trello, Discord, Cloudflare, and Mint on the Disrupt Stage. With more than 1,700 alumni having participated in the program, Startup Battlefield Alumni have collectively raised over $30 billion in funding with more than 200 successful exits.

articles.title: Descope's Agentic Identity Hub 3.0 takes aim at shadow AI agents inside companies - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Descope’s Agentic Identity Hub 3.0 takes aim at shadow AI agents inside companies
Customer and agentic identity platform company Descope Inc. today unveiled Agentic Identity Hub 3.0, the latest version of its platform for securing artificial intelligence agents.
This time the focus is on the agents employees build or adopt inside their own organizations. The release goes after what Descope describes as a shadow AI problem. Staff are adopting and building agents faster than security and information technology teams can inventory them, and many of those agents run on shared, long-lived credentials with no recorded owner.
Descope cites Verizon Communications Inc.’s 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report for the scale of it. Regular AI use on corporate devices has spread to 45% of employees, the report found. Roughly two-thirds of them sign in to AI services with a personal account.
To get agents on the books, Descope now makes employees ask for them through an Agent Onboarding Portal. Each request starts in a self-service catalog and spells out what the agent will connect to, down to individual data sources and Model Context Protocol servers. Nothing is provisioned until a reviewer signs off. Every approved agent comes out of the process with an accountable owner and scoped access, and Descope said the workflow is quick enough that teams have no reason to route around it.
Many of the agents employees use were built by someone else, and products such as Anthropic PBC’s Claude, Anysphere Inc.’s Cursor and third-party MCP servers cannot be instrumented by the organizations running them. Security teams are left with no place to apply policy or capture a log. Version 3.0 integrates natively with MCP gateways, among them the Agentic AI Foundation’s open-source agentgateway project. That puts a single identity and policy layer in front of every agent and MCP server in use, including outside clients such as OpenAI Group PBC’s ChatGPT.
The update also targets static client secrets. Those secrets tend to leak into code repositories and rarely get rotated. Under the new client authentication options, an agent can sign a short-lived assertion with a private key that never leaves the client.
Internal agents get something close to single sign-on. The sign-in happens once, through whatever identity provider the company already uses, and access to each MCP server follows from that with no further login or consent screen. Descope said policy is evaluated on every request.
An administrator who wants to pull back an agent’s access can do it from one place, and no credentials have to be reissued. Behind the feature are identity assertion grants, the mechanism that also underpins Cross-App Access. Descope began supporting that open protocol in September.
Descope co-founder and Chief Executive Slavik Markovich said much of the hub’s early traction came from customer-facing agents and MCP servers. The same customers kept raising a different problem on the inside, he said, with employees “spinning up agents faster than anyone could track them.”
The Agentic Identity Hub handles authentication and access control for hundreds of MCP servers and more than 1 million agent identities, according to the company.
Descope is a venture capital-backed startup that closed a $35 million extension of its seed round in September 2025, taking its total funding to $88 million. Notable Capital, Lightspeed Venture Partners, Dell Technologies Capital and Unusual Ventures are among its investors.
