articles.title: Malicious Russian disinformation bot traffic barely flinches after Ukraine strikes Yandex data centers and auto-migration kicks in — Cloudflare tracks 170 million automated attacks shifting to alternate cloud hosts
articles.text:
Malicious Russian disinformation bot traffic barely flinches after Ukraine strikes Yandex data centers and auto-migration kicks in — Cloudflare tracks 170 million automated attacks shifting to alternate cloud hosts
Taking out malicious bots is a game of whack-a-mole.
Russian bot traffic showed signs of slowing down after Ukraine bombed some of Yandex’s biggest data centers. Unfortunately, while the attacks have slowed down overall bot traffic from Russia, Cloudflare reports that malicious bots appeared to have simply transferred to other hosting ASNs like Radist and Selectel. Overall traffic on Yandex Search and Yandex.Cloud continues to stay at 10% to 15% of normal traffic levels, meaning the network remains disrupted. Cloudflare noted that traffic from the former is composed mostly of verified search crawlers indexing websites, meaning traffic from this service is mostly legitimate. On the other hand, the latter experienced a drop in malicious activities such as vulnerability scanning and probing after the data center bombings, but Cloudflare says that “high-volume automation did not vanish — it simply migrated to other hosting providers.”
This was evident with one Cloudflare customer in the gambling sector: it saw malicious bot requests from Yandex.Cloud drop to zero but started seeing the same activity being routed through other networks. “Overall, Russian bot traffic targeting gambling accounts remained essentially flat over the week, moving from 167.7 million to 170.1 million requests (+1.4%),” the company wrote in its analysis. “The automation never stopped running; the operators simply migrated their workloads to alternate cloud providers once Yandex.Cloud became unavailable.”
The company also looked at social media traffic and found a similar result — traffic from Russian-origin IPs only dropped by 0.6% in the same period while Russian bot traffic hitting “post,” “reply,” and “like” on one platform only decreased by 5.7%. Because of this, Cloudflare debunked the theory that Ukrainian strikes have caused a drop in social media manipulation, although it also noted that the scope of its analysis is limited to traffic that passed through Cloudflare services.
Since cloud-based workloads can easily be transferred between data centers, taking a few out will not necessarily end the services running out of them. Instead, owners and operators could simply migrate to another data center, which is exactly what Amazon advised its clients who have been affected by Iranian strikes on AWS Bahrain and AWS Abu Dhabi.
Cloudflare pointed out that this is why it’s difficult to defend against automated threats like bot networks — even though an IP prefix gets blocked or the physical infrastructure behind them gets annihilated, their operators could simply move their operations to another provider in a matter of hours and quickly return to normal traffic levels.

articles.title: Verbraucherzentrale gewinnt gegen Starlink
articles.text:
Verbraucherzentrale erfolgreich gegen Starlink: Wie Nutzer ihr Geld zurückfordern können
Im Mai 2026 hatte Starlink in Deutschland den Abopreis für den Tarif Privathaushalt (200 Megabit pro Sekunde) während der Laufzeit von 49 auf 55 Euro im Monat erhöht. Zudem soll auch die angebotene maximale Geschwindigkeit geschrumpft sein.
Starlink: Rechtswidrige Preiserhöhung
Die Abonnent:innen hatte der Satelliteninternet-Anbieter zwar per E-Mail über den Schritt informiert. Eine aktive Zustimmung holte Starlink aber nicht ein. Zudem beschwerten sich einige Kund:innen, dass sie ohne ausdrückliche Zustimmung in den deutlich teureren Tarif Privathaushalt Max umgestellt worden seien.
Dies rief die Verbraucherzentrale Niedersachsen auf den Plan, die unter anderem eine aus ihrer Sicht intransparente Vertragsklausel beanstandete. Eine entsprechende Abmahnung Starlinks durch die Verbraucherschützer:innen hatte jetzt Erfolg, wie es in einer entsprechenden Mitteilung heißt.
Erfolg für Verbraucherzentrale
„Wir begrüßen, dass Starlink in den beanstandeten Punkten Einsicht gezeigt hat“, erklärte Jana von Bibra, Rechtsexpertin der Verbraucherzentrale Niedersachsen. Schließlich müssten sich die Verbraucher:innen darauf verlassen können, „dass die vereinbarten Leistungen und Preise nicht nach Belieben geändert werden“. Wer einen Vertrag abschließe, so von Bibra, habe Anspruch „auf klare und nachvollziehbare Regelungen“.
Von der Erhöhung betroffene Verbraucher:innen können unrechtmäßig gezahlte Beträge jetzt zurückfordern, heißt es vonseiten der Verbraucherzentrale Niedersachsen. Allerdings gilt zu beachten, dass Starlink vor allem bei kurzen Kündigungsfristen wie bei Monatsverträgen eine Kündigung aussprechen könnte. Um den Dienst weiter nutzen zu können, müssten Nutzer:innen dann in einen neuen Tarif wechseln.
Amazon verliert vor Bundesgerichtshof
Erst Anfang Oktober 2026 hatte Amazon in einem ähnlich gelagerten Fall auch in dritter Instanz vor dem Bundesgerichtshof verloren. Geklagt hatte die Verbraucherzentrale Nordrhein-Westfalen. Hintergrund ist, dass Amazon 2022 den Preis für das Prime-Abonnement in Deutschland erhöht hatte, ohne die Millionen betroffenen Kund:innen ausdrücklich um deren Zustimmung zu bitten.
Zwar gibt sich Amazon noch nicht mit dem Urteil zufrieden. Bis auf Weiteres gelten für Altkund:innen damit aber wieder die alten Preise. Kund:innen können darüber hinaus für mindestens drei Jahre das zu viel gezahlte Geld entweder individuell zurückfordern. Oder sie schließen sich einer Sammelklage der Verbraucherzentrale an.

articles.title: How Fraunhofer Supplies Chips for Advanced EUV Lithography - EE Times
articles.text:
At the Fraunhofer Institute for Silicon Technology (ISIT) in northern Germany, engineers manufacture a very small number of specialized semiconductor chips. By the standards of an industry accustomed to producing millions of chips, the output is negligible. Yet these components help operate equipment used by Intel and TSMC to manufacture some of the world’s most advanced semiconductors.
The customer is IMS Nanofabrication, an Austrian company that builds multibeam electron-beam systems for rapidly writing photomasks used in EUV lithography at technology nodes of 5 nm and below. Fraunhofer supplies a critical component of those machines: a chip containing hundreds of thousands of individually controlled structures that allow each electron beam to be controlled independently.
The relationship illustrates a little-recognized part of the semiconductor value chain. While governments compete to attract advanced fabs, Europe already supplies specialized technologies on which those fabs depend.
“We’re operating in a niche that conventional semiconductor foundries aren’t really set up to serve,” Fabian Lofink, deputy director of Fraunhofer ISIT, told EE Times. “The volumes are very small. The technology is extremely complex. At these production levels, you can’t rely on statistical process control the way high-volume fabs do, so engineers need to be closely involved in manufacturing every day. “
From a thousand beams to hundreds of thousands
The collaboration began in 2005 through publicly funded research. As semiconductor features shrank, the corresponding lithography masks required increasingly dense patterns, driving up electron-beam writing times. Multibeam technology offered a solution by allowing many electron beams to write in parallel.
“As feature sizes shrink, you need to write far more data onto the mask,” Lofink explained. “With a conventional single-beam writer, that directly translates into longer write times. The idea behind multibeam technology was to parallelize the process, enabling high-throughput mask writing even for the most advanced technology nodes.”
The first demonstrator measured one square millimeter and contained 1,000 cells. By 2012, Fraunhofer and partners had developed a chip with approximately 262,000 individually controlled cells.
Fraunhofer does not manufacture the underlying CMOS circuitry. Instead, the chips are fabricated using advanced CMOS technology with feature sizes below 50 nm to achieve the data rates required for multibeam operation. Fraunhofer then adds the structures that enable individual electron beams to be controlled.
This post-CMOS processing requires electroplated gold electrodes, chosen for their high conductivity and ability to support rapid beam control.
“Gold is normally something you don’t want anywhere near a CMOS fabrication line because of contamination,” Lofink said. “But in our application, even the slightest charging effects can distort the electron beam trajectories. Gold provides both the excellent conductivity needed for high-speed beam control and a reliable path for dissipating charge. Our expertise is in combining these materials after the CMOS process without damaging the electronics.”
Some gold structures approach 50 micrometers in height, far beyond conventional planar semiconductor dimensions.
Around 2015, IMS began selling mask-writing systems incorporating the second-generation TROM2 chip to produce photomasks for the 7-nm technology nodes. Fraunhofer continues to manufacture that component.
Too specialized for conventional foundries
The biggest question is: Why does IMS continue to buy from a research organization rather than a commercial foundry?
“Conventional foundries are looking for business cases involving at least 10,000 wafers a year,” Lofink said. “We’re operating at volumes roughly two orders of magnitude below that threshold. That’s a completely different manufacturing environment.”
The Fraunhofer process also involves approximately 15 lithography levels beyond the CMOS fabrication, specialized materials, and demanding quality requirements.
“High complexity, low volume—that’s our niche,” Lofink said. “You cannot manufacture these products simply by putting operators in front of machines and asking them to push buttons. You need engineers working with the process every day to maintain the required quality.”
High-volume manufacturers use extensive production data to identify variations and stabilize processes. Very small production runs provide fewer opportunities to accumulate such data, increasing the importance of direct engineering supervision.
Fraunhofer also combines experimental research with the ability to supply components reliably. “What differentiates us from a university is that we can take research into an industrial environment,” Lofink said. “We can deliver the same quality repeatedly, and we can deliver it when the customer needs it.”
A small supplier with strong influence
The arrangement has created a supply chain dependency. Fraunhofer remains the key source of TROM2, and transferring production elsewhere would require substantial development.
“If our production stopped, IMS would have a serious problem,” Lofink said. “They have some stock, of course, but you cannot simply move this technology to another supplier. Developing the process takes years.”
For the latest version, TROM3, which is the third generation of the chip, IMS has expanded its manufacturing ecosystem. According to Lofink, it contains approximately 590,000 control cells and supports higher data rates.
The importance of the chips extends far beyond their production volume. IMS’s systems write masks for advanced semiconductor manufacturing, including EUV processes. Lofink identifies Intel and TSMC as major users.
The chips themselves use comparatively mature CMOS technology. “The CMOS in our chip might use a 100-nm or 50-nm process, but the equipment it goes into is used to make masks for 5-nm or 2-nm technology,” Lofink explained.
Extending the model across Europe
For Dirk Schumann, director of the APECS pilot line at the Research Fab Microelectronics Germany (FMD), the IMS relationship illustrates an industrial model that Europe can expand. “If you compare the price of the components we supply with the industrial business they enable, the leverage can be a factor of 50 to 100,” he told EE Times.
The estimate reflects his assessment of the potential downstream value of specialized components, rather than a measured return for the IMS collaboration. Schumann distinguished between the requirements of high-volume chipmakers and those of equipment manufacturers, medical technology companies, and other specialized customers.
“If you’re talking about a company such as Intel or TSMC, they may come to a pilot line for early development, but once they move toward volume manufacturing, they need a different infrastructure,” he said. “For an equipment manufacturer, it’s different. They may need only a limited number of very advanced components, and we can continue supplying those components.”
FMD operates through 13 Fraunhofer institutes and two Leibniz institutes, offering capabilities from technology development through prototyping and small-volume manufacturing. “Our customers don’t need to own the entire infrastructure by themselves,” Schumann said. “We can take a company from an initial idea through technology development, design, prototyping, and even small-volume manufacturing.”
The IMS collaboration predates APECS by many years. Although it didn’t create that relationship, APECS seeks to extend the underlying model through additional capabilities and European partners. Its distributed network aims to give industrial customers access to specialized facilities through a single point of contact, spanning materials, semiconductor processing, and advanced packaging.
Schumann emphasized that developing new technologies is only part of Fraunhofer’s mission. “The real difference comes when we can turn those technologies into industrial value by supplying components that companies can use in their products,” he said.
From technical capability to industrial delivery
APECS is developing 11 demonstrators across four technology areas: high-performance computing, sensors, optical technologies, and RF applications. Beyond proving the technologies themselves, the projects are testing whether geographically dispersed research facilities can operate as a coordinated industrial supplier.
“Technically, moving wafers or chiplets between different institutes isn’t necessarily the biggest challenge,” Schumann said. “The interesting part is making the whole system work as a business: preparing quotations, planning production, coordinating the different facilities, and delivering what the customer has ordered.”
Industrial interest is emerging. According to Schumann, four demonstrators have attracted customers seeking evaluation hardware. “The total number of project requests at APECS, primarily from industrial customers, has already exceeded 200,” he said. How many will lead to sustained commercial production, and when, remains uncertain.
The Fraunhofer–IMS relationship demonstrates what that transition requires: not simply manufacturing a specialized component, but delivering it consistently, reliably, and on schedule. APECS aims to replicate that model across a much larger European network.
Europe’s contribution to advanced chipmaking cannot be measured by production volume alone. Fraunhofer manufactures the specialized chips it supplies to IMS in tiny quantities, yet they play a critical role in equipment used by some of the world’s largest semiconductor manufacturers.

articles.title: This 11-year-old built an AI smart cane for ₹10,000 and took it to the UN
articles.text:
This 11-year-old built an AI smart cane for ₹10,000 and took it to the UN
Noida’s Aaradhya Jain, 11, built STAMBHA, an AI cane that guides users, tracks their health and alerts family after a fall. She presented it at the UN.
On 25 September, inside the UN Conference Centre in Bangkok, the youngest speaker in the room walked up holding a cane.
Aaradhya Jain was there as a youth speaker at the Second World Summit on Sustainable Health and Well-Being. The cane in her hand was STAMBHA (स्तम्भ, “the pillar”), which she designed, wired and programmed herself. After her talk, she found herself explaining it to a WHO regional adviser and to Hungary’s Ambassador to Thailand.
It was a long way from where the idea began: her own living room in Noida.
Why an 11-year-old built a cane
STAMBHA started with a question most adults never think to ask.
“When I was small, someone was always checking on me,” Aaradhya says. “Then they got old, and no one was checking on them.”
She means her grandparents. They used to fuss over whether she was warm, whether she was safe. As they aged, she noticed the roles never reversed. Her conclusion is disarmingly simple: a life should be held all the way through, not just at the beginning.
A second spark came from the screen. Watching Srikanth, the biopic of visually impaired industrialist Srikanth Bolla, made her wonder what moving through the world without sight actually feels like.
So she tried it. She shut her eyes and walked around the house. “Naturally, I was banging everywhere,” she told Digit. That bruising experiment became her first piece of user research.
A guide to the world, and a guardian for the person holding it
Most smart canes look only outward, at the ground ahead. STAMBHA also looks inward, at the person gripping it. In the world of assistive tech, that usually means three separate products. Aaradhya put them in one stick.
Facing outward. A laser rangefinder spots obstacles ahead and warns the user with a buzz in the palm. A camera describes the scene and reads signs aloud.
Facing inward. Sensors in the grip track pulse, blood oxygen and balance. The cane also knows whether a hand is still holding on.
Just talk to it. Users speak to STAMBHA in Hindi or English. “What does this sign say?” “Where is the nearest chemist?” “Is my walk steady today?” It answers using both the world around the user and the user’s own past readings.
When something goes wrong, it alerts family with the user’s location. Crucially, it can tell a stumble from a fall, so a minor trip doesn’t set off a panic. False alarms are a big reason people abandon such gadgets. It also works without a phone, so a dead smartphone battery doesn’t leave the user unprotected.
Aaradhya is careful to say STAMBHA is not a medical device and makes no diagnostic claims. It is a working prototype built to notice change.
Built at home, tested on family
STAMBHA runs on an ESP32-S3 microcontroller. Aaradhya worked on it for about a year, with her father and her uncle Nitin Jain, CTO of ShareChat, often beside her. The trickiest soldering she watched rather than did, and she says so herself.
Much of the code was written with AI programming tools, which Nitin estimates handled about 80% of it. “If you have the concept, if you have the idea, you can do it,” he told Digit.
But the AI didn’t decide what the cane should notice, or when it should stay quiet. Aaradhya did. Early builds kept failing as sensors malfunctioned wherever she mounted them. She kept moving them until they worked.
Her test users were the people closest to her: parents, grandparents and her elder sister. Between 25 August and 23 September she ran 16 test sessions. They produced more than 22,600 sensor records, over 8,500 obstacle records and nearly 20,000 balance records. That is closer to a small field trial than a school project.
The effort has already been recognised. Aaradhya was named a Global Child Prodigy Award winner and one of the Top 100 Child Prodigies of the World 2025, at a ceremony held at the UK House of Commons.
Why India needs a cane like this
India is ageing fast. About 149 million Indians are over 60 today, a number expected to reach about 347 million by 2050, according to the UNFPA India Ageing Report 2023. Many of them live alone or with children who work long hours far away.
The tools that could help them are out of reach. Comparable smart canes sold abroad cost ₹80,000 or more. STAMBHA’s parts come to about ₹10,000, roughly an eighth of the price.
That gap is the real story. A cane that talks in Hindi, reads a pharmacy sign and calls home after a fall could matter most to people who will never shop for imported assistive tech.
What’s next for STAMBHA
On 17–18 October, Aaradhya presents STAMBHA again, this time on Innovation World’s global GIFT livestream.
After that comes the harder test. She plans to put the cane in the hands of real elderly and visually impaired users, then redesign it around what they tell her.
Ask her what success looks like and she doesn’t mention funding, scale or a startup. “My goal is to make it reach the right people,” she says. “I built this for the right people.”
She named it “the pillar” for a reason. At 11, Aaradhya Jain is building something for the people who once held her up, so they never have to walk alone.

articles.title: Proofpoint gives MSPs a Microsoft 365 risk dashboard, Teams training and an AI assistant - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Proofpoint gives MSPs a Microsoft 365 risk dashboard, Teams training and an AI assistant
Cybersecurity company Proofpoint Inc. today unveiled new Microsoft 365 security features meant to get managed service providers and the businesses they look after ready to adopt artificial intelligence tools safely.
The four new features land in the Microsoft 365 security products sold by Proofpoint MSP Platform, the business unit that handles the company’s work with managed service providers and small and midsize businesses. Tenant Risk Exposure maps permission and sharing risks across Microsoft 365 tenants. Email verdicts from the unit’s AI now arrive with an explanation of how they were reached.
Security awareness training has been extended into Microsoft Teams, where an AI coach quizzes employees after they finish a course. The fourth is an AI assistant for partners and administrators, built into their control panel.
Daniel Hofmann, who runs Proofpoint MSP Platform as general manager and executive vice president, said the data and channels an AI tool can reach matter as much as the choice of tool. Overly broad permissions and unclear sharing settings were there before AI arrived, he said, and using the technology “can amplify their impact.”
Tenant Risk Exposure is aimed at administrators who already rely on Proofpoint’s 365 Permission Manager to keep track of access rights in Microsoft 365. The new dashboard shows them, tenant by tenant, where anonymous access and inactive guest accounts have crept in, and a shortcut beside each finding lets them close it off by hand. Remediation can also run automatically.
Security teams reviewing a message in Email Live Tracking will now see why the AI reached its verdict on it. Proofpoint says that should speed up work on the rare false positive.
The AI-powered Security Awareness Service now works inside Microsoft Teams. Employees who finish an e-learning session hear from AI.MY, the unit’s AI Cyber Assistant, acting as a coach.
Its three follow-up questions are pitched at each person’s awareness level, and feedback comes back immediately. Answers go into a knowledge profile that organizations can use to measure learning progress and work out who needs more training.
The AI assistant for partners and administrators lives in the control panel of Proofpoint 365 Total Protection, a Microsoft 365 security suite originally developed by German security company Hornetsecurity GmbH. It answers conversational questions on onboarding, configuration and day-to-day security operations.
Managed service providers can also use it to match products to a given customer and find places to extend that customer’s protection. Proofpoint expects that to cut the effort providers put into customer consultations.
Proofpoint closed its $1.8 billion purchase of Hornetsecurity in December, then built the MSP unit on top of that business in May. More than 12,000 managed service providers and channel partners now sell the unit’s products to upward of 125,000 customers, and the four new features are scheduled to reach them in the fourth quarter.

articles.title: Astrophysiker zweifeln an Hypernovae – warum die riesigen Sternenexplosionen womöglich nie stattfanden
articles.text:
Rätsel um Hypernovae: Haben die riesigen Explosionen im All nie stattgefunden?
Die vermeintlichen Spuren sogenannter Hypernovae in alten Sternen lassen sich vollständig durch gewöhnliche Sternenexplosionen erklären. Zu diesem Ergebnis kommen der Doktorand Anmol Aggarwal und der Astrophysiker Ralph Schönrich vom britischen University College London (UCL). Das erläutern sie in einer Mitteilung der Hochschule, die zwei aufeinander aufbauende Studien zusammenfasst.
Wenn massereiche Sterne am Ende ihrer Lebenszeit ihren Kernbrennstoff verbrauchen, kollabiert ihr Inneres und schleudert die äußeren Hüllen in einer Supernova ins All, wobei sich die Forschung immer wieder mit verschiedenen Arten von Sternenexplosionen beschäftigt. Für vier besonders eisenarme Sterne im Halo, dem kugelförmigen Außenbereich der Milchstraße, sowie in einer benachbarten Zwerggalaxie reichte diese normale Explosionsenergie in bisherigen Computermodellen jedoch nicht aus, weshalb Wissenschaftler:innen zehnmal stärkere Hypernovae als Ursprung postulierten.
Asymmetrische Supernova statt Hypernova: Warum das Zwiebelschalen-Modell die Abweichungen erklärt
In ihrer bereits im Frühjahr 2026 in der britischen Fachzeitschrift Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society veröffentlichten ersten Arbeit weisen Aggarwal und Schönrich nach, dass frühere Analysen auf einer falschen Grundannahme beruhten. Bisherige Berechnungen setzten voraus, dass eine Supernova ihre chemischen Elemente bei der Detonation gleichmäßig im Raum verteilt und benachbarte Gaswolken mit einem Durchschnittsmix aller Stoffe anreichert.
„Wenn wir uns heute eine Supernova ansehen, sind die Materialien des Sterns nicht gleichmäßig verteilt: Sauerstoff fliegt möglicherweise überwiegend in die eine Richtung, Schwefel in eine andere“, erklärt Erstautor Aggarwal in der Mitteilung des UCL. Kurz vor der Explosion besitze ein Stern Schichten wie eine Zwiebel mit schwereren Elementen im Zentrum und leichteren weiter außen, ergänzt Mitautor Schönrich.
Weil reale Sternenexplosionen durch physikalische Instabilitäten asymmetrisch ablaufen, treffen oft nur Fetzen einzelner Schichten auf jene benachbarten Gaswolken, aus denen später neue Sterne entstehen. Als die beiden Forscher diese unvollständige Durchmischung mathematisch modellierten, ließen sich drei der vier untersuchten Sterne statistisch besser durch normale Supernovae mit 13 bis 15 Sonnenmassen erklären als durch Hypernovae.
Roter Riese SMSS 2003–1142: Neutronensterne und eine Zwerggalaxie lösen das Uran-Rätsel
Als letztes Argument für eine Hypernova verblieb zunächst der Rote Riese SMSS 2003–1142 im äußeren Halo der Milchstraße, den ein internationales Forschungsteam im Jahr 2021 in einer im Wissenschaftsmagazin Nature veröffentlichten Studie untersucht hatte. Da dieser alte Stern neben leichteren Stoffen auch hohe Mengen schwerer Elemente wie Silber, Thorium und Uran enthält, galt er bisher als Beleg für eine stark magnetisierte, schnell rotierende Hypernova.
Gewöhnliche Supernovae können solche schweren Elemente oberhalb von Eisen und Nickel nicht erzeugen, und eine Kollision zweier extrem verdichteter Neutronensterne schlossen Forscher:innen damals aus, weil in der jungen Milchstraße bis zur Geburt des Sterns schlicht die Zeit dafür gefehlt hätte. In ihrer im Spätsommer 2026 ebenfalls im Fachblatt Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society publizierten Folgestudie widerlegten Aggarwal und Schönrich jedoch auch diese Herleitung.
Anhand von Bewegungsdaten des europäischen Weltraumteleskops Gaia zeigen die Autoren, dass der Rote Riese mit rund 368 Kilometern pro Sekunde entgegen der Rotationsrichtung der Milchstraße durch den Halo fliegt und somit aus einer später eingefangenen Zwerggalaxie stammt. Dort reicherte sich das Gas über Milliarden Jahre hinweg nur langsam mit Eisen an, was genügend Zeit für eine Neutronensternkollision ließ, deren Auswurf die Forscher mithilfe von Simulationsdaten aus dem Archiv des Max-Planck-Instituts für Astrophysik im bayerischen Garching mit einer normalen Supernova kombinierten.
Während das frühere Hypernova-Modell mehrere im Stern gemessene Stoffe wie Stickstoff, Natrium oder Titan ausklammern musste, bildet die Kombination aus gewöhnlicher Sternenexplosion und Neutronensternverschmelzung sämtliche nachgewiesenen Elemente ab und halbiert dabei nahezu die durchschnittliche Abweichung zwischen Modellrechnung und Teleskopmessung. „Alle Belege, die wir für Hypernovae sehen, sind plötzlich verschwunden“, fasst Aggarwal das Resultat der beiden Untersuchungen zusammen.
Rückwärts gerechnet: Warum das neue Supernova-Modell noch Lücken aufweist
Trotz der besseren Trefferquote ist das Modell der beiden UCL-Forscher noch kein Beweis dafür, dass die untersuchten Sterne tatsächlich auf diese Weise entstanden sind. Aggarwal und Schönrich haben im Grunde rückwärts gerechnet und am Computer ausprobiert, in welchem Verhältnis man sechs bis sieben Schichten einer normalen Supernova mischen muss, um die heute gemessene Zusammensetzung der alten Sterne zu erhalten.
Ob eine echte Explosion ihre Trümmer in der Realität genauso in eine benachbarte Gaswolke schleudert, wissen die Forscher bislang nicht. „Trotz jahrzehntelanger Arbeit auf diesem Gebiet wissen wir noch immer nicht, wie gut das Supernova-Material durchmischt wird, bevor es neue Sterne bildet“, räumt Mitautor Schönrich ein.
Wenn die ausgeschleuderten Schichten mit rund 1.000 Kilometern pro Sekunde durch das All fliegen und auf umliegendes Gas prallen, entstehen komplexe Turbulenzen, die bisherige dreidimensionale Simulationen noch nicht im Detail abbilden. Zudem lässt das neue Modell der unvollständigen Durchmischung auch eine noch unspektakulärere Möglichkeit zu: Statt einer einzelnen Supernova könnten schlicht die Überreste und Winde mehrerer gewöhnlicher Sterne dieselbe Gaswolke angereichert haben.

articles.title: We test the RTX Spark Superchip in Microsoft's Surface Laptop Ultra — Nvidia's Windows on Arm platform impresses in local AI, but gaming isn't its strong suit
articles.text:
We test the RTX Spark Superchip in Microsoft's Surface Laptop Ultra — Nvidia's Windows on Arm platform impresses in local AI, but gaming isn't its strong suit
Laying the foundation for the reinvention of the PC in the agentic AI era
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang announced the RTX Spark platform with the grand ambition to “reinvent the PC” back at Computex 2026. By pairing the GB10 Superchip with a version of Windows on Arm tailored for the secure and contained execution of local AI agents, Nvidia and its partners at Microsoft, Dell, HP, MSI, Lenovo, and Asus are all hoping to pave the way to a future where the PC is an active, autonomous companion for work and creation.
The hardware foundation for that vision of the future is now in place. Last week, we flew out to San Francisco to get all the details on the RTX Spark platform, and we returned home with Microsoft’s Surface Laptop Ultra in top-end trim to put it all to the test.
This system has the full RTX Spark Superchip with 20 CPU cores and 6144 CUDA cores alongside 128GB of LPDDR5X-9400 RAM, and I’ve been putting it through its paces over the past week to see just what it can do.
The embargoes for the RTX Spark launch are a bit peculiar. Today, we’ll be sharing our broad experience with the Spark platform, as well as competitive performance evaluations, but not any system-specific results such as battery life, build or display quality, or other details of that nature. We have other RTX Spark laptops in the Tom’s Hardware labs, and detailed reviews of those systems will be coming soon.
No, this approach doesn’t make a lot of sense when the experience of a mobile platform is intimately and inextricably tied to the specific implementation of that chip in a particular laptop design. And we know that battery life is the first and foremost concern of many interested in this platform. But again, all that information is coming soon.
For this first round of testing, we compared the Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra with RTX Spark against two systems. The first is a 14" MacBook Pro with Apple's highest-end M5 Max SoC inside. That Mac has a 40-core GPU and an 18-core CPU, as well as 128 GB of LPDDR5X RAM. We don't have a mobile Ryzen AI Max+ 395 system in the labs right now, but we do have AMD's compact Ryzen AI Halo as a source of fresh data with the latest ROCm stack and llama.cpp builds.
Local AI performance
Judging local AI performance is a constantly moving target, and this review is no different. Our past testing has exercised the prompt processing and token generation phases of AI inference separately, with the understanding that a system that's fast at both those phases provides the best experience.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
But in an agentic workflow, that benchmarking technique doesn't capture the total time required to complete a task across all the inference turns needed to reach a particular goal. To capture that entire end-to-end time, the folks at Artificial Analysis have developed a new benchmark, AgentPerf-local, that precisely replays inference traces across several agentic AI tasks. The value of this approach should make immediate sense: the faster an AI agent finishes a job, the more productive a system can be.
So instead of presenting raw time-to-first-token and tokens-per-second figures, as we have in the past, we’re sharing time-to-completion values as we would for more traditional CPU and content creation benchmarks.
Again, local AI benchmarking is a continuous work in progress, so let us know what you think of this approach, and we’ll take that feedback into account as we continue to develop our methods.
We ran AgentPerf-local with two compatible models: the dense Qwen 3.8-27B, which is popular as one of the most intelligent local models available for its size, and the Qwen 3.6 35B A3B mixture-of-experts model, which is less intelligent but easier for a wide range of systems to run quickly. We used the latest build of llama.cpp as our inference backend and built it from source on each test system to take advantage of CUDA, Metal, or ROCm acceleration, as appropriate.
Let’s look at Qwen 3.8 27B’s behavior first. We used Unsloth’s Q4_K_M quantization of the model. We ran it with DFlash2 speculative decoding on the RTX Spark and MacBook Pro, and with Qwen 3.8 27B’s built-in MTP on the Ryzen AI Halo for the best performance.
As we found in our benchmarking of Apple's Mac Studio with the M4 Max SoC, memory bandwidth is only one constraint for local AI performance. Despite its memory bandwidth advantage on paper, the M5 Max MacBook Pro still ends up taking about 25% longer to finish the AgentPerf benchmark with Qwen 3.8 27B than the Surface Laptop Ultra with RTX Spark.
Part of that may be down to software maturity, but it's also worth remembering that our Surface Laptop Ultra is a 15" system with a much larger 140W power adapter versus the 14" MacBook Pro's 96W charger.
The 16" M5 Max MacBook Pro also comes with a 140W adapter, and we'd be curious to see whether the extra power and higher thermal headroom afforded by that system’s larger chassis help close the gap here. But in any event, the RTX Spark platform is the fastest overall at this task today.
Meanwhile, AMD's nearly two-year-old Ryzen AI Max+ 395 just can't keep up with either of these newer systems in this demanding test. It needs about twice as long to finish our agentic tests with Qwen 3.8 27B as either the RTX Spark or the MacBook Pro do, at a whopping 40 minutes.
The fact that the Ryzen AI Halo is a mini desktop form factor rather than a notebook doesn’t much matter to these results, as any power and thermal headroom that design might afford can’t possibly overcome the performance gap here.
Next up, we have the lighter-weight Qwen 3.6 35B A3B. We ran Unsloth’s Q4_K_M quantization of this model with MTP enabled.
The Surface Laptop Ultra ends up completing this test in just eight minutes, or about 25% faster than the 14” MacBook Pro’s 10 minutes. This test is also much friendlier to the Ryzen AI Halo, which finished the benchmark in a more reasonable 13 minutes. But that just emphasizes that you have to trade away model intelligence to get a reasonable level of performance out of Strix Halo.
AMD has recently gone on a publicity blitz to highlight the relatively low cost of entry for Strix Halo systems versus DGX Spark desktops and now RTX Spark laptops. But if time is money, and getting more intelligent tokens out of your local AI system faster means more potentially profitable agentic work gets done, then a more expensive system upfront will be able to do more of that work and potentially generate more value over time.
Gaming performance: first impressions
Despite its RTX branding and the emphasis Nvidia places on its 6144-CUDA-core GPU (or 48 SMs), the RTX Spark platform faces some tough challenges for gaming. Most games available today are not going to be natively compiled for its Arm CPU, and even for those that might be, the maximum 300 GB/s of shared memory bandwidth the platform offers is well below that of even the RTX 5060 Mobile's dedicated 384 GB/s feeding 26 SMs.
The entire GB10 SoC is competing for a relatively small amount of memory bandwidth, and because graphics is generally a memory-bandwidth-bound workload, that's not a great start for feeding all of those SMs in games.
I started my gaming explorations with Gears of War: E-Day. In this exceptionally CPU-heavy game, it's clear that the baseline performance of the Grace CPU cores and the added overhead of the Prism x86 emulator are doing this title no favors.
GPU utilization only reaches the 85% mark on average at a near-1080p (1908x1272) render resolution with the High preset and 2X framegen, and we saw at least one major hang during a map transition that was less than confidence-inspiring for an immersive experience as we progress further into the game.

|---|---|---|---|
| Row 0 - Cell 0 | Average FPS | 1% Low FPS | Avg PC Latency (ms) | 
| Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra with RTX Spark | 77.7 | 39.9 | 83.5 | 
Because of its CPU dependence, Gears is probably a worst-case scenario for this platform, but the fact remains that it's not a great experience, and turning down settings or lowering upscaling input resolutions just exacerbates the CPU-boundedness of this title. If any game could use a native Arm build, this is the one.
Control Resonant is significantly less dependent on the CPU, but that just means that the other potential gaming shortcomings of the RTX Spark Superchip seem to come into play.
After struggling a bit to achieve a solid frame rate and input latency at the Surface Laptop Ultra's native 3270x2180 output resolution even with DLSS upscaling, I found that running the game in windowed mode at 2560x1440 with DLSS Performance upscaling, the High preset, and MFG 3X to keep frame rates near the Surface Laptop Ultra's 120Hz refresh rate provided better results. (This system's tall 3:2 aspect ratio means that 16:9 fullscreen games don't cleanly scale up.)
| Control Resonant (2560x1440, High Preset, RT Off, MFG 3X) |  |  |  | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Row 0 - Cell 0 | Average FPS | 1% Low FPS | Avg PC Latency (ms) | 
| Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra with RTX Spark | 109.2 | 51.6 | 78.3 | 
But even then, input latency was above what I would consider acceptable on our standard GPU test rig, and enabling ray tracing at all dipped frame rates and spiked input latency even further, so I had to stick to raster-only rendering for the best results.
Overall, my early RTX Spark gaming verdict is that you can do it, and you can have a fine enough time, but it is not the primary focus of this platform. Gaming performance with the relatively limited memory bandwidth of the RTX Spark Superchip, combined with the system's CPU performance and the overhead of Prism emulation, mean that you'll be searching for a narrow range of settings where baseline frame rates, upscaling, image quality, and the smoothness boost of frame generation still yield acceptable input latency.
When I first approached gaming on this platform, I had expected that DLSS upscaling would be a required part of the experience, but in practice, you really need to lean on DLSS Frame Generation, as well, whether that's for added smoothness (as in Gears of War) or for both smoothness and the benefits of Nvidia Reflex due to developer choices behind the scenes (as in Control Resonant).
Even with Reflex, though, the Grace CPU generally seems to deliver input latencies significantly higher than I'm used to on our Ryzen 7 9800X3D test rig, and it's hard to get them much lower in these AAA titles by tweaking settings.
If you demand the lowest input latency and the highest performance with cutting-edge games, especially if you plan to enable RT, a separate gaming laptop with a dedicated RTX 50-series GPU will still provide a superior experience. And if you just don’t care about local AI at all, that advice applies even more strongly.
Bottom line
Nvidia's RTX Spark is an ambitious new PC platform for the traditional workloads of today and the potential agentic AI work of tomorrow. How often do we see an entirely new player try to elbow into the crowded and competitive PC space, especially one with a sweeping vision for how the PC will be used in the years to come? An incremental move this is not.
Our general performance tests and new agentic AI tests show that despite providing merely solid CPU performance and relatively low bandwidth for a unified memory architecture on paper, the Blackwell GPU on board GB10 has enough AI horsepower in practice to let the RTX Spark platform come out ahead of Apple's latest top-end M5 Max and AMD's Ryzen AI Max+ 395, aka Strix Halo, SoCs.
Whether you choose the highly intelligent dense Qwen 3.8 27B model and trade raw speed for intelligence, or make the opposite trade with the lighter and faster Qwen 3.6 35B A3B, the RTX Spark comes out on top. That bodes well for pairing popular agents like Hermes with intelligent local models on this platform.
But Nvidia's mission to reinvent the PC isn't a total grand slam in this first iteration.
First, this platform won't replace a dedicated gaming laptop. Even for those who only game on the side and have more forgiving standards for frame rates and input latency, the RTX Spark's gaming performance may not measure up to expectations.
When you put the overhead of Prism x86 emulation on top of the merely adequate performance of the Grace CPU, it’s clear that the Spark platform will have to work hard to keep up in the vast range of games that don’t have an Arm port.
The CPU-heavy Gears of War: E-Day is particularly unkind to the Prism-on-Grace stack, but even when a title like Control Resonant doesn't lean so heavily on the CPU, the limited and shared memory bandwidth of the GB10 SoC still poses an obstacle to cranking settings to the max despite the large amount of theoretical compute horsepower on tap.
We're also still waiting for Windows to fully catch up to Nvidia's ambitions for secure, manageable local agents. Our laptop expert Andrew Freedman and I couldn't test Microsoft's secure agentic AI promises within Windows 11, as the supporting features that Microsoft and Nvidia have promised to that end just aren't ready yet.
Still, for a first-generation mobile platform that joins complex silicon IP from multiple design teams onto one chip and relies on several OEM partners to bring it to life in highly integrated notebook form factors, the maturity of the RTX Spark platform is an impressive achievement. (Take it from someone who has seen a couple of rough product launches from the inside.)
Over the past week, I've been using the RTX Spark-powered Surface Laptop Ultra as I would any other Windows laptop, and aside from a couple of tiny paper cuts, I have mostly just gotten my work done as I would with any other computer. And that’s a great — albeit a very, very expensive — place to be as the local agentic AI future coalesces.
Perhaps the biggest challenge for the RTX Spark platform is that the eye-watering price tags for the range of systems available at launch still buy a lot of cloud tokens from OpenAI and Anthropic. Emphasis on a lot. The Surface Laptop Ultra we tested lists for $5899 with only 1TB of storage, and lead times for that system are already out to late December.
If you're not as concerned about keeping sensitive data out of those labs’ clouds, or you don't expect to run afoul of acceptable usage policies, you'll get much smarter tokens much faster than you will from a local token factory like the RTX Spark, and you can get them on most any reasonably powered traditional PC you have available.
But if you're surfing the AI wave on local hardware for reasons of privacy, offline model availability, freedom to tinker, or just because you think it's cool, the RTX Spark platform blends the memory capacity, compute performance, and software resources you need to get there with the familiarity and broad compatibility of Windows on top. The fact that Nvidia, Microsoft, and their partners have delivered such a capable, compatible, and polished platform even in its first at-bat should put the rest of the PC industry on notice.
Nvidia’s efforts to reshape personal computing will face strong headwinds in the immediate future from the sky-high DRAM and NAND price hikes that the company’s own Vera Rubin rollout is partially responsible for. Perhaps when the dust settles in the next two to three years, and products built around the next-generation RTX Spark Superchips arrive, we can more confidently assess whether the company has accomplished its goal.
For now, the RTX Spark feels like a platform for those who fervently believe that open AI models will continue to get more intelligent within relatively small memory footprints, and that those potential future improvements are worth a hefty chunk of change to get ready for today. Maybe that's a smart bet in a world where compute is an increasingly precious resource. But unless you're a true believer with cash to burn, our first impressions suggest that you should wait until Microsoft and Nvidia fully lay the software foundation needed for this platform to deliver on its promises.
As the Senior Analyst, Graphics at Tom's Hardware, Jeff Kampman covers everything that has to do with graphics cards, gaming performance, and more. From integrated graphics processors to discrete graphics cards to the hyperscale installations powering our AI future, if it's got a GPU in it, Jeff is on it.

articles.title: Netgear’s Orbi 770 is our top Wi-Fi 7 pick to wipe out dead zones
articles.text:
Netgear’s Orbi 770 is our top Wi-Fi 7 mesh router for large homes and WFH offices — and it's cheaper at Amazon right now than anywhere else
Cover up to 8,000 square feet with powerful tri-band Wi-Fi 7 connectivity
There's nothing more frustrating than paying for fast broadband only to discover that the signal barely reaches certain rooms. The Netgear Orbi 770 Series Wi-Fi 7 Mesh System could be the upgrade you're looking for, and it's reduced in price right now.
Rather than relying on a single router to reach every corner of your home, the Netgear Orbi 770 uses three coordinated units to distribute the wireless signal throughout. The package includes one Orbi RBE771 router and two RBE770 satellites, making it suitable for larger properties, and Netgear advertises coverage of up to 8,000 sq ft. and supports up to 100 connected devices.
• Best for: Larger homes, multi-story properties, and busy households and offices with numerous connected devices.
• The deal: The Netgear Orbi 770 Series three-pack is $628 (was $700) at Amazon.
Today's best Wi-Fi 7 mesh router deal
The Netgear Orbi 770 includes one WiFi 7 router and two satellites, offering tri-band connectivity, up to 8,000-square-foot coverage, 11Gbps combined wireless speeds, 100-device capacity, and 2.5Gbps Ethernet support.
Why we recommend it
In his four-and-a-half star review, our expert Cliff said it offered "excellent performance for home users and small businesses."
He added that "the Orbi 770 doesn’t cut any corners when it comes to performance. Its 11Gbps speed is more than fast enough to cope with most domestic broadband services, and even many business networks as well, and it’s not even slightly bothered by the troublesome Wi-Fi ‘deadspot’ that we have in an office located towards the back of our building."
It supports WiFi 7, with combined theoretical wireless speeds of up to 11Gbps. Enhanced Backhaul technology helps maintain fast, reliable connections between the router and satellites.
We rated it the top pick for homes in our guide to the best mesh Wi-Fi systems.
Price Context & Historical Value
Amazon usually sells the Netgear Orbi 770 three pack for $699 but it's currently down to $627.72 right now, a $72.27 (10%) discount.This isn't the cheapest price it's been at Amazon, as we've seen it there for $569.89 in the past, but this is still a solid reduction. For comparison, Best Buy currently lists the same system at $699.99, as does Netgear direct. However, I have found a refurbished three-pack for $574 at Target if you don't need to buy new.
Should you buy it?
✅ Buy the Netgear Orbi 770 if...
You have a large home with unreliable Wi-Fi coverage, particularly if — like in my house — the signal weakens across floors or in rooms far from your existing router. It's also worth considering if your house has dozens of connected devices.
❌ Skip the Netgear Orbi 770 if...
You live in a smaller apartment or already have reliable Wi-Fi coverage throughout your property. A less expensive router or two-unit mesh system could meet your needs.
More Wi-Fi 7 mesh router deals
This cheaper dual-band WiFi 7 mesh system offers speeds up to 5Gbps, coverage of 6,000 square feet, support for 70 devices, 2.5Gbps Ethernet connectivity, built-in security features, and straightforward app-based setup.
This tri-band WiFi 7 mesh system offers 10Gbps speeds, four 2.5Gbps ports, wired backhaul, AI roaming, HomeShield security, VPN support, and coverage of up to 7,600 square feet across homes.

articles.title: Federal government announces $500 million round of AI funding
articles.text:
The federal government has announced an additional round of funding for Artificial Intelligence (AI), including $500 million to be spent over five years to expand and enhance the Regional Artificial Intelligence Initiative.
The press release notes that the initiative is part of Canada’s National Artificial Intelligence Strategy, which is also known as “AI for all.” Announced in June 2026, the federal government says that the strategy “aims to build trust, strengthen Canadian AI capabilities and sovereignty, and ensure all Canadians can use AI responsibly to build and benefit from it.”
Interestingly, this round of funding brings the total amount spent on the initiative to $700 million.
It was also noted that the initiative will be delivered by Canada’s regional development agencies, and the support will focus primarily on “sectors where Canada has strong expertise and economic potential,” which includes health and life sciences, energy and natural resources, transportation, agriculture, manufacturing and robotics, alongside other regional strengths and priorities.
Interestingly, the federal government added that the initiative is designed to help Canadian AI businesses gain customers, attract investment, and commercialize and scale Canadian-made products and services while supporting regional organizations that connect businesses with the support they need to adopt/commercialize AI tech — Ironic, considering that some LLMs ignore small Canadian businesses.
Honestly, I’m curious about how this round of investment will actually be used. While this investment is framed as making sure the country benefits from a global AI buildout, but this is a unique time for the AI industry. There are lots of concerns regarding the safety of AI and its usage by major companies (looking at you, DraftKings), alongside its environmental impact. Plus, there are still calls for AI regulations, which still haven’t been fully addressed.
Image credit: Shutterstock
Source: Government of Canada

articles.title: 120ft raises angel funding to build autonomous microfactories run by humanoid robots - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
120ft raises angel funding to build autonomous microfactories run by humanoid robots
Swedish robotics startup 120ft Factory AB launched today with 576,000 euros ($644,000) in new funding from 22 angel investors to build autonomous microfactories run by humanoid robots.
120ft builds and operates small factories that fit inside three 40-foot shipping containers, and the combined length of those containers gives the company its name. Customers never buy a robot. Brands pay for each finished product and keep their existing component suppliers, which send parts to a 120ft site where robots shared among several customers handle final assembly, inspection and packing.
The first customers 120ft is chasing are design-led consumer brands, such as makers of small appliances and consumer electronics. Smaller brands can be forced to place production orders months before they know what will sell. Their parts often come from around the world and go to China for assembly before the finished goods are shipped back to Europe. The company frames that reliance on distant factories as a geopolitical risk.
On the production side, 120ft’s software takes product designs, parts lists and quality requirements and converts them into digital instructions. Every job runs in a simulation first. Missing information and bottlenecks are meant to show up there before production starts. Once a line is running, the company’s orchestration software coordinates robots, tooling and quality checks and decides what happens when a task fails.
120ft has demonstrated the system on a lamp, with robots assembling a cylinder lock and threading the bulb fitting before running a functional test. Instructions and data from each production run are kept so that tasks can be reused and improved for later products. It took seven weeks in 2025 to teach the robots one end-to-end assembly skill, according to 120ft, and the same work now takes seven hours. The target for 2027 is seven minutes.
Martin Willers, 120ft’s founder and chief executive, started the Stockholm company in 2025. He previously built and sold hardware design firm People People AB and co-founded Transparent AB, a Swedish maker of repairable, upgradable speakers.
Transparent is where he ran into the same ordering problem. The speaker maker could spend months waiting for thousands of products to arrive before it knew which colors customers wanted most, he recalled.
“For a smaller brand, that means tying up cash and making decisions about demand far too early,” Willers said.
120ft will put the funding toward reaching commercial production and further development of its software and factory infrastructure. Longer-term, the company plans to take the same local production model into repair, upgrades and remanufacturing.
The 22 angel investors include Ted Persson, co-head of EQT AB’s Scaleup Europe Fund; Sophia Bendz, a partner at Cherry Ventures Management GmbH; and Matthias Dantone, a co-founder of Fashwell AG, which Apple Inc. acquired. Sam Baker, an investor at Planet A Ventures with more than a decade in manufacturing, is also among them.
“A robot on its own does not solve the manufacturing problem,” Baker said. Brands also need tooling, software and quality control around the machines, in his view. Decentralized manufacturing capacity is part of Planet A’s thesis for how Europe regains its industrial autonomy, he added.

articles.title: Tesla présente enfin son Roadster définitif : il roule, il vole, il bat tous les records d'accélération
articles.text:
En novembre 2017, Tesla présentait la seconde génération de son Roadster, censée devenir la voiture la plus sportive de sa gamme. Depuis, les milliers de personnes intéressées par le modèle, dont certaines n’ont pas hésité à poser un acompte, attendent de découvrir la version définitive.
Près de neuf ans se sont écoulés, et le grand jour est enfin arrivé. Tesla a officialisé son nouveau Roadster ce jeudi 15 octobre 2026 (dans la nuit du 15 au 16 en France), lors d’une démonstration diffusée en direct sur X et sur YouTube, avec des démos jamais vues dans l’industrie automobile.
Le Roadster peut… décoller
On attendait les propulseurs annoncés depuis des mois, et au mieux un vol stationnaire de quelques secondes. Le Roadster a fait bien mieux. Oui, le Roadster est bien capable de décoller. Tesla a fait deux démonstrations. Dans la première, le Roadster a roulé tête en bas sur une rampe, plaqué contre elle par ses ventilateurs, avant de la quitter et de se retourner en l’air pour revenir au sol. Dans la deuxième, il a carrément quitté le sol pour « sauter » au-dessus d’autres véhicules, en réalisant un tonneau en l’air. Les deux démonstrations ont été des réussites.
« Le système de propulseurs de la Roadster génère 4 à 5 fois la force que les pneus peuvent supporter. Plus de force sur la même masse signifie une accélération significativement meilleure — la physique fait le reste », explique Tesla.
Un 0 à 96 km/h en moins d’une seconde
Tesla revendique un 0 à 96 km/h en 0,81 seconde, chronométré en direct avec l’aide des propulseurs. C’est deux fois moins que la Rimac Nevera R (1,66 seconde), qui détient le record pour une voiture de série. Le chrono de Tesla a toutefois été réalisé par un prototype. Lors de sa présentation en 2017, la sportive promettait 1,9 seconde.
L’autonomie est annoncée à plus de 480 kilomètres, et la vitesse maximale à plus de 370 km/h pour le modèle le plus radical.
Côté aérodynamique, le Roadster reçoit un aileron arrière mobile capable d’ajuster l’appui au sol en temps réel (système actif), assisté par des ventilateurs et un diffuseur spécifique.
Ces chiffres ne concernent pas tous le même modèle. Tesla décline son Roadster en trois versions :
- La Performance, la seule pensée pour la route, se contente des ventilateurs et de l’aileron actif, avec un 0 à 96 km/h en moins de 1,6 seconde.
- La Thrust ajoute des propulseurs à l’arrière et descend sous les 0,9 seconde. Elle est pensée pour le circuit et sera produite en série limitée.
- La Rocket, monoplace et réservée aux invités, ajoute des propulseurs tout autour de la carrosserie pour décoller et pivoter en l’air. Elle revendique moins de 0,59 seconde. Tesla précise qu’elle n’est pas autorisée sur la route : les cascades de la soirée ne montrent donc pas la voiture que la plupart des clients pourront acheter.
Quand la voiture décolle : des propulseurs SpaceX à bord
L’élément le plus fou de cette présentation reste la démonstration en vol. Le Roadster est équipé de propulseurs à gaz froid développés avec SpaceX, qui fonctionnent à l’air comprimé stocké dans des réservoirs en fibre de carbone. Il s’est élancé sur une rampe avant de « sauter » par-dessus cinq Tesla alignées (Cybercab, Cybertruck, Semi, Model Y et Model 3). Dans les airs, les propulseurs permettent à la voiture d’effectuer un tonneau complet avant de se reposer sur ses quatre roues.
Elon Musk concèdent que le véhicule est « loin d’être sécurisé, mais extrêmement fun ».
Un design futuriste et un cockpit épuré
Visuellement, le design a nettement évolué par rapport au prototype présenté en 2017. Tesla cite l’avion espion SR-71 et le chasseur F-35 comme sources d’inspiration, avec des lignes plus incisives et futuristes.
Dans l’habitacle, le Roadster fait le choix du minimalisme :
- Deux places seulement ;
- Le volant Yoke, couplé à la technologie de direction électrique steer-by-wire déjà aperçue sur le Cybertruck ;
- Des commandes manuelles pour réduire la masse ;
- Des matériaux légers à haute résistance (titane, fibre de carbone).
Tesla n’a donné aucun prix, pour aucune des trois versions. En 2017, le Roadster était annoncé à partir de 200 000 dollars (environ 170 000 euros), et à 250 000 dollars (environ 215 000 euros) pour la série Founders. Les réservations ont rouvert aux mêmes conditions qu’il y a neuf ans : 50 000 dollars d’acompte (environ 43 000 euros), dont 5 000 dollars à verser tout de suite et le reste sous dix jours. Côté calendrier, Elon Musk vise une production en 2028. Il avait déjà promis 2020, puis 2023.
Tesla confirme sa volonté de commercialiser ce monstre de puissance, l’un des objets roulants (et volants) les plus extravagants jamais montrés par un constructeur. Les cascades de la soirée reposent pourtant sur des versions réservées au circuit ou distribuées sur invitation, et la version de route n’arrivera pas avant 2028, si Elon Musk tient enfin un calendrier.
La présentation, minute par minute
Enfin la présentation du Roadster
Vous avez du café ? Vous avez du pop-corn ? C’est parti pour la grande présentation du Tesla Roadster, la supercar électrique qui promet une fiche technique dantesque, via un show inouï. Début des hostilités à 2h55, heure française, dans la nuit de ce jeudi 15 à ce vendredi 16 octobre, depuis le site d’essais de SpaceX à McGregor, au Texas.
Du retard à prévoir ?
Est-ce que ça va vraiment commencer à 2h55 ? Tesla est habitué aux retards. Le flux vidéo vient bien de débuter, avec un logo Roadster au style rétro qui défile à l’écran.
Une rampe ?!
Tesla a semble-t-il prévu une rampe pour l’une des démonstrations, à en croire un message publié sur X par Sawyer Merritt… Nous ne sommes pas prêts, je crois.
Teasing d’Elon Musk
« Le nouveau Roadster est au-delà des films, au-delà de l’imagination, au-delà de l’humain, mais toujours fait par des humains sur Terre », a écrit sur X Elon Musk, patron de Tesla et de SpaceX, quelques heures avant le show.
5 minutes de retard
Ça commence ! Les gens sur place applaudissent déjà !
FRANZ EST LÀ
Le designer star de Tesla, Franz von Holzhausen, va-t-il encore taper sur une voiture avec une masse, comme sur le Cybertruck en 2019 ?
Curieux rappel
On nous rappelle qu’un Roadster a été envoyé dans l’espace. Lol !
Et voici ELON !
Elon Musk arrive, avec un t-shirt Roadster et une grosse ceinture du Texas. « Vous allez voir quelque chose de fou ce soir », prévient-il. On n’en croira pas nos yeux, paraît-il… Le Roadster est, selon lui, le fruit de deux ingénieries de pointe, celles de Tesla et de SpaceX. Mieux que dans un film…
« Le succès n’est pas garanti…»
La démo pourrait mal se passer, prévient Elon Musk, qui assume. Mais on va s’amuser… et personne ne sera tué dans l’exercice. Ouf !
Le but est simple
Le Roadster doit dépasser les limites, martèle Elon Musk.
VOICI LE ROADSTER !
LE DÉCOLLAGE !
La voiture a décollé ! La démo fonctionne ! La voiture a roulé sur une rampe en restant plaquée dessus, l’a quittée puis est revenue sur terre en se retournant et en se posant grâce à des propulseurs !
Des propulseurs piqués à SpaceX
Le Roadster est équipé de propulseurs à air comprimé conçus avec SpaceX pour se retourner dans les airs, et de ventilateurs qui l’aspirent vers la route pour le plaquer au sol.
Starman est là !
Voiture loin d’être sécurisée mais fun
Dixit Elon Musk…
Nouvelle démo
Cette fois, le Roadster a décollé et a « sauté » au-dessus d’autres véhicules pour réaliser un tonneau et se remettre sur ses roues. On reste loin de la voiture volante, mais le saut est réussi.
Le design a bien changé
Le design du Roadster est bien plus radical que celui présenté en 2017, et la voiture est désormais un coupé à portes en élytre. Il est inspiré de l’aérospatial.
Une deux places
Dans l’habitacle, on découvre deux places et un volant en forme de manche d’avion (yoke), avec une direction steer-by-wire, sans liaison mécanique avec les roues, comme sur le Cybertruck.
Un gros aileron à l’arrière
Un gros aileron arrière, qui peut changer de position, ajuste l’appui aérodynamique. Une fois en l’air, la voiture se retourne grâce à ses propulseurs. Les propulseurs et les ventilateurs sont logés à l’arrière, dans la zone du diffuseur. Ils fonctionnent à l’air comprimé, sans carburant, et les deux réservoirs haute pression en carbone se rechargent tout seuls.
Accélération fulgurante
Le 0 à 96 km/h est réalisé en moins d’une seconde, selon le chrono annoncé par Tesla ! Le record de la Rimac Nevera R (1,66 seconde, mesuré de façon indépendante en 2025) est pulvérisé, sur le papier du moins. Quand elle accélère.
C’est déjà fini ?!
La récréation est finie ! Tesla a terminé les démonstrations et dévoilé son Roadster, qu’il promet toujours de commercialiser.
Bonne nuit !
