articles.title: Valve Index VR drops to $400 as production ends, leaked code hints at 4K OLED Steam Frame upgrade
articles.text:
In a nutshell: VR users looking for whatever cheap headset they can get their hands on should consider snagging a discounted Valve Index while they can. However, those happy to wait and pay (a lot) more might want to hold off, as recently leaked code suggests a mid-generation refresh of the Steam Frame is on the horizon.
Valve has unsurprisingly ended production of its first VR headset, the Index, and has begun clearing stock with a 20% discount on the headset and all accessories. Meanwhile, although the company only recently launched the Index's successor, the Steam Frame, hints of an upgraded model have already emerged.
The Index headset is currently available from Steam for $400 while supplies last. The replacement tether is now just $103.20, while the base station and replacement left controller are discounted to $120. The bundle is no longer available, but its individual components would now total $741, down from $926.
Meta's Quest 3 and Quest 3S have long since eclipsed the Index in both price and performance, but some VR enthusiasts might want to take the opportunity to acquire a relatively cheap headset that doesn't require a Meta account. Plus, while Valve's new standalone Steam Frame includes more modern hardware, its RAM-crisis-inflated $1,060 starting price likely puts it out of reach for many shoppers. Meanwhile, the Steam Frame's kernel source code, which evlaV mirrored on GitHub, reveals early work on an updated model with OLED lenses and higher frame rates.
Codenamed "Plano," the new model would replace the current Steam Frame's 2160 × 2160 per-eye LCD panels with 3552 × 3840 OLED displays. The new OLED panels support a 90Hz refresh rate, with an experimental 120Hz mode in development.
However, because Plano reuses the original Steam Frame's Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 processor, its default operating resolution is limited to 1776 × 1920, with an experimental 1.5x scaling mode that increases this to 2368 × 2560. According to Steam Frame Hub, the panels are likely the same MicroOLED displays used in the Samsung Galaxy XR.
To save horsepower and enhance performance, Plano would also introduce foveated scaling, using the Steam Frame's eye-tracking capabilities to detect where users are looking and render only those pixels at native resolution. The current Steam Frame uses eye-tracking for foveated streaming, which applies the same basic concept to conserve bandwidth when wirelessly streaming software from PCs.
The leaked code includes development records from as recently as October 2, indicating Plano remains deep in development. However, there is no telling how close the refresh is to launch.

articles.title: Nvidia squeezed a 74B agent model into 24GB so it can run on your laptop
articles.text:
Nvidia squeezed a 74B agent model into 24GB so it can run on your laptop
Nvidia on Thursday announced a few new additions to its Nemotron family: Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, a 120B vision-language model for enterprise agents and two small Bolt models (Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB and Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB) for running coding, research, and conversational workloads locally.
The Bolt models, Nvidia says, are meant to run “everyday agentic tasks on laptops, balancing speed and intelligence needed to handle multistep reasoning, tool calling, and web browsing.”
And while they come in very different sizes and are meant for different use cases, the focus for all three is on speed and efficiency.
The two larger models are available today, while the smaller Bolt E4B 4G model will launch in the near future.
Nemotron 3.5 Super VL
The marquee release here is Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, a 120-billion-parameter model that combines reasoning and tool use with image and document understanding.
In the announcement, Kari Briski, Nvidia’s VP for open models and software, notes that the large model is meant to deliver “leading accuracy on multimodal agentic tasks — instruction following, tool use, multistep business workflows, and visual understanding — comparable with NVIDIA’s largest reasoning model at roughly one-fifth the parameter count.”
Super VL builds on Nemotron 3 Super, which launched in March. Both have 120 billion total parameters, with 12 billion active during inference, and context windows of up to 1 million tokens. But while the earlier model only accepted text, Super VL now adds support for image and video input (though not output).
Mixed results against Qwen
But when it comes to the benchmarks, though, especially when compared to other open models of comparable size, the results are mixed.
In Nvidia’s own evaluations, Super VL outperforms Alibaba’s Qwen3.5-122B-A10B on scientific reasoning and terminal tasks, while scoring slightly lower on SWE-bench Verified and document understanding.
The five tests are GPQA-Diamond, Terminal-Bench 2.1, SWE-bench Verified, IFBench, and MMLongBench-Doc. Super VL scores 66.7 on Terminal-Bench, compared with Qwen3.5’s 48.7, but trails it on SWE-bench Verified, 71.1 to 71.9.
Qwen has 122 billion total parameters and 10 billion active, compared with Super VL’s 120 billion and 12 billion. The newer Qwen3.8-Flash-Next scores higher on all five tests, though its additional embedding and prediction components bring its total parameter count to about 180 billion.
Thinking Machines’ Inkling-Small has 276 billion total parameters and 12 billion active. It also trails Super VL on terminal tasks but scores higher on instruction following.
Nvidia also reports Super VL ahead of Ultra on Hermes Bench and LangChain behavioral evaluations, scoring 63.44% versus 56.33% and 87.05% versus 84.3%, respectively.
Overall, though, the focus here was clearly on speed.
Nvidia reports fourfold faster completion of 10,000 SWE-bench Pro tasks on four B200 GPUs, though its chart shows lower accuracy than Qwen3.8-Flash-Next and DeepSeek V4 Flash.
Hybrid Mamba architecture, faster decoding
As for how Nvidia built the model, it’s worth noting that the Nemotron coalition is sticking to the 3.5 family’s hybrid architecture, which combines Mamba-2, attention, and mixture-of-experts layers — but with the addition of a vision encoder. Nvidia also continued training the language model using distillation from Nemotron 3 Ultra before further training for software engineering, vision, and agent tasks, according to its model card.
To speed up text generation, Nvidia also uses LiLiCorr, a technique for speculative decoding. With this, a smaller helper model drafts several tokens ahead, which Super VL checks together instead of generating each token individually. Nvidia says this speeds up token generation on DGX Spark by up to 2.3 times compared with decoding without speculation.
For document workflows, Nvidia says Super VL focuses on optical character recognition, tables, charts, and structured information.
On CharXiv, a chart-reasoning benchmark, Nvidia reports 80.8% accuracy, compared with Nano Omni’s 63%. Python code interpretation raises Super VL’s result to 84%.
Bolt runs 74B in 24GB
If you’re interested in running local models, the new Bolt models may be the most interesting release here — and their benchmarks tend to outperform most comparable models.
Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB is derived from Super VL. Its hybrid mixture-of-experts architecture activates 9 billion of its 74 billion parameters at a time.
In Nvidia’s tests, Bolt scores 51.0 on Terminal-Bench 2.1, versus 44.4 for Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and 37.2 for Gemma4 26B-A4B, both tested in BF16. Bolt uses mixed precision, including two-bit experts.
To get to this size, Nvidia used two-bit quantization to reduce the 74B model’s memory footprint to 24GB. The company says it is optimizing the model for RTX Spark and DGX Spark systems, with support for llama.cpp, Ollama, LM Studio, and vLLM.
A second, even smaller version of this model, Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB, is scheduled for later this month. With this one, Nvidia is targeting conversational and physical agents on GeForce RTX, Jetson, and Spark hardware, including device assistants and interactive characters that need multiturn tool use and awareness of application state.
Availability
The new models are now available for download on Hugging Face under the OpenMDW 1.1 license, which permits commercial use and modification.

articles.title: Microplastics in water aren’t inert and make damaging chemicals on their own
articles.text:
One reason plastics are used so often is that they’re chemically inert, meaning bags, food containers, and cups don’t react with what we put in them. Yet they can still break down into microplastics, which turn up in drinking water, human blood, arteries, and brains. The consequences of that are uncertain.
“Whether microplastics can directly cause human disease is still being researched,” said Wei Min, a chemist at Columbia University. In a new Nature study, Min’s team took a step toward answering this question by demonstrating that microplastics are likely not as chemically inert as we might expect.
Microdroplet chemistry
Min’s lab has spent years working on microdroplet chemistry, studying how water broken into tiny droplets behaves at its boundary with air. These droplets have been reported to generate reactive oxygen species, or ROS, a family of harmful, oxygen-containing molecules. “ROS will essentially bump into proteins, lipids, DNA, and cause damage,” Min said. “You could break a DNA strand into segments. You could mutate DNA; you could misfold proteins.”
Many animal studies have tied microplastic toxicity to oxidative stress, which is caused by ROS. So the team wondered if the boundary between water and plastic might do something similar. “We got inspired by that field,” Min said.
In the first test, the team stirred polystyrene powder into water containing methyl orange, a yellow dye that ROS break apart. Over 10 days, the solution faded almost to colorless, losing nearly 90 percent of the dye. In ethanol or other solvents, the dye stayed intact. Min and his colleagues concluded that whatever chemistry polystyrene was undergoing needed water to happen. So they ran more tests.
Water under stress
First was electron spin resonance, a technique that directly detects radicals—atoms or molecules with an unpaired electron that makes them particularly reactive. The polystyrene powder and water mixture contained hydroxyl radicals, a highly reactive ROS.
Next, the team used a fluorescent sensor that lights up only when it reacts with hydroxyl radicals. “You don’t see it, but once it reacts with local ROS, it turns into a bright color,” Min said. Under a microscope, the glow concentrated on the surfaces of the plastic particles and kept building over time.
The effect was not unique to polystyrene either. Scientists tested six common plastics—polyethylene, polypropylene, polystyrene, PVC, PET, and acrylic—and all of them generated radicals. The most water-repellent plastics, polyethylene and polypropylene, were the most active, while PET and acrylic, which contain chemical groups that attract water, were the least.
“The simplest answer is the most water-repellent ones change the water structure the most,” Min said. In ordinary, or bulk, water, each molecule is held in a network of hydrogen bonds with its neighbors. But a few layers of water molecules pressed against a water-repellent surface lose some of those partners. “Their structure is no longer the regular water structure. They are perturbed, and their energy is also significantly increased,” Min said.
Water always contains a small number of hydroxide ions, and turning one into a hydroxyl radical requires stripping away an electron. In bulk water, that costs a lot of energy. But simulations run by the group showed that, at a polyethylene surface, hydroxide ions short on hydrogen bonds needed far less energy to form radicals. On top of that, the plastic surfaces build up a negative electric charge in water, which further lowered the energy cost.
But Min’s team still had doubts to address before making any conclusive claims.
Ruling out the dirt
Min’s earlier work on microdroplet chemistry has drawn a lot of criticism, with some researchers arguing that the reported reactive chemicals come from contamination or measurement artifacts.
To avoid similar objections, Min and his colleagues used several independent detection methods. They also added a detergent-like surfactant that coats the plastic and disrupts the water layer at its surface. They found that the more surfactant they added, the weaker the plastic’s electric charge became and the fewer radicals it produced. “We only change one parameter while keeping all the rest [the same],” Min said. “We’re using exactly the same plastics, the same water, the same everything.”
Impurities, Min explained, are typically stable molecules with no reason to spontaneously generate radicals. He is careful not to overstate it, though. “To be absolutely clear, we cannot 100 percent rule out the involvement of impurities,” he said. “But our controls and our theoretical computation studies highly suggest that this is intrinsic to the microplastic-water interface.”
Finally, the team tested if this interface chemistry matters for biological molecules. And it most likely does.
Proteins and blood cells
Proteins and DNA can gather on plastic surfaces, and lysozyme, a common test protein, also began clumping into aggregates there. Adding caffeine, which mops up radicals, largely stopped the clumping, pointing to the radicals as the cause.
Mouse red blood cells that touched polystyrene particles broke into fragments, and the damage from each type of plastic tracked how many radicals it produced. The effect also persisted in blood serum.
Min stressed, though, that this indicates that microplastics make people sick by generating ROS. While animal studies often point to ROS as possible roots of oxidative stress and chronic inflammation, ROS can be produced in many ways, including through basic metabolic activity.
Min admitted comparing the magnitude of this effect to the impact of ROS our own cells make is rather tricky.
A local problem
“If you are really at the interface, you could be significantly affected by this effect, whereas if you are just a few microns away, you don’t feel it anymore,” Min said. Exposure is another unknown here. Min also emphasized that no one can yet say how many microplastics an average person takes in each year from food, water, and air.
The plastics in the study were mostly fresh, lab-bought powders, unlike weathered particles we encounter in the environment. In the team’s tests, older particles with more oxidized surfaces produced somewhat weaker signals. “This aging process is very heterogeneous,” Min said. “Some microplastic particles were made 50 years ago, some were made five days ago.” Finally, there is the question of size.
Microplastics are usually defined as particles smaller than five millimeters, while the minimum cutoff varies between 100 and 1,000 nanometers. Min’s team did not test how variation in microplastic particle size affects water-interface chemistry, but the researchers suspect it might play a role. The same mass of plastic broken into nanoparticles has far more surface area, which might make the effect larger. “This may be another reason for nanoplastics to be more dangerous,” Min said.
The researchers argue that if water-repellent surfaces drive the water interface chemistry, plastics could be designed to be less water-repellent, either by changing their molecular structure or including additives. First, though, the team wants to focus on the question their study left open. “We definitely want to see how much this effect is directly contributing to disease or biological problems in animals and humans,” Min said.
Jacek Krywko is a freelance science and technology writer who covers space exploration, artificial intelligence research, computer science, and all sorts of engineering wizardry.

articles.title: El próximo 'Call of Duty' no será 'Modern Warfare' ni 'Black Ops': Activision confirma que una nueva saga está en marcha
articles.text:
Modern Warfare 4 posiblemente sea uno de los Call of Duty que menos expectación ha generado en los fanáticos en mucho tiempo, al menos en lo que respecta a esta subfranquicia del shooter bélico. Algo así ya había sucedido en 2025 con Black Ops 7, por lo que el sentimiento no es del todo desconocido para Activision. La empresa sabe que existe un desgaste y un descontento entre el público, y por eso planean dar un golpe de timón de cara al futuro.
Tyler Bahl, jefe de marketing de Activision, confirmó en una entrevista con The Game Business que la compañía está trabajando en una saga de Call of Duty totalmente nueva. La idea es distanciarse de Modern Warfare y Black Ops por un buen tiempo, y para ello necesitan algo fresco y nuevo.
Los detalles respecto de cómo será la nueva subfranquicia de Call of Duty y qué estudio la encabezará son todavía un misterio. Sin embargo, Bahl ha dejado en claro que la respuesta de los jugadores a los lanzamientos consecutivos de los últimos años no fue tan buena como esperaban.
Recordemos que, si bien Modern Warfare 2 (2022) recibió muy buenas críticas, no sucedió lo mismo con Modern Warfare 3 (2023). Algo similar sucedió con Black Ops 6 (2024), que recibió críticas mixtas y fue seguido en 2025 por un Black Ops 7 que fue un fiasco tanto comercial como de reseñas.
"[Los lanzamientos consecutivos] no eran algo que nuestra comunidad estuviera buscando. Querían algo fresco y, aunque existían diferentes ambientaciones temporales y formas de jugar con nuevas funcionalidades, ese cambio de tono es precisamente lo que buscaban. Por eso, ya hemos anunciado que un futuro título constituirá una nueva subfranquicia, para lo cual ya hemos sentado las bases. Pero estamos muy entusiasmados con Modern Warfare 4, que da respuesta a parte de esos comentarios", explicó Bahl sobre el futuro de Call of Duty.
Call of Duty se aleja de Modern Warfare y Black Ops para explorar una nueva saga
Que Activision no repetiría la estrategia de lanzamientos en años consecutivos para Call of Duty: Modern Warfare y Black Ops, no era sorpresa. La compañía lo anunció en diciembre del año pasado, cuando dijo que aspiraban a una innovación significativa, en lugar de incremental, y que ya estaban construyendo el futuro de la franquicia.
Claro que por entonces todavía no se sabía que la idea era poner a descansar a sus dos sagas principales para abrir un camino totalmente nuevo. Todavía es muy temprano para saber qué le depara el futuro a Call of Duty, aunque hay varios rumores en circulación. Uno de los más fuertes sostiene que la subfranquicia actualmente en desarrollo podría debutar en 2027 de la mano de Sledgehammer Games, cuyo últimos juegos como desarrollador principal fueron Vanguard (2021) y MW3 (2023).
También se especula con la posibilidad de que Call of Duty comience a explorar otros elementos relacionados con el combate cuerpo a cuerpo y las artes marciales, sin alejarse al 100 % de su esencia como shooter bélico.

articles.title: Google reorganiza sus planes IA: los modelos Gemini Pro pasarán a ser exclusivos de la tarifa Pro
articles.text:
Google comenzó a notificar por correo a los suscriptores de Google AI Plus un cambio en sus condiciones de servicio. A partir del 13 de noviembre de 2026, el acceso a los modelos Pro dentro de la aplicación de Gemini y el modo IA integrado en el buscador quedará bloqueado para quienes paguen la tarifa económica.
“Seguirás teniendo acceso a nuestro último modelo Flash-Lite y a Flash, diseñados para ofrecer velocidad e inteligencia”, señala la compañía en la comunicación enviada a los usuarios.
El movimiento amplía la diferencia de rendimiento entre Google AI Plus y Google AI Pro, este último con acceso al nuevo Gemini 4 Argon, y plantea a los usuarios la duda entre mantener una cuota reducida con prestaciones limitadas o asumir un otro precio para conservar las funciones de razonamiento avanzado.
Cómo cambia la suscripción económica de Google
Los usuarios que mantengan la cuota de 4,99 euros mensuales quedarán relegados en exclusiva a los modelos Flash y Flash Lite, sin acceso a la selección de motores Pro.
Estas variantes ofrecen mayor velocidad para consultas cotidianas, pero carecen de la capacidad de deducción, el músculo analítico y la precisión de redacción que distinguen a la rama Pro en tareas complejas.
El recorte afecta al trabajo ya realizado dentro de la aplicación. Las conversaciones y proyectos abiertos en los que se utilizó previamente un modelo Pro no desaparecerán del historial, pero la plataforma impedirá continuar esa misma charla con el motor original.
Para enviar nuevos mensajes en esos hilos, se deberá cambiar de manera manual la conversación a un modelo inferior, lo que implica una pérdida de contexto y de calidad en las respuestas frente a lo que ofrecía antes el sistema Pro.
Cuánto cuesta mantener las funciones de razonamiento profundo de la IA de Google
El cambio deja fuera del plan de 4,99 euros las herramientas de razonamiento profundo y obliga a contratar la modalidad Google AI Pro, cuya cuota asciende a 21,99 euros mensuales en España.
No obstante, el plan gratuito de Google sigue dando acceso al modelo Flash-Lite, y las suscripciones de pago continúan incluyendo beneficios adicionales como almacenamiento en la nube y YouTube Premium.
Quienes opten por el nivel más alto, Google AI Ultra, con un costo desde 99,99 euros mensuales, mantienen acceso pleno tanto a Gemini 4 Argon como al resto de funciones avanzadas sin restricciones adicionales.
Qué aporta Gemini 4 Argon frente a sus los modelos antecesores de Google
Gemini 4 Argon se distingue en el análisis de tareas complejas del mundo real en ámbitos como programación, finanzas, derecho, ciberseguridad y ciencia.
Su precisión en tareas de múltiples pasos le permitió ocupar el primer puesto en el índice Vals, que mide el rendimiento de los modelos de inteligencia artificial en sectores económicos clave como finanzas, programación, derecho e impuestos.
El modelo ya está disponible a nivel mundial para desarrolladores y empresas a través de la API en AI Studio y la plataforma Gemini, para suscriptores de Google AI Ultra en Google Antigravity, y para usuarios de AI Ultra y AI Pro en la aplicación Gemini y el modo IA de la búsqueda.
Cuáles resultados reporta Google con el uso de Gemini 4 Argon
Dentro de la propia compañía, grupos de ingeniería han utilizado Argon para acelerar la entrega de código con agentes en más del 35%, al tiempo que redujeron las reversiones de código en casi un tercio.
Un caso destacado fue el trabajo del grupo de Chrome, que usó el modelo para separar el manejo principal de páginas web de una carpeta heredada de aproximadamente seis millones de líneas de código, dentro de una base de 40 millones de líneas de Chromium, un proceso que redujo de meses a semanas.
En el ámbito científico, investigadores lograron que el paquete de química cuántica de código abierto xTB fuera hasta 2,3 veces más rápido en la predicción de estructuras moleculares.
Asimismo, el uso de Argon permitió una aceleración de inferencia de 2,85 veces en los modelos abiertos Gemma, con una paridad de tokens del 100% y sin pérdida de calidad, un avance que normalmente habría requerido meses de desarrollo y que el modelo completó en pocos días.

articles.title: Canada has few gaming events -- VGLX aims to change that
articles.text:
Canada is one of the largest producers of games in the world, and yet you wouldn’t know it based on how relatively few consumer gaming events we have here.
The U.S. has PAX. Europe has Gamescom. Japan has Tokyo Game Show. Canada, however, doesn’t have any sort of equivalent. Toronto’s Fan Expo Canada, our largest pop-culture event, generally has minimal gaming programming, while Edmonton’s burgeoning Game Con Canada, while home to a big indie game showcase, is nonetheless focused more on tabletop games like Warhammer.
That might soon change, though, if Jason Lepine has anything to say about it. As the founder and CEO of XP Gaming, he’s put on numerous successful business-to-business (B2B) gaming events across Canada, including the XP Game Summit and Montreal International Game Summit (MIGS). And prior to starting XP Gaming in 2019, Lepine cut his teeth working at Enthusiast Gaming, which put on the Enthusiast Gaming Live Expo (EGLX) events before COVID permanently shut them down.
Building on all of that experience, Lepine started Video Game Live Expo (VGLX) last year, a fan convention featuring all kinds of gaming programming. After the inaugural show last October, VGLX returns to Mississauga this year on Oct. 24 and 25 at the International Centre. This year’s highlights include playable games (both indie and AAA, including this year’s Modern Warfare 4), guests like Craig Burnatowski (Wesker/Zeno from Resident Evil) and Jon McLaren (Star-Lord in Marvel’s Guardians of the Galaxy), numerous vendors and OverActive Media esports reveals.
MobileSyrup sat down with Lepine to discuss his ambitions with VGLX, overcoming challenging market conditions, the importance of building community, and what makes Canada’s gaming scene so special.
What inspired you to start VGLX?
So when I got the chance after the pandemic, an old friend of mine who works in events and who’s a partner of mine on VGLX, that’s Mikey [Singer] from MKEM, He does events. He approached me. I was already doing B2B events. He was like, “Why don’t we kickstart a B2C [business-to-consumer] event again? It’s something you’ve always shared you wanted to do.” I wasn’t too willing to do it while I was focused on B2B. Myself, the XP gaming team, were quite busy with all our B2B events. But having a partner that was now offering to come in and help me do the heavy lifting on the event was really kind of the gateway that said, “Yeah, let’s do it.” Pre-pandemic, we were successful. We had built an event that had over 30,000 attendees, and it was the largest video game con in Canada.
But the pandemic made that go away, and there’s not been really any that have come back. There’s a big one in Alberta now that’s set up in Edmonton, Game Con Canada, which I haven’t been to. It sounds fantastic what they’ve built there. But there’s nothing here on the East Coast. So that’s really what kind of triggered the decision to build a new consumer event, and that’s where Video Game Live Expo came from.
You mentioned Game Con Canada. I was actually there this year, it was my first time. That is an interesting show because it is cool what they’re building, especially as a small team. But it is very tabletop heavy, so there’s not as much in the way of video game stuff right now. They’re hoping to expand that. But what you’re doing with VGLX, which is focused specifically on video games, is more relevant to this larger conversation about the lack of gaming events.
Lepine: I will say it’s not easy. I made a LinkedIn post about a month ago declaring this is my vision [with VGLX], what I want to do, and it was a very well-supported post. But there was a lot of valid criticism of the business model for a video game event, “it doesn’t make a lot of sense anymore,” and you hear this in a lot of the circles.
And you see it when you go to events, especially post-pandemic, that a lot of things have changed. You don’t see all these mega booths from the major publishers. It definitely has changed the business model. It doesn’t really make sense for a massive publisher to spend a lot of money to have a massive booth to show a game to, I don’t know how many attendees they can go through in a booth in a weekend, let’s be generous and say it’s 5,000 attendees. You compare the cost to how many people can play that versus getting a demo out on Steam or online and getting that into the hands of hundreds of thousands, and you boost it with a little bit of a marketing boost. The economics are just not the same.
And so it’s important to be aware of that, especially on my team side when we are looking to build a consumer show from the ground up. How do you do that in 2026? Because the budgets aren’t there like they used to be. The publishers are not going to have all these earmarked budgets for “Yeah, let’s build a big booth at VGLX.” And my answer to that is we have to lean on community, and I think that’s always been at the heart of all of our shows.
And when you look at PAX and how they all started — it was through community, and that is very much, I think, a business model for the post-pandemic era where studios are looking to engage with their communities. And one way to do that is in person. There is nothing that replaces the in-person experience. I was at China Joy over the summer, and one of the differentiators there — someone pointed out all these publishers; their games are free to play. So why do they need to be investing money, have booths and physical presence at these shows when you can pick up their game for free on phones or anywhere? And it’s because they’re developing community. It’s all about investing in the community, giving them an experience, a shared experience that you can’t get anywhere else by just being online.
That’s a great point. You mentioned taking this on with your partner. Working on EGLX on the B2C side, and then obviously, your extensive B2B background as well with XP Game Summit and MIGS… What were some of the lessons you took from doing all of those events, and how did that help you organize and execute on your VGLX strategy?
Lepine: That’s a very good question, and I’ll be honest in saying that the B2B and the B2C business model surprised me at how different [they were]. For example, one of the simple differences: B2B, the attendees tend to plan well ahead. A lot of the times, they’re international attendees, so they’re planning their hotels, their flights. The programming needs to be up far earlier in advance, and so you’re working with these timelines that are spread out over far more time. And also, the ticket price for a B2B event is significantly higher. It’s hundreds of dollars for a ticket. A B2C event is far more affordable, and it’s far easier to be impulsive about it. You could wake up one morning and say, “Do we have plans this weekend? Let’s go to VGLX.” And it just costs you $20 or $25 depending on what day you go, and it can be a family activity.
So there was a lot of learning to be done there in adapting a lot of our B2B strategies to B2C. For the most part, how things are structured is very similar, where partner onboarding is very similar […] All of that is already built into our company, so fine-tuning it and directing that towards a B2C is a good starting point, because a lot of our B2B attendees enjoy B2C shows as well, but now, it’s all about building that consumer side.
And the third thing is the experiential, which is something I’ve always taken to heart. My conferences, I’ve always approached them from a creative angle. I’ve been a massive gaming fan my whole life, and I’ve always wanted to be a part of the gaming community. And I recognize I have no skill to make a game, or I don’t want to learn how to make a game because I’ve seen how difficult it is. But what I can do is I can build events, and an event is an experience. And so I always look to games. Games evoke these emotions when you play them. And I always think, “How can my events be like a game? How can I evoke emotions from the moment you walk in, from the moment you experience the event? What are these little things that you can take away from as memories with your friends, with your family?”
And that’s one of the things that we take to heart when we design this — not just myself, but all my partners on this event. VGLX is an experiential event. The last thing we want to do is create an event where it’s just a hall filled with vendors, and it’s pretty much what I call the “shopping mall.” We want to create the “theme park” experience where there are vendors, but there’s also experiences, and we look usually for about a 50/50 ratio of when you’re in VGLX, you get all of these experiences included with your ticket, and then of course there’s the vendor experience where you can find stuff in Artist Alley, retro games, cool gaming swag and so on.
Having successfully put on an event last year, what were some of the biggest lessons that you learned that you’ve taken into this sophomore year?
Lepine: It was really the fact that the world has changed post-pandemic, and also recognizing that I started XP Gaming five years ago, so I haven’t been at the “build it from the ground up” [level] in a while. It’s been five years, and I remember my first B2B show was XP Games Summit, and that took a lot of grinding. And so VGLX in year one was exactly that. It’s a lot of grinding. Nobody knows about this show. It’s not just a “build it, and they will come.” You have to advertise. You have to hustle, and you have to get out there. But one of the things that we definitely learned from our inaugural show is we leaned into that experiential vision that I shared, where I think our ratio ended up being like 60 per cent experiential. There was a Minecraft zone last year. There was the esports tournaments. There was a lot of like Pokémon mini-games and scavenger hunts throughout the hall. We had a Monster Hunter hunt, which was inspired by a game I love to play.
So that resonated very well with our audience, and it was an indicator that we were on the right track, and so we leaned more into that this year. I remember one of my colleagues actually brought their daughter to the show, and this was a spontaneous decision, and he just came to support. So he came for an hour, and when it came time to leave, Zara’s like, “I don’t want to leave! I have all these things I want to check out.” And they ended up staying for five hours. And that’s just kind of one anecdote.
But it’s something that we heard consistently throughout the weekend that once people were there, they were having fun. They didn’t want to leave. And that, to me, is the biggest indicator of success that we are on the right path of creating an experiential event. Because when you think about it, when you go to a theme park, you don’t go in there and you ride one ride, and you leave; you stay there all day. That’s what we’re seeing early on with the VGLX concept that we’re testing out.
This year, you’re in the International Centre in Mississauga, which is a much bigger venue. As you were planning this second show in a larger space, what were some of the things you wanted to double down on, expand upon, that sort of thing?
Lepine: One of the things that we always felt was an iconic aspect to a show is our esports tournament, and we’ve done it differently this year, where we’ve partnered with Incendium Games, and they’ve been running their tournament Electric Clash every year. And so this year, instead of us saying, “Well, let’s put on this VGLX tournament,” we decided, “Why don’t we give Electric Clash a home and a stage, and we can use the infrastructure and we can partner? You’re already doing this event annually.” And this was kind of the building blocks I saw when we were building EGLX pre-pandemic of working with community members, working with existing communities that are already doing things, and just bringing it together. So that was one of the key pieces.
Another thing that we really wanted to lean more into was to create more gaming experiences. So our indie game zone from last year was very well-received. I think it was the most bustling space in our show in year one. So in year two, we gave it more room to breathe, and we also have attracted a lot more partners, such as [Toronto-based indie] Torn Banner, which is going to be there with their game No More Room in Hell 2, which just launched this year to great success. We have [Canada’s largest independent game developer] Behaviour Interactive [Dead by Daylight] bringing their indie horror titles through their new publishing label, Misbehaviour. So, on top of the indie game zone that features roughly 40 indie games, we have all of these other gaming experiences from larger studios coming into the show. That’s another very exciting kind of indicator of growth and success with the show.
You touched on it a bit. With digital distribution being so big nowadays, it’s easier than ever for developers to reach their audiences. But because of that, people may underestimate the value of being able to connect directly in-person with fans at events like VGLX. From your experience, having talked to developers and put on these events, why is it important for games to have this kind of platform at something like VGLX?
Lepine: I think it really gives that unique value proposition to develop community here in Ontario. I think the gold standard that we can look to is [Warframe developer] Digital Extremes and their TennoCon event that happens every year in London, Ontario. Again, a free-to-play game, but they host this massive event that draws thousands of fans from all over the world, and I’m pretty sure they sell out very quickly of their tickets because it gives them a platform. There’s another event that just launched in Canada earlier this year from Behaviour Interactive celebrating their 10-year anniversary of Dead by Daylight. It was a fan event that, again, drew thousands of fans from around the world. So already, that is a testament to the in-person experience and developing a culture around your game and a community, because when a community loves your game, there’s going to be ROI there because they’re going to tell their friends and they’re going to invite their friends to join the community.
So you know there’s a play to be made in community to invest in community. And not every studio can put on their own TennoCon? Putting on events is very expensive, especially when you start talking about thousands of attendees. So VGLX gives studios the chance to build their community at a very cost-effective price, where the ROI makes a lot of sense. They’re not dropping half a million dollars just to put together an event around their game. They can now be alongside these other studios in a way that makes sense for them financially. And a show like ours gives us a lot of entry points, whether you’re indie and you’re just starting out and you need a table for a few hundred dollars, all the way up to whatever level of partnership makes sense for a studio.
As we talk about growing VGLX and looking at your long-term, multi-year vision. We’re in this unique geopolitical climate right now where a lot of people don’t want to do as much business with the U.S. Based on conversations and trends that you’ve been having and observing, are you optimistic that this might drive more international interest in an event like VGLX?
Lepine: Definitely optimistic. It’s something that we’ve seen on the B2B side of our events where there is a lot more international attention happening just for having events in Canada as people look for new opportunities in all sorts of markets. On the B2C side, I think it’s not just a geographical consideration, but I think it’s a business model consideration. Like I’ve shared, it’s a fairly new shift of what I’m seeing, where it’s not about having a booth to sell your game at the show. It’s about building community. I really think studios like Digital Extremes and Behaviour Interactive are at the forefront of that mindset and are discovering the value.
And I don’t think necessarily it’s caught on as “This is what we need to do.” I think we’re maybe five years away from the bulk of these major studios saying, “We need to be back in events, in a position and a strategy to grow our community.” And as that trend turns, we will be there ready to accept them at a show like VGLX. And maybe there will be more than one show. So right now, we’re building one show in Toronto, but there’s a lot of room for shows like this all over the world and all over Canada. We’re a very large country! So my hope is that we would attract more international publishers to be developing community, to engage with community here in Canada and North America, and be a destination for these community-focused events.
You’ve mentioned a lot of gaming events of different sizes and formats. You have something like TennoCon or the DBD event which hit a few thousand people. You did EGLX, which reached 30,000. And there’s larger events like PAX and whatnot. As you envision and build upon this idea for VGLX, in terms of scope, where do you envision this fitting into all of that? Hypothetically, 5 years out, 10 years out — is this more like “Canada’s PAX?” Is it something smaller-scale? Is it more like “EGLX 2.0?” Where do you see it heading?
Lepine: It’s a great question, and the simple answer is: time will tell us. I’m very receptive to the market. I used to build my B2B shows with the vision of, “I’m going to build GDC on the East Coast.” That was my original pitch, only to discover that the mid-size B2B events I had made were actually what the industry wanted as the alternative. They wanted these smaller spaces to connect and do business. I’m seeing a trend where these massive conventions of hundreds of thousands of people have their drawbacks. They’re very difficult, to some extent, to scale to that size, and there is definitely a market for a more mid-size event, anywhere from, let’s call it 5,000 to 50,000 people, where you’re not being slammed into a crowd. That is not a great experience if you’re spending your whole day wedged in a crowd, just shuffling between tables.
That goes counter to what we’re trying to build as this vision of “a theme park for gamers.” So I think we need to be very receptive and listen to what the community wants, while at the same time assessing what makes sense to the business model. But I would say it’s not an easy answer of “we just want to be the biggest with the biggest crowds.” I can tell you that is not the intent right now. It’s “how can we build the richest experience?” And maybe that means at one point it becomes exclusive to a set number of tickets, and once they’re sold out, they’re sold out. But I think having the ability to make that decision and control is very important. It’s not about just reaching max capacity all the time.
I think that’s a great answer, and a very honest and mature answer. This year, especially, Fan Expo Canada got a lot of criticism for that. It’s always been packed, but this year, there were many overcrowding concerns and complaints. So, approaching VGLX with the right sort of mindset and managed scope is very smart.
Lepine: I believe in thinking long-term for the consumer. They trust us with their time. They trust us with their money. If they’re coming out for a weekend or a day at VGLX, it’s saying, “We trust you, we’re going to give you our time and our money.” And we have to reward that trust and, hopefully, build a long-term loyalty and relationship with the attendees that they can continue to trust us in building what the gaming community here wants to see in Toronto and the Greater Toronto Area.
This interview has been edited for language, clarity and length.
VGLX runs Oct. 24 and 25 at the International Centre. Tickets start at $20 and are available on the official VGLX website. You can also use our community discount code MOBILESYRUPVGLX26 to get 15 per cent off.

articles.title: Meta launches an open-weight AI model that runs on Macs | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Meta has launched what it calls the “most capable” open-weight model in the United States. Dubbed Muse Spark Open, the model also has the distinction of having been designed to work with Macs.
The new model, which leverages 816 billion parameters and a 1 million token context window, claims to offer superior performance to other popular open-weight models, according to evaluation results released by Meta on Thursday.
Muse Spark Open is natively multimodal and built for complex coding tasks and agentic labor. It has also been designed to run locally on Apple’s computers. However, you will still need a lot of power to run the model locally, with a requirement of at least 1 terabyte of RAM, per Engadget. The model will run best via the Mac Studio that comes equipped with the M5 Ultra chip.
Still, if you can muster the memory, Muse Spark Open may prove a significant work horse for coding and other desktop tasks. Meta says that it paired the model with Muse Code, its AI coding terminal, and deployed it to various agentic workflows, including coding fixes for a Mastodon client that included “bug fixes, new features, [and] full build.”
The company says it also deployed it in the service of running DaVinci Resolve, the high-end video editing software, revealing that the model was capable of reviewing and cropping footage.
Open-weight models provide a number of distinct industry advantages that aren’t afforded by closed and proprietary models. Open-weight models can be significantly more cost-efficient and can also offer transparency and flexibility that closed source models don’t allow.
Meta is making the new model available now through a number of different API platforms.

articles.title: Strengthening Advanced-Node Interconnects Through Automated Via Insertion
articles.text:
Short-resilient via insertion improves reliability and performance.
As the semiconductor industry pushes deeper into the sub-5nm realm, the physical design landscape has shifted from being dominated by gate delays to being defined by interconnect performance. In modern system-on-chip (SoC) designs, the wiring that connects billions of transistors has become the primary bottleneck for power, performance, and area (PPA). Among the various components of the interconnect stack, vias – the vertical connections between metal layers – represent one of the most significant points of vulnerability.
At advanced process nodes, via resistance increases exponentially as dimensions shrink. This rising resistance, coupled with higher current densities, exacerbates challenges related to electromigration (EM) and IR drop. Traditionally, design teams addressed these issues during the final signoff phase, often resulting in late-stage engineering change orders (ECOs) that could delay a project by weeks. To maintain aggressive time-to-market schedules while ensuring long-term silicon reliability, a new approach is required: shifting signoff-aware interconnect optimization into the implementation phase.
To understand the need for automated via optimization, first consider the physical challenges at play. In a typical advanced-node interconnect, the resistance of a single via can be significantly higher than that of a corresponding length of metal wire. As current flows through these narrow vertical structures, the resulting heat and atomic displacement can lead to electromigration – the gradual movement of metal atoms that eventually creates voids or shorts.
Plus, the cumulative effect of via resistance across a massive power delivery network (PDN) leads to IR drop. If the voltage reaching a logic gate falls below a certain threshold, the gate’s switching speed slows down, potentially leading to timing failures. In the worst cases, the gate may fail to switch entirely.
Historically, designers mitigated these risks by manually adding redundant vias to critical signal paths and power grids. The redundant vias provide parallel paths for current, lowering the effective resistance and reducing the current density through any single via. However, at 5nm and below, the sheer density of the layout and the complexity of foundry design rules make manual insertion practically impossible. Figure 1 illustrates the problem.
Fig. 1: The increasing complexity of advanced-node layouts requires automated solutions to identify valid locations for redundant via insertion without violating foundry rules.
Most place-and-route (P&R) tools include basic capabilities for via redundancy. However, these routers are primarily optimized for connectivity and timing closure, not for the exhaustive reliability enhancement required for high-performance silicon. Router-based via insertion typically comes with several limitations:
To overcome these hurdles, many design teams adopt a “shift-left” methodology that uses signoff-quality engines earlier in the design cycle. By integrating the same logic used for final verification into the enhancement process, designers can achieve “correct-by-construction” results that are guaranteed to pass final signoff.
The shift-left approach to via optimization involves a specialized enhancement platform that operates on the design database during the implementation phase. This platform reads standard design formats – such as LEF/DEF or OASIS – and applies a multi-step process to strengthen the interconnect.
The first step is a comprehensive analysis of the existing layout to identify every potential location where a redundant via could be placed. This is not a simple proximity check; the tool must account for complex multi-patterning constraints, voltage-aware spacing rules, and enclosure requirements. By leveraging a signoff-grade geometry engine, the tool can navigate these constraints with a level of precision that far exceeds traditional routers.
Once the valid insertion points are identified, the tool strategically adds redundant vias to the user-selected nets. This can be applied globally to the entire power grid or targeted toward specific high-priority signal nets, such as clock trees or long-distance bus lines. The result is a layout that is significantly more robust, with lower overall resistance and improved EM margins.
Fig. 2: By moving signoff-aware optimization into the implementation phase, design teams can resolve interconnect issues before they become late-stage bottlenecks.
One of the most innovative aspects of modern automated enhancement is the ability to handle “dirty” or incomplete layout data. A typical design database is rarely perfectly clean during the implementation flow. Localized shorts, routing overlaps, or incomplete power grid definitions are common as the design matures.
Traditional optimization tools often fail when encountering these imperfections, either crashing or producing illegal layout modifications. A robust enhancement platform must be “short-resilient.” This means the tool can identify regions with existing connectivity conflicts and automatically designate them as keep-out areas (Figure 3).
Fig. 3: Short-resilient DE-Via flow; avoiding insertion on identified short-prone regions.
By protecting these suspicious regions, the tool can continue to optimize the rest of the design. This lets design teams run via enhancement early and often, even before the layout is fully DRC-clean. This iterative approach is essential for maintaining productivity in a fast-paced design environment, as it prevents minor layout issues from stalling the overall reliability enhancement of the chip.
The technical benefits of automated via insertion are most evident in the power delivery network. In high-performance SoCs, the PDN must deliver massive amounts of current with minimal voltage drop. As the number of metal layers increases, the vertical resistance through the via stacks becomes a dominant contributor to the total IR drop.
By maximizing the number of vias in the PDN, automated enhancement significantly lowers the vertical impedance of the grid. This leads to a more uniform voltage distribution across the die, providing more timing margin for the logic gates. In many cases, this enhancement can be the difference between meeting a performance target and having to down-clock the final product.
From an EM perspective, additional vias provide a critical safety net. Electromigration is a statistical phenomenon; while a single via might be designed to handle a specific current, manufacturing variations can lead to localized “hot spots” where the current density exceeds the safe limit. By providing parallel paths, automated insertion ensures that the current is distributed more evenly, reducing the likelihood of a catastrophic failure over the lifetime of the device.
As SoC designs grow to include billions of transistors and tens of kilometers of wiring, the scalability of the enhancement platform becomes vital. The tool must be able to process massive data volumes quickly enough to fit within a standard overnight implementation run. This requires a highly parallelized architecture that can distribute the layout analysis and insertion tasks across hundreds of CPU cores.
Furthermore, the platform must integrate seamlessly into the existing EDA ecosystem. By supporting standard industry formats and providing clear reporting on the enhancements made, the tool allows designers to maintain full control over their layouts. The ability to run “what-if” scenarios – such as testing the impact of different via densities on IR drop – provides designers with the insights needed to make informed trade-offs between PPA and reliability.
In the advanced-node era, the distinction between implementation and verification is blurring. The challenges of 5nm, 3nm, and beyond require that signoff awareness be present at every stage of the design cycle. Automated via insertion is a prime example of how this shift-left methodology can provide tangible benefits in terms of silicon reliability and schedule predictability.
By automating a traditionally manual and error-prone process, design teams can focus their efforts on higher-level architectural innovations, secure in the knowledge that their interconnects are built on a foundation of signoff-verified robustness. As interconnect challenges continue to mount, the adoption of automated, signoff-aware enhancement platforms will become not just an advantage, but a necessity for any team aiming to deliver high-performance silicon in the modern era.

articles.title: Hackers exploit Collabora RCE flaw to backdoor Nextcloud servers
articles.text:
Threat actors are exploiting a critical command execution flaw, now tracked as CVE-2026-110447, in the Collabora Online - Built-in CODE Server app (richdocumentscode) for Nextcloud.
Multiple administrator reports indicate that attacks began in mid-September, roughly a month before the formal security bulletin, the GitHub advisory, and CVE publication.
CVE-2026-110447 impacts richdocumentscode versions before 26.4.303 and resides in the Nextcloud app’s mechanism for starting the bundled Collabora server.
The flaw affects only the optional built-in CODE server app. Standalone Collabora Online servers, Docker and RPM/DEB installations, and Nextcloud All-in-One deployments remain unaffected, according to Collabora.
The attacks involve sending a malicious request to the app’s proxy.php endpoint, triggering OS command injection.
A key prerequisite for successful exploitation is that the built-in CODE server must be stopped (e.g., after a restart, upgrade, crash). Authentication or user interaction is not required.
System administrators impacted by malicious activity reported attacks against multiple endpoints dating back to September 10.
According to the reports, the attacker planted PHP webshells and used them to search for password databases, password manager artifacts, and cryptocurrency wallets.
Some users also reported that ransomware operators are exploiting the flaw, but BleepingComputer could not independently confirm this.
System administrators are recommended to upgrade to version 26.4.303 or later, or remove the server app if not needed. The vendor warned that disabling the app is insufficient.
Beyond the mid-September warnings from maintainers, a community warning was also published on October 3, urging administrators to update immediately due to ongoing exploitation.
However, the lack of a CVE ID made it more difficult for administrators to pinpoint the issue correctly and implement efficient defenses.
A study from cybersecurity company Second Security illustrates the gap between security fixes and formal vulnerability notifications.
The firm analyzed real-world examples from open-source flaws and found that the median interval between public fixes and CVE publication was 39 days in August, up from 5.1 days in January.
The researchers suggest that growing volumes of AI-assisted vulnerability discoveries are straining CVE processing and contributing to publication delays.
In many cases, the researchers found public exploit code emerged online within hours of a security fix and several days before the corresponding CVE was published.
Second Security notes that the use of AI tools makes it easy for attackers to generate working exploits for published fixes.
In Collabora’s case, the fix was committed on September 9, and version 26.4.303 was released on September 11. The advisory and CVE were published on October 14, a gap of more than four weeks.
BleepingComputer contacted Nextcloud with questions about its response to the malicious activity reports, as well as details about the attacks and the number of impacted systems.
Nextcloud told BleepingComputer that Collabora reported the vulnerability in mid-September and that an update became available through the app store.
The company justified the disclosure delay by saying it gave users time to update and that it had not observed widespread exploitation.
In a blog post earlier today about the activity, Collabora attributed the delayed announcement primarily to GitHub CVE-processing backlogs, which it said were under strain from increasing volumes of AI-driven security reports.

articles.title: ‘We cannot wait 75 years’: ANRF CEO Shivkumar Kalyanaraman on scaling India’s research multiplier
articles.text:
‘We cannot wait 75 years’: ANRF CEO Shivkumar Kalyanaraman on scaling India’s research multiplier
To boost India’s R&D spend toward 3% of GDP, ANRF CEO Shivkumar Kalyanaraman revealed a patient-capital architecture combining private investment, open IP licensing, and national mission programmes.
India cannot afford to replicate the 75-year evolutionary timelines of Western institutions like the US National Science Foundation or DARPA, according to Shivkumar Kalyanaraman, Chief Executive Officer of the Anusandhan National Research Foundation.
Speaking at TechSparks 2026, YourStory’s annual summit, Kalyanaraman made it clear that under an impatient Prime Minister, the organisation must bypass traditional bureaucratic friction and drive scientific discovery into the real economy at unprecedented speed.
Describing the foundation as an institutional startup, Kalyanaraman outlined how the nation is altering its approach to scientific research and technology commercialisation. Formalised by parliament in 2023 following recommendations in the National Education Policy 2020, the foundation operates as an autonomous statutory body presided over by the Prime Minister of India.
The organisation was established to transform the country into a global innovation powerhouse by linking higher education, private industry, venture capital, and global philanthropy, ensuring rapid funding flows from foundational research to market implementation.
Patient capital
At the centre of this financial transformation is the Research, Development, and Innovation fund, a government-backed pool of Rs 1 lakh crore. Designed as a patient capital instrument, the fund provides long-term financial support tailored to research-intensive and deep-tech enterprises that require extended gestation periods without demanding immediate short-term returns.
Instead of disbursing capital directly to individual businesses, the foundation acts as an apex funding architecture that routes money through secondary fund managers.
Under this fund-of-funds structure, an initial allocation is provided to nineteen selected fund managers and specialised statutory entities, which in turn attract additional private investment. This arrangement creates a financial multiplier expanding capital reaching real-world technology ventures.
“This is a patient capital fund and our Rs 1 lakh crore of government money or taxpayer money will catalyse a lot more anywhere from Rs 5 to 10 lakh crores by the time it hits the real economy,” he said.
To complement government allocations, the foundation aggregates corporate social responsibility grants, diaspora contributions, and global philanthropic partnerships.
The ultimate objective is to raise national expenditure on research and development from sub 1% of gross domestic product to 3% or more through a compound annual growth rate of 20 to 25%.
Democratising excellence
Beyond commercial capital, the foundation addresses structural imbalances across the higher education sector. Historically, advanced scientific research in India remained concentrated within a small cluster of elite institutions, such as the Indian Institutes of Technology and the Indian Institute of Science.
Pointing to the need for broader participation, Kalyanaraman noted, “India has a very tiny sliver of institutions that are deep in R&D and deep in the excellence of R&D. So, we would like to broaden this distribution, but our goal is not just to throw money at different places, but to really broaden the distribution of excellence.”
To achieve wider distribution without lowering standards, the foundation launched the Partnerships for Accelerated Innovation and Research initiative. This framework uses a hub-and-spoke mentorship structure in which top-tier research universities guide regional institutions from Kashmir to Nagaland.
To ensure academic research yields practical benefits, the foundation established targeted sectoral initiatives known as Maha programmes covering electric mobility, medical devices, space technology, artificial intelligence for science, drones, water security, and critical minerals.
A major bottleneck in commercialisation has been transferring intellectual property from universities to commercial startups. To resolve this, discoveries under programmes like artificial intelligence for science are released under open licensing frameworks derived from the MIT licence model, allowing startups to rapidly adopt university research and de-risk laboratory discoveries at regional translational test facilities.

articles.title: El caso de “la más celosa de Reino Unido”: le compraba consolas a su esposo para alejarlo de otras mujeres
articles.text:
Debbi Wood, una mujer de Leicester, Inglaterra, se convirtió en 2024 en noticia mundial al revelarse que utilizaba parte de los más de 100.000 dólares que recibía en beneficios estatales para comprarle consolas de videojuegos a su esposo con el objetivo de mantenerlo alejado de otras mujeres.
El caso, conocido ahora como el de “la más celosa de Reino Unido”, reflejó las consecuencias extremas de un trastorno psiquiátrico poco difundido. La estrategia formaba parte de un patrón de conductas que medios británicos calificaron como tóxicas y que convirtieron a la pareja en protagonista recurrente de programas de televisión y portadas de diarios locales e internacionales.
Quién es Debbi Wood y cómo surgió el apodo
Wood, de 43 años, y su esposo Steve Wood, de 32, saltaron a la fama después de aparecer en el programa británico This Morning, donde Debbi admitió someter a su pareja a pruebas periódicas con un detector de mentiras cada vez que salía de la casa.
La práctica comenzó luego de que Steve, en tono de broma, dijera que estaba dispuesto a tomar una prueba de este tipo para demostrar su fidelidad. Debbi tomó la frase al pie de la letra y compró el dispositivo.
A esa medida se sumaron otras formas de control que la pareja detalló públicamente a lo largo de los años:
- Revisión constante del teléfono, el correo electrónico y los estados de cuenta bancarios de su esposo.
- Instalación de filtros infantiles en la computadora y el celular de Steve para impedir que viera imágenes de mujeres.
- Prohibición de ver programas de televisión con presencia femenina, incluido el concurso The Weakest Link, conducido por Anne Robinson.
- Compra de tres consolas de videojuegos como estrategia para mantener ocupado a su esposo y reducir el tiempo que pasaba fuera de casa o en contacto con otras personas.
Steve relató que, a raíz de estas restricciones, “probablemente pasamos más de la mitad del día jugando”, y mencionó entre sus títulos favoritos “Gran Turismo” y “Call of Duty”.
El origen del dinero y las críticas públicas
Wood recibía entonces alrededor de 1.500 dólares mensuales en concepto de apoyo de ingresos, movilidad, discapacidad y beneficios de vivienda, otorgados por el Estado británico debido a una condición de movilidad reducida vinculada con el sobrepeso.
Ante los cuestionamientos sobre el uso de esos fondos, la mujer defendió su postura: “He pagado al sistema, tengo derecho a recibir las cosas que recibimos. Mi discapacidad, mi subsidio de cuidado, mi apoyo a los ingresos. No puedes darte la vuelta y decirle a alguien: ‘Oh, porque eres obeso es tu culpa’. No fue culpa mía que subiera de peso”, sostuvo.
El diagnóstico detrás de la conducta
Con el paso del tiempo se reveló que los celos extremos de Wood respondían al Síndrome de Otelo, un trastorno psiquiátrico que lleva a quienes lo padecen a convencerse de que su pareja les es infiel, incluso sin ninguna prueba que lo sustente.
El nombre del síndrome proviene del personaje de la obra de Shakespeare que asesina a su esposa tras sospechar, de forma infundada, que lo había engañado. Especialistas señalan que la condición puede tratarse mediante terapia y medicación.
Wood atribuyó el origen de su inseguridad a una relación traumática anterior que le dejó secuelas de desconfianza. En busca de una solución, anunció que se sometería a una cirugía financiada por el sistema de salud público, con un costo cercano a los 3.000 dólares, con la expectativa de perder diez kilos y reducir así el nivel de ansiedad que, según explicó, alimentaba sus sospechas constantes sobre una posible infidelidad de su esposo.
A pesar de las restricciones impuestas dentro del matrimonio, Steve sostuvo en distintas apariciones públicas que la relación funcionaba bien fuera de los episodios de celos: “Cuando no estamos discutiendo por esto, nuestra relación es absolutamente increíble”, afirmó.
La exposición mediática de la pareja, lejos de resolver el conflicto, funcionó como un espejo de cuánto cuesta todavía reconocer los celos patológicos como un problema de salud mental y no como un simple rasgo de carácter.

articles.title: Frigos de supermarchés piratés : Claude a reproduit la cyberattaque en 28 minutes
articles.text:
La cyberattaque contre les frigos des supermarchés français était à la portée de n’importe quel hacker. Les chercheurs de Claroty, l’entreprise de cybersécurité israélo-américaine, ont d’ailleurs réussi à reproduire la même attaque avec Claude, l’IA d’Anthropic. Il n’a fallu que 28 minutes à l’intelligence artificielle pour prendre le contrôle d’un système de refroidissement et activer la fonction de dégivrage à distance.
Le test a été mené sur un contrôleur de Danfoss, la marque danoise qui équipe les frigos de milliers de supermarchés. Ce sont les dispositifs électroniques de ce groupe qui ont été piratés dans le cadre de la cyberattaque nationale à l’encontre d’Intermarché, Leclerc, Carrefour ou encore Netto. Évidemment, l’appareil était déconnecté d’Internet afin que le test se déroule sans le moindre dégât.
« On se rend compte qu’il n’est plus nécessaire d’avoir des compétences poussées », explique Amir Preminger, directeur technique de Claroty, à La Tribune, qui relaie les découvertes des chercheurs.
À lire aussi : Cyberattaque nationale : pourquoi les pirates s’attaquent maintenant aux supermarchés ?
Une attaque à la portée de n’importe quel hacker
Avec l’aide de l’IA, un pirate peut automatiser toute l’attaque. Il n’a pas besoin de développer des compétences en informatique ou en piratage pour arriver à ses fins. « Il y a deux ans, on se serait forcément penché sur la piste d’un acte commis avec beaucoup de moyens », souligne Amir Preminger. Le chercheur précise que le modèle d’IA utilisé dans le test n’était même pas la version la plus récente de Claude. Bref, l’attaque était vraiment à la portée de tout le monde. Il suffisait d’avoir accès à un modèle de langage.
Plusieurs experts interrogés par 01net abondent dans le même sens. Pour Samuel Hassine, PDG de Filigran, « ce n’est pas une attaque sophistiquée ». En effet, « la barrière d’entrée est très basse, donc le nombre d’acteurs capables de le faire est très élevé ». C’est pourquoi il est difficile de déterminer d’où vient l’offensive. « Trouver et exploiter ce type de faille n’est plus si complexe aujourd’hui », nous confirme Romain Ponceau, directeur général d’Opinion Act. Selon lui, les attaquants profitent surtout de « l’absence de correctifs sur des équipements que l’on peut facilement trouver en ligne ».
Une faille divulguée depuis des mois
La faille exploitée n’avait d’ailleurs rien d’un secret. Elle se situe dans le mécanisme de secours, baptisé « code du jour », des contrôleurs Danfoss. Chaque jour, le boîtier génère un mot de passe administrateur temporaire, calculé uniquement à partir de la date et de l’heure internes. En réalisant le même calcul, un pirate peut ouvrir se connecter à l’appareil sans connaître le véritable mot de passe. L’attaquant est ensuite libre de lancer le dégivrage, et de porter la température au-delà des 50 degrés.
Notez que Claroty a divulgué cette faille de sécurité en août 2026, soit deux mois avant la cyberattaque. Danfoss a publié un correctif, mais estime que certains appareils sont trop anciens pour être mis à jour. Par ailleurs, la société française Synacktiv a signalé des vulnérabilités analogues trois ans plus tôt. Kevin Tellier, chercheur chez Synacktiv, se souvient d’un constructeur plutôt réactif. Danfoss avait « pris en compte, sous quinze jours, le rapport que nous lui avions soumis », explique-t-il à 01net. La vulnérabilité avait ensuite été rendue publique sur le site du fabricant.
« Les systèmes affectés n’étant plus pris en charge par le constructeur, Danfoss nous a indiqué avoir notifié les clients concernés et leur avoir recommandé d’isoler les équipements vulnérables », précise le chercheur.
Des milliers de frigos encore exposés
Amir Preminger souligne que de nombreuses interfaces de pilotage des frigos Danfoss ou Dixell, l’autre constructeur piraté dans le cadre de la cyberattaque, sont exposées sur Internet, à la portée du premier pirate venu. La France en compte des milliers. C’est même le pays le plus exposé, estiment les chercheurs. Selon Claroty, de nombreuses interfaces sont toujours en ligne, même si certains distributeurs ont commencé à les retirer à la suite de la cyberattaque nationale.
Romain Ponceau redoute aussi un « effet d’imitation » à très court terme. En clair, d’autres cybercriminels pourraient vouloir se connecter aux frigos de supermarchés à distance. Le directeur général d’Opinion Act évoque par ailleurs la présence hypothétique de « programmes malveillants dormants, capables de s’activer même si les équipements ont été déconnectés ». Sur le papier, les pirates pourraient frapper ultérieurement, sans devoir se reconnecter aux appareils via Internet. Selon lui, les attaques pourraient aussi s’étendre « aux étiquettes électroniques (bloquant la mise à jour des prix), aux caméras de vidéosurveillance ou aux systèmes logistiques ». L’Agence nationale de la sécurité des systèmes d’information (ANSSI) appelle toutes les entités concernées à corriger les failles et à ne plus exposer d’équipements sur Internet. Gageons que la grande distribution puisse agir avant que des pirates ne repassent à l’action.

articles.title: Tamron 16-50mm F2.8 A : un zoom lumineux, polyvalent et compact pour les hybrides APS-C
articles.text:
Tamron 16-50mm F2.8 A : un zoom lumineux, polyvalent et compact pour les hybrides APS-C
Tamron vient de dévoiler un 16-50 mm f/2,8 destiné aux hybrides APS-C Sony, Canon, Nikon et Fujifilm. Avec son ouverture constante, son grand-angle et son prix contenu, ce zoom Tamron 16-50mm F2.8 A se veut super polyvalent pour moins de 500 €.
Les zooms fournis avec les appareils photo permettent de débuter à moindre coût, mais leur ouverture limitée et leur qualité optique peut vite donner envie de passer à autre chose. Avec son nouveau 16-50mm F2.8 A, Tamron veut ainsi proposer une optique lumineuse, très polyvalente, plus compacte que le 17-70mm F2.8 de la marque, et à bon rapport qualité-prix !
Un zoom 16-50 mm à ouverture constante f/2,8
Conçu pour les capteurs APS-C, ce Tamron offre un cadrage équivalent à un 24-75 mm en plein format sur les boîtiers Sony, Nikon et Fujifilm, et à un 25,6-80 mm chez Canon. Une plage polyvalente, qui permet de passer d’une vue d’ensemble à un portrait sans changer d’objectif.
Son deuxième intérêt réside aussi dans son ouverture maximale f/2,8, conservée sur toute la plage de zoom. Par rapport à un objectif de kit moins lumineux, elle permet de limiter la montée en sensibilité ou d’utiliser une vitesse plus rapide lorsque la lumière vient à manquer. Elle facilite également le détachement du sujet sur un arrière-plan flou, particulièrement à fond de zoom.
Un autofocus VXD dans un objectif de 305 g
Tamron annonce une longueur de seulement 79,6 mm en monture Sony E, pour un poids de 305 g. Les versions Canon RF et Fujifilm X affichent la même masse, tandis que la déclinaison Nikon Z atteint 315 g.
La mise au point repose sur une motorisation linéaire VXD, que le fabricant promet rapide et discrète. La distance minimale de mise au point descend à 15 cm au grand-angle et à 29 cm au téléobjectif, pour photographier de petits sujets de près. La construction bénéficie également de joints contre l’humidité et d’un traitement fluoré sur la lentille avant pour faciliter son nettoyage.
Côté vidéo, les versions Sony E et Nikon Z sont compatibles avec Tamron Lens Utility pour accéder à des fonctions de personnalisation. Attention toutefois aux différences entre montures : la version Canon RF se limite actuellement aux mises à jour du micrologiciel, tandis que le modèle Fujifilm X n’est pas compatible avec l’application.
Prix et disponibilité du Tamron 16-50mm F2.8 A
Le Tamron 16-50mm F2.8 A est proposé à partir de 470 €, un tarif très intéressant vu la configuration proposée. La commercialisation est échelonnée sur cette fin d’année : les premières livraisons sont annoncées pour le 29 octobre 2026 en montures Sony E et Canon RF, puis le 19 novembre en Nikon Z et le 17 décembre en Fujifilm X.

articles.title: Netflix supprime 1 000 emplois : derrière les licenciements, un malaise plus profond
articles.text:
Netflix vient d’annoncer la suppression d’environ 1 000 emplois, sa plus importante vague de licenciements depuis 2022. Derrière cette décision, le géant du streaming doit composer avec une croissance de son audience qui peine à suivre celle de ses revenus.
Netflix continue de gagner des milliards, mais cela ne l’empêche pas de sortir la calculatrice. Mercredi 14 octobre, le géant du streaming a annoncé une vaste réorganisation qui se traduira par la suppression de près de 6 % de ses effectifs. Une décision surprenante pour une entreprise qui enchaîne les résultats financiers solides, mais dont les perspectives de croissance inquiètent de plus en plus les investisseurs. Les licenciements ne touchent d’ailleurs pas seulement les équipes administratives ou techniques. Plusieurs responsables des productions cinématographiques et télévisées quittent également la plateforme, signe que Netflix revoit certaines de ses priorités. Et derrière ces coupes, une question commence à se poser : comment continuer à faire grandir un service qui compte déjà des centaines de millions d’abonnés ?
Netflix taille dans ses effectifs, jusque dans ses équipes de production
Selon les informations de Reuters, qui a consulté une communication interne, Netflix supprime environ 1 000 emplois, soit 6 % de ses effectifs. Les équipes chargées des produits, des technologies, des ressources humaines et des affaires juridiques sont principalement concernées.
Dans leur message aux salariés, les codirecteurs généraux Ted Sarandos et Greg Peters expliquent vouloir concentrer les ressources de l’entreprise sur les activités présentant le plus fort potentiel. Netflix assure néanmoins maintenir ses objectifs financiers pour l'année.
La réorganisation touche aussi les contenus. D’après le média spécialisé TheWrap, Doug Belgrad, vice-président de la division cinéma et proche collaborateur du responsable des films Dan Lin, figure parmi les départs. Sheroum Kim, chargée des productions indépendantes, est également concernée.
Du côté des séries, plusieurs responsables quittent leurs fonctions, notamment Carolina Garcia, qui avait travaillé sur Stranger Things, ainsi qu’Andrew McQuinn et Lisa Lang McMullen. Des départs qui témoignent de l’ampleur de la réorganisation, même s’ils ne permettent pas, à eux seuls, d’affirmer que Netflix prépare un changement radical dans sa politique de production.
La plateforme avait déjà commencé à revoir ses relations avec certains grands noms du cinéma. Ces nouvelles suppressions de postes interviennent donc dans un contexte où le groupe cherche à mieux répartir ses investissements entre films, séries, événements en direct et nouvelles formes de divertissement.
Netflix gagne toujours des milliards, mais peine à capter davantage notre attention
Car Netflix n’est pas en difficulté financière. Au deuxième trimestre 2026, la plateforme a réalisé 12,56 milliards de dollars de chiffre d’affaires et environ 3,4 milliards de bénéfice net. Des résultats qui feraient rêver bien des entreprises.
Le problème est ailleurs. Dans sa dernière lettre aux actionnaires, Netflix indique que ses abonnés ont regardé plus de 97 milliards d’heures de programmes au premier semestre 2026. Un chiffre impressionnant, mais en progression de seulement 2 % sur un an.
Cette croissance reste positive, et représente même une légère accélération par rapport à 2025. Elle montre néanmoins combien il devient difficile pour Netflix d’augmenter sensiblement le temps passé sur sa plateforme, alors que ses revenus progressent beaucoup plus rapidement.
On connaissait déjà les difficultés de certaines grandes séries Netflix à conserver leur audience d’une saison à l’autre. Mais le problème dépasse désormais les seules productions originales.
La concurrence ne vient plus uniquement de Disney+, Prime Video ou HBO Max. Selon les mesures de Nielsen, YouTube représentait 14,2 % du temps passé devant un téléviseur aux États-Unis en juillet 2026, contre 7,8 % pour Netflix. Les deux plateformes ne proposent pas exactement les mêmes contenus, mais elles se disputent les mêmes heures disponibles dans la journée.
Netflix tente de trouver de nouveaux relais de croissance avec les événements sportifs, les jeux vidéo, les podcasts filmés et la publicité. Ces activités peuvent attirer de nouveaux publics ou renforcer la fidélité des abonnés, mais leur contribution à long terme reste à démontrer.
C'est tout le paradoxe de la situation. Netflix continue de prospérer, tout en cherchant à réduire ses coûts et à réorganiser ses équipes pour préserver sa croissance. Les résultats du troisième trimestre, attendus le 20 octobre, apporteront un nouvel éclairage sur ses performances. Mais ils ne régleront pas forcément son principal défi : convaincre des spectateurs déjà sollicités de toutes parts de lui consacrer encore davantage de temps.
