articles.title: Mondial de l’Auto 2026 : nos 9 coups de cœur, de l’Alpine A310 Vision à la Citroën 2CV
articles.text:
Le Mondial de l’Auto 2026, organisé du 12 au 18 octobre à Paris, semble faire du bien au cœur des automobilistes. Après deux éditions sans grande conviction à la suite du covid (surtout celle de 2022), cette année, l’ambiance est bien plus réjouissante. Les 60 marques présentes ont une foule de nouveautés à présenter au public, et elles le font en mettant les formes.
Qu’il expose des véhicules abordables ou des concepts ultra-désirables, le salon parisien ne nous a pas laissés indifférents chez Numerama. Nous étions tous les deux sur place (Raphaëlle et Robin, les deux journalistes de la rubrique Vroom de Numerama), à arpenter le salon pour découvrir les différents modèles. Et bien entendu, nous avons chacun nos petits chouchous… certains en commun, mais d’autres non !
Les coups de cœur commun
Alpine A310 Vision
- L’avis de Raphaëlle : Alpine a su garder le secret jusqu’au bout, la surprise était totale. Et clairement, le design de ce concept a fait grimper mon rythme cardiaque en flèche. Tout y est pour créer la désirabilité.
- L’avis de Robin : À défaut de montrer sa nouvelle A110, Alpine nous a mis une claque avec cette réinterprétation de l’A310. Mon coup de cœur ultime du Mondial 2026.
Denza Z
- L’avis de Raphaëlle : Même si l’on a découvert les premières images des différentes versions de la Denza Z plus tôt cet été, les voir sur le Mondial de Paris a permis de réaliser à quel point le design fonctionnait bien, autant en Coupé qu’en Spider. Entre les deux, mon cœur balance.
- L’avis de Robin : Denza a montré lors de ce Mondial qu’une voiture chinoise pouvait être spectaculaire et séduire même les plus passionnés. Mention spéciale pour la version découvrable Spider.
Smart #2
- L’avis de Raphaëlle : Une fiche technique qui tient la route pour un tout petit gabarit, et le tout à un tarif quasi 10 000 €, moins cher qu’on l’imaginait. Cette Smart #2 m’a surprise à plus d’un titre, elle est à découvrir.
- L’avis de Robin : On l’attendait depuis des lustres, la « vraie » smart est enfin de retour. Elle s’offre en prime une fiche technique intéressante.
Les coups de cœur de Raphaëlle
Citroën 2 CV Concept
Je suis apparemment bon public pour les véhicules au design néo-rétro. En dehors de la couleur extérieure qui pousse le curseur un peu trop loin à mon goût, je trouve la proposition particulièrement séduisante. Certains clins d’œil au passé sont vraiment fun (notamment le pommeau de vitesses qui sert en fait de selecteur). Reste à voir ce qui sera conservé sur la version de série, mais rapporté au prix promis de 15 000 €, Citroën frappe fort. Au passage, c’est valable également pour la version fourgonnette.
Renault Twingobay
La Renault Twingo n’est clairement pas la nouveauté du salon 2026. En revanche, l’ajout de son toit panoramique au contour arrondi était un secret bien gardé qui a créé la surprise, et ça apporte un plus à ce modèle déjà fort sympathique.
DS F3VER Concept
Mon dernier choix est également un peu spécial pour un article coup de cœur. J’apprécie le concept DS F3VER, sans pour autant l’aimer dans sa globalité. Je n’apprécie pas spécialement l’arrière du concept qui est trop chargé. En revanche, de face et de profil, j’y vois bien les lignes de ce que pourrait devenir une DS 3 de retour au format « berline compacte » (abandonnant la SUVisation du modèle).
Les coups de cœur de Robin
Lucid Gravity
Oui, j’aime les voitures chères, haut de gamme et d’un certain gabarit. Le genre de modèle que je (et une bonne partie de la population) ne peut pas se payer. Et au Mondial de Paris, il y a une marque de voitures électriques qui coche parfaitement toutes ces cases : Lucid. J’ai craqué en particulier pour le grand SUV Gravity avec son élégante teinte verte combinée à sa sellerie en cuir caramel. Mais mon détail préféré est bien son capot s’ouvrant en grand pour se transformer en mini banquette.
Peugeot RCZ Vision
Dans la folie néorétro, Peugeot a carrément sauté des décennies pour réinterpreter un modèle plutôt récent : le RCZ. C’est probablement mon concept favori ex-aequo avec l’Alpine A310. En même temps, ils portent tous les deux le suffixe « Vision », ça ne peut qu’être un signe. Plus sérieusement, étant un amateur du modèle original, je ne suis pas insensible à ces courbes délicieusement modernisées. Et que dire du fameux vitrage à double bosse, waouh !
Renault E-Space Concept
Après avoir vu les photos du dossier de presse, je n’aurais pas pensé aimer le nouveau concept star de Renault baptisé E-Space Concept. On peut dire qu’il en impose, que ce soit par ses dimensions ou sa calandre illuminée qui vient vous chatouiller la rétine. Justement c’est toute cette partie avant que je préfère, avec son grand pare-brise profilé. Le retour en force des monospaces, qui aurait pu le prédire ?

articles.title: What it takes to become an AI company: Four lessons from the top
articles.text:
What it takes to become an AI company: Four lessons from the top
Every company is under pressure to become “an AI company.” Over the past several months, we’ve been undertaking that transformation at Precisely, changing how we build, work, and measure progress.
That experience has reinforced something for me: the hardest parts of becoming an AI company have relatively little to do with the technology.
AI can help an organization move faster, automate work, increase capacity, and fundamentally change what people can accomplish. But none of those things guarantees better business performance.
“The hardest parts of becoming an AI company have relatively little to do with the technology.”
Four leadership lessons have emerged from that experience:
- Start with the business objective
- Simplify before accelerating
- Redesign how people work
- Measure the results that matter
Start with the business objective
First, clarify what the business is trying to achieve. That needs to be a business outcome: growth, faster innovation, stronger customer relationships, better products, improved margins, or something else that matters to the strategy.
AI dramatically expands what is possible. That makes focus critically important. Leaders must establish clear priorities: what needs to improve, what the organization needs to start doing, and just as importantly, what it needs to stop doing.
That clarity filters where to invest, which processes to change, and where AI can create the most value.
Without it, AI can proliferate complexity rather than reduce it. Organizations deploy more tools, launch more agents, and generate more activity without a clear connection to the business outcome they are trying to achieve.
That’s why I think of AI as an operating model, not a strategy. Strategy establishes where the business is going and why. AI can change how quickly and effectively you get there.
Simplify before you accelerate
Once the objective is clear, leaders need to examine how work gets done.
AI can make almost anything move faster. That’s both the opportunity and the problem.
Apply AI to a process that no longer adds value, and you’ve simply made a bad process run faster. Automate one step while leaving the same unnecessary approvals, handoffs, meetings, and decision points around it, and the bottleneck moves from one point to another.
“Apply AI to a process that no longer adds value, and you’ve simply made a bad process run faster.”
I’ve seen this firsthand. As AI accelerates areas like software development, constraints often shift to the processes around the work. If an engineer can generate code 4x faster, but that code still waits in the same queues and moves through the same handoffs, the organization hasn’t created 4x the value.
The entire system has to evolve.
The principle is straightforward:
Eliminate what doesn’t add value à Simplify what does à Then use AI to accelerate it
Redesign how people work
Technology alone doesn’t transform an organization. People have to change how they work.
I saw this in an unexpected place at Precisely: our summer intern program.
Our interns arrived with different levels of AI experience and different ideas about what it might mean for their careers. Over ten weeks, I watched those perceptions change. Once they could apply AI to real work, they moved faster, explored challenges more deeply, and became more confident in what they could accomplish.
What struck me most was how quickly their sense of what they were capable of changed, and how contagious that confidence became.
That experience reinforced something I believe leaders need to understand about AI: the baseline for what people can accomplish is changing. And this extends well beyond people entering the workforce.
As AI takes on more execution and routine work, people at every level have greater capacity to set direction, evaluate outputs, solve difficult problems, build relationships, and apply judgment and expertise.
“Giving employees access to AI and measuring usage will only take an organization so far. Leaders need to examine how the work itself should change.”
That has significant implications for how leaders think about jobs, skills, and development. The assumptions we have built around what a role looks like, how long it takes someone to become proficient, and what people at different career stages can contribute will have to evolve.
Workflows need to evolve, too. Giving employees access to AI and measuring usage will only take an organization so far. Leaders need to examine how the work itself should change: where AI belongs in the process, what it can take on, where human judgment remains essential, and what people can now accomplish with the capacity AI creates.
Our interns gave me an early glimpse of what that can look like. The leadership challenge is creating the conditions for that same shift to happen across the organization.
Measure what the business gets back
Finally, leaders need to be disciplined about measuring progress.
At some point, AI adoption became a business metric. Organizations track how many employees are using AI, how many agents they’ve deployed, or how many tokens they process.
Those numbers can tell you whether people are using AI. They can’t tell you whether AI is creating value.
We never measured the ROI of email. We didn’t track spreadsheet adoption or ask for weekly reports on how many documents were created in Word. We treated them as infrastructure and measured what the business did with them.
Adoption is an input, not an outcome.
Productivity should create capacity. That capacity should let teams move faster, bring ideas to market sooner, spend more time on work that requires judgment and expertise, and create better customer experiences. Those gains then need to translate into growth and stronger business performance.
“Adoption is an input, not an outcome. The greater opportunity is expanding what an organization can accomplish with the people and expertise it already has.”
That’s why I believe leaders should see AI as an opportunity to do more with the same, not as an opportunity to do more with less.
If your AI strategy focuses on headcount reduction, you’re treating AI as an efficiency tool. That can reduce costs in the short term, but it doesn’t provide long-term value. The greater opportunity is expanding what an organization can accomplish with the people and expertise it already has.
The leadership challenge ahead
I’m optimistic about what AI will mean for work.
Technology has always changed what people do and raised the ceiling on what they can accomplish. AI is accelerating that pattern.
But simply having the technology won’t create competitive advantage.
The differentiator will be how organizations use it.
That means staying focused on the business objective, eliminating complexity before accelerating it, redesigning work around what people and AI can accomplish together, and holding the transformation accountable to business results.
The true measure of AI is what your business can now do that it couldn’t do before.

articles.title: Malatsi: SA’s AI policy scandal ‘cannot be allowed to slide’
articles.text:
Five months after fabricated academic references forced South Africa to withdraw its draft national artificial intelligence (AI) policy, one of the two officials suspended over the scandal has resigned. Disciplinary proceedings against the other communications department staffer are still under way.
Solly Malatsi, South Africa’s communications minister, says the government remains confident that Cabinet will finalise the replacement AI policy before the end of March 2027, with public consultation expected to begin in April.
But the unfinished disciplinary process leaves questions about accountability for a scandal that embarrassed a government seeking to position South Africa as a continental leader in AI governance.
Malatsi told TechCabal in an interview on Thursday that the department could not allow the incident to pass without consequences, acknowledging the damage caused by AI-generated material use that went undetected during the AI policy’s preparation.
“Having such a major stain on an important policy is something that cannot just be allowed to slide,” he said.
The minister confirmed that the department suspended two officials for failing to disclose AI use in preparing material that contributed to fabricated references appearing in the policy.
“The appropriate processes were followed, and two officials were suspended,” Malatsi said. “The ongoing processes now relate to the one official who remains an employee of the department.”
In May, TechCabal reported that South Africa withdrew its draft AI policy after fictitious academic references were discovered. The setback triggered renewed scrutiny over how generative AI is used in policymaking and exposed weaknesses in government oversight.
Malatsi said the department’s director-general acted after he instructed that those responsible be held accountable.
“It was clear that there had been non-disclosure around the use of AI, which contributed to the hallucinations that emerged in the policy,” he said.
The minister described the withdrawal as necessary despite the damage it caused to the government’s policymaking process.
At CollectiveXchange 2026, a national digital skills and jobs summit, in Johannesburg earlier on Thursday, Malatsi acknowledged that the process had experienced a “false start.” He stressed that the government was working to complete its internal processes before opening the replacement policy to public consultation.
“Yes, it is very late, and that is the consequence of having a false start,” he told delegates.
However, Malatsi rejected the suggestion in the interview with TechCabal that the government had introduced a new deadline for the AI policy. He said the January 2027 reference and the end of the 2026/27 financial year were not separate dates, while reiterating his confidence that the policy would be finalised by the end of March.
The timetable places responsibility on the independent AI review panel team led by Professor Benjamin Rosman of the Machine Intelligence and Neural Discovery Institute at the University of the Witwatersrand to restore confidence in the policy after the original draft’s credibility collapsed.
Malatsi said the panel had been working at pace and that he remained confident it would deliver a draft Cabinet could finalise. When the AI policy enters public consultation, he said, government departments would have made inputs, followed by engagement with civil society, residents, the private sector and other stakeholders.
The replacement policy will need to address more than the failures exposed by the citation scandal. Despite the fabricated citations, Malatsi said the withdrawn draft contained credible provisions, including protections for South Africans’ rights and dignity online.
“As unfortunate as the withdrawal of the policy was, it was necessary given the stain that it had,” he stated. “Much of the policy’s substance was credible, and everyone who has engaged with it has acknowledged that.”
The minister also pointed to the need for safeguards governing the ethical use of AI, including avenues for redress when the technology is used improperly.
“The important thing for us is to ensure that when we create a regime for the ethical use and ethical adoption of AI, where the use is not ethical, there’s got to be an avenue for recourse,” he said.

articles.title: Los expertos lo tienen claro: "Los que beben café tienen un microbioma intestinal más diverso que los que no beben café"
articles.text:
Durante años, la ciencia ha intentado desentrañar los secretos del café, buscando justificar nuestro 'amor' por tomar a diario esta bebida que a veces ha sido demonizada. Y es que, entre los muchos beneficios que tiene, destaca uno que se está investigando ahora mucho mejor, y hablamos justamente de la alteración que hace sobre nuestra microbiota. Pero casi siempre para nuestro bien.
Unas bacterias. El gran protagonista de esta historia es un estudio publicado en el año 2024 en el que participó el conocido epidemiólogo genético Tim Spector. En este se analizaron datos de más de 22.000 participantes en Estados Unidos y Reino Unido, integrándolos con datos públicos de más de 54.000 personas.
Y el resultado apuntaba a que existe una asociación muy fuerte entre el consumo de café y la presencia de la bacteria Lawsonibacter asaccharolyticus en nuestros intestinos. Y es que esta especie bacteriana era entre 4,5 y 8 veces más abundante en quienes bebían café.
Lo interesante es que este efecto no depende de la cafeína, sino que se ha visto que la bacteria crece más rápido con café descafeinado, apuntando a que la clave podría estar en los polifenoles o en metabolitos como el ácido quínico y la trigonelina que está presente en esta bebida.
Pero hay un matiz muy importante, puesto que de momento no conocemos efectivamente si este cambio en la microbiota es algo positivo para nosotros, puesto que sigue bajo investigación.
El café para el microbioma. La idea de que el café es un alimento clave para el microbioma humano no es nueva, puesto que ya en 2021 se apuntaba en esta dirección. En este caso, al analizar más de 150 alimentos, encontraron que el café era el que mostraba una mayor correlación con la composición del microbioma en unas 1.000 personas.
Aunque hay detractores, ya que otras investigaciones nos apuntan a que el café altera poblaciones microbianas concretas, pero no cambia la diversidad global de la microbiota. Es decir, cambia el "quién es quién" del intestino, pero no necesariamente hace que haya más variedad.
La fibra. Otro argumento frecuentemente esgrimido a favor del café es su contenido en fibra, y se ha llegado a afirmar que una taza de café tiene más fibra que un vaso de zumo de naranja. Esta idea proviene de un estudio de 2007, que encontró que el café preparado contiene entre 0,47 y 0,75 g de fibra soluble por 100 ml, siendo el café soluble aún más rico en fibra. De aquí sale la famosa cifra de "1,5 g por taza" que menciona Spector. Sin embargo, el propio investigador español advirtió de que no está demostrado que esta fibra específica tenga los mismos beneficios para la salud que la fibra de frutas o verduras.
Salud cardiovascular. Más allá del microbioma, nos encontramos con un estudio publicado en 2022 que analizó a casi medio millón de personas durante 12,5 años. En este se encontró que el consumo de café, especialmente entre 2 y 3 tazas al día, se asociaba con reducciones significativas de enfermedades cardiovasculares y mortalidad.
Por otro lado, una revisión general concluyó que el mayor descenso en el riesgo de diversas enfermedades aparece con un consumo de 3 a 4 tazas diarias. Sin embargo, los autores señalan que se necesitan ensayos aleatorizados para confirmar si estas asociaciones son causales y recomiendan precaución durante el embarazo y en mujeres con alto riesgo de fracturas.

articles.title: Anthropic ditched Git for its own version control system because Claude is writing too much code
articles.text:
First look: Anthropic has replaced Git in its main code repository as AI-generated changes outpaced the infrastructure built to manage them. The new system, called "Scion," moves most source-control operations to servers, reducing the amount of data that agents and automated jobs must download.
Anthropic detailed the system in a recent engineering post, reporting that it averaged about 2,500 merged code changes a day in May. By September, that figure exceeded 30,000.
Anthropic says Scion uses just one two-hundredth as much CPU power and memory as the Git mirror infrastructure it replaced. Code checkouts for continuous integration (CI) and research jobs now take seconds instead of minutes. Anthropic says the change freed up 25% of the CPU capacity used by its CI infrastructure. A seven-person team built Scion and its supporting tools and completed the migration in five months.
Scion puts commits, merges, rebases and file-history queries on the server. The client tracks local edits, manages files and keeps a limited cache. It does not need to hold enough repository data to perform those operations independently.
That approach suits Anthropic's workload. Most clients are agents and automated jobs that stay online, so Git's offline support offers little benefit. Centralizing the work reduces local storage and synchronization, though it makes server performance and availability more important.
Jobs that need files can download selected directories through sparse checkouts or use virtualized checkouts, which retrieve files as they are read. Both approaches avoid fetching code a job will never use.
The size of Anthropic's repository helps explain the change. Its main-branch history approaches 100 GB, and a compressed working copy exceeds 25 GB. CI alone performs about 25 million checkouts each day, excluding developer environments, agent sandboxes and research jobs.
Downloading a full compressed copy for every CI checkout would generate more than 600 petabytes of daily traffic, according to the company. That estimate reflects what a naive implementation would require, not actual traffic.
Anthropic had already tried shallow clones, sparse checkouts, promisor remotes, snapshots in blob storage and internal mirrors. At one point, the company operated several hundred Git mirrors. The arrangement bought time but became harder to maintain as more changes entered the repository.
Scion records each change as a changeset in a write-ahead log. Each changeset lists files modified relative to its first parent and points to their compressed contents in blob storage. A Git commit instead points to a repository tree. Creating a changeset therefore takes resources proportional to the change, not the whole repository.
Higher merge volume has also forced Anthropic to rethink testing. The company says it could not effectively use a merge queue with a global repository lock at this scale. Hundreds or thousands of changes can merge while tests are still running.
Anthropic now relies more on automated testing after merges and before deployment. Conflicts still occur, and the company says Claude usually fixes them quickly. That puts more weight on catching problems after changes merge but before they are deployed.
Claude also helped build Scion. An early internal version of Claude Mythos Preview rewrote a Git-to-Scion ingestion pipeline. Anthropic says the replacement ran four times faster and used one-twentieth the memory. Engineers still set the system's constraints and rejected shortcuts, including attempts to scan commit logs when an agent should have queried the code review service.
Anthropic says that Scion would be difficult for other organizations to adopt because it requires custom review, search and CI tools, and that Git remains suitable for most repositories. But it sees room for existing platforms to adopt parts of the design, particularly server-side APIs that let agents work without repeatedly fetching a local copy of the code.

articles.title: Trump cancels Pentagon plans to livestream firing squad execution
articles.text:
On Thursday, Donald Trump called off the Pentagon’s highly controversial plans to livestream a firing squad execution that is still on schedule for December 3.
Trump supports the execution of Nidal Hasan, who was convicted of killing 13 people and wounding more than 30 others in the 2009 mass shooting at Fort Hood. But sources close to Trump told CNN that the president was blindsided last week when Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth announced that the event—which is the first US execution of a soldier since World War II—would be livestreamed.
Backlash to the livestream was immediate and crossed political divides. On the morning Trump canceled the plans, an ABC News poll found 8 in 10 Americans were against the livestream, including a 55 percent majority of MAGA Republicans.
Insiders told ABC News that Trump feared that “broadcasting the execution could super charge anti-American propaganda or reflect poorly on the US.” Privately, Trump had remarked that “he did not initially know that Hasan was paralyzed from the waist down,” CNN reported. As one Army officer appalled by Hegseth’s announcement explained in a separate CNN report, livestreaming the execution “takes away everything America stands for.”
“The generational harm caused by allowing troops in uniform to stand in front of a man in a wheelchair and watch him get shot to death is irreparable,” the officer, who was deployed multiple times in the Middle East, told CNN.
Livestream risked identifying US soldiers
On Truth Social, Trump confirmed that Hasan “will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed.” Families of victims will still be able to watch the execution, but the execution will not be broadcast for the public.

articles.text:
'Close to perfect': Creality’s K1 Max is $350 off in the Halloween sale, just in time to print life-size props and masks
AI-assisted monitoring helps you keep an eye on printing problems
If you've been thinking about getting into 3D printing, or upgrading from a smaller machine, the Creality K1 Max 2025 3D printer, currently discounted as part of the company's Halloween sale, combines a generous build area with fast printing speeds and AI-assisted features.
The K1 Max is particularly appealing if you've outgrown a smaller 3D printer or want to tackle more ambitious projects without spending hours waiting for each print to complete. We tested out the 2023 model and came away highly impressed with its speed and accuracy.
• Best for: Hobbyists, makers, designers, and small businesses that want to create larger models, prototypes, and functional parts.
• The deal: The Creality K1 Max 2025 3D printer is $549 (was $899) at Creality Store.
This enclosed 3D printer offers 600mm/s maximum printing speed, 300mm cubed build volume, AI LiDAR, camera monitoring, automatic leveling, 300°C nozzle, dual-gear extrusion, Wi-Fi connectivity, and power-loss recovery for projects.
Why we recommend it
In his four-and-a-half-star review, our expert Alastair said: "The Creality K1 Max offers an impressive blend of innovation, speed, and quality... The machine's AI-driven capabilities certainly set a new standard in handling complex designs, while the extensive material compatibility and decent build volume make it an ideal solution for all levels of 3D print enthusiasts."
He added that "The K1 Max offers something new and completely refined. The enclosed design, network operation, AI monitoring and print quality make it stand out", describing the machine as "close to perfect".
Price context & historical value
Creality Store has reduced the price of the K1 Max 2025 3D printer from $899 to $549 as part of its Halloween sale, saving you a huge $350. We've seen it on sale for a few dollars cheaper in the past, but this is a great deal and one I'd definitely recommend.
Should you buy it?
✅ Buy the Creality K1 Max 2025 if...
You want to create larger 3D prints, work on detailed prototypes, or move beyond the limitations of a smaller printer. It's also worth considering if automatic bed leveling and AI-assisted monitoring appeal to you.
❌ Skip the Creality K1 Max 2025 if...
You only plan to print small objects occasionally. A compact, less expensive printer may be more than enough.

articles.title: FBI fecha fazendas de notebooks usadas em fraude norte-coreana • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
FBI fecha fazendas de notebooks usadas em fraude norte-coreana
Ação no Texas atingiu mais de 40 endereços. Esquema usava identidades falsas para obter empregos remotos em empresas dos EUA.
O FBI realizou buscas em mais de 40 residências no Texas usadas ou suspeitas de funcionar como “fazendas de notebooks” para trabalhadores norte-coreanos. A operação apreendeu cerca de 187 dispositivos que, segundo as autoridades, ajudavam a obter empregos remotos em empresas americanas com identidades falsas ou roubadas.
O governo dos EUA alega que os salários recebidos nesses esquemas ajudam a financiar o regime da Coreia do Norte, contornando sanções internacionais. A ação ocorreu entre 21 e 25 de setembro e foi divulgada na terça-feira (13/10). Entre os equipamentos estavam notebooks e dispositivos que permitem controlar teclado, tela e mouse remotamente.
As fazendas são mantidas por facilitadores nos Estados Unidos. São eles que recebem os computadores enviados pelos empregadores, deixam as máquinas conectadas à internet e instalam recursos de acesso remoto. Os operadores, que estão em outros países, passam a trabalhar nesses equipamentos como se estivessem em território americano.
O endereço local ajuda a disfarçar a localização real de quem executa as tarefas. Segundo o New York Times, o FBI decidiu interromper a rede no Texas, sem esperar acusações formais. Não houve prisões nessa etapa. Os envolvidos foram avisados que poderiam enfrentar punições criminais se continuassem colaborando com as fraudes.
O FBI afirma que os facilitadores nem sempre sabem para quem estão trabalhando. Os recrutadores procuram pessoas em dificuldades financeiras e oferecem serviços aparentemente simples, como receber encomendas ou manter notebooks ligados em casa, em troca de pagamento.
O esquema atingiu até empresas de segurança. A KnowBe4 admitiu ter contratado um funcionário norte-coreano com identidade roubada e foto alterada com inteligência artificial. A Amazon também identificou o que seria um infiltrado após detectar um atraso na digitação: o notebook estava nos Estados Unidos, mas era controlado remotamente, com tráfego rastreado até a China. Uma facilitadora mantinha o equipamento conectado e a latência serviu como sinal para uma investigação.
O Departamento de Justiça também fez a denúncia de um esquema que afetou mais de 70 empresas entre 2019 e 2025 e gerou aproximadamente US$ 3 milhões (cerca de R$ 15,1 milhões em conversão direta), que teriam sido encaminhados à entidades norte-coreanas.
Vale lembrar que os EUA já aplicaram sanções contra facilitadores e empresas de fachada envolvidos nesses esquemas.

articles.title: Epic Games brags about faster vibe-coded app as Steam quietly beats it
articles.text:
Epic Games just rebuilt its game launcher, promoting the revamped app as being “vibe-coded” and “faster than the other guy.” Well, it didn’t last long — a day later, and Steam is back to being faster.
In a recent Steam update, Valve noted in the patch notes that it “improved Steam Client startup performance,” with user testing putting the new launch time at around 5.23 seconds. Meanwhile, Epic was just patting itself on the back for the 5.47-second launch time of its AI-built Epic Games Store (EGS) launcher.
When Epic debuted the new app, it made a big deal about the launch time, even going so far as to commission an independent third party called Keyword Studios to run tests. Keyword compared the Steam and EGS launch times in five tests across 13 machines, averaging the results while dropping the three lowest-end PCs tested. The results showed Epic’s new launcher starting in 5.47 seconds compared to Steam’s 10.07-second average.
this is such a good day to be a sweeney hater.. not even 24h later lmao https://t.co/XXLcIqYTT7
— dea (@girlglock_) October 15, 2026
Of course, we’re only going off limited tests here, and a variety of factors can influence start times. In a quick test I ran on my own machine, Steam launched in about 6.25 seconds. But a variety of things will impact start times, from your internet connection to your hard drive, to other hardware specs like CPU and RAM.
The thing is — and as many people were quick to point out — most people don’t care how fast EGS or Steam launches. People generally choose a store based on the games they have and the features on offer. I don’t think anyone is going to ditch their platform of choice over a few seconds’ difference in launch times.
The whole launch time thing is really silly, and Valve’s quick response to undermine Epic’s claims by improving Steam’s start time is honestly pretty funny.
@Wario64 Oh yeah Epic Games the reason we all use Steam is because of how fast it launched https://t.co/dcDgnhHXHl
— Phil Miyamoto (@PhilMiyamoto) October 14, 2026
Moreover, Epic can’t just “vibe code” EGS into popularity. There are tons of reasons people don’t like EGS, like frustrating exclusivity deals, lack of features, a general disdain for Epic’s dweeby CEO, Tim Sweeney, or the company’s obsession with AI. (Not that Valve and Steam are perfect, mind you, with Steam arguably being a monopoly in PC gaming.)
The point about AI is particularly salient, given Epic told developers to stop hand-writing code and to use AI to generate art — things that gamers have been particularly outspoken about. And Epic laid off 1,000 employees earlier this year, though Sweeney claimed AI wasn’t to blame.
It also doesn’t instill much confidence in Epic’s products when the company itself admitted that “programming is hard.” I mean, it took Epic years to finally add a shopping cart to its store, a standard feature of most online shopping platforms. At least Epic’s AI was able to keep that “advanced digital commerce technology” in the new app.
Source: @girlglock (Twitter) Via: Videocardz.com

articles.title: Steve Walton’s 3C merges with UK’s Datalec to build full-service data centre platform | BetaKit
articles.text:
A liquid cooling startup spearheaded by former CoolIT alumnus Steve Walton has merged with the UK’s Datalec Precision Installations to create a multifaceted data centre services platform.
The news: The merger was announced on Oct. 14, with the new entity operating under the 3C Datalec moniker. The new company will pair 3C’s liquid-cooling data centre infrastructure services with Datalec’s engineering capabilities, allowing the company to design, build, and operate data centre infrastructure. The financial terms of the merger were not disclosed.
From the source: “Liquid cooling is no longer optional,” Walton, who will take the role of CEO at 3C Datalec, said in a statement. “At CoolIT, we spent years preparing for this moment and became a global leader in liquid cooling. The hard part now is making cooling, power, construction, and operations work as one system.”
The context: In March, Walton’s former company, the Calgary-based CoolIT Systems, sold to Minnesota’s Ecolab for $4.75 billion USD ($6.5 billion CAD). Walton left the company in 2024, but his tenure as CEO helped set the stage for the deal, which became one of the largest acquisitions in Alberta’s tech ecosystem to date and underscored the growing value of data-centre-related infrastructure. Walton later founded 3C, which helps data centres move away from air cooling systems to closed-loop, liquid cooling systems.
Final thought: With the backing of venture capital firms like Longbow Capital, S2G Investments, Apogem Capital, and QIC, 3C Datalec is forecasting annual revenue of $400 million USD and has active projects in 16 countries. Over the next 12 months, the company said it is planning to hire 200 engineers ahead of opening new facilities in Calgary, Austin, and Warsaw. With demand for compute showing no signs of slowing, the merger seems to be the logical next step for Walton’s latest company, as 3C Datalec positions itself as a one-stop shop poised to capitalize on the complete data centre boom value chain.

articles.title: Samsung actualiza uno de sus mejores móviles de los últimos años a One UI 9 y Android 17
articles.text:
Samsung continúa con la expansión de One UI 9 y Android 17, y acaba de lanzar la actualización a la versión estable para varios dispositivos que llegaron al mercado en los últimos tiempos. Entre ellos se encuentra el Galaxy S23, uno de los mejores móviles que la marca coreana ha lanzado en años recientes.
La actualización a One UI 9 y Android 17 abarca los modelos más importantes de la citada familia; es decir, el Galaxy S23, el S23+ y el S23 Ultra. Por lo pronto, no hay novedades sobre si el software también estará disponible para el S23 FE, ni cuándo podría estar disponible.
Otros móviles de Samsung que también están recibiendo la nueva versión del sistema operativo de la mano de One UI 9 son los Galaxy Z Fold 5 y Z Flip 5. Aunque la historia no se limita a modelos insignia con cierta antigüedad, puesto que el update también ha comenzado a llegar a teléfonos de la línea Galaxy A.
Para ser más específicos, los usuarios de los Galaxy A56, Galaxy A36 y Galaxy A27 también pueden instalar la actualización estable a One UI 9 y Android 17. Eso sí, el despliegue del software puede que demore algunos días (o incluso semanas) en llegar a todas las unidades a nivel global. Como es costumbre, el SO está llegando primero a usuarios en Corea del Sur y paulatinamente se expandirá a otros mercados.
One UI 9 y Android 17 llegan a más móviles Samsung con su actualización estable
La llegada de One UI 9 y Android 17 al Galaxy S23 y otros dispositivos ya mencionados, no sorprende. Después de todo, muchos usuarios ya venían probando el software desde la fase beta. Sin embargo, es una buena noticia que la versión estable esté ganando espacio en el mercado.
Es cierto que One UI 9 no trae un arsenal de novedades de suma importancia, pero el hecho de que llegue acompañado de la versión más reciente del SO es para destacar. También hay que mencionar que introduce mejoras en algunas aplicaciones de Samsung, en el modo DEX (el entorno de escritorio del software) y en la personalización de la interfaz gráfica.
Si tienes un Galaxy S23 o cualquier otro de los móviles antes indicados, la actualización a One UI 9 y Android 17 pesa casi 484 MB. Si quieres chequear manualmente si el firmware está disponible, tienes que ingresar en Ajustes > Actualizaciones de software > Buscar actualizaciones.

articles.title: Nouvelle app Photos sur Windows 11 : ce qui change et comment l'essayer avant tout le monde — Frandroid
articles.text:
Quelque chose est en train de changer chez Microsoft. La firme de Redmond semble avoir pris conscience qu’il fallait absolument faire évoluer Windows 11.
Ce jeudi 15 octobre, Microsoft a présenté dans un billet du Windows Blog une version entièrement refaite de Photos, l’application qui ouvre par défaut les images sur Windows 11. La galerie, l’éditeur et la visionneuse changent tous les trois, avec un peu plus d’IA au passage.
Si vos photos sont éparpillées entre le PC, OneDrive et un iPhone, la nouvelle app les affiche toutes au même endroit. Pour l’instant, seuls les membres du programme Windows Insider, les volontaires qui testent les préversions de Windows, y ont accès.
La nouvelle galerie réunit les photos stockées sur le PC, dans OneDrive et dans iCloud, le service de stockage en ligne d’Apple. On peut y chercher une image en la décrivant avec ses propres mots, par exemple « un pique-nique en famille », plutôt qu’en tapant un nom de fichier ou une date. Des filtres par personnes permettent aussi de retrouver les photos d’un proche grâce à la reconnaissance des visages.
De son côté, la fonction Moments regroupe automatiquement les photos OneDrive en souvenirs à thème, à regarder en diaporama ou à enregistrer en vidéo. Les albums, eux, s’organisent à la main et se partagent. Et pas besoin de se connecter à OneDrive pour parcourir ses photos locales ou sa bibliothèque iCloud (seul Moments l’exige).
Relight arrive sur tous les PC, sans qu’on sache où tourne l’IA
Microsoft a reconstruit l’éditeur avec WinUI 3, sa boîte à outils pour dessiner les interfaces des applications Windows. D’après ses propres tests, il se charge 25 % plus vite que l’ancien. Il sait maintenant retoucher les photos HDR (à plage dynamique étendue, avec des zones claires et sombres plus détaillées). Surtout, il enregistre les fichiers HEIC, le format des photos d’iPhone, et WebP, très courant sur le Web, sans les convertir.
Pour les retouches, on peut effacer un objet gênant en le coloriant au pinceau. La fonction Relight permet aussi de rééclairer une photo après coup, avec jusqu’à trois sources de lumière dont on règle la couleur et l’intensité. Jusqu’ici, elle était réservée aux PC Copilot+, équipés d’une puce dédiée à l’IA (le NPU). Elle arrive maintenant sur toutes les machines.
La visionneuse promet d’ouvrir les photos « jusqu’à 30 % plus vite ». Pourtant, en moyenne, le gain mesuré par Microsoft tombe à 15 %, et les 30 % ne concernent que les fichiers HEIC. Elle affiche aussi mieux le HDR et ouvre plus de formats, dont le SVG (des images vectorielles). Microsoft insiste beaucoup sur la vitesse en ce moment, après avoir annoncé que la version 26H2 de Windows 11 libère jusqu’à 2 Go de mémoire vive.
Côté IA, l’éditeur repose sur un « modèle IA amélioré », d’après Microsoft. Par contre, l’entreprise ne dit pas s’il tourne sur le PC ou sur ses serveurs. Pour l’ancienne gomme générative, Microsoft exigeait une connexion internet et un compte Microsoft, d’après sa page d’aide.
Et Microsoft n’est pas plus précis pour la recherche en langage naturel de la galerie. La recherche de Windows 11 retrouve déjà des photos par description sans service cloud, mais uniquement sur les PC Copilot+ et dans le dossier Images. Le sujet est sensible pour Microsoft, qui tente déjà de regagner la confiance perdue avec Recall.
Comment tester la nouvelle app Photos dès maintenant
Pour essayer la nouvelle app avant sa sortie, il faut passer par le programme Windows Insider. Même un PC à jour avec la grosse mise à jour d’octobre garde l’ancienne version. Vous aurez besoin d’un PC sous Windows 11, d’un compte Microsoft et d’accepter l’envoi des données de diagnostic facultatives.
- Ouvrez Paramètres, puis Windows Update et Programme Windows Insider.
- Cliquez sur Commencer et liez votre compte Microsoft.
- Choisissez un canal, puis redémarrez le PC.
- Mettez à jour Photos depuis le Microsoft Store.
Depuis avril 2026, le programme ne compte plus que deux canaux. Expérimental remplace les anciens Canary et Dev, et Bêta reste plus proche de la version finale. Microsoft n’a pas dit lequel reçoit Photos en premier, et le déploiement se fait par vagues. Tous les PC inscrits ne l’auront donc pas tout de suite.
Les préversions peuvent planter, alors installez-les plutôt sur un PC secondaire ou depuis une partition. D’ailleurs, depuis la refonte d’avril, quitter le programme ne demande plus de réinstaller Windows.

articles.title: Amazon devices chief Panos Panay sees a future where AI devices replace the need to use apps | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Amazon is placing its bets on ambient computing, not apps, as the future of personal AI.
Alongside the launch of the company’s new AI wearables from Bee, Panos Panay, who serves as Amazon’s SVP of Devices, Alexa & Leo, took the stage at TechCrunch Disrupt on Thursday to talk more in depth about where he sees personal computing headed.
“A lot of times, what you’re doing right now — what we all do right now — is we have to remember what we’re asking our tool to do for us,” Panay began, explaining that this is how we engage with our modern smartphones. “It’s like point, shoot, return,” Panay continued. “I think where we’re headed is a world [that] starts with ambient devices.”
By “ambient devices,” he means those that work quietly in the background, using sensors and AI to help you figure out what needs to be done, instead of the other way around, where you’re telling the device what you need to do.
“As it works in the background, you’re able to stay more present. You’re able to get more done. You’re about to spend more time with people … you’re not afraid if you miss something. It’s incredibly powerful,” Panay said.
Amazon’s biggest entry into this space is the set of new Bee devices it introduced on Thursday, which include a band you can wear on your wrist or detach to wear as a pendant, as well as a new credit-card-sized device that attaches magnetically to the back of your smartphone.
These gadgets passively record audio and take notes about your day, finding the to-dos, reminders, and insights you may later need to refer back to. To balance the need to be useful with user privacy, Bee’s devices don’t actually store the raw audio from your conversations; they process the audio in real time and then delete it when done. Transcripts of conversations are encrypted using keys that your device creates and controls. That means no one else, including Amazon employees, can access those files unless you intentionally share them.
Panay said that privacy was a key consideration for how these new ambient devices should work.
“You have to give customers that control,” he said. “Every product is different, but for Bee specifically, as an example in the ambient space like that, you have to design with privacy in mind. And that’s what we do. That’s critical.”
The executive, who came to Amazon after 19 years at Microsoft where he oversaw the development of Surface devices, has spent a lot of his life thinking about how personal computing will evolve. With Bee — and ambient computing more generally — Panay also envisioned a future where the idea of interacting with apps becomes less important, as more tasks are handled via AI.
“Do I think we have a future where there’s a bit of a balance — a whole generation that doesn’t say ‘give me the app’ for that, but says it should just understand what I need? Yeah, I do. I think that transformation is coming. I think that is the next generation,” he said.
That doesn’t necessarily mean the smartphone itself won’t continue to be an important personal computing device (as much as Amazon would like it to be an Alexa tablet or Echo smart speaker), Panay pointed out. Rather, he believes a new crop of devices will emerge that use sensors to understand users better, and to bring intelligence to the world around you.
“I’m not a proponent that says one form factor is going to replace another. I don’t think that’s the case,” he clarified. “I think there’s an intelligence layer that connects it all … and it has to be useful.”

articles.title: Instagram Modernized its UI with an AI-Native Architecture, Cutting Token Costs by 33%
articles.text:
Instagram Direct migrated its Android UI from the legacy Android View system to Jetpack Compose, creating an AI-native UI codebase that is easier for AI coding agents to understand, modify, and maintain. According to Instagram engineers, the migration reduced UI code volume by 50% and token costs per AI agent session by 33%.
One of Instagram engineers' key claims is that "designing an AI-native architecture led to significant wins". Rather than taking a piecemeal approach where agents are prompted to migrate individual components, the emphasis should be on evaluating whether the underlying architecture makes correct implementations easy to produce. In fact, as the engineers point out, "AI tools often take the path of least resistance", which is likely to introduce "subtle bugs, tech debt and performance regressions".
Optimizing the codebase for AI, Instagram engineers explain, means establishing correct architectural boundaries around state management, predictable behavior, and which development patterns makes it so that the least resistance path for agents is the one that leads to the best conversion. Instead of simply letting the AI patch design gaps, the goal is to design the codebase with an understanding of how AI agents actually modify code:
AI agents naturally take the path of least resistance, so the design should make that path lead to correct, high-quality code, while making poor design decisions hard and expensive to express.
Another key principle is minimizing context dependency, which means that rather than requiring AI agents to rely on codebase-specific knowledge, they favor established best practices and familiar patterns that help them produce more reliable results.
The migration was carried through without disrupting the wider team's work, allowing engineers to continue shipping new features. AI-assisted workflows were standardized to promote consistency and ensure alignment with shared architectural conventions and best practices across the team.
With this approach, the Jetpack Compose migration reduced UI code volume by 50%, while cutting AI agent execution time by 35%, token costs per agent session by 33%, and engineer–agent exchanges by 32%.
A major challenge was ensuring that the migration did not introduce performance regressions. The team focused on three key production metrics: time to interact, i.e., the time it takes for a screen to become usable after opening it; time to fully load, i.e., the time for all screen content to load; and scroll performance, i.e., measuring how smoothly screen contents scrolls.
These metrics are tracked at runtime in production, making it possible to run A/B tests comparing the migrated Compose UI against the legacy UI and evaluate the performance impact of this effort.
One significant finding for Instagram engineers was that performance could not be assessed reliably until entires screens were ported to Compose, eliminating any remaining legacy Views that could distort performance measurements.
This means Compose UI components should be abstracted away from the framework they are enclosed in while still being compatible with both RecyclerView and LazyColumn at the same time. Equally important is the ability to switch between the two at runtime via feature flags, to enable A/B testing.
Eventually, the team replaced the legacy RecyclerView, initially retained as a container for the new Compose-based composables, with LazyColumn, Compose native solution for efficiently rendering scrollable lists.
As a final note, the migration also improved startup performance in other areas in the app. This was partly because Compose has a runtime warmup cost that is incurred only once per app session, allowing other Compose-based screens to benefit from the runtime already being initialized rather than paying that cost again.

articles.title: ASML reports record quarter, vows to expand capacity as clients eager to place orders to 2030
articles.text:
ASML reports record $13 billion quarter, vows to expand capacity as demand for lithography equipment soars — customers eager to secure orders in 2030 as demand is expected to outstrip 2027 and 2028 supply
As the world needs more chips, ASML is the one who always wins.
ASML this week reported record quarterly revenue of $13.06 billion (€11.66 billion) and profitability of nearly $5.79 billion (€5 billion) as demand for advanced semiconductor manufacturing equipment continues to accelerate and investments in AI infrastructure continue to increase. The company now expects demand for its lithography systems to exceed its production capacity in 2027 and 2028, despite plans to increase output substantially. Some clients are already interested in placing orders for equipment as far ahead as 2030, which makes ASML consider further capacity expansions beyond its previously announced intentions.
Record financial results
ASML reported third-quarter 2026 revenue of $13.06 billion USD (€11.66 billion), up 55% year-over-year and 25% sequentially. The company's gross margin reached a record 57.5%, up from 51.6% a year earlier, while operating income rose to $5.79 billion (€5.17 billion). Net income reached $5.56 billion USD (€4.96 billion) , although this figure includes approximately $570 million (€510 million) from the re-evaluation of the company's investment in Mistral AI.
During the quarter, ASML sold 121 lithography systems, including 113 new and eight refurbished machines, up from 91 systems in Q2 2026. The company generated $4.59 billion USD (€4.1 billion) from 17 EUV lithography systems and $4.82 billion USD (€4.3 billion) from 85 DUV (including 45 ArFi scanners) and 19 i-line litho tools. In addition, ASML recognized revenue from one High-NA EUV system in Q2. Of total equipment revenue, 54% came from logic chipmakers and 46% from memory manufacturers.
Taiwan accounted for 32% of ASML's equipment sales in Q3 2026, followed closely by South Korea at 31%. China represented another 23%, while the United States accounted for 13% and the rest of Asia contributed just 1%. Combined, Taiwan and South Korea generated 63% of ASML's equipment revenue, which reflects substantial investments in advanced logic and memory manufacturing capacity that by far exceed those in the U.S. and Japan.
ASML’s Installed Base Management business generated $3.68 billion (€3.29 billion), approximately $450 million (€400 million) above guidance, largely due to strong demand for productivity upgrades (more on this later), which contributed to the company’s record profitability.
For the fourth quarter, ASML expects revenue of $15.9 billion to $17.0 billion (€14.2 billion to €15.2 billion) and gross margin of approximately 57%. Full-year revenue should reach $49.3 billion to $50.4 billion (€44 billion to €45 billion), up approximately 36% YoY. The company projects EUV revenue should increase by more than 45% year-over-year, while memory-related equipment sales are expected to rise by approximately 75%, which indicates growing demand from DRAM producers.
Demand for litho tools spans to 2030
One of the biggest learnings from these results and accompanying statements is that semiconductor manufacturers are increasingly interested in securing lithography equipment years before they actually need it. According to ASML CEO Christophe Fouquet, customers expect demand for its products to exceed available supply through at least 2028, which encourages them to accelerate construction of new fabs as well as expand their existing capacity.
"Our leading-edge high-volume customers are sharing very good visibility as a result of the increasing number of long-term commitments they are securing with their customers," Fouquet said during the company's conference call with analysts and investors. "This extended visibility has led them to conclude that demand for their products will outpace supply through at least 2028. As a result, customers are accelerating capacity build-out plans and preparing for further expansion beyond 2028 in order to better meet the anticipated level of demand."
ASML is already receiving orders that are to be delivered in 2028, while some customers have expressed interest in equipment for 2029 and even 2030.
"As customers shift focus to their needs beyond 2027, our order momentum continues to build," Fouquet added. "We are increasingly receiving orders for 2028, and customers are also expressing interest in placing orders for 2029 and even 2030."
To address this demand, ASML plans to manufacture approximately 65 Low-NA EUV systems in 2026, up from 44 scanners shipped in 2025. Production of immersion DUV systems should remain approximately at last year's level, even though proveiously the company expected shipments of DUV tools to decline.
The company previously announced plans to increase production capacity for both Low-NA EUV and immersion DUV systems by 30% in 2027, followed by another potential 30% increase in 2028. Based on its 2026 EUV production target, this implies capacity for approximately 85 Low-NA EUV systems in 2027 and roughly 110 in 2028, assuming both increases materialize.
However, ASML now believes even this level of output will be insufficient and is investigating ways to expand its 2028 capacity beyond the previously planned 30% increase. However, the company has not disclosed revised production targets.
"Looking further ahead, we shared our intent last quarter to increase our capacity in 2027 by 30% for both Low NA EUV and DUV immersion systems, as well as to investigate adding a further 30% in 2028," explained Roger Dassen, Chief Financial Officer at ASML. "However, given the dynamics of this quarter, we now anticipate that our current planned levels of output in 2027 and 2028 will not fully meet the demand of our customers."
High-NA EUV adoption
Meanwhile, High-NA EUV adoption is progressing. Intel has already exposed more than one million wafers using High-NA systems and plans to start using High-NA EUV with its 14A process technology in 2028. Samsung plans to introduce High-NA EUV into high-volume manufacturing (HVM) in 2028 for DRAM and for logic later, while TSMC plans to use High-NA EUV scanners by 2030 – 2031. ASML says availability across its installed High-NA fleet is approaching 90%, which suggests that the tools are becoming mature enough for HVM deployment.
Interestingly, Samsung's planned 2028 introduction may create additional demand for High-NA equipment from memory manufacturers, as they will need to compete against their larger rival. However, ASML has not disclosed specific shipment targets for these tools.
New tools, more capacity
ASML also intends to increase semiconductor production capacity by introducing more productive lithography systems. Its upcoming Twinscan NXE:3800F, scheduled for introduction in early 2027, will process up to 260 wafers per hour, compared with 230 wafers per hour for the existing NXE:3800E. While this represents 'only' approximately 13% higher throughput, this translates to 21,600 extra EUV exposures per month without corresponding increases in cleanroom space. Three such tools per fab enable 90 additional EUV exposures per hour, 2,160 per day, or 64,800 per month. The company also plans to introduce a new critical-layer immersion DUV system capable of processing 330 wafers per hour.
Keep in mind that the actual fab capacity improvements depend on the number of lithography exposures required per wafer on a particular node, as well as the capabilities of other manufacturing equipment.
Another important element of ASML's strategy is its growing portfolio of productivity upgrade packages for existing EUV and DUV systems. Such upgrades enable chipmakers to increase wafer throughput without purchasing additional scanners, which can provide additional capacity considerably faster than procuring new tools or constructing new fabs.
Value-based pricing is a go
One of the controversial things that ASML discussed back in early Q2 was its value-based pricing, which many thought was a blanket price hike. This is not and CFO Roger Dassen this week confirmed that negotiations with major customers have been completed, although the financial benefits for ASML will not become visible immediately.
The company expects the first effects of higher pricing to appear during 2027, with the full impact becoming apparent in 2028 and beyond, which essentially means that the company is not setting new prices on its backlog, but generally setting new prices on new tools.
"We completed those conversations," said Dassen. "So that has been done with the key customers. The effect of that is not really visible in 2026. It will start to become visible partly in the course of 2027. The full impact of that you will start to see in 2028 and beyond."
This strategy could further improve ASML's already substantial gross margins, particularly as customers have no alternatives for advanced lithography equipment.
China remains important
Despite export restrictions that prevent Chinese chipmakers from acquiring EUV scanners and advanced DUV systems, China remains a substantial market for ASML. The company expects China to account for approximately 20% of its total revenue in 2026, which implies annual sales of roughly €8.8 billion to €9 billion based on current guidance.
Although China's share of ASML's business has declined from its levels in 2023 - 2025, the country's semiconductor manufacturers continue to invest in mature node capacity and equipment that remains available under existing export regulations. Meanwhile, it is impossible to predict what is going to happen if the U.S. lawmakers approve the MATCH Act.
Yet, ASML management emphasizes that its key growth opportunities lie with advanced logic and memory manufacturers, which are accelerating their investment in advanced lithography tools, including sophisticated DUV systems, Low-NA EUV machines, and High-NA EUV scanners.
The future of ASML
Thanks to gaining momentum in AI infrastructure investments, ASML reported record quarterly revenue of $13.06 billion (€11.7 billion) as demand for advanced lithography equipment continued to accelerate. The company expects demand to persist for years as its customers are interested in placing orders for tools to be delivered as far ahead as 2030. To meet growing demand, the company plans to expand production capacity beyond its previous targets for 2028. ASML also intends to introduce new EUV and DUV systems with higher productivity, offer productivity upgrades, and raise equipment prices to capitalize on unprecedented demand.
Anton Shilov is a contributing writer at Tom’s Hardware. Over the past couple of decades, he has covered everything from CPUs and GPUs to supercomputers and from modern process technologies and latest fab tools to high-tech industry trends.

articles.title: Lebensfreundlicher als die Erde – warum Astronom:innen jetzt nach einer neuen Art von Planeten suchen
articles.text:
Lebensfreundlicher als die Erde: Warum Astronomen bei der Suche nach Exoplaneten umdenken
Anfang 2027 will die Europäische Weltraumorganisation ESA das Weltraumteleskop Plato ins All schicken, um nach Gesteinsplaneten außerhalb unseres Sonnensystems zu suchen. Dabei rücken neben klassischen Doppelgängern der Erde verstärkt sogenannte superhabitable Welten in den Fokus, die für biologische Prozesse günstigere Voraussetzungen als unser Heimatplanet bieten könnten.
Dieser Strategiewechsel hängt auch mit Ernüchterungen der vergangenen Jahre zusammen, nachdem Untersuchungen mit dem James-Webb-Weltraumteleskop zahlreiche nahe Gesteinsplaneten um kleine, kühle Rote Zwerge (sogenannte M-Zwerge) näher analysiert haben. Wie eine im Wissenschaftsmagazin Nature veröffentlichte Studie unter Leitung des Astrophysikers Thomas Greene vom Ames Research Center der US-Raumfahrtbehörde Nasa am Beispiel des Planeten Trappist-1b zeigt, haben Strahlungsausbrüche dieser Sterne die Atmosphären der eng kreisenden Planeten oft vollständig abgetragen.
ESA-Weltraumteleskop Plato und K-Zwerge: Warum die Erde kein Idealmaß ist
Statt auf Rote Zwerge oder kurzlebigere sonnenähnliche Sterne richten Astronom:innen ihre Instrumente zunehmend auf sogenannte K-Zwerge, also orangefarbene Sterne, die etwas kühler und masseärmer als unsere Sonne sind. Wie die New York Times berichtet, bezeichnet die Planetenforscherin Johanna Teske von der Carnegie Institution for Science in der US-Hauptstadt Washington, D.C. diese Sternklasse als einen günstigen Mittelweg für die Beobachtung.
Während unsere Sonne ihren Wasserstoffvorrat nach insgesamt rund zehn Milliarden Jahren verbraucht haben wird, verbrennen K-Zwerge ihren Kernbrennstoff so langsam, dass sie über Dutzende Milliarden Jahre hinweg gleichmäßig leuchten. Auf der Erde hingegen wird es durch die zunehmende Leuchtkraft der Sonne bereits in rund 500 Millionen Jahren zu heiß für komplexe Pflanzen und Tiere, zumal unser Planet ohnehin nah am inneren Rand der habitablen Zone kreist, also jenem Abstandsbereich um einen Stern, in dem flüssiges Wasser auf der Oberfläche existieren kann.
Dass sich die Raumfahrt dennoch lange auf die Suche nach einem Erdzwilling konzentrierte, führt der Astrophysiker René Heller vom Max-Planck-Institut für Sonnensystemforschung im niedersächsischen Göttingen gegenüber der New York Times auf eine menschheitszentrierte Sichtweise zurück: „Natürlich ist die Erde für uns etwas Besonderes. Aber warum sollte die Erde aus einer universellen Perspektive die Referenz sein?“ Gemeinsam mit dem Physiker John Armstrong von der Weber State University in Ogden im US-Bundesstaat Utah legte Heller bereits 2014 in einer im Fachjournal Astrobiology veröffentlichten Arbeit dar, welche Eigenschaften ein Planet aufweisen müsste, um eine größere Artenvielfalt als die Erde hervorzubringen.
Supererden um K-Zwerge: Schwerkraft, Atmosphäre und Schattenseiten
Nach diesen Modellen wäre eine solche Welt eine sogenannte Supererde mit etwa der doppelten Masse und einem um 20 bis 30 Prozent größeren Durchmesser als unser Planet. Durch die um rund 30 Prozent höhere Schwerkraft flachen hohe Gebirge und tiefe Ozeangräben ab, sodass eine Welt mit vielen flachen Meeren und Inselketten entsteht, während ein größerer Eisenkern ein stärkeres Magnetfeld gegen kosmische Strahlung aufbaut.
In einer 2020 ebenfalls im Fachblatt Astrobiology publizierten Untersuchung grenzte ein Team um den Astrobiologen Dirk Schulze-Makuch von der Technischen Universität Berlin gemeinsam mit Heller zudem 24 mögliche Planetenkandidaten ein und bezifferte die günstigste globale Durchschnittstemperatur auf etwa fünf Grad Celsius oberhalb des irdischen Mittelwerts. Allerdings hat das Konzept auch Kehrseiten: Keiner der 24 Kandidaten ist bislang zweifelsfrei bestätigt, alle liegen mehr als 100 Lichtjahre entfernt, und eine noch größere Masse würde schnell zu einem hohen Atmosphärendruck führen oder den Gesteinsplaneten in einen lebensfeindlichen Mini-Neptun mit dichter Gashülle verwandeln.
Photosynthese im Labor und die Grenzen künftiger Teleskope
Ob irdische Organismen mit dem rötlicheren Lichtspektrum eines K-Zwergs überhaupt auskommen, prüfte ein Team um die Astrobiologin Iva Vilović, die heute am Leibniz-Institut für Astrophysik im brandenburgischen Potsdam forscht, im Jahr 2024 in einer im International Journal of Astrobiology veröffentlichten Studie. Unter simuliertem K-Zwerg-Licht keimte gewöhnliche Gartenkresse zwar schneller und wuchs höher als unter künstlichem Sonnenlicht, wies am Ende jedoch einen höheren Wasseranteil und eine geringere Trockenmasse auf, weil der höhere Rotlichtanteil vor allem das Längenwachstum der Stängel anregte.
Ob solche Welten in unserer kosmischen Nachbarschaft tatsächlich existieren, soll ab März 2027 zunächst die ESA-Mission Plato klären, an deren Vorbereitung auch Heller in Göttingen beteiligt ist. Gegenüber der New York Times dämpft der Wissenschaftler jedoch zu hohe Erwartungen: „Wir werden wahrscheinlich einige von ihnen finden – vielleicht ein Dutzend. Aber wir werden noch nicht viel über sie erfahren.“
Denn Plato kann über regelmäßige Helligkeitsschwankungen von Sternen zwar die Größe und Umlaufbahn vorbeiziehender Planeten bestimmen, nicht aber die chemische Zusammensetzung ihrer Lufthülle. Für die Suche nach biologischen Spuren wie Sauerstoff oder Methan in den Atmosphären dieser Kandidaten werden Astronom:innen auf das im Bau befindliche Extremely Large Telescope der Europäischen Südsternwarte ESO sowie auf das Habitable Worlds Observatory der Nasa warten müssen, dessen Start erst für die 2040er-Jahre vorgesehen ist.

articles.title: Save $249 on 32GB of DDR5 with this 3-item Newegg bundle — score 32GB of G.SKill Trident Z5 NeoX RAM, a Ryzen 7 9800X3D, and an MSI X870E Motherboard for only $1,094.99

Save $249 on 32GB of DDR5 with this 3-item Newegg bundle — score 32GB of G.SKill Trident Z5 NeoX RAM, a Ryzen 7 9800X3D, and an MSI X870E Motherboard for only $1,094.99

articles.title: Private Internet Access adds 10 new server locations to its network – but it seems the truth is better than PIA lets on
articles.text:
Private Internet Access adds 10 new server locations to its network – but it seems the truth is better than PIA lets on
Yet more locations have arrived, but more so than PIA suggests
Private Internet Access (PIA) has announced the addition of 10 new locations to its server network, building on recent expansions by adding servers in the Americas, the Middle East, Africa, and Australia.
The announcement follows the addition of 15 new locations in September 2026 and forms part of a larger effort to improve and expand the Colorado-based VPN’s server network.
The full list of new locations includes:
- Bermuda
- Brooklyn, NY
- Dominican Republic
- Honduras
- Puerto Rico
- Trinidad and Tobago
- Ghana
- Kenya
- Lebanon
- Woolloomooloo (Sydney, AU)
PIA says the new locations include some virtual servers, writing in the announcement: “Virtual server locations allow us to offer our users more locations while ensuring they meet our strict privacy and security standards”.
Virtual servers are employed by all major consumer VPNs and are considered as safe and reliable as on-site servers if properly managed.
As we recently covered, previous expansions have focused on the Caribbean, Central and Southeast Asia, with new dedicated streaming servers in Europe and the Americas.
According to PIA, these recent expansions bring the total number of locations in its network to 170 locations across 104 countries and territories.
However, our independent tracking suggests the firm might be speaking a little too modestly about its total number of locations – our testing suggests PIA currently offers 176 server locations in 112 countries.
More curiously, our numbers match what PIA's Windows app shows too, so it seems PIA's press release isn't quite showing just how vast its improvements have been in recent months.
Like most consumer VPNs, PIA leans towards North America and Europe with its server network, offering 69 locations in the former and 50 in the latter.
Asia comes in third with 33 locations to choose from, while South America, Oceania and Africa get nine, eight, and seven locations respectively.
PIA is certainly no slouch when it comes to choice of server locations, but it still falls behind industry leaders like NordVPN (225 locations in 150 countries) and ExpressVPN (196 locations in 113 countries).
Why does having more VPN server locations matter?
As our Private Internet Access review details, PIA fills a niche for budget-conscious users looking for solid privacy tools and customization – and by expanding its server network, PIA has made itself even easier to recommend for a wider range of potential users.
For certain use cases, a VPN is only as strong as its server network. Users hoping to stream high-definition video over a VPN will look for options with dedicated streaming servers, and those wanting to access content in other countries while travelling will opt for a VPN with plenty of server locations across the globe.
Multiple locations within the same country or region are also welcome – if a VPN has multiple servers in, say, California, users have options if one starts lagging or goes offline altogether.
The five options in our list of the best VPNs all offer a large, varied server network, with some offering dedicated locations for streaming and gaming
Though it is one of the best cheap VPNs, PIA doesn’t rank in our main list just yet – but continued expansion of its network is sure to make this budget-friendly option a stronger contender.

articles.title: Ce vélo électrique de ville de Decathlon aux 110 km d'autonomie perd 300 €
articles.text:
Le passage à l’heure d’hiver tombe le dimanche 25 octobre. Pour celles et ceux qui vont au travail à vélo, cela veut dire rentrer de nuit, souvent sur des routes mouillées. Pour ces trajets, l’éclairage, les garde-boue et un bon freinage comptent plus que la fiche technique du moteur.
Decathlon a justement baissé le prix de son vélo électrique de ville Elops LD 500 E équipé, en version cadre haut. Il passe à 1 199,99 € au lieu de 1 499,99 €, soit 300 € de réduction. L’offre est affichée jusqu’au 31 octobre 2026.
Que vaut le vélo électrique longue distance 500 de Decathlon ?
Ce vélo électrique longue distance de Decathlon possède un cadre haut, avec une barre centrale qui demande de lever davantage la jambe pour l’enjamber. Un détail à prendre en compte au quotidien, notamment en hiver lorsqu’on porte un manteau. En contrepartie, ce cadre offre une silhouette classique, dans l’esprit des vélos de ville traditionnels. Sa position de conduite légèrement inclinée vers l’avant permet de conserver un bon compromis entre confort et efficacité, tout en gardant une bonne visibilité sur la route.
Pour faire avancer l’Elops LD 500 E, Decathlon a opté pour un moteur de 250 watts intégré à la roue arrière, capable de délivrer un couple de 45 Nm. Une configuration qui privilégie une assistance progressive et agréable au quotidien, que ce soit pour relancer le vélo après un feu rouge ou aborder une côte sans trop forcer sur les pédales. Sa batterie de 504 Wh promet, selon Decathlon, jusqu’à 110 km d’autonomie en mode éco et 60 km avec l’assistance au maximum.
Avec ses 23 kg, batterie comprise, le vélo reste néanmoins assez encombrant à manipuler à l’arrêt, notamment pour franchir des marches. Côté équipement, il dispose de freins à disque hydrauliques Tektro et d’une transmission Microshift à huit vitesses.
À ce prix, le vélo électrique longue distance 500 est-il une bonne affaire ?
Avec 20 % de réduction, l’Elops 500 devient encore plus intéressant, d’autant qu’il est livré avec tout l’équipement nécessaire pour rouler au quotidien : éclairage, garde-boue, porte-bagages et béquille. Pas besoin de prévoir un budget supplémentaire pour ces accessoires.
La promotion se termine le 31 octobre, six jours après le passage à l’heure d’hiver, au moment où l’on commence à rentrer de nuit avec l’éclairage allumé. Decathlon garantit le cadre et le cintre à vie, et les éléments électriques deux ans. Les 300 € économisés peuvent servir à acheter un bon antivol et des sacoches pour le porte-bagages.
