articles.title: Tesla annonce son Roadster : 0 à 96 km/h en 0,81 seconde, et la voiture vole vraiment — Frandroid
articles.text:
Il est 3h du matin, on a les yeux qui piquent, et une voiture blanche vient de rouler à l’envers sur une rampe de 15 mètres avant de se poser sur des propulseurs.
    Pour aller plus loin
Tesla lance enfin son Roadster : revivez le direct de ce lancement mythique
            
Pendant neuf ans, le Tesla Roadster a surtout existé sous forme de promesses, de reports et de messages sur X. Cette nuit, sur le site d’essais de fusées de SpaceX à McGregor, au Texas, il a enfin pris une forme physique. Elon Musk, CEO de Tesla, n’a pas fait les choses à moitié : looping, saut par-dessus une rangée de Tesla avec le mannequin Starman au volant, et chrono en direct.
Le Roadster est une biplace aux lignes très tendues, clairement de la famille du Cybertruck. Franz von Holzhausen, designer en chef de Tesla, cite plutôt l’avion espion SR-71. Les phares sont escamotables, un feu arrière court sur toute la largeur et les surfaces affleurantes gomment les appendices aérodynamiques. La peinture « Ano White » s’inspire des revêtements qui protègent les fusées, et les vitres teintées imitent le reflet doré des visières de combinaisons spatiales, avec quelques touches de titane. Les jantes ultralégères à rayons fins participent à la rigidité de l’ensemble.
Elon Musk annonce que ce sera, à terme, la seule Tesla qu’on conduira soi-même, le reste de la gamme devant basculer vers l’autonomie. L’habitacle joue donc la carte de la voiture de pilote : intérieur blanc avec détails en microdaim gris, sièges renforcés pour mieux tenir le corps en virage, et direction, freins et accélérateur entièrement à commande électrique. Les sièges sont moulés dans le châssis, en position fixe, pour gagner du poids. Tesla mise aussi sur le magnésium, le titane et la fibre de carbone pour alléger l’ensemble.
Jusqu’à 330€ d’avantages avec nos offres Hello Prime ou Hello Prime Duo, dont 80€ cash à l’ouverture de compte !
Pour coller à la route, un système de ventilateurs et de jupes d’étanchéité aspire l’air sous la voiture et génère jusqu’à 2 g d’appui, quand une sportive classique plafonne entre 1 et 1,2 g grâce à ses seuls pneus. Associé à des ailerons actifs, il produit un appui important même à l’arrêt, assez pour maintenir la voiture à l’envers selon Tesla. La voiture de démonstration embarquait en plus deux réservoirs en carbone de 600 litres au total, environ 250 kg d’air comprimé et dix buses. Des actionneurs électriques les pilotent en une fraction de seconde pour stabiliser la voiture en vol. La poussée annoncée dépasse 80 kN, à peu près un dixième d’un moteur de fusée Falcon 9.
0,81 seconde, sur le chrono maison
Le chiffre qui va faire le tour du web, c’est ce 0 à 96 km/h en 0,81 seconde, réalisé en direct avec les propulseurs allumés. En 2017, Tesla promettait 1,9 seconde. Les voitures de série les plus rapides sur l’exercice, comme la Rimac Nevera ou la Corvette ZR1X, tournent autour de 1,8 à 1,9 seconde.
Le Roadster ferait donc plus de deux fois mieux, avec une accélération moyenne de plus de 3 g. Le chrono a pourtant été mesuré par Tesla, sur son propre terrain, sur une piste qu’elle reconnaît elle-même trop courte, et par une voiture de démonstration qui roulait en mode autonome. Sur son site, Tesla donne un temps par version : moins de 1,6 seconde pour la Performance, moins de 0,9 seconde pour la Thrust et moins de 0,59 seconde pour la Rocket. Même la version de base, sans propulseurs, battrait donc la Rimac Nevera et la Corvette ZR1X. Elon Musk parle déjà de la « voiture de série la plus rapide du monde » pour un modèle qui n’est toujours pas produit.
Trois versions, et 50 000 euros pour réserver
Sur son site, Tesla ouvre déjà les réservations pour trois versions du Roadster :
- Performance : biplace pensée pour la route, avec aérodynamique active et système d’aspiration, sans propulseurs. 0 à 96 km/h en moins de 1,6 seconde. Réservation de 50 000 euros, dont 5 000 euros à la commande et 45 000 euros sous dix jours ;
- Thrust : série limitée, biplace pensée pour la piste, avec en plus des propulseurs à gaz froid à l’arrière. 0 à 96 km/h en moins de 0,9 seconde. Réservation de 250 000 euros, dont 245 000 euros sous dix jours, limitée à une commande par client ;
- Rocket : sur invitation uniquement, monoplace, avec des propulseurs tout autour de la voiture pour accélérer, décoller et pivoter. 0 à 96 km/h en moins de 0,59 seconde et plus de 370 km/h en pointe. Tesla assume : elle peut voler.
Attention, ce sont des montants de réservation, pas des prix de vente. Tesla n’affiche aucun tarif final, et seuls les 5 000 premiers euros sont présentés comme entièrement remboursables. Sans le reste du paiement sous dix jours, la réservation peut être annulée. Le schéma rappelle celui de 2017, quand Tesla réclamait déjà 50 000 dollars pour réserver la version de base.
2028, 480 km d’autonomie et toujours pas de prix
Tesla annonce une production en 2028, « pour de vrai » selon Elon Musk. L’autonomie annoncée dépasse 480 km, soit moins de la moitié des 1 000 km promis en 2017. La vitesse de pointe de plus de 370 km/h ne concerne que la version Rocket, et reste en dessous des plus de 400 km/h promis à l’époque. Prix de vente et capacité de batterie restent inconnus. En 2017, la marque annonçait 200 000 dollars en version de base et 250 000 dollars pour la Founders Series.
Reste la question de l’homologation. Tesla l’écrit noir sur blanc : la version Rocket n’est pas approuvée pour la voie publique, et la disponibilité de chaque version dépend de la législation locale. Elon Musk concède aussi que la voiture n’est « pas forcément optimisée pour la sécurité ». On a du mal à imaginer l’Europe homologuer les propulseurs de la version Thrust sur une voiture de route. Le Roadster vise donc surtout des collectionneurs fortunés, à commencer par ceux qui ont réservé il y a des années.
Elon Musk a même lancé un nouveau défi à ses équipes : retenter le saut du Snake River Canyon, raté par le cascadeur Evel Knievel en 1974, à environ 600 km/h. « Là où on va, on n’a pas besoin de pneus », a-t-il lancé, en détournant la réplique de Doc Brown dans Retour vers le futur.
Tesla a livré cette nuit le plus beau numéro de cirque automobile qu’on ait vu depuis longtemps. La prochaine démonstration attendue sera moins spectaculaire : une production lancée en 2028 comme promis. Depuis 2017, la marque n’a tenu aucune de ses dates, ce qui ne l’empêche pas de réclamer à nouveau 50 000 euros pour réserver.

articles.title: McKinsey lässt Bewerber mit KI-Kunden sprechen: Was der Test zeigen soll
articles.text:
KI-Kunden sollen Bewerber testen: Was sich das Beratungsunternehmen McKinsey davon erhofft
Künstliche Intelligenz kommt nicht mehr nur beim Schreiben von Bewerbungen und beim Bewerten selbiger durch Personaler:innen zum Einsatz. Auch im nachfolgenden Bewerbungsprozess nimmt KI jetzt ihren Platz ein. So ist es zumindest seit Herbst 2026 in den nordamerikanischen Büros des Beratungsunternehmens McKinsey. Dort müssen sich Bewerber:innen im ersten Schritt dem Gespräch mit einer KI stellen.
So nutzt McKinsey KI bei Bewerbungen
Wie das Wall Street Journal berichtet, handelt es sich dabei nicht um Gespräche per Zoom-Call, sondern vor Ort in den Büros des Beratungsunternehmens. Die Kandidat:innen sprechen etwa zehn Minuten lang mit einer KI, die eine:n Kund:in imitiert. Währenddessen sollen sich andere Menschen mit im Raum befinden, um die Entscheidungen der Bewerber:innen zu überwachen und zu bewerten. Die KI selbst soll keinerlei Bewertung am Ende des Prozesses abgeben.
Zudem wurde die KI nicht speziell darauf trainiert, besonders knifflige Fragen zu stellen oder cholerische Kund:innen nachzuahmen, um die Bewerber:innen unter Druck zu setzen. Stattdessen sollen damit die Alltagszenarien abgedeckt werden, die die Interessent:innen in ihrem potenziellen Job immer wieder vorgesetzt bekommen.
Saleem Zafar, McKinsey-Partner und einer der Mitverantwortlichen für das KI-Projekt, sagte dazu: „Die Dinge, auf die ich achte, sind: Hast du wirklich zugehört, als es um wichtige Dinge ging? Hast du anhand dieser Informationen gehandelt? Oder hast du alles nur schnell abgewickelt? […] Was wir wissen wollen, ist, wie du auf sich verändernde Stimuli reagierst.“
Als Beispiel nennt Zafar dafür einen theoretischen Fall einer Stadt, die sich bei McKinsey Rat für den Bauplatz eines neuen Stadions einholen möchte. In diesem Fall würde die KI die Rolle der Bürgermeisterin übernehmen: „Die Bürgermeisterin hätte dabei einige Dinge zu sagen, die ihr wirklich wichtig sind, und sie will deine Empfehlungen. Aber während du die Empfehlungen aussprichst, könnte sie weitere Sorgen äußern oder zusätzlichen Kontext einfließen lassen.“
Zunächst soll das KI‑Tool bei McKinsey eingesetzt werden, um Student:innen zu bewerten, die sich auf eine Position in der Business-Analyse bewerben. Voraussichtlich wird es dabei hunderte Kandidat:innen geben, die den Job haben möchten und mit einer KI sprechen werden. Sollten sich die Tests als effektiv erweisen, plant McKinsey, sie im nächsten Jahr auch für andere offene Jobpositionen zu nutzen.

articles.title: Optimizing Software Workflow: Exploring Fundamental Impacts in Technology
articles.text:
Software only has value when shipped; faster release cadence matters. Development, deployment, and operations require different thinking, metrics, and investments, Titus Winters explained in his talk Software Workflow Optimization at Craft Conference. He mentioned four impacts in tech: product success, compute capacity, engineering capacity, and strategic innovation. The biggest expense is people, not compute, which goes mostly unmeasured. AI shifts engineers toward deeper problem understanding, not fewer engineers, he argued.
Developing software with or without AI, we have to carefully reason about the goals, inputs, and outputs of each phase of the software workflow, Winters mentioned. He referred to the paper Develop, Deploy, Operate - a holistic model for understanding the costs and value of software development that he wrote with Leah Rivers and Salim Virji, which provides guidance for reasoning about impact and efficiency in the software process, whether AI-assisted or not.
Software only has value when you have shipped it to customers, Winters argued. When bugs happen in production, you are risking actual bottom line losses, he added. There is value in being able to remedy an issue by shipping a well-tested update quickly and reliably. Faster release cadence is almost always better, and probably better than your leadership recognizes.
Development is a creative process; this is what we want humans to spend time on, Winters argued. Deployment is a factory process, and operations is an automation process:
These three processes aren’t just different activities; they require different thinking, different metrics, and different investments.
Winters mentioned four fundamental impacts in tech:
- Product success: Revenue, adoption, customer satisfaction, NPS, etc
- Compute capacity: Cloud costs, storage, networking, etc
- Engineering capacity: "Productivity", human efficiency
- Strategic innovation: Make new good things cheap/possible, make existing bad things rare/impossible
We have to be looking at all four of these things and balancing the impact mixture, Winters mentioned:
Running fewer tests might save you on compute costs, but the resulting quality issues might cause actual bottom-line losses or engineering burnout when you try to get the product to stability.
The biggest expense is rarely compute; it’s people, Winters said. We cannot directly measure what those people are producing or what the production of it actually costs. We’ve been measuring everything except the biggest line item, which hardly seems rigorous, he added.
Software engineering is not just coding; it’s also people and time, and we cannot measure the people part. Winters mentioned that with the shift to AI for coding tasks, we might have the potential to build experiments using AI as a proxy for the human parts of development.
We want our engineers to be solving problems primarily, Winters argued. With AI, developers are going to remain in the loop, but no longer free of guardrails. They work within a system that has encoded expert knowledge and organizational policies, so they don’t have to internalize all of the details and can focus on the unique problem at hand. The shift that we are looking towards is not a reduction in the number of engineers; it will be a shift away from focusing only on raw software expertise, in favor of a deeper understanding of the actual problem that is being solved, he concluded.
InfoQ interviewed Titus Winters after his talk.
InfoQ: What are the challenges of managing the impact of engineering capacity, and how can we deal with those challenges?
Titus Winters: Compared to tracking token costs or cloud spend, it’s a lot harder to track where engineering time is going. Even for companies that do, we need enough understanding of the engineering process to decide whether a given task is wasteful, and that requires some subtlety.
We were making good inroads on explaining that developer experience and productivity are important related concerns, but AI seems to have sucked the air out of that. Not because the necessary investments changed, but because the discourse is so messy. The same lessons are still true post-AI, just accelerated: we need clear processes, clean code, good tools, fast feedback signals, good tests, etc.
InfoQ: How can we build experiments with AI to evaluate the human parts of development?
Winters: If we accept that token consumption is a tolerable proxy for human effort in software tasks, we can start to build experiments to put a quantitative cost or benefit on various aspects of software.
What we need is a robust set of evals for software agents: across a variety of software tasks (new feature, bugfix, refactoring), across the platforms we care about (frontend, backend, mobile, etc), across the languages we care about, and at a range of difficulties. Each software task in this eval suite needs a set of functional and quality acceptance criteria, hidden from the AI. And we need the ability to measure token costs for each eval run.
With that setup, we can now run empirical tests. Do you want to measure whether good unit test coverage is actually a good thing? Get two agents, one that is prompted to follow all of our practices in unit testing, one that actively doesn’t write unit tests. Run the eval suite, probably repeatedly. Measure token consumption. Important practices should likely reduce token cost across the board. Specialized practices may only apply in some regions of the eval space.
The same thing applies to tools. Would a semantic index help humans navigate a large codebase? Or more specifically, how much? Give the experimental agent access to a good indexer, leave the control agent with its standard out-of-the-box approach. We spend a few more tokens explaining how to use the tools, but if the tool pays off in net token costs, we should invest in that tooling.

articles.title: Batterie de 6 500 mAh et stockage de 512 Go : le POCO M8 Pro 5G est à 329 €
articles.text:
Le smartphone POCO M8 Pro 5G 12/512 Go est à 329 €
Le POCO M8 Pro 5G associe un écran AMOLED 120 Hz, une batterie de 6 500 mAh et un appareil photo principal stabilisé. Cette version dispose de 512 Go de stockage.
Amazon propose le POCO M8 Pro 5G 12/512 Go argent à 329 €, contre un prix conseillé de 403 €. L’écart atteint 74 €, soit environ 18 %. L’offre concerne un smartphone neuf, vendu et expédié par Amazon. Il s’agit bien du modèle Pro avec 12 Go de mémoire vive, distinct du POCO M8 également proposé sur la fiche.
Un écran AMOLED 120 Hz et un capteur photo stabilisé
Le POCO M8 Pro 5G possède un écran AMOLED de 6,83 pouces, affichant 2 772 × 1 280 pixels. Son taux de rafraîchissement atteint 120 Hz dans les applications compatibles. La prise en charge de Dolby Vision et du HDR10+ complète l’affichage pour les contenus adaptés, tandis que les haut-parleurs stéréo accompagnent la lecture des vidéos.
La partie photo comprend un capteur principal Light Fusion 800 de 50 Mpx avec stabilisation optique, ainsi qu’un ultra grand-angle de 8 Mpx. La caméra avant affiche 32 Mpx. Le smartphone peut enregistrer des vidéos en 4K à 30 images par seconde avec la caméra arrière.
Une batterie de 6 500 mAh et une charge compatible 100 W
Le Snapdragon 7s Gen 4 est associé à 12 Go de RAM et 512 Go de stockage. Cette capacité permet de conserver applications, photos et fichiers téléchargés, même si le système en occupe une partie. Le téléphone dispose également d’un lecteur d’empreintes sous l’écran, de la connectivité 5G et du NFC.
Sa batterie de 6 500 mAh est compatible avec la charge HyperCharge 100 W. Le chargeur secteur n’est toutefois pas inclus : il faut prévoir un adaptateur compatible pour profiter de la charge rapide. Une fonction de recharge inversée filaire jusqu’à 22,5 W permet aussi d’alimenter un accessoire compatible depuis le téléphone. L’autonomie réelle dépend notamment de l’écran, des applications et du réseau utilisé.

articles.title: Police seize humanoid robot after it allegedly sexually assaulted 16-year-old girl in Germany
articles.text:
WTF?! Makers of humanoid robots often claim they can do anything a human can. Unfortunately, that might include sexual assault. Police in Germany have seized a robot believed to have groped a 16-year-old girl while it was controlled by two male teenage boys. The whole thing was reportedly livestreamed with commentary, too.
The alleged incident took place overnight on October 10-11 in the city of Cologne, reports AP.
The robot stood about 3 feet 11 inches tall and wore a white tank top, black sweatpants, a gold chain, and sunglasses. It was also sporting a fake mustache, giving it an Iron Man meets Dr. Disrespect vibe.
Videos posted online show two young men escorting the robot toward a group of women. The machine bumps into one and hugs others on the lively street. The police allege that at one point, the robot touched the buttocks of a 16-year-old girl and made thrusting movements toward her.
Emergency teams that were dispatched to the scene near a fast-food restaurant found the robot in the trunk of a vehicle. The robot and the two young men's mobile phones were seized by officers.
A police spokesperson said the robot's suspected 16-year-old owner and a 19-year-old companion filmed the alleged assault. The pair have not been charged but are considered suspects. Investigators were examining whether the robot's movements were preprogrammed or controlled in real time, which may influence what actions the police take.
"We have not been aware of this phenomenon so far," Cologne police spokesman Christoph Bermel told AP, adding that this sort of incident is "new territory for us."
It wasn't too long ago that humanoid robots were only sold to enterprise users, and the few available commercial ones were priced beyond what most people could afford.
But that's changed over the last few years. Unitree has several commercial humanoid robots for sale at prices that range from the cost of a high-end gaming laptop to that of a second-hand car. We also saw what was described as the first of the machines aimed at consumers, 1X's Neo, in 2025. It carries a $20,000 price tag, can do household chores, and, concerningly, will occasionally allow a human operator to take control and see through its eyes.

articles.title: Quiénes son las protagonistas de ‘Las Guerreras K-pop’ y qué canciones las hicieron famosas
articles.text:
Más de un año después de su estreno mundial, Las guerreras K-pop mantiene su presencia en las plataformas de streaming gracias a una banda sonora que reúne canciones de sus protagonistas y de sus principales antagonistas.
La película animada de Netflix, conocida en inglés como K-Pop Demon Hunters, combina música, acción y fantasía en una historia protagonizada por tres estrellas del pop coreano que llevan una doble vida.
Rumi, Mira y Zoey forman HUNTR/X, un grupo musical que, además de presentarse ante miles de seguidores, tiene una misión secreta: proteger a la humanidad de los demonios. Sus canciones cumplen una función fundamental en la trama, ya que sus voces y actuaciones ayudan a mantener una barrera de energía que impide que las criaturas invadan el mundo humano.
Rumi, Mira y Zoey: quiénes integran HUNTR/X
Rumi es la líder del grupo y una de las figuras centrales de la historia. Mientras cumple con sus compromisos como estrella del K-pop, debe enfrentarse a un conflicto relacionado con su identidad, que amenaza con cambiar la forma en que se ve a sí misma y a sus compañeras.
Mira destaca por su personalidad decidida y su habilidad para combatir a los demonios. Zoey, por su parte, completa el trío con su energía y sus capacidades musicales. Juntas combinan coreografías, voces y destrezas de combate para enfrentarse a las amenazas que se esconden detrás del espectáculo.
Las voces cantadas de HUNTR/X corresponden a EJAE, Audrey Nuna y Rei Ami, mientras que Arden Cho, May Hong y Ji-young Yoo interpretan a las protagonistas en la versión original en inglés. Esta separación entre las voces de actuación y las musicales permitió construir personajes animados con identidades propias dentro de la historia.
Las canciones más populares de ‘Las Guerreras K-pop’
La banda sonora es uno de los principales motores del éxito de la película. Entre los temas asociados con HUNTR/X y los Saja Boys destacan cinco canciones que combinan el pop, el rap y las referencias a los conflictos de la trama.
“Golden”, interpretada por HUNTR/X, se convirtió en el tema más reconocido de la producción. Su mensaje gira alrededor de la confianza personal, la aceptación de la propia identidad y la decisión de dejar de esconderse. La canción también trascendió la película y alcanzó reconocimiento en la industria musical, con un Grammy obtenido en 2026 por sus intérpretes.
“How It’s Done” presenta el lado más contundente de HUNTR/X. Con una base marcada por el rap y una interpretación enérgica, la canción acompaña la faceta de las protagonistas como cazadoras de demonios y muestra cómo su vida musical convive con el peligro.
“What It Sounds Like” ofrece un registro más emocional. El tema aborda la aceptación de las heridas personales y la posibilidad de encontrar valor en aquello que se considera imperfecto. Su mensaje se relaciona con los conflictos internos que atraviesan las protagonistas durante la historia.
Saja Boys: los rivales detrás de “Soda Pop” y “Your Idol”
La película también presenta a los Saja Boys, una banda masculina que aparenta ser un grupo de ídolos del K-pop, pero esconde una identidad demoníaca. Sus integrantes —Jinu Saja, Abby Saja, Mystery Saja, Romance Saja y Baby Saja— buscan atraer a sus seguidores para apoderarse de sus almas.
“Soda Pop” utiliza un ritmo ligero y pegadizo para presentar al quinteto con una imagen atractiva e inofensiva. Sin embargo, detrás de su sonido festivo se ocultan las intenciones de los personajes.
“Your Idol”, también interpretada por los Saja Boys, tiene un tono más oscuro y cumple una función decisiva en la historia. La canción representa el poder que el grupo ejerce sobre sus seguidores y convierte la devoción por los ídolos en una herramienta de control.
Una banda sonora que trascendió la pantalla
El impacto de Las guerreras K-pop se extendió más allá de Netflix. Sus canciones ganaron popularidad en plataformas de streaming y redes sociales, donde los usuarios compartieron coreografías, versiones y fragmentos de las actuaciones.
La producción también obtuvo reconocimiento en las listas musicales estadounidenses, con varios temas en el Billboard Hot 100 y una destacada presencia de su banda sonora en el Billboard 200.
La combinación de personajes, música y fantasía explica parte de la conexión con el público: cada canción no funciona únicamente como acompañamiento, sino que desarrolla la personalidad de los grupos y refleja el conflicto entre HUNTR/X y los Saja Boys. Así, Rumi, Mira y Zoey se consolidaron como figuras centrales de una historia en la que el K-pop es tanto espectáculo como herramienta para salvar al mundo.

articles.title: Building AI Infrastructure For Greater Choice And Flexibility
articles.text:
Open interfaces and interoperability allow designers to choose technologies based on the needs of the system.
AI infrastructure is changing fast. Training and inference are putting different demands on compute, memory, connectivity, and networking, and there is no single architecture that fits every workload.
For system architects, this opens up an important question: How much flexibility can be built into the system from the start?
The answer increasingly involves giving designers more choices across memory, compute, connectivity, and packaging, while making sure those technologies work together.
AI training and inference may run on much of the same underlying infrastructure, but they don’t behave the same way.
Training places heavy demands on memory and communication between accelerators. Inference has a different mix of requirements, including memory capacity, latency, throughput, and efficiency.
Those differences matter when choosing an architecture. A memory technology that’s right for one workload may not be right for another. The same applies to interconnects and networking.
This is why AI infrastructure is becoming more heterogeneous. Architects are combining different technologies based on what they need the system to do, rather than trying to force every workload into the same design.
Fig. 1: Heterogeneous applications demand distinct solutions for optimized implementations.
Open standards give designers more options for how they put those systems together.
UCIe is one example. The standard provides a common approach to die-to-die connectivity and is aimed at supporting an open chiplet ecosystem. It gives the industry a standardized way to connect dies within a package rather than tying the architecture to a single implementation.
System architects are also working across a wider range of process technologies, packaging approaches, and functions. A chiplet-based approach provides another way to partition those functions, allowing compute, I/O, memory interfaces, and other functions to be integrated within the same package.
UCIe provides a standardized die-to-die connection for that environment. This gives designers a common interface as they evaluate how different functions should be partitioned and integrated.
For designers, the value is choice. Different functions can be brought together in a package while using a common interface between them.
That freedom becomes particularly useful when architects are balancing performance, power, cost, packaging, and process technology.
Open standards provide a common foundation for bringing technologies from different suppliers and foundries into the same system. Interoperability helps designers understand how those different implementations will work together.
Verification plays an important role here, particularly as systems incorporate more functions, interfaces, and technologies.
The need for choice doesn’t stop at the package.
An AI system can include several kinds of connectivity, each serving a different role. PCIe, CXL, UCIe, UALink, and Ethernet-based technologies address different parts of the architecture. Memory brings another set of decisions.
Fig. 2: Different connectivity, different scope, same goal: economical, rapid data transfer.
The requirements also change depending on where data is moving. HBM4E and LPDDR6 address different memory needs, while PCIe supports high-speed host and device connectivity. UALink addresses accelerator-to-accelerator communication, 224G high-speed SerDes provides the underlying high-speed signaling needed for demanding connectivity applications, and UCIe connects dies within packages.
Designers need to consider what they are connecting, how much data needs to move, and the requirements of the workload. Looking at those decisions together provides a more complete view of the system than treating each interface independently.
That perspective changes the design conversation. Rather than optimizing individual pieces independently, architects can look at how memory, compute, and connectivity fit together across the system.
AI infrastructure will continue to change as workloads, memory technologies, accelerators, and interconnects advance. Building flexibility into the architecture gives designers more options as those requirements change.
Open interfaces and interoperability are an important part of that flexibility, allowing designers to choose technologies based on the needs of the system rather than a single approach.
For a deeper look at the memory, compute, and connectivity technologies shaping these systems, read our Building AI Factories with IP Solutions white paper.

articles.title: À 24 heures près, GTA 6 pourra participer in extremis aux Game Awards 2026
articles.text:
Depuis que Rockstar a fixé la sortie du jeu au 19 novembre, beaucoup se demandaient si GTA VI arriverait à temps pour les Game Awards 2026. Le jeu pourra bien concourir cette année, et ainsi venger Red Dead Redemption 2, battu en 2018 par God of War dans la catégorie du jeu de l’année.
Le titre de jeu de l’année est aujourd’hui détenu par Clair Obscur: Expedition 33, du studio montpelliérain Sandfall Interactive, grand gagnant de l’édition 2025.
Pour être éligibles à la cérémonie, qui se tiendra dans la nuit du 10 au 11 décembre 2026, à 1h30 du matin heure française, « les jeux doivent être mis à la disposition des clients, dans le commerce, au plus tard le vendredi 20 novembre 2026 à 21h (heure du Pacifique) », précise le site officiel des Game Awards.
Le blockbuster de Rockstar, qui s’est dévoilé dans un nouveau trailer de lancement, est attendu pour le 19 novembre 2026, et passe donc tout juste sous la barre. Au moment de la date limite, le jeu sera en vente depuis à peine plus de 24 heures. Cette confirmation ne signifie toutefois pas que GTA VI sera automatiquement nommé dans la catégorie jeu de l’année.
Comme le rappelle le règlement des Game Awards, les nominations dans la plupart des catégories sont déterminées par un jury international composé de plus de 100 médias et créateurs de contenu du monde entier. Chacun liste ses cinq jeux favoris par catégorie, et les cinq titres les plus cités deviennent les finalistes.
GTA VI en lice, mais pas encore nommé
Les Game Awards ont-ils repoussé leur date limite spécialement pour accueillir GTA VI ? L’hypothèse a circulé sur les réseaux sociaux. Pourtant, rien ne semble la confirmer. La date limite tombe, comme d’habitude, le troisième vendredi de novembre. En 2025, elle était fixée au 21 novembre.
La présence de GTA VI devrait attirer du monde devant la cérémonie, créée et présentée par Geoff Keighley. Le jeu de Rockstar croisera aussi d’autres grosses sorties de fin d’année, comme le remake de The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, attendu le 5 novembre sur Switch 2.
La sortie, fixée au 19 novembre, tombe après l’annonce des nominations, attendue à la mi-novembre selon le site officiel. Entre sa sortie et la cérémonie du 10 décembre, il ne s’écoulera que 21 jours. Le jury ne pourra donc juger GTA VI que si Rockstar lui donne accès au jeu en avance, ce que le règlement des Game Awards autorise. L’attente autour de GTA VI, élu jeu le plus attendu aux Game Awards 2024 puis 2025, devrait peser dans le choix des votants.

articles.title: How Zambia’s CherryPick is building more resilient food systems for Africa - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Zambia’s CherryPick is an agro-processing company that is helping to build more resilient, inclusive and adaptable food systems while encouraging healthier eating habits, one healthy snack at a time.
Founded in 2016 by Zama Bbuku and her husband Lwando, CherryPick started as a modest strawberry-growing venture keen to contribute meaningfully to Zambia’s agricultural landscape.
“This exposed us to a reality shared by farmers across Zambia – abundance at harvest and loss shortly after due to challenges with market linkages. This sparked a defining question for us – what if we could preserve more of what we grow, add value locally and make nutritious food accessible year round,” she said.
“At the heart of what we do is a very simple idea – Zambia produces a lot of good food, but too much of it is lost after harvest, while at the same time consumers are looking for healthier and more convenient food options.”
CherryPick sources seasonal, nutritious produce from small-scale farmers and transforms it into quality, shelf-stable, conveniently-packaged dried fruit and cashew nut snacks.
“By extending the shelf-life of fresh produce, we are able to reduce post-harvest losses, create market opportunities for farmers and give consumers convenient healthier alternatives to ultra-processed foods,” Bbuku said.
Improving traceability and quality
The startup is currently in the process of developing AgroChain360, a technology platform designed to improve traceability, farmer coordination, production planning and quality assurance across the agricultural value chain.
“Ultimately, we want consumers to have greater visibility of where their food comes from while creating stronger and more reliable links between farmers and markets,” said Bbuku.
“We saw two sides of the same problem. On one side, farmers can have good produce but struggle with reliable markets, and because fresh produce is highly perishable, anything that isn’t sold quickly can become a loss. On the other side, consumers increasingly want convenient snacks, but many of the readily available options are highly processed.”
CherryPick saw an opportunity to connect those two problems.
“We are not simply trying to sell another snack. We are building a farm-to-shelf model around local sourcing, value addition, healthier eating and traceability. AgroChain360 will strengthen that differentiation by helping us build greater transparency and coordination into the supply chain,” said Bbuku.
Finding support to grow
Cherry-Pick has been grown through a combination of founder investment, business revenues and grant funding.
“One of our most important milestones has been our participation in the Standard Chartered Women in Tech programme implemented by BongoHive, through which we received both funding and business support. We have received three grants since inception, which has helped us expand our operations.”
This refers to the Standard Chartered Foundation’s Women in Tech Accelerator, implemented by BongoHive in Zambia, with support from Village Capital. The program is part of a multi-region initiative which supports impact-creating, tech-enabled, women-led startups in building thriving businesses across Africa, the Middle East, and Pakistan.
“Other important milestones have included obtaining our ZABS certification, expanding our retail presence, building partnerships within Zambia’s entrepreneurship ecosystem, and continuing to grow our production capacity despite operating in a very challenging environment,” Bbuku said.
Building traction
“We have built up a lot of traction over the years with uptake and growth increasing year-on-year by over 60 per cent. The response has been highly encouraging, particularly as more consumers become conscious of what they eat and look for convenient but healthier alternatives.”
The business has grown through a combination of retail sales, direct customers, corporate orders and partnerships.
“One of the things that has encouraged us most is repeat consumption. When somebody tries the product and comes back for it, that tells us we are not simply benefiting from curiosity around a new product, we are building something people genuinely want,” said Bbuku.
“We have also learnt that building a food brand takes time. It involves educating consumers, getting them to try something different and then consistently delivering the quality that makes them come back.”
Expanding beyond Zambia
CherryPick’s ambition goes beyond Zambia.
“We believe the challenges we are addressing such as post-harvest losses, fragmented agricultural value chains and growing demand for healthier foods, are shared across many African markets,” said Bbuku.
“Our longer-term plan is therefore to expand our product distribution into regional and export markets while also scaling AgroChain360. We want Cherry-Pick to demonstrate that African agricultural businesses can create value locally and build products and systems capable of competing beyond their home markets.”
Bbuku’s background is not in the food business, but rather the ICT regulatory space, where much of her work involved licensing, regulation, stakeholder engagement and understanding how businesses operate within structured environments. Entrepreneurship came from a desire to build something of her own, but also something that could solve a real problem.
“The journey has definitely not been a straight line. We started small and have had to learn almost every aspect of the business along the way – from production and packaging to certification, getting products onto retail shelves, managing cash flow and building a brand. We’ve also had to navigate challenges such as load shedding, access to equipment, sourcing consistently and finding the right markets for our products,” she said.
“For me personally, entrepreneurship has been a journey of resilience. I have had to learn that you don’t need to have everything figured out before you start. You build, you make mistakes, you adjust, and you keep going.”

articles.title: Peak XV is taking bigger bets as Indian startups grow more ambitious: Mohit Bhatnagar
articles.text:
Peak XV is taking bigger bets as Indian startups grow more ambitious: Mohit Bhatnagar
At TechSparks 2026, Peak XV's Managing Director Mohit Bhatnagar said the venture capital firm is increasingly willing to back ambitious, high-risk startups as AI opens up new opportunities for Indian founders to build global companies.
Indian startup founders are increasingly aspiring to build companies worth $50 billion or even $100 billion, a shift that is prompting venture capital firms such as Peak XV Partners to take bigger risks, according to its Managing Director Mohit Bhatnagar.
During a fireside chat with Shradha Sharma, Founder and CEO of YourStory and The Bharat Project, at TechSparks 2026 in Bengaluru, Bhatnagar said the success of companies such as Zomato and the growing acceptance of startups in India's public markets have fundamentally changed what founders and investors believe is possible.
Bhatnagar was gungo-ho about the ambition and aspiration of Indian founders which has grown multifold over the years. "The startup ecosystem is in a much better place today than it was 20 years back. The biggest difference is in ambition," he said.
According to him, the ambition of startup founders is at a different level now than what was seen in the past. Bhatnagar, who has two decades of experience as a venture capitalist, sees ambition from Indian startups only getting bigger going forward.
Peak XV is one of the leading venture capital firms in the country with investment bets spread across sectors, including companies such as Zomato and Meesho.
Bhatnagar said Peak XV has had about 37 IPOs in the country, and 22 of them have happened in the last five years.
“The total market cap of all startups that have gone public in India today is somewhere around $170 billion. That number, by the way, used to be 1/10 or much smaller than that 10 years back,” Bhatnagar remarked and added that public markets are embracing startups like never before.
“The Indian public markets in the last five years have truly been a massive blessing to the entire startup ecosystem,” he remarked.
There have also been other changes across the world, driven by artificial intelligence (AI).
Bhatnagar believes AI can be a big advantage for a country like India. “AI tools are now available to everybody. Everyone here should be dreaming about building a company that is rooted in India and really think global,” he said.
He emphasised that every founder should leverage the AI opportunity to build global companies. He highlighted that, as the cost of tokens fall over a period of time, consumer AI applications will be unleashed across sectors such as health, financial services, and education.
He was also of the firm opinion that AI will bring in efficiency as smaller teams will be able to quickly come out with better solutions.
At the same time, he said, there is no easy yardstick to identify the right companies. Founders need to sustain their hard work to build a durable business, which might take even a decade.
Bhatnagar said India remains a very attractive destination for investors seeking to back startup founders. “I really hope we now see a 10x unleashing of entrepreneurial energy because it's become so much easier to launch a product, to try it in the marketplace, than ever before. You don't need as much capital.”

articles.title: Yellowjackets : Paramount+ dévoile un trailer intense pour l'ultime saison
articles.text:
Yellowjackets : Paramount+ dévoile un trailer intense pour l'ultime saison
La série Yellowjackets prépare son retour sur Paramount+ et dévoile une bande-annonce de sa saison 4 qui laisse entendre que le retour des footballeuses à la civilisation ne vas pas être évident.
La série Yellowjackets revient le 20 novembre prochain sur nos écrans avec sa quatrième et dernière saison disponible sur le service de streaming Paramount+. Il est donc temps pour cette équipe de football féminine perdue dans la nature de rentrer chez elle et de faire face aux conséquences de leurs actes, comme l'indique la bande-annonce du show.
Retour au bercail
Dans l'ultime saison de Yellowjackets, les survivantes rentrent chez elles après 19 mois passés dans la forêt du Grand Nord, "hantées par ce qu'il leur en a coûté pour s'en sortir vivantes," comme l'indique le synopsis officiel de la série. On retrouvera aussi bien entendu en parallèle Shauna (Melanie Lynskey), Taissa (Tawny Cypress), Misty (Christina Ricci) et compagnie 25 ans plus tard, alors que leur passé continue de les rattraper.
La distribution de la série demeure composée de Sophie Nélisse (Heated Rivalry), Jasmin Savoy Brown (The Leftovers), Sophie Thatcher (Heretic), Samantha Hanratty (Shameless), Courtney Eaton (Mad Max: Fury Road), Liv Hewson (Santa Clarita Diet), Warren Kole (Shades of Blue), Kevin Alves (Locke & Key), Sarah Desjardins (The Night Agent), Nia Sondaya (Heart Shot), Jenna Burgess (Lies Between Friends), Hilary Swank (Million Dollar Baby) et Elijah Wood (Le Seigneur de Anneaux).
Pour rappel, Yellowjackets est à la fois un récit de survie, un thriller psychologique aux accents horrifiques et une chronique adolescente, créée par Ashley Lyle et Bart Nickerson.
La série est produite par Lionsgate Television pour Showtime et distribuée par Paramount Global Content Distribution, et ces trois premières saisons sont donc disponibles en streaming sur Paramount+.

articles.title: Google a laissé traîner un faux Chrome frauduleux sur le Play Store
articles.text:
Google veut sécuriser Android. C’est d’ailleurs la raison pour laquelle la firme de Mountain View a récemment dévoilé son intention de compliquer la tâche des utilisateurs souhaitant installer des applications en dehors du Google Play Store.
Pour ce faire, Google a prévu de rendre le sideloading beaucoup plus compliqué à mettre en place. Une façon pour l’entreprise de forcer les utilisateurs à ne télécharger que des applications vérifiées et censées être sécurisées, depuis son Google Play Store.
Malheureusement pour Google, sa boutique d’applications mobiles est loin d’être parfaite. Si celle-ci a déjà été épinglée à plusieurs reprises par le passé pour avoir laissé passer des applications peu recommandables, l’entreprise avait, en principe, renforcé la sécurité de sa boutique pour éviter ce genre de mauvaise surprise. C’est d’ailleurs ce qui lui a permis, l’an dernier, de bloquer quelque 1,75 million d’applications potentiellement dangereuses de sa boutique officielle. Mais visiblement, Google a encore quelques efforts à faire pour que son Play Store soit irréprochable.
Un faux Google Chrome frauduleux promu et téléchargé plus de 100 000 fois
Aussi incroyable que cela puisse paraître, une fausse version de Google Chrome, non détectée par Google, a été proposée au téléchargement sur le Play Store. Téléchargée plus de 100 000 fois, cette application malveillante était proposée par un développeur nommé « Hizbartech », et n’avait en réalité rien d’un navigateur Web. Il s’agissait en réalité d’une application de discussion fonctionnant avec des réponses préenregistrées.
Comment Google a-t-il pu laisser passer ça ? Pour bien comprendre, il faut remonter au 22 août dernier, date à laquelle l’application a été publiée à l’origine sous un autre nom, « Ball Bounce », sous la forme d’un simple jeu. Le développeur de ladite application a pu, dès la fin du mois de septembre, modifier le nom de son application, sa description mais aussi et surtout son icône pour faire passer celle-ci pour la version légitime de Google Chrome.
Le développeur usurpateur a ensuite payé pour sponsoriser son application sur le Google Play Store, faisant ainsi apparaître celle-ci en haut des résultats de recherche, au-dessus de la version légitime de Google Chrome, lorsque les utilisateurs lançaient la requête « Chrome » dans le moteur de recherche.
Il a finalement fallu qu’un utilisateur de Reddit dénonce l’opération suspecte dans une publication envoyée sur le forum, et rapidement relayée par Piunikaweb et Android Authority pour que Google réagisse finalement et procède au retrait de l’application malveillante.
Google pris à son propre piège
Pour Google, c’est un peu la douche froide. Depuis plusieurs mois, Google prône sa boutique d’applications comme le moyen le plus sûr d’installer des applications face aux risques générés par le sideloading. Pourtant, force est de constater que le Play Store n’est pas aussi parfait en termes de sécurité que veut bien le faire croire Google.
Cette affaire, qui a le don de mettre Google face à ses contradictions, démontre que la firme de Mountain View a encore un peu de travail devant elle pour ce qui est de sécuriser le Play Store. Comment est-il possible qu’un développeur puisse modifier aussi facilement le nom et l’icône d’une application dans la boutique ? Surtout, comment les équipes de Google justifient-elles l’absence totale de vérification des annonces publicitaires payantes qui ont en l’occurrence permis à un fraudeur d’acheter de la visibilité pour une application malveillante ?
En attendant que Google prenne les mesures nécessaires pour qu’un tel épisode ne se renouvelle pas, il est conseillé de toujours vérifier l’identité exacte du développeur des applications que vous téléchargez sur le Play Store, ainsi que le nom du package de l’application. Surtout, évitez autant que possible de cliquer sur les résultats sponsorisés affichés tout en haut des résultats de recherche.

articles.title: Android gets AI defenses against messaging scams, fake calls
articles.text:
Google announced new AI-powered defenses against scam messages and call-forwarding abuse on Android, currently rolling out to eligible devices.
The new measures aim to address the increased sophistication of scams targeting mobile users, including fraudulent bank alerts and voice-cloning attacks.
“Mobile scams have evolved far beyond basic robocalls and phishing texts, turning into sophisticated operations that use spoofed numbers, fake bank alerts, and AI voice cloning,” Google says.
“With scams growing harder to spot, it’s nearly impossible for users to catch every red flag themselves,” added the tech giant.
Google says its existing Phone and Messages scam detection flags more than 5 million suspected scam calls and texts monthly, but the new measures are expected to catch even more threats.
Cloud-based scam analysis
The new protections focus on Google Messages and rely on cloud-based Gemini-backed analysis for complex conversations, scrutinizing them for signs of fraud.
The system analyzes conversations with unknown senders within the encrypted Private AI Compute environment, protecting user privacy at all times.
The new mode also adds on-device Gemini Nano (local AI model) checks for unfamiliar links using real-time web signals, plus clearer warnings before opening links from unsaved numbers.
The new cloud-based protections are currently disabled by default, allowing users to activate them.
Other improvements
Apart from the Google Messages protection, Google has also implemented the enhancements in other areas of the Android system:
- On-device scam detection in chat notifications, previously launched on Pixel, will reach hundreds of millions more users through Android device partners later this year.
- Android’s existing sensitive-information masking is now expanding to Chrome and Android WebView, hiding login fields and payment screens during live screen sharing.
- Android blocks apps from silently enabling call forwarding in the background and warns users before manually entered MMI forwarding codes take effect.
Google is also expanding its verified bank calls system, introduced earlier this year, adding financial institutions from more.
This system checks whether a real bank’s call center initiated an incoming call or if it is a spoofing attempt. If the verification fails, the call is automatically ended.
Google says that since June it has blocked over 3 million fraudulent calls of this kind for Banco do Brasil and Itaú Unibanco alone. Revolut and other global financial institutions are also supported.
Android users should upgrade to the latest release, keep apps updated, and independently verify caller/sender identities when receiving requests for account-related action or sensitive information.
Once attackers have valid credentials, only 37% of their actions are blocked
Overall prevention scores can hide what happens after initial access. Once attackers are using valid credentials, prevention drops sharply.

articles.title: Free tient (enfin) sa promesse et laisse choisir le pays de sortie de son VPN gratuit
articles.text:
Free fait évoluer mVPN, le VPN gratuit intégré à ses forfaits mobiles. L'opérateur renforce son service, avec le choix entre huit pays de connexion, le filtrage des sites malveillants et pour adultes, et un widget dédié.
Un peu plus d'un an après son lancement, mVPN, le VPN gratuit intégré aux forfaits Free Mobile, s'offre sa mise à jour la plus copieuse ce jeudi 15 octobre 2026. L'aiguillage imposé vers l'Italie ou les Pays-Bas est terminé, puisque l'abonné choisit désormais son pays de sortie parmi huit destinations, et règle lui-même le niveau de filtrage de sa navigation. Ironie de l'histoire, le réglage le plus strict bloque les sites pour adultes, ceux-là mêmes que mVPN permettait de rejoindre à sa sortie, comme l'avait reconnu Xavier Niel.
Free mVPN fait le plein de nouveautés
Principale nouveauté de cette mise à jour, le VPN gratuit de Free laisse désormais choisir entre trois niveaux de protection. Le mode Standard chiffre la connexion, c’est-à-dire qu’il rend les données échangées illisibles pour qui tenterait de les intercepter, mais ne filtre aucun site. Le niveau Essentiel bloque en plus l’accès aux sites malveillants ou frauduleux, comme ces fausses pages de livraison ou de banque vers lesquelles renvoient certains SMS et e-mails piégés. Le niveau Renforcé y ajoute les sites pour adultes. Ce blocage des liens dangereux était déjà mis en avant au lancement, où il s’appliquait automatiquement, mais il devient aujourd’hui un réglage que chacun choisit, et qu'il est possible de modifier à tout moment.
Pour faire le tri, Free mise sur ses propres résolveurs DNS, qui on le rappelle sont des annuaires du web qui traduisent le nom d'un site en adresse joignable. Ils sont complétés par plusieurs sources qui recensent les sites jugés dangereux, frauduleux ou réservés aux adultes. L'opérateur imagine par exemple le niveau Renforcé sur la ligne d'un adolescent, ou lorsque toute la famille se branche sur le même partage de connexion.
Les parents gardent la main sur l'outil. Un contrôle parental activé par le titulaire du compte reste en place quand mVPN tourne. Sur une ligne secondaire, seul le titulaire principal peut autoriser l'usage du VPN. mVPN vient ainsi s'ajouter aux outils que Free fournit déjà sans surcoût aux familles. L'opérateur reconnaît d’ailleurs lui-même les limites de l’exercice, car aucun outil de sécurité ne met totalement à l’abri des risques en ligne. Le filtrage s’appuie en effet sur des listes de sites déjà identifiés comme dangereux, et une arnaque toute récente peut encore passer entre les mailles du filet.
Huit pays au compteur et un widget pour gagner du temps
Le choix du pays de sortie, promis dès le lancement et que beaucoup attendaient, est enfin là. Un VPN chiffre la connexion et la fait ressortir sur Internet depuis un serveur situé ailleurs. Jusqu'ici, ce serveur se trouvait d'office en Italie ou aux Pays-Bas. Huit destinations sont désormais proposées avec la Suisse, les États-Unis, l'Italie, le Royaume-Uni, les Pays-Bas, le Canada, le Brésil et le Japon, en plus d'un mode automatique. Notez que les pays et niveau de protection se modifient à tout moment.
Il n'y a toujours aucune application tierce à installer. Tout passe par l'application Free, qui facilite désormais l'ajout d'un widget mVPN sur l'écran d'accueil, sur iOS comme sur Android. Ce raccourci allume ou éteint le VPN sans ouvrir l'application. Les nouveautés sont disponibles dès aujourd'hui pour les abonnés Forfait Free 5G+, Forfait Free Max et Série Free, via l'app, le widget ou l'Espace Abonné, rubrique « Mes options ». Si les mises à jour automatiques sont désactivées sur le téléphone, il faudra mettre l'app à jour à la main.
Le mode d'emploi, lui, ne bouge pas, par exemple, mVPN s'active par sessions de 12 heures, qui s'arrêtent seules ou à la demande de l'utilisateur. Il fonctionne uniquement en France métropolitaine et sur le réseau mobile de Free, c'est-à-dire qu'il faut couper le Wi-Fi. Il n'a pas de quota dédié, mais puise dans la data du forfait, y compris en partage de connexion. Les MMS restent indisponibles. Et sur iPhone, le filtrage n'est pas compatible avec le Relais privé iCloud ni avec l'option « Masquer l'adresse IP » de Safari. Free, qui comptait 15,8 millions d'abonnés mobiles fin juin 2026 et revendiquait au lancement une première mondiale, est à ce jour le seul opérateur français à inclure un VPN sans surcoût.

articles.title: Anthropic’s been eyeing confidential AI. It just made its move with another acquihire.
articles.text:
Anthropic’s been eyeing confidential AI. It just made its move with another acquihire.
Anthropic’s done it again. On Tuesday, Opaque Systems announced a new agreement with Anthropic that “carries Opaque’s work forward.”
Vague wording aside, the agreement marks another acquihire for Anthropic, with the AI juggernaut licensing Opaque’s technology and bringing on board some (but not all) of its employees, including Opaque CEO Aaron Fulkerson and CTO Rishabh Poddar, reports The Information.
The agreement gives Anthropic access to expertise in confidential AI, the “real-world technology” and category Opaque claims it helped define after starting as a research project at UC Berkeley’s RISELab 10 years ago with the goal to “enabl[e] organizations to use their most sensitive data while keeping it private, even while it’s being used.”
For now, both Anthropic and Opaque are pretty mum on the details of the deal, leaving one obvious question on everyone’s mind:
What will happen to Opaque’s open-source ecosystem? And what does that mean for the developers relying on them?
What is confidential AI? And what does Opaque bring to the table?
On LinkedIn, where he shared news of the agreement, Fulkerson reflected on Opaque’s work defining the category of confidential AI, what he described as “verifiability for the AI stack.”
When asked for more information on the term, Arjun Jaggi, associate director of R&D innovation at Cognizant, describes confidential computing in AI to The New Stack as “running workloads on sensitive data while the data stays protected by the hardware itself, even while it’s being used.”
Whether or not it truly defined the category, the startup’s sure been making its mark. Earlier this year, it closed a $24 million Series B with a $300 million valuation. It’s also spearheaded a slew of industry initiatives.
It created the Confidential Computing Summit, an event Fulkerson says it has now handed over to the Linux Foundation, which already co-hosted this year’s June summit with Opaque. Working with the UAE’s Technology Innovation Institute, it created an open standard for verifiable AI governance. In June this year, it launched AgenTrust, an open-source community for verifiable agent governance, and Confidential MCP, which Opaque bills as the first verifiably governed, secure MCP implementation.
Now, as Opaque enters into a deal with one of the biggest names in the AI space, the obvious question is what will happen to the technology and community it helped build. So far, reactions are mixed.
Anthropic’s been transparent about its interest in confidential AI
In 2024, Jason Clinton, Anthropic’s chief information security officer, appeared on Opaque’s AI Confidential podcast, where he discussed the importance of confidential computing for the future of AI. Afterward, Fulkerson recapped the conversation with a post, the title of which made clear Anthropic’s confidential AI aspirations: “The Mathematical Case for Trusted AI: Why Anthropic is All-In on Confidential Computing.”
Then in 2025, Anthropic published research with Pattern Labs on confidential inference, an approach to protecting sensitive data and AI model weights: “Confidential Inference via Trusted Virtual Machines.” The AI company acknowledged the work was still preliminary, calling it “just a sketch of our research” that was “still early.”
And by early 2026, Anthropic was named in Opaque’s list of customers and partners.
“When a frontier lab like Anthropic takes a promising confidential computing tool and puts real resources behind it, that’s often how a research stage project becomes something hardened enough for production — and an under-funded startup might never get it there on its own.”
Looking back, those public statements suggest Anthropic has been thinking about confidential AI well before its Opaque deal. Whether the new agreement will benefit the industry as a whole, though, remains unknown.
Jaggi, at least, is taking an optimistic stance, telling The New Stack Anthropic’s resources could give the technology the push it needs to grow:
“I’d actually frame this more positively than most. When a frontier lab like Anthropic takes a promising confidential computing tool and puts real resources behind it, that’s often how a research stage project becomes something hardened enough for production — and an under-funded startup might never get it there on its own.”
Others are more skeptical, though.
When asked for his take, Michael Heinrich, co-founder and CEO of 0G Labs, tells The New Stack he sees the agreement as a good move for Anthropic, which can piggyback on Opaque’s decade of confidential computing research. What he expresses caution about is a potential conflict of interest:
“The whole point of confidential computing is that you don’t have to trust the operator. When the tools that produce that proof sit inside a model vendor, the party being checked now owns part of the checking.”
Both are opaque on the details of the deal
In his LinkedIn post, Fulkerson describes his move to Anthropic as a natural fit, writing, “Their culture, their mission and their values align with mine, personally and professionally.”
In its announcement, Opaque itself is similarly vague, calling the agreement a “next chapter” that “carries Opaque’s work forward.”
Anthropic, for its part, has told The Information that it’s licensing Opaque’s technology and hiring some of its engineers but has otherwise released no further information.
“The whole point of confidential computing is that you don’t have to trust the operator. When the tools that produce that proof sit inside a model vendor, the party being checked now owns part of the checking.”
So the (unanswered) elephant in the room is: What happens to all of Opaque’s existing initiatives? The governance framework? AgenTrust? Confidential MCP?
We know that Opaque has passed its summit to the Linux Foundation. But questions remain about the startup’s open-source projects, as neither Opaque nor Anthropic has made any statements about maintenance commitments.
Heinrich seems relatively unconcerned for now, telling TNS that Confidential MCP is MIT-licensed, so anyone can continue using it. He also adds, “Anthropic has set a good precedent here: It gave MCP to the Linux Foundation’s Agentic AI Foundation so no single company controls the protocol.”
Nevertheless, both he and Jaggi advise developers to take precautions now by pinning versions of the tools they rely on and mirroring repositories to preserve code access.
For now, it seems clear Anthropic will benefit from Opaque’s expertise—whether the rest of the industry will, too, remains to be seen.

articles.title: Kaspersky’s African business is profitable. Now it wants bigger clients.
articles.text:
Kaspersky has spent over a decade building its African business. Its next phase is about winning a bigger role in the systems that keep the continent’s economy running.
Kaspersky, the Russian-founded global security company, said Africa is becoming a key market for the group. Its operations across Sub-Saharan Africa are now profitable, executives told TechCabal on the sidelines of GITEX Nigeria in Lagos in September.
The company plans to expand its business with banks, governments, and critical infrastructure operators as the growth of digital financial services creates more systems that need protection. Its African sales rose 12% in 2025, following 19% growth in 2024, according to its executives.
Nigeria is Kaspersky’s top priority market in Africa, according to its executives. Ghana, Côte d’Ivoire, Senegal, and Cameroon are also high priority; Kenya is rated “very high,” and Uganda and Zambia are growth markets.
The expansion would give Kaspersky a deeper role in institutions whose security failures can disrupt payments, expose customer information, and interrupt public services. The company said it helped build and continues to run Rwanda’s national security operations centre infrastructure. It also said several East African central banks use its products, and that Ethiopia contributes 60% of the region’s revenue.
Kaspersky wants a larger role in institutional customers’ operations by monitoring networks, investigating attacks, and supporting recovery. African institutions gain capabilities they may struggle to build themselves, but also become more dependent on its software and expertise. Choosing a security supplier means assessing both the protection it offers and the institution’s ability to oversee its work.
Kaspersky is trying to address those concerns through products customers can operate within their own environments and a transparency programme that allows scrutiny of its technology. The challenge is whether those arrangements give institutions enough control as the company takes on more sensitive work.
Moving beyond antivirus
Financial institutions account for much of Kaspersky’s private-sector business in Africa, said Bethwel Opil, its enterprise business sales manager. Government accounts are smaller but strategically important because they include regulators and institutions responsible for national systems.
The attraction of these customers extends beyond selling additional software licences. A supplier that monitors networks, investigates incidents and supports recovery becomes part of an institution’s daily operations. Its relationship with the customer can extend across several security functions.
Kaspersky’s global results show the commercial importance of that shift. Its sales reached $836 million in 2025, with business-to-business (B2B) sales rising 16% and enterprise sales growing 21%. Products protecting infrastructure beyond traditional computers and servers recorded 29% growth, compared with 1% for endpoint products.
Kaspersky’s push into African businesses has yet to produce the growth it is seeing among consumers. Consumer sales growth has averaged 36% in Africa, compared with 10% for business, Opil said. The company did not provide revenue totals for either segment, leaving the size of its institutional business unclear.
However, its case for selling broader protection across the continent rests on changes in how attacks have evolved. In 2025, the company said it detected about 500,000 malicious files daily across its customer base. Ransomware attackers can steal information before locking a customer’s files, then threaten to publish it even if the organisation has backups that allow it to restore its systems. Restoring operations leaves the risk of a data leak unresolved.
Staff using public AI tools add another route for data to leave. Employees who paste sensitive documents into chatbots to summarise or polish them can expose corporate data, Kaspersky said. It said its tools can show organisations which unsanctioned AI tools their staff use, so they can set rules and risk controls.
Institutions need to know how attackers broke in, which systems and data they accessed, and whether they can still get in. Kaspersky’s tools collect and analyse logs, the records of activity kept by computers, email systems and networks, to help security teams trace the attack.
Moses Munguti, a security consultant and Kaspersky Africa lead, said customers have different budgets, staffing levels and security capabilities. Combining several functions in one product can help smaller teams manage that work, giving Kaspersky a way to expand its role within the organisations it already protects.
The benefit is a more coordinated defence. The trade-off is greater dependence on the supplier. The more security functions an institution buys from Kaspersky, the harder it could become to switch providers. Leaving may mean replacing several tools at once and retraining the staff who use them.
Kaspersky is competing for that role with companies such as Sophos and Microsoft. Sophos completed its $859 million acquisition of Secureworks in February 2025, expanding its threat detection, investigation, and response capabilities. The combined company said it served more than 28,000 organisations through managed detection and response services, which provide security specialists to monitor and help contain attacks.
The competition already extends into Africa. Johannesburg-based BUI offers a security operations service built on Microsoft Sentinel, providing monitoring, threat detection, and investigation across South Africa and other African markets, according to a Microsoft case study. Kaspersky must compete with both rival software platforms and service providers using those platforms to manage customers’ security.
Local deployment does not settle control
Kaspersky faces additional scrutiny because of its Russian origins. In June 2024, the US Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) restricted the export of its cybersecurity software, citing risks stemming from potential Russian government influence and the software’s access to customers’ systems. Kaspersky disputed the decision, attributed it to geopolitical and theoretical concerns, and denied that it threatened US national security.
Kaspersky subsequently announced it would wind down its US operations from July 20, 2024, and eliminate US-based jobs. The restrictions also prohibited antivirus software and software updates for US customers as of September 29, 2024.
While the restrictions do not establish that Kaspersky compromised African customers, they highlight a risk institutions must assess when choosing security software: the supplier’s access to their systems and the laws under which it operates.
These concerns extend beyond Kaspersky. In its 2026 Africa Cybersecurity Threat Outlook, consulting firm EY identified third-party and ecosystem risk as a major blind spot, noting that vulnerabilities can spread through vendors and their suppliers. An institution can strengthen its own defences and remain exposed through a company it relies on.
This complicates Africa’s push for digital sovereignty. Keeping data within national borders addresses where it is stored. Institutions must also establish who can access it, control the software that handles it, and maintain the systems that support it.
Kaspersky said customers can run its security products on their own premises, giving their IT teams greater control over the infrastructure.
“Based on the functionality of the product or service our customers want to use, in most cases they can choose if and how much data they want to provide,” Munguti told TechCabal. “Kaspersky products never process sensitive personal data. We just need a unique identifier to check against our cloud-based database. That can give our customers confidence that there’s no likelihood of [data] leaving the environment.”
Some detection runs locally, allowing devices to identify threats without constant Internet connectivity, he said. Other checks use Kaspersky’s cloud-based threat intelligence. Customers need to understand which functions operate locally, what information is transmitted, and how their chosen settings affect protection, according to Munguti.
In 2023, the company opened a Transparency Centre in Kigali, Rwanda—one of 13 such centres globally and the only one in Africa—offering customers and regulators information on its engineering and data-processing practices, including source-code review demonstrations.
These measures give institutions ways to scrutinise Kaspersky’s assurances. Using them requires expertise to assess the software and verify how it operates within their own systems. Customers buying security tools to compensate for limited technical capacity may also need help evaluating those tools.
Kaspersky’s expansion could strengthen those institutions’ defences. The risk is that they become better protected without becoming better equipped to oversee the supplier. As the company takes on more sensitive assignments, customers need both: protection against attackers and enough control to maintain that protection if the relationship ends.
True scale demands moving beyond surface-level integrations to robust execution. We’ve filtered the noise out of Moonshot 2026, optimising the conference strictly for high-calibre connections between startup founders, global financial operators, enterprise leaders, and individuals rewiring Africa’s technical frameworks.
