articles.title: A new mod brings Apple's classic iPods into 2026 with Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, USB-C, and Spotify support
articles.text:
In brief: Those who still love the iPod's iconic click wheel and simple interface may soon be able to use one without relying on wired headphones or Apple's old proprietary USB interface. An upcoming project aims to update certain models to support modern accessories while retaining the legendary MP3 player's simple user experience.
Interested iPod owners can now sign up for updates on the development of a mod that adds support for Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, USB-C, expandable storage, additional media formats, and more. Built from Raspberry Pi boards, the mod requires no soldering.
The Sprout Pico and Sprout Pi are open-source drop-in replacement mainboards that make the obsolete 3rd- and 4th-generation iPods, as well as the iPod mini, compatible with modern wired and wireless interfaces. The Raspberry Pi RP2350 boards also come pre-installed with a custom OS that supports various new features and apps, mixing today's functionality with an early-2000s monochrome user interface. The project supports older iPod models because they are cheaper and more readily available than the 5th-gen iPod Video.
While pricing information is not yet available, the Sprout Pico will presumably be the cheaper model. It adds Bluetooth audio to support modern AirPods, a hi-fi DAC through the 3.5mm headphone jack, USB-C with digital audio out and inline remote controls, Wi-Fi support, two GPIO pins, up to 2TB of microSD card storage, and a 1,200 mAh or 2,500 mAh battery. Modded iPods also gain support for AAC, ALAC, FLAC, Opus, and podcast downloads. Meanwhile, the Sprout Pi adds a Raspberry Pi Compute Module Zero to support AirPlay, custom apps, and streaming via Apple Music or Spotify.
The Apple iPod: Pocket Music Before That Phone – A Legends of Tech feature
A trailer shows the installation process, which is reversible, followed by shots of the iPod interacting with AirPods, a HomePod, and other Bluetooth devices. The custom interface squeezes AirPods controls, the latest podcasts, and music from Spotify and Apple Music onto the iPod's low-resolution, black-and-white screen. Additional apps include MacPaint, a calculator, and Crash Bandicoot.
While MP3 players already existed when Apple launched the first iPod in 2001, the iconic device certainly popularized them. However, after multiple design revisions over two decades, Apple ultimately discontinued it because the iPhone had subsumed all of its functionality. The final iPod model, the iPod Touch, was essentially an iPhone without cellular connectivity.
However, in recent years, widespread frustration with the streaming business model has driven some users back to standalone MP3 players. Prior iPod mods have also added features like microSD support and (ironically) Spotify, but Sprout Pi appears to take things further.

articles.title: Context Is King in the Fight Against Modern Cyberattacks
articles.text:
For most of its history, cybersecurity has been reactive by design. Spot the bad event, shut it down. But as cyberattacks evolve, this thinking must evolve too. In the past, attackers relied on a single dramatic exploit to access the crown jewels. But the nature of attacks has changed.
Defenders see ordinary events they don’t think are important enough to follow up on, but before they realize it, these events lead to a dramatic breach. A breach can start with a common event like an admin login or an unfamiliar tool being downloaded after office hours. This first step, if left unchallenged, leads to each following step growing more severe, resulting in a security incident.
Lack of Data Sensibility
It’s wrong to assume that attackers have more data than defenders do about their own environment. Defenders know their users, devices, applications, network traffic, and vulnerabilities. Having access to such diverse data volumes, there should be no reason why defenders end up on the losing side, but they do. The reason is data fragmentation, with information sitting across various disconnected tools. There are different tools tracking identity, endpoints, and network flow. The data is visible to defenders as disparate strands with no clear clasp tying them together. These disjointed threads create blind spots that attackers can exploit, and they do this faster than humans can stitch together the moving pieces of the attack.
Therefore, the focus should shift from flagging isolated events to contextual, agentic defense, where security systems look at multiple signals as a whole, catching early signs of an imminent attack forming.
The OODA Loop offers a useful way to structure this process: Observe what is happening. Orient those observations with the right context. Decide on the appropriate response, and act. This should help teams move before a small anomaly turns into a larger incident, without reacting blindly to an isolated event.
From “Is This Bad?” to “Where Is This Heading?”
Traditional security detections check whether an event is malicious. Contextual defense asks what an attacker is likely to do next and what the smallest possible move is to stop them, without causing a disruption.
Consider a scenario where a user in the finance department downloads legitimate software that enables remote administration. This is the kind of tool IT teams use every day. This action doesn’t normally flash suspicion. But additional context will inform you this was the first time this user downloaded this tool, and they did it from a low-reputation domain. Putting two and two together, you realize this might be outside the norm. Contextual defense helps to answer the who, when, and where behind the event and accordingly flags it as an early warning sign. The downloaded tool wasn’t bad, but the pattern surrounding this download was flashing red. Imagine the same user downloading yet another tool. In this case, your context-aware system will look at it as a closely related event. It will link this download to the previous one and connect the dots. If needed, it will block future downloads before the attack can escalate further.
This kind of reasoning draws on several signals at once:
- Identity and user behavior matter because the same action can look completely different depending on who’s doing it.
- Not every device or application carries equal risk, which is why device and asset context matter just as much.
- Network activity often gives away intent well before anything looks outright malicious.
- A device or account with known vulnerabilities or a history of past incidents makes any suspicious activity more likely to be a real attack, not a false alarm.
- Unusual data activity rarely appears out of nowhere; threat intelligence often shows it fits a known attack pattern.
A cybersecurity framework that is context-aware shouldn’t be seen only from a tech upgrade perspective. Contextual defense also enables a shift in the way security teams function. Teams that previously spent time chasing disconnected alerts can focus on the handful of incidents that showed early relevance. They can also deliver proportionate responses. If you lock an employee out of their device because of a false positive, it will disrupt their day. But contextual defense can make a request for additional login verification or restrict access to an application.
Contextual Security in Practice
Some action items that will lay a strong contextual security foundation:
- Start with auditing data quality: Contextual reasoning depends on the quality of the data feeding it, including identity records, asset inventories, and telemetry.
- Clear authority boundaries: Decide explicitly the actions that a system can take autonomously and which need human oversight, especially for privileged accounts or sensitive customer and financial data.
- Keep actions visible and reversible: Every automated action should be recorded, easy to explain, and easy to undo if new information changes things.
- Plan for scale: AI-driven attacks generate much more activity than traditional attacks. The security systems doing the detection need to handle that volume without slowing down, which means they need to be built on infrastructure that can scale up on demand, not fixed-capacity systems that get overwhelmed under load.
- Measure results, not just activity: Track time-to-detect, time-to-contain, and business disruption from false positives, not just the number of alerts correlated.
Do not think that contextual agentic defense is a recipe for eliminating uncertainty or a replacement for foundational security controls. What it does is close the gap between having data and making sense of it. As attacks increase in sophistication, organizations must be able to see the connections between signals and act on them with precision.

articles.title: Tem eletrônico parado? Correios agora fazem o descarte gratuito • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Tem eletrônico parado? Correios agora fazem o descarte gratuito
Estatal vai descartar seu lixo eletrônico gratuitamente e de maneira correta. Iniciativa fica disponível em mais de 6 mil agências pelo país.
Os Correios anunciaram um novo serviço de coleta de lixo eletrônico no Brasil. A novidade foi revelada nesta quarta-feira (14/10), data que marca o Dia Internacional do Lixo Eletrônico. Os produtos dispensados pelos cidadãos serão encaminhados para recicladores homologados sob os cuidados da Circular Brain, empresa parceira no projeto.
O descarte correto de computadores, celulares e mais dispositivos ainda é insuficiente no Brasil. Segundo pesquisa da Global E-waste Statistics Partnership (UIT/Unitar), apenas 3% das mais de 2,4 mil toneladas de lixo eletrônico produzido por aqui é direcionada para reciclagem ou tratamento.
A estatal leva a iniciativa para 6.868 agências pelo país por meio do Balcão do Cidadão. Para utilizar o serviço, basta levar seus eletrônicos antigos embalados em uma caixa e solicitar o descarte. Os Correios então enviam os produtos para reciclagem e você recebe um comprovante ao final do procedimento.
O lixo eletrônico não deve ser jogado fora junto a outros materiais. Isso porque há um alto risco de contaminação ambiental em locais sem o devido preparo para receber esses materiais. A partir da decomposição de pilhas e baterias, por exemplo, metais pesados são liberados ali, alterando a composição química do solo e da água.
Segundo a Superintendência de Gestão Ambiental da USP, a presença dessas substâncias prejudica não apenas a região inicial, mas pode alcançar rios e afluentes, por exemplo, sendo inclusive causa de doenças em humanos.
Existe hoje a Política Nacional de Resíduos Sólidos, que obriga empresas responsáveis pela fabricação e distribuição de eletrônicos a garantirem soluções de descarte correto para seus consumidores. É por isso que você pode encontrar locais de coleta de lixo eletrônico em lojas físicas de operadoras ou mesmo serviços do tipo sendo ofertados por fabricantes e empresas de tecnologia em geral.
O reaproveitamento dos materiais provenientes de eletrônicos pós-consumo é interessante para a indústria de tecnologia. Componentes e carcaças podem passar por tratamento e serem reutilizados na produção de novos dispositivos. Apesar disso, apenas 3% do volume de lixo eletrônico produzido no país vai parar em coletas oficiais, conforme aponta a Global E-waste Statistics Partnership (UIT/Unitar). Os dados são de 2022.
Em 2025, a Rede Circulare processou 83 mil toneladas. A empresa promete não só tratar esse lixo, mas também ofertar os materiais disponibilizados a partir disso para serem reaproveitados por fabricantes.
Segundo o CEO da Circular Brain, Marcus Oliveira, esse processo é importante não só pelo descarte correto em si, mas pela utilidade dos eletrônicos que estão parados em casa. Ele afirma que, com produtos nessa situação, “a indústria perde muitas matérias-primas que poderiam voltar à cadeia produtiva sem a necessidade de explorar novamente o meio-ambiente”.
Configuram lixo eletrônico produtos como celulares, notebooks, tablets ,fones de ouvido, cabos, caixas de som, controles, microfones, monitores, TVs e mais. Com o limite de 30 kg definido pelos Correios, alguns dispositivos precisam ser coletados, em serviço oferecido pela Circular Brain. Outra opção é recorrer às respectivas fabricantes, que, vale lembrar, precisam garantir esse descarte correto por lei.
O envio pelos Correios é gratuito e não precisa de agendamento prévio. Você pode separar seus eletrônicos em uma caixa e o atendente responsável vai fechá-la por lá. A coleta fica disponível apenas em agências que ofereçam o serviço de Balcão do Cidadão, portanto, vale buscar essa informação na hora de procurar o endereço mais próximo. Para confirmar a coleta, é necessário informar seu nome, endereço, CPF, telefone e e-mail.

articles.title: What 25 Trillion Tokens Reveal About How Developers Actually Adopt AI Agents
articles.text:
Transcript
Brendan O'Leary: My name is Brendan O'Leary. I'm a founding developer relations engineer at Kilo Code. How many people have heard of Kilo Code? That's key, because I'm about to present you a whole bunch of our data. If you don't know who we are, not really helpful. How many have heard of Codex or Claude Code, or OpenCode maybe? What Kilo Code is, is an open-source agentic engineering tool. You can think of it as like a Claude Code or a Cursor, but it's open source. We have surfaces in the CLI, like a Claude Code or a Codex. We have surfaces inside of VS Code, so like a VS Code extension. You can think of like a Cline, or maybe like a Cursor, if Cursor is a fork of VS Code, in some ways you can think of it the same way. Then we also have cloud agents. The only point in telling you all that is like, where does all this data come from?
It's all real-world data from our gateway. We'll talk a little bit more about the specifics of the data. Being that I'm at Kilo, and we're this open-source competitor in this highly competitive space, I'm sitting at an uncomfortable intersection of like, what is the data that we can see about how developers actually use AI tools? Then the story that industry is telling us, especially the larger players in the industry are telling us about how AI adoption works. I think the problem is that not always do those stories match up really well. That's why I wanted to bring some real-world data to this talk to try and talk about like what we're seeing, and how that matches or doesn't match with the industry narrative. The industry narrative is a lot about capability, a capability narrative. This model X scored better than this model on benchmark Y, and model Z has this size of a context window.
This new release beats the old release on human eval by 0.02 points. It's not that that information is useless, but it has very little to almost nothing to do with whether developers can actually adopt those models to use it in an agentic tool like ours. I think thus also has very little impact on how you might choose what model you're going to use as you're building an agentic workflow. I've watched teams get access to the best models, the best capabilities, best benchmarks, and not use them at all. Or other teams build real dependency on tools that actually benchmark worse than other models maybe, but really work for them in their use case for certain reasons. I don't think that gap is random. I think it really is a lot about trust. I want to talk about that specifically in the context of developers using, and pull from this dataset that gives us a pretty clear view into what's actually happening on the ground. We're talking about from the title, 25 trillion tokens. We'll see in a minute that's not quite right.
Outline
What are we going to learn from that? I want to leave you with three things today. One is developers don't adopt the AI tools and the models in the way that I think we tend to assume, and not in the way that we think about adopting other tools. I think that's partially because the nature of AI is very different as a tool, being non-deterministic. I think that creates what we call this trust ladder. We'll talk about it in specifics, but we had auto-complete, and then we had chat with some agents in code. Then now we have this idea of like let's orchestrate many agents to do all kinds of things at once. Unlike tools in the past, you really have to have a solid foundation. Three Failure Points
I think there's three failure points that I've tried to bring out from what we've seen in terms of teams trying to adopt more and more of this trust. I think each one manifests at a different point in that. Then, again, it affects everything above that if you're not able to accomplish it. Let's go through those one by one. The first failure point is what I call context construction. I think this is where the most friction happens, because it's all the things that happen before you send the request to the model. Like which files are included? Like, should we index the codebase or not? Should we do semantic reasoning against the codebase? Does the model understand the relationships between things when it's looking at a problem? Have I stated the problem well to the model? It's like a model that I've given one file, and a model that can reason across hundreds of thousands of tokens and actually understand a representation of the project.
Again, when autocomplete's bad, if it suggests something that doesn't make sense in the structure, that's not a bad model. It's typically bad context. Like have we given the model enough relevant signal, or did it have the wrong signal? Or did we let it have the wrong signal for a long period of time, and now we've got this polluted context that we're not taking care of. If I say, where does the auth logic in this project live? The agent starts to walk down the wrong path, then that retrieval failure can have impacts for the rest of that chat. Because the context doesn't have the right information, it's going to start making guesses. Then by the time you get to, I want to have an agent go run by itself, or I want to have orchestrators run through the code, if that construction is broken, you're going to just multiply that failure.
If it's working from this incomplete set of context, then it's going to be much harder to walk it back and get it to deliver you meaningfully working code at the end. I think this shows up in the usage data indirectly. Developers are stuck with that heavy chat, but haven't started to use agents, consume a lot higher token counts per request. We see the tokens per request growing. They're doing this manual thing of pasting in a bunch of context themselves, or walking down the road when the context isn't right. I think that signal, for us, means that if context construction doesn't work right, and the developer doesn't know how to solve for that, they try to start patching it manually, which could work, but if the task is big enough, you can't solve that problem. Again, if you give it the wrong context, you can't get out of that.
I think there's three things to get right here. One, context windows have to scale with the task complexity. Here, people talk about models and the size of their context window. Trust Is Measurable
I've been using that word trust, and I think it's a mushy word to use in an engineering talk. I do think it's measurable. I promise that I would talk a little bit about how I think we can measure it. I think the measurements then matter for how you design these feedback loops we were talking about. There's a couple of things we use that I'll give you as proxies, again that are specific to the AI agent use case, but hopefully gives you some idea. One is, at autocomplete rung, we look at the override rate. What percentage of suggestions get rejected? Then, can we tell if that's model related? Is it context related? Is it folks that just haven't empirically learned that that judgment is better than the suggestion? Is it bad pattern matching? That maybe is recoverable, but if you don't measure this then we're not going to be able to trace it back.
At the chat level we look at session depth and follow-up rate. Developers stop asking for follow-ups and will reject it or treat their first response as final. That can be a trust deficit sign for us. They have decided that's not worth iterating. This is not right. I'm not getting that value. For agents we look at session completion rate. Did the developer let the task run to completion? Did they interrupt it? What is the interruption rate for an agent session? That's like a proxy for us for that trust then. It's hard to distinguish like the developer correctly interrupted, it's like a bad run where it was walking down from the developer just got anxious and took over. It gives us signal about that feedback loop design. Have we exposed enough of the feedback loop to the developer to tell them when they need to intervene and when they don't?
Again, it's very asymmetric, this trust. Many positive experiences are required to build a meaningful amount of trust. Only one bad experience can really destroy that. We talked about that in the last slide. I think this also has a social dimension that is also underweighted in most deployment strategies for agents. What I think that looks like is, yes, it's often a social failure rather than a technical failure. One highly visible failure of an agent in front of the wrong audience, in our example would be a senior engineer who's already very skeptical of AI, or in a high stakes moment with an audience like if I was live demoing on stage, which is why I'm not, can create this narrative inside of an org that is going to take a very long time to reverse. I think the counterintuitive implication there is you have to have the right rollout strategy. Moving to a more, they're motivated to iterate. I talked early on about our dataset being focused on those early adopters. I think that's how organizations have to think about adoption too. It's like you're going to have a set of folks who can build that trust and iterate and figure out the right way to build social proof for the adoption from skeptics. Again, depending on where you are in that rung of the ladder, the stakes are different. Unlike most technology, AI failures are very visible. It's like if you think about Waymo or other self-driving, it's like you hear about every self-driving accident that exists versus you don't hear about every single human driving accident that exists. Then, I also think as you're building that like, do developers actually, for us, build trust over time? This is when we're looking at retention. Do developers move up that ladder? If I said APIs or REST APIs, I don't think that's a great answer because if you just give it whatever you want it's going to be really messy, versus if you have a really well-established pattern of APIs, it's going to be great at like, I need this next thing. It's going to be like this but a little bit different like this. It's going to be really good at following those patterns.
Participant 2: Piggybacking off of that, are you seeing any patterns when it comes to popular sub-agents, so like UX review, or QA? There are so many ways to slice and dice your sub-agents with coding. I'm curious if you're seeing just even one or two that stand out, like you are gun to head, I only got two agents that ride or die with me. Who are you bringing with you?
Brendan O'Leary: I think the models have gotten a lot better at reviewing even their own code. Of course, they don't have any real bias towards their code, so we added a local review agent at the end of a turn. I used to not use that at all and now I use it almost every time. I think that reviewing the code for a given goal is something that the models are getting really good at. The thousands of other skills and agents that exist, I don't know. I don't know that there's a standout there. I think reviewing code for intent is something that they're getting really good at doing.
Participant 3: What I had observed while also using OpenRouter is that depending on what provider you choose for a specific model, the performance changed, and that, of course, how their inference settings were set up for their vLLMs and all of that stuff. Is that showing up somehow and is that an angle that gets lost in some of the metrics that you are looking at? How are you compensating for that?
Brendan O'Leary: OpenRouter which is one of the backends that we use, it also has multiple providers. If you're talking about especially an open weight model, you can end up with very different implementations of the same model. Normally it's not something I think most people care about, but you care about it, so it's good. It's almost all we think about. What we've found is that people just expect it to work. What we end up doing is building a lot of filtering there in order to make it work the way you expect. Because there's a lot of things that once you start getting in an LLM, like how well are you doing caching, like all of that stuff then starts really mattering for the frontend performance to the developer and of course to anybody using that. That's then when we end up spending a lot of our time in thinking.
See more presentations with transcripts

articles.title: Startup de exGoogle recaudó 300 millones de dólares para que la IA diseñe chips
articles.text:
La startup Ricursive Intelligence, fundada por dos exinvestigadoras de Google DeepMind, presentó su apuesta para que la inteligencia artificial diseñe chips de computación de forma autónoma, con el objetivo declarado de aliviar la escasez de capacidad de cómputo que enfrenta toda la industria de IA.
Anna Goldie y Azalia Mirhoseini, cofundadoras de la compañía, contaron cómo su plataforma de inteligencia artificial diseña chips, aprende de cada iteración y mejora los diseños siguientes. “Hay un entendimiento de que en los próximos cinco años vamos a tener al menos 10.000 veces más demanda de cómputo, y eso es potencialmente conservador”, dijo Goldie durante el evento TechCrunch Disrupt.
La fundadora explicó que construir más centros de datos no alcanza para cubrir ese salto de demanda. “No queremos construir 10.000 veces más centros de datos. Creemos que tenemos que ayudar haciendo chips más eficientes, que usen mejor el ancho de banda de esos centros de datos, que usen mejor las obleas y las fábricas”, señaló, y agregó que incluso construir centros de datos en el espacio no resolvería el problema de fondo.
Cuál es el origen en AlphaChip de Google
Goldie y Mirhoseini no llegan a este problema de la nada. Antes de fundar Ricursive Intelligence, a fines de 2025, ambas codesarrollaron AlphaChip, el sistema de inteligencia artificial de Google DeepMind capaz de generar diseños de chips en horas en lugar de los meses o años que demandan los equipos humanos.
Esa tecnología se usó en el diseño de cuatro generaciones de las unidades de procesamiento tensorial (TPU) de Google y también fue adoptada por empresas externas del sector de semiconductores, según reportó TechCrunch.
El antecedente explica por qué los inversores reaccionaron rápido: Ricursive levantó una ronda semilla de USD 35 millones liderada por Sequoia Capital y, meses después, una Serie A de USD 300 millones liderada por Lightspeed Venture Partners que llevó su valuación a USD 4.000 millones, con Nvidia entre los inversores a través de su brazo de capital de riesgo.
Diseños que un ingeniero no imaginaría
Las fundadoras sostienen que la inteligencia artificial puede desafiar los métodos tradicionales de diseño de chips al descubrir distribuciones poco convencionales que superan a las convencionales. Citaron como ejemplo a AlphaChip, que produjo un arreglo circular de componentes, con forma de rosquilla, que sorprendió a los ingenieros antes de demostrar que funcionaba mejor.
A diferencia del método tradicional, que divide un chip en decenas de bloques más pequeños para optimizarlos por separado, Ricursive optimiza el chip completo de una sola vez. Esa estrategia le permite a la inteligencia artificial generar patrones más complejos, incluidos diseños ondulados, sobre los que las fundadoras dijeron que compartirán más detalles en el futuro.
Goldie planteó que acortar los tiempos de diseño abre la puerta a chips que hoy no se justifican económicamente. “Si te lleva seis meses, un año o dos años diseñar un nuevo chip, tenés que ser extremadamente selectivo con los chips que diseñás. Pero si podés diseñar un chip en una semana, podés crear chips a medida para todo tipo de aplicaciones, como espacio, realidad aumentada y virtual, o computación biológica”, explicó.
La fundadora remarcó además que ese diseño más rápido también puede traducirse en chips más eficientes energéticamente, un punto sensible para una industria que multiplica el consumo eléctrico de sus centros de datos.
Una apuesta frente a los gigantes del sector
Ricursive busca usar inteligencia artificial para diseñar chips y competir con Synopsys y Cadence Design Systems, firmas que ya aplican estas herramientas al diseño electrónico automatizado. La empresa reunió investigadores e ingenieros que trabajaron en Google DeepMind, Anthropic, Apple y Cadence.
Su meta es crear un ciclo entre la IA y el hardware: chips más avanzados permitirían entrenar modelos más capaces, que luego diseñarían mejores procesadores. Para Goldie, los ingenieros deberían aportar las ideas y dejar la ejecución a la inteligencia artificial.
Ricursive no informó nuevos contratos con fabricantes ni fechas para llevar sus diseños a producción masiva. Antes de fabricarse en plantas como las de TSMC o Samsung, los diseños deben superar verificaciones físicas rigurosas.

articles.title: Neutron's first launch slips again amid trouble with carbon composites
articles.text:
Rocket Lab announced Wednesday that its Neutron launch vehicle won’t fly until 2027, citing an issue discovered during manufacturing of the rocket’s carbon composite structures.
The announcement was public confirmation of what nearly everyone inside Rocket Lab and the wider space industry already knew. The most recent official update from Rocket Lab in August suggested the company still held hope of delivering the first Neutron rocket to its launch pad at Wallops Island, Virginia, before the end of this year, a schedule that would have almost certainly pushed the first flight into 2027.
But Rocket Lab’s statement Wednesday about Neutron’s schedule suggests the company is still struggling with manufacturing the rocket’s large booster stage. Neutron’s reusable first stage is made of carbon composite structures, which offer low weight, high strength, and corrosion resistance. But carbon composites in aerospace are generally harder to manufacture than metallic structures.
Peter Beck, Rocket Lab’s founder and CEO, identified a manufacturing defect as the reason for Neutron’s latest schedule slip. The problem lies in the dome sections at the ends of the rocket’s first stage propellant tanks.
“Recently, we identified an issue with the manufacturing process for the propellant domes specifically, and this caused us to delay production and investigate further,” Beck said in a video released by Rocket Lab.
Scaling up
Engineers discovered voids, or air pockets, between layers of carbon fiber that make up the domes’ composite structure. Carbon composite manufacturing involves laying down carbon fiber layers in a mold, then curing, or heating, the material to bind the fibers together. But this is a tricky process, especially for large structures that won’t fit into an autoclave, a high-pressure thermal curing chamber common in modern aerospace factories.
The Neutron rocket’s first stage is the “largest pressurized structure ever made out of carbon composite,” Beck said. “Because of its scale, we’ve had to develop new out-of-autoclave processes to build Neutron, and this includes custom cure cycles for the very large pieces, like the forward and aft domes for the propellant tanks on Stage One.”
Inspections revealed voids in a newly cured forward dome, defects that could affect the structure’s strength, durability, and reliability, Beck said. “They don’t necessarily mean that the dome would fail in flight, but our practice is to proceed only when we believe the system has the appropriate margins.”
Engineers traced the voids to a recent design change intended to strengthen the rocket’s structure. Rocket Lab introduced the design change after a Neutron propellant tank unexpectedly ruptured during a hydrostatic pressure test in January, a failure blamed on a manufacturing defect at a “critical join” in the tank.
Officials said the failed carbon composite tank was manufactured by a “third-party contractor using a manual hand-lay process,” a decision made to allow tank testing to move forward while Rocket Lab brought online an automated fiber placement machine, which is now operational. Rocket Lab also deleted joints in the first stage tank structure and increased the thickness of some sections of the carbon composite.
“Those thicker sections are where the voids formed,” Beck said.
Propellant domes inside Rocket Lab’s Neutron factory.
Credit:
Rocket Lab
Propellant domes inside Rocket Lab’s Neutron factory.
Credit:
Rocket Lab
Curing the void
Rocket Lab said the problem appears to be solved after modifying the manufacturing process again. An aft propellant dome made with the updated procedure passed inspection.
“We’ve solved the problem,” Beck said. “That gives us complete confidence to move forward with the new forward dome. That process to make a new forward dome, combining with all the time that it took to investigate, identify, and resolve the issue, has pushed Neutron’s first launch date to next year.”
The Neutron rocket is significantly larger than Rocket Lab’s Electron launch vehicle, also made of carbon fiber. The light-class Electron rocket is 3.9 feet (1.2 meters) in diameter, while the medium-lift Neutron measures 23 feet (7 meters) across at its widest.
Rocket Lab completed qualification testing on Neutron’s expendable second stage and payload fairing last year. The rocket’s design is unique: The upper stage and payload rest inside the first stage’s nose cone during the initial phases of launch. A few minutes after liftoff, Neutron’s booster stage will open its clamshell-like nose cone to release the upper stage and payload to continue accelerating into orbit. Then the first stage will close its payload fairing and return to landing on an offshore platform for reuse.
Neutron’s first stage methane and liquid oxygen tanks are the largest elements of the rocket, and they must withstand internal pressure and the rigors of launch and reentry.
Rocket Lab’s checklist for the first Neutron flight is long. Final qualification of the first stage is still pending, as is qualification of the rocket’s methane-fueled Archimedes engine, nine of which will power the Neutron booster. Rocket Lab reported in August that it was heading into the “final stretch” of engine qualification testing.
Once that is complete, teams will begin the launch campaign on Virginia’s Eastern Shore. Launch campaigns for new rockets often take months before a first flight, involving multiple integrated fueling tests, countdown rehearsals, and a static fire.
Engineers often discover new problems during integrated testing, requiring repeat tests and tweaks to procedures and hardware on the launch pad and the rocket. That is the purpose of such testing.
Rocket Lab announced the Neutron rocket in 2021, aiming for a first flight in 2024. The Neutron development timeline has now doubled.
Beck said Wednesday that Neutron’s development remains “on an ambitious timeline.” In previous statements, Beck has emphasized Rocket Lab’s focus on quality and its unwillingness to launch an “unproven product.”
“Our aim is to make orbit on the first try,” Beck said last year. “You won’t see us using some qualifier about us just clearing the pad, and claiming success and whatnot, and that means that we don’t want to learn something during Neutron’s first flight that could be learned on the ground during the testing phase.”
Rocket Lab has achieved great success with its Electron rocket, with a capacity of deploying up to 660 pounds (300 kilograms) of payload into a low-altitude orbit. Electron has made 97 flights to date, with 56 consecutive successes.
With Neutron, Rocket Lab seeks to compete for a wider range of launch contracts, eyeing opportunities to sell launches to the US military and operators of satellite megaconstellations. Its lift capability to low-Earth orbit is nearly 29,000 pounds (13,000 kilograms).
“We’re building the program’s long-term infrastructure at the same time as we build our first rocket, so that we can scale quickly, unlock global launch crunches, and commercial customers, governments, and our own future satellite services are also counting on it,” Beck said Wednesday. “But I’ve also said that we won’t rush to the pad with unnecessary risk, and that development programs like Neutron have their challenges.”
Neutron’s latest challenge popped up just as the rocket’s prospective customers clamor for more launch capacity. SpaceX, the market leader, is pivoting to the giant Starship rocket and will, in the next few years, retire from commercial service its workhorse Falcon 9 rocket, without which many satellite startups would be unable to put their payloads into orbit affordably.
That puts Rocket Lab in the mix to scoop up business from satellite operators whose payloads don’t match up with Starship’s capabilities. But there’s stiff competition. Other rocket companies, such as Relativity Space, Stoke Space, and Firefly Aerospace, are working on medium-lift rockets to address the same market.
Stephen Clark is a space reporter at Ars Technica, covering private space companies and the world’s space agencies. Stephen writes about the nexus of technology, science, policy, and business on and off the planet.

articles.title: The Xreal 1 Pro+: better image quality and 2D-to-3D conversion
articles.text:
Xreal is launching new AR glasses called the Xreal 1 Pro+. The 1 Pro+ launches globally on October 15 and will be available through Xreal.com
The new model now features the X1 spatial computing chip, native 3DoF spatial anchoring, and a 57-degree field of view. The screen reaches up to 1,200 nits of peak brightness from 700 nits and also includes AI HDR to improve the perceived image quality across supported content. Standard, Movie and Reading viewing modes, so you can control how the content is presented.
The Xreal also upgraded the 2D-to-3D conversion capability from 30fps to 60fps, delivering smoother motion when viewing converted spatial content. This means that any 2D content can be seen smoothly in 3D.
The 1 Pro+ has a new ergonomic nose pad system for better stability and comfort while helping users keep a consistent field of view. The Xreal 1 Pro+ is available globally on October 15 at Xreal for US$599 (C$850).
I’ve used the Xreal 1 Pro+ for a short flight to New York. I liked watching content; using the 2D-to-3D conversion was also pretty interesting. Some content, like Drag Race, worked really well. It was pretty crazy, all of a sudden, watching a YouTube video in 3D.
But I watched Phantom Blade Zero gameplay, and the rapid movements would occasionally show some artifacts. It was cool, though, that it was able to showcase the RPG in 3D, even though it wasn’t perfect. I also thought it was comfortable enough to wear for the entire hour pretty easily. I liked that you can black out the world around you, control how far away the display is and how big it is.
I would need to spend more time putting the Xreal 1 Pro+ through its paces, but so far they are a pretty cool pair of AR glasses.

articles.title: U of T’s Citizen Lab exposes “nightmare” spyware hack that requires no clicks from users | BetaKit
articles.text:
Researchers at the University of Toronto have identified, for the first time, a spyware hack run simply through targeted ads—no clicking necessary.
The news: A joint report by the University of Toronto’s Citizen Lab and cybersecurity firm Confiant found that dozens of devices at Al Jazeera were compromised with mercenary spyware from Israeli spyware firm Candiru through malicious ads.
The ads themselves were purchased by Israel-based advertising company Discover-Tech, which runs a platform allowing spyware partners to identify and infect devices. The ad secretly directs the device to contact Candiru’s servers, most likely for “tracking and reconnaissance.”
The researchers said it’s the first confirmation of a “zero-click mercenary spyware attack” delivered through targeted ads, which they’re calling “AdFection.” Citizen Lab explains that the malware works by displaying ads across various platforms, from dating apps to articles on news sites, including CBC. Once a user is shown the ad, the user’s IP address is transmitted to Discover-Tech’s servers. If that user is then targeted for hacking, the device is sent malicious code that is executed by the user’s browser or app and placed onto their device, without the user ever clicking on it. The ads were shown on nearly 200,000 websites and apps in dozens of countries, the report said.
From the source: “The risk of having your device infected with spyware simply by using a website or app that displays ads is a nightmare scenario,” senior Citizen Lab researcher Wolfie Christl told WIRED.
The context: The Citizen Lab is a research unit at the University of Toronto’s Munk School of Global Affairs and Public Policy that investigates digital threats to democracy, human rights, and global security. Citizen Lab and Confiant said they shared these findings with ad vendors including Google and Beeswax, both of which removed Discover-Tech’s access to their digital ad marketplace.
Final thought: The worrying situation doesn’t stop there, the researchers said. A separate threat actor Citizen Lab is calling “Dark Cartographer” is using Discover-Tech’s infrastructure to exploit vulnerabilities across numerous mobile carriers, which will be the subject of a forthcoming report. The researchers called on cybersecurity agencies and other regulators in the US, Canada, and Europe to take action to detect and block this type of “AdFection” attack. Citizen Lab also detailed steps users can take to protect themselves, from setting up a security plan to using privacy-protecting web browsers.
Feature image courtesy Unsplash. Photo by Jonas Leupe.

articles.title: Descubren un malware que te infecta con solo ver un anuncio
articles.text:
Una empresa israelí de publicidad colaboró con empresas de spyware para infectar equipos con solo mostrar un anuncio. De acuerdo con una investigación del Citizen Lab y la firma de seguridad Confiant, Discover Tech utilizó su red publicitaria para servir anuncios que parecían legítimos, pero que en el fondo escondían un malware diseñado para espiar a los usuarios. Los investigadores afirman que esta es la primera evidencia de un ataque zero-click entregado mediante publicidad segmentada.
Según el informe, el malware identificado en la investigación está vinculado a Candiru, una compañía israelí que desarrolla software espía y que se encuentra en la lista negra de Estados Unidos desde 2021. La característica más peligrosa de este spyware es que no requiere interacción: basta con que el anuncio infectado se cargue en una web o aplicación para que comience la recopilación de datos o intento de infección, sin necesidad de que el usuario haga clic en él.
El spyware se distribuyó a través de Discover-Tech, una agencia de publicidad que funciona como intermediaria para que grupos de hackeo coloquen anuncios maliciosos por todo internet. Los anuncios, a menudo de productos corrientes como móviles o auriculares, llegaron a más de 120.000 sitios web y 75.000 aplicaciones. Esta publicidad podía rastrear usuarios, extraer ciertos datos y facilitar la instalación de otro software malicioso asociado con Candiru.
El Citizen Lab menciona que una variante potente del software, entregado mediante los anuncios infectados, comprometió 45 ordenadores de la cadena Al Jazeera entre 2024 y 2025. Confiant calcula que Discover-Tech difundió al menos 10 millones de anuncios al día y era posible realizar seguimiento a las víctimas a través del cruce de cookies.
Ahora te puedes infectar con solo ver un anuncio en internet
Los anuncios que aparecen en cualquier página web o aplicación móvil se sirven mediante redes que recopilan datos sobre millones de personas todos los días. Ese ecosistema ha generado preocupaciones entre los expertos en privacidad y reguladores, quienes intentan acotar el alcance para proteger a los usuarios. El hallazgo de Citizen Lab y Confiant deja claro que esta infraestructura ahora es un vehículo para vulnerar los equipos de personas para espiarlas.
“La forma en que funciona la publicidad en línea hoy en día es una amenaza sistémica para la seguridad”, señaló Wolfie Cristl, investigador principal de Citizen Lab, en una entrevista con Reuters. “Para los estados, el sector privado, la sociedad civil y todos los demás por igual”.
Por su parte, Confiant, afirmó que cientos de millones de personas quedaron vulnerables a este malware. La firma de seguridad dijo que los anuncios se mostraron a usuarios en cientos de redes de categorías sensibles, como el Pentágono, la Corte Penal Internacional o el Organismo Internacional de Energía Atómica. Los investigadores del Citizen Lab encontraron evidencia en la ONU, OTAN, la Comisión Europea y empresas de chips como NVIDIA o Micron.
Lamentablemente no existe un modo de saber si te infectaste, ya que los anuncios no dejan rastro en el ordenador. Los investigadores recomiendan usar bloqueadores de anuncios, desactivar el seguimiento y restablecer periódicamente los identificadores publicitarios del móvil. Estos se encuentran como "Restablecer ID de publicidad" dentro de Ajustes > Privacidad > Anuncios, aunque puede cambiar dependiendo del dispositivo o sistema operativo.
Otras recomendaciones incluyen mantener tu sistema operativo actualizado, usar un software de seguridad confiable y revisar cualquier comportamiento sospechoso.

articles.title: Bluesky wants to make it easier to buy, sell, and fundraise on the network | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Bluesky plans to introduce payments in the coming months, a first step in its strategy to make money without relying on advertising. CEO Toni Schneider and COO Rose Wang outlined the plans Thursday at TechCrunch Disrupt, explaining how the company hopes to build on the commerce and fundraising activity already happening on its decentralized social network.
“People are actually selling things, fundraising very successfully, supporting each other on the network,” Schneider said. “We want to make that easier, and the way we’re going to do this is if you see something on the network that you like and support, you can support that monetarily, and we want to do it in a way that works for Bluesky and for all the other apps out there as well, so that it works across the entire network.”
Schneider, the former CEO of Automattic, took the reins of the company in March after longtime CEO Jay Graber stepped down. He said, while onstage, that he was surprised by the reaction to his appointment, with some users joking that it marked the beginning of the end for the platform. Those comments reflected fears that a leadership change would bring unwanted changes to Bluesky.
Schneider said he understands that users can leave Bluesky for another platform if the company introduces features or changes they dislike, a reality that he said keeps the leadership team accountable as it prepares to introduce monetization in the coming months.
The executives argued that advertising isn’t the only viable business model for a social network.
“I think there’s a story around monetization that feels like advertising is the inevitable thing we have to do that will ruin the network,” Wang said. “What was really promising about having Toni join us is he built at WordPress Automatic a $10 billion business where a billion of it goes back to the parent company and the rest of it goes to the ecosystem.”
Wang also pointed to Bluesky’s status as a Public Benefit Corporation (PBC), which she said puts the company’s mission at the center of its business strategy.
“Yes, we need to make money, but because of our infrastructure, we cannot lock people in,” Wang said. “And so the thing that really matters for us is the people who are creating value on the networks these days are the ones who are getting the value that is coming in or the money that’s coming in. And I kind of think of it as like feudal society where we’re working for a few landlords and they dictate everything, and then we have to pay up our dues as tariffs.”
Bluesky aims to give users ownership of their digital identities and control over their networks while creating a more open internet where value and revenue can flow directly to the people who generate them.
“First, we’ll start with payments, but I think it’s about disrupting the actual infrastructure layer, which is what we’re doing, and not just building another app,” Wang said.

articles.title: Need more Plex storage? Seagate’s 16TB IronWolf NAS drive is $119 off
articles.text:
Seagate's 16TB IronWolf NAS hard drive is a massive storage upgrade with $119 off at Newegg
It's built for continuous operation in multi-bay network storage systems
If you're building a NAS or running out of room on your existing one, you'll know that high-capacity hard drives can be expensive. But one I'd definitely consider is the 16TB Seagate IronWolf, which is tailored for adding more space for backups, media libraries, or shared files.
Ideal for NAS owners, home server enthusiasts, content creators, and small businesses needing large amounts of always-accessible storage, the 16TB Seagate IronWolf NAS hard drive is $671 (was $790) at Newegg.
Unlike an ordinary desktop hard drive, the IronWolf NAS is designed to operate continuously in NAS systems that remain powered on throughout the day and night. The drive uses conventional magnetic recording (CMR), useful in RAID configurations, and it spins at 7200 RPM and includes a 256MB cache.
Today's best Seagate NAS drive deal
The 16TB Seagate NAS drive features 7200 RPM performance, 256MB cache, SATA 6Gbps connectivity, CMR recording, rotational vibration sensors, AgileArray optimization, IronWolf Health Management, and 24/7 operational support capabilities.
Why we recommend it
While we haven't tested the 16TB capacity drive, we have gone hands-on with the 8TB Seagate Ironwolf. We scored it 4 stars in our review, and Seagate NAS drives have always proved reliable in our tests - although the skyrocketing component prices are starting to bite now.
16TB of hard drive space is enough to comfortably store thousands of high-resolution photographs, large video libraries, computer backups, and shared documents.
Seagate's AgileArray technology helps optimize performance in multi-bay NAS systems, while rotational vibration sensors help maintain stability. There's also IronWolf Health Management, which provides monitoring and diagnostic information on compatible devices.
The 180TB/year workload rating makes the drive suitable for demanding home and small-business environments.
Price Context & Historical Value
Newegg is selling the 16TB Seagate IronWolf for $670.99, down from $789.75. That's a saving of $118.76, or approximately 15%, bringing the cost to around $41.94 per terabyte. This is far from the cheapest it's every been however, as we've seen it as low as $579.99 in the past year, and even cheaper when it first came out. But that's the component cost crisis for you, pushing up prices even on HDDs.
Should you buy it?
✅ Buy the 16TB Seagate IronWolf NAS hard drive if...
You own a NAS and need more room for backups, media files, or shared storage. The combination of 16TB capacity, CMR recording, and NAS-specific features make this a practical upgrade.
❌ Skip the 16TB Seagate IronWolf NAS hard drive if...
You only need a small amount of additional storage or want a portable drive that connects directly to your computer. You should also look for an SSD if transfer speed is your main priority.

ASML struggling to keep up with demand for chipmaking equipment as AI spending continues to boom — chipmakers are already looking to place orders for 2029 and 2030 output, CEO says demand could surpass capacity despite massive expansion plans
ASML to increase prices starting in 2027
ASML has said that the unprecedented spending and investment brought about by the artificial intelligence (AI) boom is not slowing down at all, as customers are already lining up to place orders for its advanced chipmaking tools for 2029 and 2030, according to a Reuters report citing ASML's Q3 2026 earnings published today, October 14. ASML CEO Christophe Fouquet said that the company would struggle to meet the demand despite plans announced in July to raise capacity by 30% in 2027 and another 30% in 2028. The company also confirmed on Wednesday that it will raise prices starting in 2027, with the full effect showing in 2028.
The Dutch company's comments follow its Q3 2026 earnings report, which detailed a net profit of €4.96 billion on net sales of €11.7 billion. It projects Q4 sales of €14.2 billion to €15.2 billion ($15.9 billion to $17 billion), boosting its full-year sales projections from at least €43 billion to €44-45 billion. ASML's shares rose 2% on Wednesday, up almost 70% so far this year, with its €586 billion market valuation making it Europe's largest firm by market cap.
According to Reuters, there had been concerns that the AI investment boom was losing steam. However, positive projections from the largest manufacturer of the tools for making AI chips and advanced semiconductors signal that chipmakers will keep expanding, sustaining demand across the AI industry well into the foreseeable future. "There were concerns that the AI trade was running out of steam," Gordon Kerr, European macro strategist at KBRA, said. "Demand for chips remains strong, and infrastructure spending is likely to continue well into 2027."
ASML's customers include logic chip manufacturers such as Samsung, Intel, and TSMC, which manufactures chips for Nvidia, all of whom are heavily investing in increasing chip production. Memory chip makers SK Hynix and Micron have also announced expansion plans that involve ASML machines. Meanwhile, the company's CFO Roger Dassen said it is "still kicking the tires on the exact size of that (Terafab) opportunity," referring to Elon Musk's 100 million square feet semiconductor manufacturing facility that aims to output millions of logic and memory chips. Terafab will reportedly receive its first EUV chipmaking tool from ASML in mid-2027.
ASML's order book reflects a wave of spending across the AI industry. As of April this year, Google, Amazon, Microsoft, and Meta reportedly collectively planned to spend $725 billion on capex in 2026, up 77% from last year's record $410 billion. Since then, Alphabet has raised its 2026 capex guidance from $180–190 billion to $195–205 billion, Amazon from $200 billion to $220 billion, and Meta has raised the floor of its range from $125 billion to $130 billion, keeping its $145 billion ceiling. Some of the spending reflects rising chip prices, with Microsoft CFO Amy Hood attributing $25 billion of the company's record capex budget to higher prices for memory chips and other components. Still, analysts such as Gartner expect global AI spending to rise 49.5% in 2026 to $2.7 trillion and another 36.2% in 2027.

articles.title: The Tesla Roadster flew, drove upside down, and hit 60mph in under a second
articles.text:
Elon Musk promised a flying car. And the Tesla Roadster did exactly that.
The Tesla Roadster flew, drove upside down, and hit 60mph in under a second
The next-gen Roadster has been in development for nearly a decade. But perhaps it was worth the wait.
Tesla demonstrated its next-generation Roadster at an event in Waco, Texas, where the electric supercar drove upside down, briefly flew, and accelerated to 60mph in under a second. It was an impressive demonstration of a car that likely will come with some heavy caveats and restrictions if it ever goes into production.
The event was less than 30 minutes and felt more like a stunt show than a product reveal. Indeed, there was no mention of price, release date, or other such mundane details. Musk promised the hypercar would go into production in 2028, but after nearly nine years who’s counting. The people were here to see a car fly, and that’s what Tesla gave them.
First, the Roadster drove up a very tall, multi-story ramp, using its incredible downforce to cling to the vertical roadway. When it reached the top of the ramp, it flipped around using its cold-gas thrusters to bring it gently back down to earth. The car uses a fan-based suction system, supplied by SpaceX and mounted underneath the vehicle, which is capable of generating up to two Gs of suction force.
Next, the Roadster flew over the rest of Tesla’s lineup, including the Model 3, Model Y, Cybertruck, Semi, and Cybercab — doing what Tesla VP for Engineering Lars Moravy called “a kick flip” in the process. Musk explained that it features attitude-control thrusters as well as main thrusters at the rear, giving the Roadster rocket-like capabilities.
“So it can basically fly like a rocket,” Musk said. “And it could do rolls. It could do, like, crazy gymnastics. Whatever you want, really. Now, I should say that this is not necessarily a safety-optimized car. But it takes the fun meter to 11 out of 10.”
The Roadster two ultra-high pressure air tanks with a combined volume of 600 liters, containing approximately 250 kilograms of air, and uses 10 nozzles to execute its maneuvers. The Roadster can even recharge its own tank, without requiring a specialized chemical propellant. The stored compressed air supplies the thrust needed to lift the car and perform the demonstrated maneuvers.
Musk claimed “This will be an actual car that’s on the roads” — though later the company admitted it would not be road legal. This seems obvious, of course. Imagine having to satisfy strict regulatory requirements from the Federal Aviation Administration and the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration. The Roadster could go into production in 2028, as Musk promised — or it could be another decade of missed deadlines and broken promises. Again, who cares? Car flew.
As for the Roadster itself, Musk called it “the last best driver’s car.” Moravy said that Tesla drew inspiration from aerospace designs such as the SR-71 reconnaissance aircraft. It’s a two-seater, with seats molded directly into the chassis. Its steering and driving controls use steer-by-wire technology, including a steer-by-wire yoke, brakes, and throttle. The rear of the car features the thrusters and fans housed around the diffuser area. And it has a retractable rear wing for added downforce.
Tesla has also said that the Roadster can accelerate from 0-60mph in less than a second. And during the event, the company claimed it did so in 0.81 seconds. Musk explained that increasing the applied force while reducing the vehicle’s mass help boost acceleration. In fact, Musk says the production Roadster should improve on the demonstrated result, although he acknowledged the extreme forces involved and the need to avoid subjecting occupants to extreme acceleration.
“You’ve got to crack halfway to the speed of sound, I think,” Musk teased. “Mach 0.5. Maybe a little higher.”
After the event, Tesla updated its website with details about the three distinct performance tiers for the next-generation Roadster, outlining how its controversial cold-gas thruster systems scale across the lineup:
- Performance (Road Ready): The entry-level variant seats two passengers and relies on an active aerodynamics package paired with a multi-mode suction system to maximize downforce on and off the track. It claims a 0–60 mph time under 1.6 seconds and a target range exceeding 300 miles.
- Thrust (Race Ready): Also a two-seater, this mid-tier version pairs the multi-mode suction system with rear-mounted cold-gas thrusters. The additional propulsion cuts the vehicle’s 0–60 mph acceleration to under 0.9 seconds. Tesla says this configuration will be in “limited release.”
- Rocket (Air Ready): The single-seat flagship model expands the hardware to a full perimeter-mounted array of cold-gas thrusters. In addition to driving forward and upward acceleration, the thrusters enable lateral and rotational movement in midair — enabling the short, low-altitude stunts showcased at the event. This top-spec version reaches a top speed over 230 mph and pushes 0–60 mph acceleration to under 0.59 seconds. Tesla says this version will be “invite only,” but also “not approved for public road use.”
The next-gen Roadster certainly took the scenic route in getting here. A prototype version was announced as a “one more thing” style surprise during the 2017 Tesla Semi event. The specs sounded ludicrous even back then: 0-60 mph in 1.9 seconds, a top speed over 250 mph, a 200 kWh battery delivering up to 620 miles of range, and a $200,000 starting price tag. Musk said deliveries would start in 2020, which sounded perfectly doable at the time.
Early adopters quickly threw down $50,000 deposits (or $250,000 for the limited Founders Series), effectively interest-free loans to help fund Tesla’s scaling ambitions. But then Tesla seemed to forget about the Roadster, as cementing its status as the ultimate vaporware. Production deadlines slipped as Tesla prioritized mass-market vehicles like the Model Y, while also wrestling with the overly complicated Cybertruck. Occasionally, when Musk would remember that the Roadster existed, he would up the ante about its capabilities. This culminated in the “SpaceX package” that would equip the supercar with cold-gas thrusters, bestowing hover powers and a 0-60 time under one second.
Musk has also sought to downplay the Roadster’s significance, calling it a “small potato situation” that will not “move the needle in a major way financially.” He’s framed the supercar more as a joint engineering collaboration between Tesla and SpaceX, even questioning whether it’s “even a car anymore” given its experimental nature. Some analysts theorize that the decision to re-release the Roadster is an attempt to set the stage for a rumored Tesla-SpaceX merger.
Tesla’s failure to bring the Roadster to market allowed other automakers to slip past the company with their own hyper-powered EVs. Rimac has smashed performance records with the Nevera, Porsche has refined electric performance with the Taycan, and Chinese giants like BYD are producing track-ready supercars at a fraction of the cost. The Roadster is no longer shocking the world as an impossible prototype; it’s playing catch-up to an industry that spent nine years building what Tesla merely rendered.
But then again, none of those cars flew.

articles.title: AMBA C2C: Moving Forward With A Converged AMBA Foundation For C2C Connectivity
articles.text:
Extending chiplet connectivity across AXI and CHI with scalable protocol subsets, interoperability, and flexible transport support.
In this blog post, we introduce AMBA C2C, a new specification being developed with the AMBA ecosystem. It provides a unified and scalable approach to connecting AMBA protocols across chiplets, including AMBA AXI and AMBA CHI.
Chiplet technology and AI are evolving rapidly, bringing new benefits and protocol requirements.
AMBA CHI C2C has established strong momentum as a foundational protocol for chiplets and chip-to-chip (C2C) connectivity. It is particularly suited to fully coherent, advanced heterogeneous compute and superchips.
However, chiplets span a much wider range of use cases. These include memory expansion, IO and accelerator attach, and advanced heterogeneous systems. Each use case comes with different requirements and trade-offs in functionality, performance, bandwidth efficiency, and implementation complexity.
AMBA CHI C2C already supports scalability in implementation complexity through a property negotiation mechanism. Implementations can support only the capabilities they need while preserving interoperability across chiplet types, vendors, and generations.
Our continued collaboration with the ecosystem has highlighted an important additional requirement. Many chiplets do not need the full feature set of advanced coherent systems and require an even simpler approach for C2C connectivity. This is particularly important for the vast installed base of AXI-based designs. These designs can benefit from the greater reuse and composability that chiplets enable.
This has been an important focus area since we first introduced AMBA CHI C2C in 2023. At that time, we discussed how C2C connectivity could extend to simpler, often AXI-based use cases. Partner feedback since then has reinforced the need for a unified and converged C2C approach for AMBA protocols. This approach includes both CHI and AXI, rather than separate, protocol-specific point solutions.
To address these evolving requirements, we are developing AMBA C2C.
AMBA C2C builds on the success of AMBA CHI C2C. It provides a converged and scalable C2C foundation across AMBA protocols, including AXI and CHI.
At the heart of AMBA C2C is protocol subsetting. Defined subsets enable the protocol feature set and complexity to scale across different use cases. For example, device or accelerator attach subsets can support the simpler requirements aligned with AXI-based IO and non-coherent traffic. More advanced subsets can support the richer functionality required by coherent and heterogeneous systems.
AMBA C2C uses defined protocol subsets to scale functionality and implementation complexity across different use cases. These subsets can align with on-chip protocols such as AXI and CHI. AMBA C2C then defines how these protocols are packetized for chip-to-chip transport. The packetization is optimized for each subset while providing a common approach across AXI- and CHI-class traffic.
Interoperability remains fundamental to the architecture. AMBA C2C builds on the property negotiation mechanism introduced with AMBA CHI C2C. This mechanism enables implementations with different capabilities to interoperate across chiplet types, vendors, and generations. This includes backwards and forwards compatibility.
An open chiplet ecosystem requires open standards and a clear, layered standardization approach. This includes a clear separation between the protocol and the underlying transport.
This is a proven industry model that UCIe and the broader ecosystem have adopted. AMBA CHI C2C, for example, uses UCIe Streaming as discussed in the UCIe 1.1 specification announcement.
Similarly, PCIe and CXL protocols can be transported over UCIe. More recently, UALink has adopted a similar layered architecture. It defines a packetization strategy alongside its protocol functionality while separating it from the underlying data-link and physical layers.
AMBA C2C follows this same principle. AMBA defines the protocol and packetization mechanism, while transports such as UCIe provide the underlying die-to-die connectivity. This enables AMBA C2C to work with a variety of die-to-die and chip-to-chip transports. More importantly, it provides a clean architectural boundary that enables AMBA protocols and underlying transport technologies to continue evolving at pace.
Fig. 1: Transporting AMBA protocols over UCIe with AMBA C2C.
For AMBA AXI, this separation is particularly important. AXI is widely adopted across the industry and continues to evolve. However, unlike packet-based protocols, AXI defines interface behavior rather than a native packet format. AXI is also highly configurable, and capabilities vary between implementations. Transporting AXI over a C2C link therefore requires an architectural definition. This definition specifies which AXI semantics are carried and how they are packetized. That definition must evolve alongside AXI itself.
AMBA C2C is the next evolution of AMBA’s C2C work. It builds on AMBA CHI C2C and extends the approach to a broader range of AMBA-based chiplet systems.
AMBA C2C provides a common foundation that can scale from simple AXI-based designs to advanced, CHI-based fully coherent heterogeneous systems. Interoperability is built into the architecture.
AMBA C2C follows the development and licensing model that has supported the AMBA ecosystem for decades. We are developing it in collaboration with industry partners. The specification will be freely available, royalty-free, and architecture-neutral. Over decades, this model has helped establish AMBA as a dependable and trusted industry foundation. It has supported widespread adoption, a thriving ecosystem, and a broad marketplace of compatible solutions.
We look forward to continuing our collaboration with the industry to enable an open, interoperable chiplet ecosystem, with AMBA C2C evolving alongside complementary industry standards.
