articles.title: South Korea removes safety barriers to let humanoid robots work alongside humans in factories
articles.text:
What just happened? Humanoid robots have long been making their way into different areas of the US workplace. It's also happening in South Korea, which has approved an exception to industrial safety rules so 20 machines can be tested alongside workers. For employees already worried about being replaced, removing these barriers – both literally and figuratively – isn't going to offer much reassurance.
South Korea's industry ministry announced the approval on October 13 through its regulatory sandbox program, which allows companies to test new technologies under exemptions from existing requirements.
The problem is that the country's industrial robot safety rules were written around machines that don't move around freely like a human would. They require fences and other barriers separating robot work areas from people, which would make it pretty difficult for humanoids to walk around factories and share tasks with employees.
As the Seoul Economic Daily reports, robotics and AI company Robros received permission to test its bipedal machines across semiconductor, automotive, shipbuilding, and logistics sites. The exemption lets the robots operate in spaces shared with human workers or adjacent to their work areas.
This doesn't give manufacturers permission to remove every single safety fence and let robots roam around without a care. The Kyunghyang Shinmun reports that the trials will operate under additional safety standards. The approval covers a specific trial, while the government plans to use the resulting data to revise industrial robot safety requirements more broadly.
The 20 robots will be split across Nepes (semiconductors), Sungwoo Hitech (automotive), HD Hyundai Samho (shipbuilding), and Delivery Lab (logistics). Their tasks will include cleaning semiconductor packaging components, positioning car body parts, stacking scaffolding brackets, and moving refrigerated logistics packaging.
Officials see humanoids as a way to address labor shortages, improve productivity, and carry out jobs considered too repetitive or dangerous for humans. Whether workers feel the same way is another matter.
Hyundai's union warned earlier this year that deploying humanoids could cause major job losses and insisted that management secure its agreement before introducing robots. Hyundai, meanwhile, responded by saying that the robots would reduce physically demanding and dangerous work.
A lot has been said about the effectiveness of these robots, but just how capable they really are remains uncertain. At the start of 2026, UBTech admitted that its Walker S2 humanoids managed only 30% to 50% of human productivity, despite growing interest from manufacturers.
Much like AI, there are fears that fully capable humanoid robots could put huge numbers of people out of work, causing a devastating impact on the economy. Bill Gates believes the solution could be to make the robots pay FICA taxes when they replace humans.

articles.title: “Everybody with a $20 account is now a researcher”: How Akrites is tackling the flood of AI bug reports
articles.text:
“Everybody with a $20 account is now a researcher”: How Akrites is tackling the flood of AI bug reports
AI is making it easier than ever to find potential security vulnerabilities in open source software. But finding something that looks like a vulnerability isn’t quite the same as finding a genuine security flaw. As such, maintainers are being inundated with AI-generated reports that are inaccurate, duplicative, or lack the information needed to deploy fixes.
It’s a problem that Akrites, an initiative announced by the Linux Foundation back in June, is striving to solve. As The New Stack reported at the time, Akrites was established to provide a shared security incident response team (SIRT) that consolidates vulnerability reports, validates findings, and coordinates fixes with upstream maintainers.
Some three months on, and The New Stack was at Open Source Summit Europe in Prague last week, where we sat down with Christopher Robinson, CTO of Akrites and chief security architect at the Open Source Security Foundation (OpenSSF); and Laura Guazzelli, the Linux Foundation’s security architect for AI and agentic systems. We discussed the mounting pressure on maintainers, why better AI models aren’t necessarily making their lives easier, and how Akrites is attempting to address the problem.
Part of the overarching challenge is that AI has massively lowered the barrier to entry for vulnerability hunting, allowing almost anyone to start probing open source codebases, regardless of their security credentials.
“Everybody with a $20 account is now a researcher,” Robinson tells The New Stack.
“Everybody with a $20 account is now a researcher.”
‘Vibe researching’: Finding the same bugs over and over
Robinson had, in fact, appeared in a separate talk the previous day at the very same conference, appearing alongside OpenSSF chief of staff Adrianne Marcum, who had half-jokingly floated the term “vibe researching” to describe the growing number of people using AI tools to hunt for vulnerabilities.
The phrase might not be standard industry parlance yet, and it might never catch on. But it’s an apt descriptor of the problem it encapsulates: an avalanche of AI-generated security reports that still require human time and expertise to separate genuine threats from noise.
The consequences aren’t merely frustrating for maintainers. Robinson estimates that reviewing a single security pull request can take an engineer up to eight hours — time that could otherwise be spent fixing bugs, improving software or developing new features.
“They’re very verbose,” Robinson says. “They’re highly inaccurate. They overestimate the severity of things. And they generally don’t give you the right data that an engineer needs to be able to write a patch, or understand what it is.”
“They’re very verbose. They’re highly inaccurate. They overestimate the severity of things.”
Part of the problem, Guazzelli adds, is that AI models can identify suspicious code without understanding the wider security architecture of a project, including protections implemented elsewhere that might render a reported vulnerability harmless.
“The robots don’t have the context,” Guazzelli says. “That’s why they can’t necessarily call something a false positive, because they don’t understand that you have controls that are additionally applied somewhere else.”
In other words, a model might flag a piece of code as vulnerable without recognising that other security measures already prevent the supposed flaw from being exploited. What looks like a serious issue in isolation may therefore be far less significant in reality.
Moreover, because many people are using similar AI models to examine the same codebases, maintainers can end up receiving multiple reports about the same issue.
“These models all kind of work similarly and they find similar bugs, so we’re getting a ton of duplicative reports,” Robinson continues.
“We’re getting a ton of duplicative reports.”
That doesn’t mean the technology isn’t getting better. Robinson says the quality of AI-generated vulnerability reports has improved considerably this year, but the benefits aren’t necessarily reaching open source maintainers.
“The better reports come from the more expensive paid models,” Robinson says. “[Enterprises] are better prepared, but they also are not necessarily taking those findings and reporting them to the upstream project.”
Yet, dismissing AI-generated reports altogether isn’t really an option. The same technology responsible for much of the noise is also becoming increasingly capable of uncovering genuine security weaknesses, including combinations of seemingly minor flaws that can be exploited together.
“They’ll take a series of low problems and be able to escalate that into a bigger exploit,” Robinson says. “That is months or a year’s worth of work that the computer can now do in just a couple hours.”
Money and minds
Akrites has had some serious industry muscle behind it from the get go, with founding members including Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, AWS, NVIDIA, Cisco, IBM, Red Hat, Citi, JPMorganChase, among others.
What, perhaps, distinguishes Akrites from most other Linux Foundation projects is that its members aren’t just being asked to write cheques. While financial contributions are very much part of the deal, members are also expected to commit engineering resources, up to 10 full-time engineers each, according to Robinson. Some, such as financial institutions with internal policies that prevent them from contributing upstream, put in more money instead.
“I have a fleet of about 200 seconded engineers,” Robinson says.
“I have a fleet of about 200 seconded engineers.”
Many of those engineers are already contributors or maintainers on upstream projects, bringing expertise in particular programming languages and codebases, as well as established relationships with the communities Akrites is trying to help.
“They’re the humans in the loop,” Robinson says. “I trust the robot, but I want to make sure I have a human set of eyes on things that are very important.”
Akrites uses AI to assess incoming reports and identify duplicates, while its seconded engineers help review the findings before they reach upstream maintainers.
“It’s my job to take those reports, make them more concise, understandable, and give the additional artifacts like test cases, proof of concept, and then patches,” Robinson says. “[We] provide that to upstream, so they can make more informed and more quick choices.”
“I trust the robot, but I want to make sure I have a human set of eyes on things that are very important.”
Who pays to fight the robots?
Akrites isn’t the only Linux Foundation effort attempting to put AI to work on open source security. A related initiative, the open source Cyber Reasoning System (OSS-CRS), is developing AI-powered tools that open source projects can use to investigate vulnerabilities and generate fixes. While Akrites focuses on coordinating the handling of security reports across projects, OSS-CRS is concerned with giving maintainers the tools to do more of that work themselves.
Guazzelli says one of the challenges is ensuring that AI-generated patches actually address the underlying problem without introducing new vulnerabilities or breaking existing functionality.
“With the CRS, what we’re trying to suggest is we not only verify that you have found a vulnerability, but we have the best patch possible,” Guazzelli says.
Of course, someone has to foot the bill. And while Akrites’ corporate members provide the financial backing, Robinson is keenly aware that the costs of tackling AI-generated security problems shouldn’t fall on the open source maintainers themselves.
“A lot of that goes towards our infrastructure and our tokens because it is highly powered and enabled by LLMs,” Robinson says. “It is not an inexpensive proposition.”
The financial backing and engineering resources are particularly important given the volume of material Akrites is dealing with. And for Robinson, there’s another consideration: making sure the resulting security improvements reach the open source projects that need them, rather than remaining exclusively available to the commercial organisations that helped uncover them.
“I literally have a backlog of hundreds of thousands of reports we have to go through, and then figure out how we’re getting those upstream,” Robinson says. “The commercial orgs are welcome to take those patches, but I don’t want to have things kind of isolated in this little jailed environment.”

articles.title: German AI startup Elevatry secures €3 million to automate procurement workflows | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Munich-based Elevatry, an AI platform for strategic procurement, has closed a €3 million pre-Seed financing round in order to enhance its platform, expand its team, and support market entry in Europe before expanding to North America.
Investors include Bayern Kapital, the management consultancy H&Z, and several business angels, among them Jan Henner-Theißen, Martin Berr-Sorokin, Mike Simon, Markus Ehrle, Andreas Junck, and Alexander Bruehl.
“Strategic purchasing is one of the biggest drivers of results in a company. So far, it’s only being used where there’s sufficient capacity and the necessary expertise,” says Heiko Schwarz, co-founder and CEO of Elevatry. “Our partners handle complex thinking and execute tasks at the highest level. This allows purchasing teams to apply the methodology of their best category managers to every product group. Our investors bring together capital, exclusive purchasing expertise, and market access. From now on, we’ll demonstrate the impact on our customers.”
Elevatry’s financing follows several European funding rounds in AI-powered procurement and related purchasing infrastructure during 2026.
These include Paris-based Pivot’s €34.4 million Series B, Italy’s Soource with €3 million, and German startups Procuros and Finches, which secured €20 million and €2 million, respectively.
Notably, Bayern Kapital also participated in Finches’ pre-Seed round, highlighting an earlier investment in AI-driven procurement technology.
Across eight selected comparable funding announcements covered by EU-Startups this year, approximately €75.5 million has been raised, rising to €78.5 million when Elevatry’s round is included.
“Elevatry combines a highly experienced founding team with a clear vision for the future of strategic procurement. The AI-native platform addresses a significant efficiency and value creation lever within companies, generating immediately tangible customer benefits through the intelligent use of procurement knowledge and data.
“At the same time, the company operates in an attractive, rapidly growing market for AI-powered procurement software. We look forward to supporting the team on its continued growth trajectory together with a strong consortium of business angels,” adds Monika Steger, Managing Director, Bayern Kapital.
Founded in 2026 by Heiko Schwarz, Christian Ruck, and Tizian Ruck and is headquartered near Munich, Elevatry is an AI platform for strategic procurement. Its companions (including Category Strategist, Negotiation Coach, and Risk & Integrity Manager) handle the routine analytical work along the source-to-contract process, providing procurement depth and industry- and commodity-group-specific expertise.
As a system of initiative, the platform plans proactively, prioritises based on impact (€), and prepares proposals – decisions are made collaboratively. Customers configure their own levels of autonomy, approvals, and data sovereignty on an open multi-LLM architecture.
According to the company, strategic procurement significantly influences the costs, quality, resilience, and compliance of the entire purchasing volume.
The potential is substantial: For a company with €1 billion in revenue and €500 million in purchasing volume, a 10 percent improvement can translate into €50 million in additional profit. At a 5 percent margin, this would equate to a doubling of revenue to €2 billion.
In practice, purchasing teams often only have the capacity to actively manage a portion of suppliers and product groups – thus leaving a large part of the potential leverage untapped.
Elevatry sees itself as a system of initiative rather than a system of record. The platform plans proactively, prioritises based on impact in euros, and prepares proposals. Decisions are made collaboratively. Customers configure their own levels of autonomy, approvals, and data sovereignty on an open multi-LLM architecture.
Each result grows into a further optimized knowledge layer that belongs exclusively to the customer.
“We have been supporting Elevatry with great conviction since its founding. Agentic AI will fundamentally change procurement by intelligently automating repetitive knowledge work and effectively supporting decision-making processes,” say Harald Enz and Jonas Harm, Managing Partners of H&Z.
“Elevatry creates a unique combination of leading AI technology and deep procurement domain knowledge. For us, it’s clear: Our clients expect us not only to observe innovation, but to actively shape it and translate it into concrete added value. That’s why we are investing in Elevatry and will closely support the company as a strategic partner on its growth trajectory.”
Elevatry will use today’s funds to further develop its platform and companion portfolio, as well as to implement the accompanying go-to-market activities for market entry. The team will therefore be expanded, particularly in engineering, AI, marketing, and customer support.
The initial focus is on market entry in the DACH region (Germany, Austria, Switzerland) and the EU, with international expansion planned for the medium term, focusing on North America.

articles.title: Grafana Tempo 3.1 Adds Query-Based Trace Redaction and Sampling-Aware TraceQL Metrics
articles.text:
Grafana Labs has released Tempo 3.1, the first minor update to the 3.0 architecture. It adds TLS and additional SASL mechanisms to the Kafka client, lets operators redact traces with a TraceQL query instead of a list of trace IDs, and introduces an experimental query-time hint that corrects TraceQL metrics for sampled data. vParquet5 also becomes the default block format. According to Grafana, simple metrics queries now run close to twice as fast.
The release builds on Tempo 3.0, published in June, which made the Kafka-compatible architecture (codenamed Project Rhythm) the default for microservices deployments. In that design, distributors write to a Kafka topic. Block-builders consume the topic to write Parquet blocks to object storage, and live-stores consume it to serve recent traces. Ingesters and compactors are gone, replaced by a backend scheduler and workers. Grafana says dropping replication factor 3 reduces storage from 3 to 3.5 times the trace volume to a single copy. Monolithic mode remains Kafka-free.
Because Kafka is now on the critical path, the 3.0 client's limits became a problem. It supported only SASL PLAIN over an unencrypted connection, so any broker requiring TLS refused it. Tempo 3.1 adds TLS, including optional mTLS, plus SCRAM-SHA-256, SCRAM-SHA-512, OAUTHBEARER, and AWS_MSK_IAM. A new client_rack option enables rack-aware fetching (KIP-392), so block-builders, live-stores, and metrics-generators can read from a replica in their own availability zone and avoid cross-zone transfer charges. It requires brokers with rack IDs configured. A new producer_compression option accepts none, gzip, snappy, lz4, or zstd; unset, it defaults to snappy. Grafana notes that this, together with TLS, makes Azure Event Hubs usable as a backend, since it accepts only gzip. All three changes came from community contributors.
Trace redaction, introduced in 3.0 through t`empo-cli redact`, previously required enumerating trace IDs. Sensitive values such as tokens or account numbers often appear across more traces than can practically be listed. In 3.1 the command takes a TraceQL query and supports --dry-run, which counts matches without modifying blocks. Grafana limits the syntax to one spanset filter. It uses equality comparisons on resource.* and span.* attributes, along with && and ||. This is because the rewrite cannot be undone. --start and --end flags narrow the time range, which matters because Tempo pauses compaction for a tenant while a redaction applies. Grafana warns that older workers ignore the window and remove every match in each block they receive, without an error. The flags should only be used once every scheduler and worker runs 3.1.
TraceQL metrics, which became generally available in 3.0, gains three changes. The experimental hint with (extrapolate=true) scales by the sampling rate in tracestate. This follows OpenTelemetry's probability sampling rules. At 50% sampling, each stored span counts as two. Spans without a recorded rate count as one, so partial adoption does not distort other services. It applies to: rate, count_over_time, sum_over_time, avg_over_time, histogram_over_time, quantile_over_time, and compare, but not to min_over_time or max_over_time. It requires vParquet4 or later and reads the rate the same way as the metrics-generator's enable_tracestate_span_multiplier setting from 3.0, so ad-hoc queries and pre-aggregated series should agree. Second, +, -, *, and / now work between metrics queries and scalars, so an error rate becomes a single query. Third, the span-only fetch path, experimental in 3.0, is now on by default for vParquet5 blocks. In one warmed-up test, { } | rate() finished in slightly over half the time.
Other additions include an experimental span pruning option on the trace-by-ID v2 endpoint, which collapses similar leaf spans into one summary span carrying count and duration statistics. The same endpoint gains TraceQL filtering. A new experimental POST /api/v2/traces/diff endpoint compares two traces and can return a compact summary instead of a span-level patch. It is exposed through gcx, tempo-cli, and the Tempo MCP server, where Grafana says the smaller payload helps LLM-driven investigations. The metrics-generator gets an unmatched_span_kind label on expired service-graph edges, support for the renamed OpenTelemetry db.system.name attribute, and pooled label buffers that Grafana reports reduce per-span allocations to zero in its service-graph benchmarks.

articles.title: Report: FTC probes Anthropic, OpenAI after Trump dismissed AI fears as “hoax”
articles.text:
Following a string of incidents where AI models hacked websites and breached government systems during testing phases, the Federal Trade Commission is officially probing Anthropic and OpenAI over consumer harms, an insider told Axios.
On Wednesday, the FTC sent out civil investigative demands seeking a wide range of information from the AI firms on recent safety incidents.
The FTC did not respond to Ars’ request to review the subpoena demands. However, Axios’ source said the requests spanned more than 50 pages of questions and sought documents related to the incidents, internal security measures taken, and marketing materials that may suggest consumers were misled.
Soon, third parties targeted by OpenAI and Anthropic agents will also be subpoenaed, Axios’ source said. Any concerning evidence gathered may support FTC litigation, should the FTC decide to sue either or both firms for releasing unsafe products.
OpenAI already faces lawsuits alleging consumer harms, including lawsuits linking its chatbot to matricide, child suicide, school shootings, and other violence. And this week, a group of eight states specifically sued OpenAI over consumer harms, Reuters reported. Like consumers suing, they argued that ChatGPT harms children and “reinforces delusions, encourages dangerous behavior, and assists users in planning violence like mass shootings.”
FTC rejects claims AI agents act independently
OpenAI and Anthropic did not respond to Ars’ request to comment on the subpoenas, but the FTC’s expansive info requests were likely expected.
In September, Reuters reported that the probe was coming, noting that an independent research group investigating the incidents, METR, would likely also be subpoenaed.
That same month, FTC Chair Andrew Ferguson told Reuters that he thinks that companies should be liable for chatbot harms. At that time, Ferguson emphasized that he was tired of people anthropomorphizing AI tools. He insisted that, “if someone tells a tool to do something, and the tool does it, I don’t think we would say, ‘Oh, what do we do about the tool?’”

articles.title: Molagri raises $5.2-million USD seed round to bolster work on pesticides that “evolve” | BetaKit
articles.text:
Toronto-based AgTech startup Molagri has emerged from Y Combinator with investor backing to hire more scientists.
The news: Molagri, which is developing easily updatable pesticides to “evolve” alongside pest resistance, announced this week that it has raised a total of $5.2 million USD ($8.2 million CAD) in seed funding. The funding comes in addition to the roughly $600,000 USD it raised before joining San Francisco-based accelerator Y Combinator, which it graduated from last month.
The seed round was led by Convective Capital, with participation from Y Combinator, Superorganism, Robinhood Ventures, and Y Combinator co-founder Paul Graham, alongside other angels.
Molagri co-founder and CEO Zaky Hassan told BetaKit in a phone call that the funding will help double its team of four and perform field trials.
From the source: “I’m just thinking of hitting our milestones and building a product that works and makes life better for farmers and consumers,” Hassan said when asked about the round. “We’re focused on building, so I feel like we have to maybe step back once in a while and smell the roses, but right now we’re just nonstop.”
The context: Molagri was founded by Hassan and Min Jin, two PhD candidates from the University of Toronto who specialize in common cold coronaviruses and were both interested in recent AI-driven advancements in protein design. The startup is synthesizing pesticides on top of a non-infectious insect virus that they can engineer to “whitelist” and “blacklist” targeted proteins, and easily tweak its formulation to stay ahead of anticipated pest resistance.
Hassan previously told BetaKit that Molagri is developing pesticides for tree nuts and tree fruits because they have an acute insecticide need.
Final thought: Hassan reaffirmed that Molagri has secured lab space in Toronto and plans to keep growing the company in the city, which he told BetaKit in August is a “crazy place for talent.” In a LinkedIn post, Hassan said the company is looking for scientists with experience in synthetic virology, insect biology, molecular display and binder discovery, and yeast expression and virus-like particle production.
Feature image courtesy Molagri.

articles.title: ¡Por fin! '007 First Light', el nuevo juego de James Bond, tiene fecha de lanzamiento en la Nintendo Switch 2
articles.text:
Después de su postergación, 007 First Light por fin tiene fecha de lanzamiento confirmada en Nintendo Switch 2. El nuevo juego de James Bond, desarrollado por IO Interactive, ha revelado desde cuándo estará disponible en la plataforma japonesa, lo cual es una muy buena noticia. La mala noticia es que los interesados en jugarlo aún tienen que esperar varios meses más antes de tenerlo en sus manos.
De acuerdo con el estudio, 007 First Light llegará a la Nintendo Switch 2 el 18 de marzo de 2027. Esto significa que el título estará disponible en la consola con casi un año de demora respecto de su fecha de lanzamiento original. Las reservas ya están abiertas e incluyen el traje de GoldenEye como beneficio para quienes concreten la compra anticipada.
Un detalle interesante a considerar es que, al menos por ahora, IO Interactive está promocionando la edición Deluxe de 007 First Light para Nintendo Switch 2. La misma cuesta 69,99 euros e incluye cuatro disfraces exclusivos, un skin de arma y el pack de gadgets que incluye un encendedor, un set de dardos, un bolígrafo y auriculares. El estudio todavía no ha mencionado si piensa ofrecer una edición estándar.
Sea como sea, los usuarios de la consola japonesa tendrán que esperar unos 5 meses más antes de acceder a 007 First Light. Ya veremos si la extensa demora en el lanzamiento de la versión para Nintendo Switch 2 termina impactando negativamente en sus proyecciones de venta. Después de todo, el juego debutará allí unos 10 meses después de su estreno en el resto de las plataformas.
007 First Light, lo nuevo de James Bond, llegará a la Nintendo Switch 2 en marzo de 2027
El caso de 007 First Light es un tanto llamativo, pues originalmente iba a debutar en simultáneo en todas las plataformas. La primera fecha pautada fue el 27 de marzo de 2026, aunque no se cumplió. IO Interactive retrasó el debut del juego en PS5, Xbox Series X|S y PC hasta el 27 de mayo, y prometió que la versión para Nintendo Switch 2 iba a llegar en el transcurso del verano.
No obstante, lo último tampoco sucedió. Si bien el juego llegó en tiempo y forma a ordenadores y consolas PlayStation y Xbox de actual generación, el verano pasó y no hubo novedades sobre 007 First Light en Switch 2. Ahora, la espera se extiende hasta marzo de 2027 bajo la promesa de ofrecer una experiencia realmente excepcional en el dispositivo portátil de Nintendo.
007 First Light es una propuesta muy interesante, pues aleja a los jugadores de la historias de James Bond ya conocidas. El juego presenta al personaje principal como un agente del MI6 que recién está dando sus primeros pasos en el mundo del espionaje. La respuesta de los jugadores ha sido bastante positiva y sus desarrolladores apuestan a lograr lo mismo en la Nintendo Switch 2.

articles.title: Measuring Human Cryptanalysis Effort - Schneier on Security
articles.text:
Measuring Human Cryptanalysis Effort
Matthew Green has a new site that tries to estimate the number of cryptanalyst-hours that have been spent analyzing different public-key algorithms:
Abstract: We estimate how much public cryptanalysis each public-key assumption has received, using the literature itself as the instrument. From roughly sixteen thousand candidate papers we classify cryptanalytic work on ECDLP, structured and plain lattices, syndrome decoding and their comparators, then convert papers into estimated research-allocation years through a person-level author map. These publication-based estimates may substantially overstate actual time spent. Lattices have overtaken elliptic curves in this cumulative measure only recently; we express that history as inference budgets under stated productivity assumptions. The study was conducted by AI models: Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Opus 5.5 built the pipeline, ran the analysis and wrote this page, with contributions from GPT-6 Astra. Matthew Green set the questions, made the key methodological decisions and oversaw the work.
There are a lot of caveats to this analysis. It relies on published work, so anything unpublished does not count. This includes both academic cryptanalysis that didn’t result in a paper, and intelligence agency cryptanalysis done in secret. But it’s a good first stab at a metric of this sort.

articles.title: Anthropic is letting METR researchers look under the hood with employee-level access | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Anthropic is giving employee-level access to six researchers from METR, a nonprofit that tests frontier AI models, to independently assess Anthropic’s models, safety practices, and risk management, the company said in a blog post on Thursday.
The arrangement comes at a time where incidents of AI agents acting outside their instructions have been disclosed every week or two since late August. The incidents have sharpened calls for independent checks on AI companies.
“We want to be publicly accountable for the decisions we’re making,” Anthropic said in the blog post. “We aim to close the gap between what evaluators understand about a frontier AI company’s systems and what the company itself understands.”
Under the new arrangement, the METR team has Anthropic-issued company laptops, office space, and access to internal tools roughly on par with what Anthropic’s own risk assessment teams use. “Anthropic employees are encouraged to share information with them just as they would with a fellow employee working on alignment risk” the company said.
Anthropic compared the arrangement to banking, similar to how regulators place resident examiners inside the largest banks.
METR will publish its own assessments of Anthropic’s risks, incidents, and practices, and the company has given up the right to block them.
“Anthropic can’t veto publication, but we can require them to redact information if it falls into narrow, pre-defined categories,” the company said, such as customer data, anything attorney-client privileged, or relating to information about its model architectures. “METR is free to characterize our redactions publicly, and say whether it believes the redactions were justified, as long as it does so without revealing the redacted information” Anthropic added.
METR is the only evaluator so far at the top of a three-tier system Anthropic is building. Evaluators in the bottom tier, like biosecurity nonprofit SecureBio, run narrow reviews and require Anthropic’s approval to publish. The middle tier gets more information and can publish without approval, while the top tier adds METR’s employee-level access.
Thursday’s announcement makes good on a promise Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei made in a September essay, where he proposed embedding outside evaluators inside AI labs as a first step toward slowing the technology’s development. OpenAI quickly pledged the same, and both companies, along with Google, Meta, Nvidia, and xAI, have since signed a White House accord committing to independent review.

articles.title: Tesla revela Roadster que “voa” e dirige de ponta-cabeça com tecnologia da SpaceX
articles.text:
A Tesla apresentou, nesta quinta-feira (15), uma nova geração do Roadster, seu supercarro elétrico desenvolvido em colaboração com a SpaceX. O modelo promete ser o veículo mais potente já criado pela montadora de Elon Musk e inclui recursos que parecem saídos de um filme de ficção científica: a capacidade de “voar” e de dirigir de ponta-cabeça.
Durante a apresentação, a empresa demonstrou o veículo preso a uma parede, sem cair. O efeito é produzido por um ventilador instalado na base do carro, que cria sucção para mantê-lo grudado à superfície.
A demonstração dá destaque às ambições da Tesla para o novo esportivo, cujo desenvolvimento se arrasta há anos. O protótipo foi apresentado originalmente em 2017, com preço anunciado de US$ 200 mil (cerca de R$ 1,1 milhão) e previsão inicial de entrega para 2020. Desde então, a empresa não atualizou o preço de tabela, e as reservas continuam abertas mediante pagamento de US$ 50 mil (cerca de R$ 270 mil).
Tesla revela versões, desempenho e previsão de produção do Roadster
A apresentação do novo Roadster trouxe detalhes adicionais sobre o desempenho e as configurações do esportivo. Durante o evento realizado no Texas (EUA), o veículo usou ventiladores de alta potência e propulsores da SpaceX para subir uma rampa invertida, girar e descer até o chão. A Tesla também demonstrou o carro saltando por cima de cinco veículos da marca: Cybercab, Cybertruck, Tesla Semi, Model Y e Model 3.
Segundo Elon Musk, o Roadster consegue acelerar de zero a 96 km/h em apenas um segundo. A Tesla afirma que todas as versões terão autonomia de aproximadamente 483 km e velocidade máxima superior a 370 km/h.
O modelo será oferecido em três configurações:
- Performance: versão para uso em estradas, com dois lugares, aerodinâmica ativa e sistema de sucção para melhorar o desempenho dentro e fora das pistas. A reserva custa US$ 50 mil (cerca de R$ 270 mil);
- Thrust: configuração voltada às pistas, também com dois lugares, equipada com propulsores de gás frio na traseira. A reserva custa US$ 250 mil (cerca de R$ 1,35 milhão);
- Rocket: versão descrita pela Tesla como preparada para voar, com apenas um assento e dez propulsores de gás frio distribuídos pelo veículo. A compra será feita somente por convite.
O vice-presidente de engenharia da Tesla, Lars Moravy, explicou que os dez propulsores estão conectados a um sistema com 600 litros de ar comprimido, usado para levantar e girar o carro no ar. O reservatório pode ser recarregado. A empresa também afirmou que praticamente todos os espaços disponíveis no veículo são ocupados por vasos de pressão reforçados com fibra de carbono.
A Tesla pretende iniciar a produção do Roadster em 2028, mas Musk não anunciou um preço definitivo para o modelo. O executivo também mencionou a possibilidade de tentar saltar o Snake River Canyon, nos Estados Unidos, um desfiladeiro conhecido por uma tentativa de travessia realizada pelo dublê Evel Knievel.
O design foi outro destaque da apresentação. Com linhas mais angulares, o carro tem inspiração declarada nos aviões militares SR-71 e F-35. A nova aparência representa evolução em relação ao protótipo mostrado em 2017.
Roadster promete voar com ajuda da SpaceX
A possibilidade de o novo Roadster voar já havia sido mencionada por Musk em outubro de 2025, durante entrevista ao podcast de Joe Rogan. Na ocasião, o executivo confirmou que o desenvolvimento do esportivo continuava e afirmou que o carro poderia sair do chão.
Musk também demonstrou frustração com a ausência de carros voadores no mundo atual e defendeu que as pessoas deveriam ter a possibilidade de comprar um.
O projeto reúne a Tesla e a SpaceX, duas empresas comandadas pelo empresário. A colaboração abre espaço para a aplicação de tecnologias associadas à indústria aeroespacial em um automóvel de produção, embora os detalhes técnicos dos recursos apresentados ainda não estejam esclarecidos no material fornecido.
Apesar da demonstração, não há data de entrega confirmada para a nova geração do Roadster. A previsão inicial de 2020 ficou para trás, e o modelo segue em desenvolvimento.
Primeiro Roadster da Tesla foi lançado ao espaço
A história do esportivo também passa pela exploração espacial. Em 6 de fevereiro de 2018, um foguete levou um Roadster da primeira geração ao espaço durante seu voo inaugural, com o carro como única carga a bordo.
O lançamento ocorreu na plataforma 39A do Centro Espacial Kennedy, nos Estados Unidos. Poucas horas depois da decolagem, o segundo estágio do foguete foi acionado para colocar o veículo em uma órbita ao redor do Sol, cuja distância máxima corresponde à órbita de Marte.
Na época, Musk afirmou que pretendia deixar o carro em órbita marciana por centenas de milhões de anos.
“Eu adoro a ideia de um carro navegando aparentemente sem parar pelo espaço e talvez sendo descoberto por uma raça alienígena milhões de anos no futuro”, disse o empresário durante o lançamento.
O Roadster chegou a se aproximar de Marte em novembro de 2018 e continua percorrendo uma trajetória elíptica ao redor do Sol, aproximando-se e afastando-se da região da órbita terrestre.
Leia mais:
- Sem volante nem pedais, Cybercab vira alvo de investigação
- Tesla é julgada por acusações de discriminação racial contra trabalhadores negros nos EUA
- Tesla muda nome do sistema de direção assistida na Europa
Roadster ajudou a consolidar os carros elétricos da Tesla
A primeira geração do Roadster foi lançada em 2008 e permaneceu à venda até 2012. O modelo utilizava o chassi do Lotus Elise e foi o primeiro carro da Tesla, ajudando a demonstrar que veículos elétricos também poderiam oferecer desempenho esportivo.
Depois dele, a fabricante ampliou sua linha com os utilitários esportivos Model Y e Model X e os sedãs Model S e Model 3.
A apresentação da nova geração acontece em meio a mudança de prioridades na empresa. A Tesla vem direcionando mais atenção à robótica e às tecnologias de direção autônoma baseadas em inteligência artificial (IA).
Neste ano, a companhia interrompeu as vendas dos Model S e Model X para abrir espaço na produção de seus robôs humanoides Optimus. A empresa também lançou o Cybercab, robô-táxi de dois lugares projetado sem volante, pedais ou retrovisores.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: Rockstar co-head says the huge GTA 6 leaks in 2022 felt 'really weirdly invasive,' and a new policy banned devs from accessing servers and tools outside the office — 'It feels like somebody’s wading through your dirty washing'
articles.text:
'It feels like somebody’s wading through your dirty washing' — Rockstar says GTA 6 leaks in 2022 felt 'weirdly invasive' and were 'hard to deal with on an emotional level'
Despite the security measure policy introduced at Rockstar, leaks have persisted
- Rockstar Games co-head of development Aaron Garbut says Grand Theft Auto 6 leaks from 2022 were an "invasive" moment
- The leaks caused a huge shift at Rockstar that forced a five-day in-office work policy for security reasons
- Rockstar’s head of publishing, Jennifer Kolbe, says Rockstar plans to reexamine the policy after GTA 6 launches
Rockstar Games has addressed the initial Grand Theft Auto 6 leaks from 2022, calling it an "invasive" moment that resulted in a huge policy shift at the studio.
In a lengthy interview with Bloomberg, where Rockstar leadership discussed GTA 6's long development period, co-head of development Aaron Garbut touched on the huge leaks from 2022 that changed how the studio works today.
In September of that year, someone hacked the company's Slack channel and leaked dozens of raw, unfinished gameplay footage before Rockstar was ready to unveil anything. Rockstar released a statement about the leaks, and despite copyright takedowns, the footage quickly spread like wildfire, and though law enforcement later tracked the alleged hacker down, it was too late.
"It feels like somebody’s wading through your dirty washing," Garbut said. "It’s like they’re inside your head. You see your early work out there. Nobody’s ever supposed to see that. It’s really weirdly invasive. And so it’s quite hard to deal with on an emotional level."
As a result, Rockstar introduced a controversial policy in 2024 requiring every developer to work in-office five days a week for security reasons; developers were also banned from accessing Rockstar’s servers and tools outside the office, which forced them to take vacation days if they needed to stay home for childcare or emergencies.
The policy set back the cultural progress the studio made after Red Dead Redemption 2's release, a game made under extensive periods of "crunch." With GTA 6, Rockstar knew it couldn't repeat those mistakes; however, the new policy following the leaks meant no more hybrid working.
Rockstar’s head of publishing Jennifer Kolbe told Bloomberg, however, that the studio plans to reexamine the policy after GTA 6 launches, though she doubts it will be able to switch to the more common three-days-in, two-days-out hybrid work model.

"The idea that we would have the game in that many environments is something that I think the security team would not love," Kolbe said. “I think if we did not have a game that people wanted to steal as much, maybe it would be an easier conversation."
Unfortunately, more leaks have since occurred, notably ahead of Rockstar's GTA 6 extended look, and persist to this day, with a prevalent leaker known as 'Cyberleek' threatening to release more in the lead-up to the game's launch on November 19.
In case you missed it, Rockstar has released the cinematic GTA 6 launch trailer, which offers a deeper look into the game's story.

articles.title: TSMC confirms it is considering Terafab chipmaking expansion with Elon Musk — CEO insists TSMC would have to run Texas-based project
articles.text:
TSMC confirms it is considering Terafab chipmaking expansion with Elon Musk — CEO insists TSMC would have to run Texas-based project
Could run Terafab too.
C.C. Wei, chief executive and chairman of TSMC, confirmed on Thursday that the company is considering expansion of its American production capacity beyond Arizona and Texas is one of the options it is evaluating. The head of the world's largest contract chipmaker also confirmed negotiations with Elon Musk regarding usage of Terafab, but stressed that to be a part of it, the fab must be managed by TSMC, which automatically excludes burgers and cigars in the cleanroom.
"We expanded our capacity consideration to see outside Arizona, whether we can get another chance to expand our capacity," said C.C. Wei during the company's earnings call with financial analysts and investors. "Texas is one [of our options]. We sent the teams to Texas to do all the evaluation. We also talked to one of our customers, who is trying to build a fab, Terafab, let me be more specific."
Recently in transpired that Elon Musk's Terafab was in talks with TSMC over using the giant semiconductor production facility together. Elon Musk confirmed the negotiations, whereas TSMC did not comment.
"We are discussing with them to see whether we can be utilizing that actual capacity also," Wei added. "So, we are still in discussion. If we have any solid conclusion, we will share with you."
The information about negotiations between Elon Musk's Terafab and TSMC immediately triggered chatter that the parties are set to adopt TSMC's typical business model it uses for ESMC and JASM facilities under which it operates fabs co-owned with other investors. However, Musk then said that Terafab's facility would be operated by Terafab and TSMC could only sub-lease part of its cleanroom. Now, C.C. Wei said that if TSMC joins the project, it will insist on operating the fab.
"We are still in discussion," Wei replied when asked whether TSMC is not becoming a part of the Terafab project. "Let me say that. […] Either way, it will be possible, but the fab has to be run by TSMC."
The key question now is whether Musk and TSMC can agree on an arrangement that satisfies both parties. Musk wants Terafab to retain control of its manufacturing complex, whereas TSMC insists on operating any fab it uses. One potential compromise would be for Terafab to own the facility and lease a portion of it to TSMC, which would independently operate its production lines. Such an arrangement would allow Musk to retain ownership of the whole complex while giving TSMC control over select manufacturing lines. However, if Terafab itself uses Intel's 14A process technology at the facility, TSMC's presence there will be extremely complicated, if possible at all. In any case, so far the parties have not come to any agreement.

articles.title: Steam can now show game achievements in separate ‘sets’
articles.text:
Valve is introducing a major new feature for Steam achievements called “achievement sets” that lets developers list different groups of achievements for a base game and DLCs.
Steam can now show game achievements in separate ‘sets’
Developers with games on Steam can split achievements from a base game and its DLC into sets with their own progress bars.
“In games that support sets, you still unlock achievements by playing the game as usual,” Valve says. “But when you browse what you have unlocked afterward, Steam will break the long list of game achievements into the developer-created sets, making it easier to see what you have completed and to find other related achievements you can unlock next.” Achievement sets have their own progress bars, and if you finish a set, you’ll get a “set complete” trophy that’s visible on your profile.
Steam will support seasonal achievement sets that developers can archive, too. “We think there are a lot of fun ways games can take advantage of the temporary nature this can add, such as adding achievements to season-based games or enabling time-limited holiday achievements,” Valve says.
A handful of games already support achievement sets, per Valve:

articles.title: Grid Modernization’s Hidden Cost - EE Times
articles.text:
The grid is being rebuilt in real time, with developers on track to add 86 gigawatts of utility-scale capacity this year, the largest single-year capacity addition in over two decades, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA).
The problem with such rapid expansion, however, is that every solar array, battery site, and electric vehicle depot introduces networked, protocol-speaking assets that need to be seen and secured. And, historically, network visibility has been a thorn in the side of energy administrators because most still can’t fully see across OT and IT. Case in point: Just 14% of organizations in Fortinet’s 2026 State of OT and Cybersecurity Report signaled full visibility into their OT systems, while roughly a quarter said they can see only half of the operational network.
Bad actors are exploiting these visibility teething pains. In August, five federal agencies warned of an active campaign targeting industrial controllers running power and water systems. Knowing that many energy operators struggle to quickly detect anomalies across connected infrastructure, attackers used AI-written scripts disguised as legitimate monitoring tools to find and probe internet-exposed assets.
This isn’t good enough. Going forward, utilities need to close the modernization-vs-visibility gap and account for every asset under their watch, both existing and incoming.
More assets and a growing attack surface
Across stakeholders, grid modernization outpacing grid visibility is top of mind. The North American Electric Reliability Corporation (NERC) highlighted this concern at the start of the year, recognizing that a more dynamic, interconnected, and digitized grid is exposed in kind to more sophisticated cyber and physical threats. In short, if not properly accounted for, more energy assets can quickly expand the attack surface.
Unfortunately, the energy sector’s track record isn’t particularly strong in overseeing information technology and operational technology. Cultural divisions between the two sides of the network often see long-term legacy infrastructure and control machinery (OT) connected without proper network oversight (IT). Disconnected defenses can and do result in successful breaches, which then spiral into real-world consequences such as production shutdowns, equipment damage, or lateral movement inside the network.
Leaders, too, know this is a problem: 83% of energy, utilities, and resources executives view cyberattacks as a serious or moderate risk (six percentage points higher than other sectors). One of the core reasons? Limited real-time awareness of OT assets. During energy assessments, I’ve seen this all-too-common problem firsthand in the form of unpatched devices, insecure external connections, and incomplete asset inventories.
Energy players need to take ownership and step up their defenses. NERC reinforced this message by finding that, while the Critical Infrastructure Protection (CIP) standards remain the backbone of mandatory security controls for bulk power system operators, the sector’s operating environment is changing faster than the standards’ scope and revision cadence. In this vacuum, all players must not only comply with current standards but also redouble monitoring efforts, build a defensible inventory, and extend oversight to operational assets.
Most operators need to go back to basics
While the immediate reflex to more threats is more defenses, the truth is you can’t secure what you can’t see. The first move to grid visibility is therefore knowing what’s connected, how it talks, and what “normal” looks like.
Similarly, IT and OT can no longer operate independently. I made the case last year that legacy PLCs don’t need ripping out, just proper monitoring. The grid is no different since operators need a single line of sight across control centers, switches and routers, and remote substations. This way, backed by tools that can poll Modbus devices, subscribe to MQTT topics, and clearly display what they see for whoever’s watching, any network problem appears in one shared view instead of multiple disconnected alerts.
Another by-product benefit of watching the grid is that operators can also close the compliance gap alongside the security gap. CIP-015 (NERC’s standard focused on internal network security monitoring) requires historical records and alert logs that back up your documented processes. Continuous monitoring creates a paper trail like this, making evidence-gathering much easier if and when auditors come knocking.
Of course, none of this replaces core tenets of energy security. Operators still need to take controllers off the public internet, agree which team owns each new asset at commissioning, and write security requirements into equipment contracts. Done right, visibility is the supporting layer beneath everything that lets teams act before problems escalate.
Energy network monitoring can’t be an afterthought
One silver lining is that large energy companies are responding and bolstering their cybersecurity. Smaller utilities, however, still struggle to allocate manpower and resources to defend themselves. This is a particular concern because low-impact systems and third-party operators represent a growing share of operational dependency. In this way, adversaries are more often trying to target these smaller systems and aggregate the compromises into large-scale effects.
For operators big and small, closing the gap doesn’t start with a bigger budget or a larger team but with oversight that scales.
Whether added capacity translates into a more vulnerable attack surface ultimately depends on energy leaders. From where I sit, connecting each new asset with visibility that surfaces issues early is the highest-leverage move stretched operators can make right now.

LinkedIn will now let you charge to share your expertise — and build stronger business relationships
LinkedIn want you to manage your connections better
- LinkedIn could soon gain a new Network feed just for your existing contacts
- Digital business cards for LinkedIn are coming to your mobile wallet soon
- In-Stream Ads are also being tested with select partners in the US
LinkedIn says more professionals are starting side hustles, so to help them, it's launching a series of new tools to help them strengthen relationships, grow their audiences and generate more income.
The Microsoft-owned platform noted that the number of founders on its platform has risen by 70%, and the number of members reporting more than one job position rising 26% since 2019.
However it also stressed that more than half of Gen Z professionals are unsure how to develop a relationship after making an initial connection.
LinkedIn wants to help the creator community
The platform is now testing a new Network feed to play home to posts from existing connections, helping users strengthen their existing relationships. This will be a separate feed to the main feed, so that they can gain better visibility into what existing contacts are saying and doing. Initial test markets include the US, UK, India and Australia, but there's no word yet on a broader rollout or general availability.
LinkedIn is also bridging the gap between physical and digital, integrating digital business cards into the app with support for mobile wallet apps for quick access. Something that could be especially useful for conferences, meetings and other networking events, with plans for a global rollout in the coming months.
Premium subscribers will also be able to add private notes to other people's profiles to help them remember key details, like where they met somebody.
On the cash front, creators are gaining a new dashboard to manage their content and keep an eye on important statistics, while In-Stream Ads are also set to come to videos for an additional monetization option – something that's currently being tested with select US creators and advertisers.

articles.title: Crecen los daños de barcos a los cables submarinos de internet: los casos que encendieron las alarmas
articles.text:
La mayor parte del tráfico de internet del mundo sigue viajando por cables de fibra óptica tendidos en el fondo del mar, y esa infraestructura enfrenta un riesgo creciente de sabotaje a medida que se multiplican los conflictos abiertos y la llamada guerra en zona gris, según un nuevo libro de la investigadora Elisabeth Braw.
Braw, investigadora sénior del Atlantic Council, un centro de estudios con sede en Washington, dirige la iniciativa sobre amenazas al orden marítimo global de esa institución. Su libro, titulado Undersea War, documenta un aumento en los incidentes sospechosos de barcos que arrastran sus anclas durante trayectos inusualmente largos y terminan cortando cables submarinos.
Según el libro, alrededor del 60% de los daños a cables submarinos se debe a errores humanos durante tareas de pesca o navegación, cuando redes con pesas o anclas rozan el fondo marino, mientras que el Comité Internacional de Protección de Cables (ICPC) ubica esa cifra entre el 50% y el 80%. Cada año se dañan entre 150 y 200 cables en todo el mundo, y en general se reparan con rapidez.
Los incidentes que encendieron las alarmas
Uno de los casos más citados en el libro ocurrió el 25 de diciembre de 2024, cuando el petrolero Eagle S, vinculado a Rusia, arrastró su ancla durante unos 90 kilómetros y cortó o dañó cuatro cables de datos además del cable eléctrico submarino Estlink 2, que conecta las redes de energía del Báltico y los países nórdicos.
Uno de esos cables de datos ya había sido cortado un mes antes por el buque de carga chino Yi Peng 3, en noviembre de 2024, en la misma región del mar Báltico. La tripulación de ese barco no fue procesada por las autoridades europeas, mientras que Finlandia sí intentó llevar a juicio a tres oficiales del Eagle S.
Del otro lado del mundo, un tribunal de Taiwán condenó al capitán del buque de propiedad china Hong Tai por cortar un cable de telecomunicaciones submarino en febrero de 2025, con una sentencia de tres años de prisión dictada en junio de ese año. Tras el caso, el parlamento taiwanés aumentó las penas por daño intencional a cables o gasoductos submarinos hasta un máximo de siete años de cárcel.
Nuevas amenazas en el mar y bajo el agua
Este año se sumaron otros episodios, entre ellos intentos de Irán de cobrar tarifas a los operadores de cables submarinos que atraviesan el estrecho de Ormuz, una vía marítima estratégica entre el golfo Pérsico y el mar Arábigo.
Por separado, una operación conjunta del Reino Unido, Noruega y Estados Unidos interceptó a submarinos rusos que practicaban el uso de una nueva tecnología para inutilizar cables submarinos en aguas árticas cercanas al archipiélago noruego de Svalbard.
Braw explicó que, durante décadas, incluso en plena Guerra Fría, existió un acuerdo internacional tácito para no dañar esta infraestructura, algo que calificó como el comportamiento de “un buen ciudadano del fondo marino”.
“Si pensás en la naturaleza absolutamente crucial de los cables y gasoductos submarinos, sobre todo los cables, si se interrumpieran aunque sea por un minuto, causarían una disrupción masiva”, dijo Braw a Ars Technica, al explicar por qué ese sistema de infraestructura se volvió un blanco cada vez más atractivo.
La investigadora remarcó que, a diferencia de la Guerra Fría, cuando existían pocos cables telefónicos y un uso limitado de las comunicaciones internacionales, hoy esos conductores eléctricos transportan sumas de dinero constantes y un volumen de datos que no tiene comparación histórica.
Las redes de fibra óptica submarina coexisten además con gasoductos y cables eléctricos submarinos, lo que multiplica los blancos posibles para cualquier ataque deliberado contra la infraestructura bajo el mar.
El propio libro de Braw plantea la pregunta de fondo: qué ocurre cuando ese acuerdo internacional de no agresión contra la infraestructura submarina, sostenido durante décadas, deja de regir para las principales potencias.

articles.title: Votre smartphone Android peut enfin éteindre ou redémarrer votre PC à distance
articles.text:
L’application Lien avec Windows de Microsoft se limitait jusqu’ici aux appels, aux messages, aux photos, au transfert de fichiers et au verrouillage de l’ordinateur (ce qui est déjà bien). Elle s’enrichit aujourd’hui d’une option très attendue pour éteindre, mettre en veille ou redémarrer à distance votre PC en utilisant votre smartphone Android.
Un nouveau menu sur l’application mobile
Source : Android Authority
Repérée en août dernier et déployée via la dernière mise à jour bêta de Lien avec Windows (version 1.26101.103.0), cette nouveauté remplace l’ancien bouton de verrouillage par une touche dédiée à l’alimentation. En touchant cette commande, un volet s’ouvre désormais pour laisser le choix entre verrouiller, mettre en veille, redémarrer ou éteindre complètement l’ordinateur. Des messages d’alerte vous préviennent évidemment si vos données ne sont pas enregistrées. La mise en veille vous rappelle aussi qu’il faudra être physiquement présent pour réveiller l’écran.
Source : Android Authority
L’application intègre également une option pour terminer les mises à jour en attente avant de couper ou de relancer Windows. Concrètement, choisir cette option ferme les applications en cours, installe les correctifs nécessaires, puis éteint ou redémarre la machine sans manipulation supplémentaire à faire depuis votre bureau.
Une meilleure intégration de Windows et Android
Si des outils comme le Bureau à distance proposaient déjà ce type de contrôle, l’intégration directe dans Lien avec Windows simplifie grandement la vie de ceux qui gardent leur téléphone à portée de main toute la journée, c’est-à-dire presque tout le monde. Cette mise à jour vient un peu plus renforcer le lien entre Android et Windows, tout en évitant de multiplier les logiciels tiers pour effectuer des actions aussi basiques.
À lire : Windows 11 : Microsoft voudrait fusionner votre smartphone Android avec votre PC
Si vous voulez en profiter dès maintenant, il suffit de vous inscrire au programme bêta depuis votre smartphone Android en allant en bas de la page de l’application sur le Google Play Store. Pour les autres, le déploiement de cette mise à jour devrait suivre une fois la phase de test validée par Microsoft. Pratique, non ?

articles.title: Programmer l’eau chaude depuis son téléphone : le chauffe-eau Comfee de 80 litres est à 174,99 €
articles.text:
Le chauffe-eau connecté Comfee D80-15EFG de 80 litres est à 174,99 €
Le Comfee D80-15EFG est un chauffe-eau électrique vertical de 80 litres avec commande électronique, connexion Wi-Fi et programmation de la chauffe.
Amazon propose le chauffe-eau Comfee D80-15EFG de 80 litres à 174,99 €, contre un prix conseillé de 209,99 €. L’écart atteint 35 €, soit environ 17 %. Par rapport au prix le plus bas des 30 derniers jours de 189,99 €, la baisse représente 15 €, soit environ 8 %. L’appareil est vendu et expédié par Amazon.
Un ballon vertical de 80 litres à réservoir unique
Cette offre concerne la version à réservoir unique de 80 litres, distincte du modèle à double réservoir également proposé sur la fiche. Ce chauffe-eau électrique à accumulation stocke l’eau chauffée pour la restituer lors des usages quotidiens. Sa puissance nominale est de 1 500 W et sa classe énergétique annoncée est B.
Le ballon mesure 81,2 cm de hauteur pour 45 cm de largeur et de profondeur. Ces dimensions doivent être prises en compte avec l’espace nécessaire aux raccordements et à l’entretien. La capacité adaptée dépend des habitudes du foyer : durée des douches, débit utilisé et consommation aux autres points d’eau influencent la quantité disponible.
Une programmation de la chauffe et une connexion Wi-Fi
La commande électronique permet de régler la température et de programmer le chauffage de l’eau. La connexion Wi-Fi ajoute le pilotage depuis un smartphone, tandis que la fiche mentionne également le contrôle vocal. Ces fonctions permettent d’adapter les périodes de chauffe aux horaires d’utilisation, plutôt que de modifier systématiquement les réglages sur le ballon.
Le prix de 174,99 € concerne l’appareil, hors pose. Avant un remplacement, il faut vérifier la compatibilité de l’emplacement, des fixations et des raccordements existants. Le manuel Comfee prévoit une installation et un entretien réalisés par un professionnel qualifié. Le budget final dépendra donc aussi des accessoires et des éventuelles adaptations nécessaires sur place.

articles.title: Fake Arch Linux packages push malware with root privileges
articles.text:
A threat actor uploaded malicious packages to the Arch User Repository (AUR) that impersonated two popular helper tools, yay and paru.
AUR is a community-maintained, widely-used package index for Arch Linux and derivative distributions that hosts package build scripts (PKGBUILDs) for third-party and proprietary tools, beta, or older package versions that are no longer available via the official Linux distribution channels.
The repository has recently become a target of malicious campaigns, including an attack in June in which 400 packages distributed credential-stealing malware with rootkit capabilities. Another campaign in July prompted Arch to temporarily disable package adoption.
The latest campaign was detected on October 13 and involved malicious packages uploaded by a user named “marchos1as” under typosquatted names mimicking the yay and paru command-line tools.
Also known as AUR helpers, these tools simplify software management on Arch Linux by streamlining the retrieval and installation of user-contributed packages.
A thread on the Arch Linux mailing list named "hundreds of aur packages were mass uploaded with malware" alerted users of the malicious uploads.
In minutes, community members confirmed that the packages contained legitimate upstream code combined with a malicious installation script that executed a remote shell script with root privileges.
“The package presents itself as a straightforward repackaging of the legitimate 'yay' AUR helper (same upstream URL, same source tarball), but the package name 'yyay' and the malicious install scriptlet reveal it is a trojanised impersonation designed to blend in with the real package,” AUR maintainer Andreas Reichel warned.
Another maintainer, Emiliano Gandini Outeda, listed some malicious packages that triggered an alert on his system using rules in his open-source application security tool, TrustSight.
The AUR team banned the account belonging to marchos1as and removed the malicious packages from the repository.
Reichel says that the payload delivered this way was fetched through a Wayback Machine URL that pointed to a personal repository (hellscripter/install-scripts) hosted on the Russian hosting service GitFlic.
Potential links to npm worm
A recent report from application security company SafeDep documented an npm campaign dubbed "DirtyBlanket" that fetched code from a ‘hellscripter/install-scripts’ repository on Codeberg.
The researchers found a Linux worm that deployed the CHAOS remote-access trojan disguised as a font service, which also injected a loader into AUR packages.
Furthermore, an OSV advisory on the "DirtyBlanket" activity describes the same Wayback Machine and GitFlic domain.
Despite the connections, there is currently no confirmation that the two operations are related.
Arch users who downloaded the suspicious packages should assume that their systems were compromised and take immediate remediation action.

articles.title: Anthropic built its own git replacement for AI-scale coding. But you can’t have it.
articles.text:
Anthropic built its own git replacement for AI-scale coding. But you can’t have it.
This week, Anthropic revealed it built an in-house version control system to handle exploding code merges. It says Claude was both part of the problem that caused the bottleneck and instrumental in building the solution.
When the AI company’s daily code merges hit more than 30,000 in September 2026 (up from just 2,500 in May), it realized this trend was likely to continue, and it needed an alternative to the git-based system that was beginning to falter: “Every bottleneck we remove immediately leads to a further increase in the amount of code we produce.”
Dubbed Scion, its in-house version control system has a 200x smaller infrastructure footprint in CPU and memory than its previous git-mirroring infrastructure, per Anthropic. Plus, it says CI and research jobs can now check out code two orders of magnitude faster.
That’s great news for Anthropic — but just a tease for everyone else. Even though Anthropic expects other companies to hit similar bottlenecks, it has no plans to release Scion or create a public version any time soon. For developers dealing with similar scaling issues, inspiration from Anthropic is all they’ve got for now — though it says it wants to partner with GitHub, GitLab and the open source community to bring some of Scion’s ideas to git.
Why Anthropic built Scion (and why it says git wasn’t enough)
Scion is Anthropic’s in-house version control system, which it says it built and fully migrated its monorepo to in just five months.
The project started around the same time Anthropic made Claude Mythos Preview and Claude Tag available internally. The AI company says those releases were part of the reason it needed Scion in the first place—and why it was able to build it so quickly.
“At Anthropic, coding is no longer the bottleneck to building systems or doing research,” the company wrote, citing Claude’s ability to write code at speed and scale as the reason why developer infrastructure is floundering to keep up. “The bottleneck, now, is all of the developer infrastructure built for human scale: source control, builds, and CI.”
git, Anthropic says, is no longer a match for high-volume AI coding, at least not for its enormous monorepo and unusually large volume of code changes. Scion, in contrast, can handle that scale and even reduce infrastructure overhead.
“Every bottleneck we remove immediately leads to a further increase in the amount of code we produce.”
For one, Scion delivers always-on server access, letting clients fetch data whenever needed. For clients that Anthropic says are always online, git’s assumption that they need to work offline with complete repository copies adds unnecessary work.
The Anthropic version control system also offers API-based source control, letting a CI job or tool ask questions about code history and other repository information without maintaining a local repository, à la git.
Plus, because Anthropic says Scion is horizontally scalable (i.e., its repository data is distributed across independently scalable components), it can expand capacity as needed without having to maintain hundreds of git mirrors.
Anthropic said Claude’s fast coding prowess also helped make Scion “among the most well-tested and well-defended codebases we have ever worked on,” with extensive simulations, fuzzing, and sophisticated rate limiting.
That’s just a taste of what Anthropic says Scion can do, likely attractive capabilities for other teams facing the same challenges. But if they want to get in on the Scion benefits, they’re out of luck.
It says the same scaling problem is coming for other AI-heavy teams
The juggernaut AI company may be dealing with more AI-generated code than the average team, but it predicts its story of AI coding outpacing developer infrastructure won’t be unique for long.
As written in its announcement, “Anthropic uses Claude to write software far more than almost any other company, so we’re often the first to see where tools built for human scale start to strain. Source control is just one example of this.”
The strain, it says, has exceeded the capacity of traditional developer infrastructure and Git’s original design assumptions.
Even though Anthropic expects other companies to hit similar bottlenecks, it isn’t offering Scion publicly and has made no commitment to a public version.
Source control, though, isn’t the only area facing a paradigm shift from AI coding agents, Anthropic reminds. Going forward, the company predicts small engineering teams will more often develop new systems quickly.
That’s what happened with Scion. Anthropic says a team of just seven built Scion (plus a new code review tool, Antique, and a half dozen other systems) in five months — a far cry from what it says would normally take a large-scale engineering team years of work.
Why it’s not sharing
Though Anthropic thinks other companies will face similar source control issues soon, it’s not sharing its solution.
For starters, it says token costs could be prohibitive for many companies: “Anthropic is unique in that our ability to spend tokens for internal use far exceeds what any other business would realistically want to spend.”
Scion is simply too niche to be broadly useful outside Anthropic’s work environment.
Plus, it says Scion is simply too niche to be broadly useful outside Anthropic’s work environment. Because the version control system is a significant departure from git, other companies would need a boatload of migration work to make it suitable.
For now, then, Anthropic is putting the kibosh on building a public version. It’s also clear about where it stands on Scion’s broader applicability, calling its source control system “by no means a suitable replacement for git for general use.”
So why all the talk? Because Anthropic believes Scion still has a role to play — however small — in addressing the scaling concerns that come with increasingly capable AI coding agents. By sharing its thinking, it hopes to peel back the curtain on its in-house solution so other developers can apply some of Scion’s most successful ideas to git.
For Scion-curious developers, that seems like the best they can hope for right now.

articles.title: World of Warcraft : Forever sera bientôt jouable gratuitement en bêta, mais ça sera très bref
articles.text:
L’heure est aux ultimes réglages chez Blizzard, avant le lancement général de World of Warcraft Forever, la version repensée du monde d’Azeroth de 2004, qui sortira le 4 novembre prochain. Et pour s’assurer que l’ouverture de ce « troisième » MMORPG (avec WoW Moderne et WoW Classic) se passe le mieux possible, quoi de mieux qu’un grand stress test ?
C’est justement ce que prévoit le studio américain dans les jours à venir. Le 17 septembre dernier, on pouvait lire dans une actualité officielle qu’un « server slam » était dans les cartons, à une date encore indéterminée. Mais le 14 octobre, Icy Veins, un site spécialisé dans l’actualité de WoW, a repéré un indice dans le lanceur Battle.net.
Le programme, qui permet d’installer et d’exécuter les jeux de Blizzard, a glissé l’information suivante : WoW : Forever – Stress Test, avec une ouverture annoncée pour le 19 octobre. Blizzard n’a pas encore confirmé cette date, mais ça concorderait bien avec les ultimes moments de la bêta, dont la date de fin est fixée au 21 octobre.
Un maximum de joueurs d’un coup, et c’est voulu
Le principe d’un server slam est simple. Blizzard laisse entrer trop de monde en même temps, volontairement, pour vérifier que son infrastructure tient le choc avant la sortie. De cette manière, le studio peut avoir ainsi une bonne idée de la charge que vont encaisser les serveurs et son réseau, et, si besoin, apporter les ajustements requis avant le jour J.
C’est une pratique plutôt habituelle dans le monde du jeu vidéo. Blizzard avait déjà fait le coup avec Diablo IV en mai 2023, quelques semaines avant le lancement du jeu. Et c’est aussi un bon moyen pour le studio de relancer l’engouement autour de WoW Forever et, peut-être, convaincre les indécis qui hésitent à se lancer dans l’aventure.
C’est aussi intéressant pour les joueurs et joueuses perplexes. Jusqu’ici, il fallait en effet acheter le pack épique ou la WoW Forever Collection, ou bien s’inscrire et espérer être tiré au sort pour entrer dans la bêta du jeu. Ce stress test sera donc une fenêtre gratuite pour découvrir notamment les Eolides, la nouvelle race jouable, et leur île de Zephras.

articles.title: Xpeng corrige un de ses points faibles dans ses voitures : des centaines d'applications grâce au Google Play dès 2027 — Frandroid
articles.text:
Xpeng nous avait réservé une petite surprise en plein milieu du Mondial de l’auto. Le constructeur chinois Xpeng a annoncé, dans un communiqué, que Google Play arrivera directement dans ses voitures à partir de début 2027.
Sur l’écran central, les conducteurs pourront télécharger des applications de musique, de podcasts, de vidéo, de navigation, de recharge ou de stationnement. Ils n’auront pas besoin de brancher leur smartphone. Xpeng promet des centaines d’applications adaptées à l’écran de bord, dans plus de 100 pays et régions.
La marque vend ses voitures électriques dans plusieurs pays européens, dont la France, et elle mise beaucoup sur la technologie. Avec Tesla, c’est d’ailleurs la seule marque à avoir fait essayer sa conduite autonome au Mondial de Paris.
Google Play fonctionnera sur Android Automotive OS, la version d’Android qui tourne directement dans la voiture. Android Auto, à l’inverse, se contente d’afficher sur l’écran de bord les applications du téléphone branché.
    Pour aller plus loin
Google Automotive ou Android Auto ? On vous explique la différence
            
Xpeng garde par contre son propre assistant vocal multilingue, qui servira à ouvrir et à piloter les applications téléchargées. Le constructeur n’a pas expliqué comment l’assistant communiquera avec chaque application. On ne sait pas non plus si Gemini sera disponible, comme c’est le cas chez Volvo et Renault.
Les applications se mettront à jour via Google Play, sans attendre une mise à jour complète du logiciel de la voiture. Les jeux, eux, ne seront accessibles qu’à l’arrêt.
Après les cartes Google, toute la boutique
Xpeng et Google travaillent ensemble depuis l’été. Le 16 juillet à Munich, le constructeur a lancé son SUV coupé L03 dans 65 pays et régions.
    Pour aller plus loin
J’ai essayé le nouveau Xpeng L03 : un SUV électrique abordable et à la recharge très rapide, mais j’ai quelques réserves
            
Sa navigation repose sur le Google Maps Auto SDK. Ce kit de développement permet à un constructeur de créer sa propre application de cartes avec les données et le guidage de Google.
Il n’y a pas d’offres pour le moment, découvrez :
- Tesla Model Y Propulsion (Standard)34 290,00 €Voir l’offre
- Skoda Elroq33 300,00 €Voir l’offre
- Renault Scénic E-Tech (60 kWh)36 620,00 €Voir l’offre
Xpeng s’était alors présenté comme le premier constructeur de la zone Asie-Pacifique à livrer une voiture avec ce kit. Hors de Chine, ces cartes servent aussi à ses aides à la conduite. Il en a besoin pour sa conduite autonome VLA 2.0, attendue en Europe en 2027.
« Avec Google Play, nous étendons cette approche de la navigation à l’ensemble de l’écosystème numérique », explique Xianming Liu, vice-président de Xpeng, dans le communiqué du 15 octobre.
CarPlay et Android Auto gardent leur place
Avec CarPlay et Android Auto, tout passe par le smartphone, qui affiche ses applications sur l’écran de la voiture. Xpeng ne les abandonne pas pour autant. Ses G6 et G9 vendus en Europe proposent CarPlay et Android Auto de série depuis leur renouvellement en 2025. Le communiqué de Xpeng parle d’ailleurs d’un téléphone « optionnel ».
Volvo et Polestar, deux marques qui appartiennent au groupe chinois Geely, utilisent Google depuis plus longtemps. La Polestar 2 a été en 2020 la première voiture vendue avec Google intégré. Volvo a d’ailleurs déployé Gemini sur la Volvo EX30, également sous Google Automotive.
En Europe, les constructeurs chinois mettent souvent en avant les caractéristiques techniques, comme BYD avec l’Atto 8 et ses 775 ch. BYD a également adopté le système Google avec le Google Play et ses applications.
Xpeng n’a pas encore dit quels modèles seront concernés ni à quelle date dans chaque pays. Ces informations viendront plus tard. Tout comme le choix d’applications qui pourra aussi changer selon le modèle et les règles de sécurité.
On ne sait pas non plus si les voitures déjà vendues, ou son SUV G9L, plus grand qu’un Range Rover, y auront droit.
