articles.title: WhatsApp ouvre ses appels aux invités sans compte, avec Meet et Teams en ligne de mire
articles.text:
La messagerie de Meta lance les appels en mode invité. N'importe qui peut rejoindre un appel WhatsApp depuis un navigateur, sans compte et sans limite de durée. Des intégrations calendrier arriveront d'ici la fin de l'année.
Jusqu'ici, il fallait un compte WhatsApp, donc un numéro de téléphone, pour participer à un appel. Ce n'est plus le cas. La messagerie autorise désormais les personnes extérieures à rejoindre une conversation depuis un simple lien.
Un invité peut rejoindre un appel, mais pas le lancer
Le principe est simple. Depuis l'onglet Appels de WhatsApp, il est possible de toucher l'icône +, de créer un lien d'appel puis de l'envoyer à une personne. Côté destinataire, rien à installer. Il ouvre le lien dans le navigateur de son ordinateur, tape son nom et attend son admission. Ces liens fonctionnent aussi bien en individuel qu'en groupe, dans la limite de 32 participants. Oui, on l'a compris, WhatsApp souhaite désormais s'attaquer à Meet ou Teams.
Rien de vraiment très nouveau sous le soleil et Apple propose depuis longtemps une option similaire sur FaceTime, avec la possibilité de rejoindre un appel sans compte ni appareil de la marque. D'ailleurs WhatsApp en reprend aussi les limites puisqu'un invité ne peut pas démarrer un appel, il répond seulement aux invitations. Ce dernier passe par une salle d'attente avant d'être validé par l'organisateur, lequel peut d'ailleurs aussi l'exclure à tout moment. Soulignons au passage que l'invité ne voit pas les numéros de téléphone des autres participants. Il ne peut pas non plus écrire de messages ni ajouter d'autres participants.
Le statut d'invité permet d'accéder aux fonctions principales comme le partage d'écran, les réactions emoji, ou les pouces et mains levés pour demander la parole. Les appels restent gratuits, chiffrés de bout en bout, sans plafond de durée.
- Chiffrement de bout en bout.
- Appels audio et vidéo gratuits.
- Compatibilité multiplateforme.
WhatsApp bientôt Google Agenda et Outlook
Forcément cela ouvre quelques perspectives pour WhatsApp avec un autre chantier : un plugin pour calendrier, promis pour plus tard dans l'année. Concrètement, une fois le module installé et connecté à son compte, l'utilisateur peut ajouter un lien d'appel WhatsApp à une invitation Google Agenda ou Outlook. Chaque personne invitée pourra alors rejoindre la réunion, avec ou sans compte.
Fin juillet, la filiale de Meta lançait les appels audio et vidéo sur WhatsApp Web, avec transfert d'appel entre appareils, salle d'attente et contrôles pour les appels de groupe. L'équipe a aussi lancé les identifiants pour masquer le numéro de téléphone, puis ouvert l'inscription depuis iPad et planche aussi sur la programmation différée de messages.

articles.title: OPINION: Are we attracting talent to live in Europe or to build here? | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Europe is an attractive place to live because of its high quality of life, job opportunities, and stability. However, attracting people to live here for the lifestyle is different from attracting talent and companies to move here and build.
The latter entails companies bringing teams with them, hiring locally, and establishing R&D that fosters an entrepreneurial ecosystem that benefits the continent as a whole. This is an area that Europe isn’t doing so well in, especially compared to the US.
The trend shows that approximately 10% of EU scale-ups relocate abroad, with around 85% moving to the United States. Furthermore, between 2008-2021, nearly 30% of unicorns moved their headquarters abroad (again, mostly to the US).
Despite this, the narrative has recently been disrupted by Langdock, a Berlin-based AI startup. They moved their parent company from the US to Germany and aim to become a “European hyperscaler”.
This illustrates that the phenomenon of startups relocating to the US from Europe isn’t set in stone. Europe can attract and retain its talent. This article explores different cases of that and explores how to get teams to build here rather than just use Europe as a stepping stone.
The US or Europe: How do startups choose?
It is imperative to understand Europe’s main competitor in order to learn where more can be done. The US isn’t just where most European startups relocate, it also captures 85% of startups worldwide. If there’s a US VC, chances are the startup will relocate there. In fact, a Delaware parent company, a US-based legal entity that owns and controls the startup’s operations, including those in Europe, is frequently a precondition US venture funds set before they’ll invest.
Then comes the fact that the US grants access to a single market compared to Europe’s 27 member states. Buyers spread across European jurisdictions take longer to close than buyers spread across US states operating under one framework. This forces European startups to cross borders earlier than many of their US counterparts (something the EU. Inc Framework is working to address). Still, 97% moves are partial exits, with companies retaining operations in their home country. Only around three-quarters of relocating CEOs physically move to the new destination.
The capital gap between Europe and the US cannot be ignored either. Contrary to popular sentiment that the US is more forgiving towards founders whose previous enterprises have failed and that they have more appetite for risk, the reality is that there is more capital to go around to fund newer attempts (€930 billion versus €150 billion in the EU, around sixfold to be precise). European investors are understandably more cautious due to this.
Having prefaced the US’s attraction for startups, how do cases like Langdock exist?
Langdock’s move was commercial. Their customers’ legal teams kept flagging the US parent company as a data-risk exposure despite the fact that it had no staff, servers, or systems access. The US Cloud Act in particular was a great cause of concern.
80% of the company was owned by founders and employees living in the EU, and the teams, coupled with approximately 13,000 client organisations, were being served from Germany.
In short, everything was already based in Europe, but the parent company was created to initially attract US investors and benefit from the start-up accelerator Y Combinator.
What Europe has been doing and what it should do instead
Europe has acted as a magnet for talent to study, train, and build. However, its retention of that same talent has proven to be less successful, as discussed previously. The focus has mostly been on easing restrictions that bring talent into the country, namely by putting in special visa schemes. That is not to say that they haven’t been successful at that.
Germany issued 72% of the EU’s Blue Cards in 2024, which fast-tracks skilled workers residing in the EU. France’s Tech Visa provides a simplified residence route for startup employees, and 1200 companies have utilised it for international recruitment since the program was launched. Portugal’s Digital Nomad Visa (D8) was launched in 2022 to attract remote workers without needing a Portuguese employer or company. It has approved 7,664 applications since then.
But talent attraction is not only about how many people move to Europe. It makes a positive impact only when people and companies build teams, hire locally, create R&D capacity, and stay long enough to strengthen the ecosystem. While founders and talented people moving for lifestyle reasons is good, it is not the same as a company bringing sales teams, engineering, and creating jobs in the area. The good part is that there are already some examples where the latter is happening.
Unicorn Factory Lisbon is one such example. Launched in 2022, has attracted 82 technology companies to set up offices in the city, creating more than 16,000 jobs.
Such clusters are important because their alumni can go on to become new founders, as seen in the case of Talkdesk and OutSystems alumni, who founded Speak, Cleverly.ai, and Screenloop.
Barcelona serves as a stronger example where 6 unicorns are headquartered in the city, and create €36 billion in combined enterprise value by locally-based companies. Whether Lisbon can transform from simply attracting branches and teams to headquarters remains to be seen.
Estonia has provided another innovative way of attracting companies. By providing individual e-residencies, it allows global entrepreneurs to register a business online, access the EU market, and enjoy a 0% corporate tax rate on reinvested and retained profits. This has resulted in dividends amounting to €124.9 million for the country.
The Next Stage for Europe’s Talent
Europe has proven that it is quite capable of attracting talent, but it has yet to stem the loss of its talent to other countries, especially the US. Different symptoms have to be addressed differently.
For example, incentivising companies to open their branches and headquarters on the continent. Providing a common framework for countries to operate with. The issues with capital cannot be ignored. Europe’s pension funds can compensate for the discrepancy to an extent. Europe has proven its innovativeness, but it is time to build it.

This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
Pig kidneys that were “frozen” for a year have been brought back to life
Pig kidneys that were cooled to -150 °C and stored in a freezer for months have been successfully rewarmed and shown to work again for the first time, say scientists.
The kidneys, which are similar in size to human ones, were left in a glass-like state, in one case for over a year. Once they had been rewarmed, tested in machines, and transplanted into pigs, the kidneys regained their color and made urine—key signs they were working.
The results are a big milestone. But the team still needs to establish whether the approach could work for humans.
Dissect what the breakthrough means for organ transplantation.
—Jessica Hamzelou
How much more can nuclear power plants give?
In this age of rising electricity demand, people are trying to squeeze every last bit of power out of every power plant. Over the past few weeks, there’s been big news about the nuclear industry trying to do just that.
Constellation, the largest nuclear operator in the US, announced plans to add nearly a gigawatt of new capacity across 11 existing nuclear reactors at six plants. On October 5, the Department of Energy awarded Vistra a $4.2 billion loan to upgrade three plants.
Pushing existing reactors to produce more could quickly provide more clean power for data centers. But just how much additional power can we count on?
—Casey Crownhart
This story is from The Checkup, our weekly climate and energy tech newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Thursday.

The company has more than 150 electric buses on the road in Kenya and Rwanda, with a reservation list of 1,200 customers. Now it’s targeting another major source of pollution on the roads: trucks.

articles.title: Google Play now lets you install your own vibe-coded apps without publishing them
articles.text:
First look: Android users who build apps in AI Studio can now install them through Google Play without making them publicly available or connecting their phones to a computer. The feature makes it easier to turn an AI coding project into a native app for everyday use. It also gives creators room to test their work before deciding whether it belongs on the public store.
Google announced the feature this week for US users. Creators can use a standard Google account, and their apps stay private. They will not appear in Play's search results or public listings, and only the creator can access them at launch.
The update makes AI-built apps easier to install. Building an Android app doesn't automatically put it on your phone. Google added Android app creation to AI Studio in May, but users could still need a computer to install their apps. Publishing on Google Play was another option, but it made the apps available to everyone. Those limitations pushed many users toward creating web apps rather than native Android apps.
Now, creators can use Play to install their apps without making them publicly available. The update changes distribution, not the app-building tools: AI Studio creates the software, while Google Play provides a way to run it on an Android device. It also lets creators start using their apps without first setting up a professional developer account.
Google says the apps will remain "secure, private, and separate from the public store catalog." They must still comply with Google Play's existing policies. The change also does not make AI-generated apps automatically eligible for public distribution.
Google plans to add small-group sharing in the coming months. Creators will then be able to give friends and family access to their apps without putting them in the public catalog.
The company also plans to provide a route from personal apps to public releases. Creators who want broader distribution will need to move to a professional developer account and complete the required reviews.
The result is a more gradual route from personal Android projects to public releases. Users can build and run an app for themselves, then share it with a limited group, and eventually pursue a public release if they choose. The first step is now available through Play. Small-group sharing will arrive later, while public releases will require developers to meet Google's existing publishing requirements.

articles.title: UK Legal Aid Agency Hack Scope Widens After Forensic Review
articles.text:
The UK’s Legal Aid Agency (LAA) has discovered that records dating back to 1978 were compromised in an April 2025 data breach.
In May last year, the UK Ministry of Justice agency said hackers had accessed and exfiltrated the personal information of individuals who applied for legal aid, but did not share the full scope of the incident.
An incident update published this week reveals that most of the compromised records are related to applications, claims, and payments submitted between 2007 and 2025.
However, forensic investigators confirmed that approximately 250,000 compromised records predate 2007.
“The overwhelming majority of these are from the 1990s and 2000s, with only a fractionally small number dating from before 1990. The earliest record currently verified dates from 1978,” the update reads.
Compromised data associated with legal aid applicants and recipients may include names, addresses, dates of birth, National Insurance Numbers, postcodes, case reference numbers, answers entered into LAA’s Client and Cost Management System (CCMS), phone numbers, and other types of information.
The hackers also exfiltrated data pertaining to legal aid practitioners who interacted with LAA, including contracts, schedules, office locations, payment details, and user account credentials.
Other affected individuals include judges, solicitors, advocates, other parties in civil certificated proceedings, and individuals who managed pay point locations.
“Our improved cyber capabilities have also identified that data relating to probation service users was also accessed. The data exfiltrated by the attackers includes some names, dates of birth, nationalities, and case reference numbers for a relatively small number of offenders who were being actively managed by Probation Services between 2010 and 2017,” LAA says.
According to the agency, its investigation into the incident took a long time because the attack involved multiple systems and significant volumes of information, most of which was unstructured, fragmented, or incomplete data.
“This has made analyzing the data complex. Therefore, since the incident, specialist technical and data teams have undertaken extensive work to understand what information the attackers accessed and exfiltrated,” the agency said.
LAA also underlined that it has no evidence that the stolen information has been released publicly or sold.

articles.title: Server-Side DPoP and Token Exchange in Spring Security 7
articles.text:
Key Takeaways
- Spring Authorization Server now lives inside Spring Security 7 under the same Maven coordinates, so moving off 1.5.x is a version bump, rather than an artifact swap.
- Demonstrating Proof of Possession (DPoP) (RFC 9449) already worked end-to-end on Spring Security 6.5 with Spring Authorization Server 1.5. The real news on the 7.1 line is that resource-server verification is no longer automatic, so an app that relied on the old auto-applied behavior silently stops enforcing DPoP after upgrading until it adds the new .dPoP() call.
- Spring binds the JWK thumbprint via cnf.jkt and the refresh token for public clients on its own, leaving two real decisions to the identity provider: the nonce policy and whether the jti replay cache, which defaults to an in-memory, single-node implementation, needs to be swapped for a distributed one across a cluster.
- RFC 8693 Token Exchange turns the bespoke "service-account swap" many identity providers (IdPs) still carry into a standard grant, with subject_token and actor_token semantics and an `act` claim that records the delegation chain.
- The two features are more useful together than apart, because a DPoP-bound subject token exchanged for a narrowed, audience-restricted downstream token is the pattern service-to-service and agentic architectures keep reaching for, but the combined pattern is only as safe as the exchange policy and token customizer you write.
Your in-house identity provider has run on Spring Authorization Server 1.x for two years. The upgrade to Spring Boot 4 looks routine on paper. You bump the Bill of Materials (BOM), fix the deprecations, and ship it. Then you open the migration guide and find that the authorization server you depend on is no longer a separate project. It moved into Spring Security 7.0 while you were on the 1.x line. On the current 7.1 line, paired with Spring Boot 4.1, the two OAuth 2.1 features you have been deferring, sender-constrained tokens and a real delegation grant, are sitting in the same module, Spring General availability (GA) release, waiting to be switched on.
This is the part of the Spring Boot 4 migration that the migration guides skip. They cover Jackson 3, the lambda DSL, and the package relocations, then stop at OAuth 2.0. The auth-layer payoff is DPoP (RFC 9449) and Token Exchange (RFC 8693), both are production-ready in official components for the first time, which is where the upgrade actually earns its keep for anyone running their own IdP. This article is the server-side walk-through, covering what has been consolidated, what changes when you turn DPoP on, what an RFC 8693 exchange looks like end-to-end, and why the two features are worth running together. It assumes you already run an OAuth 2.0 / OIDC server and know the protocol. It does not re-explain OAuth from scratch.
What Spring Boot 4 Consolidated
Spring's November 2025 release train shipped in three steps: Spring Framework 7.0 on November 13, Spring Security 7.0 on November 17, and Spring Boot 4.0 on November 20. The release notes lead with modularization, JSpecify null-safety, API versioning, and the Jackson 3 baseline. The OAuth server story sits underneath these modules The changes had been announced two months earlier.
On September 11, 2025, the Spring team announced that Spring Authorization Server, a standalone project since 2020 and GA since November 2022, was moving into Spring Security 7.0. The standalone 1.5.x branch is the last generation with new development happening inside Spring Security. Spring Security shipped 7.1.0 in June 2026, paired with Spring Boot 4.1, then 7.1.1 in August 2026, so the current coordinates are org.springframework.security:spring-security-oauth2-authorization-server:7.1.1. The consolidation itself happened at 7.0. The examples here target 7.1.1 specifically, because that is where both version-specific details this article covers land: the resource-server .dPoP() opt-in (new in 7.1.0) and the pluggable jti replay cache, which were new in 7.1.1 Each is called out where it appears. For a team that has been treating "the authorization server" as a separate dependency with its own release cadence, the consolidation is the headline. There is now one security module, one version, and one set of release notes to track.
There is a subtlety here worth getting right, because it is the single most common thing people get wrong about this migration. The Maven coordinates did not change. The standalone project was already published under org.springframework.security:spring-security-oauth2-authorization-server and the merged module in Spring Security 7 uses the same groupId and artifactId. Only the version moved from the 1.5.x line onto the Spring Security version line (7.0.x, now 7.1.x). If you read somewhere that you need to rename a spring-authorization-server artifact, that artifact never existed. One genuine rename does apply if you pull the authorization server in through the Boot starter rather than the library directly. In Boot 4, the starter gained a security- prefix, so spring-boot-starter-oauth2-authorization-server is deprecated in favor of spring-boot-starter-security-oauth2-authorization-server with both still published through 4.1.1. Beyond that, the migration is a version bump plus the same package relocations. Jackson moves every Spring Security 7 consumer absorbs. It is not a coordinate swap.
Xml
<!-- Before: standalone Spring Authorization Server on the 1.5.x line -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.security</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-security-oauth2-authorization-server</artifactId>
    <version>1.5.7</version>
</dependency>
<!-- After: same coordinates, version tracks Spring Security (current line) -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.security</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-security-oauth2-authorization-server</artifactId>
    <version>7.1.1</version>
</dependency>
                                    By moving to the 7.x line you inherit a module where DPoP issuance, refresh-token DPoP binding, and Token Exchange already coexist with the resource-server DPoP support that reached GA in Spring Security 6.5. Before this consolidation, getting all of those in one place required pinning a specific standalone authorization server version to a specific Spring Security version and hoping the matrix lined up. Now it is one version number.
Figure 1. The Spring Boot 4 consolidation. (Source: created by author.)
As shown in Figure 1, the standalone Spring Authorization Server (1.5.x, last generation) folds into the Spring Security 7.x line under the same Maven coordinates, consolidating DPoP and Token Exchange into a single module.
The Migration Tax, Paid Once
Before any of the new features, Spring Security 7 charges a baseline migration tax that is mostly not OAuth-specific: and() is gone from the HttpSecurity builder, Jackson 3 replaces Jackson 2, and a couple of JSON Web Token (JWT)-decoder defaults change. Spring's own migration guide and its OAuth 2.0-specific page walk through the mechanics; the concrete steps are items 2 through 4 in the playbook below.
The guide does not spell out two things, because they are specific to running an authorization server rather than any Spring Security app. First, the typ header change is not a loosening of validation. Rather, it is Spring finally wiring in automatically what the 6.5 preparation steps asked you to add by hand: validateTypes(false) turning off Nimbus's own typ check so you could register JwtTypeValidator.jwt() yourself and in 7.0 both halves of that dance happen for you. The actual audit point is narrower than "will my tokens still validate?". JwtTypeValidator.jwt() requires typ to be JWT or absent, so any token your server issues or accepts with a different typ, such as the RFC 9068 at+jwt access-token type, now fails validation by default unless you register a validator that allows it. Second, if you persist OAuth2Authorization objects to a database with Spring's Jackson modules, that registration has to move from the Jackson 2 SecurityJackson2Modules to the Jackson 3 SecurityJacksonModules in the new org.springframework.security.jackson package, or deserialization of previously persisted authorization state will break.
A team that is already up to date with Spring Security 6.5 deprecations can plan the baseline migration as roughly a one-sprint effort before touching any new OAuth 2.1 features. A team several versions behind should treat the baseline migration and the feature adoption as two separate efforts.
DPoP, End-to-End
DPoP (RFC 9449) constrains an access token to a key the client holds. The client generates an asymmetric key pair and, on each request, signs a short-lived proof JWT. The authorization server validates that proof at the token endpoint and binds the issued access token to the proof's public key. The resource server then refuses to honor the token unless it arrives with a fresh proof from the same key. A stolen token is inert without the private key. That is the whole point and it is the subject of this article's browser-side companion, which addresses the hard problem of where a browser can safely keep that key. Here the concern is the other end of the wire, namely what the server does when the proof arrives.
The proof itself is specified in RFC 9449 §4.2. The header carries typ: dpop+jwt, an asymmetric alg, and the client's public key inline as a jwk. The payload binds the proof to the request with htm (HTTP method), htu (target URI, query and fragment stripped), iat, and a unique jti. When the proof accompanies an access token to a resource server, it also carries the base64url SHA-256 hash of that token.
Figure 2. The DPoP loop, server side. The authorization server binds the token to the client's key, and the resource server refuses it without a matching proof. (Source: created by author.)
Issuance: Two Decisions the Defaults Leave to You
On the authorization-server side, Spring wires the proof-verification machinery for you. DPoPProofVerifier and the supporting DPoPProofJwtDecoderFactory perform the RFC 9449 §4.3 checks: a well-formed JWT, a typ of dpop+jwt, a non-none asymmetric alg, a signature that verifies against the embedded jwk, and htm/htu matching the token request. Two things that look like decisions aren't. What is actually left to you is building the nonce challenge yourself (if you want it at all) and the reach of the replay cache.
The cnf.jkt binding is handled for you. The access token must carry a cnf claim whose jkt member is the base64url-encoded JWK SHA-256 Thumbprint (RFC 7638) of the proof key. Spring populates this key automatically when DPoP is in play; the only thing to watch for is a token customizer that overwrites cnf by accident. The resource server later compares against the thumbprint, not the public key and not a certificate hash.
JSON
{
  "sub": "service-a",
  "aud": "https://orders.internal",
  "cnf": {
    "jkt": "0ZcOCORZNYy-DWpqq30jZyJGHTN0d2HglBV3uiguA4I"
  }
}
First, consider the nonce challenge, which Spring does not implement at all. RFC 9449 §8 lets the authorization server demand a server-chosen nonce inside the proof, which stops a client from pre-minting proofs; the resource server has the parallel mechanism in §9. When a server requires a nonce the client did not supply, it answers with error: use_dpop_nonce and a DPoP-Nonce response header, 400 at the authorization server, and 401 at the resource server. As of Spring Security 7.1.1, none of that exists in Spring's DPoP code on either side: no issuance of a DPoP-Nonce header, no handling of use_dpop_nonce, and no validator checking the proof's optional nonce claim. The nonce challenge is a SHOULD in the RFC, not a MUST, which is presumably why it has shipped without one, but if your threat model needs it, you are building the entire mechanism yourself: issuing nonces, returning the challenge response, storing what you issued, and validating the claim against it.
Also Handled for You: Refresh-Token Binding for Public Clients
RFC 9449 §5 requires that when a public client presents a DPoP proof at the token endpoint, the refresh token it receives is bound to that key, and later refreshes must prove the same key. Spring Authorization Server added this key automatically in the 1.5.0-RC1 milestone (April 2025) and carried it into the 7.x line; there is no switch to flip. Confidential clients lean on their existing client-credential binding instead, so this approach matters most for single-page apps (SPAs) and native apps.
Second, there is the replay cache. RFC 9449 §11.1 requires rejecting a proof whose jti has already been seen, within an acceptable time window. On Spring Security 7.0.x and 7.1.0, that check was hard-coded: a fixed, thousand-entry in-memory cache buried inside DPoPProofJwtDecoderFactory, with no way to swap it out. Since Spring Security 6.5.12 / 7.1.1, it is the pluggable DPoPProofReplayValidator, wired by default with its own InMemoryCache (one hundred thousand entries, capped per key). That default implementation's own Javadoc says plainly that it "only works in a single-node setup" and names Redis and Hazelcast as the kind of distributed Cache a clustered deployment needs to supply instead.
Verification Is Now Stock at the Resource Server
The resource-server side is where Spring 7 removes the most custom code. DPoP-bound access-token verification arrived through the Spring Security 6.5.0 milestones and went GA in 6.5.0 (May 2025). One version detail matters here. In Spring Security 7.0 that support was applied automatically whenever the DPoP classes were on the classpath, with no DSL hook. Spring Security 7.1 added an explicit dPoP(Customizer) method to the resource-server DSL (@since 7.1), making support opt-in and customizable; in 7.1, you call .dPoP() to enable it. This is a genuine behavioral change on upgrade, not just a new option: an application that relied on the auto-applied verification in 6.5 or 7.0, including one built entirely on Spring Boot's default resource-server autoconfiguration, which never called the new hook either, silently stops enforcing DPoP the moment it moves to 7.1 until .dPoP() is added explicitly. A DPoP-bound token arrives under the DPoP authentication scheme, not Bearer. Sending it as Bearer is a common and incorrect shortcut. Spring's DPoPAuthenticationProvider does the work.
One naming trap is worth flagging, because it will bite during code review. The resource-server provider is DPoPAuthenticationProvider, with no OAuth2 prefix, unlike OAuth2TokenExchangeAuthenticationProvider in the next section. The converter and provider also live in different packages. DPoPAuthenticationConverter sits in ...resource.web.authentication, while DPoPAuthenticationProvider and DPoPAuthenticationToken sit in ...resource.authentication, without the web.
Java
// Resource server: accept DPoP-bound access tokens.
@Bean
public SecurityFilterChain resourceServer(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
    http
        .authorizeHttpRequests(authorize -> authorize.anyRequest().authenticated())
        .oauth2ResourceServer(oauth2 -> oauth2
            .jwt(Customizer.withDefaults())   // validates the access token
            .dPoP(Customizer.withDefaults())  // validates the proof: signature, htm/htu, ath, cnf.jkt
        );
    return http.build();
}
With .dPoP() configured, the resource server verifies the proof signature, confirms htm/htu against the incoming request, checks that the proof's path equals the hash of the presented token, and confirms the proof key's thumbprint equals the token's cnf.jkt. Before Spring Security 6.5 this was hand-written filter code. Now it is one line in the DSL.
Token Exchange Without the Bespoke Plumbing
Most in-house IdPs carry some version of "service-account swap". Service A needs to call service B on behalf of a user, so it reaches for a second set of credentials, mints a fresh token through a side channel, or passes the user's own token downstream and hopes the audience checks are lenient. RFC 8693 replaces that approach with a standard grant.
Token Exchange landed in Spring Authorization Server 1.3.0-M3 (March 2024) and is in the 7.x module. The grant type is urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange. The request includes a subject_token, the token representing the party on whose behalf the call is made, and an optional actor_token representing the party acting, along with the audience, resource, and scope the caller wants on the way out.
Http
POST /oauth2/token HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
DPoP: eyJ...                     # the edge service's proof, so the issued token re-binds to its key
grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange
&subject_token=eyJ...            # the incoming user token, on whose behalf the call is made
&subject_token_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:access_token
&actor_token=eyJ...              # the edge service's own token; this is what produces the act claim
&actor_token_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:access_token
&audience=https://orders.internal
&scope=orders:read
The exchange matters most for the two semantics that RFC 8693 §1.1 distinguishes. Impersonation issues a token that appears to be the subject and the actor disappears. Delegation preserves both identities, the issued token carries the subject and an act (actor) claim identifying who is acting. Which one you get is decided by a single parameter. Send only a subject_token and Spring's OAuth2TokenExchangeAuthenticationProvider issues an impersonation token with no act claim. Send an actor_token alongside it and the provider builds a delegation token, deriving the act claim from the actor_token rather than from the authenticated client. For anything you will need to audit later and for service-to-service calls, delegation is exactly what you want.
RFC 8693 §4.1 represents a multi-hop chain by nesting act claims, with the outermost being the current actor and each nested one a prior actor. The nested entries come from the subject token. If the gateway's earlier exchange already left an act claim on the token the edge service now presents as its subject_token, Spring carries that prior actor through as the nested entry. So in this example, edge-service, the actor token's owner, becomes the current actor, and gateway-service is nested beneath it as the earlier one.
JSON
{
  "sub": "user-123",
  "aud": "https://orders.internal",
  "scope": "orders:read",
  "act": {
    "sub": "edge-service",
    "act": {
      "sub": "gateway-service"
    }
  }
}
On the Spring side, the grant is handled by the OAuth2TokenExchangeAuthenticationProvider, which is registered through the authorization-server configurer. The grant is not enabled by default per client. The calling client's RegisteredClient must declare it, or the provider rejects the request with unsupported_grant_type.
Java
RegisteredClient.withId(UUID.randomUUID().toString())
    .clientId("edge-service")
    // ... client authentication, scopes ...
    .authorizationGrantType(AuthorizationGrantType.TOKEN_EXCHANGE)
    .build();
The act claim, itself, is the framework's job, built from the actor token as described above, so you do not assemble it by hand. What is left to you is narrowing the issued token by dropping scopes or switching the audience, which is the job of an OAuth2TokenCustomizer<JwtEncodingContext> bean, the same hook you would use for any claim shaping.
Java
@Bean
public OAuth2TokenCustomizer<JwtEncodingContext> tokenCustomizer() {
    return context -> {
        if (AuthorizationGrantType.TOKEN_EXCHANGE.equals(
                context.getAuthorizationGrantType())) {
            // Narrow the audience and trim scopes on the exchanged token.
            context.getClaims().audience(List.of("https://orders.internal"));
            context.getClaims().claim("scope", "orders:read");
        }
    };
}
One principle is worth holding on to. The exchange is where you reduce authority, so never widen it. A token-exchange endpoint that can be leveraged to access a broader scope than the subject token holds is a privilege-escalation bug, not a feature.
The Pattern That Needs Both DPoP and Token Exchange
The two features are each useful alone. Composed, they cover a problem neither closes by itself: propagating constrained authority across a chain of services without handing every hop a bearer token it could replay.
Picture an edge service that receives a DPoP-bound access token from a client. It needs to call an orders service on the user's behalf, but it should not forward the user's token wholesale. That token's audience is the edge and forwarding a bearer copy gives the orders service something it can, in turn, replay anywhere. Instead, the edge service performs a token exchange. It presents the user's token as the subject_token, its own token as the actor_token, and a DPoP proof on the exchange request, then asks for a token scoped to orders:read, audience https://orders.internal. The authorization server issues a narrowed token, records the edge service in the act claim from that actor token, and, because the edge sent a proof, binds the new token to the edge service's own key through cnf.jkt.
Figure 3. DPoP-bound token exchanged for a narrowed, re-bound downstream token. Scope shrinks, audience switches, the actor is recorded, and each hop is sender-constrained. (Source: created by author.)
The result is concrete. The orders service receives a token it can verify is sender-constrained to the caller it is actually talking to, scoped to exactly what that call needs, with an audit trail of who delegated to whom. No hop holds a replayable credential for a service it does not call. This is the shape that modern service meshes and agentic systems keep reinventing badly with ad hoc header passing. RFC 8693 plus RFC 9449 are the standards-track versions and Spring Security 7 is the first official Spring surface where both halves ship together.
There is a real caveat. The narrowing is yours to enforce. Spring gives you the grant and the customizer hook, but it does not stop you from writing an exchange that widens scope or skips the audience switch. The security of the pattern lives in the OAuth2TokenCustomizer you write. That code deserves its own tests.
A Migration Playbook
Two starting points cover most teams. The first is Greenfield on Spring Boot 4.1. A new IdP starts on the 7.x module with DPoP and Token Exchange available from day one. The work is configuration, not migration: register clients, decide your nonce policy, write the narrowing customizer, and turn on .dPoP() at every resource server. Treat the OAuth2TokenCustomizer as security-critical code from the first commit.
The second starting point is an existing standalone Authorization Server 1.5.x. This is a version bump on coordinates you already use, not a re-platforming. The sequence:
- Move to the Spring Boot 4.1 / Spring Security 7.1 BOM. Bump spring-security-oauth2-authorization-server from 1.5.x to 7.1.x, same groupId and artifactId.
- Convert any remaining and()-style filter chains to the lambda DSL.
- Audit JwtDecoder configuration for validateTypes(false) and confirm the new JwtTypeValidator defaults accept your tokens.
- Update Jackson module registration where you persist authorization state, so SecurityJackson2Modules becomes SecurityJacksonModules.
- Only then, as a separate change, enable DPoP for new client registrations and stand up the token-exchange grant, after the baseline migration is green.
The production rollout has its own decisions. The decisions that turn a feature flag into a deployment. Keep the issuer URL stable across the cutover. Advertise DPoP and the token-exchange grant in the authorization-server metadata so clients can discover them. Roll out resource-server .dPoP() support before you start issuing DPoP-bound tokens, so the verifier is ready when the first bound token arrives. Plan a dual-stack window in which bearer and DPoP-bound tokens coexist as clients migrate. Enable DPoP per client registration rather than globally, so the existing fleet keeps working while new registrations opt in.
The metadata is what lets clients discover all of this functionality. The authorization server's /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server document should advertise both capabilities: the DPoP signing algorithms it accepts and the token-exchange grant in its grant-type list.
JSON
{
  "issuer": "https://idp.internal",
  "grant_types_supported": [
    "authorization_code",
    "refresh_token",
    "urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange"
  ],
  "dpop_signing_alg_values_supported": ["ES256", "RS256"]
}
What Comes Next
Watch the nonce gap specifically. The RFC marks it a SHOULD, not a MUST, and there is no open feature request for it in Spring Security's issue tracker as of this writing, so an identity provider that wants it is building it alone and should plan for that rather than wait on a future release.
The more durable trend sits a level above this one release. Multi-hop service calls and increasingly chains of autonomous agents acting across trust boundaries need both proof of key possession and an audited, narrowing delegation chain, not just a bearer token and a scope check. RFC 8693's nested `act` claim already models that chain. As that architecture spreads, the pairing this article covers, DPoP binding plus token exchange, looks less like a Spring Security 7 feature pairing and more like a default expectation for identity providers generally.
References
- RFC 9449, OAuth 2.0 Demonstrating Proof of Possession (DPoP), IETF, September 2023.
- RFC 8693, OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange, IETF, January 2020.
- RFC 7638, JSON Web Key (JWK) Thumbprint, IETF, September 2015.
- "Spring Authorization Server is moving to Spring Security", Spring blog, September 11, 2025.
- "Spring Framework 7.0 General Availability", Spring blog, November 13, 2025.
- "Spring Boot 4.0.0 available now", Spring blog, November 20, 2025.
- Spring Security 7.0.0 release, GitHub, November 17, 2025.
- Spring Security Reference, OAuth 2.0 DPoP-bound Access Tokens.
- Spring Security issue #16940 / PR #17202, "Add support dpop customization" (dPoP(Customizer), @since 7.1).
- "The DPoP Storage Paradox: Why Browser-Based Proof-of-Possession Remains an Unsolved Problem", InfoQ, April 2026 (companion article).

articles.title: ChatGPT can peek at your Chrome tabs now
articles.text:
OpenAI’s ChatGPT Atlas browser is gone, but now ChatGPT’s Google Chrome extension is getting some upgrades that allow it to use the browser tabs you already have open. With the extension installed, OpenAI says ChatGPT can now view your browser tabs when you tag Chrome in ChatGPT’s web or desktop app, posting a demo video showing someone asking ChatGPT to compare the three tabs they have open with sofas they’re considering.
ChatGPT can peek at your Chrome tabs now
With the ChatGPT extension installed, it can pull information from your open tabs or bring the AI bot into the sidebar.
Here are some of the sample queries OpenAI listed for using the upgraded add-on:
- Use the details in this event brief to fill out the registration form, and stop before submitting.
- Put the vendors in these tabs into my comparison sheet, with pricing, key features, and source links.
- Look at all the tabs I have open and compare the contractor services. Then draft an email to the one that fits my home renovation.
- Fill out the form I have open in @chrome ahead of seeing my new dentist. Also, can you add the appointment to my work and personal calendar.
It’s also updated ChatGPT in the sidebar, with “the full power of ChatGPT” and your entire conversation history in Chat or Work to use without leaving the page you’re viewing. It also enables ChatGPT Work to “control” your Chrome tabs for tasks like “sending messages, filling out forms, or downloading files,” similar to Google’s Gemini-powered “auto browse” feature, as well as organize or group open tabs.

articles.title: Why Open-Weight AI Matters
articles.text:
Proprietary models still hold the edge, but open-weight models add more flexibility for deploying AI.
Key Takeaways:
Open-weight AI models are creating new challenges for chip architects as rapidly changing workloads strain memory, interconnects, and compute flexibility.
The focus is no longer just peak TOPS. The checklist has grown to include the best way to feed memory-hungry models, sustain performance across long-context and multi-agent inference, support rapidly changing numeric formats and sparse computation, and isolate models, data, and tools as part of the security boundary. Model architectures can change in weeks while silicon takes years, so the winners will build adaptable hardware-software platforms, rather than accelerators optimized for a benchmark that may be obsolete before tape-out.
Massive data centers are not a prerequisite for AI-driven scientific advances. Science has different infrastructure needs from consumer AI platforms serving millions of users. Open-weight AI models — whose trained parameters are publicly available — can be deployed locally, potentially widening access, improving compute efficiency, and supporting independent research.
Open weights also raise questions about control, cost, and who can build on AI technology.
Sharad Chole, chief scientist and co-founder at Expedera, said publishing weights can reduce vendor lock-in as it allows users to host a model themselves or choose a service provider. “If you want to use a service, or host it yourself, there is no vendor lock-in in terms of who is providing the next token for you or who is servicing your next request. But there are geopolitical and investment sides to it. There is also a push for open hardware, like what Meta and others do to enable different competing solution providers. As of September 2026, the larger open-weight models come primarily from outside the U.S., either Europe or Asia, and we are moving toward trillion-parameter models.”
Open-weight models make trained parameters downloadable, letting users run and adapt them on their own hardware rather than relying on a provider’s API, according to Guillaume Boillet, vice president of strategic marketing at Arteris. “They are not necessarily open source: training data, code and usage rights may remain restricted.”
While open-weight AI model releases publish trained parameters, open-source releases aim to publish the full recipe, and closed models publish neither, said Ashish Darbari, CEO of Axiomise.
Representative open-weight releases include Meta Llama, Alibaba Qwen, DeepSeek, Mistral, Google Gemma, Microsoft Phi, and OpenAI’s gpt-oss family. OpenAI reports that gpt-oss-120b runs on a single 80 GB GPU and gpt-oss-20b can run on devices with 16 GB of memory; both use MXFP4 quantization, Darbari noted. “These specifications illustrate the widening range of deployment options, but memory fit alone does not establish useful performance.”
Some U.S.-based AI companies use knowledge distillation to develop smaller models from larger teacher models, but approaches vary. Smaller models may also be pretrained independently or developed through a mix of techniques. Large-scale pretraining remains computationally intensive, while distillation and post-training are important parts of the model-development process.
Chole said the largest models continue to push toward trillion-parameter scales, while models intended for devices or local AI are often distilled into smaller versions. “It’s not like suddenly we’re going to have 100-billion-parameter models breaking all the benchmark records,” he said. He cited an effort to distill a 400-billion-parameter DeepSeek-C model into an 8-billion-parameter Qwen model, while noting that model distillation itself is not new. The broader point is that users now have many choices across model size, capability, and deployment method, and the largest model is not necessarily the right choice for every task.
On Hugging Face, the ‘GitHub for AI models’, there have been approximately 250 open-weight models released in the last two years by major companies, not including quantized variants or models from smaller companies, Chole noted.
But abundance is not the same as readiness, and turning this expanding model catalog into useful design intelligence requires EDA teams to supply trusted domain data, workflow context and rigorous ground truth.
From general-purpose models to EDA workflows
Whether commercial or open-source, general-purpose LLMs aren’t built for chip design tasks, according to Thomas Andersen, vice president for AI and machine learning at Synopsys. “A lot of them are very good at common tasks. They’re very good at creating PowerPoints and summarizing things. They’re good at coding, obviously, because there’s a lot of code out there. Those have been optimized to death. They’re not necessarily well suited to hardware development, not even the RTL coding, because even the RTL that’s out there is just not nearly as much as software. Because of that, every party, including EDA vendors and customers, needs to add their data, and that data is obviously proprietary. This is the difference versus all these models that take public knowledge and put it into the training data. There are both pre- and post-training capabilities, even beyond the weights themselves, where you can add data, and that’s an important key point. Otherwise, it just doesn’t work. It’s like asking a chatbot a question. It doesn’t always give the right answer because it has conflicting data, searches the internet, and people say all kinds of things. What’s the ground truth?”
Accurate results rely on both the query and the quality of the source data.
“The source data itself needs to be very clear, very crisp,” Andersen said. “On the internet, it doesn’t exist. You go on Reddit, people will say five different things when you ask them a question. That becomes the problem of the LLM. In our case, we obviously need very crisp data. In a corporate environment, it’s different. You have much better documentation of processes, of tools, and so on, so it’s a little bit easier. Without that, it doesn’t work. Still, general training of run-of-the-mill models is absolutely required.”
That said, open-weight models will have a place in chip design. “An open-weight model simply means you have an LLM model where you can train the weights of the model,” Andersen explained. “Agentic is a loop that sits around this LLM and then does certain tasks, so it’s a means to an end. There are multiple ways to train the model, which is more like tuning the answer’s correctness, but it doesn’t actually add data itself. There are other ways to add data. Once you have, let’s say, an LLM that knows everything the way you as a human would, then agentic just means you’re building an agentic loop that essentially optimizes your workflow, that does a sequence of tasks the way you as a human would do, rather than one-shot things. Or, you just ask a question and it comes back.”
That distinction between the model and the workflow around it leads directly to a practical deployment question: How should EDA teams route each task to the right model while balancing capability, cost, and control?
Ankur Gupta, executive vice president and head of EDA IC software at Siemens EDA, noted that anyone who is super cost-conscious, from a big chip design company to a small one, still wants to optimize. “They want to pay for the best commercial model, as long as it fits the task, so key architects can solve the hardest problems. It’s called model routing. We know that open-weight models are very useful. They’re effective. EDA companies are playing with them. We certainly are. Many of our developers are using open-weight models extensively because you don’t need to go pay a bunch of money for every single task. And I see this in our customers. They have pulled back on opening up the highest-strength models to everybody, and they’re doing model routing internally. We haven’t.”
Gupta suggests thinking about it in the context of an iceberg. “What you see above the water level is GPU and costs and tokens and all that. That’s on every CIO’s dashboard. It hasn’t gone away. What’s under the surface is also equally important. It’s connecting the silicon to the system to the facilities. There’s lossiness there that you have to recover cost from. Somebody’s going to figure out how to make token cost very viable, just like the entire semiconductor industry has been operating that way, like building in functionality and making that functionality cheaper. It’s just a matter of time before that happens.”
Steven Woo, fellow and distinguished inventor at Rambus, sees open-weight AI models as very helpful to chip designers. “You look at the success stories from companies like OpenAI with the Jalapeno chip and using their own tools, having a smaller team that was both nimbler and more able to do more turns more quickly. Designing that chip in nine months and getting it to work the first time out was incredible. We know that work has been going on in this area, and the tools are just getting better.”
The caveat is that organizations need to maintain control of data that distinguishes them from competitors. “In the beginning, when you had to access these things on the web, there weren’t private, walled areas where a company could ensure its data stayed inside, and many companies were reluctant to let employees use the technology,” Woo said. “But the industry heard and said, ‘Okay, well now we’re going to set up walled areas where we can be certain that your information won’t leak.’ The general idea of how to design a chip — for example, writing RTL to do certain functions and doing place-and-route — there are many examples out there that you can use to train a large language model or an AI entity to do this. Different industries and different companies have very specific ways they approach solutions to problems. Those you can’t really let out because they’re more like trade secrets. So then the question is, ‘How do I take these models that are trained on more general sets and tune them — really fine-tune them — to the specifics of what I do and what my customers care about, and that can’t leave the walled area?’ I’m hopeful that that kind of thing gets solved.”
Open-weight AI models might also be useful in the EDA tool flow to help control costs. “Cost is a big deal, and we want our customers to pay us, not the AI vendors,” said Chuck Alpert, AI fellow at Cadence. “The idea is that open-weight models are going to help keep the costs under control for customers. How do we do that? If you have an open-weight model, you can put it on a machine and never leave your network. If you’re using, say, Claude Opus [a closed, proprietary model by Anthropic], you have to leave the network. Some customers — maybe defense customers especially, who are very sensitive about their information — are part of an ecosystem that says they want to use agentic AI but don’t want to leave their system. A customer like that has to use Openlayer [an enterprise AI evaluation, observability, and governance platform]. There’s also currently the issue that open-weight models may not perform well. They’re getting better, and I’m finding some of them are quite good. But they’re still lagging, which is where doing some training of open-weight models could be a real improvement and an important development, and that we’re actively pursuing.”
One of the keys here is clearly defining the problem statement. “If you think about what chip design is, there’s a massive, multi-physics component, and then you distill it down to a math model, which is extensive — it could be 100,000 lines of the transistor model,” said Mo Faisal, CEO of Movellus. “After that, it is just matrix multiplication. When and how, I’m not sure, but it probably will be one of the new startups that is building semiconductor-specific models. They may start opening up the older things that are maybe trained on 180nm, and you can go build a chip of that and not open up whatever works with the more advanced nodes or more advanced architectures. There’s probably a surprise coming from the Googles or Microsofts or Metas of the world. Why can’t they open-weight their silicon models, since they do have internal silicon design models that they use?”
That possibility shifts the discussion from whether open-weight models can serve EDA to how their business model shapes where — and on what hardware — those models are deployed.
Distinguishing features
Open- and closed-weight models can use similar underlying architectures.
“The architectures are the same — the same transformer blocks, the same attention mechanisms, the same quantization tricks,” said Steve Roddy, chief marketing officer at Quadric. “A chip architect looking at the two would not be able to tell them apart from the compute graph. The difference is entirely a business model distinction. One vendor publishes the parameters for download, the other sells access by the token.”
That difference is what drives deployment. “In practice, the small and mid-sized open-weight models are the ones technically sophisticated users — engineers mostly — download and run on their own hardware, and the motivation is overwhelmingly cost,” Roddy said. “Some run locally to keep prompt data private, and that matters in regulated industries, but token economics is by far the bigger driver today.”
Roddy expects the closed-model vendors to come after that local token volume. “It would surprise no one to see the large private model companies orchestrate split deployments — a midsize front-end model running on the user’s own hardware, with the large model in the cloud handling what the local model can’t. Those big model companies absolutely do not want some other vendor or other model running locally to become the front door that gates access to the big paid model in the cloud. The pricing incentive is obvious — offer dramatically cheaper (maybe free) tokens for the ones the user generates on their own machine, on their own electricity, and cut the data center rental bill enormously. When an offhand tweet (Sam Altman, April 2025) says that the cost of users typing ‘thank you’ runs to tens of millions of dollars, the pressure to offload inference to the edge is not subtle.”
All of that puts pressure on local machines to run larger models, or portions of those models that are disaggregated into smaller models. “The world cannot build data centers fast enough, and it is not going to. But we can plug something the size of a household appliance into every home and office,” Roddy said. “That opens a new category of compute — the agentic computer, architected around running AI models as its primary workload, not as an afterthought bolted onto a phone or PC designed for something else. Today’s devices treat inference as a guest. The next generation will treat it as the host. The question chip architects should be asking is not, ‘How do I add an NPU to my SoC?’ It’s, ‘What does a system look like when model execution is the main job?’ Memory bandwidth and capacity, not TOPS. Sustained throughput, not burst benchmarks. Thermal envelope for continuous rather than intermittent load. And a software stack that can absorb a new model architecture every few months without a silicon respin.”
One of the problems here is the mismatch between chip and model cycles. “If you’re designing a chip for a particular model, models are changing on a weekly basis, or at best monthly, and your chip design cycle is in the best-case scenario 2.5 years,” said Vishal Chandrasekar, director of product management at Ayar Labs. “So how you are intercepting something over that kind of a time frame is hard to see. At the same time, chips that were made in 2019 are still valuable today, because now maybe you’re compute-limited. So a model that’s released today, even if there are 10 new models in two years, is still useful for some application.”
That mismatch makes adaptability the central design requirement — and it frames the practical questions chip architects must answer before committing to an open-weight AI platform.
Solaiman Rahim, chief product officer at ChipAgents, said chip designers should understand that the weights are open, so anyone can use them. “Not only the weights, but also the task list and the dataset they were trained on are provided with the model. So, if anybody wants to rebuild the model, they can. The goal of open-weight models is to give you a base model you can fine-tune to your needs, and performance and cost vary depending on the model. People think open-weight models perform poorly and cost little, but that’s not true. If you look at the latest open-weight model, GLM 5.3, the performance is pretty good. It’s in the 70% to 80% range, but the cost is also very high. It’s not because it’s open-weight that you necessarily get the lowest performance and the lowest cost. The cost and performance of many open-weight models really depend on which model you’re using. But it’s a good base model to fine-tune and build your workflow on top of to get your desired outcome. You also need to figure out how to integrate an open-weight model into your infrastructure.”
Deployment may be on-premises or in a cloud environment such as a virtual private cloud, depending on security requirements and whether a company is comfortable sharing data with its provider. “If you go to AWS, their cloud is very secure. Many customers use VPCs in AWS or other cloud providers, so you need to decide how you want to deploy that model,” Rahim said. “The model alone isn’t enough to start a cost-effective design task. You need to build the ontology layer yourself. You have to build the workflows. Our platform does that automatically so you don’t spend your time and investment trying to reinvent the same way that EDA was built 30 years ago. When everyone did their own synthesis, they came up with Design Compiler, which showed them they could do it with one and didn’t need to reinvent everything. The same thing is happening right now. We have our ontology, our workflows, and our own model layer. Our model layer can pick the best model for you automatically based on the task.”
Other considerations the architecture and design team should ask about include defining the range of models the system must support rather than predicting a single future model size, said Arteris’ Boillet. “Important variables include active parameter count, precision, context length, modality, concurrency, and latency. Teams should ask whether a smaller specialized model is sufficient, where the working set will reside, and how energy use changes under realistic loads. The meaningful measure is energy per useful result, not just TOPS or TDP.”
Taken together, those workload variables turn model selection into a system-architecture problem, with direct consequences for memory, compute, interconnect, and verification.
Axiomise’s Darbari noted that if more inference moves out of hyperscale data centers, it could shift inference silicon toward institutional servers, workstations, laptops, and edge SoCs running 1 billion to 100 billion parameter mixture-of-experts models locally, with a number of architectural implications such as:
Those architectural priorities become concrete when teams estimate what it takes not merely to fit a model in memory, but to run it responsively in daily engineering workflows.
“Capable language, vision-language, and reasoning models with 20 billion to 30 billion parameters can now fit in roughly 16 to 24 GiB of memory after quantization,” Boillet said. “In my own synthetic benchmark on a 36 GB MacBook, models in this range fit. But fitting in memory was not the same as running productively. For the responsiveness needed to replace cloud models in daily work and agentic workflows, the cost can still climb above $10,000. Chip architects need to size compute, memory, and interconnect for the intended application while leaving room for the model mix to change. Being open-weight does not change the underlying model arithmetic. It does let users change precision, sparsity, fine-tuning, and model structure, so memory bandwidth, data movement, numeric flexibility, and quality of service matter more than peak TOPS alone. A dense model and a mixture-of-experts model with the same total parameter count can load the system very differently. Security priorities include authenticating model files and updates, protecting memory and DMA paths, isolating workloads, and supporting rollback.”
Conclusion
Open-weight AI will not eliminate the tradeoffs facing chip architects, but it will make them more explicit. Successful platforms will be designed around adaptable model mixes, sustained memory and interconnect performance, realistic energy and latency targets, and security that extends from authenticated weights through runtimes, tools, and data. For EDA teams, the advantage will come not from choosing open or closed models in isolation, but from combining the right models with trusted domain knowledge, disciplined routing, and hardware-software systems that can evolve long after tape-out.
Leave a Reply

articles.title: Moroccan, Ugandan startups among prize winners as SANAD ElevateHer selects 22 for further support - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Moroccan solar irrigation startup MIRRIAH and Ugandan food preservation company Freza Nanotech are among the cash prize winners after the SANAD ElevateHer accelerator selected 22 startups from across Africa and the Middle East for further support.
The ElevateHer programme, delivered by Seedstars and funded by the SANAD Fund for MSME through its advisory and capacity-building arm, managed by Finance in Motion, supports 38 startups from prototype to growth stage. It focuses on women-led businesses, as well as companies that boost women’s participation through ownership, leadership, employment or their customer base.
Startups pitched at Techne Summit Alexandria, held at the Bibliotheca Alexandrina in Egypt on October 3, with 22 selected for the next phase. Prize winners were announced the following evening at the Seedstars Villa networking event.
MIRRIAH, led by CEO Nidal Tafah, supplies solar irrigation to smallholder farmers and trains rural women and young people to install and sell its systems. Freza Nanotech, represented by COO Samantha Ainembabazi, develops products that preserve fruit and vegetables where cold storage is limited. The third prize went to Jordan’s SmartWTI, led by CEO Hebah Asa’d, which uses connected sensors to monitor water consumption and detect leaks.
The selected startups come from nine markets, with Kenya – Riziki Nature Based Solutions, Soko Kijiji, VunaPay and Wavu – and Ghana – Biowax, Gardpath Technologies, Sackan Farms and SmartWatt Company – providing four apiece.
Alongside MIRRIAH, Morocco was represented by a further two startups, in the shape of Jafife and SMART COLLECTE, while Tunisia also has three representatives – E-Tafakna, GoToGreen and Pixii Motors.
Egyptian startups EcoDahab and TSNGF were also selected, and Uganda had an additional representative in the shape of Essymart Africa. Zimbabwe was represented by Nyamula Logistics Solutions, and Jordan also had a further startup selected. One Lebanese startup was also selected.
The first phase of the programme combined workshops, one-on-one mentoring and practical work on business models, with training in Marrakech covering pricing, unit economics, sales and investor readiness. A founders’ bootcamp ahead of the Alexandria event focused on refining pitches through peer feedback and guidance from coaches and investors. All startups will now receive further coaching and investment-readiness support, including tailored guidance on fundraising, partnerships and scaling.
“Making technology work for customers means deciding who installs it, how it is delivered and what people can afford to pay. We help founders test those choices and build a business around them,” said Sabrina Salama, MENA partnerships lead at Seedstars.

articles.title: WhatsApp : tout le monde peut désormais rejoindre appel, même sans compte
articles.text:
WhatsApp veut que tout le monde puisse profiter de sa plate-forme, et cela, même sans compte. Après plusieurs mois de tests, la messagerie vient d’annoncer l’arrivée d’une nouvelle fonctionnalité d’appels invités, accessible gratuitement sans qu’il soit nécessaire de posséder un compte WhatsApp.
Des appels WhatsApp pour tous, sur invitation
Très concrètement, cette nouvelle fonctionnalité d’appels invités permet à n’importe quel utilisateur de la plate-forme d’inviter un tiers à un appel WhatsApp, même si celui-ci ne possède pas de compte sur la plate-forme. Ces appels réalisés avec des utilisateurs invités sont gratuits, chiffrés de bout en bout et sans aucune limite de temps, comme n’importe quel appel classique sur le service.
Pour en profiter, il faut toutefois qu’un utilisateur disposant d’un compte WhatsApp initie l’opération en créant un lien d’appel directement depuis l’onglet Appels, puis en sélectionnant le bouton + qui permet dorénavant de créer un Nouveau lien d’appel.
Les invités pourront ouvrir le lien depuis le navigateur Web de leur ordinateur et n’auront qu’à saisir leur nom pour rejoindre la salle d’attente de l’appel individuel ou de groupe (maximum 32 personnes) en cours. Il faudra ensuite que l’organisateur de l’appel valide l’arrivée de l’invité pour que celui-ci accède à l’appel.
À noter que WhatsApp applique certaines restrictions à l’ensemble des participants invités. Ces derniers n’ont ainsi pas accès aux numéros de téléphone des autres participants et ne pourront pas, non plus, envoyer des messages textuels ni ajouter d’autres personnes. Ils pourront cependant profiter de certaines fonctions collaboratives comme le partage d’écran, ou encore la possibilité de réagir avec des émojis ou de lever la main.
Une intégration à venir dans Outlook et dans le calendrier Google
WhatsApp a par ailleurs précisé que cette nouvelle fonctionnalité bénéficierait un peu plus tard dans l’année de nouvelles possibilités. La messagerie a en effet prévu de proposer un plugin dédié pour vous permettre d’intégrer la fonction directement dans Google Agenda ou dans Outlook.
Vous pourrez alors ajouter des liens d’appels directement dans les événements de vos calendriers ainsi que dans les invitations que vous envoyez.
La possibilité de générer un lien d’appel n’est pas vraiment nouvelle, WhatsApp l’ayant introduit pour la première fois en 2022. Mais l’utilisation de celle-ci pour rejoindre un appel n’était jusqu’à présent réservée qu’aux seuls utilisateurs disposant d’un compte WhatsApp. Une restriction qui est à présent levée et qui donne tout son sens à la fonction.

articles.title: Les quadricycles électriques font aussi leur show au Mondial de Paris - Numerama
articles.text:
Si notre découverte de La Bagnole de Kilow transformée en mini-camping-car avec Decathlon prouvait déjà que le quadricycle pouvait s’émanciper du simple trajet urbain pour adolescents, le reste du salon enfonce le clou.
Les voitures sans permis et quadricycles lourds (catégories L6e et L7e) ne sont plus de simples cubes en plastique réservés aux sans-permis. Ils incarnent aujourd’hui une solution de mobilité décomplexée sur le marché automobile : voici notre tour d’horizon des nouveautés au Mondial de l’Automobile, organisé du 12 au 18 octobre à Paris, qui redéfinissent la micromobilité en 2026.
Fiat Multiplina : la Topolino s’étire pour quatre passagers
Chez Stellantis, le carton commercial de la Citroën Ami et de la Fiat Topolino donne des ailes aux designers. La marque italienne a profité du salon pour dévoiler au public le concept Multiplina, ainsi que de nouvelles versions de la Topolino.
Fini le strict format biplace : la Multiplina est pensée comme un quadricycle lourd (L7e) vraiment capable d’accueillir quatre personnes et de filer jusqu’à 90 km/h. Avec sa bouille tout en rondeur et son agencement optimisé, elle préfigure ce que pourrait être la voiture urbaine et périurbaine de Fiat à l’horizon 2028, notamment pour barrer la route au futur projet Dacia Hipster.
Kilow : La Bagnole progresse encore
Pionnier du genre, l’artisan haut-savoyard Kilow ne s’est pas contenté d’exposer son étonnant mini-camping-car conçu avec Decathlon. La marque en profite pour enrichir sa gamme :
- Panneaux interchangeables : des habillages de carrosserie vendus séparément, à monter soi-même, avec 24 teintes au catalogue pour changer facilement de look.
- Offre Kilow Pro : des aménagements de benne sur mesure pour les artisans (150 kg de charge utile).
L’entreprise annonce une cadence de production de 20 exemplaires par semaine et vise 600 livraisons d’ici à la fin de l’année.
Ipop : le buggy alsacien fabriqué par Dangel
Non loin de Kilow, un autre projet tricolore fait tourner les têtes : l’Ipop. Imaginé en Alsace et produit chez le spécialiste de la transmission Dangel, l’engin ne passe pas inaperçu avec son coloris jaune. Nous vous avions déjà présenté ce projet sur Numerama en avril 2026. Il évolue à mi-chemin entre le buggy des plages et l’utilitaire de poche.
L’Ipop se distingue par l’adoption de moteurs électriques intégrés directement dans les roues, libérant un espace précieux à bord. Il se décline en deux variantes :
- Ipop 45 (L6e) : bridé à 45 km/h, accessible dès 14 ans avec le permis AM, à partir de 11 000 €.
- Ipop 90 (L7e) : capable d’atteindre 90 km/h avec 140 km d’autonomie. Facturé 15 000 € en propulsion, il monte à 17 000 € dans une version à quatre roues motrices conçue main dans la main avec Dangel.
Avec sa petite benne arrière de 350 litres et ses carrosseries modulables (portes souples, hard-top), l’Ipop apporte une vraie proposition rustique et polyvalente.
Liux Big : une carrosserie qui pousse dans les champs de lin
Le jeune constructeur espagnol Liux présente la Big pour la première fois sur un grand salon international. Longue de 2,76 mètres, cette biplace L7e (90 km/h) s’attaque frontalement au bilan carbone de la fabrication automobile.
Sa structure et ses panneaux de carrosserie font appel à un biocomposite à base de fibre de lin, associé à un châssis en acier ultraléger. Selon la marque, ce procédé allège la structure de 40 % face à une caisse en acier classique tout en réduisant drastiquement l’empreinte environnementale.
Sur la route, la Liux Big ne pèse que 648 kg et promet entre 215 et 270 km d’autonomie grâce à des packs de batteries de 15 ou 20 kWh, pour un tarif ciblé sous les 18 000 €.
EZI et Linktour : la déferlante des microcars tech venues d’Asie
La micro-mobilité aiguise aussi les appétits asiatiques, avec deux philosophies très différentes :
- EZI : une microcar connectée et « AI-native », avec une version cabriolet et un pilotage gestuel via une bague connectée. C’est sans aucun doute le quadricycle le plus technologique de tous.
- Linktour (Alumi) adopte une approche plus industrielle et pragmatique. Avec ses modèles Alumi (L6e, 45 km/h, dès 10 690 €) et Alumi Elite (L7e, 90 km/h, jusqu’à 180 km d’autonomie en cycle WMTC), le constructeur chinois met en avant une finition soignée et un équipement généreux pour la catégorie.
Qu’il s’agisse de capitaliser sur des matériaux comme le lin, de proposer quatre places dans un mouchoir de poche ou de greffer une transmission 4×4 à un tarif raisonnable, le quadricycle prouve qu’il n’est plus une punition pour conducteur sans permis, mais une réponse évidente à la démesure de nos voitures modernes. On apprécie la proposition. Et si vous voulez les découvrir : rendez-vous au hall 7 (à l’exception de Fiat).
