articles.title: Muse Spark Open : le nouveau modèle ouvert de Meta tourne en local sur deux Mac Studio M5 Ultra — Frandroid
articles.text:
Mark Zuckerberg, CEO de Meta, a annoncé sur X ce jeudi 15 octobre la publication des poids de Muse Spark Open, le dernier modèle de la famille Muse. Les poids sont les paramètres qui font fonctionner le modèle.
En les publiant, Meta laisse n’importe qui le télécharger et le faire tourner sur ses propres machines, sans passer par ses serveurs. Et d’après Mark Zuckerberg, le modèle « tourne très bien sur les nouveaux Mac Studio », grâce à un travail mené avec John Ternus et Apple.
Le modèle est pourtant énorme. Dans son billet de blog, Meta le présente comme « le modèle open-weight américain le plus performant à ce jour », avec 816 milliards de paramètres. Meta affirme aussi qu’aucun autre modèle de cette catégorie n’avait encore tourné sur un ordinateur de bureau.
John Ternus, CEO d’Apple depuis le 1er septembre, a répondu moins d’une heure plus tard. Il félicite l’équipe et trouve « incroyable » de faire tourner un modèle de ce « calibre » aussi efficacement « depuis son bureau ». Selon lui, le Mac Studio « continue de repousser les limites de l’IA embarquée », c’est-à-dire de l’IA qui tourne sur la machine plutôt que dans le cloud. Le message suit la ligne d’Apple, qui fait de l’IA locale le grand argument de ses nouveaux Mac.
Jusqu’à 330€ d’avantages avec nos offres Hello Prime ou Hello Prime Duo, dont 80€ cash à l’ouverture de compte !
Des mois de travail entre deux ennemis d’hier
Apple et Meta évitaient de s’afficher ensemble depuis des années. Les relations avaient touché le fond en 2021, quand Apple a limité le pistage publicitaire sur iPhone. Le ciblage des publicités, qui fait vivre Meta, était alors devenu plus difficile.
Pourtant, ce rapprochement ne date pas d’hier. On parle ici d’une réelle optimisation et d’une « alliance » pour mieux faire tourner les modèles Muse sur Mac. Alexandr Wang, responsable de l’IA chez Meta, a précisé à Axios que les deux équipes travaillaient ensemble depuis plusieurs mois. Daniel Gross, ancien cadre d’Apple passé chez Meta, aurait joué un rôle clé, et Alexandr Wang se dit ravi de voir « papa et maman » s’entendre de nouveau.
Aucun accord commercial n’a été annoncé pour autant. Interrogés par CNBC, les deux groupes ont refusé de dire si ce projet préparait une relation plus large.
Meta, de son côté, garde ses meilleures cartes. Muse Spark Open reste moins avancé que Muse Wonder, le modèle fermé haut de gamme du groupe. Alexandr Wang l’admet lui-même auprès de CNBC : « ce ne sont pas les modèles les plus performants que nous ayons développés ». Avec ce modèle ouvert, Meta se démarque d’OpenAI, Google ou Anthropic, qui gardent leurs modèles phares fermés. Par contre, Meta n’est pas seul sur ce créneau : le français Mistral a lui aussi publié de nouveaux modèles ouverts la semaine dernière. Sans oublier l’ensemble des labos chinois, Z.ai (GLM-5.3), DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813 (DeepSeek), Qwen3.8 Max (Alibaba), Kimi K3 (Moonshot) ou encore MiMo 3 (Xiaomi).
Deux Mac Studio et un très gros budget
Pour faire tourner Muse Spark Open chez soi, Meta prévoit deux Mac Studio M5 Ultra reliés entre eux en Thunderbolt, chacun avec 512 Go de mémoire unifiée. Le tout passe par MLX, la bibliothèque logicielle open source d’Apple conçue pour cette mémoire que se partagent le processeur et la partie graphique de la puce.
Pourquoi deux machines ? Le modèle repose sur une architecture dite « mixture d’experts » : seuls 42 milliards de ses 816 milliards de paramètres travaillent pour chaque token (un fragment de mot). Pourtant, tous doivent rester chargés en mémoire, et une seule machine n’y suffit pas. La puce M5 Ultra peut ensuite lire 1,2 téraoctet par seconde dans sa mémoire, assez pour aller chercher vite la petite partie utile à chaque étape.
Meta a testé l’ensemble sur des tâches entièrement locales. Le modèle a corrigé des bugs et ajouté des fonctions à Ice Cubes, une application iOS open source pour le réseau social Mastodon. Il a aussi piloté le logiciel de montage DaVinci Resolve pour repérer les meilleurs plans d’une vidéo et les recadrer à la verticale.
Côté prix, ça calme vite. Le Mac Studio M5 Ultra démarre à 6 599 euros avec 96 Go de mémoire. La configuration en 256 Go est affichée à 16 279 euros avec 8 To de stockage. Le Mac Studio M5 Ultra en version 512 Go, celle qu’il faut acheter en double, n’arrive qu’à la fin octobre. Apple n’en a pas encore donné le prix.
Avant de casser votre tirelire, lisez pourquoi acheter un Mac mini M6 pour l’IA locale est souvent une mauvaise idée, et si un Mac peut vraiment remplacer un abonnement à Claude ou Codex.
Sans Mac, le modèle reste accessible : les poids sont sur Hugging Face, et des services comme Groq, OpenRouter ou Together AI le proposent en ligne.

articles.title: Climb Up visé par une fuite de données, un pirate prétend vendre les informations de 151 000 clients
articles.text:
Un pirate affirme détenir les données de 151 000 clients du réseau français de salles d’escalade Climb Up. Selon l’analyse d’un échantillon diffusé par le pirate, le fichier contiendrait également des informations concernant des enfants et leurs familles.
Les données personnelles enregistrées par les salles de sport peuvent intéresser les cybercriminels, et celles de Climb Up pourraient bien être tombées entre de mauvaises mains. Mercredi 14 octobre, un individu utilisant le pseudonyme Alduin a publié sur un forum spécialisé dans la revente de données volées une annonce concernant le réseau français de salles d’escalade. Il affirme posséder quelque 151 000 fiches clients provenant de 29 établissements. Une revendication qui n’a pas encore été confirmée par l’enseigne, mais dont les premiers éléments examinés révèlent des informations personnelles détaillées, y compris sur des personnes mineures.
Des coordonnées personnelles issues de plusieurs salles d’escalade
Repérée par le site spécialisé FrenchBreaches, l’annonce porte sur un fichier d’environ 93,5 Mo, dont les données s’étendraient de janvier 2016 à mars 2026. Le pirate propose cette base à deux acheteurs au maximum et fournit un échantillon pour en montrer le contenu. On ignore toutefois si la base complète a déjà trouvé preneur.
Le site Cyberattaque.org indique avoir examiné 1 001 enregistrements issus de cet échantillon. Les fiches concernent 13 établissements différents, parmi lesquels figurent plusieurs salles Climb Up à Lyon, Dijon, Limoges ou encore en région parisienne, mais aussi des structures MROC, une enseigne fondée conjointement par Climb Up et Arkose, et SOLO Escalade. Une répartition qui laisse penser que les informations pourraient provenir d’un outil de gestion commun à plusieurs établissements, plutôt que d’une intrusion visant une seule salle.
Les données sont particulièrement détaillées. Sur les 1 001 fiches analysées, 991 contiennent une adresse électronique, 979 au moins un numéro de téléphone et 485 une adresse postale. On y trouve également les noms, dates de naissance, identifiants clients, établissements fréquentés et dates de dernière activité. Aucun mot de passe ni numéro de carte bancaire n’a en revanche été identifié dans cet échantillon.
Des informations sur des enfants et leurs parents également exposées
Plus préoccupant, les fichiers permettent aussi de retrouver les liens familiaux entre les personnes enregistrées. Cyberattaque.org a identifié 280 profils comportant au moins une relation avec un autre compte, pour un total de 517 liens recensés. Parents, enfants, frères et sœurs peuvent ainsi être associés dans les données.
L’analyse a également permis de relever 259 identifiants distincts correspondant à des mineurs dans ces relations familiales, dont des enfants âgés de seulement deux ans. Ce chiffre ne signifie pas que 259 dossiers complets de mineurs ont été exposés, mais confirme que des informations les concernant figurent dans l’échantillon.
De quoi alimenter des tentatives d’hameçonnage particulièrement ciblées. Avec le nom d’un parent, celui de son enfant, leur salle d’escalade et leurs coordonnées, un escroc pourrait se faire passer pour l’établissement et envoyer un faux message concernant une inscription, un stage ou un paiement en attente.
L’origine de cette fuite présumée demeure inconnue. FrenchBreaches évoque la possible compromission d'un compte utilisateur, sans confirmation officielle. Quant aux 151 000 fiches annoncées, rien ne permet pour le moment de vérifier qu’elles correspondent à autant de personnes distinctes, ni que la totalité des données proposées à la vente est authentique.
En attendant d’éventuelles précisions de Climb Up, les clients du réseau ont donc intérêt à se méfier des messages inattendus évoquant leur abonnement ou les activités de leurs enfants, en privilégiant les canaux officiels de leur salle pour vérifier toute demande de paiement ou de renseignements personnels.

articles.title: The permission you denied today is your safety net for tomorrow
articles.text:
The permission you denied today is your safety net for tomorrow
What happens when you give an AI support agent a permission it never needed, then assign it a task the underlying data does not support? The result is entirely predictable. During a test with customer invoices, an agent pulled up a record, confirmed the charge had failed, and no money had left the customer’s account, and refunded it anyway. It repeated the mistake five times without hesitation.
That was Claude Haiku 4.5 going six for six on tasks designed to catch that exact logic flaw. Claude Sonnet 5 identified all six edge cases on its own. Adding a single line to Haiku’s system prompt instructing it to verify transaction state before executing financial actions also resolved the issue.
I had two working fixes and felt reasonably confident until I realized I control neither variable. The moment someone reroutes support traffic to a cheaper model next quarter to trim inference costs, the first fix evaporates. If someone trims or rewrites the system prompt during an experiment, the second fix disappears, leaving no record of the safety guardrail it maintained.
“The only safety control that survives your own cost-cutting is the permission you never granted in the first place.”
The only run that held up reliably was the one where the agent lacked the authority to make the decision. Because its role excluded billing:refund, the execution failed at the permission layer, making the underlying model completely irrelevant.
This is the core argument for least privilege in AI architectures. It isn’t just about malicious actors or leaked tokens; it is about preventing a well-behaved agent from faithfully executing a flawed instruction at machine speed with zero human oversight. The only safety control that survives your own cost-cutting is the permission you never granted in the first place.
Roles are drawn in advance; agent work is not
A standard service account receives a role because a microservice performs one predictable job forever. The payment service handles payments; you scope it once, review it annually, and move on.
An agent’s workload changes on every invocation. The same support agent reads a ticket at 09:00, issues a refund at 09:04, and modifies a seat count at 09:11. The union of everything it might do over a week bears no relationship to what it needs in a single run.
Asking “how much of its permission set does an agent use?” yields a useless metric because that number reflects how generously you provisioned the credential. Grant 400 scopes, and utilization looks catastrophic; grant four, and it looks efficient. You end up measuring an arbitrary configuration choice rather than systemic risk.
A meaningful calculation evaluates the task distribution independently of the grant:
This metric represents the blast-radius multiplier. In a compromised run, an agent reaches the total union of scopes rather than the per-task subset. Across my test suite, that factor reached 11.0. The union across 20 tasks totaled 22 scopes, while the median task required only two.
The experimental framework
I constructed a test environment with 30 scopes across nine domains of a mock enterprise API covering tickets, users, billing, subscriptions, files, messages, audit, admin, and search. Thirteen of these scopes modify or exfiltrate state. Every command maps to exactly one scope, and the system logs every attempt — whether allowed or denied.
The suite comprises 20 tasks, each ending in a state change verifiable mechanically rather than by evaluating the agent’s prose (e.g., closing a ticket, refunding an invoice, or calculating seat overages and commenting the total).
Before running any agent, I authored a reference solution for every task to serve two functions:
- It confirms the task is solvable via the CLI, ensuring a run failure stems from the agent rather than an impossible environment.
- It establishes the minimum required scope set by observing the exact endpoints a correct solution touches.
I evaluated four permission models that differed strictly by which credentials were active at the moment of execution:
- Broad: One long-lived credential holding all 30 scopes.
- Role: A static support-agent role holding 17 scopes derived from a typical job description.
- Task: Scopes issued per run based on a declared plan, expiring when the run completes.
- Just-In-Time (JIT): Starts at zero scopes, requesting each scope on demand with a stated rationale.
Each model ran against two LLM tiers — Claude Haiku 4.5 and Claude Sonnet 5 — totaling 160 runs. The test stack relies strictly on standard-library Python with zero external dependencies or API keys, allowing full reproduction of the reference runs and metrics.
Blast radius against completion
| Permission model | Live scopes | Destructive scopes | Task completion (Haiku / Sonnet) | Call overhead | 
| Broad grant | 30 of 30 | 13 | 20/20 · 20/20 | Baseline | 
| Role-based | 17 of 30 | 2 | 10/20 · 9/20 | Baseline | 
| Task-scoped | 2 of 30 | 1 | 20/20 · 20/20 | Negligible | 
| JIT escalation | 2 of 30 | 1 | 19/20 · 20/20 | +79% / +84% calls | 
Task-scoping achieved complete task execution while holding one-fifteenth of the credentials compared to the broad grant. The occasional denied call and subsequent retry did not meaningfully increase overall API call volume, making the reduction in blast radius effectively free.
The minor completion gap under role-scoping did not stem from permission failures. Both models stalled on the same ten tasks. The single-task variance occurred because one task dataset contained three open tickets with identical subjects. Sonnet declined to guess which ticket to close under the role configuration, yet selected the lowest-numbered ticket under the other three models — even though the role grant contained every scope that task required. This represents standard run-to-run variance on an ambiguous prompt.
“Role-based provisioning is simultaneously too broad and too narrow because it assigns permissions based on a job title rather than the underlying work.”
Role-based scoping performed worst across both axes: it held 8.5 times more credentials than task-scoping while completing half as many tasks. Comparing the role grant against actual task requirements explains why: it granted four scopes no task ever invoked while missing nine essential scopes. Expanding the role until every task passed required 26 scopes — compared to a median task requirement of two. Role-based provisioning is simultaneously too broad and too narrow because it assigns permissions based on a job title rather than the underlying work.
Under role-scoping, each model hit ten permission denials (one per blocked task) and failed every blocked run. These ten denials hit eight of the nine missing scopes (billing:refund and files:upload each blocked two tasks). The ninth missing scope, admin:update_settings, was never reached because the task failed a step earlier at admin:read_settings.
Under task-scoping, Haiku encountered one denial, and Sonnet hit six across four total tasks — yet all four tasks verified successfully. Because a task-scoped grant contains the primary permissions required, denials hit only optional exploratory paths the agent tried (such as querying a search endpoint instead of a list endpoint). Conversely, because a role grant lacks required scopes, its denials are terminal.
JIT escalation achieved the same low blast radius without advance declaration, but it cost ~80% more API calls.
Evaluating the three defensive layers
| Configuration | Executed harmful refund | Caught issue via reasoning | 
| Haiku 4.5 (No prompt hint) | 6 of 6 | 0 of 6 | 
| Sonnet 5 (No prompt hint) | 0 of 6 | 6 of 6 | 
| Haiku 4.5 (One-line system prompt hint) | 0 of 6 | 6 of 6 | 
| Role arm (Lacking billing:refund) | 0 of 6 | 0 of 6 (Blocked by policy) | 
Model capability cannot serve as a primary security control because you do not own the model lifecycle. The day an operations team routes traffic to a cheaper model to cut inference spend, your safety guarantees disappear without triggering an error in your test suite.
Similarly, system prompts are fragile controls. Prompts drift over time; an engineer might trim the prompt to save tokens or rewrite it for an experiment, silently stripping the guardrail.
“A scope that was never granted holds firm regardless of which model runs behind it, how the prompt is modified, or whether the team remembers why the guardrail existed.”
A scope that was never granted holds firm regardless of which model runs behind it, how the prompt is modified, or whether the team remembers why the guardrail existed.
To be clear: this data does not show that agents are inherently reckless. Across standard workflows, agents invoked only 4% to 5% more scopes than the reference minimum — demonstrating disciplined execution. The problem is scale: when a well-behaved agent carrying 30 scopes encounters an edge case, it executes mistakes at a 30-scope scale.
Requirements for a purpose-built agent identity model
- Scope credentials to the task, not the actor: Task-scoped credentials yield identical completion rates with one-fifteenth the blast radius and no measurable overhead. The execution run is the primary identity, not the agent.
- Tie credential expiration to the run lifecycle: A task-scoped credential that outlives its task degrades into a broad credential. The median run in this test suite required permissions only for a single operation.
- Deploy escalation paths over static ceilings: JIT permissions increased call volume by ~80%, which represents the operational cost of runtime discovery. Use declared scopes when a planner can predict them, use JIT escalation when it cannot, and treat every escalation as an auditable event.
- Design permission denials to redirect rather than block: Denials under task-scoping were non-fatal because the grant contained the core permissions needed to finish the task. If permission denials consistently break your workflows, your scoping model is flawed, and widening the static grant is the wrong fix.
Audit logs as primary security artifacts
Every experiment in this framework runs on an append-only log that tracks allowed and denied execution attempts. This log provides the primary telemetry needed to investigate operational incidents.
Denied calls are as critical as successful ones. A denied attempt signals that an agent’s active grant does not match its workflow — indicating either a scoping error or prompt injection. Under JIT escalation, every privilege expansion records a timestamp and an explicit rationale, replacing guesswork with concrete audit records when investigating why an agent accessed a resource.
The audit log also verified experimental integrity, proving no agent bypassed the API by directly modifying fixture states. A task that reports completion without a corresponding mutating call in the log indicates out-of-band tampering. All 160 runs remained consistent because the system verified the execution log directly.
Analyze one week of your agent’s production traffic and evaluate two metrics:
- The total union of scopes exercised across all runs.
- The median number of scopes exercised per individual run.
Divide the first number by the second. If the ratio approaches 1.0, your agent performs a single, static task, and a fixed credential is sufficient. If the ratio approaches 11.0, each run carries an order of magnitude more permission surface than it needs — leaving excess authority waiting to be exploited.
Finally, review the last destructive action your agent executed incorrectly and determine which layer should have prevented it. If you rely on the model or the prompt for safety, your security model is vulnerable to the next cost-optimization ticket. In these test runs, the cheaper model executed six out of six harmful financial actions with contradictory data displayed directly on screen. The only configuration that stopped execution every time was the one where the permission didn’t exist.

articles.title: Tech can improve governance, says Krishna Byre Gowda; Why Indian startups should build for the world from day one
articles.text:
Tech can improve governance, says Krishna Byre Gowda; Why Indian startups should build for the world from day one
At TechSparks 2026, Karnataka Minister for Greater Bengaluru Development, Krishna Byre Gowda, acknowledged the challenges facing Bengaluru and said there is plan to address some of key issues.
Dear Reader,
TechSparks 2026 continued to enthral and inspire.
Day 2 of YourStory’s flagship tech-startup summit saw key conversations around deeptech, venture capital, and technology in governance.
Krishna Byre Gowda, Minister for Greater Bengaluru Development, Government of Karnataka, highlighted technology’s role in improving governance, enhancing transparency, and reducing corruption. He also said technology can help bridge the trust gap between people and the government.
Highlighting Bengaluru’s economic weight in GCC investments and IT service exports, he urged entrepreneurs and builders to apply their innovation beyond commercial software to real socio-economic challenges.
“Bengaluru continues to be the centre for dynamism that nurtures talent and is able to be the home for a lot of people who contribute productively to their own lives, the economy, and the services of the country as well as the larger global space,” said Gowda.
In a panel discussion on deeptech capital, venture capitalists said the deeptech ecosystem is giving rise to new kinds of founders and bold ideas. VCs focused on the deeptech segment believe Indian founders have several differentiated capabilities that can lead to the creation of self-reliant technologies.
The panellists emphasised that deeptech founders must identify niche areas and build solutions around them, as the traditional manner of creating products will no longer work.
In a fireside chat with Shradha Sharma, Founder & CEO, YourStory and The Bharat Project, Tally’s Managing Director Tejas Goenka and Executive Director Nupur Goenka spoke about how the company has stayed relevant for 40 years.
Here’s what’s in store for Day 3, the final day of TechSparks 2026.
In today’s newsletter, we will talk about
- Why Indian startups should build for the world from day one
- Govern like a bank, build like Big Tech: PhonePe’s Sameer Nigam
Here’s your trivia for today: What is the name of the Japanese optical giant, founded in 1919 as Takachiho Seisakusho, famous for pioneering medical endoscopes and cameras? (Scroll down for the answer)
TechSparks
Why Indian startups should build for the world from day one
Indian startups no longer need to wait until they establish themselves at home to expand internationally. Manish Maheshwari, Managing Director of Stripe India, says founders can think global and build for international markets from day one. At TechSparks 2026, he highlighted the role of payments infrastructure, localisation and AI in helping Indian businesses scale across borders.
Key takeaways
- AI is making it faster and cheaper for Indian founders to build businesses for international markets, without waiting to establish a strong domestic presence.
- Stripe data shows 76% of customers prefer paying in their own currency, while offering local payment methods beyond cards can increase revenue by around 12%.
- As AI adoption increases spending on tokens and computing, Stripe’s planned OpenRouter acquisition aims to help businesses manage AI costs while building sustainable business models.
TechSparks
Govern like a bank, build like Big Tech: PhonePe’s Sameer Nigam
PhonePe is balancing the demands of regulatory compliance with the need to innovate and scale, CEO Sameer Nigam said at YourStory’s TechSparks 2026. The fintech company is preparing to revive its IPO plans when global markets stabilise, while expanding its payments business internationally. Nigam also spoke about taking UPI to feature phones and making financial services accessible to more Indians.
Key takeaways
- Nigam stressed that trust, strong governance and non-negotiable ethics must go hand in hand with technology-led innovation. PhonePe undergoes around 130–140 external audits annually.
- PhonePe hopes to resume its listing plans once global markets stabilise, after completing much of the groundwork before pausing the process in March 2026.
- PhonePe’s feature-phone UPI offering is gaining traction, while the company is preparing to expand its full-stack payments business into the UAE, subject to final regulatory approvals.
News & updates
- AI for MSMEs: The/Nudge, an Indian action institute focused on livelihoods and economic inclusion, is receiving a $15 million commitment from Google.org to develop AI tools for India’s micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs).
- Jio IPO: Jio Platforms, the digital arm of billionaire Mukesh Ambani's Reliance Industries, will launch what is expected to be India's largest initial public offering on October 21, a company filing showed.
What is the name of the Japanese optical giant, founded in 1919 as Takachiho Seisakusho, famous for pioneering medical endoscopes and cameras?
Answer: Olympus

articles.title: 'GTA 6' lanza un nuevo tráiler de alto voltaje: acción y romance en Vice City
articles.text:
Rockstar Games acaba de lanzar un nuevo tráiler de GTA 6 que nos ha tomado a todos por sorpresa. El avance en cuestión se presenta como un "tráiler de lanzamiento" enfocado en PlayStation e incluye nuevo material que brinda un poco más de contexto a los orígenes de Jason y Lucía, los protagonistas.
Al igual que los tráiler previos de GTA 6, los desarrolladores no desaprovechan la oportunidad de introducir escenas de alto voltaje. Pero en este caso no se limitan a persecuciones, tiroteos y otras situaciones cargadas de acción y adrenalina, sino que también hay lugar para el romance y las situaciones "cuerpo a cuerpo" (guiño, guiño).
El tráiler de GTA 6 se inicia revelando nuevos detalles del pasado de Jason Duval. El protagonista menciona que se metió en problemas durante su paso por el Ejército y que no se fue en los mejores términos. También, que la gente de su tipo no recibe préstamos ni ningún tipo de ayuda.
Básicamente, el personaje se presenta como un paria que se ve empujado a una vida delictiva para tratar de salir adelante. El avance de GTA 6 también muestra un contacto telefónico con Lucía Caminos, de quien ya sabíamos sobre su pasado en prisión. Así, Rockstar sienta las bases de esa relación a lo Bonnie y Clyde, con ambos personajes trenzándose tanto desde lo romántico como desde lo criminal.
En esta oportunidad, GTA 6 también elige mostrar un poco más de piel, con Jason y Lucía compartiendo un momento íntimo bajo la ducha. Es evidente que Rockstar no piensa contenerse con absolutamente nada, algo que una reciente filtración había dejado entrever al mostrar que sería posible jugar con los personajes totalmente desnudos.
GTA 6 estrena un nuevo tráiler en la recta final para su lanzamiento
El nuevo tráiler de lanzamiento de GTA 6 no ha tardado en viralizarse en YouTube. Al momento de redacción de este artículo, acumula más de 1,2 millones de reproducciones en la plataforma cuando ni siquiera ha transcurrido una hora desde su lanzamiento. Un número que quedará rápidamente desactualizado con el correr de los minutos.
Más allá de lo que se presenta a nivel visual, el tráiler de GTA 6 también permite conocer una nueva canción que forma parte de su banda sonora original. Se trata de Flower in a Hurricane, de Justice. El dúo francés de música electrónica ha colaborado con Tame Impala, SZA y King Gizzard & the Lizard Wizard en esta producción. Puedes escucharlo completo a continuación.
La música siempre juega un rol crucial en Grand Theft Auto y los tráiler previos de GTA 6 hicieron disparar la popularidad de las canciones que utilizaron. No sería raro que suceda algo similar con esta nueva pieza que forma parte de la banda sonora oficial, que Rockstar Games ha lanzado a la venta en CD y vinilo.
GTA 6 debuta el próximo 19 de noviembre en PS5, PS5 Pro y Xbox Series X|S.

articles.title: Is AI pentesting as good as a human pentester?
articles.text:
With the rise of AI pentesting, a lot of people are wondering if it’s as good as a human. Having started as a pentester twelve years ago, and having moved through similar roles to working on Intruder’s AI pentester,
I've come to understand the advantages and disadvantages of both. Here’s how they compare.
The strict methodology was never the good bit
You may expect AI pentesters to follow strict methodologies in the way that many human pentests do.
At Intruder, we experimented with this approach early on - structured systems where each agent had a specific vulnerability type to look for. What we found was that agents would miss things outside their remit entirely, or miscategorize what they did find as the one thing they'd been told to look for, causing confusing reports.
A complete lack of structure also failed to produce good results, as completely free agents without any guidance couldn’t break down and manage large applications properly. They could find interesting things, but at the cost of missing a load of other vulnerabilities in our targets.
We’ve put a lot of testing into finding the balance between these approaches, and settled on giving agents freedom with broadly defined roles to help them approach and manage large applications, and stricter guardrails to stop them causing damage.
This does mean that our AI pentester doesn’t tick off the parts of a methodology document that you’d typically see in a human pentest. That may make some people uncomfortable - a strict methodology gives people assurance that someone has gone through your application and tested everything on the list. An unauthenticated SQL injection needs to be found, and a checklist is there to make sure it does.
The methodology gives a lot of people the idea that a human pentest is a perfectly repeatable product, as any tester will be able to follow the methodology, and everything important will get found. The reality is a lot more nuanced than that though, as pentesting is a skilled job, and many of the most impactful findings on a pentest will come from the tester being experienced in noticing weird behaviours and following up on them.
For our AI pentester, we ended up with much more interesting and impactful results by not trying to guide our agents through specific vulnerability types. A good example is a complex authentication bypass the agents found that had been sitting in a codebase through five years of pentests without any human testers picking it up.
The mechanics of that issue mean that you’d never think to write a testing guide that could be strictly followed to identify it, and if we’d tried to limit our AI pentester too much it never would have found it either.
You could say that only finding the common things would still be pretty good, but there's such an array of vulnerabilities that aren't common that you find during a pentest. And just because they’re not common, it doesn’t mean that an attacker can’t find them too, especially now AI is being used to enable attacks more.
A strict methodology being carried out by a competent tester only ever provided a low baseline of reliability, and it didn’t even do that perfectly. What makes a pentest good is the part that a skilled tester does outside the checklist, and that's where AI thrives - following its nose through your application and finding the things that were never going to make a list.
Pentest with every major release. Security that keeps up with engineering.
Intruder's AI pentesting agents deliver the depth of a manual engagement on-demand: no lead time, no scoping calls, a fraction of the cost.
Test with every release, close your window of exposure, and get an audit-ready report in hours.
Book a Demo
What they know, and what they can’t ask
Our AI pentests take a white box approach, which means the agents get the source code. They work through the entire codebase and build a picture of not just what every page is, but how the application is meant to function and what requests can be made. Doing this to the level of detail that the AI is able to isn’t feasible for a human pentester during a typical time window for a pentest.
The AI pentester also builds up a sense of what the application is for, and a good example of this is access control - it doesn’t need to be told that low privileged users shouldn’t be able to reach admin functionality, or that a particular bit of data is sensitive.
You can give them extra information as well, just like a human tester. For example, people often specify that they’re worried about their customers being able to access each others’ data, and the pentester has done a great job of focusing on these issues and identifying a lot of them.
What the agents can't do is ask you for anything you didn't already give or tell them. If I don't understand what a part of an application does while I’m doing a pentest, I can ask my contact, and those conversations can be very useful for testing the application properly, and assessing risk in the final report.
I can also clarify the scope with my contact if needed, or ask for permission to verify something when I’m unsure if there’s a risk of disruption.
We’ve had to deliberately make our AI pentesting agents cautious on this front to avoid going out of scope.
Neither finds everything
The freedom that lets AI pentesting agents find something like a complex auth bypass is the same thing that makes them less predictable. They decide where to dig, and that won't be identical every time.
But pentest results have always varied with the person doing them. It's why many consultancies will rotate your tester each year - different people find different things on the same application.
This comes down to people’s experience, specialisms, and incidental knowledge.
I’ve found issues because of a blog post or specification I happened to read years earlier and was left sitting in the back of my head. And even the things on a checklist get missed sometimes. People are fallible, and covering an entire application methodically over multiple days can be hard.
Consistent coverage is something we're actively working to improve, but it’s not something that was ever offered perfectly from anyone. It's why every human pentest report comes with a disclaimer saying as much, even though most people read it as a formality.
The remediation I couldn’t have written
Every pentester has strong opinions about what makes a good report. I’ve built up many of my own over the years, as have the rest of the current and former pentesters at Intruder. These opinions are what we built our report around.
The executive summary is the hardest page of a report to get right. For a lot of people it's their entire experience of your work, and at a good consultancy a lot of effort goes into it. We’ve worked to get to the point where the agents are now writing genuinely good ones, and I often read them first on our own reports to get a good overview before diving into detail.
Where they're still off is scoring risk. They rate things higher than I would, partly because they can't have the conversations with you that would bring a rating down, and partly because LLMs err towards caution when you start talking about cybersecurity.
That's the right direction to be wrong in, but it does mean you'll see things flagged as more serious than they are, and it's something we're working on.
Remediation guidance is where the agents excel. After a long week on a pentest it's tempting for a human to write generic advice, and you catch yourself and try to do better. Unfortunately, you're usually limited by time and usually by not having the source code.
The agents don't have either problem, so they'll tell you the line of code to change, and what to change it to on every issue. They also write about mitigating controls that can help reduce the impact of the issue, or provide a temporary fix.
We're seeing that speed up how quickly people actually fix things. We had a customer with 78 issues who fixed all of them within a few days, which as a human pentester I have never seen happen. I couldn't have written the level of detail that made those fixes possible in the time I'd have had.
So is AI pentesting as good as a human?
AI pentesting and human pentesting are different, and once you stop trying to rank them the comparison gets a lot more useful.
The agents are finding serious issues in applications that human testers have already been through multiple times. They'll read a whole codebase, work through every path in it, and write up every instance of what they find with the fix down to the line of code.
And you can run one whenever you want. For what a single human engagement costs you can run four AI pentests, which means you can do deep testing on a regular basis rather than once a year.
That’s a key thing that is missed by human pentesting, and often applications have undergone a lot of untested changes in between pentests.
See what Intruder’s AI pentester finds in your application. Learn more.
Author
Written by Daniel Thatcher, Security Research Engineer, Intruder
Daniel is a security researcher at Intruder with a background in penetration testing, and a focus on exploiting web applications in black-box scenarios.
Sponsored and written by Intruder.

articles.title: Kenya’s fintech reforms could delay ecosystem investment
articles.text:
Kenya is proposing approval requirements for significant investments in payment companies, potentially lengthening fundraising for startups as the central bank strengthens its oversight of the industry.
The draft National Payment System Bill, 2026 would require investors acquiring at least 10% of a licensed payment service provider or payment system operator to obtain written approval from the Central Bank of Kenya (CBK). Incoming significant shareholders would also undergo regulatory vetting, a standard process at other financial institutions, such as banks.
The proposals would make approval a condition of completing investments. Fintech founders could face a longer time between securing an investor’s commitment and completing the transaction. A company running short of cash would have to account for a decision that neither its board nor its prospective backers could control.
“A significant change of ownership of a licensed payment service provider or a licensed payment system operator shall be subject to the prior written approval of the Central Bank,” clause 58 of the Bill states.
Repeal of old laws
The requirements are part of a proposed repeal of Kenya’s fintech law, which would establish separate licensing categories for businesses including electronic wallets, payment gateways, and money remittance providers. The overhaul introduces measures that the regulator says will encourage competition in a sector dominated by banks and telcos, and also bring tighter controls over capital, ownership and management.
Agnes Aistleitner, managing partner of First Circle Capital, tells me that the proposal adds complexity and costs to investing in Kenya, which is already very expensive and, so far, hasn’t been the most lucrative fintech market, apart from Safaricom and a few others. “Ultimately, I think it raises the bar for investment opportunities in Kenya,” she says.
While the draft sets a threshold for ownership approval, it does not specify how quickly CBK must decide on a transaction.
The uncertainty would concern the closing date. An investor could agree to fund a business but make the funding contingent on regulatory approval, leaving the company unable to count on the money until approval is granted. A provider with limited cash would need to begin raising earlier or arrange financing to cover the wait.
The timing could become particularly important for providers raising money to meet the bill’s capital requirements. The draft proposes a minimum capital requirement of KES 250 million ($1.9 million) for electronic money issuers and KES 50 million ($385,178) for wallet providers, with existing payment businesses given 1 year from the law’s commencement to comply. A company bringing in a significant shareholder to meet those requirements would need to complete both the investment and the ownership approval within its compliance timetable.
A temporary cash injection would not necessarily resolve the problem. Clause 10 excludes “shareholder loans or advances” and “unpaid, partly paid, or contingent capital commitments” from paid-up capital. A founder could therefore secure sufficient funds to keep the business operating without meeting the regulatory minimum.
Investor scrutiny is already part of Kenya’s fintech industry. The 2014 regulations require CBK to assess and approve significant shareholders, directors and senior managers. They set the threshold at 5% for unlisted providers and 10% for listed companies.
Therefore, the bill’s proposed 10% threshold would be higher for unlisted providers. The effect of the proposed changes would depend on how the approval process works alongside shareholder vetting, and whether it becomes predictable.
“The new significant shareholders shall undergo the same vetting as the existing shareholders,” clause 58 says.
Such assessments could cover matters including integrity, competence, business conduct, and bankruptcy, with investors subject to an examination of their suitability.
The requirements could also reach investments below the headline threshold. Clause 11 of the proposed law allows the CBK to vet smaller shareholders when it suspects that a holding has been reduced to avoid certification, or when an investor exercises control through associates.
“It’s not very attractive for investors. If we have to look at bridge financing or restructuring down the line, that would make it even more complicated. That would also factor into whether we would want to do a deal in the first place,” Aistleitner said.
Exit plans would face scrutiny too. The draft says “no merger or acquisition of a payment service provider or payment system operator shall be done without the prior written approval of the Central Bank”.
For a company unable to raise capital independently, a sale to a larger rival could thus require regulatory clearance as well. The same would apply to investors seeking an acquisition as their exit from the business, subject to any applicable competition review.
These requirements could favour investors able to commit time and resources to regulatory due diligence. They could also encourage companies to begin fundraising earlier, negotiate more time between signing, and completion, and prepare ownership and governance information before approaching CBK.
Bringing certainty
There is a benefit in some of these changes. Currently, Kenya’s fintech sector is regulated by the Central Bank of Kenya Act, the National Payment Systems Act, the National Payment Systems Regulations of 2014, and the e-money Regulations of 2013, all of which apply to fintechs.
This has put remittance and payment startups on a collision course with Kenyan authorities, with law enforcement agencies, including the Financial Reporting Centre (FRC) and the Asset Recovery Authority (ARA), freezing accounts and seizing assets of sector players on money-laundering charges.
In 2022, CBK ordered local financial institutions, including banks and mobile money service providers, to cut ties with fintechs, citing unspecified threats to the country’s financial systems. The regulator said at the time that the firms were operating without authorisation.
Clear licences and a consistent approval process could make payment businesses easier to assess and reduce uncertainty about their right to operate. The Treasury and CBK say the overhaul is intended to promote competition and innovation while protecting consumers and financial stability.
A well-run process could allow investor vetting to proceed alongside commercial negotiations. A slow or unpredictable one could leave a company with an agreed deal but insufficient certainty to plan hiring, expansion, or even its next few months of operations.
True scale demands moving beyond surface-level integrations to robust execution. We’ve filtered the noise out of Moonshot 2026, optimising the conference strictly for high-calibre connections between startup founders, global financial operators, enterprise leaders, and individuals rewiring Africa’s technical frameworks. articles.title: “Programmer, c'est difficile” : Epic vibe code et assume un nouveau Epic Games Store plus rapide
articles.text:
“Programmer, c'est difficile” : Epic vibe code et assume un nouveau Epic Games Store plus rapide
Mauvaises vibes
Epic a visiblement décidé d'embrasser l'IA à pleine bouche. Après les rumeurs d'un futur jeu au développement sérieusement dopé à l'IA, c'est son launcher maison, l'Epic Games Store, qui va faire sa révolution grâce au vibe coding.
Alors que la situation dans le jeu vidéo n'a jamais été aussi sombre, tant les fermetures de studios et les licenciements massifs d'artistes et développeurs se multiplient à toutes les échelles, Epic semble pleinement assumer de verser de l'essence sur l'incendie. Plutôt que de recruter pour améliorer son launcher Epic Games Store, toujours à la traîne et boudé face à Steam, la société assume avoir vibe codé une nouvelle version pour rattraper la concurrence.
Une nouvelle version de l'EGS en IA et légère en fonctionnalités
"Programmer, c'est difficile", déclare d'entrée de jeu et sans trembler des genoux Epic dans l'annonce concernant son nouveau launcher. Il ajoute : "Du coup, au lieu de faire ça, nous avons vibe codé un nouveau lanceur Epic Games qui est bien plus rapide et réactif que l'actuel, et qui arbore un nouveau look."
Les développeurs qui ne trouvent plus de travail à cause de l'IA générative qui code à leur place seront sans doute ravis. Nul doute qu'Epic fera appel à eux quand il s'agira de corriger les bugs et failles généralement laissés par le vibe coding, et déjà repérés dans cette nouvelle version.
Sur Windows, par rapport à Steam, le nouveau EGS s'ouvrirait à froid 46 % plus rapidement, à savoir 5,47 secondes contre 10,07 secondes. Un chiffre qui ne veut pour le moment pas dire grand-chose, car cette version preview est, de l'aveu d'Epic elle même, encore légère en fonctionnalités. Il est cependant possible d'acheter, télécharger et lancer des jeux, tandis que le système de groupe et de chat est également là, avec une expérience de navigation globalement plus rapide et fluide.
L'Epic Games Store et Fortnite arrivent sur Linux
Pour tester ce nouveau Epic Games Store, il faudra récupérer la version Preview sur le site dédié. On relèvera que cette nouvelle version concerne Windows et macOS, mais aussi pour la première fois Linux. Ainsi, Fortnite pourra être jouable sur Linux, via un nouveau système anti-triche.
Signalons que ce nouveau launcher s'inscrit dans une volonté visiblement assumée d'Epic d'adopter toujours plus l'IA générative. Il y a quelques jours, le journaliste souvent bien informé Jason Schreier rapportait qu'un futur jeu Epic Games mêlant les univers Marvel et Star Wars était en retard. Pour rattraper cela, la stratégie adoptée est claire : ne plus écrire le moindre code à la main et s'appuyer au maximum sur l'IA.

articles.title: Meta's smart glasses were recording conversations without the wake phrase, company admits
articles.text:
A hot potato: If there's one product that really doesn't need any more negative stories, it's Meta's smart glasses, but here we are. Some users discovered that the wearables were recording their voices without the wake phrase, an issue the company says has now been resolved.
A redditor recently wrote that they'd noticed something concerning with Meta's Ray-Ban glasses: they were capturing conversations when they were talking to other people despite the "Hey Meta" wake phrase not being used.
The conversations appeared in the Meta AI app as saved audio recordings and text transcripts. It's also noted that the "Respond without Hey Meta" setting was turned off, and that the white notification light was sometimes activated when the person was speaking normally.
This could have been a problem with a single pair of Meta's glasses, but the same behavior was present on three different pairs, including 2nd- and 3rd-generation models. Most tellingly, it appeared after a firmware update was rolled out to the devices.
Meta support was contacted about the strange behavior, but its response was to recommend disabling microphone and camera permissions, turn off Wear Detection, delete voice history, and disable automatic updates.
The user complained that these steps would not only disable the product's core functionality but also fail to explain or address the problem.
The post adds that the user is consulting with a lawyer about the possibility of initiating a class-action lawsuit if other customers discovered the same unwanted voice recording.
Several responses to the post confirm that other Meta Ray-Ban users experienced the same issue: the glasses randomly recording conversations without the wake word.
Meta has since responded to the Reddit post, though it never gave any information on exactly what happened and why. "This issue has been resolved. People can manage, review and delete voice logs of their interactions with Meta AI via settings at any time," the company told Android Authority.
Wearing smart glasses in public is becoming about as socially acceptable as walking around sporting a swastika badge. Norway is considering temporarily banning them in parks, beaches, and schools, and they're being banned in courtrooms across the US and elsewhere.
This isn't the first privacy nightmare involving Meta's smart glasses. In March, contractors in Nairobi said they'd been paid to study hours of raw footage captured through Meta's "live AI" feature, analyzing everything from simple interactions to some very intimate moments. This data labeling allows Meta to train its computer vision systems, though the people who were recorded using bathrooms, getting dressed, and having sex might not care too much about the reasons.

articles.title: Supermarket Refrigeration Attack Widens to Copeland, Dixell Controllers
articles.text:
The cyberattack that disrupted refrigeration at hundreds of French supermarkets this week also affected equipment from Copeland and its Dixell brand, according to France’s national cybersecurity agency ANSSI.
ANSSI’s CERT-FR first warned on October 12 of numerous compromises involving Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC series refrigeration controllers. A day later, the agency updated its alert to include Copeland XWEB and Dixell XWEB systems.
Copeland initially declined to confirm the agency’s findings, but it has since acknowledged a vulnerability. “We are currently working with impacted customers to mitigate the risk,” the company said.
This summer, Claroty detailed flaws in Danfoss’s AK-SM 800A, along with 23 vulnerabilities in Copeland’s XWEB Pro controller. Copeland patched them in a firmware update.
It is still unclear how the attackers gained access. The CERT-FR alert does not link the compromises to any specific vulnerability, and neither Danfoss nor French authorities have tied the attack to the flaws Claroty disclosed.
Danfoss said most of the affected devices are older AK-SM 800 and AK-SC 355 systems, which have reached end of life and are no longer patched. The vendor stopped supporting the AK-SM 800 in May 2021, and the AK-SC 355 was discontinued in 2016. Some current AK-SM 800A controllers that were running outdated firmware were also affected.
CERT-FR has urged operators of the affected controllers to take them off the internet and restore remote access only through a secure VPN or protected network. Filtering connections by IP address is acceptable only as a temporary emergency measure, the agency said.
For compromised end-of-life devices, a factory reset alone is not enough as the device will remain vulnerable and is likely to be compromised again if it stays exposed.
Hundreds of supermarkets affected in France
Supermarket chains that have confirmed being affected include Carrefour, Coopérative U, E.Leclerc, Intermarché, and Monoprix.
About 700 of France’s roughly 10,000 supermarkets were affected, Finance Minister Roland Lescure told lawmakers on Tuesday. Earlier reports had put the number at 300-350.
At Intermarché, about 150 stores were affected, according to owner Les Mousquetaires. Refrigeration units there ran at 50 degrees Celsius for six hours, and all the food was discarded. Carrefour said 80 of its stores were impacted.
Coopérative U CEO Dominique Schelcher said 80 of the group’s stores were targeted, but only a minority had to throw away products. Two supermarkets in Alsace reported combined losses of €270,000 ($300,000).
The Paris prosecutor’s office, whose cybercrime unit has opened an investigation, said the attack caused fires in addition to food losses. According to Le Monde, the attackers lengthened defrost cycles from one hour to as many as eight, which delayed alarms.
Investigators are reportedly puzzled by the lack of either a claim of responsibility or a ransom demand, Reuters reported, citing a source familiar with the probe.
Sekoia’s Félix Aimé told Reuters that stores in Spain, Portugal, Poland, Germany, and Belgium were also affected, but did not provide details. The Dutch NCSC said it did not believe a cyberattack against Ahold Delhaize was connected to the attack on refrigerators.
Censys counted nearly 3,000 internet-exposed Danfoss StoreView control panels on October 11, more than 1,800 of them in France. By October 14, the French count had dropped to 537, while the number elsewhere barely changed.
Patched and unpatched versions disappeared at roughly the same rate, suggesting that operators are disconnecting the controllers rather than updating them, Censys noted.
The attack has also raised questions about liability. Les Mousquetaires said the refrigeration systems were managed by Danfoss and that it is therefore up to the supplier to file a complaint with the authorities, Bloomberg reported.
Related: CenterPoint Energy Data Breach Impacts 1 Million Texans
Related: Meta Says Hackers Took Code, Personal Data of 1,500 in GitHub Breach

articles.title: Singer or clanker? YouTube Music will tell you with new gen AI labeling.
articles.text:
Genuine human creativity takes time, but you know what doesn’t? AI slop. There are countless AI models out there that can make something that passes for music, and you might come across those tracks on streaming services without realizing it. Google says it will begin labeling that content in YouTube Music, building on similar disclosures in the main YouTube app.
Google is not outright banning AI music or even speaking ill of it. “Generative AI is opening up new ways for artists to create, experiment, and share music,” the company says in a blog post.
However, the company also acknowledges that people want to know if a song was created with generative AI tools. A new label for AI content on YouTube Music is now rolling out in the app and on the website, which looks a lot like a label Google began adding to AI-generated videos on YouTube earlier this year.
The AI label will be visible on the player page, and a tap will open a menu with more information. The label will be applied to songs that were created entirely or altered significantly with AI. But how will Google know when to apply that label? That could be a little tricky.
The process of labeling AI music will be similar to Google’s detection setup with YouTube videos. Google says it is working with partners and using its own detection tools to identify AI music. When publishers upload content, they can specify how much (if any) gen AI was used. The tiers are fully gen AI, partially gen AI, and no gen AI. However, this is optional.

articles.title: Epic Games programó con IA su nuevo lanzador y asegura que es 46% más veloz que Steam
articles.text:
Epic Games lanzó una versión de prueba de su nuevo Epic Games Launcher, reconstruida con herramientas de inteligencia artificial a las que la compañía llama vibe coding (programar guiando a una IA con instrucciones en lenguaje simple en vez de escribir el código a mano). Según pruebas que la empresa encargó a un proveedor externo, el programa arranca 46% más rápido que su rival en la venta de juegos para PC.
En su anuncio oficial, la compañía escribió que “programar es difícil, así que en vez de hacerlo, programamos con IA un nuevo Epic Games Launcher que es mucho más rápido y responsivo que el actual, y tiene un diseño nuevo”. La frase, con tono de broma, acompaña una decisión que la empresa no oculta.
La medición oficial muestra un arranque en frío de 5,47 segundos, contra 10,07 segundos de Steam. El nuevo programa también abre la tienda tres veces más rápido y restaura la ventana desde la bandeja del sistema en 0,36 segundos, frente a los 0,42 segundos de la competencia.
Esa última diferencia, de apenas 0,06 segundos, resultó marginal en las pruebas independientes que realizaron medios especializados como Tom’s Hardware y GamesRadar+, que la calificaron de poco perceptible para un usuario común.
Un equipo y una base de código nueva
Las mediciones fueron encargadas a Keywords Studios, una firma que presta servicios de evaluación técnica para la industria de los videojuegos. Los resultados surgen de cinco pruebas realizadas en 13 computadoras con Windows, según detalló Tom’s Hardware.
Martin Keely, vicepresidente y gerente general de Epic Games Store, explicó a PC Gamer que el equipo “empezó desde cero”. “Esto es una arquitectura completamente nueva tanto para la tienda como para el programa del lanzador”, dijo Keely, y agregó que la IA funcionó “como una herramienta para escribir y revisar nuevas funciones y capacidades desde cero, en una base tecnológica distinta a la que teníamos antes”.
En otra entrevista con IGN, Keely precisó que el uso de inteligencia artificial los “hizo más eficientes” y que permitió que un equipo chico reescribiera la base de código y pudiera lanzarla más rápido en distintas plataformas. Según indicó, el nuevo lanzador tiene soporte para Windows y Mac, y también tendrá una versión para Linux.
Epic había anticipado parte de este trabajo en junio, durante una presentación de su evento Unreal Fest, cuando prometió una “rearquitectura total” de su tienda y un arranque “cinco veces más rápido” que el de entonces.
El relanzamiento llega días después de que el director ejecutivo, Tim Sweeney, describiera en redes sociales un “gran giro” en la compañía hacia el uso intensivo de inteligencia artificial en el desarrollo. “La meta no es hacer lo mismo con menos gente, sino permitir que todos acá construyan más y mejores cosas, y llevar esos beneficios a todos los equipos que usan Unreal”, escribió Sweeney.
La agencia Bloomberg había informado días antes que empleados fueron instruidos para dejar de escribir código a mano en un proyecto no anunciado con personajes de Star Wars y Marvel, y usar en cambio modelos de IA como Claude, de Anthropic.
Lo que todavía falta en la versión de prueba
Epic Games admitió que la versión preliminar está “ligera en funciones”: todavía faltan paneles sociales completos y opciones de gestión de cuenta que sí tiene el programa anterior. Por eso recomendó a los jugadores de Fortnite y Rocket League mantener el lanzador clásico mientras el nuevo todavía no alcanza paridad de funciones.
Steam mantiene, según estimaciones de la industria citadas por el sitio especializado Neowin, entre 74% y 75% del mercado de tiendas de juegos para computadora. Epic Games compite contra esa posición dominante desde que abrió su propia tienda hace casi ocho años.
La compañía dijo que seguirá recogiendo comentarios de los usuarios de la versión de prueba antes de avanzar hacia un lanzamiento estable del nuevo lanzador.

articles.title: The Canadian entrepreneur has changed. Has banking kept up? | BetaKit
articles.text:
Picture a Canadian entrepreneur, and there’s a good chance that image is already out of date.
That’s according to the Modern Entrepreneur Report, a new study from Tangerine Bank and PwC Canada. Over half of the 552 Canadian business owners surveyed for the report said the traditional definition of ‘entrepreneur’ does not quite fit them: many are working solo, building businesses alongside other jobs, and keeping teams small.
The ways these entrepreneurs define success are changing, too. Headcount, growth, and exits are becoming less useful as shorthand for what makes entrepreneurship worthwhile, according to the report, with many placing greater value on freedom, flexibility, and the difference they make in their communities.
The report’s findings suggest that the banks serving entrepreneurs have not fully caught up with these changes. Only half of those surveyed feel their bank treats them as a business owner, rather than simply an individual customer.
BetaKit spoke with Jodi Kovitz, Managing Director of Business at Tangerine, about her perspective on how the profile of Canada’s modern entrepreneur is shifting, and where banking still has some catching up to do.
The following Q&A has been edited for brevity and clarity.
Why did Tangerine produce this report?
Entrepreneurship in Canada is changing rapidly, but perceptions of what it means to be an entrepreneur have not always kept pace with the realities of how modern businesses are being built. As Tangerine took a closer look at how we can support the business community, we spoke with entrepreneurs across the country and heard incredible stories from people building businesses in very different ways, often alongside other work, with small teams, or as solo operators.
That’s why we collaborated with PwC Canada to develop the report: to better understand who today’s entrepreneurs are, what motivates them, what challenges they face, and what they need to thrive.
The research confirmed what we were hearing firsthand: entrepreneurship is being redefined, and many entrepreneurs don’t feel fully recognized by the institutions built to serve them. We saw an opportunity to shine a light on this evolving segment and start a broader conversation about how financial institutions can better support entrepreneurs as they build and grow.
What is the most surprising thing you learned when reviewing the report?
What stood out to me most in the report was just how many businesses are thriving without having to scale and expand. Since 2020, businesses without employees have grown by 24 percent, compared to just four percent for employer businesses. This revolution isn’t just being driven by tech startups; it’s being built by freelance graphic designers, content creators, registered massage therapists, and so many more.
These entrepreneurs aren’t necessarily trying to get bigger. While 93 percent of those we surveyed said they are proud of the business that they’ve built, fewer than half (45 percent) expect their businesses to grow, and only 22 percent identified long-term financial security as motivation for starting their business, signaling how important passion and improving their quality of life are as drivers.
More than half of respondents say the traditional label of “entrepreneur” no longer fits them. What do you make of that?
For a long time, entrepreneurship was associated with traditional markers like employees, office space, rapid growth, and scale. While those businesses still exist, many of today’s entrepreneurs are building successful businesses with different goals in mind.
Nearly 40 percent of respondents said greater independence and control were key motivations for starting their business, and many now define success by the freedom, flexibility, and community impact their business creates, not just revenue or headcount. That challenges businesses and financial institutions to look beyond traditional measures of success and take a more holistic view of entrepreneurs.
That’s precisely what we’re doing at Tangerine. We’re building a new model for business banking that recognizes that entrepreneurs need more than a place to manage their money.
Through the Tangerine Business Community, we’re creating opportunities for entrepreneurs to connect, share experiences, and learn from one another, while continuing to build banking experiences informed by their feedback and shaped around their needs.
How does today’s entrepreneur look compared to the traditional archetype?
What we consider a traditional entrepreneur is pretty typical and actually embodies how most large enterprises today got their start: creating a company, scaling it, hiring a team, and eventually selling. What’s changing is that there are now many more paths.
Entrepreneurs may start quietly alongside another job, operate successful businesses without employees, juggle multiple income streams, or intentionally keep their businesses lean. The report calls this “the quiet start” and highlights that entrepreneurship increasingly begins through a series of small steps rather than a single leap. Technology has been a major enabler of this shift. Today’s entrepreneurs have access to tools that allow small teams and solo operators to achieve things that once were only possible for much larger organizations.
When you look at the typical banking experience today, where do you see the biggest friction points for entrepreneurs, and how is Tangerine working to better serve this segment?
Canada’s modern entrepreneurs already wear multiple hats, from operator and marketer to book keeper and technology decision-maker. The last thing they need is unnecessary friction, whether that’s administrative complexity, disconnected banking experiences, or a lack of support as they move their business forward.
At Tangerine, we’re focused on addressing that in two ways: first, by building a streamlined banking experience designed around how entrepreneurs today actually operate; and second, by creating opportunities for entrepreneurs to connect, learn, and grow together.
We know entrepreneurship can feel isolating at times, and the report reinforced the importance of community. While the broader Tangerine Business community creates opportunities for entrepreneurs to connect, share ideas, and learn from one another, we also wanted to bring entrepreneurs directly into the build process. That’s why we established the Tangerine Business Founders Circle, a group of entrepreneurs from across industries who work closely with us to share candid feedback and help shape the future of Tangerine Business.
If the financial sector gets this right, what would real progress look like for businesses over the next few years?
Real progress starts with recognition. The insights from the report make it clear that entrepreneurship has evolved, but many of the systems designed to support entrepreneurs haven’t evolved at the same pace, which tells us there’s still work to do. Progress means creating a financial system that reflects how entrepreneurs build businesses today, not how they built them 20 years ago.
When we get it right, every entrepreneur, whether they’re a creator, driver, consultant, or side-hustler, will be able to work within a system that’s been built with them, not just for them. We’ll know we’ve succeeded when our clients tell us they feel seen, supported, and more confident in how to move their businesses forward.
What has inspired you most personally from listening to the feedback and stories behind the report?
One of the report’s most striking findings was that 81 percent of entrepreneurs surveyed are optimistic about the future of their business. That optimism isn’t about certainty; it’s about having the confidence to keep moving forward despite it.
We saw that spirit come to life through the Tangerine Business Elevator Pitch competition in September. Nearly 200 entrepreneurs stepped forward for the chance to receive $50,000 to help accelerate momentum for their businesses. Their enthusiasm, conviction, and willingness to back themselves reflected exactly what we heard in the report: entrepreneurs remain overwhelmingly optimistic about what’s possible.
Our goal is to keep building Tangerine Business with the needs and input of our clients top of mind, helping entrepreneurs spend less time navigating complexity and more time focused on achieving their goals.
What advice would you share with founders who feel their current banking setup isn’t keeping pace with where their business is heading?
Expect more from the people and institutions that support your business. You shouldn’t have to adapt your way of working to fit into outdated models of support. Look for partners who understand how you’re building your business, who help reduce friction, and who give you confidence and clarity to focus on what matters most.
PRESENTED BY
What does today’s Canadian entrepreneur look like? Dig into the full Modern Entrepreneur Report from Tangerine and PwC Canada to find out. Get the report here.
Feature image courtesy Tangerine Bank.

articles.title: Is EU Inc in trouble? European innovators warn landmark startup reform is being stripped of its purpose | EU-Startups
articles.text:
“Dear Europe, why are you killing EU Inc?” That’s how many in the European startup community were greeted when they read this morning’s brief by the highly supported EU–INC initiative.
Backed by some of Europe’s most prominent startup founders and investors, the initiative has issued an urgent warning that the European Union’s proposed ‘EU Inc’ pan-European company framework is losing the very provisions that made it attractive to entrepreneurs.
In a public statement released on 15 October 2026, the campaign accused European policymakers of weakening the proposal through months of negotiations, reducing an ambitious effort to little more than a fast-track company registration system.
Since launch, the EU-INC campaign has since attracted more than 26,000 supporters from across 27 countries, including founders associated with Stripe, Mistral AI, Klarna and Wise, alongside investors from Atomico, Index Ventures and Seedcamp. Its central ambition has been to establish a common European company structure that would help startups access international investment, recruit talent and expand across borders without navigating fragmented national corporate systems.
In its latest statement, addressed directly to Europe’s Heads of State and Government, EU–INC declared: “The EU Inc you championed – one that will enable Europe to compete at scale – no longer exists. Months of negotiations have removed the core of the proposal. As it stands, it will do nothing to improve Europe’s competitiveness.”
The initiative has not been formally cancelled, and negotiations remain ongoing. However, campaigners argue that the emerging compromises threaten to undermine its original purpose.
From European dream to compromise
Known as the 28th regime, EU Inc was introduced by the European Commission on 18 March 2026 as an optional corporate framework operating alongside the 27 existing national systems.
The Commission’s original proposal would allow entrepreneurs to establish a company digitally within 48 hours for no more than €100, without minimum share capital requirements. It also envisaged simplified share transfers, digital insolvency procedures, access to modern financing instruments and a common employee stock option scheme with deferred taxation.
One of its central elements was freedom to choose the EU country in which a business incorporates, regardless of where its employees and operations are based. This would allow companies and investors to converge around familiar legal jurisdictions and standardised investment documentation, similar to the role Delaware plays in the United States.
The EU–INC campaign argues that restrictions on this freedom would prevent a recognised European corporate standard from emerging.
Stock options on the chopping block
Another major disagreement concerns employee stock options, which startups frequently use to attract skilled workers when they cannot match the salaries offered by larger companies.
The Commission originally proposed a harmonised framework under which taxation would be deferred until employees sold their shares, avoiding situations where workers face tax liabilities before receiving any proceeds.
However, the Irish presidency of the Council of the EU introduced restrictions in its July compromise text, limiting the proposed stock option scheme to companies with fewer than 1,000 employees and turnover below €450 million. Subsequent negotiations have raised further questions about whether the provisions will survive at all.
According to Agence Europe, discussions among EU ambassadors on 30 September failed to resolve disagreements over stock option taxation.
Stéphane Séjourné, European Commissioner responsible for Prosperity and Industrial Strategy, had already warned against weakening the framework during a meeting of industry ministers in Brussels on 24 September.
Séjourné said: “I cannot see the 28th regime and the Commission’s proposal without stock option harmonisation.”
The proposed central digital company register has also become a point of contention. The Commission initially envisaged an EU-level registration interface followed by a central register, designed to make company information accessible across Member States and simplify procedures such as opening bank accounts, verifying ownership and conducting compliance checks.
Yet the first Council compromise text removed plans for the central register, prompting criticism from campaigners who consider a shared digital infrastructure essential to establishing trust in the new corporate framework.
Workers’ rights enter the fray
Beyond these disagreements, EU Inc has encountered opposition from European trade unions concerned about its potential impact on workers’ rights.
On 24 September, hundreds of trade union activists demonstrated in Brussels, arguing that the proposed framework could enable companies to register in countries with less demanding corporate rules while operating elsewhere.
The European Trade Union Confederation (ETUC) has warned of potential risks to collective bargaining, employee representation and national labour protections.
The Commission maintains that EU Inc. would not override national employment and social legislation. EU–INC emphasised that workers would remain protected by the labour laws of the countries where they work, while companies and employees would continue to pay taxes according to applicable national rules.
Taxation represents another unresolved dimension. In July 2026, the European Parliament adopted recommendations for an optional tax regime accompanying EU Inc, including a single EU VAT number, centralised VAT declarations and refunds, and simplified corporate tax procedures.
This leaves open questions about how much administrative friction EU Inc would actually remove for businesses operating across multiple European markets.
A make-or-break moment for Europe
The dispute comes at a sensitive moment for European competitiveness. The EU has repeatedly identified fragmented regulation, limited access to growth capital and difficulties retaining entrepreneurial talent as barriers to building globally competitive technology companies.
With EU institutions targeting a political agreement before the end of 2026, the coming negotiations will determine how much of the Commission’s original proposal survives.
EU–INC is now appealing directly to Europe’s national leaders to intervene, reverse objections to its central provisions and restore what it considers the minimum requirements for a functioning European startup standard.
“If Europe’s leaders cannot even align on a solution like EU Inc, Europe’s founders will lose more than a proposal. They will lose faith in Europe’s ability to face the challenges of our time. Europe’s founders will have a future. Whether that future is European is in your hands.”
