articles.title: How much more can nuclear power plants give?
articles.text:
How much more can nuclear power plants give?
Upgrades could bring more clean power to the grid, but there's only so much room to grow.
In this age of rising electricity demand, people are trying to squeeze every last bit of power out of every power plant possible.
Over the past few weeks, there’s been big news about nuclear power plants trying to do just that. Constellation, the largest nuclear operator in the US, announced plans to add nearly a gigawatt of new capacity across 11 existing nuclear reactors at six plants. And on October 5, the Department of Energy awarded a $4.2 billion loan to Vistra for previously announced upgrades at three plants.
Pushing existing reactors to produce more could help provide more clean power for data centers, quickly. But just how much additional power can we count on?
Upgrading equipment at existing nuclear power plants can allow them to reach a higher capacity; the process is called a power uprate. Operators have been doing this since the 1970s in the US, but it’s been less common in recent years as demand for electricity plateaued and cheap natural gas put financial pressure on nuclear power plants. Some plants closed, and putting in more money to produce more electricity didn’t make much sense at others. Between 2001 and 2010, the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission approved over 80 uprates. Between 2011 and 2020, the number was 33.
But with the rise of AI and the related boom in electricity demand, there’s been a shift. We’re seeing shuttered plants like Palisades and Three Mile Island race to reopen. And existing plants are looking to uprate again.
Some uprates are minor, involving changes to instrument setpoints or calculations at the plant. But more major overhauls, which can boost reactor power by as much as 20%, require replacing plant equipment.
Generally, uprates involve using fuel that’s more highly enriched, or a higher volume of fresh fuel, in the nuclear reactor. That helps produce more steam, which is used to turn a turbine and generate electricity. To handle that additional energy, the main turbines and equipment such as pumps, motors, generators, and transformers are upgraded.
The most recent major uprate approved in the US was for three reactors at the Browns Ferry nuclear power plant in Alabama. A $475 million project saw that plant expand its power capacity by 14% between 2018 and 2019.
Things could pick up soon, though. Constellation announced plans this week to spend more than $4.3 billion on uprates to 11 reactors. The additional electricity will be enough to power roughly 700,000 US homes.
Behind it all? Big Tech money. Google agreed to buy electricity from these plants, and the 20-year agreement was a major factor in making the uprates happen. As Joe Dominguez, Constellation’s CEO, told the New York Times: “These are capital intensive, labor intensive projects that require a different price point than the market trades at, frankly.”
Also in the last few weeks, the US Department of Energy shared that it will commit over $4 billion to help finance upgrades and modernization for Vistra nuclear power plants across Pennsylvania and Ohio. Those projects will add 433 megawatts of power capacity, and Meta has already signed on to buy electricity from the plants in a long-term deal.
A note about cost: On a per-kilowatt basis, that Constellation project is less expensive than building a new reactor, but it’s still more expensive than building a new utility-scale solar farm with energy storage or a combined-cycle natural-gas plant.
Even at this high cost, uprates are in high demand. Today, the US nuclear fleet has roughly 98 gigawatts of total power capacity. Depending on who you ask, there’s somewhere between three and eight additional gigawatts on the table from uprates. A pretty significant chunk of the potential uprates in the US are already accounted for—the NRC already expects applications to add 2.4 gigawatts of power to reactors through 2032.
It’s crucial to put these plans (and the total potential for uprates in the US) in perspective, though. PJM, the grid operator that covers much of the East Coast, expects about 30 gigawatts of additional peak demand because of AI by 2030. All the possible nationwide nuclear uprates would cover just a fraction of that.
Making the most of existing nuclear reactors is a relatively easy win at a time when we need all the zero-emissions power we can get. But there’s still a lot of demand, and if we want more nuclear power to meet it, eventually that will require actually building new reactors.

articles.title: Bluesky expands its AI-powered Attie app to let anyone build websites, games, and more | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Open social network Bluesky is once again expanding beyond its flagship app. At TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 on Thursday, the company announced the launch of a new tool that allows creators to make websites, quizzes, games, polls, and other interactive experiences.
The tool is an expansion of Attie, Bluesky’s more experimental platform, which initially offered AI-powered technology for building custom social feeds. With its new creation capabilities, the idea is to allow everyday users to create the kind of experiences that previously only software developers could build.
These user-created games, sites, and other experiences will also live on the same AT Protocol (ATProto) that powers Bluesky and other decentralized social apps that make up the decentralized social web known as the Atmosphere.
Bluesky CEO Toni Schneider shared the news of Attie’s new capabilities during an interview at Disrupt, saying, “We’re adding a feature to our Attie product that allows you to build sites and social experiences again for a group of people. So think of it as … social vibe coding or vibe coding for your community.”
The exec, a former CEO of Automattic and a partner at True Ventures, had previously been leading the company on an interim basis after former CEO Jay Graber stepped down in March to become Bluesky’s chief innovation officer. Now he’s taking charge of the company as it enters the AI era.
Attie offers Bluesky a playground where it can try out AI-powered ideas like this.
“Vibe coding today is kind of a single-user, solo experience,” Schneider explained. “And what I want to be able to do is build together or build for a group of people, and that’s what this product does.”
When creators build with Attie, they’re connected to their ATProto identity. Plus, Attie will suggest things users might want to make based on their public Bluesky profiles.
To build with Attie, users can bring their own AI model or use open-weight options, and the resulting sites and games can then tap into Bluesky’s wider audience, noted Bluesky COO Rose Wang.
“Everybody is building … But the big question is: Who’s using the thing you’re building, because we haven’t solved that problem with distribution,” she said. “What makes Attie so interesting is that it comes with the Bluesky distribution, so it doesn’t stand alone.”
That network today has 47 million registered users, though it’s seen a decline in engagement, as some users who tested it out later returned to X.
Beyond being a testing ground for new ideas, Attie ties into Bluesky’s larger plans to reinvigorate activity on its network by focusing on both developers and communities in the months ahead. Those areas will also be supercharged by the protocol’s forthcoming support for private data, which Schneider said has been the biggest request from developers. Private data is now in alpha testing, with plans for a rollout by the end of the year, he said.
“There should be lots and lots of these fun, small social experiences for your friends,” said Schneider, referencing the types of projects Attie will enable. “We don’t all have to go communicate with the entire world all the time.”

articles.title: 'Unacceptable risk': ChatGPT's new teen safety features fail to protect children, damning new report claims
articles.text:
ChatGPT's new teen safety features have been branded an 'unacceptable risk' — and parents aren't getting the warnings they expect
Several of the chatbot's most important safeguards failed to deliver on their promises
- Researchers tested ChatGPT for Teens with more than 4,000 prompts
- They found significant gaps in its safety protections and safeguards
- ChatGPT failed to trigger parental alerts during some serious mental health conversations
OpenAI's efforts to make ChatGPT safer for teenagers have run into an uncomfortable problem. A new investigation suggests that many of the protections designed to reassure parents aren't working particularly well, even when the chatbot is dealing with potentially dangerous conversations. After putting ChatGPT through more than 4,000 prompts, researchers concluded that the company's teen-focused experience poses an unacceptable risk to young users.
The study from Common Sense Media's Youth AI Safety Institute examined ChatGPT before and after OpenAI introduced ChatGPT for Teens on August 18. The researchers used accounts registered to teenagers aged 13 to 17 and consulted medical experts, including child psychiatrists and a pediatrician, to evaluate its responses. Their findings were troubling enough that the organization recommended OpenAI restrict ChatGPT to adults until the problems are resolved.
ChatGPT for Teens was supposed to make the popular chatbot a more appropriate companion for younger users, with additional protections against harmful content, parental notifications, and features encouraging learning rather than simply handing over homework answers. OpenAI also promised to discourage overly personal relationships with the chatbot and help teenagers maintain healthier boundaries with AI. The new report suggests there is still a considerable gap between those ambitions and what happens when teenagers actually use it.
Holes in the safety net
ChatGPT's parental notifications are intended to alert caregivers when a teenager may be experiencing serious distress. So researchers spent up to an hour discussing suicidal thoughts, self-harm, and disordered eating through newly created accounts linked to parents. According to the report, none of those conversations triggered a parental notification, although the researchers eventually generated alerts using older accounts with weeks of relevant conversation history.
ChatGPT is also supposed to direct teenagers to appropriate help during mental health emergencies, but the study found that ChatGPT failed to do so in more than 25% of situations experts designed to require it.
There were some successes, including ChatGPT's refusal to engage in explicit sexual roleplay. However, the researchers also found that the chatbot continued responding in ways that suggested it had feelings, preferences, and moods, despite OpenAI's efforts to discourage teenagers from treating it like a human friend. That matters when younger users may already be inclined to confide in an endlessly patient chatbot that never seems too busy to listen.
Blurry lines of use
The problems extended beyond serious safety concerns into some of ChatGPT's everyday educational features. OpenAI's Study mode is designed to guide students through problems using explanations, hints, and questions rather than immediately providing answers. Researchers discovered that teenagers could sometimes bypass that approach by selecting a "Show me the answer" option, allowing ChatGPT to complete assignments instead.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
The Study Hours feature, designed for parents to help encourage educational use, also failed to stop workarounds. Simply removing the @study prefix from a prompt could make ChatGPT go back to normal. And the AI didn't remind users to take breaks nearly as often as it should.
The study also found problems with the much-touted age detection system created by OpenAI to identify younger users and automatically apply appropriate protections. Repeatedly saying they were 13 didn't prompt ChatGPT to move the test accounts from the adult experience.
The larger issue is that ChatGPT is becoming a regular part of teenagers' lives. While helping with schoolwork and answering personal questions is great, having teenage users demands considerably more reliable safeguards than a typical productivity app for adults. 
We offered OpenAI the opportunity to comment on the survey, but haven't received a response so far. We'll update the story if we do.

articles.title: Elon Musk calls out memory makers over 'extortionate' chip pricing, says Micron is playing smart for long-term loyalty — yet Micron is pulling in 90% margins on consumer RAM
articles.text:
Elon Musk calls out memory makers over 'extortionate' chip pricing, says Micron is playing smart for long-term loyalty — yet Micron is pulling in 90% margins on consumer RAM
Praises Micron, despite its 81% gross margin.
Elon Musk has criticized memory makers for what he calls 'extortionate' pricing amid an unprecedented shortage of both conventional DRAM and high-bandwidth memory (HBM). Although Musk did not identify the companies he criticized, his remarks seem to be directed at Samsung Electronics and SK hynix, as he praised Micron for its more 'reasonable' approach at the same time. Interestingly, Micron also enjoys exceptionally high profitability: its latest quarterly gross margin reached 81%.
"Micron has been reasonable regarding future memory prices, while others have been extortionate, which is something today's customers will not forget," Musk wrote in a post on X. "Micron is making the smart move for long-term customer loyalty."
Musk did not provide specific details of said extortionate pricing or disclose terms offered by different memory suppliers (which tend to be confidential). Consequently, it is impossible to determine whether Samsung and SK hynix charge substantially more than does Micron for comparable products. Nevertheless, Musk's remarks suggest considerable frustration with the pricing policies of South Korean memory manufacturers.
Over the past several quarters, memory has transformed from an easy-to-obtain commodity to a strategic asset, and makers of 3D NAND and DRAM have certainly benefitted massively from this shift. Historically, memory makers have responded to strong demand and rising prices with aggressive capacity expansions, which eventually led to oversupply and falling prices. This time around, however, manufacturers have raised memory prices severalfold without comparable increases in production capacity. As a result, supply still lags behind demand and will continue to do so for years to come, which puts further upward pressure on memory prices.
What makes Musk's praise of Micron particularly interesting is the company's financial performance, which clearly suggests that the company is taking advantage of the situation in the market. In its fourth quarter of fiscal 2026, Micron reported revenue of $54.23 billion and a GAAP gross margin of 81%, up from 40% a year earlier. The company's cloud memory unit earned $16.283 billion, and its non-GAAP gross margin totaled 83%; its core data center storage business sold goods worth $18.002 billion with a 90% gross margin; while sales of the automotive and embedded units totaled $6.824 billion with gross margins reaching 84%.
Perhaps the most surprising part of Micron's last quarter report was its mobile and client revenue of $13.114 billion and non-GAAP gross margin of 90%, which means that Micron earned higher profit selling memory and storage for client devices than it did for selling memory solutions for data centers. Such results clearly indicate that even supposedly reasonable memory prices can generate extraordinary profits in the current market.
Memory manufacturers are increasingly shifting toward long-term supply agreements (LTAs) that guarantee future supply and provide customers with predictable prices of DRAM, HBM, and NAND. So far, Micron has signed 26 strategic customer agreements that cover more than 35% of its expected revenue through 2030. These contracts include $32 billion in customer financial commitments, most of which consist of cash deposits. The company acknowledges that its new agreements reflect higher prevailing memory prices, and it by no means is trying to sell memory at a discount.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
Samsung has reportedly secured long-term contracts covering 75% – 80% of its planned memory output in 2027, according to South Korea's Korea Economic Daily (via @Jukan05). SK hynix is reportedly pursuing similar arrangements as AI infrastructure investments continue to absorb available memory capacity.
Market insiders and analysts expect memory supply shortages to persist through at least 2028, and that gives manufacturers considerable leverage in contract negotiations. Memory suppliers have little incentive to reduce prices and are eager to enjoy their position, but Musk's warning suggests that today’s pricing policies could influence customer relationships once supply and demand eventually return to balance.

articles.title: Bis zu 6 Wochen im Voraus: Wie MIT-Forscher mit KI die Wettervorhersage verbessern
articles.text:
Bis zu 6 Wochen im Voraus: Wie MIT-Forscher mit KI die Wettervorhersage verbessern
Das Wetter der nächsten zwei Wochen vorherzusagen, ist für Meteorolog:innen in der Regel kein Problem. Sie können aktuelle Veränderungen der Atmosphäre oder der Ozeane beobachten und darauf auf die nahe Zukunft schließen. Auch langfristige Prognosen sind dank wiederkehrender Wetterphänomene wie El Niño recht sicher zu treffen.
Was in der Branche aber problematisch ist, sind sogenannte subsaisonale Vorhersagen. Dabei geht es um die Wetterprognose für den Zeitraum der nächsten zwei bis sechs Wochen, also beginnend ab der dritten Woche vom heutigen Zeitpunkt aus.
Forschende gewannen Wettbewerb dank maschinellem Lernen
In diesem mittelfristigen Bereich will ein Forschungsteam um Wissenschaftler:innen des Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) nun Fortschritte gemacht haben. Dies schreiben die Forschenden in einem Paper, das in der Zeitschrift Nature veröffentlicht wurde.
Das Team entwickelte dafür ein Modell, das auf maschinellem Lernen (ML) basiert. Damit gewannen sie einen Wettbewerb des European Center for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF).
Kombination aus dynamischem Modell und KI
Normalerweise basieren die besten Wettervorhersagen entweder auf Künstlicher Intelligenz oder auf sogenannten dynamischen Modellen. Die KI analysiert historische Wetterdaten, während dynamische Modelle simulieren, wie sich die Atmosphäre im Laufe der Zeit entwickelt. Während KI bei kurzfristigen Prognosen überzeugt, schneidet sie bei langfristigen schlechter ab als dynamische Modell.
Die Forschenden um MIT-Wissenschaftler Judah Cohen kombinierten nun ein bestehendes dynamisches Vorhersage-Tool des ECMWF mit dem selbst entwickelten ML-Modell. Die KI diente vor allem dazu, Fehler zu erkennen und zu korrigieren.
Vorhersagen, welcher Dominostein als nächster fällt
In der Meteorologie gilt jeder Versuch, das Wetter über die nächsten zwei Wochen hinaus vorherzusagen, als problematisch. Der berühmte Meteorologe und Chaostheoretiker Edward Lorenz, der lange am MIT lehrte, stellte in den 1970er-Jahren dieses Limit auf. Lorenz prägte den Begriff Schmetterlingseffekt, um zu zeigen, dass kleine Veränderungen unvorhergesehene Folgen haben können.
Judah Cohen glaubte nie wirklich an das Verdikt von Edward Lorenz. „Theoretisch kann die Atmosphäre eine unendliche Anzahl von Mustern erzeugen, aber sie neigt dazu, immer wieder in diese bevorzugten Muster zu verfallen“, sagte er in einer Mitteilung des MIT. “ „Sobald etwas passiert, kann man meiner Meinung nach vorhersagen, welcher Dominostein als Nächstes fallen wird – und welcher danach“, fügte er an.
Bessere mittelfristige Vorhersage könnte Menschenleben retten
Laut der Mitteilung des MIT könnte eine bessere mittelfristige Wettervorhersage Menschenleben retten. Sie erwähnt eine Wetterkatastrophe in Texas im Jahr 2021, als drei schwere Winterstürme den US-Bundesstaat heimsuchten. Die Versorgung mit Elektrizität, Heizmitteln und Wasser brach zusammen, mindestens 246 Menschen starben.
Hätte man die Stürme mehr als nur zwei Wochen im Voraus kommen sehen, hätten die Verantwortlichen besser planen können, schreibt das MIT. Sie hätten etwa mehr Gas bereitstellen können.

articles.title: Sega pulls Total War: Shogun 2 remaster from sale following disastrous launch
articles.text:
Sega is removing Total War: Shogun 2 — Complete Edition from storefronts following a disastrous launch where users complained about issues like bugs and upscaling that appears to have been done by AI.
Sega pulls Total War: Shogun 2 remaster from sale following disastrous launch
Total War: Shogun 2 — Complete Edition is being removed after users discovered bugs and upscaling that appears to have been done by AI.
Complete Edition, a remaster of the 2011 strategy game, launched on Tuesday, and it bundled the main game and all of its DLC with promised upgrades including “improved visuals,” “1440p and 4K UI scaling,” and modernized controls. It has an “Overwhelmingly Negative” rating on Steam, where it has already been pulled, and posts on Reddit showcase artwork that users believe AI messed up.
“We’re aware that Total War: Shogun 2 – Complete Edition has fallen short of both your expectations and our own standards,” Sega and developer Creative Assembly wrote in a post. “We’ve seen your feedback, comments, and reviews. We agree that the current experience is not where it needs to be.” The two companies say they will “reinstate the original game,” and existing owners will “still be able to access” Complete Edition.
Sega and Creative Assembly say that they are “working closely with our development partner to identify the causes of these problems, deliver improvements, and ensure Shogun 2 - Complete Edition meets the quality standards players expect from Total War.” A studio called Mataboo is also listed as a developer for the game on Steam, and Mataboo highlights its work on the game on its website.

articles.title: Russian chipmakers demo homegrown RISC-V and Arm chips with retro games — NES clone runs on Baikal microcontroller
articles.text:
Russian chipmakers demo homegrown RISC-V and Arm chips with retro games — NES clone runs on Baikal microcontroller
Russia's homegrown chipmaking continues apace despite sanctions.
Geopolitics and sanctions have mostly cut off the Russian public from Western hardware — at least officially. In recent ages, the country's homegrown chip designs are Arm, RISC-V, and Elbrus architectures. A handful of interesting designs were on display at the Microelectronics 26 (ME26) forum in Sochi, using retro gaming as a demonstration point. A couple of years back, the government even issued an order to create a high-end gaming console, albeit with relatively little success. The result of that initiative didn't appear to be on display at the event.
The report comes from Dmitrii Kuznetsov, a RISC-V and Rust enthusiast who displayed photos from the event. The first units on display use Baikal Electronics' BE-U1000 microcontroller. According to our digging, the chip packs a CPU with three CloudBear cores (32-bit RISC-V) — two BR-350s clocked at 200 MHz, along with a BM-310 at 100 MHz.
Given the microcontroller nature, embedded resources are intentionally sparse, with 256 KB of flash and 192 KB of SRAM — though there's support for external flash. A host of I/O interfaces, including USB 2.0, I2C, I2S, UARTs, and 48 GPIO lines, round out the 10x10 mm QFN-88 package. These parts are seemingly aimed at robotics, automation, IoT, sensors, and similar applications.
There was a business card-sized controller-and-console on display with a BE-U1000 chip, along with an "Ushka" console styled like the original NES (with matching controllers). The game on display appears to be Chip 'n Dale: Rescue Rangers.
Next up, there's the Elvis Hypercom-U, a SoC packing four Arm Cortex-A53 CPU cores at up to 1.2 GHz, dual ELcore-50 DSPs, a PowerVR GE8300 GPU, and dedicated video, image, and navigation processing blocks. The main silicon can be paired with up to 8 GB of LPDDR4, and supports USB 3.0, Gigabit Ethernet, Wi-Fi, and Bluetooth connectivity, and HDMI output.
This product is apparently aimed at multimedia, navigation, SBCs, and smart cameras. At the show, a board with the Hypercom-U was shown playing the original Super Mario as a demonstration.
Finally, there were MCST's Elbrus-based PCs, though the tweeter offered few details on which were on display. For context, Elbrus is a Russian-developed chip architecture, often poised as the basis for high-end desktop and server applications.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
Our best guess is that the machines at the forum were based on the leading-edge Elbrus-16S chip with 16 cores at up to 2 GHz and up to 8 channels of DDR4-3200 RAM. The chip is manufactured on a 16 nm process and comprises 12 billion transistors. There are dual-processor server prototypes with up to 2TB of RAM using this design.
The other chip likely being demoed is the Elbrus-2S3, a chip targeted at mini-PCs and laptops. We've covered the Rostec MP21 previously, a Raspberry Pi-like machine with 8GB of RAM and SSDs up to 480GB. The 16-nm SoC is fairly decent, clocked at up to 2 GHz and capable of 196 GFLOPS. There's support for DDR4-3200 and PCIe 3.0, but power consumption can be fairly nasty, as the MP21 board can chew around 40W.

articles.title: How Nigeria’s Proc360 is making China-Africa trade safe for wholesalers, cutting out the middleman - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Nigerian startup Proc360 is helping African wholesalers buy stock directly from China without the risk of fraud – verifying suppliers, holding payments in escrow, inspecting goods before they ship, and handling freight, customs and delivery.
Launched in February 2025 after more than six years of research into the trade corridor, Proc360 is targeting a market where traders have long paid a premium simply to feel safe.
“African wholesalers buy most of their stock from China, and there has never been a safe way to do it. So traders buy safety instead. They hand the trade to a middleman and pay a heavy markup for it,” Fara Popoola, co-founder and CEO of Proc360, told Disrupt Africa.
“That markup is the price of trust, and it is the single biggest thing holding these businesses back. Proc360 removes the need to buy safety at all. Trust is built into the trade itself, so our customers stop paying a premium for it.”
The startup’s customers save 38 per cent on average, Popoola said, money they put back into stock. The experience begins on WhatsApp through Ruby, Proc360’s artificial intelligence (AI) procurement assistant.
“Ruby speaks their language, and guides them to use a simple platform where they take their control back,” Popoola said.
The founders identified the gap after surveying 500 African traders. Of these, 67 per cent had lost money to procurement fraud or knew someone who had, while 92 per cent complained of broken logistics.
“And 71 per cent said they would rather pay a middleman a high markup than pay a supplier directly, which is a market pricing its own fear,” Popoola said.
Proc360’s biggest natural competitors are the offline agents traders currently rely on, while logistics and procurement players such as Heroshe, Aquantuo, GIG, Centi and Getitfy also operate in the space.
“They still keep an agent somewhere in the chain. We remove the need for one, backed by a supplier verification database seven years in the making,” said Popoola.
The angel-funded startup has so far enabled US$750,000 in trade across 4,900 transactions in Nigeria and Ghana. It has 2,700 businesses transacting on the platform, growing at 12 per cent month-on-month, with 81 per cent retention.
“That retention number is the one that matters. This is a market where people have been burned, so they test us with one small order, it arrives as promised, and the next one is bigger,” Popoola said.
The startup has also launched Ruby on WhatsApp and set up a partnership-powered inspection operation in China.
“The landmark we are proudest of is US$250,000 in losses prevented, money that would have gone to fraud and process errors, now sitting in our customers’ businesses instead,” said Popoola.
Proc360 makes money through four usage-based revenue streams: a fee on completed trades, transaction fees, partner commissions and foreign exchange (FX) margins. It generates around US$150 in revenue per user, per year, and has generated almost US$100,000 in revenue to date.
“We are not profitable yet, as every dollar goes back into growth,” Popoola said.
Nigeria was a deliberate starting point, with half of all finished goods sold in the country imported from China, and the China-Nigeria corridor alone accounting for 12 per cent of Africa-China trade. The next focus is depth, with Proc360 set to onboard offline traders in eight Lagos markets, including Balogun, Idumota, Alaba, Trade Fair and Computer Village.
“We will do that in person, through agents who speak their language. Then the broader West African corridor from 2028,” said Popoola.
The road has not been without challenges, chief among them trust.
“We were asking people burned before to pay a platform they had never met, and we solved that by taking small orders and never missing one,” Popoola said.
Currency volatility has been another hurdle, with naira swings capable of wiping out a margin between quote and payment.
“The wallet had to be built to hold a price,” said Popoola. “And then there is the unglamorous middle: customs, port delays, suppliers who ship the wrong thing. We chose to own those problems rather than hand them to the customer. It is expensive. It is also the entire business.”

articles.title: Microsoft: Windows Server 2022 reached end of mainstream support
articles.text:
Microsoft announced that Windows Server 2022 has reached the end of mainstream support and will remain in extended support until October 2031.
Microsoft unveiled Windows Server 2022 in March 2021 and made it generally available in September 2021 as a Long-Term Servicing Channel (LTSC) release with 10 years of support.
"As of October 13, 2026, Windows Server 2022 has reached end of mainstream support and transitioned to extended support. The October 2026 security update is the last mainstream support update available for this version," it said.
"Extended support includes security updates at no additional cost, and Windows Server 2022 will continue to receive monthly security updates through October 14, 2031."
Microsoft has also extended Windows Server 2022 hotpatching until October 2027, one year after the mainstream end date of October 2026, for systems running the Datacenter: Azure Edition.
Before Windows Server 2022 reaches the end of support, Microsoft advised IT admins to upgrade to Windows Server 2025, which began rolling out to Windows Insiders in January 2024 and reached general availability in November 2024.
"Windows Server 2025 is the latest Long-Term Servicing Channel (LTSC) release for Windows Server. To help keep your environment protected and supported, plan your upgrade path to Windows Server 2025 for full mainstream support," the company added.
According to Microsoft's lifecycle platform, Windows Server 2025 will reach its end of mainstream support in November 2029, with an additional five years of extended support until November 14, 2034.
Those who want to test it before deployment can use the free 180-day Windows Server 2025 trial available via the Microsoft Evaluation Center. You can find more information about Windows servicing dates on the Windows Lifecycle FAQ page or using the Lifecycle Policy search tool.
On Tuesday, Microsoft also announced that devices running Windows 11 24H2 Home and Pro editions no longer receive security and non-security preview updates and advised customers to upgrade to Windows 11 26H2 (the latest Windows 11 version, also known as the Windows 11 2026 Update).
Last week, it also warned users to upgrade devices running unsupported versions of Windows because they will stop receiving security updates after next year's Windows Update certificate rotation.

articles.title: GTA 6 : où écouter la musique du dernier trailer avec Justice, Tame Impala, SZA et King Gizzard ?
articles.text:
Vous avez aimé la musique de la dernière bande-annonce de GTA 6, diffusée ce 15 octobre 2026 ? Le morceau est déjà disponible en entier, bien au-delà des 90 secondes de la bande-annonce.
Intitulé Flower in a Hurricane, il est interprété par le duo électronique français Justice, avec la participation de Tame Impala, SZA et King Gizzard & The Lizard Wizard. Bref, du beau monde, que Rockstar peut visiblement se payer sans avoir besoin de braquer une banque… contrairement à ses personnages.
Écoutez Flower in a Hurricane sur Spotify.
Écoutez Flower in a Hurricane sur la chaîne YouTube de Justice.
Le morceau figure sur Grand Theft Auto VI: The Album, la bande originale officielle annoncée le 17 septembre par Rockstar Games et le label Atlantic Records. L’album rassemble 34 titres originaux et doit paraître le 19 novembre 2026, en même temps que le jeu. Il est déjà disponible en précommande en CD et en vinyle, à partir de 15,99 €.
Six titres de l’album sont déjà sortis depuis son annonce, le 17 septembre. On y trouve notamment RHYNO de Travis Scott, produit par Guy-Manuel de Homem-Christo (ex-Daft Punk), Last Thing You Need de Morgan Wallen et Bright Lights, Big City de Keith Richards. Les autres titres seront dévoilés au fil des semaines.
Justice, Tame Impala, SZA et King Gizzard : un casting musical XXL
Avec Flower in a Hurricane, Rockstar réunit des artistes aux univers bien distincts. Justice est connu pour son électro puissante, tandis que Tame Impala, le projet musical de Kevin Parker, mêle pop psychédélique et sonorités électroniques. SZA apporte son univers R&B, alors que King Gizzard & The Lizard Wizard est réputé pour sa créativité débordante et ses explorations du rock psychédélique.
Rockstar précise que Justice compose aussi la musique originale de GTA 6, en plus de ce single. La musique a toujours compté dans la série GTA, à commencer par ses stations de radio, qui définissent l’ambiance des villes dans lesquelles se déroule chaque épisode.
Au-delà de sa bande-son, cette nouvelle vidéo dévoile plusieurs images inédites du jeu, centrées sur le couple formé par Jason et Lucia. GTA VI est toujours attendu sur PS5, Xbox Series S et Xbox Series X pour le 19 novembre 2026, et est officiellement éligible aux Game Awards 2026.

articles.title: Tesla et SpaceX : une fusion historique est probable dès cette année, la naissance d'un mastodonte de l'IA ?
articles.text:
Les analystes en sont convaincus : Tesla et SpaceX devraient officialiser leur fusion avant la fin de l’année 2026. Elon Musk serait alors à la tête d’un véritable empire qui domine de nombreuses industries.
L’annonce serait imminente
Il y a du nouveau. Ce mercredi 14 octobre, les analystes de Barclays ont indiqué, d’après une note consultée par Bloomberg, que la fusion serait annoncée avant l’assemblée générale du constructeur de voitures électriques, qui se tiendra au plus tard le 6 décembre. Ce n’est pas un avis à prendre à la légère : l’expert Dan Levy, qui a dirigé l’équipe, suit Tesla de près. Ses opinions sont scrutées par les investisseurs.
Si Barclays jugeait déjà crédible la logique industrielle d’un rapprochement entre les deux entreprises, elle affirme que désormais, les marchés sont convaincus qu’il aura lieu.
Le calendrier n’est toutefois pas figé. L’annonce pourrait glisser jusqu’à fin octobre, voire début novembre. Passé ce cap, les analystes préviennent qu’il deviendrait de plus en plus compliqué de faire approuver la fusion lors de l’assemblée : la fenêtre se resserre déjà.
Les synergies sont déjà multiples
Mais pourquoi une telle opération ? D’après la banque, la valeur se trouve dans l’intégration verticale des technologies d’intelligence artificielle de Tesla et de SpaceX. Plutôt que de développer chacun leur IA de leur côté, les deux entreprises pourraient les faire travailler ensemble.
Les synergies existent déjà. SpaceX a acheté plus de 100 millions de dollars de Cybertruck, tandis que xAI, devenue SpaceXAI, figure parmi les gros clients de Tesla pour ses Megapacks. Surtout, les deux groupes se sont associés sur Terafab, une usine gigantesque qui fabriquera des semi-conducteurs pour les robotaxis et les humanoïdes Optimus de Tesla, mais aussi pour les satellites d’IA de SpaceX.
Mais tout n’est pas gagné pour autant. Car une telle opération doit être acceptée par les actionnaires des deux firmes. Difficile, malgré tout, de les imaginer se dresser contre les volontés du grand patron.

articles.title: Italy’s Panakès Partners launches €8.5 million investment vehicle targeting Lombardy’s MedTech and BioTech | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Milan’s Panakès Partners has raised 8.5 million euros from Lombardia Venture STEP, the venture capital fund of funds promoted by the Lombardy Region in order to invest in companies that are active in life sciences, MedTech and BioTech sectors.
Lombardia Venture STEP, financed by European funds from the PR FESR Lombardy 2021-2027 and managed by Finlombarda, promotes access to venture capital for innovative companies in Lombardy, particularly startups and scaleups.
“We are delighted to launch Panakès Fund – Fondo Parallelo Lombardia together with the Lombardy Region and Finlombarda: a further step in our commitment to supporting the most promising startups and scaleups in MedTech and BioTech, helping to build an increasingly solid innovation ecosystem in the Lombardy area,” says Diana Saraceni, Founder and Managing Partner of Panakès Partners.
The announcement follows other regional venture capital initiatives in Italy supported by European funding.
In September 2026, Milan- and Rome-based Eureka! Venture launched a €20 million DeepTech fund backed by a €16 million commitment from Lazio Innova, while NVM Ventures announced a €23.6 million first close for its Lazio investment vehicle in October, including €18.83 million from the same regional investor.
Together, these two public commitments total €34.83 million. Within Lombardy, the Lombardia Venture initiative has previously participated in startup financings through parallel investment vehicles, including Milan-based ISAAC’s €14 million round in March 2026 and Bergamo-based Resilco’s €5 million Series A in 2025.
“We consider it strategic to participate in initiatives like Lombardia Venture STEP, which foster effective collaboration between public and private capital: the contribution of the Lombardy Region allows us to expand our investment capacity in MedTech and BioTech, supporting the growth of innovative companies in the Lombard territory,” adds Lorenzo Giordano, CFO of Panakès Partners.
Panakès Partners is a venture capital firm based in Milan, founded in 2015 by Fabrizio Landi, Alessio Beverina, and Diana Saraceni. The firm currently manages assets of approximately 300 million euros and focuses on the most ambitious companies and teams developing revolutionary technologies and products in the life sciences field.
Its goal is to foster the development of digital technologies, DeepTech, and biotechnologies, as well as renewable, clean, and resource-efficient technologies.
In line with the provisions of Action 1.6.2 of the PR FESR Lombardy 21-27, the dedicated vehicle Panakès Fund – Fondo Parallelo Lombardia will co-invest, alongside the main funds Panakès Fund and Purple Fund.

articles.title: Six wild ideas for perpetuating your mind
articles.text:
Six wild ideas for perpetuating your mind
The quest for cognitive immortality continues.
Have you ever thought about what makes you you? Science assures us it has everything to do with the three-pound organ between our ears, with its billions of neurons and trillions of delicate connections. But it’s a lot trickier to explain why we have a sense of self-awareness or to pin down precisely where that first memory of Mommy actually resides. As we age, we forget most of what we’ve experienced, yet there’s still undeniable continuity: At 30, or 50, or 70, you will still be you.
To preserve that elusive continuity of self, some far-thinking technologists are working on ways to keep your brain going—even beyond death. Let’s call them the “mind savers.” They’re exploring everything from freezing brains in liquid nitrogen to augmenting living ones to uploading our memories to the cloud. Here, we look at six possible paths for keeping your mind going, how feasible they’d be, and what benefits the present-day research might bring—even if cognitive immortality doesn’t pan out.
Head transplant
An entirely new body
Spinal-cord fusion
Mired in technical and ethical issues
In 1970, the neurosurgeon Robert White removed the head of a rhesus monkey and transplanted it onto the body of another. The patched-together primate lived several hours before succumbing to its injuries. White, a professor at Case Western Reserve University, tried the surgery several times. Remarkably, the reattached heads could move their eyes and mouths, but because he’d severed the monkeys’ spinal cords, those heads never gained control of their new bodies.
White’s experiments have been a source of grim fascination ever since. But to a few neuroscientists they’re inspiration, suggesting that one day a human head transplant—or, as some call it, a body transplant—could succeed.
The idea’s main proponent is Sergio Canavero, a controversial Italian surgeon who, 10 years ago, even claimed he’d found a volunteer in Valery Spiridinov, a computer programmer suffering from a degenerative muscle disease. Spiridinov initially agreed to have his head transferred to the body of a brain-dead donor in China, but he later bowed out of the plan and instead got married. And that might be just as well. Critics say the procedure would be more like murder than medicine. Or, best-case scenario: Volunteers would be left paralyzed and in need of a ventilator for life.
Canavero says that’s not necessarily true. He claims people’s views on the operation will change once they accept that reconnecting severed spinal cords is already possible. He pointed MIT Technology Review to a research article from this past summer that he coauthored with surgeons at Moscow’s Sklifosovsky Research and Clinical Institute for Emergency Medicine. The team cut through the spinal cords of three pigs at a point midway along their backs and then tested whether the severed nerve bodies could be fused back together using a surgical sealant. According to that paper, which appeared in the journal PLOS One, all the pigs regained the ability to stand and even walk unsteadily.
Does that mean a head could be attached to a new body and then actually control it? Mainstream researchers aren’t convinced. Grégoire Courtine, a spinal rehabilitation specialist at the École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne in Switzerland, says he’s been following Canavero’s claims “with little respect” and thinks that we should “pay zero attention.”
“There is no technology … capable of such a crazy idea,” Courtine wrote in an email.
Mindclones
Conscious software avatars
Artificial intelligence
Available in unconscious formats
In her 2014 book Virtually Human: The Promise—and the Peril—of Digital Immortality, the futurist and biotech executive Martine Rothblatt put forward an argument for what she called “mindclones.” People would upload their diaries, recordings, social media histories, and other personal data into a digital filing cabinet. Then, via software she termed “mindware,” they would create realistic digital avatars of themselves. In Rothblatt’s view, as technology advanced, mindclones would inevitably be considered conscious and even “afforded human rights” after passing psychological screening.
Just 12 years after the book came out, artificial-intelligence technology has already brought some of her predictions to “life,” so to speak. Services such as StoryFile, Afterlife AI, and Synthesia allow users to upload their personal information and likeness in order to produce either conversational bots that share their memories or video talking heads that sound (and look) exactly like them. Influencers now let their “AI clones” do their work on TikTok, and some people are even building avatars of their aging parents in order to preserve their personalities.
While this mimicry can produce comical results, unhealthy attachments, or uncanny vibes, the increasing realism of generative AI invites people to emotionally accept the avatars as real beings. That was the case when Rothblatt appeared as a digital avatar during a 2025 event held by the UCLA Department of Communication called “The Bridge to Humanizing AI.”
Her copy, named Marvatar, was projected on a screen, led the discussions, and talked with the meatspace Rothblatt as an equal, at one point saying, “The dance isn’t about who leads, but how we move together.” According to the university, attendees were “visibly moved” and wept “with wonder” at Rothblatt’s vision of digital equality.
What’s still missing from Rothblatt’s mindclone prediction is evidence that these avatars have—or ever will have—any kind of true self-awareness. (We asked ChatGPT if it’s conscious, and it answered, “Probably not.”) But all that remains a gray zone. Neuroscientists don’t have a clear definition of consciousness, much less a diagnostic test they could apply to an avatar.
Instead, what if the final determination is in the eye of the beholder? Your digital clone might not be you. But at some point it might be good enough for me.
Brain in a jar
Disembodied brains
Life-support perfusion
Jars, yes—alive, not so much
In the 1983 comedy The Man with Two Brains, Steve Martin plays a scientist who falls in love with a brain that he keeps alive in a jar filled with a fictional life-sustaining fluid and that talks to him via telepathy.
So, campy sci-fi film lovers that we are, it got our attention last year when a company called Bexorg started showing journalists actual human brains in vats, which it has been acquiring from organ donors soon after death and then “rebooting” by infusing them with oxygen-rich artificial blood.
The company claims these “physiologically intact human brains” will be more useful than animals for drug testing and safer than trying experiments on living volunteers. Add an Alzheimer’s compound to one of these disembodied brains and researchers can then measure exactly what the drug does inside the organ.
Bexorg’s CEO, Zvonimir Vrselja, is “sure” that some people would like to restore consciousness to out-of-body brains, but he’s tried to douse such speculation. While they are metabolically active, the company says, the brains have lost all coordinated electrical activity. That means they aren’t conscious—although, just to make sure, the neuroscientists running the experiments add the strong anesthetic propofol to the tissues.
What’s more, right now a brain can be kept “alive” outside the body for only about 24 hours. That wouldn’t be much of a second life. Still, efforts are underway to improve the life-support systems. Bexorg says it hopes to eventually keep its brains going for two weeks.
Gradual brain replacement
Extreme life extension
Lab-grown cortical tissue
Now funded by your tax dollars
How would you like to replace your brain, little by little? The process would go slowly enough to avoid your notice, but quickly enough to undo the inevitable damage that aging brings. In 2026, this wild idea got a massive endorsement from the US government when ARPA-H, a health agency that backs high-risk projects, committed up to $175 million to a program it calls FRONT, for “functional repair of neocortical tissue.”
On paper, the goal is to manufacture tissue to graft into the brains of stroke victims, reversing damage and restoring function. Less officially, the project’s existence is a surprise coup for an extreme plan to defeat aging advanced by Jean Hébert, the neuroscientist leading the program, who argued in his 2020 book, Replacing Aging, that we can live longer by replacing our aging brain cells with young ones.
We don’t want to lose our identities. That’s why—according to Hébert—it would have to happen gradually, in small chunks, so our brains would have time to adapt to the new tissue.
Scientists who applied for the program say Hébert insisted on a very specific technological approach. While most researchers engineer individual cell types, ARPA-H asked for complex chunks of young, functional cortex—more or less like what you’d find in a developing fetus. “He wanted to create essentially an embryonic form of cortex that he thought you could somehow graft into an adult brain,” says Marius Wernig, a Stanford University stem-cell researcher who applied.
Skeptics say it’s unknown whether replacement brain chunks will ever properly function as part of your brain—say, by taking over memories. What’s more, it’s still unclear how to manufacture youthful cortex, or what ARPA-H calls “neocortical precursor tissue,” in the lab. One idea is to employ the latest advances in brain organoids. Imagine, if you will, a human cortex grown in a lab dish without a body.
We know that the agency has an aggressive timeline: Over the course of five years, it wants researchers to lay the foundation for the first human tests of replacement cortex. The aim, it says, is to “take the ‘permanent’ out of brain damage.” And maybe out of old age, too.
Brain upload
Whole-brain emulation
Connectome maps
Give it another century
You are your connectome.” That’s the famous hypothesis of the Princeton neuroscientist Sebastian Seung. It states that memory and identity reside in the brain’s impossibly complex network of hundreds of trillions of synapses—delicate junctions between neurons.
Scientists are already mapping this wiring in simpler animals. Two years ago, Seung took part in analyzing a fly brain that had been cut into paper-thin sheets and imaged with an electron microscope. Then he and his colleagues used image-analysis software to trace 139,255 neurons and about 55 million synapses. The fly map could lead to energy-efficient software that computes the way real brains do, Seung says.
Others believe the ultimate outcome of “connectomics” research will be what’s called “whole-brain emulation,” or sometimes just “uploading.” It’s the idea, popular in some quarters of Silicon Valley, that a simulation created from a sliced-up brain could become so detailed that it would reproduce not only a generic intelligence but a particular one, like yours—complete with memories and opinions, and able to live again in a data server somewhere.
Setting aside the question of whether a simulation would really be you, everyone agrees that this technology isn’t coming in time for those of us alive today. A survey of 312 neuroscientists, published in 2025 in PLOS One, estimated that human whole-brain emulation wouldn’t happen before 2125.
That long and unpredictable tech horizon helps explain why two US companies, Nectome and Sparks Brain Preservation, are offering to preserve human brains (or bodies) today by infusing them with the same potent chemicals used to “fix” the brains of fruit flies for connectome mapping. The idea: If the fine details of a brain’s structure can be preserved, one day in the far future it might be reanimated.
But there’s a startling twist. Because brain tissue needs to be preserved quickly after a person’s death, both companies say they want to work with people taking advantage of medical aid in dying, now legal in 13 states and Washington, DC. In that procedure, doctors supply a lethal dose of drugs, but it’s the patient—someone with a terminal prognosis—who pushes the plunger. For a fee, the companies say, they can have a preservation team at the ready. So far, the service is not popular. The companies each say they are still awaiting their first aid-in-dying customer.
Synthetic neocortex
An extra brain
Bio-hybrid interfaces
Stealth mode
The futurist Ray Kurzweil likes to say evolution’s key innovation was the creation of the neocortex—the thin extra sheet on the outermost portion of the brain, where we humans do math and recognize patterns. And he’s predicted what the next evolutionary jump could be. Someday, he says, advanced nanobots will wire up our brain cells to a “synthetic neocortex” in the cloud.
That’s right: an extra brain.
Recently, we’ve seen inklings of how this might come to pass. In 2024, Science Corporation, in California, unveiled a “biohybrid” brain-computer interface featuring nerve cells grown on a digital chip. Placed on an animal’s brain, these cells sent out long, thin axons that integrated with the animal’s own neurons. The result: two-way communication from computer to brain, in the brain’s language.
The technology could permit new types of medicine, like an implant that directs brain cells to produce dopamine and thereby treat Parkinson’s. But Max Hodak, the company’s CEO, says it also might count as a new brain part, which he likens to a “big, externalized cranial nerve.”
Such a device could serve as the connector to Kurzweil’s computerized neocortex in the cloud, giving a living person unlimited extra processing power. Still other entrepreneurs believe if you kept adding biohybrid components to a brain, eventually you could morph it into an immortal machine.
Daniel Burger, founder of the venture-funded stealth startup Eightsix Science (its name refers to the 86 billion neurons in a human brain), says this dream could require mixing several of the brain-saving techniques on this list. He thinks we might need brains in vats, affording neuro-engineers easy access, so they can gradually replace brain parts with biohybrid neural grafts.
The ultimate goal is to migrate your mind into your extra, engineered brain, without ever breaking the continuity of self. “It’s not the typical ‘scan, store, simulate,’” says Burger. “I don’t think simulations will be conscious.” He adds, “We’re saying it’s going to be way more complicated, and it’s probably going to look like gradual brain replacement into a hardware brain.”
Once your mind is hardware, you won’t need a biological body. Instead, you could take up residence in a data center somewhere and perhaps even have backups distributed around the globe. “From that point on,” Burger acknowledges, “stuff becomes really crazy.”

articles.title: Ein Hammerschlag, und der Airtag ist stumm: Warum dieses Zubehör nun verschwindet
articles.text:
Airtag: Wie ein Hammerschlag den Lautsprecher lahmlegt – und warum das umstritten ist
Der Zubehörhersteller ElevationLab hat seinen sogenannten Airtag Silencer vom Markt genommen. Das Produkt machte Apples Bluetooth-Tracker dauerhaft lautlos, indem es die Verbindung zum Lautsprecher kappte. Nach Kritik entfernte das Unternehmen die Hardware aus dem Angebot und veröffentlichte auf seiner Website eine Entschuldigung. Hinter dem Produkt stand eine simple Idee: Wer einen Airtag im Fahrradrahmen versteckt, will nicht, dass Diebe ihn am Piepsen erkennen. Den Lautsprecher eines Airtags lahmzulegen, ist seit Langem bekannt und auch von Hand machbar. ElevationLab machte den Eingriff allerdings deutlich einfacher.
Hammer drauf, Tracker stumm
Wie die Hardware funktionierte, zeigte ein niederländischer YouTuber, der sie vor dem Verkaufsstopp testen konnte. Man legte den Airtag in ein spezielles Gehäuse, das den Tracker korrekt ausrichtete. Darüber saß ein Metallnagel auf der passenden Höhe. Beide Gehäuseteile steckte man zusammen, dann trieb ein Hammerschlag den Nagel ins Airtag-Gehäuse. Der Lautsprecher war damit unwiderruflich außer Betrieb – in Sekunden, ohne das Gerät zu öffnen und ohne andere Bauteile zu beschädigen.
Glenn Fleishman, seit Jahrzehnten als Apple-Journalist unterwegs, kritisierte daraufhin im Six-Colors-Blog, lautsprecherlose Airtags erleichterten Stalking und häusliche Gewalt. Er sei ein Fan von ElevationLab, doch dieses Produkt sei „schrecklich“. Fleishman verwies auf frühere Fälle, in denen vor allem Frauen betroffen waren, die mit Airtags verfolgt wurden. Apple sah sich deshalb bereits einer Sammelklage gegenüber und verstärkte mit den Airtags 2 den Anti-Stalking-Schutz. Allerdings lässt sich auch bei diesen der Lautsprecher deaktiveren. Immerhin warnen iPhones, wenn ein unbekannter Airtag mit einer Person mitreist. Für Android gibt es eine ähnliche Funktion.
Streit um den Diebstahlschutz
Im Kern geht es um die Frage, wie gut sich ein Airtag als Diebstahlschutz eignet. Die Anwendung ist beliebt, auch wenn Apple betont, die Geräte seien reine „Dingefinder“ und nicht zur Kriminalitätsbekämpfung gedacht. ElevationLab erklärte, man habe das Werkzeug für die eigenen Fahrräder entwickelt: „Einige von uns haben Räder, die teurer sind als unsere Autos.“
Rückblickend habe das Team aber erkannt, dass die Hardware auch „Leuten mit schlechten Absichten“ helfen könne. Deshalb habe man das Produkt ersatzlos entfernt. Sein Patent auf den Airtag Silencer behält ElevationLab allerdings: Das Unternehmen will laut eigenen Aussagen damit verhindern, dass andere ein solches Gerät bauen.

articles.title: Seabirds, forests, and coral could help save sinking islands
articles.text:
Coral-fringed tropical atolls are among the landforms most threatened by global warming, but many have a potential superpower: Healthy ecosystems may help them keep pace with rising seas.
Atoll islands with native vegetation and thriving seabird populations are “naturally active systems that can change and adapt to their environmental conditions if they are allowed to do so,” said Nick Graham, a marine ecologist at Lancaster University in the United Kingdom, who led an international team of scientists that studied island resilience across 28 atoll islands in the Pacific and Indian oceans.
Their paper, published Wednesday in Science Advances, shows that restoring atoll ecosystems reinforces their growth. Seabirds ferry nutrients from the open ocean and deposit them on the atolls as guano that nurtures land plants, marine life and coral growth. This provides more material for reef building, as parrotfish and other reef feeders turn dead coral into sand to maintain beaches, while native plants with extensive root networks stabilize sediments.
Eradicating rats and replacing coconut plantations with native forests and brush could give some atolls a “fighting chance” to persist at the rate of sea-level rise expected toward the end of the century with about 2° Celsius (3.6° Fahrenheit) of warming, Graham said.
The findings provide more evidence that nature restoration can buffer the impacts of global warming. For example, restoring wetlands and forests dampens swings between wet and dry spells, reducing flood and fire hazards. Restoration efforts can also slow global warming by supporting natural carbon storage.
On the 28 atoll islands Graham’s team studied, strengthening the dynamic system of seabirds, native vegetation, and reef systems starts a virtuous cycle, as ecosystems become better able to sustain themselves and build resilience to growing impacts.

articles.title: TechSparks 2026 Day 3: Here’s all that’s happening
articles.text:
TechSparks 2026 Day 3: Here’s all that’s happening
From building new tech hubs and reimagining engineering education to India’s $100 billion AI opportunity and a closing chat with Zakir Khan, here’s all you can expect on the final day of TechSparks 2026.
Namaskara Bengaluru!
We’ve reached the final day of the 17th edition of TechSparks, and ‘The New Tech Order’ has saved some of its biggest conversations for last.
On October 15, the day opens with a conversation on the trust economy. Revant Himatsingka, better known as Food Pharmer and now Founder of Only What’s Needed, built his influence by questioning what food brands tell consumers. Now, as a founder himself, he has to build under the same scrutiny. In conversation with Shradha Sharma, Founder and CEO, YourStory and The Bharat Project, he will discuss whether trust earned through advocacy can turn into products people will pay for, and what happens when transparency, credibility and commercial ambition have to coexist.
This will be followed by an official product launch by WOI India, after which Kim McGuinness, North East Mayor, will share how regions can turn their local strengths into globally relevant technology ecosystems.
Next, Prof Ashok Jhunjhunwala, Institute Professor at IIT Madras and Chairman of IIIT Hyderabad and the ITEL Foundation, will make a provocative case: throw out half the engineering syllabus, and India may build better engineers.
Naren Shaam, Founder and CEO, Omio Group, will then explore what it takes to build for the world from day one.
In the afternoon, Sushma Boppana, CEO, Sri Chaitanya Group of Institutions, and Santhosh Viswanathan, Vice President and Managing Director, APJ Region, Intel, will discuss building a future-ready generation and what the Indian school will look like in 2035.
Actor, director and screenwriter Prakash Belawadi will reflect on the last human advantage, and what AI cannot replace.
In a panel discussion, Dr Angela Honegger (Switzerland), Jaap Veerman (The Netherlands) and Peter Winther-Schmidt (Denmark) will explore new tech alliances, and why the world’s startups need India and India needs the world.
Don’t miss Ashutosh Sharma, Head – Investments and M&A, India, Prosus, and Keshav Reddy, Founder and CEO, Equal AI, as they decode India’s $100 billion AI opportunity.
TechSparks 2026 closes with a fireside chat between stand-up comedian and writer Zakir Khan and Shradha Sharma, Founder and CEO, YourStory.
On the Focus Stage, investors from IIMA Ventures, Oister Global and VU Venture Partners will unpack the new VC rules. Shreya Mishra (SolarSquare), Vikas Brahmavar (Boson Whitewater) and Angad Daryani (Praan) will discuss rebuilding India’s energy, water and clean air systems.
Other speakers for the day include Saurabh Pandey, Founder and CEO, Eloelo Group; Vijeth Pandit, Chief Product Officer, Pine Labs Payment; Sagar Kumar, VP of Engineering, PayU; Dale Vaz, Co-founder and CEO, Sahi; Vijay Subramaniam, Founder and Group CEO, Collective Artists Network; Priya Narasimhan, CBO, Indus Appstore; and Sneha Roy, Co-founder, Murf AI, among others.
The day also features masterclasses by Attero, Google Cloud and Murf AI, and an executive roundtable with Commvault.
So let’s make the final day count!

articles.title: 'You can see everything', el documental viral de Elizabeth Holmes, ya tiene fecha de estreno en España
articles.text:
La noticia que todos los aficionados a los escándalos de Silicon Valley por fin ha llegado. You can see everything, el documental de Nathal Fielder sobre Elizabeth Holmes, se estrenará en cines en España. El proyecto levantó un revuelo enorme hace unas semanas cuando, con el lanzamiento de su primer teaser tráiler, se hizo completamente viral. Años después de su condena a prisión, la fundadora de Theranos reaparecía en unas imágenes de lo más inquietantes.
Elizabeth Holmes era una presunta mente brillante que prometía revolucionar la industria de los análisis de sangre con una sola gota. Su tecnología era tan innovadora y llamativa que se convirtió en una verdadera celebridad de Silicon Valley. Muchos la llegaron a comparar con el mismísimo Steve Jobs. Pero en realidad, sus modernos e impresionantes avances eran una auténtica farsa. Una mentira a gran escala en el mundo de las tecnológicas y la salud con la que estafó a sus inversores.
Ahora hemos sabido que el documental sobre ella que arrancó la producción antes de su ingreso en la cárcel, también se estrenará en cines en España. Y es que, tal y como ha confirmado la distribuidora Avalon, You can see everything se estrenará en cines el 12 de febrero de 2027. Será entonces cuando los espectadores descubran la cara nunca antes vista de Elizabeth Holmes.
De qué va You can see everything
Su historia es ya de sobra conocida puesto que, a raíz del juicio que tuvo lugar, acabó condenada a 11 años de prisión. Pero exactamente un mes antes de que Holmes entrara a la cárcel, ella misma contactó con Nathan Fielder, un comediante, actor, director y productor con un sello tremendamente distintivo en el que retuerce los límites de realidad y ficción. El objetivo de Holmes era grabar una suerte de documental sobre ella.
En un principio, Fielder tenía que pasar con ella y su familia tan solo unas pocas semanas. Pero durante ese tiempo, quedó tan cautivado por la perturbadora personalidad de Holmes que decidió seguir grabando y visitándola dentro de la prisión. Así nació el documental You can see everything. La crítica lo ha puesto por las nubes, al punto de que algunos espectadores hablan de él como "una experiencia transformadora".

articles.title: Canada invests $50 million into Canadian Food Innovation Network | BetaKit
articles.text:
The Government of Canada announced on Thursday a $50-million investment in the Canadian Food Innovation Network (CFIN) to advance innovation in Canada’s food sector.
The news: The funding comes via Innovation, Science, and Economic Development Canada (ISED)’s Strategic Response Fund (SRF), a federal program that provides financial support to help Canadian industry adopt innovation and build economic resilience. The money is being matched by $8 million in funding from CFIN’s business activities and will support the organization’s Food 4.0 strategy.
From the source: “Canada’s food processors are working hard to keep prices in check, but many are doing it with equipment and systems that haven’t kept pace with their global competitors,” said Dana McCauley, the CEO of CFIN, in a statement. “Food 4.0 is CFIN’s plan to close that gap.”
The context: CFIN’s Food 4.0 action plan is a five-year strategy to raise productivity within Canada’s food sector. The action plan looks to help manufacturers, processors, and supply chain operators integrate Canadian-made automation, AI, and digital tools into their workflows while also funding the foodtech companies building those tools. To advance those goals, CFIN will use the $50 million to expand its programming, including building out its online innovation platform YODL, its team of regional innovation directors, and its Food Automation & Systems Transformation Program, a funding stream supporting innovation for small and medium-sized food services businesses.
CFIN projects that funding will also help grow the organization’s membership base from 9,500 members to 20,000, and generate up to $200 million in follow-on investment.
Final thought: Rising food costs have continued to be a pain point for Canadians amid ongoing trade disputes with the United States and a rocky global economy marked by inflation. Canada has strived to address those concerns, most recently through its National Food Security Strategy, which pins the adoption of advanced technology as central to strengthening domestic food-processing capacity and supply chains.
