articles.title: Agentic AI Alters The CPU-GPU Balance
articles.text:
Agentic workloads increase CPU demand, while reasoning models, MoE architectures, and reservoir computing fuel AI acceleration.
Key Takeaways:
Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and large language models (LLMs) have dominated commercial AI for some time. Proprietary recommender models for companies such as Meta have also had significant societal impact even though only one company employs each such model. GPUs perform the heavy lifting for many of those types of models. But agentic AI needs more orchestration, and that’s a job for CPUs.
When AI’s only job is to run a model, it turns to GPUs or dedicated neural processing units (NPUs). Agents still use these models, but each is only part of the solution. Those agents must make decisions based on what the models return, and that requires if-then-else logic, and that’s what CPUs are good at. GPUs, not so much. According to some industry estimates, agentic workloads could alter the ratio of CPUs to GPUs from 1:4 to as low as 1:1.
Newer model types are also emerging, most of which are still based on LLM fundamentals. Unlike agentic AI, reasoning models, mixture-of-expert (MoE) models, and reservoir computing still rely on GPUs. But they’re also ripe for use by agents.
Pixels and parsing
For several years, practical, commercial AI meant CNNs and recurrent neural networks, or RNNs. The former were good at analyzing camera input, while the latter were proficient at analyzing sound and language. The second “L” in LLM means “language,” but LLMs do much more than language today. The notion is that some piece of text is abstracted into a token, and now practically anything can be a token.
The benefit of LLMs over RNNs is that they can maintain an arbitrarily long context, making them better at picking the right words when interpreting and generating text. In addition to requiring fewer resources, RNNs can analyze incoming frames of sound immediately without waiting to establish context, improving real-time response.
The challenge with early LLMs was that they had one job — to predict a likely next word in a sequence. That word had to make sense syntactically, but not necessarily semantically, and it certainly didn’t check facts to ensure correctness, hence the frequent “hallucinations.”
One way to improve that was through retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Instead of just figuring out a word that could maybe work, models could access “embeddings” that contained real facts, helping generate text that was both syntactically, semantically, and factually correct.
Secret agent man
Today’s hot topic is, of course, agentic AI. An agent is a new entity, not one that replaces or modifies an LLM (or any other model). It effectively represents a higher level of abstraction, acting as an orchestrator of models. It’s not a model itself, although it must be trained.
“There is some new research out there that says agentic inference is going to dwarf everything else put together before it,” said Ed Doe, CEO and co-founder of Delos Data.
The whole point of an agent is that it does more than find an answer to a question. It does something with that answer. What it does will likely depend on the answers it’s received so far. In other words, it can send tokens to a model and, when it receives the result, decide what to do next, embarking on a sequence of decisions and actions.
A well-trained agent is meant to handle a set of tasks without tight supervision. “If, as a leader, you have to tell your team every step to accomplish, you’re going to be more consumed with every step of the way,” explained Rob Knoth, product management director, digital and signoff group at Cadence. “But if you say, ‘I need you to go over there and get this work done,’ then you can go focus on another task, occasionally looking over to make sure that things are going well.”
This is a new space. “Since last year, agentic AI took off,” noted Satadal Bhattacharjee, global head of cloud and AI infrastructure silicon at Arm. “Now you can say, ‘I want to go to Costa Rica for 10 days. I need hotels, car rental, and entry tickets for these parks. Here is my budget. Go and reserve all of that.’ You give it an outline, just like to a travel agent, then the agent calls APIs to take action on your behalf.”
A new job for CPUs
An agent’s decisions typically involve if-then-else branching, and that’s not what GPUs are good at. CPUs do far better at such decision-heavy code, so they’re becoming a more important part of the computing cluster. For typical LLMs, they mainly serve as hosts, setting things up and managing communication through PCI for things like scale-out. That’s a relatively light CPU load, allowing it to handle host duties for multiple GPUs at the same time. The ratio of CPUs to GPUs will vary by system, but it’s around 1:4 for typical LLMs.
With agents, CPUs will be far busier doing actual work (rather than just enabling the GPUs to do work). So while the GPU has been the belle of the ball for a long time, CPUs are getting renewed respect as the CPU: GPU ratio moves closer to 1:1. That will also raise demand for CPUs, which can nudge prices upward.
“The challenge used to be how many AI accelerators we can get per CPU,” said Ron Lowman, strategic marketing manager for IP at Synopsys. “With agentic AI, there’s more CPU load demand, and therefore the ratios have changed.”
Bhattacharjee agreed. “Demand for CPU has risen a lot because everyone is looking for a lot more compute and in a power-efficient way to run these agents,” he said.
“In the last 18 months, everyone is clamoring over agentic AI,” said Yong Meng Sua, CTO at QCI. “This is why CPUs are getting very expensive right now.”
“The CPU is back, but is being used in a very different way than it was used in the rest of the data center,” Doe said.
Agentic queries are also more compute-intensive because, instead of just one query, sending a request to an agent typically results in many queries as the agent completes its series of tasks.
More advanced agents must also understand sequencing, and that can be programmed. “There is a programming part as well,” Arm’s Bhattacharjee said. “You can run JSON scripts to tune it and sequence it. There’s a lot more that can be done with agents.”
Show your work
The other challenge with early models is that humans can’t understand them. Models are a big cloud of numbers, and no single number can realistically be tied to anything physical or factual. The weights achieved during training aren’t sacrosanct. Training starts with random weights that get refined over many passes. Start with a different random assignment and the training will evolve to a different — and yet still correct — model.
So how do you prove that your solution is correct even if it is one of many possible correct models? There’s no deterministic way to trace how a basic model performs its calculations, making it hard to certify systems that must, for example, be safe. And the notion of safety is expanding as frontier models behave badly and escape their sandboxes, for example.
Reasoning models use additional inferencing before generating answers to queries, and in some cases they provide an accounting of how they arrived at an answer. “Reasoning is where it uses its knowledge of the topic, the context from previous discussions that you had with the model, and your knowledge of the person that is asking,” said Bhattacharjee. “So reasoning is where the model now does a next level of thinking and comes up with a better response. It’s more holistic in terms of covering a wider spectrum rather than just answering the question that is being asked.”
Reasoning models are also subject to training, so if a particular step in the reasoning was incorrect, that feedback can improve performance on future queries.
The reasoning element involves calculations better suited to GPUs than CPUs. “Reasoning is typically part of model inference and runs primarily on GPUs or other AI accelerators,” said Bhattacharjee. “Thinking involves generating additional tokens and neural-network computation that is best done by accelerators.”
Reasoning models have been commercially released. “OpenAI’s O-series models and DeepSeek-R1 are examples of commercially deployed reasoning models,” added Bhattacharjee.
Crowdsourcing (or cloudsourcing?)
LLMs are enormous models, and running each token through the entire model is resource-intensive. Two approaches attempt to tame the extent of these models.
The simple one is a small language model (SLM). Instead of trying to capture all of the internet and human knowledge in one model, it focuses on a specialty and is very well trained on that specialty, but on nothing else. An SLM is a self-contained model that can run independently.
Then, an increasingly popular technique segregates portions of individual model layers as experts in a mixture-of-experts (MoE) model. On a given layer, one can establish multiple experts that are independent of each other. Each has its own set of weights, making it better at dealing with certain tokens.
“Some of the model’s dense feed-forward network (FFN) layers are replaced by multiple separate FFNs, or ‘experts,’ together with a learned router,” explained Bhattacharjee.
“Earlier we had this scaling in large language models where if you just added more parameters, you got better performance,” explained Priyank Shukla, director of product management, interface IP at Synopsys. “With a mixture of experts, you not only have one large parameter model, but you have expert models, so you don’t need 10 trillion parameters for the whole process. You split it, and you have, let’s say, 1 trillion, which will do, let’s say, legal work. 1 trillion will do math work. And the front-end model will give the query to the right model.”
There’s a generic model that says, ‘Let me understand what question is being asked,’ called the pre-fill phase. “During that phase, it parses out your prompt to understand the context,” said Bhattacharjee. “Then there’s a series of experts that it works with. Once it understands that your question is related to, say, healthcare, there’s an expert trained on healthcare.”
A gating function or router decides, for a given token, which expert to send it to. Theoretically, it could send it to all experts, but typically only one or two get a shot at it. Training happens in the usual way, but the router is also trained by watching which experts perform best on different tokens during training. That allows it to direct tokens appropriately during inference.
The context reflecting everything that’s happened so far in the inference process is stored in the key-value cache (KV cache). It gets larger as processing continues and drives future decisions. This will be sent to the selected expert.
“We have to transmit the KV cache from the first model, which interacts with the relevant mixture of experts,” said Synopsys’ Shukla.
The router also executes on the accelerators. “The routing or gating function is part of the model itself and generally executed on the accelerator alongside the model,” Bhattacharjee noted.
Finally, the segregation of experts happens at training. “The experts are trained jointly and aren’t normally manually assigned,” he said.
That distinction becomes clearer when MoE is compared directly with the other specialization strategy: small language models.
SLMs vs. MoE
SLMs and MoEs are distinct in two critical ways. SLMs can process an entire string of tokens, whereas a given expert will handle only certain tokens within a string. SLMs are smaller models and require fewer resources to run. MoEs make bigger models. An ordinary LLM would have only one expert (on everything), while an MoE provides multiple experts for the same task, making the model larger than its pure LLM equivalent. But it’s still likely smaller than what would be necessary if the entire model had to be trained to cover all areas without experts.
Fig. 1: SLM vs. MoE. A specialized LLM can be condensed into an SLM, whereas a MoE model has multiple options for critical parts of the model, with a router that decides which “experts” will handle the next token. Source: Bryon Moyer/Semiconductor Engineering
In addition, an MoE model can have broader coverage, with embedded experts covering a wide range of topics. An SLM covers only a narrow range and is therefore more limited in the material it can consume.
MoE models tend to be larger than regular “dense” models, because one critical feed-forward layer may be replaced by several experts. That means the total parameter count may exceed that of a standard model, but since only a few experts run at any given time, not all of those parameters need to be fetched.
“An MoE model can have a very large total parameter count because it contains multiple experts, but only a subset of those experts is activated for each token,” explained Bhattacharjee. “That sparse activation is the key advantage. It allows the model to increase its overall capacity without requiring every parameter to participate in every inference operation.”
Less clear are the power implications of MoE models. “Although an MoE model may contain more total parameters, only a subset of its experts is typically activated for each token,” said Bhattacharjee. “That means it can require less computation per token than a dense model with a comparable total parameter count. The tradeoff is that routing, memory access, and communication between devices can introduce additional overhead, so efficiency increasingly depends on the design of the overall system rather than parameter count alone.”
Random reservoirs
A rather obscure type of model is called reservoir computing. With a limited remit for handling time sequences, it’s much easier to train than typical models since most of the model is random. The training process affects only the last layer, which takes whatever the random bits produce and maps it to a correct answer.
“It’s a specialized approach for dynamic temporal inputs, particularly for low power, fast adoption, and where you know simple training is valuable,” said Bhattacharjee.
Because most of the model’s contents don’t matter, they can be hard-coded into silicon, with only the last layer accepting trained weights. It also requires far less energy since only weights for the last layer must be fetched.
Not much is heard about this type of AI, but it can be useful for speech or audio recognition, processing sensor data and controlling motors on robots, and modeling sequences, including time-series prediction for applications such as weather and financial markets.
Quantum Computing Inc. (QCI) has a photonic version of a reservoir computer being readied for launch. “You can implement reservoir computing using other methods, but among all the methods, photonics is one of the best choices because of the bandwidth,” said Prajnesh Kumar, quantum technology lead at QCI.
One benefit of photonics is that it can eventually use wavelength-division multiplexing (WDM) to boost productivity. “Say you have 10 wavelengths,” explained Kumar. “You can put 10 different tasks on these wavelengths. Then if your kernel is the same for all of them, you can perform 10 operations in parallel without any sort of interference.”
That way, they’re addressing specific tasks that require high performance and low power. “There are certain future applications such as vertical takeoff vehicles where you need to do trajectory planning,” said Kumar. “You don’t want vehicles to collide. I have also been talking to one of the professors who’s been using our previous-generation product to analyze brain signals and figure out whether we can classify epilepsy versus other conditions based on brain activity. There are other applications, more toward certain military and defense applications.”
Taken together, these specialized approaches broaden the AI landscape rather than pointing to a single dominant architecture.
Many model types
The number of different model types keeps evolving, and that’s unlikely to change anytime soon. Today, CNNs still have a home, while LLMs and agentic AI are the big powerhouses, with MoE now gaining traction. Reasoning models aren’t as widespread but have their niche, as does reservoir computing.
Most of these technologies continue to rely on GPUs (or other NPUs) for the heavy lifting. The big exception is agentic AI, which is putting a premium on CPUs while not removing any of the pressure on GPUs.
It remains to be seen whether new breakthroughs such as attention and transformers occur regularly, but for now, developers are running hard with what is available today to find better ways to use it—with no end in sight.
Reference
1. Michael te Vrugt, “An introduction to reservoir computing,” book chapter to appear in: Artificial Intelligence and Intelligent Matter, Springer, Cham, arXiv:2412.13212v1

Standalone GPUs are being replaced by heterogeneous SoCs and chiplets that combine CPUs, GPUs, and NPUs to eliminate memory bottlenecks, reduce latency, and boost efficiency.

articles.title: Test Asus Chromebook CM14 (CM1406) : notre avis complet
articles.text:
Gratuit pour des dizaines de milliers de lycéens d’Île-de-France et des Pays de la Loire, le Chromebook CM1406 d’Asus est aussi un ordinateur portable disponible à la vente pour le grand public. Sa particularité vient de la présence du système d’exploitation ChromeOS de Google, encore relativement méconnu en France face à Windows, macOS et des distributions Linux. Ce n’est toutefois pas la seule curiosité de cette machine que nous avons testée dans sa version commerciale.
Très proche du modèle distribué aux élèves, cette variante se distingue en intégrant un écran tactile et n’embarque pas de chargeur de 45 W dans la boîte. Tout le reste est identique, à l’exception du coloris et d’une version de ChromeOS qui offre plus de liberté. Alors, est-ce un ordinateur portable trop limité pour séduire le grand public ou une bonne affaire en puissance qui peut quitter les salles de classe ? On a voulu vérifier et voici notre test complet.
Prix et date de sortie de l’ASUS Chromebook CM14 (CM1406)
L’Asus Chromebook CM1406 a fait son apparition en France juste avant la rentrée. Notre version tactile coûte 449,99 € (499,99 € avant la remise en cours) avec 8 Go de mémoire, 128 Go de stockage, une housse de transport et Google AI Pro (5 To) sans frais pendant 12 mois.
Design : du métal, et ça se voit
Pensés pour être accessibles, les Chromebook ont parfois renvoyé une image de PC portables relativement « cheap ». Ce n’est pas le cas du CM1406 qui opte pour des lignes modernes et des finitions de bonne qualité. Asus a soigné les détails sur ce modèle qui se présente un gabarit de 31,37 x 22,61 x 1,56 cm pour un poids de 1,32 kg sur notre balance. C’est un 14 pouces classique, ni plume ni brique qui ne passera pas totalement inaperçu dans un sac à dos, sans pour autant se montrer trop encombrant.
Le capot s’ouvre facilement, d’une seule main, et l’ensemble respire la solidité. Un bon pour l’élève scolarisé au lycée qui va garder son modèle durant l’année scolaire (les établissements doivent opter pour un système de rotation chaque année) et l’utilisateur classique qui devrait le conserver pendant quelques années.
Détail appréciable, Asus fournit une pochette de transport avec la machine, un détail appréciable.
Sous le capot, on trouve un clavier relativement classique sans pavé numérique. Les touches sont souples, la frappe confortable et très silencieuse.
Le rétroéclairage est présent, mais en tout ou rien, c’est-à-dire qu’on l’allume ou on l’éteint, sans réglage d’intensité. L’ensemble reste proche d’un clavier de PC Windows ou de macOS, avec une touche Google pour nous rappeler que nous sommes bien sous ChromeOS.
Quant au trackpad, il mesure 13 x 8,5 cm d’après nos mesures, soit environ 15,5 cm de diagonale. Il assure une glisse fluide et se montre réactif. Rien d’exceptionnel, mais c’est un bon trackpad à l’usage,
Connectique : la bonne surprise
Le Chromebook CM1406 d’Asus se montre généreux sur ce point. Le flanc gauche accueille deux ports USB-C 3.2 Gen 1 (recharge et sortie vidéo), un USB-A, une sortie HDMI 1.4 et une prise jack. Le flanc droit ajoute un second USB-A et un emplacement Kensington. Une connectique relativement complète qui permet de brancher de nombreux périphériques (clé USB, disque dur, écran externe, casque filaire…) sans chercher un adapateur.
Deux bémols sont quand même à noter : le HDMI 1.4 limite l’affichage externe, et il n’y a pas de lecteur microSD. Côté sans-fil, notre exemplaire est en Wi-Fi 6E avec Bluetooth 5.4. Certaines configurations d’ASUS annoncent du Wi-Fi 7, mais pas la nôtre.
Écran : lisible, précis dans ses angles, mais fade
La dalle IPS tactile de 14 pouces (1920 x 1200, 16:10) offre une surface d’affichage appréciable, légèrement plus grande que celle de l’ancien modèle fourni aux élèves (13,3 pouces). Le choix du format 14 pouces est plutôt équilibré, notamment pour l’éducation, offrant plus de confort qu’un 13 pouces sans se montrer aussi imposant qu’un 15 pouces.
Asus fait des choix pertinents en optant pour une dalle mate qui évite grandement les reflets tandis que l’IPS assure d’excellents angles de vision. En prime sur notre modèle grand public, le tactile réagit bien.
Le constructeur annonce 400 nits pour cette version et si je n’avais pas de sonde sous la main pour le vérifier précisément, la promesse semble conforme à ce que j’ai constaté à l’usage. Les couleurs apparaissent plutôt fidèles, mais nous restons en présence d’une dalle plutôt orientée vers l’entrée de gamme et l’IPS ne fait pas de miracle. Le contraste n’est pas exceptionnel et les noirs peuvent apparaître un peu gris, mais ce n’est pas le principal défaut de cet écran.
Pour autant, l’image m’a paru assez sage. Nous restons sur une dalle IPS d’entrée de gamme : le contraste donne des noirs un peu grisâtres, et le sRGB ne produit pas les couleurs éclatantes d’un écran OLED ou d’un MacBook. Le résultat est correct pour la bureautique, la navigation et la vidéo, un peu terne pour qui vient d’un bon smartphone ou d’un écran plus haut de gamme. Pour de la retouche photo ou de l’étalonnage sérieux, mieux vaut s’orienter ailleurs.
Note : Asus propose aussi une dalle non tactile à 300 nits et 45 % de NTSC, celle des modèles distribués aux lycéens.
Logiciel : ChromeOS, pour qui sait ce qu’il veut
Notre exemplaire tourne sous ChromeOS (en version 154.0.8037.96 à la publication de ce test). Développé depuis de nombreuses années par Google, il a pris son temps avant de réellement émerger, notamment dans nos contrées où il reste en retrait. Il faut dire que ce système d’exploitation peut surprendre par son fonctionnement puisqu’il s’articule principalement autour d’un navigateur très populaire : Chrome.
Ce dernier est à la base et s’accompagne du Google Play Store, la même boutique d’applications que l’on trouve sur les smartphones et tablettes Android. Vous y trouverez donc de nombreuses applications mobiles, mais pas forcément les logiciels en local que vous avez l’habitude d’avoir chez Windows, macOS ou Linux. L’argument numéro un de ChromeOS reste l’utilisation en ligne et des services dans le cloud, ce qui peut autant séduire que rebuter.
Pour des usages simples (et le plus souvent en ligne), cela convient très bien. Pour des logiciels métiers lourds, ce n’est pas la bonne plateforme. Même si ChromeOS et les services Google permettent une utilisation « hors ligne », il reste dépendant d’une connexion. Après tout, cela reste plutôt logique pour un système qui dépend grandement d’un navigateur internet.
Rien à redire sur son fonctionnement sur notre Chromebook, le système d’exploitation de Google se montre léger et peu gourmand en ressources. Notez la possibilité d’accéder à un conteneur Linux, ce qui peut être pratique pour les bidouilleurs. Du côté des lycées, il faudra composer avec une version limitée et associée à l’ENT de l’établissement.
Côté durée de vie, Google affiche sur notre exemplaire des mises à jour logicielles et de sécurité jusqu’en juin 2036. À noter toutefois que la FAQ Googlebook publiée en septembre fixe la fin du support de ChromeOS à la mi-2034, avant une migration vers Googlebook OS réservée aux modèles éligibles. La liste n’est pas publiée. Cela laisse plusieurs années devant soi, mais c’est une donnée à connaître pour qui compte garder la machine très longtemps.
Audio et webcam : le strict minimum
Les deux enceintes, placées sous le châssis, font le travail pour regarder des vidéos YouTube. Elles privilégient les voix au détriment des basses : c’est suffisant pour un cours en ligne ou une série, un peu juste pour de la musique.
La webcam filme en 720p. Sa qualité est juste correcte pour des visios, sans plus, mais on apprécie son cache de confidentialité physique.
Performances : un moteur de smartphone de milieu de gamme
Le Chromebook CM1406 est animé par la puce MediaTek Kompanio 540 : huit cœurs, deux Cortex-A78 à 2,6 GHz et six Cortex-A55 à 2,0 GHz, gravés en 6 nm avec un GPU Mali-G57 MC2. Elle est épaulée par 8 Go de LPDDR5X soudés. Sur le papier, la configuration nous rappelle plus celle d’un smartphone que d’un ordinateur portable classique, mais ce n’est pas une surprise si l’on est familier de l’univers de ChromeOS.
Ce système est d’ailleurs un peu plus particulier qu’un Windows (ou macOS) pour mesurer les performances. J’ai pu lancer plusieurs benchmarks, mais il s’agit le plus souvent d’applications conçues pour Android, disponibles sur le Play Store et compatibles avec ChromeOS, ainsi que de tests web dans Chrome.
Les résultats ci-dessous risquent de vous paraître bien faibles, et pour cause : ils le sont si on les compare à ceux d’un portable Windows. Toutefois, ce n’est pas la bonne échelle ici. ChromeOS est peu outillé pour ce type de mesures, et la plupart des tests habituels n’y existent pas. J’ai néanmoins tenu à le faire pour avoir un aperçu et disposer d’une base de comparaison avec d’autres Chromebook, mesurés de la même façon.
| Test | Résultat | 
| Speedometer 3 | 7,90 | 
| JetStream 2 | 153 | 
| Geekbench 6 (monocœur) | 1 010 | 
| Geekbench 6 (multicoeur) | 2 125 | 
| Geekbench 6 GPU | 1 786 | 
| 3DMark Wild Life | 1 441 | 
| 3DMark Wild Life Extreme | 412 | 
| 3DMark Wild Life Extreme Stability | 99,2 % | 
| 3DMark Steel Nomad Light | 171 | 
Pris seuls, ces chiffres disent peu, mais ils racontent trois choses. Premièrement, on observe un net progrès sur la génération précédente. Si on le compare aux scores habituels du Kompanio 520, qui équipait l’ancien CM14, le 540 gagne environ 60 % en monocœur et 38 % en multicœur sous Geekbench 6. Cela suit l’annonce de MediaTek et se traduit par plus de réactivité à l’usage, sans pour autant en faire une foudre de guerre.
Deuxièment, Kompanio 540 a beau être un compagnon volontaire, il reste en retrait face à l’Intel N100. Cette puce populaire dans les Chromebook et PC bon marché conserve une longueur d’avance en matière de performance brute et pourra se montrer plus véloce sur certaines tâches. En pratique, nous restons sur des puces limitées et le Kompanio 540 garde certains atouts dans sa manche.
Troisièmement, outre l’autonomie que nous verrons un peu plus loin, ce Kompanio 540 se distingue par sa stabilité en ne chauffant que très peu, quelles que soient les circonstances. Ainsi, ce Chromebook se permet une conception entièrement sans ventilateur et fonctionne dans un silence complet. C’est appréciable pour nous, mais aussi pour une utilisation en classe ou à la bibliothèque pour les lycéens.
Stockage : le maillon faible
Le vrai talon d’Achielle en matière de performances est ici. Le CM1406 embarque 128 Go d’eMMC, soudés et non extensibles. Nous l’avons mesuré avec fio, depuis l’environnement Linux de ChromeOS, ce qui passe par une couche de virtualisation : les valeurs ne reflètent donc pas parfaitement le composant seul.
En lecture séquentielle, le débit est de 64 Mo/s. L’écriture séquentielle atteint 204 Mo/s, mais cette valeur est sans doute gonflée par un cache. C’est en accès aléatoire que le résultat est le plus parlant : environ 16 Mo/s en lecture et 19 Mo/s en écriture par blocs de 4 Ko, soit 4 000 à 4 500 opérations par seconde. Un SSD NVMe fait des dizaines de fois mieux. Ce sont ces valeurs qui expliquent les à-coups quand la RAM sature et que le système bascule vers le stockage.
Vous l’aurez compris, notre machine ne fait pas rêver par ses performances et son utilisation se limite principalement aux applications installées ou des services en ligne. Cela tombe bien, ce Chromebook CM1406 répond présent sur ces tâches simples en faisant tourner ChromeOS de manière stable et fluide avec plusieurs onglets ouverts. En dehors de ces usages, le CM1406 n’est tout simplement pas fait pour jouer ni monter de la vidéo.
Autonomie : le point fort annoncé
Avec ses 70 Wh, le Chromebook CM1406 d’Asus s’offre une batterie généreuse et le constructeur promet un alléchant « jusqu’à 23 heures d’autonomie ». Un résultat qui dépend évidemment de nombreuses conditions (utilisation, paramètres, conditions réseau…), mais néanmoins atteignable en lecture vidéo par exemple.
Avec une utilisation multitâche consistant à utiliser plusieurs onglets, services en ligne et programmes préinstallés, l’autonomie se situe autour de 16 heures.
Ce résultat très solide permet d’envisager deux à trois jours d’utilisation complète avant de recharger le Chromebook. Côté recharge, Asus nous a fait parvenir notre modèle de test avec un chargeur 45 W qui, rappelons-le, n’est pas fourni dans la version commerciale. Il ne permet pas une recharge ultra-rapide et il faudra près de 2 heures pour une charge complète.
 👉🏻 Suivez l’actualité tech en temps réel : ajoutez 01net à vos sources sur Google, et abonnez-vous à notre canal WhatsApp.

articles.title: Aldi traerá el altavoz Bluetooth supercompacto por 7,99 euros. Incluye micrófono, un imán y una pinza de sujeción
articles.text:
Aldi renueva su catálogo de productos semanalmente, por lo que con el paso de los días podemos ir encontrando una gran variedad de dispositivos orientados al hogar. El próximo 24 de octubre llegará el altavoz Bluetooth Workzone, y lo mejor es que se lanzará a un precio de 7,99 euros.
Como alternativa, Amazon tiene de oferta el Soundcore Select 4 Go por un precio de 24,99 euros. Se trata de un altavoz Bluetooth que, pese a tener un precio bastante más alto que el de Aldi, incluye un pequeño cordón para poder colgarlo en diversas superficies.
Soundcore Select 4 Go
Un altavoz para colgarlo en diferentes superficies
Este altavoz Bluetooth no tendrá el mejor diseño para colocarlo en la casa, pero sí que es bastante útil gracias a que cuenta con algunas características muy particulares. En este sentido, viene tanto con un imán como con una pinza de sujeción, algo bastante práctico para colgar el altavoz en diferentes superficies.
El altavoz cuenta con conectividad Bluetooth 5.1 y viene con micrófono integrado. Además, no funciona a pilas, sino que incorpora una batería que ofrece una autonomía de hasta seis horas, una cifra que, si bien es cierto que se aleja mucho de lo que solemos ver en otros modelos, es suficiente para poder utilizarlo durante bastante tiempo.

articles.title: Police arrests 95 suspects in international CSAM crackdown action
articles.text:
Law enforcement authorities from 17 countries in Latin America and Europe have arrested 95 suspects in an INTERPOL-coordinated operation targeting the distribution of child sexual abuse material (CSAM) through online messaging groups.
The joint action, dubbed International Effort Confluencia, included four law enforcement operations between March 2026 and September 2026.
"Effective cross-border cooperation between law enforcement and the private sector has never been more urgent," said Stephen Fry, Executive Director of INTERPOL Investigation Support. "Behind every file is a child who was abused, and who is revictimized every time that image recirculates. Wherever offenders move, we have to move faster."
The investigators executed 127 search warrants to arrest nearly 95 suspects and rescued a five-year-old victim whose parent had been producing and selling abuse material online.
Ecuadorian authorities found one individual part of a group sharing CSAM who had approximately 15GB of abuse images and more than 4,000 files, while investigators in Panama arrested the administrator of a group disseminating abusive material depicting children with more than 700 users.
In Argentina, another suspect who was allegedly in contact with over 260 girls worldwide allegedly threatened victims who tried to refuse his requests for increasingly explicit content and is now accused of sextortion of minors.
"These platforms are increasingly used to groom children, coordinate abuse, connect offenders and receive payment for illegal content. They also enable the recirculation of abuse content, resulting in continued revictimization of children," INTERPOL said, referring to the messaging platforms used to disseminate and commercialize abuse content.
"Material seized during the investigation is expected to lead to further identifications of offenders and children at risk, as well as additional safeguarding action."
Last year, in February, 25 other suspects linked to a large criminal ring distributing AI-generated CSAM were arrested as part of Operation Cumberland. German cybercrime prosecutors also took down Kidflix in April 2025, one of the largest child sexual abuse material (CSAM) platforms on the dark web, and made an additional 79 arrests after identifying 1,393 suspects.
European and Latin American authorities from over a dozen countries arrested 20 more suspects in June 2025 as part of a separate joint operation targeting the production and distribution of CSAM via instant messaging groups.
More recently, in March, a global law enforcement action supported by Europol and named "Operation Alice" shut down more than 373,000 dark web sites that offered fake CSAM packages following an investigation that started in mid-2021.

articles.title: iPhone Duo : ce que vous allez perdre en choisissant le premier iPhone pliant d’Apple
articles.text:
Avec son écran pliable de 7,6 pouces, l’iPhone Duo propose un format inédit au sein de la gamme Apple. Mais ce changement de design s’accompagne de plusieurs concessions face aux iPhone 18 Pro, y compris sur des fonctions utilisées au quotidien et sur les capacités photo.
L’iPhone Duo s’annonce comme l’un des appareils les plus novateurs d’Apple ces dernières années, avec son écran pliable de 7,6 pouces et les possibilités qu’il pourrait offrir au quotidien. Nous avons d’ailleurs déjà évoqué à plusieurs reprises ses atouts, mais ce nouveau format ne vient pas sans compromis. Face aux iPhone 18 Pro, le smartphone pliant fait l’impasse sur plusieurs fonctions, parfois bien installées dans les habitudes des utilisateurs. Et son prix élevé rend ces concessions d’autant plus difficiles à ignorer.
Un iPhone pliant plus cher, mais moins pratique sur plusieurs points
Mettons immédiatement les pieds dans le plat avec l’un des principaux sujets qui fâchent : le prix. À capacité de stockage équivalente (256 Go), l’iPhone Duo coûte 2 339 euros, soit 860 euros de plus que l’iPhone 18 Pro et 710 euros de plus que le Pro Max. Et la différence ne s’arrête pas au moment de l’achat : les tarifs d’AppleCare+, les réparations et le remplacement de la batterie sont également plus élevés que sur les modèles Pro.
Le format pliant impose aussi quelques concessions à prendre en compte avant l’achat. Replié, l’appareil mesure 11,3 mm d’épaisseur et pèse 254 grammes, soit 43 grammes de plus que l’iPhone 18 Pro. Son écran extérieur de 5,4 pouces est également plus petit que celui des deux modèles Pro, qui affichent respectivement 6,3 et 6,9 pouces. Pour profiter de la dalle intérieure de 7,6 pouces, il faut donc ouvrir le téléphone (c’est le concept même d’un téléphone pliant). Cette dernière affiche par ailleurs une densité de 430 pixels par pouce, contre 460 sur les Pro.
De plus, malgré les efforts d’Apple pour réduire la pliure au centre de l’iPhone Duo, celle-ci devrait rester visible sous certaines conditions d’éclairage.
Face ID, bouton Action, autonomie : ce que l’iPhone Duo abandonne
Plusieurs fonctions du quotidien sont également absentes. Face ID cède sa place à un Touch ID intégré dans le bouton latéral et le bouton Action personnalisable des modèles Pro disparaît. MagSafe reste heureusement compatible avec les coques et les chargeurs sans fil, mais pas avec les portefeuilles de la marque. Autre particularité : l’iPhone Duo fonctionne exclusivement avec une eSIM, alors que certains iPhone 18 Pro conservent un emplacement pour carte nano-SIM selon les marchés, dont la France.
Enfin, l’autonomie annoncée atteint 24 heures en utilisation typique. C’est autant que l’iPhone 18 Pro, mais six heures de moins que le Pro Max. La recharge filaire est également plus lente. Apple annonce environ 20 minutes pour atteindre 50 %, contre 15 minutes sur les deux modèles Pro.
La photo et la vidéo font aussi les frais du pliant
C’est sans conteste sur la photo que l’iPhone Duo creuse le plus l’écart avec les modèles Pro. Faute de téléobjectif dédié, il doit se contenter d’un zoom de qualité optique 2x, alors que les iPhone 18 Pro disposent d’un téléobjectif 4x et d’un zoom numérique pouvant atteindre 40x. Le capteur principal perd également l’ouverture variable des modèles Pro. Son ouverture fixe à f/1,6 laisse moins de latitude pour ajuster la capture de lumière et la profondeur de champ.
Les amateurs de photo et de vidéo avancées devront aussi faire des concessions. L’iPhone Duo fait l’impasse sur le scanner LiDAR, la capture ProRAW et les formats vidéo ProRes et ProRes RAW. Il ne prend pas non plus en charge les photos et vidéos spatiales, Apple Log 2 ou le système ACES, utilisés dans certains flux de production professionnels. Les commandes avancées des modèles Pro, qui permettent notamment d’ajuster la vitesse d’obturation et la balance des blancs, sont elles aussi absentes.
À l’avant, la caméra Center Stage extérieure passe de 18 à 12 mégapixels, avec une ouverture moins grande. Et la caméra intégrée sous l’écran intérieur va encore plus loin dans les compromis puisqu’elle se limite à la vidéo en 1080p et ne propose ni mode Nuit, ni mode Portrait, ni styles photographiques. Le grand écran pliable de l’iPhone Duo ne s’accompagne donc pas de toute la polyvalence photo des iPhone 18 Pro.
L’iPhone Duo n’en reste pas moins une proposition inédite chez Apple, dont le grand écran pliable pourrait ouvrir de nouvelles possibilités intéressantes. Reste que son intérêt dépendra aussi des fonctions auxquelles chacun est prêt à renoncer. Le smartphone sera pour rappel disponible à la vente dès le 23 octobre prochain, tandis que les précommandes débuteront ce vendredi 16 octobre.

articles.title: The code confidence gap nobody’s talking about
articles.text:
The code confidence gap nobody’s talking about
AI has changed the economics of software creation: A task that once took hours to implement can now start with an agent producing an initial solution in minutes. As agents take on broader assignments, like changing code across a repository, refactoring services, writing tests, and preparing pull requests, output volume will continue to rise.
That is an extraordinary opportunity, and it’s also why the next challenge for engineering organizations isn’t generating more code, but building confidence in the code that reaches production. In the agentic software factory, agents write, test, and propose changes faster than people can review them line by line.
Code creation is becoming abundant; code confidence is not.
This distinction matters because a completed pull request is not the same as a dependable outcome. The code may compile and pass a narrow test suite while still violating an architectural convention, introducing a security weakness, duplicating existing functionality, or creating maintenance costs that surface much later. The faster an organization generates changes, the less feasible it becomes to rely on heroics and manual review alone to catch every issue.
“Code creation is becoming abundant; code confidence is not.”
The way forward is to treat code confidence as something you can design into the software delivery system. A useful formula is Intent × Guiderails × Verification × Evidence. (And yes, the multiplication sign here is deliberate.) Each of these four pieces is crucial. Strength in three cannot make up for weakness in the fourth.
Clear intent without verification does not prevent mistakes. Strong verification without evidence does not create accountability. Guiderails without clear intent merely automate ambiguity. Evidence without independent verification is only a record of what an agent claimed.
Here is what each part of the formula means in practice.
Intent: Make the standard explicit
Agents are remarkably capable at pursuing a stated objective. But “build a payments feature” or “modernize this service” is not a sufficient objective for a production codebase. An organization’s definition of good software includes much more, such as business logic, security expectations, design patterns, performance needs, dependencies, and conventions accumulated through years of engineering.
Intent is the discipline of making those expectations explicit. It means defining the goal of a change and the standards it must meet before an agent begins work. The better the context, the fewer cycles agents spend producing plausible but unsuitable answers, and the less rework falls to developers later.
Guiderails: Shape the work before it creates risk
Guiderails translate intent into boundaries that guide how agents operate. They may define which repositories, dependencies, data, or actions are permitted; where human approval is required; and what policies apply to a given class of code.
The purpose is not to constrain every useful action. It’s to give agents enough structure to operate productively and predictably. A well-designed guiderail lets teams safely grant more autonomy because everyone understands the conditions under which that autonomy applies.
The result is repeatable autonomy. Rather than treating every agent-driven change as a one-off experiment, teams can apply consistent boundaries and expand agentic development with confidence.
Verification: Check every change independently
Verification is where confidence is tested. As agents generate code at increasing scale, every change needs consistent evaluation for the qualities that matter: correctness, reliability, security, maintainability, and compliance with the organization’s own standards.
“A model can assist in reviewing its own work, but an organization should not rely solely on the same probabilistic system that produced a change to determine whether that change is safe to ship.”
Independence is essential. A model can assist in reviewing its own work, but an organization should not rely solely on the same probabilistic system that produced a change to determine whether that change is safe to ship. Repeatable, independent checks provide a common standard across models, agents, and toolchains. This is especially important when the AI tools themselves are evolving quickly.
Verification also needs to occur in the flow of work, not as a slow, final checkpoint. The goal is to identify and fix problems at the source, while the agent or developer still has the context needed to resolve them.
Evidence: Make confidence visible and auditable
A change may be well-intentioned, carefully governed, and thoroughly checked. But engineering leaders, auditors, and the teams responsible for production still need to know what happened and why. Evidence is the durable record: what standards applied, what was checked, what was found, and how the issue was resolved.
This matters most in complex and regulated environments, but it’s valuable everywhere. Evidence makes quality measurable, allows teams to improve their practices over time, and gives organizations a defensible basis for moving quickly.
Building the factory around confidence
The most promising vision for agentic software development is not one in which people disappear from the process. It’s one in which people, agents, and verification systems each contribute their strengths. Agents accelerate execution, and engineers provide judgment and direction. The delivery system supplies the standards, controls, and evidence that allow autonomy to scale.
“The most promising vision for agentic software development is not one in which people disappear from the process. It’s one in which people, agents, and verification systems each contribute their strengths.”
The organizations that succeed will be the ones that build code confidence into every change, at any volume, and at agent speed.
That is the real work of the agentic software factory, producing software an organization has the confidence to stand behind.
Start with four questions the next time an agent opens a pull request:
- Did the agent know your standards before it started?
- What was it allowed to touch, and what needed a human decision?
- Did something other than the model that wrote the change check it?
- Can you show what was found and how it was resolved?
Wherever the answer is “no,” that is where your confidence gap lives. Close it there first.

articles.title: On a vu le Tesla Cybercab : ce n’est pas l’absence de volant qui nous a le plus marqués au Mondial — Frandroid
articles.text:
J’avais déjà croisé un des premiers prototypes du Cybercab, et l’absence de volant fait toujours son petit effet. On s’attend à trouver quelque chose devant le siège gauche, et on ne trouve qu’une planche de bord nue et un grand écran central. Et j’avoue que je ne m’attendais pas à la trouver au Mondial de l’auto, sachant que la voiture ne roule pas pour le moment en Europe. Elle ne peut pas être homologuée dans l’état actuel des choses.
Cette fois, sur le stand Tesla du hall 7.1, j’ai surtout découvert ce que je n’avais jamais vu : le coffre.
Le hayon levé révèle un volume qu’on n’attend pas sur un engin dont la silhouette évoque une Model 3 raccourcie. Le Cybercab n’a que deux places, mais il a manifestement été dessiné autour des valises.
Présenté en octobre 2024 lors de la soirée « We, Robot », le Cybercab est produit en série depuis février 2026 à la Gigafactory du Texas. Depuis le 4 septembre, il transporte des passagers à Austin via l’application Tesla Robotaxi, sur une zone de 264 miles carrés, soit environ 680 km², qui couvre l’essentiel de la ville.
Tesla revendique plus de 300 Cybercabs en service sur place, aux côtés de Model Y modifiées, et Dallas devrait suivre. La fiche technique reste modeste, avec une batterie de 48 kWh, un moteur de 219 ch et 1 412 kg sur la balance. La charge doit à terme passer par induction, sans câble ni prise visible.
Un coffre de SUV pour deux passagers
Selon le guide passager publié par Tesla, le coffre arrière cube 572 l. C’est plus qu’un Peugeot 3008 (520 l), pour une voiture qui ne transporte que deux personnes. C’est étrange, mais il y a une explication.
Un robotaxi passe ses journées à faire des allers-retours vers l’aéroport ou la gare, et deux voyageurs avec deux valises en soute et deux bagages cabine doivent y tenir sans négociation. Tesla limite toutefois le coffre à 100 kg et la charge utile totale à 280 kg, occupants compris. Deux adultes costauds et des valises bien remplies, et on frôle déjà la limite.
Taxi d’abord, voiture perso ensuite ?
La stratégie de Tesla consiste d’abord à vendre des trajets plutôt que des voitures. Elon Musk vise pourtant aussi les particuliers : il a répondu « oui » en février à la question d’une vente avant 2027, avec un objectif de prix sous les 30 000 dollars.
La question est de savoir qui achèterait une voiture sans volant, utilisable seulement là où Tesla est autorisé à rouler sans conducteur.
Aux États-Unis, l’agence de sécurité routière NHTSA a ouvert en septembre un audit sur la façon dont Tesla a autocertifié environ 1 000 Cybercabs, sans demander d’exemption comme l’a fait Zoox. En France, le Cybercab n’a aucune autorisation de circuler, et même la conduite supervisée FSD n’y est pas encore permise.
Sur un stand, c’est l’une des voitures les plus réussies du salon, et la plus radicale. Si le Cybercab bouscule l’automobile, ce sera surtout en installant l’idée qu’on peut disposer d’une voiture sans en posséder une.

articles.title: OnePlus 16 vs RedMagic 12 Pro+: Which gaming phone wins?
articles.text:
Table of contents
Comparing the OnePlus 16 vs RedMagic 12 Pro+ comes down to one question: what do you want besides gaming?
Both phones run Qualcomm’s new Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 chip. OnePlus started sales in China on October 13. RedMagic will launch its phone in China on October 15 at 2:30 pm China time (7:30 am in Lagos).
This guide compares both phones on price, gaming, battery, and cameras. It also shows you which one you can get in Africa.
Quick answer: Pick the OnePlus 16 if you want one phone for gaming and photos. Wait for the RedMagic 12 Pro+ launch if fan cooling for long gaming sessions matters most to you.
| Feature | OnePlus 16 | RedMagic 12 Pro+ | 
|---|---|---|
| Chip | Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 | Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 | 
| Screen | 6.78-inch OLED, up to 185Hz in supported games | Size not out yet; 0.96mm borders with the selfie camera under the screen | 
| Battery | 9,000mAh | 8,400mAh (leak) | 
| Charging | 100W wired, 50W wireless | 120W wired, 80W wireless (leak) | 
| Main camera | 200MP | Not out yet | 
| Cooling | Large vapour chamber | Liquid cooling plus a fan | 
| China starting price | CNY 5,699 ($847) (first sale) | Out on October 15 | 
| Sales | On sale in China | Launches October 15 | 
Gizmochina reports the leaked RedMagic battery and charging figures. RedMagic still has to confirm them.
Price and availability
OnePlus 16 price in China
OnePlus sells the phone in four memory sizes. These are its prices in China.
| RAM and storage | First-sale price | Normal price | 
|---|---|---|
| 12GB + 256GB | CNY 5,699 ($847) | CNY 5,999 ($892) | 
| 12GB + 512GB | CNY 6,499 ($966) | CNY 6,799 ($1,011) | 
| 16GB + 512GB | CNY 7,199 ($1,071) | CNY 7,499 ($1,115) | 
| 16GB + 1TB | CNY 8,199 ($1,219) | CNY 8,499 ($1,264) | 
Dollar figures use the People’s Bank of China rate of CNY 6.7249 to $1 on October 14, 2026.
- The base model costs CNY 5,699 ($847) in the first sale. Its normal price is CNY 5,999 ($892).
- Buyers in China can drop the base model to CNY 5,199 ($773) with a government subsidy. This subsidy works only inside China.
A dollar or naira conversion shows you only the China price. Your final cost also includes four extras:
- Currency conversion fees
- Shipping
- Import charges
- The seller’s margin
Ask the seller for the full delivered price in writing before you pay.
Where OnePlus sells the OnePlus 16
OnePlus sells the OnePlus 16 in China. Android Authority reports it will skip Europe and North America, and TechRepublic notes that OnePlus confirmed in July it would stop launching new phones in those regions.
For India, tipster Yogesh Brar says, via TechRepublic, that the OnePlus 16R may become OnePlus’s top phone there instead. OnePlus has not confirmed this.
OnePlus has not announced a launch for Nigeria, Kenya, Ghana, or South Africa. A local seller with stock is importing the phone, so confirm the exact model you get.
RedMagic 12 Pro+ price
RedMagic shares the price at its October 15 launch. In China, you can reserve the phone now with a CNY 100 ($15) deposit on RedMagic’s website or JD.com.
The global version may differ from the China model. For example, the global RedMagic 11 Pro came with a 7,500mAh battery and 80W wired charging. The China model had an 8,000mAh battery and 120W wired charging. Check the specs of the exact version you buy.
Compare both phones again when RedMagic posts prices for matching memory sizes.
OnePlus 16 vs RedMagic: Can you buy either phone in Africa?
RedMagic’s global store ships to a fixed list of countries. Egypt is on the list. Nigeria, Kenya, Ghana, and South Africa are missing, and RedMagic’s policy says a missing country gets no direct delivery.
| Country | Direct RedMagic delivery? | What you can do | 
|---|---|---|
| Nigeria | No | Ask a trusted reseller or forwarding service for a full quote | 
| Kenya | No | Confirm stock and the full delivery cost | 
| Ghana | No | Check the seller’s return and repair terms | 
| South Africa | No | Confirm the model, delivery route and who provides the warranty | 
If you buy either phone from a reseller, ask these four questions:
- Which region is the phone from?
- What software does it run?
- Does it support your network’s bands?
- Who handles warranty repairs?
If a seller says the phone has a “global ROM”, ask if the factory installed it or the seller added it later.
RedMagic’s warranty covers phones from its official store. RedMagic says it offers no extra help for phones from other sellers, so the reseller’s own warranty matters a lot.
Performance and gaming
Same chip, different results
Both phones use the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6. The same chip gives you a fair starting point. Cooling and game tuning still change how each phone plays.
A quick benchmark score tells you little about long matches. When reviews come out, look for these four results after 30 minutes of play:
- Average frame rate
- Sudden frame drops
- Battery used
- How hot the back gets
OnePlus 16 focuses on touch, screen and network
OnePlus packs a 6,428mm² vapour chamber to move heat away from the chip. It also adds these gaming parts:
- G3 chip for a steadier network connection
- P4 chip for the display
- T3 chip for faster touch response
- 800Hz gyroscope for motion aiming
Check that your favourite games support high frame rates on the version you buy. Game support in China can differ from global versions of PUBG Mobile and Call of Duty Mobile.
RedMagic 12 Pro+ focuses on cooling
RedMagic pairs a liquid cooling engine with fan-powered air cooling. This setup helps the chip maintain peak performance in long games. Reviews still need to test fan noise and frame-rate stability.
A Geekbench 7 listing, which Gizmochina and Android Headlines link to the 12 Pro+, shows 3,677 single-core and 12,679 multi-core points. RedMagic has not confirmed the listing.
At launch, check for these four gaming features:
- Shoulder triggers
- A headphone jack
- Touch-control settings
- Bypass charging
Gaming verdict: RedMagic’s fan cooling gives gamers a good reason to wait for its launch. Long-session tests will show which phone holds up better.
Detailed specs
1. Display
| Detail | OnePlus 16 | RedMagic 12 Pro+ | 
|---|---|---|
| Size and type | 6.78-inch flat LTPO OLED (BOE X4) | Not out yet | 
| Resolution | 1.5K | Not out yet | 
| Top refresh rate | 185Hz in supported games; up to 165Hz for apps | Not out yet | 
| Peak brightness | 2,000 nits | Not out yet | 
| Borders and selfie camera | 1.15mm borders | 0.96mm borders; selfie camera hidden under the screen | 
Some apps and games run below the top refresh rate. Your frame rate depends on each game’s settings.
2. Design and build
| Detail | OnePlus 16 | RedMagic 12 Pro+ | 
|---|---|---|
| Thickness | 8.45mm to 8.55mm, by colour | Thinner than the 11 Pro+, final figure not out yet | 
| Weight | 217g to 220g, by colour | Lighter than the 11 Pro+, final figure not out yet | 
| Water and dust | IP66, IP68, IP69 and IP69K | Not out yet | 
| Colours | Tomorrow’s Starlight (with rear lights), Dark Forest and Mars Masterpiece | Transparent Dark Night, Transparent Silver Wing and Transparent Ice Blue | 
Hold each phone sideways before you buy, if you can. Check that your fingers reach the controls and that your grip doesn’t block the camera.
3. Cameras
| Camera | OnePlus 16 | RedMagic 12 Pro+ | 
|---|---|---|
| Rear cameras | Three | Two, flush with the back | 
| Main | 200MP, 1/1.4-inch sensor, OIS | Not out yet | 
| Ultra wide | 50MP | Not out yet | 
| Zoom | 50MP 3x periscope telephoto | Not out yet | 
| Selfie | 50MP | Under-display camera, megapixels not out yet | 
Megapixels tell only part of the story. Wait for sample photos in daylight and at night before you decide.
Camera verdict: The OnePlus 16 is the safer pick for photos. It has a 3x zoom camera, and RedMagic hasn’t shared its camera specs yet.
4. Battery and charging
| Detail | OnePlus 16 | RedMagic 12 Pro+ | 
|---|---|---|
| Battery | 9,000mAh | 8,400mAh (leak) | 
| Wired charging | 100W | 120W (leak) | 
| Wireless charging | 50W | 80W (leak) | 
| Bypass charging | Yes | Not out yet | 
If the leak holds, the OnePlus 16 carries 600mAh more. Lab tests will show which phone lasts longer in games.
Bypass charging sends power straight to the phone while you play plugged in, which keeps the battery cooler. Check when the feature turns on before you count on it.
For both phones, check whether the charger is included in the box, and price any wireless charger separately.
5. Software and updates
| Detail | OnePlus 16 | RedMagic 12 Pro+ | 
|---|---|---|
| Software | ColorOS 17 on Android 17 (China model) | Android 17, based on a Geekbench listing | 
| Update promise | Six-year smoothness claim from OnePlus’s lab tests | Two Android updates and three years of security fixes for the 11 Pro and newer models | 
OnePlus’s six-year claim covers smoothness tests and differs from a promise of six years of Android updates.
If you import a China phone, ask the seller to show you four things working:
- Google Play
- Your banking apps
- Notifications
- English language settings
Ask for the exact model number and check its network bands against what your network needs.
6. Other features
| Detail | OnePlus 16 | RedMagic 12 Pro+ | 
|---|---|---|
| Wi-Fi and Bluetooth | Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6.0 | Not out yet | 
| Fingerprint | Ultrasonic, under the screen | Not out yet | 
| IR blaster | Yes | Not out yet | 
| USB | USB 3.2 Gen 1 | Not out yet | 
Which phone should you buy?
Pick the OnePlus 16 if:
- You want one phone for gaming and photos.
- You have checked the imported model’s software and warranty.
Wait if:
- Fan cooling for long gaming sessions matters most to you.
- You want RedMagic’s final price and global specs first.
- You need tested battery life and camera results.
- You want a local warranty and easy returns.
Before you pay for either phone, get the full price in writing and confirm the exact model.
Frequently asked questions
Q) Is the OnePlus 16 coming to Nigeria?
- OnePlus sells the phone in China and has announced no Nigerian launch. Local sellers may import it, so check the model and warranty before you pay.
Q) When is the RedMagic 12 Pro+ launching globally?
- RedMagic launches the phone in China on October 15, 2026. It has not shared a global launch date yet.
Q) Which phone has the bigger battery?
- The OnePlus 16 has a 9,000mAh battery. Leaks put the RedMagic 12 Pro+ at 8,400mAh. If the leak holds, the OnePlus 16 wins on battery size.
Q) Do the OnePlus 16 and RedMagic 12 Pro+ use the same chip?
- Yes. Both use the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6. Cooling and software still change how each one performs.
Q) Can RedMagic ship directly to my country?
- RedMagic’s shipping list excludes Nigeria, Kenya, Ghana, and South Africa. Check its latest list before you order.

articles.title: CikaBika Bot RAT Uses Discord for C&C
articles.text:
Darktrace has uncovered a new malware campaign distributing a Rust-based RAT that relies on Discord for command-and-control (C&C).
Dubbed CikaBika Bot, the malware has been distributed via document-themed lures, likely as part of phishing attacks, and provides attackers with reconnaissance, remote execution, and data exfiltration capabilities on infected systems.
Victims receive a PDF file containing a disk image with a Windows shortcut (LNK) posing as a Word document. Once opened, it displays a decoy document and launches a hidden PowerShell process to decode and run an embedded executable.
The executable is a Nim-based loader containing a Rust DLL and a PowerShell deployment script that are written to temporary files. The script then attempts to move the DLL into the protected Edge directory to bypass Windows’s User Account Control (UAC).
According to Darktrace, the attackers likely attempt to sideload the malicious code through DLL search-order hijacking by exporting functions associated with Microsoft’s debugging library.
The final payload is the CikaBika Bot RAT, which immediately registers the infected machine with Discord and starts its reconnaissance routine, harvesting system information, processes, and network configuration, and taking a screenshot.
Commands and reports are transmitted via Discord, which is used as an interactive interface. The operator can issue command execution, reconnaissance, process enumeration/termination, file upload/download, and surveillance (screenshot, camera, streaming, and broadcasting) commands.
According to Darktrace, the attackers can use the RAT to compress directories into ZIP archives and exfiltrate them via Ngrok, and can request specific documents from the victim’s system.
“The observed use of Discord channels for individual victims, alongside additional data exfiltration through Ngrok, shows how legitimate services can be repurposed to support malicious operations,” Darktrace notes.

articles.title: Nueva solución para la escasez de energía: baterías usadas de autos eléctricos que alimentan centros de datos y fábricas
articles.text:
La escasez de energía eléctrica se convirtió en un obstáculo central para fabricantes y operadores de centros de datos en Estados Unidos. Conseguir nuevas conexiones a la red eléctrica puede demorar años, lo que obliga a las empresas a buscar alternativas más rápidas para obtener electricidad. Redwood Materials propone usar baterías de autos eléctricos retiradas de circulación como una vía para cerrar esa brecha.
La compañía trabaja junto a Rivian en la instalación de sistemas de almacenamiento de energía en las plantas de fabricación del fabricante de vehículos eléctricos. El acuerdo da una segunda función a las baterías una vez que dejan de usarse en los vehículos y vincula de forma directa la recuperación de baterías con la creciente demanda de energía industrial confiable.
Las baterías agotadas para conducir aún sirven para almacenar energía
Una batería de auto eléctrico puede perder la capacidad necesaria para la conducción sin volverse inservible. Algunos paquetes conservan suficiente potencial de almacenamiento energético para aplicaciones estacionarias, donde el peso y el empaquetado dejan de ser limitaciones relevantes.
Redwood recolecta las baterías usadas que provienen de Rivian y evalúa el destino de cada una. Los paquetes aptos para otro uso pasan a sistemas de almacenamiento de energía, mientras que el resto se somete a procesos de reciclaje para recuperar materiales de valor.
Rivian ya opera un sistema de baterías de segunda vida con una capacidad de 10 megavatios-hora en su planta de Normal, en Illinois. Redwood señala que se trata de la primera instalación de este tipo en una fábrica de un fabricante de automóviles de Estados Unidos.
Los centros de servicio de Rivian también constituyen una fuente constante de baterías retiradas durante tareas de mantenimiento y reparación. La recuperación de esos paquetes le da a Redwood acceso a materiales que, de otro modo, generarían costos adicionales de manipulación y transporte. Este esquema crea un vínculo entre el servicio técnico de los vehículos y el abastecimiento eléctrico de las fábricas: las baterías que regresan luego de circular en la calle podrían contribuir, con el tiempo, a alimentar las plantas donde se producen vehículos nuevos.
Integrar baterías distintas en un solo sistema exige resolver un desafío técnico
Combinar baterías retiradas en un único sistema de energía confiable representa un reto de ingeniería considerable. Los paquetes varían en química y antigüedad, y su rendimiento cambia según el uso que hayan tenido. Un sistema de almacenamiento debe contemplar esas diferencias para entregar electricidad de manera estable.
Redwood sostiene que su trabajo de recuperación de baterías le aporta información valiosa sobre cómo se deterioran los paquetes con el tiempo. Los ingenieros de la compañía utilizan ese conocimiento para decidir cómo incorporar baterías distintas dentro de un mismo sistema de almacenamiento.
La empresa también desarrolla sus propios convertidores DC-DC y software de control. Estos componentes permiten administrar la energía eléctrica a través del sistema y hacen posible que baterías con características diferentes aporten a una misma instalación. Controlar una mayor parte de la tecnología le permite a Redwood evitar algunas demoras en la adquisición de equipos y le otorga mayor flexibilidad al diseñar sistemas según las necesidades de cada cliente.
La demanda de los centros de datos amplía la oportunidad
El uso de baterías de segunda vida no se limita a las fábricas de automóviles. Los centros de datos que sostienen cargas de trabajo de inteligencia artificial requieren cantidades sustanciales de electricidad, y sus operadores no siempre pueden esperar a que lleguen las mejoras en la red eléctrica.
El problema no se reduce a la generación de electricidad: transformadores, inversores y otros equipos eléctricos también enfrentan demoras prolongadas en su adquisición. El almacenamiento en baterías ofrece una forma de administrar la energía disponible, aunque no reemplaza la necesidad de contar con una capacidad de generación adecuada.
Redwood planea combinar sus sistemas de baterías con energía solar y otras fuentes de generación, con el objetivo de desarrollar microrredes de gran escala capaces de abastecer sitios industriales y centros de datos. Este tipo de sistemas podría permitir que las empresas pongan en marcha sus instalaciones sin depender por completo de nuevas conexiones a la red eléctrica, aunque su eficacia dependerá de la demanda local de energía, la generación disponible y el costo de instalación.

articles.title: Superwhisper, Cohere partner on meeting recorder for enterprise clients | BetaKit
articles.text:
Superwhisper is partnering with Cohere to launch a local meeting recorder, putting the consumer AI dictation tool it in competition with enterprise meeting assistant companies like Granola and Otter.
The companies, which are both headquartered in Toronto, announced on Thursday that Superwhisper users can now access Cohere’s AI models to record and transcribe meetings, allowing them to take advantage of the enterprise AI company’s smaller language models, which are trained with far fewer parameters than large language models. Cohere’s Transcribe model will transcribe what was said, while its Tiny Aya model will provide meeting summaries and action items.
“Having our core audience realize the power of a tool like this is going to be big for our growth strategy.”
Brendan James, Superwhisper
Notably, using this feature with Cohere’s models lets it run locally on a user’s device, without storing that data with Superwhisper, the company said. Meeting recorder competitors such as Otter have seen legal action alleging privacy breaches, including a lawsuit claiming that it deceptively recorded and stored private user conversations. Otter was also embroiled in a controversy in an Ontario hospital when sensitive patient data was mistakenly shared with dozens of people.
“Privacy has always been a main point of our brand, because dictation is obviously so sensitive,” Superwhisper head of growth Brendan James said in an interview.
Founded in 2023 by PartnerStack co-founder Neil Chudleigh, Superwhisper is on a mission to allow people to do work primarily through voice dictation instead of typing on keyboards. The startup’s platform allows users to select different AI models of varying sizes to perform voice-to-text transcription, and previously partnered with Cohere to use its AI transcription model. It also released its own small, open-weight transcription cleanup model, S1, which appears as a default when users sign up.
Superwhisper already had a setting for meeting recording in its consumer dictation product, James said, but it wasn’t the easiest to find and was mostly employed by technically minded users. The team felt that with Cohere’s locally run models, they could offer an edge over other transcription services that are largely cloud-based (meaning the data is stored in the cloud rather than on a user’s device).
“This tool is our biggest swing at a full-company suite of products,” James said.
The tool doesn’t join meetings as an individual participant (a phenomenon some tech leaders have complained about), and James said this was intentional because the team finds it “invasive.” Canadian meeting-assistant startup Fellow works similarly and has called the feature “botless recording.”
RELATED: Cohere to acquire Czech AI cybersecurity firm Aisle, set up new cyber division
With the launch, Superwhisper is envisioning a push toward more enterprise clients. A significant portion of its user base consists of software developers dictating instructions to AI coding assistants—essentially, speaking code into terminals. The idea is to have its most frequent users try out the new tool and encourage adoption across their companies.
“Meeting tools are a dime a dozen. There’s so much competition,” James said. “Having our core audience realize the power of a tool like this is going to be big for our growth strategy.”
The company currently has professionals at big-name tech companies OpenAI, Meta, and Shopify using its transcription tools, James claimed. Earlier this summer, Superwhisper told BetaKit that its revenue split used to be mostly from individual users, but has increasingly grown toward enterprise plans.
Superwhisper prices its pro subscriptions at monthly, annual, or a one-time flat rate, but for the moment, it isn’t charging a premium for access to the meeting tool. In the near future, James said, they’ll likely revisit enterprise pricing.
Feature image courtesy Superwhisper.

articles.title: PlayStation podría quedarse sin 'Fallout' y 'Minecraft': Xbox estudia hacer exclusivos todos sus juegos
articles.text:
Xbox podría tomar un camino arriesgado para sus próximos juegos. La compañía estaría considerando volver a la estrategia de juegos exclusivos para su consola, olvidándose para siempre de Sony y Nintendo. Una nueva encuesta interna deja entrever que la compañía está pensando en los juegos exclusivos a futuro, excepto la franquicia Call of Duty.
En los últimos años, la estrategia de Microsoft con sus videojuegos ha consistido en llevarlos a todas las plataformas posibles. A diferencia de lo que ocurrió con la Xbox original, la compañía decidió que era más rentable acabar con la exclusividad, lanzando franquicias emblemáticas como Halo o Gears of War en PS5. Este enfoque multiplataforma generó rumores sobre una eventual muerte de la división de juegos de Microsoft.
Los tiempos cambian y la nueva CEO, Asha Sharma, quiere regresar a los exclusivos. Según Windows Central, una encuesta de Xbox Research plantea un escenario en donde todos los juegos de Xbox Game Studios serían exclusivos de sus consolas, con la excepción de Call of Duty. La estrategia no solo abarcaría juegos como Elder Scrolls 6 o el próximo Halo, sino también a Minecraft.
Minecraft, Diablo y el próximo juego de Hideo Kojima serían exclusivos de Xbox
Para Minecraft, la propuesta es más compleja, puesto que la franquicia es increíblemente popular en PlayStation y Nintendo. Si bien las versiones actuales seguirían funcionando y tendrían soporte, los usuarios que compraron el juego en estas consolas podrían quedarse sin recibir contenido nuevo.
La encuesta también pregunta por otras franquicias como Fallout, The Elder Scrolls, DOOM o Diablo, así como también PHYSINT, el próximo juego de Hideo Kojima. Si hacemos memoria, Xbox se hizo de los derechos para publicar el título de espionaje de Kojima, luego de que Sony cancelara el acuerdo con el reconocido desarrollador japonés.
Imagina que se anunciara que todos los futuros lanzamientos de Fallout serán exclusivos para la consola Xbox y no estarían disponibles en PlayStation o Nintendo.
En este escenario, ¿cuál de las siguientes opciones describe mejor dónde es MÁS PROBABLE que juegues a este nuevo contenido exclusivo?
- En una consola Xbox que ya poseo.
- En una nueva Xbox Series X|S que decidiría comprar.
- En una PC.
- No jugaría, ya que no estaría disponible en mi consola preferida.
- Otra opción (por favor, especifica).
- No me interesa jugar a este contenido exclusivo.
Xbox menciona que nada cambia en PC con este anuncio, puesto que los títulos seguirían publicándose en esa plataforma. Recordemos que Project Helix tiene un fuerte componente de PC y Microsoft ha confirmado que su próxima consola será compatible con juegos de ordenador.
Es una encuesta, no una realidad
Antes de adelantarse, vale la pena indicar que esto es una encuesta de mercado y estas se utilizan para medir las reacciones. Microsoft no ha confirmado ningún cambio, pero ya dejó claro que no tiene problemas en cerrarle la puerta a PlayStation. El ejemplo más evidente es Gears of War: E-Day, un juego first party que estaba considerado para PS5 y que cuyo lanzamiento en esta consola se canceló en el último minuto.
Asha Sharma ha indicado que busca recuperar la esencia de Xbox y devolverle esa autoridad que tuvo durante la Xbox 360. El problema es que esos tiempos en los que importaban los exclusivos ya no resultan tan rentables, sobre todo cuando se carga una deuda tan grande por comprar Activision. Es probable que Microsoft haya perdido decenas de millones de dólares por no lanzar el nuevo Gears en PS5 y por retrasar Forza Horizon 6 hasta 2027.
El caso de Minecraft es notable y siendo honestos, no creemos que se vuelva exclusivo. La franquicia es una mina de oro para Xbox y no hace sentido limitarla a una sola plataforma.
