articles.title: ChatGPT ganha acesso às abas do Chrome e pode executar tarefas no navegador
articles.text:
A OpenAI atualizou a extensão do ChatGPT para o Google Chrome com recursos que permitem à inteligência artificial (IA) consultar informações de diferentes abas abertas e executar tarefas diretamente no navegador. A novidade aproxima o assistente de ferramentas capazes de interagir com páginas da web, em vez de apenas responder a perguntas sobre elas.
Com a atualização, usuários podem pedir ao ChatGPT que analise várias páginas simultaneamente, compare informações e use esse contexto para elaborar respostas. Em demonstração divulgada pela OpenAI, por exemplo, o assistente compara sofás abertos em diferentes abas do navegador.
A empresa também ampliou as funções disponíveis na lateral do Chrome, permitindo acessar o histórico de conversas e utilizar os recursos do ChatGPT sem precisar sair da página em que se está trabalhando.
O que o ChatGPT consegue fazer no Chrome?
A atualização permite usar as abas abertas como contexto para solicitações feitas no ChatGPT. Isso pode ajudar em pesquisas, comparações de produtos e outras tarefas que exigem reunir informações espalhadas por diferentes páginas.
Entre as possibilidades estão:
- Comparar páginas: analisar informações de diferentes abas para comparar produtos, preços ou características;
- Preencher formulários: inserir dados em páginas da web durante a execução de uma tarefa;
- Enviar mensagens: realizar ações em serviços acessados pelo navegador;
- Baixar arquivos: executar downloads necessários para uma atividade;
- Organizar abas: agrupar e organizar páginas abertas para facilitar o trabalho.
Essas funções ampliam o uso do ChatGPT como agente de IA, ou seja, um sistema que pode não apenas fornecer informações, mas também executar etapas de uma tarefa. A extensão pode trabalhar em segundo plano sem assumir o controle da sessão de navegação ativa, segundo a descrição oficial do produto.
Como usar a novidade?
A extensão do ChatGPT pode ser instalada pela Chrome Web Store. Para aproveitar os recursos de controle do navegador, é necessário também utilizar o aplicativo do ChatGPT para computador e configurar o acesso correspondente.
Depois da configuração, o usuário pode mencionar abas abertas para fornecer contexto ao assistente ou solicitar que ele execute uma tarefa no navegador. A disponibilidade de alguns recursos depende das configurações da conta e do ambiente de trabalho.
A novidade também reforça a integração entre o ChatGPT e o navegador. A barra lateral permite consultar conversas anteriores e continuar trabalhando com o assistente ao lado da página aberta, sem alternar constantemente entre janelas.
Leia mais:
- 8 estados dos EUA processam OpenAI e acusam ChatGPT de colocar jovens em risco
- OpenAI alerta Polícia Federal sobre ameaças contra Lula feitas no ChatGPT
- ChatGPT ganha vozes mais naturais e melhora reconhecimento de sotaques; veja novidades
ChatGPT terá acesso a tudo o que faço na internet?
Não automaticamente. Embora a extensão tenha capacidade para interagir com páginas e possa solicitar permissões amplas durante a instalação, o acesso a sites e a determinadas informações depende das permissões configuradas pelo usuário.
A documentação da OpenAI informa que o sistema solicita autorização antes de interagir com um novo site, salvo quando já existe uma permissão aplicável. A empresa também afirma que pede confirmação para ações sensíveis, como consultar o histórico de navegação e baixar ou enviar arquivos.
A OpenAI acrescenta que não mantém registro separado e completo de todas as ações realizadas pelo navegador. As informações de navegação são armazenadas quando passam a integrar o contexto do ChatGPT, por exemplo, por meio de textos lidos, capturas de tela, chamadas de ferramentas ou mensagens.
Mesmo com essas proteções, é importante revisar as permissões concedidas e acompanhar as ações realizadas pelo assistente. O acesso a páginas autenticadas, como serviços de e-mail e plataformas de trabalho, pode facilitar tarefas, mas também exige atenção ao tipo de informação disponibilizada.
Aposta em agentes de IA
A atualização faz parte de movimento mais amplo para transformar assistentes de IA em ferramentas capazes de executar atividades digitais de ponta a ponta.
Em vez de exigir que o usuário copie informações de várias páginas e realize cada etapa manualmente, o ChatGPT pode utilizar o conteúdo disponível no navegador e atuar em tarefas que envolvem diferentes sites.
A OpenAI também oferece suporte à extensão em outros navegadores baseados em Chromium, incluindo Microsoft Edge, Brave, Opera e Vivaldi. A disponibilidade da conversa lateral varia: o recurso está disponível no Chrome, Edge, Brave e Vivaldi, mas não no Opera, de acordo com a documentação da empresa.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: Novel Android RAT ‘Hirudo’ Replaces Banking Apps With Trojanized Copies
articles.text:
A novel RAT uses trojanized replacements of legitimate banking apps to neutralize security controls from inside itself.
Hirudo is a remote access banking trojan for Android that combines elements of a traditional banking trojan and a full-featured RAT: it includes on-device credential theft with live remote control of the same phone. Remote control provides live screen viewing via WebRTC, remote camera access, and remote interaction through Android Accessibility Services.
The malware, tracked and analyzed by ThreatFabric, is delivered via a dropper contained within genuine-looking downloaded content (a shopping app, an adult video app or a short drama app advertised via social media). Victims install what appears to be a legitimate application, but once installed, the contained dropper checks whether the Hirudo RAT is already present and installs it if not.
The Hirudo payload currently targets eight Indonesian banking apps. Internal code suggests it could also be used to target banks in China, India, Mexico, Morocco and Thailand. The malware detects the specific Indonesian banking app in use on the device, displays a fake update prompt and proceeds to uninstall the true app and download its own modified bank-specific replacement.
This modified version of the app includes a hooking engine to blind signature, Accessibility, screen-capture and Play Integrity checks from within the app. “When the app asks Android for its signing certificate, the hook substitutes the genuine certificate and hides the test-key signature. When it queries enabled Accessibility services, the hook returns an empty list, so the controlling service is invisible,” comment the researchers.
The Hirudo RAT will steal banking credentials, gain real-time remote control of victim devices, provide live screen viewing of front- and rear-camera sessions, and SMS collection, including a 90-day initial scan and a configured list of bank and wallet senders.
The significance, say the researchers, is that “Hirudo marks a deliberate escalation in how Android bankers approach hardened applications. By moving its tampering inside the target app, the operation shifts the contest from the device to the application’s own integrity checks, and from a bespoke patch to a reusable engine that can be retargeted at other apps and regions.” Signals produced locally by an app which may have been replaced cannot be trusted on their own.
ThreatFabric offers fourfold advice to financial institutions. Play integrity should be verified and enforced server side. A valid verdict on its own is not enough since Hirudo relays Integrity requests through its own server.
Layered defenses with additional behavioral analytics should be applied. Behavioral data can help spot fraudulent activity, while the lack of behavioral data would be suspicious in itself.
Accessibility and screen-capture signals should be treated as supporting evidence rather than blocking evidence since fake apps can hide their own Accessibility service. Checks should feed risk scoring rather than stand on their own.
Backend transaction-risk controls at login, credential recovery, beneficiary creation and payment approval should be retained. A forged local result cannot substitute for a server-side decision.
Related: RatHat Android Trojan Uses AI for Automation
Related: XWorm RAT Evolves Into Surveillance Platform
Related: Fortinet Code Execution Flaw Exploited in PivotC2 RAT Attacks
Related: New ‘Mistic’ RAT Opens Door to Several Ransomware Families

articles.title: Nvidia is investing heavily into Europe - why now? | EU-Startups
articles.text:
NVIDIA has had a busy week on this side of the pond. From announcing new investments in British and French startups to launching collaborations in Sweden, supporting AI research and bringing developers together in Barcelona, Paris and London, the US chipmaker appears determined to play a bigger role in the continent’s technological future.
The activity comes ahead of NVIDIA GTC Berlin, taking place from 20 to 22 October 2026, where founder and CEO Jensen Huang will deliver a keynote.
But beyond the conference preparations, the announcements reveal a wider strategy involving startup funding, computing infrastructure, research partnerships and the development of AI applications across European industries.
NVIDIA’s 2026 European investment trail
This week builds on an investment footprint already documented by EU-Startups throughout 2026. The company has participated in funding rounds involving French AI developers Mistral AI (€3 billion) and AMI (€890 million), alongside British companies Nscale (€1.7 billion), Wayve (€1 billion), Ineffable Intelligence (€937 million) and Orbital Industries (€43 million).
In Spain, Valencia-based iPronics secured €107.6 million with NVIDIA backing, while its venture arm, NVentures, joined a €42 million extension for Sweden’s Legora.
Together, these eight announcements represent approximately €7.72 billion in company financing, although NVIDIA’s individual contributions have not been disclosed. Earlier investments in British startup PhysicsX and France’s Scintil Photonics further illustrate its established involvement in European AI development.
Fresh bets on British and French startups
Continuing this investment commitment in Europe, NVIDIA unveiled planned investments in five startups: Boltz, Foresight, Hiverge, Prima Mente and Riverlane. Although the individual investment amounts have not been disclosed, the selection of companies provides an indication of where NVIDIA sees opportunities for technological development.
These companies join NVIDIA’s existing investment activity in the UK, where it has previously supported startups including Synthesia, Wayve, Basecamp Research and Ineffable Intelligence.
The announcement also highlighted the role of NVIDIA’s Inception programme, which now includes more than 3,100 UK companies. The programme provides eligible startups with access to technical resources, expertise and opportunities to connect with NVIDIA’s wider network.
Across the English Channel, NVIDIA announced planned minority investments in four French startups: Doctolib, Entalpic, Genesis AI and Pigment. As previously reported by EU-Startups.
On 13 October, Huang attended an AI ecosystem reception in Paris alongside founders, researchers and policymakers, including France’s Minister of the Economy, Roland Lescure. Later that evening, he met President Emmanuel Macron at the Élysée Palace to discuss AI infrastructure, investments in French technology companies, open-source development and AI safety.
Speaking at the Paris reception, Jensen Huang, founder and CEO of NVIDIA, said, “Europe is one of the great regions of industrial manufacturing,” adding, “This is the beginning of the AI journey for the EU.”
This week also saw the launch of the Startup Ireland AI Accelerator Programme, which aims to support 1,000 new startups by 2030. NVIDIA is among the technology partners associated with the initiative, further extending its involvement in Europe’s entrepreneurship networks.
Sweden’s AI ambitions take shape
Beyond France and the UK, the Nordics have emerged as another focus of NVIDIA’s European activities. The company highlighted how startups and technology companies across the region are building products using its computing platforms and open models. With several companies demonstrating applications ranging from intellectual property management to autonomous transportation.
Stockholm-based Stilta is using NVIDIA’s Nemotron models to analyse patent portfolios, helping businesses monitor intellectual property across large numbers of patents. Agaton is applying similar technology to real-time sales intelligence, while Swedish speech technology company Klang has developed Pianissimo, a transcription model trained on more than 50,000 hours of Swedish speech.
Meanwhile, Gothenburg-based Embedl, a member of NVIDIA Inception, has collaborated with Space Cargo Unlimited to develop an onboard AI prototype that monitors protein crystallisation experiments in space without requiring continuous connectivity to Earth.
Perhaps one of the most interesting Nordic announcements for founders was NVIDIA’s collaboration with the Norrsken Foundation to establish the Stockholm AI Lab.
Scheduled to open in 2027, the new hub will bring together AI-focused entrepreneurs working on challenges in healthcare, climate, food and society. Located in central Stockholm, it will also house NVIDIA’s local office, bringing the company physically closer to entrepreneurs developing AI technologies.
Another important development comes from Sweden AI Factory, one of Europe’s 19 EuroHPC-funded AI factories, which announced a collaboration with NVIDIA to open its infrastructure and expertise to startups and SMEs.
The expansion of AI infrastructure across the Nordics is also gathering pace. NVIDIA reports that regional cloud providers are working towards approximately one gigawatt of AI cloud capacity by the end of 2027, with companies including Nscale, Verda and Volta among those participating in the expansion.
“Physical AI is the next big opportunity,” said Deepu Talla, vice president of robotics and edge computing at NVIDIA. “Around 70% of GDP is in the physical world, and that makes physical AI one of the largest opportunities ahead of us. Europe can combine AI with its human capital, engineering expertise and industrial capabilities to create more value.”
Europe’s AI opportunity comes with a catch
Taken together, this week’s announcements suggest that NVIDIA’s strategy in Europe extends well beyond financial investments.
By supporting startups, offering access to computing resources, collaborating with research institutions and establishing closer relationships with developer communities, NVIDIA is positioning itself across multiple stages of the European AI development process.
At the same time, NVIDIA’s expansion raises questions about Europe’s technological independence. While access to funding, computing infrastructure and technical expertise could help European startups compete internationally, greater adoption of NVIDIA’s technology could also increase their dependence on a single US supplier.
The bigger question is whether Europe’s startups can use this momentum to build lasting, globally competitive companies of their own. If they succeed, NVIDIA could benefit from supplying the infrastructure behind their growth, while European founders have an opportunity to capture more of the value created by the next generation of AI technologies.

articles.title: Pig kidneys that were “frozen” for a year have been brought back to life
articles.text:
Pig kidneys that were “frozen” for a year have been brought back to life
One day human organs could also be banked safely for future transplantation.
Pig kidneys that were cooled to -150 °C and stored in a freezer for months have been successfully rewarmed and shown to work again for the first time, say scientists. They hope to replicate the findings with human organs.
The kidneys—which are similar in size to human ones—were left in a glass-like state, in one case for over a year. Once they had been rewarmed, tested in machines, and transplanted into pigs, the kidneys regained their color and made urine—key signs they were working.
“Ten years ago … I wouldn’t say I had high hopes it was actually going to work,” says Erik Finger, a transplant surgeon at the University of Minnesota who co-led the work. “After we did the last transplant, I walked out of the room and said, ‘This is a big deal.’” The research was shared at the preprint server bioRxiv and has not yet been peer-reviewed.
The kidneys aren’t perfect, and the researchers have yet to demonstrate that they can sustain life over the long term. But the results represent a milestone achievement, say others in the field.
“Thank God that someone’s actually managed to do it in one organ and prove that it works,” says Peter Kilbride, a cryobiologist and cofounder of Kyros Kairos, a company focused on improving funding for cryopreservation research, who was not involved in the research. “For years, people have been trying and failing to get to this step. Finally, we’ve got this breakthrough.”
“Their work is amazing and will enable us to truly, indefinitely bank organs,” says Korkut Uygun, a biomedical engineer and professor of surgery at Harvard Medical School, who was also not involved in the research. “It is a revolutionary time for transplantation.”
Buying time
Every year, tens of thousands of organ transplants take place in the US alone. These procedures are thought to have saved 2 million years of life in the last 25 years. But there’s plenty of room for improvement.
One major challenge is the lack of available organs. Even when an organ becomes available, it can be difficult to get it to the right recipient within 24 to 36 hours, which is the current limit for preserving human organs.
People who receive organ transplants must also take drugs that suppress their immune systems for the rest of their lives. These drugs are meant to stop their bodies from rejecting the new organs. But they come with side effects and increase the risk of infections and cancer.
The ability to bank organs for long periods of time holds the promise to address all these challenges. Doctors would have more time to match organs to recipients. They’d be able to limit the risk of organ rejection, too—potentially by preparing recipients, and their immune systems, beforehand.
“With real organ banking … instead of the patients waiting for the organ, it’s the organs that are waiting for the patients,” says Finger.
Scientists have been able to cool cells to ultra-low temperatures through a process called vitrification, which essentially turns them to something like glass. This procedure is already used to store eggs, sperm, and embryos. Vitrifying whole organs is much harder.
Some problems can be avoided with cryoprotectants—chemicals that work like antifreeze and prevent damaging ice crystals from forming. But these chemicals tend to be incredibly toxic. It’s also difficult to rapidly and uniformly cool large tissues, and just as hard to evenly rewarm an organ all the way through.
Working with John Bischof, a bioengineer at the University of Minnesota, Finger and colleagues have come up with a solution. Once an organ has been loaded with a cryoprotectant, they infuse it with iron oxide nanoparticles. These nanoparticles don’t do anything to the cells. But when it’s time to rewarm the organ, they can be activated with an electromagnetic field.
When the radiofrequency of that field switches between two states, the particles also flip, realigning themselves with the field. That causes them to release heat throughout the organ. Adjusting the power of the field allows the team to control the rate of heating so that it gets faster once the organ reaches -120°C.
The researchers successfully vitrified rat kidneys using this approach in work published in 2023. Back then, they were able to rewarm kidneys that had been kept in a freezer for up to 100 days before transplanting them into rats.
Since then, the team has been trying to achieve the same success with bigger organs. Pig kidneys are thought to be a good model for human ones—they’re about the same size and look similar. Rat kidneys weigh around one gram; pig kidneys are around 100.
It hasn’t been easy. The cryoprotectant used for vitrifying rat kidneys didn’t work as well in the pig organs. “We had to rediscover and modify the cocktail,” says Bischof. “That’s why it’s taken us three years.”
Deep-freezing kidneys
The first step in the procedure is to remove a kidney from a donor pig. Once it’s out, the kidney is flushed with a commonly used organ preservation solution to remove the blood, bagged, and temporarily laid on a bed of ice in a cooler so it can be taken over to the engineering lab.
There, team members unpack the kidney and hook it up to a device they’ve designed to control the organ’s temperature and pressure. Then they start to load it up with the cocktail of cryoprotectants, slowly enough to ensure an even spread through the organ but quickly enough to minimize any toxic effects. It takes around two hours.
The next step is to infuse the organ with the iron oxide nanoparticles, which are pumped through the organ for around seven to eight minutes, says Finger. Then it’s time to cool the organ by pumping cold nitrogen vapor into a chamber housing it.
It’s a delicate process, and the team must ensure that the organ is cooling all the way through. At the same time, they must lower the kidney’s temperature as quickly as possible to prevent ice from forming. “Oftentimes there are multiple people doing different things to make sure that things don’t go awry,” says Bischof.
Once the organ reaches the vitrified state at around -120 °C, it “behaves like a glass,” says Finger. “At that point, you can stay stable for long periods of time—we think indefinitely.” The team then pauses the cooling process to ensure that the organ is glassy throughout. Otherwise, it could crack.
After the pause, if everything goes well, the kidney is ultimately cooled to -150 °C. Once it’s in the freezer, it can stay there for days, weeks, or even months. The team has kept a small number of kidneys banked for over a year.
Pink right up
The real test of these kidneys comes when they’re taken out of the freezer, rewarmed, and flushed of their chemicals and nanoparticles. Can they support life? So far, the team has tested some of them in a couple of different ways.
In one set of experiments, the researchers put rewarmed kidneys on perfusion devices—systems that are already used in transplant surgeries both to provide organs with nutrients and to help doctors assess them while they’re out of the body.
In another set of experiments, Finger and his colleagues transplanted rewarmed kidneys into pigs and monitored them for two hours. In both experiments, the rewarmed kidneys seemed to recover, says Finger. “They pink right up,” he says.
There are lots of ways to measure the function of a kidney, but one key test is whether or not the organ can make urine. By this measure, the rewarmed kidneys did well, although they produced around two-thirds of the amount that would normally be expected. “They produce urine … within a minute or so,” says Finger. “We know that they work.”
Most of the rewarmed kidneys had been banked for days or weeks. But one had been in the freezer for just over a year. When Finger and his colleagues rewarmed it and put it on a perfusion machine, they found that it produced urine “immediately.” “It actually looked better than many of the [other] kidneys,” says Finger. “We’re comfortable now saying we can store them for a year and rewarm them with excellent function.”
“It’s a very big deal to go a year,” says Kevin Myer, president and CEO of LifeGift, an organ procurement organization based in Texas. Being able to store organs for that length of time would transform organ transplantation. He envisions banks of organs that could be used on demand in emergency cases where people can’t wait, such as for some drug overdoses or gunshot wounds.
Final hurdles
But the procedure isn’t ready for prime time just yet. As well as producing less urine than expected, the rewarmed kidneys also showed signs of injury. The damage seems to be caused by the cryoprotectant chemicals, say the researchers.
“This is one big breakthrough that solves half the problem,” as Kilbride puts it.
The team has shown that the rewarmed kidneys can regain blood flow, which is “very important," says Greg Fahy, a cryobiologist who is considered a pioneer in the field. But he’s worried about the extent of the damage to the organs. “We can’t tell from these experiments whether these kidneys might have supported life or not.”
But Fahy, who is chief scientific officer at the biotech companies Intervene Immune and 21st Century Medicine (where he is also executive director), acknowledges that it’s not clear how these kidneys might fare once they’re inside a living animal for the long term.
Finger also hopes to find ways to repair the damage seen in the kidneys. Other research has shown that the health of transplant organs can improve while they’re on perfusion machines. And damaged kidneys might undergo some level of self-repair once they’re in a body. At any rate, human kidneys may cope better with the process than pig kidneys, says Finger.
The next step will be to test the kidneys in pigs over longer periods of time. The team, along with many other researchers in the field, will continue the search for less toxic cryoprotectants, too. Finger, Bischof, and their colleagues are also planning experiments with human kidneys.
Finger is optimistic. “We’re going to see that there’s injury, and it’s not perfect ... but now we’ve got to the point where it works,” he says. “These are big, historic milestones in our field, and we’re excited about it.”

articles.title: Microsoft y la policía de Japón desarticularon una red que envió más de 1.000 millones de mensajes de estafa
articles.text:
Microsoft y la Agencia Nacional de Policía de Japón desarticularon una red de cibercrimen que, desde enero de 2026, facilitó el envío de más de 1.000 millones de mensajes de estafa por correo electrónico y SMS a más de 75.000 organizaciones en más de 150 países, informó la empresa tecnológica.
La operación se apoyó en una orden de la Corte de Distrito de Estados Unidos para el distrito sur de Florida. Con ese respaldo judicial, Microsoft y la organización sin fines de lucro Health-ISAC incautaron y redirigieron los dominios que sostenían la infraestructura criminal.
La compañía ya deshabilitó más de 20.000 cuentas vinculadas a la red y bloqueó más de 100.000 dominios usados para suplantar marcas y cometer fraude. Más de 750 millones de los mensajes maliciosos detectados tenían como blanco a clientes de Microsoft.
Los mensajes replicaban los avisos que millones de personas reciben a diario: una alerta de que un paquete no pudo entregarse, un peaje impago, un problema con la cuenta bancaria o una deuda impositiva pendiente, según describió Microsoft en el comunicado que acompañó el anuncio.
Un mercado clandestino en chino
La investigación arrancó a fines de 2025, cuando la Agencia Nacional de Policía de Japón alertó a Microsoft sobre campañas de mensajes fraudulentos que afectaban a personas y empresas japonesas. Ese dato llevó a los investigadores a un entramado mucho más amplio.
Microsoft identificó un mercado clandestino en idioma chino al que denominó YAM Store, que vendía cuentas robadas o fraudulentas de Microsoft y Google junto con el acceso a servicios de alojamiento. Los compradores podían elegir el tipo de cuenta según su antigüedad o el tipo de organización asociada.
Para confirmar cómo operaba la tienda, los investigadores de Microsoft realizaron compras controladas de cuentas y herramientas, lo que les permitió reconstruir la cadena completa del negocio, desde el robo de las credenciales hasta la reventa a otros delincuentes.
Ese mercado abastecía a otros tres kits de phishing, llamados CoGUI, Haozi e Iron Man, que ofrecían sitios y mensajes listos para usar con apariencia de bancos, organismos de gobierno, empresas de logística y entidades de salud.
Iron Man, el más reciente de los tres, incluye más de 2.300 plantillas que imitan organizaciones de más de 150 países. En conjunto, los tres kits usaron cerca de 17.000 dominios únicos para sus campañas, según un análisis de la empresa de seguridad Proofpoint.
CoGUI fue el kit más usado contra víctimas en Japón y Estados Unidos desde al menos octubre de 2024, con campañas que suplantaron marcas de consumo y financieras como Amazon, Apple y Rakuten. Proofpoint llegó a bloquear más de 100 millones de mensajes mensuales vinculados a ese kit.
El kit empezó a perder terreno frente a Iron Man desde junio de 2026, según el relevamiento de Microsoft. Los operadores cobraban en criptomonedas, entre ellas USDT y Ethereum, para dificultar el rastreo de sus ganancias.
Los compradores de estas herramientas apuntaron, sobre todo, a organizaciones de los sectores de salud, servicios financieros, distribución mayorista y tecnología, con víctimas concentradas en Japón, Estados Unidos, Australia e India.
Una red con alcance global
La empresa de ciberseguridad Resecurity colaboró en el rastreo técnico de los kits, mientras que Cloudflare, Oracle, Proofpoint y la firma de inteligencia sobre criptoactivos TRM Labs aportaron información para sostener la demanda civil contra los operadores.
El Centro Japonés de Control del Cibercrimen, que agrupa a más de 130 organizaciones miembro, ayudó a confirmar la magnitud del fraude contra empresas y consumidores japoneses. La red generó decenas de millones de dólares para sus operadores, según Microsoft.
TRM Labs, especializada en el seguimiento de movimientos con criptomonedas, contribuyó a ubicar el dinero recaudado por los operadores y a sostener los pedidos judiciales para congelar activos vinculados a la operación, de acuerdo con el detalle que publicó esa firma.
Health-ISAC, la organización que nuclea a hospitales y empresas de salud para compartir información sobre amenazas digitales, se sumó como codemandante en la causa civil después de que varios de sus miembros fueran blanco repetido de los kits de phishing.
“Lo que empezó como actividad de estafa dirigida a personas y organizaciones en Japón llevó a los investigadores a una economía de servicios clandestina que abastecía a criminales en todo el mundo”, escribió Steven Masada, gerente general de la Unidad de Delitos Digitales de Microsoft.
Masada agregó que YAM Store, CoGUI e Iron Man son apenas una parte de una red criminal más grande, aunque su desarticulación complica el acceso de los delincuentes a las cuentas, herramientas e infraestructura que necesitan para operar.
“El mensaje de estafa es a menudo la única parte que ven las víctimas. Los negocios detrás son los que lo hacen posible”, escribió el ejecutivo en el comunicado conjunto de Microsoft y Health-ISAC.
Microsoft aclaró que el ecosistema identificado no se limita al abuso de sus propios servicios y que continúa eliminando infraestructura alojada en su plataforma mientras avanza el bloqueo de nuevos dominios fraudulentos.
.

articles.title: Volvo makes a bigger bet on Nvidia for hands-free automated driving | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Volvo is leveling up its automated driving system through an expansion of its nearly decade-long partnership with Nvidia. The companies announced on Thursday that Volvo will use three pieces of Nvidia hardware and software in its future vehicles to provide an automated driving system that can navigate urban streets and highways.
Under the expanded partnership, Volvo will combine its vehicle safety systems and engineering with Nvidia’s Hyperion sensor and compute architecture, Alpamayo driving software stack, and Halos safety evaluation layer.
The Alpamayo stack is redundant and diverse, according to Ali Kani, who heads up Nvidia’s automotive division. It combines Alpamayo, a family of AI models, datasets, and simulation and development tools used to build autonomous-driving software, with classical software that uses machine learning and camera and radar perception, he said.
“The point is we run these two stacks at the same time, and we have multimodal sensors in our philosophy because it’s a safer product that way,” Kani said, adding that the open source Alpamayo software has now been downloaded by more than 650,000 developers.
Volvo didn’t reveal the value of the partnership or which vehicle model would be the first to use this new Nvidia tech stack. But Alwin Bakkenes, Volvo’s head of software development, hinted at the scale of the deal and how it represents the automaker’s evolution toward developing a full-tech stack designed for its electric vehicles as well as its plug-in hybrids and gas-powered vehicles.
“Automakers used to be very much like car-line-based development and working with various suppliers, etc. and we have completely changed and migrated into being a full-tech stack company,” Bakkenes said, adding that Volvo will start this partnership with a brand new vehicle that “will come in the not-too-near future.”
He said the first vehicle with this new Nvidia tech stack will debut within the decade, and “then of course the technology can go beyond that.”
While Volvo’s relationship with Nvidia isn’t new, the expanded partnership represents the automaker’s effort to bring the latest automated driving software to all of its vehicles — not just its EVs.
All of Volvo’s battery-electric vehicles use Nvidia’s Orin computer chip, which processes information from cameras, radar, and other sensors to help a vehicle understand its surroundings and make driving decisions.
“What we’re going to do in the future is actually standardize more on Hyperion — also from a sensor set perspective — to really open up the stack for the wider partnership with Nvidia,” Bakkenes said.

articles.title: The tech backlash is now in theaters
articles.text:
Though movies about disruptive tech founders are nothing new, 2026 has been unusually stacked with features that take a much more critical look at how Silicon Valley is reshaping our reality. Aaron Sorkin’s The Social Reckoningframes Mark Zuckerberg as a robotic villain whose ambitions are destabilizing society. Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s You Can See Everything paints a damning picture of Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes as she prepares for her ongoing stint in prison. After years of being widely celebrated as a visionary, you can see how the larger narrative around Elon Musk has shifted in projects like Alex Gibney’s Musk documentary. And while Luca Guadagnino’s Artificialis a dark comedy, it is also a character study that makes Sam Altman look like a manipulative sociopath.
The tech backlash is now in theaters
Between The Social Reckoning, You Can See Everything, Musk, and Artificial, filmmakers are taking Big Tech to task.
The tech backlash is now in theaters
Between The Social Reckoning, You Can See Everything, Musk, and Artificial, filmmakers are taking Big Tech to task.
Even though some of these movies are fictionalized dramas, each of them draws from the wealth of critical reporting that has revealed their subjects to be less-than-savory characters. You get the sense that these filmmakers are trying to tell stories that are meant to resonate with audiences whose views of Big Tech have long since begun to dim. But it also feels like some of Hollywood’s biggest studios are finally embracing the idea that the tech backlash isn’t letting up anytime soon.
Especially when you compare them to classics like The Social Network, the latest wave of cinematic dramas based on Silicon Valley power struggles has been far less sympathetic to their central figures. David Fincher’s 2010 film starring Jesse Eisenberg presented Zuckerberg as a complicated and misunderstood savant, but The Social Reckoning builds its story around the idea that the Facebook / Meta head is a man whose obsession with growth poses an existential threat to democracy. By focusing on the allegations leveled by whistleblower Frances Haugen, the movie is able to highlight Zuckerberg’s public transformation into a powerful executive who wields autocratic control over a multibillion-dollar social media empire.
What The Social Reckoning lacks in timeliness (The Wall Street Journal began reporting Haugen’s warnings in 2021) and stylistic flair, it makes up for in the way it connects Facebook / Meta’s past internal decisions to events that are still playing out in real time. The movie’s scenes that dig into Instagram’s negative impacts on teens’ mental health and the relationship between Facebook’s algorithm and the spread of misinformation feel as if they’re speaking directly to present-day concerns about how much influence Meta has over people’s lives. Similarly, Gibney’s Musk documentary acts as both a chronicle of the xAI / SpaceX head’s past and an inquiry into why the public was ever willing to let Musk accrue so much power within governments across the world.
Musk’s response to Gibney’s film has been telling. X has blocked the feature from being advertised on the platform, and Musk — a self-proclaimed “free speech absolutist” — has threatened to take legal action against Gibney for producing a “hit piece.” It wasn’t entirely surprising to see Musk personally badmouthing a project that casts him in a negative light, but it was curious to see the Musk ads initially missing from other social media platforms, including YouTube, Facebook, Instagram, and TikTok.
Though the Meta subsidiaries and YouTube ultimately reversed their decisions, TikTok has stuck to its guns — which feels notable given the company’s indirect connections to the Trump administration by way of Skydance Corporation CEO David Ellison. David’s father — Oracle cofounder Larry Ellison — is a longtime Donald Trump supporter and one of the American billionaires who led the consortium of investors that purchased TikTok’s US business late last year. Ellison has reportedly promised Gibney that Musk will air on HBO (now a part of Skydance) sometime next January. The film is currently screening in select theaters, but it is hard to argue that it hasn’t had to deal with an unusual amount of outside interference in the weeks leading up to its release.
Guadagnino’s Artificial — which was originally going to be released by Amazon — also faced unexpected marketing challenges this year. The streaming giant backed out of its deal to distribute the film this past June, just months after announcing that it was investing $50 billion in OpenAI. All of that made it seem very much like Amazon and other studios financially involved with AI companies might be cooling on the idea of releasing projects critical of the technology’s creators. Now that Artificial has begun screening and people have a sense of how it takes Altman to task, it’s easy to see why Amazon didn’t want to have its name attached. More than anything else, that decision may be what convinces people to see Artificial in theaters when it releases widely on December 25th, and OpenAI’s impending IPO could make the movie’s messages about Altman feel that much more relevant.
What sets Fielder’s You Can See Everything apart from each of these other recent tech films is how direct a view it gives you into the actual life of its subject. The documentary’s production began well after Holmes had already been sentenced to more than 11 years in prison, and Fielder uses his access to grill her about why she doesn’t believe that she defrauded Theranos investors. Invited to live with Holmes and her partner William Evans in a rental home during the month before she was set to begin her sentence, Fielder allows himself to become a character who can’t entirely tell whether his hosts’ supposed wish for radical transparency is genuine.
That central tension turns You Can See Everything into a surprisingly fascinating watch that challenges you to consider who’s actually in control of the documentary. Throughout the movie, Fielder repeatedly wonders if Holmes is using him as part of her recent PR campaign, and he leaves the audience to draw their own conclusions.
It often feels like Fielder is asking viewers to really listen to how Holmes presents herself on camera and then reconcile that person with what you might have read about Holmes in the news or seen in Hulu’s The Dropout. Whether or not Holmes is really just a committed performer who’s trying to manipulate the public shapes every beat of the film, and it makes You Can See Everything feel like a truly in-depth and honest examination of one of Silicon Valley’s most infamous figures — one who’s already captured so much of the public’s attention.
Even though some of these films have been box office flops, their existence reflects a larger cultural shift in how people are thinking about modern technology and the powers behind it. Hollywood has spent years poking fun at and mythologizing founders, and portions of the industry are finally beginning to take a more critical view. As we continue to deal with the fallout of things like Elon Musk’s tenure at DOGE and OpenAI’s quest to bake generative AI into every aspect of our lives, audiences’ appetites for movies like these could grow. And with all of these founders racing to monopolize the next tech frontier, the entertainment industry will probably have plenty of source material to draw from.

articles.title: UFO-Alarm nach SpaceX-Start? Das steckt hinter der spektakulären "Weltraumqualle"
articles.text:
UFO-Alarm nach SpaceX-Start? Das steckt hinter der „Space Jellyfish
Die Mission SpaceX CRS-35 ist am 13. Oktober um 6:33 Uhr Ortszeit von der Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida gestartet. An Bord der gestarteten Cargo-Dragon-Rakete befinden sich laut dem Kennedy Space Center der Nasa eine Reihe von wissenschaftlichen Geräten, Experimenten und Fracht, die als Nachschub zur Raumstation ISS geliefert werden sollen. Doch die Nachschubmission sorgt derzeit nicht mit ihrem Ziel, sondern mit ihrem Start für breite Aufmerksamkeit.
Wie entsteht der „Space Jellyfish“ am Himmel?
In den sozialen Medien werden unzählige Bilder und Videos gepostet, die einige Zeit nach dem Start aufgenommen wurden. Am Himmel ist dabei ein bläulicher Schimmer zu sehen, der die Form einer Qualle hat. Was zunächst wie ein KI-generierter Fake aussieht, ist ein echtes Phänomen, das unter bestimmten Umständen nach einem Raketenstart auftreten kann.
Der „Space Jellyfish“, der auch als „Jellyfish Ufo“ oder „Rocket Jellyfish“ bezeichnet wird, besteht aus den Abgasen der Rakete, die sich in den höheren Luftschichten sammeln und dort verharren. Das Phänomen wird allerdings nur sichtbar, wenn der Raketenstart in den frühen Morgen- oder späten Abendstunden stattfindet. Genau dann, wenn die Sonne nicht auf die Erde scheint, aber noch den Himmel beleuchtet.
Dadurch trifft das Sonnenlicht auf die Raketenabgase und erleuchtet sie. Da wir auf der Erde im Dunkeln stehen, werden sie für uns sichtbar. Die aktuelle Weltraumqualle von SpaceX ist dabei kein einzelnes Phänomen. Schon seit den 70ern gab es zahlreiche Raketenstarts, die einen „Space Jellyfish“ nach sich gezogen haben. Als das Phänomen noch nicht weitläufig bekannt war, wurden die Sichtungen oftmals als Ufos oder Anzeichen für nukleare Raketenschläge gehalten, wie die Washington Post schon 2017 berichtete.
Für SpaceX ist das Phänomen natürlich eine willkommene Werbung für den Flug zur ISS. Ob die Uhrzeit so gelegt war, dass die Möglichkeit eines „Space Jellyfishs“ erhöht ist, ist nicht bekannt. SpaceX musste den Flug schon zweimal verschieben. Er sollte ursprünglich im November 2026 stattfinden, wurde dann aber aufgrund von Schäden an einem russischen Launch-Pad auf August vorgezogen. So sollte sichergestellt werden, dass die Astronaut:innen auf der ISS ausreichend Nachschub für das kommende Jahr bekommen. Als das Launch-Pad schneller als erwartet repariert werden konnte, wurde der Start wieder nach hinten geschoben.

articles.title: How Close Are We To Fully Autonomous Chip Design?
articles.text:
Synopsys CEO Sassine Ghazi talks about AI agents, the limits of autonomous engineering, digital twins, and the challenges facing 3D-ICs.
Key Takeaways:
Sassine Ghazi, president and CEO of Synopsys, sat down with Semiconductor Engineering to discuss how AI is transforming chip design and engineering. What follows are excerpts from a keynote interview at SEMICON West this week, which was conducted before a live audience.
SE: The big change over the past year, and really the big story right now, is AI. We’re processing more AI data. Chips need to run faster. They need to run cooler. Do we really need to rethink how we’re developing these chips?
Ghazi: Absolutely. Actually, we started talking about how to re-engineer engineering, because you need to co-design and optimize across multiple intersections, starting at the physics level, material, process technology, architecture, design, along with the software and the model itself, because the model itself is what’s defining the workload, and how do you optimize along that stack?
SE: So where does AI actually fit into chip design? We’ve been dealing with computational software since what, the 1980s?
Ghazi: Yes. Around the 2016 time frame, we introduced reinforcement learning in a number of our technologies and tools to take advantage of a large space of parameters that you need to optimize, and to use AI to assist the human engineer in optimizing that large space. Today, we’ve moved from an assistant to an actual orchestration of multiple task agents. We have more than 40 task agents. Those task agents are experts of the tools, where you feed them all the knowledge, the capabilities that the tools need in order to optimize for a certain outcome. So those are specific task agents. The magic that has happened over the last year or so is the advancement in intelligence and reasoning of these models. You have long-horizon orchestration, where these models can orchestrate multiple agents, and all you have to do is give it an outcome you’re trying to achieve. That’s where we are today. So it is truly amazing the progress that we’ve made.
SE: Where do you see this going? We’ve gone from GenAI over the past four years to Agentic AI. What comes next?
Ghazi: You can look at it this way. We started from an assistant copilot, to generative capability, to now what we’re describing as long-horizon autonomous agents, where instead of giving a prompt, you give an outcome, and you expect that model is able to reason and trigger actions for multiple agents to achieve that task. So it’s autonomous engineering. Now the question typically comes up then, ‘What happens to the human engineer? What is the role that they play, and is that a risk for the industry?’ Actually, I don’t see it that way at all. Today, there’s a massive demand for more companies to define and specialize silicon, to customize silicon. And if you think about the challenges that the industry is having, it’s the shortage of human engineers to be able to architect, take a spec, define the silicon, and drive toward an outcome. So the whole autonomous orchestration is a very positive thing for the industry, where you still need the human judgment to define the architecture, to guide, and to sign off the final check before you go into product manufacturing.
SE: At the Converge conference earlier this year, some of the big chipmakers said that they will be able to develop chips with no human in the loop. Is that realistic? And if so, where does the human play? Is it a matter of, ‘Check this, make sure it’s accurate, it actually works as I expect?’
Ghazi: That’s the ambition. Today, we do have a number of engagements and technologies where you can start with a spec. The spec comes from a system company. The system company can be — think of any hyperscaler, any frontier AI lab, any EV automotive, drone. Think of a system company defining a spec. That spec is based on the end product. At some point, you need to translate it into the electronic spec. Today, we have engagements where the customer can provide a spec to Synopsys Autonomous Agent, and it moves it to a verified RTL, which is the starting point for the chip design. That process used to take many months for many human engineers, to go from the spec to writing the RTL, verifying the RTL, and ensuring that it can be physically implemented and manufactured. So today we have that step being done autonomously. We have it. We have a number of customers engaged in it now. With the intelligence and the reasoning, can it expand into the physical implementation, physical verification, into the sign-off of the chip? I have no doubt we’ll get there. Is this here today? No. Is there an ambition to have more autonomy in that workflow? Absolutely.
SE: So do agents now become the new IP?
Ghazi: Maybe a different way to ask the question is, ‘What will be the core IP for Synopsys? Is it the tool itself? Is it the agent who is the expert on the tool and needs the tool in order to perform a task?’ So today, the model is fantastic at reasoning and exploring. You still need the tool, i.e., the agent, in order to generate and to validate. Because you can generate an outcome, you can explore many design options and possibilities. But at the end, you have to decide on one implementation that provides the best performance, power, cost, etc.
SE: The reason I ask that question is that when Synopsys was developing — and still is developing — IP, almost all of that ended up as custom IP because your customers demanded that it fit into something. Do AI agents now fill that because they do adapt?
Ghazi: There is what I describe as the classic EDA products — the tools used for design. And then there’s the IP, which is the interface IP. These are needed to connect chip-to-chip and the chip to the system. Those are increasingly customized. Let’s say you’re a hyperscaler. You’re trying to optimize your chip and customize it for a specific workload in order to achieve performance, power targets, etc. If the interface IP is general, and not customized, then you’re losing competitiveness. The area may not be optimized. The performance is not optimized because it’s general-purpose IP.
SE: Changing topics, there’s a whole new market opening up in physical AI, but there’s a lot of dependencies that you have to think about. There’s a lot of data orchestration, and it’s a brand new opportunity. Elon Musk was promoting this as a $25 trillion to $30 trillion opportunity [just for Tesla] as we go forward. What do you see?
Ghazi: As AI expands from digital to physical, the silicon is powering both. You need customized silicon for both. The moment you start moving to physical application, it’s software-defined. The automotive industry has been heading down that path for at least 7 to 10 years with the software-defined vehicle. As the vehicle becomes autonomous, you need to model not only the electronics and the physics of the end product. You need to model for the environment in which it’s operating. So it’s a multiple optimization opportunity between silicon, the system itself — that includes multiple engineering of structure, fluid, the actual mechanical system — and how to model the environment in which that system is going to operate. So it’s a massive engineering opportunity, and we play from the silicon to the system. The system is through the acquisition of Ansys. We have the multi-physics sign-off. If you want to sign off either a chip or an end system, i.e., a car, a robot, anything that is an intelligent system, you need to make sure that you’re not overdesigning the product. You’re not overbuilding it. So how do you design it just right and be able to sign off across multiple physics before you commit to manufacturing?
SE: And this isn’t just a system of systems. It’s a system of heterogeneous systems, right?
Ghazi: Yes. The hardest part for me to describe is the definition of ‘system’ at multiple levels of abstraction, because an advanced package is a system. But that’s a component when you start thinking of a rack. It becomes a component as you’re thinking of a subsystem or a data center. So it’s a different level of abstraction of a system.
SE: One of the ways that people have talked about controlling AI — and we’ve all heard the stories about escapes from sandboxes — is with digital twins. We’ve been hearing about digital twins for probably a decade at this point. Has anybody actually produced one? And if not, what’s the problem?
Ghazi: The concept of digital twin or virtualization has existed for a very long time. Actually, Synopsys made two acquisitions about 15 or 17 years ago in virtualizing chips, meaning creating a digital twin for a chip in order for the customer to start designing software before the chip is manufactured. So it gives the customer optionality of models to determine which chip is most appropriate for the system. Now, if you go to the system or a digital twin of a whole car, we do have customers that are able to create a digital twin for the entire electronics — a digital twin to do crash testing for the material and the structure and the physics of the car, so you don’t have to do physical prototypes and crash testing. There are parts of digital twins for different engineering domains. Today customers are using it. But is there a digital twin that encompasses the electronics, the physics, the environment in which that system operates, that today is available and broadly used by customers? Not really. But that’s part of the journey. And I’m not sure how you can build a future sophisticated intelligent system without having a digital twin. It will take you forever, and the cost will be astronomical.
SE: But it’s still the classic divide-and-conquer, right?
Ghazi: Yes, because unless you’re starting completely from scratch, you typically start from the prior design and architecture, and you move to the next one. The one place I’m always amazed at, because they started from scratch, is China when it comes to robotics and EVs. There are many customers I visit in China, where the whole company started two or three years ago, and they started with a fully digital approach for design. The silicon just taped out, they put it on a board, they put it in a car or whatever the end system is, and the software is running within weeks. That’s a transformation in the way our customers are doing engineering. So is it possible? The answer is yes. But what are the constraints and the starting point in order to motivate an established engineering company to jump into that new way of working?
SE: And also, where in the lifecycle of a car does this actually play? Because this takes an enormous amount of computing.
Ghazi: Yes, but if you think of the traditional OEMs, they create a new platform every four or six years — the platform meaning the whole car itself. The example I just gave happens every nine months to a year. So it’s almost at the same rhythm where as they’re updating the electronics, they’re updating the whole car. Of course, it takes a lot of compute investment, but at the end, net-net, your end product is more differentiated and you are at a much faster rhythm and pace of innovation.
SE: And you’re also monitoring the health of these systems as they go forward too, right? Can you imagine a 3 nanometer chip lasting 15 years in a car?
Ghazi: The more you architect the system as individual components, where you’re able to validate it as a whole system, then it does give you the optionality based on cost, based on supply chain, based on many, many vectors that you can optimize.
SE: Let’s shift topics here. 2026 was supposed to be the year of the 3D-IC. Is it real?
Ghazi: Yes. There are many chips sitting in data centers today that are 3D-ICs. It’s complex. There are challenges beyond the electronics where customers and manufacturing are struggling. It’s not the architecture of the electronics. It’s the physics and mechanical effects of that 3D-IC. What’s happening as you’re running the workload at a high level of intensity, and as it’s intended, is that you’re running into thermal [issues] inside the package. It’s causing some of the chiplets to warp or to crack. So it’s a mechanical challenge. The industry is absolutely working toward addressing it early, during the architecture of the 3D-IC, along with the workload that is running on them. That was actually the key thesis for Synopsys to acquire Ansys — how do we bring that physics simulation early during the design phase so you can take this into account, because absolutely the future is a heterogeneous integration of multiple chips.
SE: And it’s a programming nightmare, because now you’ve got things like, ‘Okay, we’re going to have a spike in heat, we’re going to have a spike in this computing, and the spike is going to occur every 3 milliseconds.’ So now, what do we do in between those 3 milliseconds? How do we cool it down?
Ghazi: Yes, actually, this is where I mentioned the workload. Designing and architecting the system, the advanced package and multi-die system, with the context of the workload becomes very essential. This is where many surprises happen in the field, where there’s a corner case you did not take into account, and that system overheats and breaks. So it’s an optimization along the stack, from the software to architecting the actual package, to implementing it, and taking into account both the physics and the design.
SE: Let’s add one more element in here, which is that the AI itself may be changing as well. So you go back and think of what you were running in Gen AI, or you’re running in agentic AI, and now the queries are getting more complicated, as well.
Ghazi: And that’s why you have every system company trying to take control over their silicon development. It’s not because the semiconductor industry is not doing a fantastic job to optimize their silicon to a specific workload. But at the pace in which things are moving, the model is changing every three to four months. You cannot have silicon being updated every two to three years. And many of our semiconductor customers are pushing to reduce it from 18 months, 16 months, 14 months, to a year. Many of the system companies are pushing us to say how we can leverage AI and change the spec-to-tape-out to shorter than a year, shorter than nine months? Where are the bottlenecks? How can we design silicon that is very specific for a workload that we’re defining?
SE: Or one that can adapt as you go forward, right?
Ghazi: Yes, the whole programmability of either a chiplet or the entire chip itself is the direction, but I’m not seeing it adopted too much by system companies compared to, ‘I need the speed in defining a spec and customizing that silicon.’ And by the way, that silicon lifecycle is not more than two years to three years, so it’s not like they’re customizing it with the intention of keeping it for multiple generations of a model. So it’s the ability to optimize and deliver to the silicon at a much faster pace, and [for] the life of that silicon, it’s okay for it to be at a much shorter duration sitting in whatever application that they’re driving.
SE: Given all this change, what worries you? What keeps you up at night?
Ghazi: The pace, the pace, the pace. You know, there’s a massive complexity that is going on. In our industry, we’ve collectively done an amazing job to innovate and to really deliver magic. I’ve never seen a pace and system-level co-design and complexity [like] what we’re dealing with right now. The companies that are able to transform from a classical traditional workflow to adopting that next workflow — it’s very easy to put it on a PowerPoint slide [but] it’s very hard for a company to deliver the current commitment to their customer and transform that same engineering workforce to deliver that future of intelligence married with the physics married with the product differentiation that each company is trying to deliver.
SE: Does it make it hard to figure out where to place your bets? If you look at EDA, it has always exceeded almost every other hardware company that’s out there in terms of how much investment [as a percentage of revenue] you put into R&D.
Ghazi: As a percentage of revenue, yes, EDA has always had the need to invest a bigger and bigger percentage of revenue to keep up. There is an opportunity with AI. I have not seen yet that it’s able to tame it [to be able to] say right now the investment will go down. So the investment that we’re making is actually continuing to increase, not decrease.

articles.title: Global smartphone shipments slump 20 per cent but Samsung still holds on to the top spot - Tech Guide
articles.text:
Global smartphone shipments have slumped by 20 per cent year on year in Q3 2026 despite new flagship launches from Samsung and Apple.
Figures released by Omdia showed the decline in shipments can be attributed to the memory and storage cost pressures which prevented price flexibility and spurred vendors to scale back shipments of cheaper products.
This downturn made the landscape even more competitive with Samsung and Apple together accounting for 45 per cent of global shipments, up 8 per cent from a year earlier.
Samsung maintained its position as the number one global manufacturer with a 23 per cent market share (up from 19 per cent a year ago) which is an increase for the brand despite the year-on-year decline in shipments.
The August launch of the Galaxy Z Fold8 and Flip8 series helped shore up Samsung’s position the premium smartphone space.
Apple ranked second with a 22 per cent market share (up from 18 per cent last year) and maintained a consistent market position despite the wider downturn.
This was helped by strong demand for the iPhone 17 and maintained its momentum with the September introduction of the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max.
And with the upcoming release of the iPhone Duo, Apple’s first foldable iPhone, the company is in a good position to expand its customer footprint with this new form factor.
The figures show that AI is still not yet a major purchase driver for customers but Apple Intelligence may play a role in differentiating the Apple experience and sustaining its ecosystem long term.
Xiaomi maintained its third position with a 12 per cent market share, followed closely by OPPO at 9 per cent, with Vivo completing the top five at 8 per cent.
Rising memory costs are affecting companies across the category, forcing companies to prioritise Average Selling Price (ASP) growth to sustain the value of their shipments and safeguard their profitability.
“Rising component costs and differing vendor responses are reshaping the competitive landscape, but market share alone does not tell the full story,” said Hayden Hou, Principal Analyst at Omdia.
“As vendors make different trade-offs between shipment scale, revenue and profitability, their performance needs to be assessed beyond unit shipments. More importantly, the strategic decisions made during this downturn could have lasting implications beyond the current cost cycle.
“Investments in new channel partnerships, device financing capabilities and stronger premium portfolios will help determine which vendors emerge with a more competitive and sustainable business model once cost pressures ease.”
Lucas Zhong, Senior Analyst at Omdia said: “For vendors competing primarily on affordability, protecting profitability without sacrificing shipment scale has become an increasingly difficult balancing act.
“This pressure is particularly acute in emerging markets, where consumers are more price-sensitive and vendors rely heavily on entry-level devices with already thin profit margins.
“However, scaling back shipments to protect margins carries long-term risks, particularly for emerging vendors, as losing market presence can weaken brand visibility and channel mindshare, which may take years to rebuild.
“Rather than withdrawing across the board, vendors need to make more deliberate choices about where to compete, concentrating resources on markets and products that can sustain both profitability and market relevance.”

articles.title: Microsoft fixes bug causing Windows black screens, Explorer crashes
articles.text:
Microsoft has resolved a known issue that was causing black screens, desktop loading issues, and Explorer crashes after installing Windows 11 updates released since August.
As Microsoft explained when it acknowledged the issue last month, affected users experienced multiple symptoms, most commonly a black screen after sign-in, being unable to access their desktop until they manually started the desktop session, and Windows Explorer crashes in application event logs.
However, this known issue mainly affects Azure Virtual Desktop (AVD) hosts using FSLogix, a software solution that speeds up user profile loading in virtual desktop environments.
Microsoft has now addressed the bug in cumulative updates released as part of this month's Patch Tuesday and asked affected users to update their systems.
"This issue was resolved by Windows updates released October 13, 2026 [..] and updates released after that date. We recommend you install the latest update for your device as it contains important improvements and issue resolutions, including this one," it said in a release health dashboard update. "If you install an update released October 13, 2026 [..] or later, you do not need to use a workaround for this issue."
Microsoft shared a temporary workaround for those who can't install this month's Windows updates, which requires them to manually launch Windows Explorer. This can be done by opening Task Manager (Ctrl+Shift+Esc), selecting Run new task, entering explorer.exe, and clicking OK.
It also mitigated the issue for enterprise customers via Known Issue Rollback (KIR), which has to be applied on enterprise-managed devices by installing one of the following group policies:
- Windows 11, version 26H1: KB5124006 Known Issue Rollback
- Windows 11, version 25H2 and Windows 11, version 24H2: KB5124010 Known Issue Rollback
"You will need to install and configure the Group Policy for your version of Windows to resolve this issue. You will also need to restart your device(s) to apply the group policy setting," Microsoft noted. "Note that this Group Policy will disable the change causing this issue until a resolution is released in a future Windows update.
IT admins can find further details on deploying and configuring KIR group policies on Microsoft's support website.
This week, Microsoft also resolved a known issue that triggered Always On VPN connection problems after installing the September 2026 security updates and confirmed that recent Windows updates may trigger Remote Desktop failures for non-admin users if the "Administrator protection" security feature is enabled.

articles.title: El plan de Renfe para sacar de la vía al AVE incendiado en Ricla pasa por desguazar la cabina y arrastrar el chasis
articles.text:
Han pasado casi 72 horas cuando escribo estas líneas desde que un AVE de Renfe se incendiara en Ricla (Zaragoza). La vía sigue bloqueada. Y lo seguirá estando durante un tiempo que está todavía por definir. La retirada de la locomotora está siendo complicada y, mientras tanto, los pasajeros seguirán sufriendo retrasos.
¿Qué ha pasado? Como probablemente sabes a estas alturas, en la tarde del pasado 12 de octubre, día de vuelta del puente de la Hispanidad, la línea Madrid-Barcelona colapsó. A la altura de Ricla (Zaragoza), un AVE salió ardiendo, provocando el paro inmediato de los trenes.
Aunque Renfe ha señalado que la evacuación de los pasajeros se ha producido con normalidad y sin lamentar heridos, el impacto del tren incendiado dejó a casi 20.000 personas tiradas esa tarde. Finalmente, algunos trenes retomaron la actividad ya por la noche pero miles de personas de Ouigo, Iryo y Renfe se encontraron desperdigadas por estaciones de la línea sin alternativa disponible.
¿Qué se hace ahora? De momento, con el visto bueno de Adif, lo que se ha decidido es pasar los trenes por la vía anexa, la de sentido contrario al tren incendiado. Eso tiene un problema fundamental: los trenes tienen que dejarse paso unos a otros.
En un primer momento, la velocidad de paso en este tramo se limitó a 80 km/h, añadiendo por tanto más minutos a una línea en la que no se ha vuelto a circular a tanta velocidad como se hacía antes del accidente de Adamuz (Córdoba). La última noticia en este sentido es que Adif ha dado el visto bueno para aumentar la velocidad hasta los 160 km/h. El tramo convertido ahora paso de los dos sentidos con una sola vía tiene una extensión de entre 20 y 25 kilómetros, explican en La Vanguardia.
Por su parte, Renfe está utilizando trenes de doble composición para que, pese a las cancelaciones, los pasajeros tengan la mayor cantidad de asientos disponibles que sea posible.
¿Hasta cuándo? Es la gran pregunta. Diferentes informaciones aportadas por fuentes de Adif a medios como La Vanguardia apuntan a que la normalidad no se espera hasta los primeros días de la semana que viene. Es decir, todo el fin de semana se esperan afectaciones sobre la circulación habitual en la línea de alta velocidad más concurrida de España.
El plan, señalan desde Renfe a preguntas de Xataka es "retirar de la vía la parte del convoy que sufrió el incendio (la unidad motriz situada en cola). Es una operación compleja que se prolongará en los próximos días porque además el convoy se encuentra en una zona de difícil acceso".
En estos momentos, es la última parte por retirar porque la compañía nos señala que "anoche remolcamos hasta la estación de Zaragoza Delicias el tren que sufrió la incidencia en Ricla". Eso sí, recuerdan que "una vez que se haya retirado la parte del tren afectada por el incendio, Adif tendrá que inspeccionar el estado de la infraestructura". Sólo con su visto bueno se recuperará la normalidad.
Una gota más. Podríamos decir que es la que colma el vaso pero dado el historial de los últimos años, cabe preguntarse qué más puede pasar en las vías españolas. El año comenzó con el grave accidente de Adamuz (Córdoba) donde fallecieron 46 personas y mantuvo la alta velocidad cortada en el corredor sur durante semanas.
Apenas unos días después, un accidente en Rodalies dejó otro fallecido y decenas de heridos en Cataluña. Las intensas lluvias obligaron a cortar las líneas de tren y dejó inutilizable el ramal a Málaga durante semanas. El año pasado, los trenes Talgo de la línea Madrid-Barcelona sufrieron fisuras en sus coches. El pasado mes de septiembre, el problema se ha repetido en la línea del Levante.
Problemas que llegan después de tener un 2025 especialmente intenso, con fallos de software en la línea gallega con el cambio de año, el incendio de un tren en la andaluza (con viajeros que no fueron atendidos en más de 13 horas) y un punto negro en Toledo al que costaba encontrar solución.

articles.title: Les prix des réparations de l’iPhone Duo vont vous donner envie de souscrire à AppleCare+
articles.text:
Si vous envisagez d’acheter un iPhone Duo, il est sans aucun doute préférable d’envisager par la même occasion de souscrire à une garantie AppleCare+. Apple vient en effet de dévoiler les tarifs demandés pour les différentes réparations de son iPhone pliant, et une chose est certaine, les sommes demandées devraient suffire à vous y convaincre.
Une souscription AppleCare+ hautement recommandée
Comme on pouvait l’imaginer, le prix des réparations pour le tout premier iPhone pliable d’Apple explose par rapport aux autres modèles. La firme de Cupertino a mis en ligne, sur sa page d’assistance, le coût estimé des différentes réparations possibles pour l’iPhone Duo hors garantie AppleCare.
Sans surprise, l’écran interne pliant constitue l’intervention la plus lourde puisqu’il vous en coûtera, hors garantie, la somme de 1149 euros, soit plus que le prix d’un iPhone 17 neuf.
Apple précise également qu’en cas de dégâts majeurs (sans doute des dégâts multiples incluant l’écran interne), l’Assistance vous demandera quelque 1719 euros de frais de réparation.
Les deux prises en charge précédemment citées ne vous seront toutefois facturées que 99 euros dans le cadre d’une prise en charge avec AppleCare+. Une somme bien plus acceptable qui devrait vous convaincre de souscrire à la garantie AppleCare+, d’autant plus si vous craignez de faire tomber accidentellement votre appareil.
Du côté de la batterie, si le remplacement de celle-ci est pris en charge gracieusement pour les détenteurs d’une garantie AppleCare+ (dès que la capacité de celle-ci descend en dessous de 80 % de sa capacité d’origine), il vous en coûtera 269 euros hors garantie.
Pour le reste, Apple vous demandera 55 euros pour le remplacement du revêtement endommagé de l’écran, 219 euros pour le remplacement du dos en verre, 269 euros pour des dommages au niveau de la caméra arrière, 489 euros pour le remplacement de l’écran externe et pas moins de 629 euros si vous devez changer le combo écran externe + dos en verre.
