articles.title: Agentic AI doesn't have a model problem. It has a retrieval problem.
articles.text:
Agentic AI doesn’t have a model problem. It has a retrieval problem.
On BrowseComp-Plus, GPT-4.1 answered 93.49% of the questions correctly when it was given the supporting documents directly. When an agent used the same model but relied on BM25 to search for evidence to pass to the model, accuracy fell to 14.58%.
That difference matters because a system that gets the answer right 93% of the time is far more useful than one that gets it right only 15% of the time.
An agent can look excellent in a controlled demo. The corpus is clean, the task is familiar, and the relevant material is easy to find. Production is messier. Documents may be duplicated, outdated drafts can remain searchable, and teams may use different terminology for the same thing. Several versions of a policy can coexist, while the task itself may unfold in ways the evaluation set never covered.
“More model intelligence does not compensate for evidence the agent never retrieved.”
Under those conditions, the agent may retrieve incomplete, stale, or simply wrong material. More model intelligence does not compensate for evidence the agent never retrieved.
This is where retrieval starts to determine what the model can actually do.
What BrowseComp-Plus shows
BrowseComp-Plus provides a useful way to separate these effects because it evaluates agents against a fixed corpus rather than a changing web-search service. The benchmark includes 100,195 documents and 830 research questions, each with human-verified supporting documents.
One evaluation gives the model all labeled positive documents directly. The paper calls this the oracle setting. Another requires the agent to search the corpus and gather the material it needs.
The difference is large. GPT-4.1 scores 93.49% with the labeled supporting documents supplied and 14.58% when the agent searches with the BM25 baseline. Qwen3-32B moves from 83.25% to 3.49% under the same two conditions.
The oracle result shows how well the model can answer when the required material is already in front of it. For system design, comparing retrieval systems is even more useful. The reasoning model stayed the same, while better retrieval improved the final answer rate and reduced the number of search calls.
“The lesson is practical: before changing the model, examine what reaches it. A capable model working from poor retrieval results still has poor material to reason over.”
The lesson is practical: before changing the model, examine what reaches it. A capable model working from poor retrieval results still has poor material to reason over.
Enterprises can build agents around proprietary information that competitors do not have, from product and customer data to internal knowledge and operational records. That advantage depends on whether the agent can find the right information and rank it well, while also keeping up with changes in the underlying data.
One task. A few minutes. A thousand retrievals.
In its Search as Code research, Perplexity describes tasks that can trigger hundreds or thousands of retrieval operations within a few minutes. Search becomes a sustained part of the agent’s workflow rather than an occasional lookup.
Traditional search usually returns one ranked result set per query. An agent can decompose a task into multiple searches, fan them out in parallel, combine the results, and issue follow-up searches as it learns more.
At that scale, fan-out becomes a normal part of the workload. If an agent runs ten searches in parallel and needs all ten results before it can continue, the slowest search sets the pace for that step. If the agent repeats that pattern several times during the task, tail latency matters even more than it does for a single interactive query.
The same multiplication shows up in capacity. One user task can generate hundreds of search operations, and many agents may be doing that at once. Measured in user requests, the service may look lightly loaded while the retrieval layer is processing a much larger volume of searches.
When one task fans out into many searches, retrieval quality matters even more. People judge search results using context they have built up over time. They know which sources they trust and can often recognize when something looks stale, unreliable, or out of place. An agent usually starts with far less background and has to build its understanding from the evidence it retrieves during the task. It is often on its first day on the job. If one of those early results is wrong, the next search may be wrong too, and the rest of the task can drift from there.
“People judge search results using context they have built up over time. An agent usually starts with far less background and has to build its understanding from the evidence it retrieves during the task. It is often on its first day on the job.”
A simple model shows why repeated retrieval steps raise the stakes. Suppose a workflow requires five retrieval steps, each with a 90% probability of supplying what the agent needs, and assume there are no retries or recovery. The probability that all five succeed is 0.9^5, or about 59%. Real agents can retry, use redundant evidence, branch, and recover, so this is an illustration rather than a measured agent success rate. It shows how small per-step weaknesses can accumulate when later work depends on earlier retrievals.
Agentic search therefore asks the retrieval layer to handle more queries for each user task, more searches running in parallel, and retrieval steps whose results influence later work. As those patterns scale, capacity, tail latency, and retrieval quality all become more important.
Your retrieval layer was tuned for a different user
Web search spent decades adapting to human search behavior.
As Jon Bratseth writes in Your agent wants to search like a 2010 quant, people are often “lazy and clueless” when they search. The wording is blunt, but the point is straightforward: people tend to enter short queries without knowing much about the corpus or the search system behind it.
Search engines evolved around those habits. Short, underspecified queries became the norm, and much of the complexity moved behind the interface, where the search system inferred intent and returned a ranked list.
An agent can use a much richer interface. It can search for exact terms, construct filters, specify dates, group results, choose among ranking strategies, and issue follow-up searches based on what it has already found. Jon gives examples ranging from proximity search for names in a legal case to semantic search over high-quality sources and grouping events by month. In an agentic workflow, those searches can be chained together as the agent narrows, expands, and verifies its answer.
That means the retrieval layer receives more than a short text query. It may receive several kinds of input: lexical terms, query embeddings, structured filters, or combinations of them. An agent-facing interface should make those choices explicit so the agent can use the right retrieval method for the task instead of collapsing every request into one text string.
Evaluation needs to reflect the same shift. A retriever tested mostly on short, human-written questions may behave differently when an agent generates its own filters, search terms, and follow-up queries. Retrieval quality should therefore be measured on the queries the agent actually sends in production, not only on the questions in the evaluation set.
Before changing the model or retuning retrieval, inspect those production queries first.
A search API returns results. An agent needs more control.
Traditional search often exposes a narrow contract: send a query, let the server run a retrieval pipeline, and receive a ranked result list.
That works well when the caller only needs the output. An agent may need more control over how retrieval and ranking are carried out at runtime, depending on what the task requires.
Vespa exposes that control through its query language and rank profiles. The caller can combine lexical or semantic retrieval, structured filters, ranking choices, and grouping in the same request, affecting how candidates are selected, scored, and returned.
The interface matters because the agent can only use the controls it can reach. A system may support filtering, ranking, aggregation, or several retrieval methods internally, but those capabilities do not help if the agent cannot invoke them when the task calls for them.
A fixed pipeline is still a good fit for many well-defined applications. Agentic workflows become more demanding when the task changes from one step to the next and the agent needs different retrieval behavior at runtime.
The goal is to expose the controls the agent needs while keeping authorization, validation, budgets, and other safeguards on the trusted server side.
Exposing the controls is not enough
An engine can expose filters, lexical matching, nearest-neighbor search, grouping, multiple rank profiles, reranking, and query-time controls. Those capabilities only become useful to the agent when the interface explains what is available and when to use it. If rank profiles, filterable fields, or grouping operations are not described, the agent may default to a free-text query and push more of the work into later reasoning or tool calls.
One way to handle this is to put a query-translation model between the agent and the retrieval system. The translator takes the agent’s request and converts it into the engine’s query syntax. This can be useful when an application wants query construction centralized behind a stable interface.
When the caller is already an agent, a separate translator often inserts a specialized model between the agent and the retrieval system. The agent already has the task, prior results, and constraints in context; the translator must reconstruct that intent from a narrower request and convert it into a query. This extra handoff adds latency and another opportunity to lose or distort what the agent meant, making retrieval harder and less reliable.
Another approach is to describe the retrieval interface directly to the agent: which fields are available and what they mean, and what rank profiles are provided.
We call that an agent-ready schema: a description of the fields, controls, and retrieval options the agent can use, along with the application-specific meaning behind them. Vespa has described work on convenience tooling in this direction, and much of that guidance can be generated from the application schema itself.
From schema to skill
A search schema already contains much of the information an agent needs: field names and types, which fields can be searched or used as filters, available rank profiles, and configured tensors and models.
What it lacks is a description of what the fields mean and how they could be used. A field called tier may represent an account plan, a service level, or something else entirely. A timestamp such as published may mean first publication, last modification, or ingestion time. A rank profile named exact tells the agent very little about the kinds of queries it was designed for.
Those meanings can be added as explanations in the schema. That gives the agent more than names and types; it gives it enough context to choose the right fields, filters, and ranking options for the task.
Schema-to-Skill is the proposed generation step: combine the Vespa application schema, engine guidance, and application-specific knowledge into a short Markdown skill the agent can consult when constructing queries. The schema provides the structure, engine guidance explains how to use the available capabilities safely, and application-specific knowledge adds the vocabulary and meaning that cannot be inferred from the schema alone.
The agent uses that skill to choose among the retrieval strategies the Vespa application exposes. Vespa still does the actual retrieval work over the corpus, including matching, filtering, ranking, and aggregation. The agent decides what to ask for; the retrieval system executes it.
Better models can help, but agents still fail when they search for the wrong evidence, cannot express the right retrieval strategy, or do not understand the search system they are calling.
“Better models can help, but agents still fail when they search for the wrong evidence, cannot express the right retrieval strategy, or do not understand the search system they are calling.”
Agentic workloads make those weaknesses more costly because retrieval happens throughout the task. Each search can affect what the agent sees next, how much context it carries, and whether it needs to search again. At scale, retrieval quality, tail latency, and query volume become part of the task itself.
That puts more pressure on the retrieval interface. Agents need access to the filters, ranking strategies, grouping, and other controls the task requires, along with enough guidance to use them correctly. An agent-ready schema makes those capabilities explicit, and Schema-to-Skill is one way to turn that structure, engine guidance, and application-specific knowledge into something the agent can use when constructing queries.
Before upgrading the model, inspect the searches the agent is issuing, the evidence those searches return, and whether the retrieval system gives the agent both the controls and the guidance it needs. Better retrieval can improve the answer, reduce unnecessary work, and make the rest of the agentic system more effective.

articles.title: GTA 6 diffuse déjà son trailer de lancement
articles.text:
La sortie tant attendue de GTA 6 approche à grands pas, et on en a encore la preuve avec la diffusion de la bande-annonce de sortie, partagée ce jeudi 15 octobre par Rockstar Games. Au menu : 90 secondes avec des images inédites et quelques détails en plus sur l’intrigue, articulée autour du couple formé par Lucia et Jason.
« Jason et Lucia ont toujours su que les dés étaient pipés contre eux. Mais lorsqu’un coup facile tourne mal, ils se retrouvent plongés dans la face la plus sombre de la région la plus ensoleillée d’Amérique, au cœur d’une conspiration criminelle qui s’étend à travers tout l’État de Leonida — forcés plus que jamais de compter l’un sur l’autre s’ils veulent s’en sortir vivants », indique la description officielle.
Encore des images inédites pour GTA 6
La vidéo permet de découvrir l’un des morceaux inédits prévus sur la bande-son de GTA 6. En l’occurrence : Flower in a Hurricane, interprété par le duo Justice en compagnie de Tame Impala, SZA et King Gizzard & The Lizard Wizard, que l’on peut déjà écouter sur Spotify et YouTube. Il sera bien évidemment présent sur le disque disponible dans la boutique, intitulé Grand Theft Auto VI: The Album et réunissant 34 morceaux.
Jason indique, au tout début de la vidéo, qu’il a quitté l’armée en mauvais termes. « J’ai eu quelques soucis dans l’armée. Je ne l’ai pas quittée en bons termes. Ils ne donnent aucune mention à des gens comme mois », précise-t-il. On comprend alors qu’il a besoin d’argent.
Les images montrent un couple uni devant les problèmes, prenant des douches ensemble ou se taquinant à la moindre occasion. On peut voir, dans l’un des plans, que Lucia porte bien un bracelet électronique. Tout porte à croire que ce dispositif aura un impact sur sa liberté de mouvement au sein des rues de Vice City, tout au moins dans les premières heures de jeu. La complémentarité entre Lucia et Jason devrait en tout cas se retrouver dans le gameplay.
Enfin, les oreilles les plus attentives auront peut-être remarqué un clin d’œil amusant à la fin de ce trailer de lancement. La voix qui annonce la date de sortie de GTA 6 est en effet la même que celle qui présentait déjà celle de GTA 5 dans son propre trailer de lancement, en 2013. Et le plus drôle, c’est que le comédien reprend exactement le même ton, comme si douze ans ne s’étaient pas écoulés.
Bonne nouvelle : le trailer affiche toujours la date du 19 novembre. Attendu sur PS5, Xbox Series S et Xbox Series X, GTA 6 ne sera plus repoussé. La version PC, quant à elle, pourrait être commercialisée dès le début de l’année prochaine.

articles.title: African startups raise $2.49B in 9 months as Q3 rebounds
articles.text: In the first nine months of 2026, African startups raised $2.49 billion across 315 disclosed deals, representing 7.8% year-on-year growth from the $2.30 billion raised across 403 disclosed deals in the same period in 2025. While overall transaction volume dropped in the first half of the year, funding activity rebounded sharply in Q3 2026. Q3 alone brought in $1.025 billion across 167 deals, up from $785 million across 149 deals in Q3 2025, driven by stronger deal flow and larger growth rounds. Energy, fintech, and clean tech lead big deals September kept up the Q3 momentum, with investors directing relatively large capital checks into energy infrastructure, mobility, and digital payments platforms. Bluecore Energy (Ghana) raised a $50 million seed round, backed by Slauson & Co., Harlem Capital, Chris Larsen, Collab Capital, HartBeat Ventures, Tesla, Uber, and Amazon, to develop maritime nuclear technology. Odyssey Energy Solutions (Nigeria) secured $74 million in combined capital, including a $47 million debt facility from BII, BIO, Cygnum Capital, and TripleJump, alongside $27 million in equity from Broadscale Group, FMO, and Al Mada Ventures. Paymob (Egypt) raised $35 million in Pre-Series C funding led by Mubadala and EBRD. Mission Mobile (South Africa) pulled in $30.7 million from DN Invest for device-financing infrastructure. ARC Ride (Kenya) completed a $33.3 million round ($23.3M equity led by Novastar Ventures, Norrsken22, and IFC, plus $10M debt) for its e-mobility battery-swapping network. Spiro added $18 million in debt from the Africa Go Green Fund, matching an $18 million debt round raised by Cold Solutions (Kenya) from Cygnum Capital. Synapse Analytics (Egypt) raised $13 million in Series A funding led by Partech, while Nawy Now (Egypt) secured a $12.3 million debt facility. Zeal (Egypt) and SunCulture (Kenya) each pulled in $10 million. Top funding destinations: Nigeria and Egypt lead Nigeria remains Africa’s top funding destination so far in 2026, pulling in $624 million across the first nine months. Egypt ranks second with $396 million, followed by Benin ($345 million), Kenya ($297 million), and South Africa ($279 million). LPs inject $3.08B into African fund managers Capital is also flowing steadily into fund managers (GPs) deploying capital on the ground. According to our State of Tech in Africa H1 2026 Report , LPs committed over $1.7 billion to fund managers in the first half of the year. Q3 2026 added another $1.23 billion in new commitments, bringing total capital raised by African fund managers to $3.08 billion between Q1 and Q3 2026. Major Q3 2026 fund closes Ninety One closed its Africa Credit Opportunities Fund 3 at $404 million to scale private debt financing. Airnergize Capital (South Africa) reached a $239 million final close for its Clean Energy Fund, backed by DBSA, Standard Bank, and Nedbank. Acumen Capital Partners reached a $90 million second close for its Resilient Agriculture Fund (ARAF) and secured $12 million for ARAF II. Ventures Platform completed an $84 million second close for its Pan-African Fund II, backed by Norfund and the European Bank. CardinalStone Capital Advisers hit a $76 million first close for its West Africa SME growth fund. AgDevCo achieved a $49 millio n first close targeting early-stage East African agritech. Fund managers have secured over $3.08 billion in new LP commitments between Q1 and Q3 2026 across climate tech, private credit, and early-stage equity. While this fresh dry powder sets the stage for a strong finish to the year, founders must adapt their fundraising strategies to access it. Securing these new funds requires startups to look beyond traditional equity, build capacity for venture debt, and demonstrate the robust unit economics that today’s capital allocators demand.

articles.title: Chrome corrige plus d'une trentaine de vulnérabilités
articles.text:
Google vient de corriger 37 failles de sécurité dans Chrome, dont sept critiques. Edge, qui repose sur le même socle, n'a pas encore reçu ces correctifs.
Le déploiement de la version 155.0.8059.79 de Chrome (avec une build .80 sur Windows et macOS) a débuté cette semaine et va durer plusieurs jours, voire plusieurs semaines. Il arrive après Chrome 154, qui avait déjà corrigé 108 vulnérabilités.
Des erreurs de mémoire côté Chrome, un correctif en attente côté Edge
Parmi les failles critiques, la CVE-2026-110152 touche ANGLE, un composant graphique du navigateur. Il s'agit d'un dépassement de tampon (buffer overflow). Chrome peut écrire des données en dehors de l'espace mémoire prévu pour une opération. Résultat, un plantage ou, dans certains cas, l'exécution de code malveillant. Elle a été signalée le 30 septembre par Zhenpeng (Leo) Lin, de depthfirst.
Google a repéré beaucoup d'erreurs de gestion de la mémoire. 25 des 37 failles sont de type "use-after-free". Le programme continue d'utiliser une zone qu'il a pourtant libérée, et un attaquant peut tenter d'y glisser ses propres données. Six de ces failles sont critiques (navigateur, PDF, réseau, composants centraux, SVG, médias). Les 29 failles de gravité élevée touchent notamment V8, le moteur JavaScript, les extensions ou WebRTC. Le bulletin liste aussi une fuite d'informations dans le gestionnaire de mots de passe et une élévation de privilèges dans l'installeur de Chrome. Google précise que les détails techniques peuvent rester restreints tant que la majorité des utilisateurs n'est pas à jour. Une prime de 1 000 dollars pour une faille de gravité élevée a été reversée à Findingz.
Le nom de Xinyang Ge revient sur au moins 15 entrées, dont trois critiques. Parmi celles-ci, une seule, la CVE-2026-110169 (un use-after-free dans V8), précise qu'il travaille chez Anthropic et qu'il a été assisté par Claude. Google signe de son côté 12 failles. Microsoft, Mozilla ou encore Apple s'appuient eux aussi sur l'IA pour leurs travaux de sécurité. En mars, nous rapportions que Claude Opus 4.6 avait repéré plus de 100 vulnérabilités dans Firefox en deux semaines, dont 14 de haute sévérité. En mai, Mozilla expliquait avoir corrigé 423 failles en avril, dont 271 attribuées à Claude Mythos Preview.
Les autres navigateurs reposant sur Chromium comme Edge, Brave, Opera ou encore Vivaldi devraient eux aussi profiter de ces correctifs.
- Respect et protection de la vie privée
- Interface et ergonomie soignée
- Le plus rapide du marché

articles.title: Teens excited, hesitant about Canada’s proposed youth social media ban | BetaKit
articles.text:
While teenagers are glad to see that the government’s new social media legislation, Bill C-34, aims to hold technology companies more accountable for online youth safety, some fear an outright ban for youth could do more harm than good.
Senator Katherine Hay told youth at the discussion that they “can still shape this legislation, and this is getting a seat at the table.”
The Government of Canada’s proposed Safe Social Media Act aims to regulate how social media and AI chatbots engage with young Canadians by implementing a 16-year-old minimum age requirement alongside other protections, and creating a commission to ensure compliance.
“It’s a good start, but I definitely think there’s work to be done,” Grade 12 student and Rally Youth Advisory Committee member Ash MacArthur told BetaKit in an interview.
Bill C-34 was a hot topic on Wednesday at Rally. Launched last year to help teens reclaim control of their online lives, Rally’s second-annual digital wellness festival drew approximately 2,700 high school students, teachers, and others from nearly 60 Greater Toronto Area schools (up from 35 last year) to Toronto’s Meridian Hall.
Hordes of Grade 9 through 12 students put their phones down for a beat to race around on roller skates, pat dogs, play with a robot, touch artificial grass, and hear from peers and experts as live DJs filled the venue with music.
This year’s Rally was bigger, louder, and made a more concerted effort to put teens front and centre, both on and off stage. After the main show, around a dozen high school students took part in a closed-door discussion that Rally organized to share their perspectives on Bill C-34 with Senator Katherine Hay, who plans to sponsor the proposed legislation as it moves from the House of Commons to the Senate.
BetaKit spoke with Hay, MacArthur, and other students involved in that conversation, as well as Rally co-founder Keith Wallace, to get a better sense of how teens are feeling about Bill C-34.
In her opening remarks, which BetaKit and other members of the media were permitted to attend, Hay’s message to participating youth was clear: “you can still shape this legislation, and this is getting a seat at the table.”
Rally co-founder Brigitte Truong moderated as Hay listened, took notes, and fielded questions. Grade 12 student Charlie Boyle called it a unique opportunity to engage with a sitting senator and said Hay’s approach made her “feel so heard,” while MacArthur was happy to see that Hay exchanged contact information and wanted to continue the conversation.
RELATED: Rally festival tells doom-scrolling teens “it’s okay to be unavailable” online
Hay plans to compile and submit her takeaways in a report to Minister of Canadian Identity and Culture Marc Miller. She told BetaKit that she approached Rally’s organizers with the idea for this conversation. The former Kids Help Phone CEO, who became a senator last year, has taken a keen interest in matters affecting youth and “AI innovation for all … for good.”
Some youth at the event expressed support for the proposed ban, while others were less certain. “A complete ban can almost be more harmful than good because of loopholes and because of problems with inclusivity,” Boyle argued.
While Boyle and MacArthur acknowledged that consuming too much social media at a young age can be detrimental to your mental health, another roundtable participant argued that not having access to it would have hamstrung their creativity.
Where there was consensus was for the plan to put more pressure on tech companies to build guardrails to protect youth from harmful content.
While Wallace doesn’t know Bill C-34 “inside out,” he told BetaKit that he is a strong believer that social media has been left unregulated “for way too long, and we need to do something.”
“If we have to ban it for under 16s and then slowly reintroduce it in a safer way, then that’s a success because the opposite [approach] isn’t helping anyone at the moment,” Wallace added.
Hay said she came out of the conversation with a deeper understanding of the positive connections and creativity social media can facilitate. She said she feels hopeful that teens are not afraid of this tech and that they are so open about their experiences and solution-oriented.
Feature image courtesy Rally. Photo by Robert Okine.

articles.title: Anthropic: investidores reduzem expectativa de avaliação para IPO de R$ 8,1 trilhões
articles.text:
A Anthropic, desenvolvedora dos modelos de inteligência artificial (IA) Claude, enfrenta revisão nas expectativas de avaliação para sua oferta pública inicial de ações (IPO, na sigla em inglês). Alguns investidores passaram a considerar valor de aproximadamente US$ 1,5 trilhão (R$ 8,1 trilhões), abaixo dos US$ 2 trilhões (R$ 10,8 trilhões) esperados anteriormente para a operação, prevista para novembro.
Segundo a Reuters, a mudança ocorre após a divulgação dos resultados financeiros mais recentes da companhia e em meio à preocupação crescente com os custos de desenvolvimento e operação de sistemas de IA.
Durante encontro com investidores realizado na quarta-feira (14), em São Francisco (EUA), a Anthropic informou que sua receita no terceiro trimestre aumentou 45% em relação ao trimestre anterior, chegando a US$ 16,8 bilhões (R$ 90,7 bilhões). A empresa também teria registrado lucro em métrica ajustada durante o período.
Apesar dos números, parte dos investidores demonstrou preocupação com a desaceleração do ritmo de crescimento. No segundo trimestre, a receita havia mais que dobrado em relação ao primeiro, alcançando US$ 11,6 bilhões (R$ 62,6 bilhões).
As informações foram relatadas à Reuters por pessoas familiarizadas com o assunto, que falaram sob condição de anonimato. A Anthropic não respondeu imediatamente aos pedidos de comentário da agência.
Custos de IA colocam avaliação em xeque
- A revisão das expectativas acontece em momento de turbulência nos mercados financeiros globais, com onda de vendas de ações de tecnologia afetando empresas de infraestrutura para IA, fabricantes de chips e provedores de computação em nuvem especializados no setor;
- A preocupação é que a expansão da infraestrutura necessária para desenvolver e executar modelos de IA esteja exigindo investimentos cada vez maiores, financiados em parte por empréstimos. Nesse cenário, investidores questionam se o crescimento das receitas será suficiente para sustentar os gastos;
- A CoreWeave, empresa de infraestrutura de IA apoiada pela Nvidia, teve ações e títulos pressionados nesta quinta-feira (15), refletindo a apreensão com o financiamento da expansão do setor;
- Uma recepção negativa ao IPO da Anthropic poderia ampliar essas preocupações. De acordo com a Reuters, investidores consideram que as perspectivas de curto prazo do mercado de IA dependem, em boa medida, do desempenho da oferta da empresa, seguida por possível abertura de capital da OpenAI no próximo ano;
- O mercado de IPOs também enfrenta contratempos recentes. A operadora de data centers SB Energy adiou sua abertura de capital no mês passado, enquanto a empresa de tecnologia nuclear Holtec Nuclear abandonou seus planos de entrar na bolsa.
Leia mais:
- OpenAI e Anthropic querem controlar relatórios de segurança da IA
- Anthropic alerta: IA pode se replicar em TVs e eletrodomésticos
- Nova York pede que Anthropic adie IPO por riscos da IA avançada
Receita cresce, mas prejuízos continuam no radar
Fundada em 2021 por ex-executivos da OpenAI, incluindo o diretor-executivo Dario Amodei e sua irmã Daniela Amodei, atual presidente da companhia, a Anthropic se consolidou como uma das principais desenvolvedoras de IA generativa, com a família de modelos Claude.
A expansão da empresa tem sido apoiada pelo Google, da Alphabet, e pela Amazon. As duas companhias são investidoras da Anthropic, fornecedoras de capacidade computacional e parceiras na distribuição de seus produtos, mas também competem com ela no mercado de IA.
No ano passado, a receita da Anthropic cresceu 12 vezes, chegando a quase US$ 4,6 bilhões (R$ 24,8 bilhões). Apesar disso, a empresa registrou mais de US$ 8 bilhões (R$ 43,2 bilhões) em perdas operacionais, desconsiderando baixas contábeis relacionadas principalmente a rodadas anteriores de captação.
Em seu prospecto de IPO, visto pela Reuters em setembro, a companhia apresentou visão ambiciosa sobre o potencial transformador da IA na economia global. Ao mesmo tempo, informou um prejuízo de US$ 42 bilhões (R$ 226,8 bilhões) em 2025 e indicou que os gastos com infraestrutura devem continuar aumentando.
A Anthropic se comprometeu a gastar pelo menos US$ 518 bilhões (R$ 2,8 trilhões) ao longo de uma década com serviços de nuvem, capacidade computacional e infraestrutura.
O desafio para a empresa é convencer os investidores de que o crescimento do negócio poderá compensar os custos necessários para desenvolver modelos mais avançados e ampliar sua operação. A revisão das expectativas de avaliação mostra que, apesar do avanço da receita, o tamanho dos investimentos continua sendo fator central na análise de seu futuro na bolsa.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: SK Hynix bargains for chip equipment exports to its China facility in return for building a factory in US | TechCrunch
articles.text:
SK Hynix appears to be navigating choppy U.S.-China chipmaking waters. The company’s flash memory unit, Solidigm, is seeking U.S. approval to send American chipmaking equipment to its factory in Dalian, China, as a condition to continue building a semiconductor factory in the U.S., Reuters reported, citing anonymous sources.
Solidigm has been reportedly chalking up plans to build a NAND flash memory chip factory in the U.S. and is considering upstate New York as a potential location for the facility.
NAND flash chips are primarily used in solid-state storage drives, which are employed in everything from laptops and smartphones to AI data centers. But the global component shortage, thanks to skyrocketing demand for AI data centers, has driven up prices for everything that goes into data centers, including high-speed RAM chips and SSDs. Research firm TrendForce expects NAND prices to rise 15% to 20% in the fourth quarter.
Reuters cited its sources as saying that Solidigm wants to install more chipmaking equipment in spare space at SK Hynix’s Dalian factory in China to boost NAND chip production.
SK Hynix told TechCrunch it is not seeking to expand capacity at its Dalian Mod B facility, which was completed in 2023. The chip giant added that the equipment installation is being carried out in consultation with and under authorization from the U.S. government.
Washington first imposed sweeping restrictions on advanced chips and chipmaking equipment exports to China in October 2022, citing national security concerns, and further tightened the rules in 2023. Then in September 2025, the Trump administration revoked special export exemptions for certain SK Hynix, Samsung, and Intel facilities in China. The U.S. has since granted an annual license to Samsung and SK Hynix for sending chipmaking equipment to their plants in China.
The U.S. has also been pushing foreign chipmakers to build and expand their manufacturing facilities in America. In July, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick said he wanted Samsung and SK Hynix to build chip plants in the country and that he was in talks with both companies.
Solidigm is said to be preparing for a 2027 U.S. IPO that could raise around $10 billion and value it at up to $100 billion.

articles.title: Unsupervised AI agent reportedly deletes TV show’s entire edit weeks before release, erasing months of work — TV show can't air, AI agent was given access to the production server and wiped the finished season
articles.text:
Unsupervised AI agent reportedly deletes TV show’s entire edit weeks before release, erasing months of work — TV show can't air, AI agent was given access to the production server and wiped the finished season
Another case of AI agents deleting something they shouldn't.
The Swedish edition of the athletic competition show The Challenge just faced a real challenge when an AI agent deleted months of work editing the show just weeks before release. The program director blames the disaster on a failed backup system, leaving no way to recover the edit and forcing them to recut the entire season from the raw footage that thankfully was not deleted.
According to Aftonbladet’s sources, the AI agent was given access to the production server and deleted the finished season. There are no reports on what the AI agent’s role on the production server is, but it seems that file management may be one of them due to file-handling permissions. TV4, the commissioner of the show, conducted an investigation and stated the mishap was due to “the human factor” and not AI.
One of the most prominent teachings of backing up is that data is still not safe from the user despite having redundancies; RAID systems protecting data from drive failures are one thing, while accidental deletions are another — however, an AI agent deleting your files is something else entirely.
We can’t speculate on what the AI agent’s job was, but file mishandling is something that isn’t unique to Mastiff’s production team. There have been several cases of AI agents deleting stuff they shouldn’t, like this story of an AI coding platform’s entire database being deleted, this story of Google’s Antigravity agent wiping a user’s entire hard drive, or Claude deleting a developer’s entire production setup, and many other catastrophic AI agent deletion cases.
However, TV4’s program director stated before its investigation of the incident that it was not an AI agent that acted independently, despite also stating that it wasn’t clear what happened. One clear thing, however, is that their backup system failed, which is worse than deletion, as the production team’s hard work can’t be recovered easily. There are ways to potentially recover the data if there are snapshots or version histories; even forensic recovery is an option, but TV4 has kept its investigation details private, so it’s hard to say how much is realistically recoverable, if at all.

articles.title: Exclusive: 'When the best light is gone, that's just the beginning' — Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026 winner explains his unusual choice of camera gear
articles.text:
'There would have been no image without it' — why WPOTY 2026 winner used an infrared camera for his comical winning shot of an elephant spraying zebra with water
Who needs golden hour?
- Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026 winners announced
- James Lewin won the Animals in their Environment category
- He used an infrared converted Nikon Z7 II camera and budget lens for his winning shot
This week I attended the press preview of the Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026 exhibition at the Natural History Museum, London, where I had the opportunity to absorb the winning photos on display and meet many of the photographers who took them, and discuss their work.
As fortune would have it, I got chatting with James Lewin, winner of the Animals in their Environment category, as we waited to get into the venue. The British photographer lives in Kenya, where he took his winning photo — it's a country I know well, having lived there for years myself, so naturally we hit it off.
We both know the challenges facing outdoor photographers in this region: a sunrise / sunset that's over in minutes, and an all-too-brief period of golden light that's quickly followed by typically harsh, bright sunlight.
Most seasoned photographers focus on this narrow window of best light, leaving most of the rest of the day alone. However, Lewin took advantage of the harsh light by adopting a niche photography genre: infrared. It's an unusual approach for wildlife photography, but with Lewin's infrared-converted camera, it's as the 'worst' light kicks in that the fun really begins...
Why infrared photography?
Lewin was observing from a hide near a waterhole in the Chulu Hills in southern Kenya. During dry season, this location gets incredibly congested, as you can see from Lewin's photo, below.
Working in the middle of the day, under bright sunlight and with strong reflections from the waterhole, his images looking unappealing. That's when he made the decision to switch to his infrared-converted Nikon Z7 II.
Lewin has had his Z7 II permanently converted, switching the camera sensor's regular filter with a dedicated 720nm infrared filter (monochrome), which accepts part of the spectrum of light that's invisible to the human eye.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
"There would have been no image without it [infrared photography]", he told me. But with it "the skies become more dramatic, the plants reflect infrared light, and you get an otherworldly atmosphere and beautifully soft scene that you cannot produce with a regular camera. It feels more timeless."
Infrared photography warnings
Lewin shared with me a couple of warnings for infrared photography newbies. "If it's beautiful light, don't use an infrared camera because you get all kinds of weird artifacts across the across the image." Nor would he use this gear for, say, a closeup portrait of a lion — the eyes can appear particularly spooky.
He also discovered that some of the latest pro lenses, which he had spent a lot of money on, weren't suitable for infrared. Like many of Nikon's newest lenses, his pricey 24-70mm f/2.8 has protective coatings that reduce things like flare and ghosting, but disturb infrared light.
"You have to go back to having an entirely different set of inexpensive, old lenses that create beautiful infrared images, because they haven't got all of these fancy lens coatings." Indeed, James used a budget friendly 28-75mm f/2.8 for his winning shot.
TechRadar's News Editor Mark Wilson has previously unpacked converting his Fujifilm X-T3 for infrared, and in the process also discovered which Fujifilm lenses were (and weren't) suitable for infrared — you'll need to do the same for your camera system if it's a technique you'd like to try.
A cost-effective alternative to permanently converting a camera is to use a threaded infrared lens filter. However, such filters (combined with a camera's regular sensor filter) reduce light intake to such a degree that a slow shutter speed is required for an accurate exposure, which wouldn't have worked for James' comical photo of the young bull elephant spraying the zebra and giraffe with water. An infrared-converted camera, on the other hand, allowed him to "work at a fast shutter speed, and so to be able to freeze that motion and the water coming out the elephant's trunk".
Traditionally, photographers on safari look for their subjects in the golden hour, and if you haven't found a subject, you'd be waiting until evening to start photographing again. Infrared, however, says Lewin, "opens up a whole new opportunity — when the [best] light is gone [in the morning], that's just the beginning".
Lewin's winning photo is on display at the Wildlife Photographer of the Year exhibition, which is open to the public from 16 October 2026 until July 11 2027 and it's well worth a visit. Tickets can be purchased on the Natural History Museum site with prices starting at £8.50 (child) / £13.60 (concession) / £17 (adult).
Wildlife Photographer of the Year is developed and produced by the Natural History Museum, London. This year's 'Wildlife Photographer of the Year Portfolio 36' book was published on October 14 and costs £28.
Follow TechRadar on Google News and add us as a preferred source to get our expert news, reviews, and opinion in your feeds.
Tim joined the TechRadar team as Cameras Editor in 2023 and has enjoyed more than 15 years as a tech journalist specializing in camera gear. He's previously worked at Amateur Photographer, for a photo accessory manufacturer and as a freelance photographer and video producer, with clients including Studio 44 and Canon. He also started a media team in Nairobi, Kenya, where he lived for a few years volunteering for a faith-based organisation. Tim is married, father of three children, and loves being active, primarily running since hanging up his football boots.

articles.title: Trump posts AI-edited photo to brag about White House restoration work
articles.text:
President Donald Trump posted a series of photos on Truth Social showing off renovations to the White House — but one of them appears to be modified with AI. The picture, which compares an old White House column to a “restored” one, has several discrepancies and was flagged by Google’s AI detector as “made or edited with OpenAI.”
Trump posts AI-edited photo to brag about White House restoration work
A ‘before and after’ photo of a freshly painted White House column was modified with AI.
As pointed out by users on Reddit, the picture of the “restored” column has an uneven number of steps on both sides of the structure. The number of steps also doesn’t match up with the ones in the “before” photo. Additionally, the before and after photos appear nearly identical in angle and detail; the reflection in the windows is nearly the same, and the protective cardboard at the bottom of the column seems to be in the same spot as well. Not to mention that the “newly-painted” one looks unnaturally smooth.
The Verge can confirm that the photo posted to Truth Social is flagged as AI-generated when uploaded to Google’s SynthID Detector, which scans images, videos, and audio for an invisible watermark that indicates it was “created or edited” with AI.
Real pictures show people painting the front of the White House in June, so it’s possible the column actually did get a fresh coat of paint — the White House didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. The SynthID watermark wasn’t detected on other pictures Trump posted, which show the White House facade and heliport. Trump is no stranger to AI tools, though, as he often posts AI-generated caricatures of himself, while the White House has been known to post racist AI memes and at least one photo deceptively edited to make a protester appear distraught.

articles.title: Account-Zwang unter Windows 11: Microsoft schließt Lücke für lokale Konten
articles.text:
Windows 11 ohne Konto nicht mehr möglich: Microsoft entfernt Option für lokale Konten
Erst vor wenigen Wochen haben Windows-11-User:innen einen nützlichen Bug im Betriebssystem gefunden. Bei der Einrichtung eines neuen Windows-PCs ließen sich so die Schritte zur Registrierung eines Microsoft-Kontos überspringen. So war es möglich, den Windows-PC direkt mit einem lokalen Konto auszustatten. Doch offenbar hat sich Microsoft an dieser Lücke im System gestört.
Windows 11: Lokale Konten werden wieder umständlicher
Zuvor konnten User:innen bei der Einrichtung von Windows 11 auf „Mehr erfahren“ klicken, wenn sie beim Schritt des Microsoft-Kontos angekommen waren. Statt tatsächlich weitere Informationen anzuzeigen, schritt das Windows-Setup fort und Nutzer:innen durften direkt ihren PC benennen und mit einem Passwort sichern. Wie Windows Latest zeigt, geht das seit dem Oktober-Update von Windows 11 nicht mehr.
Bei der Einrichtung eines neuen Windows-PCs passiert bei einem Klick auf den Textlink jetzt genau das, was Microsoft von Anfang an wollte. User:innen werden auf eine Infoseite mit weiteren Details zum Microsoft-Konto geführt. Dort haben sie nur noch die Möglichkeit, auf den „Zurück“-Knopf zu klicken, und landen so wieder in der Anmeldemaske.
Das ist nicht das erste Mal, dass Microsoft gegen lokale Konten unter Windows 11 vorgegangen ist. Schon im Oktober 2025 kündigte das Unternehmen an, bekannte Workarounds während des Windows-Setups endgültig zu schließen. Allerdings gibt es auch heute noch Wege, um das System auszutricksen und direkt einen lokalen Windows-Account einzurichten. Wie das geht, zeigen dir unsere Kolleg:innen von Heise im verlinkten Ratgeber.
Für die meisten Windows-User:innen dürfte es aber weiterhin einfacher sein, mit dem Account-Zwang zu leben. Immerhin bringt die Verknüpfung auch einige Vorteile bei der Nutzung von Windows 11 mit sich. Dazu zählt etwa die Synchronisation über mehrere Geräte hinweg oder das Aufspüren und Sperren von verlorenen Windows-Geräten aus der Ferne über „Mein Gerät suchen“.

articles.title: Test de l'Asus Googlebook 14 (2026) : un excellent PC qui méritait un bien meilleur OS — Frandroid
articles.text:
La première salve de PC portables Googlebook est enfin là, après leur annonce par Google le 12 mai dernier. Ces PC portables sont l’occasion pour la firme de présenter l’avenir de ChromeOS sur ce type de machine. Car on le sait, les Chromebook n’ont malheureusement pas eu le succès escompté dans le monde entier, même s’ils trouvent leur public dans certains marchés.
Google et ses partenaires veulent marquer le coup en commençant sur le marché des ultraportables premium, un segment qu’Asus maîtrise parfaitement avec ses gammes Zenbook.
Mais si le châssis et la configuration proposée sont globalement réussis, cet Asus Googlebook, comme les autres, est fortement limité par son OS.
Asus Googlebook 14 (2026)Fiche technique
| Modèle | Asus Googlebook 14 (2026) | 
|---|---|
| Dimensions | 310,9 mm x 16,4 mm | 
| Définition | 2880 x 1800 pixels | 
| Technologie d’affichage | OLED | 
| Écran tactile | Oui | 
| Processeur (CPU) | Core Ultra 7 355 | 
| Puce graphique (GPU) | Intel Graphics | 
| Mémoire vive (RAM) | 16 Go | 
| Mémoire interne | 512 Go | 
| Apparence | Metal | 
| Système d’exploitation (OS) | Googlebook OS | 
| Poids | 990 grammes | 
| Profondeur | 212,8 mm | 
|  | Fiche produit | 
La machine est prêtée par Asus pour ce test.
Asus Googlebook 14 (2026)Design
L’esthétique du Googlebook d’Asus s’inscrit dans la lignée de ses Zenbook en Ceraluminium, même si son châssis n’en profite pas pour autant. La machine, ultra légère (990 grammes), est faite d’un alliage magnésium-aluminium recouvert d’un revêtement nano céramique du plus bel effet. Elle est en plus peu sensible aux traces de doigts.
Sur le dos du PC, on retrouve le logo Asus ainsi qu’une petite barre lumineuse blanche qui indique que la machine est allumée et sert de témoin de notification, comme sur tous les Googlebook. On n’est pas dépaysé donc, la marque fournit ici un châssis solide qui ne souffre d’aucun jeu ni craquement à la manipulation.
Sa teinte grise « Dusk Ash » est somme toute assez classique, avec un clavier au gris plus clair qui offre ainsi un camaïeu qu’on reconnaît aussi de chez Asus.
Clavier et pavé tactile
Le clavier est peu ou prou le même que celui des Zenbook, avec une course d’activation plutôt satisfaisante et une expérience de frappe globalement fluide. Le clavier est légèrement plus bruyant que la moyenne cependant.
Le large pavé tactile est très pratique à utiliser et dispose d’un retour haptique lors du clic. Étrangement, la glisse est un peu moins fluide que sur certains Zenbook et MacBook, sans que cela gêne au quotidien.
Connectique
Asus n’a pas lésiné sur la connectique de son Googlebook avec pas moins de quatre ports USB : deux ports USB-C Thunderbolt 4 et deux ports USB-A 3.2 Gen2. Nous aurions préféré un troisième port USB-C à la place du second USB-A, maintenant que le standard s’est généralisé. On retrouve aussi un port HDMI 2.1 ainsi qu’une prise audio jack.
Niveau connectivité, la machine supporte le Wi-Fi 7, mais à l’instar des derniers MacBook, seulement une largeur de canal de 160 MHz au lieu des 320 MHz dont la technologie est capable. Le Bluetooth 6 est quant à lui supporté pour vos appareils sans fil.
Webcam et audio
La webcam 1080p est assez basique, elle manque de piqué et d’un vrai traitement d’image. Elle suffira pour la visio, mais on a vu mieux à ce prix.
Niveau audio, les performances sont tout a fait excellentes pour le format, bien supérieur à ce que nous avons vu sur l’Acer Googlebook 14. Le son est puissante, assez clair dans les mediums et avec des basses satisfaisantes, même si limitées. Une bonne surprise.
Jusqu’à 330€ d’avantages avec nos offres Hello Prime ou Hello Prime Duo, dont 80€ cash à l’ouverture de compte !
Asus Googlebook 14 (2026)Écran
Les Googlebook disposent quasiment tous d’une dalle Oled, ce modèle Asus ne fait pas exception. On est ici sur une belle dalle 3K de 14 pouces compatible HDR (ce n’est pas le cas de tous) avec un pic de luminosité annoncé à 1 000 cd/m², une couverture annoncée de 100 % de l’espace DCI-P3 et une précision des couleurs exemplaire.
Sous notre sonde avec le logiciel Calman Ultimate, nous mesurons une couverture de 93 % de l’espace DCI-P3 (contre 100 % annoncés) et 136 % du sRGB. La technologie Oled nous a habitués à une précision des couleurs excellente et c’est le cas ici aussi avec un Delta-E de 2,03 avec un écart maximal qui ne dépasse pas les 4. Pour rappel, sous un Delta-E de 3, l’œil ne perçoit quasiment pas les écarts de couleur.
La luminosité n’est pas en reste, avec un pic à 970 cd/m² sur une petite zone de 10 % et 650 cd/m² en plein écran, en HDR. Parlons du HDR justement. Comme sur le Googlebook d’Acer que nous avons testé, l’Oled de ce modèle déçoit en HDR sur le bureau, avec des noirs rehaussés comme en SDR. Ce sont vraiment sur ces contenus HDR purs (films, vidéos) que vous profiterez de tout son potentiel.
Le problème a cependant été remonté à Google et la bonne nouvelle, c’est qu’il vient du firmware même de la machine et non de l’écran lui-même. Une fois que nous aurons vérifié que le souci a été corrigé, nous revisiterons ce test.
Asus Googlebook 14 (2026)Logiciel
Au premier lancement du Googlebook d’Asus, mon Google Pixel 10a m’a automatiquement proposé de se synchroniser avec le PC. Il suffit alors de scanner le QR Code avec l’appareil photo. Comme sur macOS, l’ordinateur récupère alors le compte Google de l’utilisateur ainsi que la connexion Wi-Fi automatiquement. Vous pourrez aussi importer vos applications automatiquement, avec leurs informations de connexion, mais aussi en installer de nouvelles parmi une sélection issue de plusieurs catégories (divertissement, communication, productivité, etc.).
Le Googlebook est opérationnel en moins de 2 minutes et vous pourrez rapidement vous mettre au travail ou simplement naviguer, car votre compte Google sera déjà synchronisé. Sans smartphone sous Android 17, cette première initialisation sera plus longue.
L’interface reste dans la continuité d’Android et de ChromeOS, Google ne touche ni aux bases logicielles ni à l’habillage graphique.
Comme c’est le cas depuis les dernières évolutions de ChromeOS, Gemini est au centre de ce Googlebook OS. Au-delà du simple assistant personnel, l’IA de Google peut avoir une véritable vision sur tout votre écosystème, vous aider à mieux gérer votre stockage ou trouver des paramètres. La fonction phare de l’OS est son curseur magique (Magic Pointer), qui s’active en secouant rapidement la souris pour afficher des actions contextuelles liées au contenu affiché à l’écran : qu’il s’agisse de copier un texte d’une image ou poser des questions à Gemini sur le contenu même. Plutôt pratique et simple d’utilisation, la fonctionnalité pourra être utile dans bien des cas.
Enfin, la recherche sémantique fonctionne aussi très bien. Vous pourrez saisir vos requêtes en langage naturel pour trouver cette « photo prise en juin dernier avec mon chat Pixel » et il pourra vous suggérer rapidement des résultats pertinents. Google rattrape ainsi Apple et Microsoft, qui proposent déjà ce type de recherche sur leurs systèmes.
L’autre promesse de Googlebook OS, c’est cette intégration native avec votre smartphone Android. Attention, il faudra nécessairement être équipé d’un appareil avec Android 17, sinon vous serez plus que bridé sur cette partie. Imaginez une version complète de Mobile connecté (Phone Link) sur Windows 11, même si Google vise surtout macOS. Vous pouvez ainsi utiliser votre smartphone directement depuis le système.
Cela inclut le lancement et l’utilisation d’applications Android, l’affichage des notifications de votre smartphone. Comme sur macOS, vous pourrez reprendre sur Googlebook OS une tâche commencée sur Android, qu’il s’agisse de retouche photo ou de la rédaction d’un mail ou d’un message. Au quotidien, cette intégration est l’argument principal de l’OS bureau de Google, une manière de légitimer encore plus l’écosystème Android hors du smartphone.
Le cas des applications
Maintenant, l’une des premières choses qui m’a interpellé lorsque j’ai lancé ce Googlebook, ce sont les applications Google. J’ai très vite remarqué de par leur comportement qu’il s’agissait en réalité d’applications web et non d’applications natives Googlebook OS. Gmail, YouTube, et bien d’autres, se lancent comme des sites web dans une fenêtre dans le système.
Google estime que les expériences de ces services, contrairement à ses applications mobiles, sont plus adaptées au format de bureau d’un PC portable. Les applications dites « natives » sont réservées à celles qui utilisent en profondeur l’architecture matérielle du PC, comme Gemini pour l’IA ou Google Maps pour le GPS.
Mais on le sait, ces sites web qui se font passer pour une application prennent plus de ressources, notamment en mémoire. De plus, nous achetons des PC plus chers pour profiter de toute leur puissance et de leur pool mémoire, pas pour les gâcher dans ces expériences web. Cela ne bloque rien au quotidien, mais Google semble avoir manqué de temps, ou d’ambition, pour porter ses propres applications sur Googlebook OS.
De plus, nous avons rencontré quelques applications tierces, comme Slack, qui ne sont pas encore optimisées pour Googlebook OS, le Play Store nous recommandant de passer par la version web, un comble sur un système qui met en avant les applications Android.
Asus Googlebook 14 (2026)Performances
Notre modèle de test est équipé d’un processeur Intel Core Ultra 7 355 avec 8 cœurs (4 performants et 4 basse consommation) et 8 threads, pour une fréquence maximale de 4,7 GHz. Une configuration Ultra 5 est aussi proposée dans la gamme. Pas de puce graphique Intel Arc ici, le Core Ultra 7 355 se contente de la partie graphique Intel Graphics à 4 cœurs Xe3.
Notre échantillon est équipé de 16 Go de RAM LPDDR5X et 512 Go de stockage en PCIe 4.0. Une version 256 Go moins onéreuse existe aussi.
Benchmarks
L’arrivée de Googlebook OS donne un petit coup de pied dans la fourmilière de notre base de données de benchmarks, car nous mesurons les performances processeur avec Cinebench. Or, celui-ci n’est pour l’instant pas compatible avec l’OS de bureau de Google, si bien que nous ne pouvons comparer le Googlebook Asus qu’avec les MacBook d’Apple sur le benchmark Geekbench 7.
Avec un score multicœur de 11 017 et un score monocœur de 2 381, l’Asus Googlebook se situe entre la puce Snapdragon X (pas la version Elite) et un MacBook Pro M1. Comme nous l’avons déjà noté dans notre test de l’Acer Googlebook 14, on entre ici dans une toute autre catégorie de performance pour la plateforme de Google, mais on reste encore loin des ténors du marché, y compris dans cette gamme de prix.
L’architecture permet une certaine polyvalence entre bureautique et création, mais reste tout de même un peu datée en termes de performances brutes. Surtout, nous avons remarqué une consommation en berne au bout de quelques minutes de test avec un thermal throttling important, de 45 à 18 watts, montrant que le Core Ultra 7 est plus que bridé dans un tel châssis. Le choix d’un modèle Core Ultra 5 moins onéreux sera à privilégier.
Sur la partie graphique, nous atteignons le score de 864 sur le 3D Mark Steel Nomad Light, soit le 3e pire score de notre base de données, juste devant le HP EliteBoard et son format clavier-PC. Ici, on imagine que les pilotes de Google sont loin d’être au point, même si on ne peut pas s’attendre à des miracles avec le simple iGPU Intel Graphics.
Enfin sur la partie stockage, nous atteignons des scores honorables au niveau de la norme PCI Gen4, Asus n’a pas fait d’économies sur cette partie fort heureusement.
Refroidissement et bruit
Rien à signaler sur le bruit et la chauffe de la machine qui resteront contenus en quasi toutes circonstances. Il faudra vraiment la soumettre à des tâches de rendu ou de benchmark lourds pour qu’on entende ses ventilateurs tourner.
Asus Googlebook 14 (2026)Autonomie
L’Asus Googlebook 14 intègre une batterie de 70 Whr somme toute assez classique sur ce format. Bien plus qu’à même de gérer une journée de travail bien remplie, la machine offre heureusement une autonomie confortable.
Je l’ai utilisé dans des conditions de travail standard, à savoir navigation web, bureautique avec plusieurs applications comme Slack et Spotify, et j’arrive à 15h45 d’usage. Ici, le Googlebook n’a donc rien à envier aux ténors du genre, notamment sur Panther Lake.
Asus Googlebook 14 (2026)Prix et disponibilité
L’Asus Googlebook 14 existe en 4 configurations, toutes à 16 Go de RAM, mais qui se partagent entre deux SoC (Intel Core Ultra 5 ou 7) et deux stockages, entre 256 et 512 Go de SSD.
Les tarifs vont ainsi de 1299 euros à 1599 euros. Nous avons testé cette dernière version, la plus puissante. Ici, l’Asus Googlebook est clairement au coude à coude avec les MacBook Air et Surface Laptop, sur cette gamme ultra-compétitive des ultraportables entre 1000 et 1500 euros.

articles.title: Test du Rog Xbox Ally X20 avec écran OLED : l'aboutissement
articles.text:
Rog Ally en 2023, Rog Ally X en 2024, Rog Xbox Ally X en 2025 et Rog Xbox Ally X20 en 2026 : chaque année, Asus lance un nouveau produit pour le segment des PC portables déguisés en console, avec à chaque fois des améliorations notables. La deuxième génération avait apporté une grosse amélioration au niveau de l’autonomie. La troisième misait sur l’ergonomie et l’intégration au sein de l’écosystème Xbox. Quant à la quatrième, elle vient apporter l’ultime touche, attendue depuis le tout premier modèle.
Disponible depuis ce jeudi 15 octobre 2026 à 1 400 €, le Rog Xbox Ally X20 célèbre les 20 ans de Rog (Republic of Gamers), la gamme gaming d’Asus. Il se distingue de ses prédécesseurs par l’intégration d’un écran OLED de 7,4 pouces. C’est une caractéristique que l’on n’espérait plus et qui fait entrer le produit dans le très haut de gamme. Après plusieurs dizaines d’heures de jeu, nous sommes conquis.
Points forts
- Écran OLED magnifique et sans concession
- Ergonomie encore améliorée
- Performances à la hauteur…
Points faibles
- … mais zéro évolution
- Windows 11 toujours pas à la hauteur
- Pas de pochette, pas de câble pour un produit à 1 400 €
L’écran OLED du Rog Xbox Ally X20 est magnifique
« Il ne lui manquait qu’un écran OLED pour être aboutie », écrivions-nous à propos du Rog Ally X, dans notre test publié en 2024. Plus d’un an plus tard, on se paraphrasait dans celui du Rog Xbox Ally X : « On rêverait d’un écran OLED. » On se doutait que l’intégration d’une telle technologie ferait bondir la facture. C’est le cas, puisqu’on passe de 900 € (prix de lancement du Rog Xbox Ally X) à 1 400 €, soit une hausse de plus de 55 %.
L’attente a été longue, mais le jeu en valait la chandelle. Le constructeur n’a fait strictement aucun compromis sur la dalle qu’arbore fièrement le Rog Xbox Ally X20. On se retrouve alors avec un écran associant les qualités immenses de l’OLED (noir parfait, couleurs éclatantes, contrastes exemplaires), une luminosité de pointe de 1 400 nits en HDR (près de trois fois les 500 nits de l’écran LCD du Rog Xbox Ally X, et ça se voit dans Forza Horizon 6 ; Asus annonce 600 nits hors HDR) et le VRR pour améliorer la fluidité. La définition est toujours en 1080p, ce qui est amplement suffisant pour un produit nomade de cette taille, tandis que le taux de rafraîchissement reste en 120 Hz.
Asus a même pensé à un filtre antireflet, particulièrement bluffant quand on sait que la dalle n’est pas matte. Le spectacle tient la route y compris en extérieur, avec 65 % de reflets en moins qu’une dalle OLED sans traitement. Sur un jeu à la direction artistique sombre mais détaillée comme Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse, l’expérience est saisissante. Essayer le Rog Xbox Ally X20 et goûter à l’OLED donnent envie de ne plus jamais revenir en arrière. Certes, le coût est élevé, mais l’écran est à la hauteur de la facture.
Quelques retouches ergonomiques bien pensées
Finition translucide
Afin de fêter les 20 ans de Rog comme il se doit, le Rog Xbox Ally X20 se pare d’une finition translucide sombre du plus bel effet, avec quelques touches de doré et un bouton Xbox illuminé. C’est joli.
Outre l’écran OLED, qui constitue son plus grand argument, le Rog Xbox Ally X20 embarque quelques petites améliorations bienvenues. La « console » est enfin dotée d’une croix directionnelle digne de ce nom. Elle détonnait totalement sur le Rog Xbox Ally X, en raison de sa finition médiocre et du ressenti à l’utilisation. Asus a revu sa copie avec une croix directionnelle bien mieux finie et, en prime, transformable. En quelques secondes, on peut passer d’une croix à quatre ou huit directions, la deuxième option étant intéressante pour les adeptes de jeux de combat et de coups impliquant des arcs de cercle.
L’autre grande évolution concerne les joysticks, toujours disposés en asymétrique. Ils passent à des capteurs magnétiques TMR qui suppriment tout risque de drift (ces mouvements fantômes qui finissent par pénaliser le gameplay). Une excellente nouvelle pour la fiabilité à long terme et les sensations en jeu.
Il faut par ailleurs souligner le grip repensé au niveau des manches. Plus prononcé, il accroche mieux la paume des mains et améliore le confort d’un objet qui pèse tout de même 756 grammes (une quarantaine de grammes de plus que les 715 grammes du Rog Xbox Ally X).
En termes de design, le Rog Xbox Ally X20 reprend la forme très ergonomique du Rog Xbox Ally X, qui consiste à placer un écran entre une manette coupée en deux. La disposition des touches est la même, y compris en ce qui concerne les deux boutons programmables à l’arrière. Attention, le Rog Xbox Ally X20 gagne un centimètre en largeur, rendant incompatibles les pochettes du Rog Xbox Ally X (aucune n’est fournie, pas plus que le chargeur).
À l’intérieur, la même puce
Asus n’a en revanche pas touché à la puce du Rog Xbox Ally X20. Seul le refroidissement a été revu pour soutenir la technologie OLED, qui supporte moins bien la chaleur qu’un écran LCD, ce qui tient davantage de l’ajustement nécessaire que d’une vraie évolution. On retrouve sinon une configuration articulée autour du processeur AMD Ryzen AI Z2 Extreme, épaulé par un NPU (pour l’IA), 24 Go de RAM et un SSD de 1 To. Le tout est alimenté par une batterie de 80 Wh.
Asus n’a pas cru bon d’améliorer la fiche technique, ce qui pourrait décevoir celles et ceux en quête de performances pures. Pas de quoi prendre en défaut cette machine capable de faire tourner des jeux comme Forza Horizon 6 sans sourciller. On a même pu réaliser le test de Valor Mortis dessus, sans aucun problème, ni effort en matière d’optimisation pour obtenir le meilleur rendu.
L’écran OLED consomme un peu plus que celui LCD du Rog Xbox Ally X, mais on parle d’une poignée de minutes perdues sur une autonomie qui varie grandement en fonction du mode de puissance (13 watts en Silencieux, 17 watts en Performances et 25 watts en Turbo) et du jeu. Comptez environ deux heures dans les conditions les plus gourmandes.
Terminons par l’interface, qui s’appuie toujours sur une base Windows 11 avec un mode Xbox pensé pour le gaming et une surcouche Asus Rog. On n’a observé aucune amélioration notable depuis la sortie du Rog Xbox Ally. Il y a toujours cette idée de proposer un agrégateur de toutes les plateformes de jeux sur PC (Steam, catalogue Xbox, Xbox Game Pass…), mais avec toujours ces frictions qui pourront parfois être pénibles dans la navigation et ces incessantes mises à jour. Au besoin, on peut aussi remplacer Windows par SteamOS, que Valve rend officiellement installable sur la gamme Rog Ally depuis 2025, pour transformer le Rog Xbox Ally X20 en Steam Deck survitaminé. Une excellente alternative pour gagner en confort et en performance.
Le verdict
Xbox Ally X20
Voir la fiche
On a aimé
- Écran OLED magnifique et sans concession
- Ergonomie encore améliorée
- Performances à la hauteur…
On a moins aimé
- … mais zéro évolution
- Windows 11 toujours pas à la hauteur
- Pas de pochette, pas de câble pour un produit à 1 400 €

articles.title: UK Legal Aid Agency: Hackers stole records dating back to 1978
articles.text:
The Legal Aid Agency (LAA), an executive agency of the UK's Ministry of Justice that manages the country's Public Defender Service, says attackers who breached its IT systems in April 2025 stole records dating back to 1978.
The agency employs around 1,250 staff, oversees billions in legal funding, and works with approximately 2,000 providers, including barristers, solicitor firms, and non-profit organizations that deliver civil and criminal legal aid services in England and Wales.
The LAA disclosed the cyberattack in early May 2025, warning that payment information for legal aid providers might have been compromised.
Two weeks later, it confirmed the resulting data breach was more serious than first believed after finding that attackers had stolen a large trove of sensitive applicant and recipient data from 2010 onward, including contact details, dates of birth, national ID numbers, criminal history, employment status, as well as contribution amounts, debts, and payments.
The threat actors have also stolen legal aid providers' data, including provider contracts, office locations, financial information, contact details, LAA Online Portal credentials (including names and email addresses), and more.
In an update published this week, the LAA said follow-up analysis of the exfiltrated data found that the stolen records go back almost five decades.
"The vast majority of the LAA data relates to applications, claims or payments submitted to the LAA between January 2007 and 16 May 2025, or to cases that were live during this period. However, we have now confirmed that approximately 250,000 records predate 2007," the agency said. "The overwhelming majority of these are from the 1990s and 2000s, with only a fractionally small number dating from before 1990. The earliest record currently verified dates from 1978."
However, it noted that records predating 2007 do not mean everyone who received, applied for legal aid, or interacted with the justice system before 2007 was affected.
"We recognise that incidents of this nature are concerning for anyone affected. That is why we published information on GOV. UK as quickly as possible and have continued to update it as our understanding of the cyber-attack has developed," a Ministry of Justice spokesperson told BleepingComputer.
"Prior to the cyber-attack, we had already committed £20 million to stabilising and upgrading the Legal Aid Agency's digital systems. We are now investing more than £200 million in modernising digital services, improving resilience and strengthening cyber security across legal aid services. There is currently no evidence that any personal data believed to have been exfiltrated has been published."
After the LAA breach, which was followed by a string of cyberattacks targeting the Co-op, Harrods, and Marks & Spencer (M&S) UK retail chains claimed by the DragonForce ransomware operation, the country's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) published guidance and advised UK organizations to follow it to strengthen their cybersecurity defenses.
In January, the UK also announced a new cybersecurity strategy, backed by more than £210 million ($283 million), to boost cyber defenses across government departments and the wider public sector.
This week, the UK Housing Ombudsman Service, a non-departmental public body sponsored by the Ministry of Housing that settles disputes between social housing residents and social landlords in England, disclosed that it is investigating a third-party IT security incident that impacted its case management system.
Once attackers have valid credentials, only 37% of their actions are blocked
