articles.title: CISO Conversations: James Robinson – Many Jobs, One Journey to Netskope CISO
articles.text:
At school James Robinson was more sporty than STEM, but after school he rose from the track to cybersecurity leader at Netskope.
The journey to becoming a CISO
The young James Robinson attended a small high school in Central Illinois and describes himself as ‘more sporty than STEM’: “I wasn’t going to knock it out of the park in the English class – but luckily the English teacher was also the track coach, so that helped.” In his final year in high school, the principal suggested going on to something vocational or trades-related rather than university. A friend was already in a vocational school doing electronics engineering, so he went that route. That school had just been included in the Cisco Networking Academy (NetAcad).
Robinson threw himself into NetAcad learning. “It was like the world suddenly became my oyster. There was no stopping me. I started doing networking at home, got connected to the internet, and studied and studied.” This was the late 1990s while he was still at school.
After school, by the early 2000s, he became a network engineer at State Farm Insurance, but now with a Cisco Certified Internetwork Expert (CCIE) certification. He decided to join Cisco itself. At that time, Cisco was the darling of the tech boom, briefly being the most valuable company in the world with a market cap in excess of $500 billion.
But then the dot-com bubble burst. It would not be a stretch to say that Cisco was caught flat-footed. Its stock price plummeted from over $80 to under $10, and the firm was forced to lay off around 8,500 employees.
For Robinson, that route to Cisco was blocked and he was forced to remain at State Farm Insurance. He asked for a different position, and was told, ‘This security thing is going to be big. Go for that.’ While doing the interviews at Cisco, he had met a guy from AT&T who had talked about the idea of shutting off internet connection and all outside communications for security reasons, so this new security idea gelled.
Robinson was in his early 20s and looking for a new direction and new challenge. In his own words, “I just kind of fell into security. I saw the opportunity, took the shot, and went for it.” He became a technical (security) analyst at State Farm Insurance.
The combination of a solid background in technology, networking and an early and growing interest in security was a solid marketable quality. In 2006 he left State Farm Insurance to become a systems engineer (info protection security architecture and analysis) at Anheuser-Busch. He moved on to Emerson Electric in 2008 and became product security assurance manager and product security officer at Emerson Network Power in 2010. In 2012 he joined Websense and became security architecture and strategy officer in 2013. He then moved to Accuvant-FishNet Security as director of information security, becoming VP of third-party risk management at Optiv in 2015.
Always in security, never staying long in any one position, but always moving up the career ladder. In 2018 he joined Netskope as deputy CISO. He seems to have found his calling. He stayed in that position for more than five years – twice his average sojourn – and became CISO in 2024. He remains CISO at Netskope today.
Advice
Every successful person has had good advice along the way. That advice is often useful to everyone, not just security practitioners.
On his journey, Robinson received and followed the advice of numerous mentors. One was his mother-in-law. “If you want to do something,” she told him, “and you keep getting blowback or being told, ‘You don’t want to do that because…’ then you’re probably not right for that position, or company, or even that career anymore.”
He also had traditional professional mentors and tries to live by one specific piece of advice: “Get close to the business. Understand how the business works. Know what makes it perform well and what makes it perform poorly.”
Some advice was more esoteric. “If you see smart people doing dumb things, you’re just not in the know.” The implication is that you shouldn’t immediately dismiss strange actions as stupidity, but you should pause and consider whether there is something you’re missing or simply don’t understand. (He added this advice could apply to the world of politics just as much as the world of business.)
“Two other pieces of advice that I try to live by are: If the door is open, see where it takes you,” he said, “and never, ever stop learning, because learning is fun when you’re in the right job.” He clearly abided by the former in his early career, rarely staying in one position beyond two years, and he welcomes the fun part of where he is now. He believes people, and especially CISOs, should have fun whenever they can, “because things happen and come at you, and there’s a lot of stress.”
He illustrated this with the advice that is almost a cultural idiom, but true all the same: it’s not about the destination, it’s about the journey. “I was at a CISO summit just last night and was talking to a CISO. She said, ‘I don’t know what I’m going to do. I’ve done everything I set out to do.’ If you make the destination the goal, what do you do next? And if you didn’t enjoy the journey, what have you got now? Sometimes we want to go so fast we simply don’t get a moment to enjoy where we’re at in the journey.”
So, he continued, “Even with my team members, who I know want to go fast, I try to get them to pause and appreciate the moment – each moment of their journey.”
Another piece of advice he offers to his team members is to ensure they always have good friends and good mentors with them both in the journey and at the destination. “There was a point in my own journey when I was struggling with some things. And then I remembered I hadn’t spoken to any of my mentors for a while. So, I called one, and we had a conversation and talked through my problem. In that discussion I realized I already knew what to do – I just needed the extra confirmation.”
Having good friends is also important. “When you move up the security ladder you increasingly become the odd duck in the company. You’re a technologist, but you deal with people. You’re the one who delivers regulatory bad news, or information that slows people down, or the data nobody wants to hear. You can find yourself a bit isolated and alone.” This is where you need good friends. They’re almost like social mentors.
“I have a few. I know I can call them or text them and no matter what, they’ll get back to me. That’s really, really helpful. I think every CISO, even if they don’t have similar friends, should stress upon their team members that developing friends along the journey is really very important.”
He finally added a combined warning and advice for people wanting to succeed in a cybersecurity career. The warning is that security people shouldn’t measure their position by their hourly wage rate, but rather by the satisfaction of doing a good job. “Security tends to push you well beyond the working day. But it’s a job that attracts people with the curiosity that sustains you so that play becomes work and work becomes play. Fourteen-hour days are not a big deal when you’re having fun, learning new things and are not too concerned with how much money you’re making each hour.”
Building the security team
That curiosity is a key element he looks for as a CISO building his security team. “Even when I’m doing mock interviews for high school students, I’ll say, ‘OK, you want to be in security. What have you been researching? What did you read last night? What did you look up? What interests you?’” he explained.
If you want to work with James Robinson, give him some insight into what you do, because you always need that curiosity and you’ve always got to be feeding it.
He does consider security certifications to be useful in choosing his team. “But it’s more about the mindset and the person,” he said. “I’m always a little bit for the underdog, the person who’s willing to put in the hard work and the time. So, I look for indicators of that.”
He gave examples. “There was a person working in healthcare. He wanted to get into security. I had to tell him there was no position for him – but that if he went to St. Louis (where we have an office) he might get an interview for an intern position. He did that. He moved to St. Louis. That’s the kind of persistence and dedication to purpose that I seek.”
In another example, “A girl was a fresh grad in Northern Indiana, who wanted to get into security. I had to tell her the same thing: I’ve got nothing for you here, but perhaps if you move… She said, ‘Yeah, I’ll move to St. Louis. I’ll go for the job. I’ll go for the role. I’ll be there.’”
She did that. She got a position. “And she’s done an excellent job. She’s now a pen tester on our team, doing attack and penetration and vulnerability assessments. It’s that kind of mindset – I’m just going to go for it – that’s something I look for, because I know that person will put in the extra effort and appreciate the journey.”
He’s as pleased for her as she was for the opportunity.
Back to certifications. He never finished his own university degree, and accepts that at certain points in his own journey there were times he wasn’t considered because he didn’t have a degree. He has no regrets because that was his choice, but he adds, “It doesn’t mean I won’t complete my degree in the future. I’m sort of in a race right now, with my kids aged 16 and 18. The 18-year-old is starting college, but he’s got a long way to go. He’s doing neuroscience and neurobiology, so maybe I’ve got up to eight years to finish my own degree and win the race.”
So, the message from Robinson for people in or wishing to be in security is simple: certifications will be useful, but attitude is even more important.
So, what keeps James Robinson up at night?
From everything he’s said so far, it will be no surprise that it’s not what you might expect. “What I think about late at night, or jot down to get it out of my mind before I go to sleep, is whether or how I can get better performance from myself and the team, whether we’re making real progress on our projects. I’m always looking and reminding myself on ways to enrich the team culture,” he said.
“I want to make sure that every individual member of the team is recognized, and that I can connect with all of them. The best leaders I ever worked with weren’t always my own managers, but they were leaders who made time for me. I try to pay that back. So, my last thoughts before sleep are often, how can I do that? Am I doing everything that I can to be the best leader for the team and is the team’s health and performance strong? Security incidents come and go. They’re like waves. They’re the job, and you handle them.”
Individual incidents do cause stress, but concern over the team is constant. Even specifically asked if AI is a concern today, he replied, “If it keeps me up it’s because I’m trying to learn more about it. It’s the excitement of AI rather than the danger of AI. It’s the team and team performance that matters most; at least for the next few years. One day, maybe everything will be agentic, including my own job. But until we get there, it’s the team and team culture that builds the company and gets things done.”

articles.title: AI can act exactly like a human, but we still don't think it's conscious
articles.text:
AI can act exactly like a human, but we still don't think it's conscious
- Date:
- October 13, 2026
- Source:
- Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München
- Summary:
- A new study reveals that people draw a surprisingly sharp line between human consciousness and artificial intelligence, even when both behave identically. Researchers found that participants considered even the most responsive AI less conscious than the least responsive human. Yet when asked about "awareness" instead, people judged humans and AI much more similarly.
- Share:
Even when artificial intelligence behaves exactly like a human, people are reluctant to consider it conscious, according to a new study from Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich (LMU).
As artificial intelligence becomes more advanced, reports of AI systems misleading users, working together, or appearing to pursue independent goals are becoming increasingly common. These behaviors often lead people to describe AI as though it can think, feel, or make decisions for itself. But does behaving like a human actually convince people that a machine has consciousness?
New research from LMU suggests that people make a clear distinction between displaying intelligent behavior and possessing a conscious mind, even when humans and AI act in precisely the same way.
How Scientists Tested Perceptions of AI Consciousness
Published in the journal Cognition, the study was led by Dr. Louis Longin of LMU's Chair of Philosophy of Mind, working alongside Dr. Bahador Bahrami, Professor Ophelia Deroy, and other researchers.
"Whereas previous studies have typically asked general questions about whether AI actually has mental states, our study is the first to directly compare how people attribute the same mental states to AI and humans behaving in exactly the same way, under identical circumstances," says Longin.
"We may be using mental terms to refer to AI, but this may only be because we lack better words," says Ophelia Deroy, philosopher and a senior author of the study. "After all, AI is trained to act and speak like a human, so these descriptions seem natural."
To investigate how people judge consciousness, the researchers conducted experiments involving nearly 1,100 participants. One group read brief descriptions of artificial agents that showed different levels of responsiveness to their environments. For example, some agents reacted to sounds or recognized the emotional states of others.
Another group encountered the same situations, except the characters were described as humans rather than AI systems. Participants then evaluated how conscious or aware each character seemed to be of its surroundings.
A Surprising Gap Between Human and AI Consciousness
The experiments revealed that responsiveness influenced how participants judged both humans and artificial intelligence. Characters that reacted more actively to their surroundings were generally considered more conscious and more aware.
However, a striking difference emerged when participants evaluated consciousness specifically. Even the most responsive AI was rated as less conscious than the least responsive human. In other words, identical behavior did not lead people to assign the same level of consciousness to humans and machines.
The results changed considerably when participants were asked about awareness instead. For this characteristic, judgments of humans and AI followed largely similar patterns, suggesting that people interpret awareness and consciousness in fundamentally different ways.
"There is a growing worry in public discussion that people will see AI behaving in a human-like way and start treating these systems as if they had human-like mental states," says Longin, lead author of the study. "We found something much more nuanced: People are quite willing to say that an AI notices things and is aware of its surroundings. But they clearly draw a line when it comes to the term 'consciousness'. People consistently attribute less consciousness to AI than humans -- even when their behavior is identical."
Although people sometimes describe AI as conscious when discussing its actions, the findings indicate that they still distinguish between artificial systems and human minds.
Why One Word Changes How We Perceive AI
The researchers believe the difference between consciousness and awareness offers an important insight into how people understand artificial intelligence.
Awareness is a relatively neutral term that can describe an agent's ability to detect and respond to information in its environment. Consciousness, however, carries deeper implications about subjective experience and what it means to have an inner mental life.
Because awareness focuses more directly on observable behavior, people appear comfortable applying it to both humans and AI. Consciousness carries a different meaning, leading people to judge the two much less similarly.
The findings also highlight why the language used to discuss artificial intelligence matters, particularly as AI systems become increasingly capable of producing convincing human behavior.
"Our study teaches us lessons for how we communicate about AI," says Bahador Bahrami, who is also a senior author of the study and an expert in social neuroscience. "Companies and journalists often reach for hyped descriptions of AI models, and credit them with intentions, plans, or even moral conscience and hesitation. What our study shows is that everyday judgments are much more discriminating: People do not simply put AI and humans on the same mental scale. But the boundary also depends on which terms we use. For more neutral descriptors such as 'awareness', the distinction can largely disappear. That makes our choice of language important."
Story Source:
Materials provided by Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Louis Longin, Jurgis Karpus, Nadine Meertens, Bahador Bahrami, Ophelia Deroy. AI is not as conscious as humans: Essentialism in mental state attributions to artificial systems. Cognition, 2027; 278: 106733 DOI: 10.1016/j.cognition.2026.106733

articles.title: Claro Colombia se pronuncia en medio de la desaparición de Movistar, ahora Tigo
articles.text:
Claro Colombia emitió un manifiesto el mismo día en que Movistar dejó de existir como marca comercial en el país para integrarse de manera definitiva a Tigo, propiedad de Millicom, la cual anunció también un plan de inversión de 8,5 billones de pesos para los próximos cuatro años, con el que busca consolidar el liderazgo del mercado móvil colombiano.
El comunicado de Claro no menciona de manera directa a Tigo ni a Movistar, pero coincide en fecha con el cambio de marca que comenzó este miércoles 14 de octubre en todo el territorio nacional. La compañía, filial de América Móvil, destacó su trayectoria en infraestructura y su transformación hacia un modelo de “empresa de tecnología” que trasciende la conectividad tradicional.
“Colombia está entrando en una etapa en la que conectar ya no es suficiente”, señaló la compañía en su manifiesto. Según el texto, el país necesita capacidad para transportar, alojar, procesar y proteger la información, además de mantener disponibles los servicios esenciales y convertir la tecnología en productividad.
Claro detalló que su red llega con 4G al 100% de las cabeceras municipales y con 5G en más de 100 ciudades y municipios, además de contar con más de 150.000 kilómetros de fibra óptica. A esa infraestructura se suman centros de datos, nube, inteligencia artificial y ciberseguridad, capacidades que, según la empresa, forman un ecosistema integrado y no servicios aislados.
“Nuestra escala es, ante todo, una responsabilidad”, afirmó la compañía en el documento, en el que vinculó su despliegue de red con la obligación de llegar a más territorios y sostener el servicio “cuando el país más la necesita”.
El comunicado también hizo referencia a cambios en la operación de Claro. La compañía indicó que está “simplificando procesos, fortaleciendo la atención y utilizando tecnología y datos para resolver con mayor agilidad”. Con esa descripción, la empresa buscó posicionarse como un actor que evolucionó “de una compañía de telecomunicaciones a una empresa de tecnología que acompaña todo el ciclo de la información”.
El mensaje se dirigió tanto a los clientes como al país en general. “A nuestros clientes se lo demostramos con una red que responde, una experiencia que mejora y una compañía que nunca deja de avanzar; al país, con compromiso”, indicó el texto, que cerró con el anuncio de que la empresa continuará “invirtiendo, innovando y elevando la calidad” de sus servicios.
Tigo avanza en el mercado de telecomunicaciones colombiano
Tigo formalizó el reemplazo de los letreros de Movistar en sus tiendas principales y dio inicio oficial a la unificación de marca. También se prevé que su nombre aparezca pronto en los teléfonos en vez de Movistar.
El cambio responde a la compra que Millicom realizó este año para quedarse con el control total de Movistar, transacción que, según el CEO de Millicom, Marcelo Benítez, representó un desembolso de 4,5 billones de pesos.
A esa cifra se suma el plan de inversión de 8,5 billones de pesos anunciado recientemente, con el que la empresa proyecta elevar su apuesta total en Colombia a 13 billones de pesos en cuatro años. Según Benítez, en entrevista con Infobae, los recursos se destinarán a ampliar la capacidad de las antenas ante un incremento del tráfico de datos cercano al 15% interanual, además de duplicar la cobertura de 5G hasta alcanzar 324 municipios y sumar más de mil nuevos sitios de conectividad.
Qué implica esta unificación para los clientes?
Los contratos firmados con Colombia Telecomunicaciones (Coltel), la sociedad que operaba Movistar, se mantienen vigentes, y los clientes continuarán con los mismos planes y canales de pago. El único cambio visible para los usuarios será el logotipo en la factura, de acuerdo con lo informado por la compañía.

articles.title: The next developer interface is ambient intelligence
articles.text:
The next developer interface is ambient intelligence
AI, agents, voice, and physical controls are shifting software development from operating tools to expressing intent—and helping developers stay focused on building.
For most of my career, building software started with the same setup: keyboard, mouse, editor, terminal, browser, and an impressive number of tabs I was definitely going to look at later. The tools changed, but the relationship did not. Like most developers, I learned commands, memorized shortcuts, and adapted my thinking to the machine.
AI is changing that relationship and not because I can prompt my way to some workable code. It’s more because the system behind it can understand a repository, choose the right model, plan work, use tools, edit files, run commands, inspect failures, and keep going within boundaries the developer controls.
We’ve made it possible for a developer to describe an outcome, and GitHub Copilot can gather repository context, inspect symbols and dependencies, edit files, run tests, and revise the implementation. In the IDE, agent mode keeps that loop interactive. GitHub Copilot coding agent can take an issue into an isolated GitHub Actions-powered environment and return a pull request for review. This is not just faster coding. It is the shift from issuing commands to making intent executable. The developer still owns the outcome, but the work looks subtly different.
AI-assisted development compresses that chain of events. We spend less time navigating tools and more time setting direction, supplying context, defining constraints, and reviewing evidence. The development workflow now is about understanding the structure of codebases, the customer, and what a good solution should feel like.
This makes developers’ jobs even more important, and their time more valuable. It makes judgment more valuable. It makes taste more valuable. An agent can generate three implementations before you finish your tea, but someone still has to decide whether the abstraction belongs, the migration is safe, the tests prove anything useful, and the result solves the problem.
That is the most important change in the craft: the developer remains accountable for the outcome, even as more mechanics are delegated.
So what does this mean for the emerging developer workflow? The goal is to embed AI into the workflow, not beside it. It’s more of an ambient intelligence.
That requires portable context. MCP connects agents to tools and services; repository instructions and skills encode conventions; hooks enforce policy and validate output. Simpler interfaces need explicit context underneath.
I see three layers: modality captures intent; the harness plans and acts; the control plane lets developers inspect, redirect, and approve. The best products connect all three without surrendering control.
Together, they let developers move across text, voice, and physical controls without losing context.
Why physical controls are interesting again
I, and many others in the maker community, have been experimenting with ambient control devices, from inexpensive hackable picture frames to ESP32 devices with screens attached. Agentic coding is past just a keyboard and a terminal into alternative interfaces.
Getting this kind of technology into everyone’s hands is something that I’m very passionate about and so over the past 18 months we’ve been working with Logitech on their MX Keypad and how it can help this new way of working.
The Logitech MX Keypad turns familiar developer actions into programmable inputs to accelerate workflows that are ambient and contextual to the work devs are doing. In GitHub Copilot app, a key can submit a parameterized prompt, open or resume a Copilot session, invoke an IDE command, or trigger a multi-step sequence. The hardware earns its place only when that shortcut removes enough friction to keep you in the code, but still gives you control.
Physical controls work when an action repeats often enough that removing a few steps preserves concentration. Not every developer needs another device on the desk, and not every interruption deserves a key. However, with this experience the developer decides which actions earn that shortcut and when the keyboard, command palette, or voice is better. Maintaining flow is the key, and a good interface gives some of that attention back.
GUIs made software visual. Mouse made navigation easier. The web made it connected. Mobile made touch natural. Agents add intent and action. The interface now includes ambient control.
The interface moves into the background
That is why GitHub worked with Logitech to integrate the GitHub Copilot app directly into the experience. Developers can run agentic workflows in control, map a repeated prompt, start or resume a session, and decide through real use whether a physical control helps you stay in flow.
This is still early, so the important questions are engineering questions. How much repository and organizational context should an agent retain? Which tool calls can run automatically? How should credentials, network access, and secrets be scoped? What evidence should accompany a change? How do multiple agents coordinate without duplicating work or creating conflicting pull requests? Products such as MX Keypad let us explore one practical part of that system: how developers invoke, steer, and resume agentic work without losing focus.
For decades, developers learned to speak computer: syntax, commands, APIs, shortcuts, and the occasional incantation copied from a seven-year-old issue comment. Now computers are getting better at meeting us halfway. The best interface will not have the most panels or AI buttons. It will understand enough context, preserve meaningful control, and get out of the way so we can build software that matters.
The goal is not to remove developers from the work. It is to remove friction around the work. Pairing MX Keypad with GitHub Copilot Pro+ gives developers a concrete experiment: choose one repeated interruption, map it to a control, and see whether it preserves focus.
If you want to try it, you can do so here and get three months of GitHub Copilot Pro+.

articles.title: AI agents are coming to Rivian's cars | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Rivian recently rolled out an AI assistant that lets drivers and passengers interact with the company’s electric vehicles just by talking to them. But the carmaker’s founder and CEO, RJ Scaringe, said at TechCrunch Disrupt this week that, in the future, Rivian’s cars will be able to run AI agents made by other companies like Anthropic.
“That’s where it becomes magical,” Scaringe said onstage.
Scaringe didn’t say when Rivian would implement this, and the company declined to offer more details, pointing instead to the “AI & Autonomy Day” event it’s hosting in December.
But it’s not hard to imagine how Rivian might integrate something like Claude, OpenAI’s Dots, or Meta’s Muse assistant into its software. The company has developed its in-car software from the ground up, instead of leaning on Apple CarPlay or Android Auto, and built a lot of its own applications, like navigation (though it has worked to integrate popular in-car apps like Apple Music).
Rivian says it has created its own in-house agentic framework that understands what action a person wants to take when they talk to the vehicle, and routes it to the right part of the car’s software. Most of the time, that involves what you’d expect: asking the car to turn down the temperature, activate the seat warmers, or summarize the news.
“Think of it as like a traffic light. So if you ask the vehicle something, it decides what model it’s going to use. It can use a local model that’s running on the edge and the vehicle. If it’s a more complex question, it can go up to the cloud. And then even for that, we have different models that we use,” Scaringe said.
As of May of this year, the agent could access external apps like Google Calendar. And Scaringe said at Disrupt the next step would be to add products from the frontier AI companies, though making them work in the car won’t be easy.
“There’s a lot of plumbing behind the scenes we have to do to make sure that that works, and it’s not just within Rivian. That’s also a lot of coordination with the labs to make sure they enable that plumbing,” he said, adding that putting this kind of software near safety-critical systems means Rivian has to be extremely careful.
“You wouldn’t want an agent to determine, ‘hey, it’s time to apply the brakes, or time to steer the vehicle.’ So anything that’s vehicle-level controls are not being handed to an agent,” he said.
Instead, he thinks the implementation will look more like an extension of how people currently use these agentic apps. That would mean Rivian would have to find a way to connect the vehicle to all of the context that apps like Muse collect on their users.
For example, Scaringe said, a driver could ask the Rivian assistant to turn on the ventilated seats before going deeper. “And then simultaneously say, ‘We were talking yesterday about this meal. I’m planning to have guests over on Friday. Can you help me think through what we’re going to make?’,” he said. The car could then pull the driver’s context from a conversation they had with the assistant on another device.
Of course, Rivian wouldn’t be the first American car company to add AI agents to a car’s software. Earlier this year, Tesla added a feature that let users talk to both SpaceX’s Grok chatbot and also its Grok Bot assistant.

articles.title: Cohere to acquire Czech AI cybersecurity firm Aisle, set up new cyber division | BetaKit
articles.text:
Cohere is hoping to make its AI platforms more resilient to cybersecurity threats by acquiring a company that detects software vulnerabilities with AI.
The news: Toronto AI company Cohere announced on Thursday that it had signed a letter of intent to acquire Prague-based AI cybersecurity company Aisle, which develops tools to identify software vulnerabilities. Aisle’s Prague headquarters, which hosts an engineering hub, will become Cohere’s Prague office, the company said. Aisle’s approximately 50 full-time employees will all join Cohere, an Aisle spokesperson told BetaKit.
Aisle CEO Ondřej Vlček will join Cohere as senior vice-president of a new cybersecurity unit called Cohere Cyber, while co-founder Jaya Baloo will become Cohere’s global chief information security officer. Aisle co-founder and CTO Stanislav Fort will become Cohere’s vice-president of AI security.
From the source: “There are meaningful gaps in solutions available for [cyber] defenders, and many are having to make the difficult tradeoff between securing their systems and exposing their [intellectual property] and telemetry to a provider that does “zero data-retention” performatively,” Cohere co-founder Ivan Zhang wrote in an X post. With Aisle, Cohere will “continue to empower defenders with a truly sovereign platform that they can fully trust to secure their most critical systems.”
The context: AI cybersecurity threats have taken on new urgency for governments and enterprises since OpenAI revealed that its agents organized to hack the AI platform Hugging Face. Since then, other AI giants, like Anthropic and Google, have also disclosed hacking incidents, and the Canadian government said there had been an attempted agentic hack of Library and Archives Canada.
Aisle was launched just a year ago by Vlček, the former CEO of antivirus company Avast, and Baloo and Fort, the latter of whom worked at Anthropic and DeepMind. It develops AI products that identify and fix security weaknesses in critical software—a capability that Cohere is hoping to bring to its platform for large companies and governments. The company drew attention this week when it claimed that its AI security system found 18 of the 24 vulnerabilities addressed in the latest release of curl, a widely used software tool for API transfer, while models from Anthropic and OpenAI found no issues.
Final thought: This move will see Cohere continue its shopping spree of European AI talent. It’s set to acquire Germany’s Aleph Alpha, subject to regulatory approvals, and also bought Montréal- and Berlin-based Reliant AI as it looks to develop a sovereign AI alternative for organizations wary of reliance on US AI giants. The German deals coincided with Canada and Germany’s digital ministers working closer together on tech policy—whether a similar scenario will play out with Czechia is unclear.

articles.title: Thermal Co-Simulation Testing Of Co-Packaged Optics
articles.text:
Ensuring optical engines can operate reliably alongside high-power AI processors in multi-chip packages.
By Vladimir Stojanovic and Igor Elkanovich
The CPO revolution is at our doorstep. But transforming data center interconnects requires overcoming new challenges in architecture, power delivery, mechanical design, and thermal management. Of these, thermal management has emerged as one of the most critical areas for successfully deploying co-packaged optics (CPO) in hyperscale AI environments.
Thermal instability has been a concern for CPO technology. Ayar Labs and Global Unichip Corp. (GUC) jointly conducted thermal co-simulation of the advanced package design and determined the thermal floor map for the package and subsequent chiplets, including air- and liquid-cooled environments.
Since thermal stability has been raised as a concern for micro-ring-based CPO, we want to address it head-on. Our co-simulation data show that CPO can operate reliably within the thermal envelope of advanced multi-chip packages. We’re sharing these results to give hyperscalers the confidence to move forward with CPO deployments at scale.
Let’s start with the new multi-chip package (MCP) design that integrates Ayar Labs’ TeraPHY optical engines into GUC’s advanced packaging and ASIC workflow. The new XPU MCP design replaces traditional electrical interconnects with Ayar Labs’ optical engines, which are attached directly to the MCP organic substrate. This architecture enables a full-duplex optical interface of more than 100 Tbps from the XPU package, an improvement of more than an order of magnitude over current XPUs.
UCIe-S provides bandwidth between the optical engines and the I/O chiplets over the MCP substrate. UCIe-A, on the other hand, is used for communication between the I/O chiplet and the main AI die over local silicon interconnect (LSI) bridges.
The scale of this design creates thermal challenges we must address. The complete package measures 105mm x 140mm, housing:
The +3 kW power envelope in a single package underscores the importance of thermal management and the need for optical engines to operate reliably alongside high-power AI processors. This complex multi-chip architecture requires sophisticated packaging. The design uses a 9-2-9 layer substrate structure to handle the complex routing requirements.
The design also addresses signal and power integrity challenges associated with the large-scale package. We perform thermal optimization at the XPU MCP level, while a stiffener design incorporates optical engines’ requirements and enables detachable fiber connections that meet mechanical stress and warpage requirements.
Thermal co-simulation is the combined simulation of electrical behavior and heat flow across a chip. It lets designers predict temperatures, hotspots, and reliability issues in integrated circuits (ICs) and packages under realistic operating conditions. The data ensures the entire system operates within required temperature specifications. This is critical for successful deployment.
In GUC’s thermal integrity design flow, we consider every chip’s power maps and perform thermal crosstalk and dynamic thermal co-simulation to ensure the MCP’s thermal integrity from early-stage through sign-off. This allows us to identify local thermal hotspots and the impact of thermal crosstalk on the optical engine.
Thermal co-simulation is crucial for GUC’s advanced ASIC workflows. In our joint analysis, the MCP includes multiple chiplets to analyze thermal crosstalk between adjacent chiplet dies. Any heat generated by the entire interposer complex may affect the optical engine’s performance.
Thermal modeling is needed to optimize optical engine performance. This joint technical exercise deliberately probes thermal hotspots and thermal crosstalk to evaluate overall CPO thermal stability in a realistic customer package form factor. Rather than avoiding the hard questions, we designed the simulation to stress the system and raise any potential concerns.
These findings are invaluable for assessing advanced packaging designs and collaborating with ecosystem partners to design optimal cooling solutions for AI server and switch applications at the most demanding Thermal Design Power levels. This testing allows us to do just that.
We performed three simulations: an analysis to determine thermal resistance targets for each chip component, plus testing of two different cooling solutions. One solution met spec, and one did not.
We tested a standard air fin heatsink at airspeeds of 5 m/s and 6 m/s at 25ºC.
Fig. 1: GUC + Ayar Labs CoWoS-L CPO simulation using heatsink.
This did not meet spec, as the temperature significantly exceeded spec for all components except the I/O die.
We analyzed the maximum junction temperature versus resistance curve to determine suitable resistance for the Chip-on-Wafer-on-Substrate with Local Silicon Interconnect (CoWoS-L) advanced packaging and optical engine to meet the temperature spec.
Fig. 2: GUC + Ayar Labs CoWoS-L CPO Thermal Resistance (Rsa) analysis.
The system-level thermal solution successfully meets the specification when RSA-ASIC is ≤ 0.008 K/W and RSA-OE is ≤ 0.15 K/W. The cold plate design achieves these targets with pressure drops of 11.2 kPa for the ASIC cold plate and 18.8 kPa for the optical engine cold plate. This ensures efficient coolant flow while maintaining thermal performance.
Finally, we tested an impingement-type cold plate thermal solution at 4.5 LPM.
Fig. 3: GUC + Ayar Labs CoWoS-L CPO simulation using cold plate.
This solution did meet spec. All components were below the temperature specifications.
We selected the impingement-type cold plate for this application because it enables higher heat flux removal than conventional parallel-channel designs. The design uses optimized fin dimensions (thickness: 0.15mm, height: 2.4mm for the ASIC and 3.0mm for the optical engine) with thermal interface materials (K=5.2 W/mK) to achieve the required thermal performance.
This approach effectively dissipates the concentrated heat from multiple high-power chiplets while maintaining the optical engines within their operational temperature limits.
Key Results
These results point to a significant breakthrough in CPO deployment. Successfully maintaining optical engines under 100ºC while dissipating over 3kW TDP from a single package (with 1,500W coming from the AI processors alone) shows that CPO operates reliably with ample junction-temperature headroom, paving the way for the most demanding thermal environments.
Our next step will focus on dynamic workload simulation to further analyze thermal impact on CPO under real-world operating conditions. The tests we’ve shared here were based on static power assumptions, where each component’s power consumption remains constant. Systems ramp up from idle, spike during training or booting, and fluctuate based on user demand during normal operations.
Large numbers of users can cause heat spikes. A dynamic workload simulation will allow us to test our design under conditions more accurate to the real world. This will help us understand how the optics respond to sudden temperature changes and ensure the systems operate efficiently.
These thermal co-simulation test results demonstrate that CPO can operate reliably in high-power AI systems when paired with appropriate cooling solutions. As the industry continues to push the boundaries of compute performance and thermal design power, CPO will play a significant role in overcoming bandwidth and power limitations.
Igor Elkanovich is the CTO of GUC.

articles.title: Bluesky’s AI tool now lets you make games and apps to share on social
articles.text:
Bluesky’s Attie AI tool, which initially launched earlier this year as a way to use AI to build your own feeds, now lets you make “small” social apps like games, polls, and dashboards that you can then share with others as their own websites. In an interview at TechCrunch Disrupt, Bluesky CEO Toni Schneider said to think of Attie as “social vibe coding or vibe coding for your community.”
Bluesky’s AI tool now lets you make games and apps to share on social
Attie launched earlier this year as a way to build your own feeds with AI, but Bluesky is expanding what it can do.
You can make your own Attie app by typing in a prompt. A simple poll I made about Pokémon Red and Pokémon Blue took a few minutes to generate. If you want to check out something more full-featured, the Attie website currently highlights a few examples like a “Flappy Butterfly” Flappy Bird clone, a drum machine, a quiz, and an idle clicker about a celery man, and each has a custom link on the attie.site domain and attribution for who made the social app at the bottom of the page. The apps I’ve messed around with are pretty lightweight novelties, though I liked the drum machine.

articles.text:
One UI 9: Samsung-Smartphone startet nicht? So löst du den Fehler
Seit einigen Tagen rollt Samsung One UI 9 für erste Galaxy-Smartphones aus. Leider läuft das Update bei einigen User:innen aber alles andere als reibungslos. Nachdem sie One UI 9 auf ihr Smartphone aufgespielt haben und einen Neustart durchführen, werden sie mit einem Setup-Bildschirm und einer Fehlermeldung statt des Homescreens begrüßt.
One UI 9: So behebst du Probleme mit dem Galaxy-Update
Wie betroffene User:innen auf X und Reddit zeigen, steht in der Fehlermeldung, dass eine XML-Datei keinerlei Informationen beinhaltet. Darunter stehen zusätzlich die Code-Zeilen: „Error. Access Denied“. Von dem Problem mit One UI 9 sind verschiedene Samsung-Geräte betroffen, darunter die S24-, S25- und S26-Reihe. Auch einige Foldable-Nutzer:innen berichten von dem Start-Bug bei ihrem Galaxy-Smartphone.
Laut Samsung-Insider Fahad Ali Javed könnte der Fehler durch eine Änderung an Samsungs Servern verursacht worden sein. Angeblich will das Unternehmen damit verhindern, dass vor einer Veröffentlichung neuer Software wie One UI 9 Leaks im Netz landen. Samsung hat diese Vermutung allerdings nicht bestätigt. Wann ein Fix für das Problem mit One UI 9 bereitsteht, ist ebenfalls nicht bekannt.
Glücklicherweise gibt es einen Weg, um die Fehlermeldung von One UI 9 herumzukommen. Wenn du davon betroffen bist, kannst du den Knopf zum Reduzieren der Lautstärke und den Power-Knopf gleichzeitig drücken, um das Gerät neu zu starten. Sobald das Samsung-Logo erscheint, halte erneut die „Lautstärke leiser“-Taste gedrückt. Dadurch startet das Galaxy-Smartphone im abgesicherten Modus.
Im abgesicherten Modus musst du dann deine WLAN-Verbindung und die mobilen Daten abschalten. Wische vom oberen Bildschirmrand nach unten, um die Schnelleinstellungen zu öffnen und die beiden Punkte zu deaktivieren. Starte dann das Gerät noch einmal regulär neu. Nach diesem Neustart sollte der Fehler nicht mehr angezeigt werden und dein Galaxy-Smartphone normal starten. Ist das der Fall, kannst du die Verbindungen wieder aktivieren.
Wie kommt man als User dazu sich mit derartigen Problemen herumquälen zu müssen ,weil Banken Apps die man nur auf einem Smartphone installieren kann für 2 Faktor Verifikation aufzwingen ? Unter solchen Bedingungen ?,weil die „so viel sicherer ist“ als die Verifikation mit 2 Faktor-SMS ? Wieso muß man das ?

articles.title: A fully programmable secure web gateway
Ihr wollt das iPhone Duo kaufen? Das ist vor der Bestellung wichtig
articles.text:
Foldables stecken nach wie vor in der Nische. Nur etwa 1,6 Prozent der verkauften Smartphones weltweit sind faltbar. Mit dem Verkaufsstart des iPhone Duo könnte sich das ändern. Schließlich hat das Gerät zur Vorstellung immense mediale Aufmerksamkeit erfahren – auch dank einer cleveren Animation beim Öffnen und Schließen. Wie bei vielen neuen iPhones werden vor allem Early Adopter früh dabei sein wollen, um zu zeigen, dass sie die begehrte Neuheit schon am ersten Tag in der Tasche haben. Entsprechend eng dürfte es bei der Vorbestellung zugehen.
Wann kann ich das iPhone Duo vorbestellen?
Der Vorbestellungszeitraum startet am 16. Oktober um 14 Uhr. Eine Woche später, am 23. Oktober, werden die Bestellungen ausgeliefert. Apple rechnet dabei offenbar mit großem Andrang – oder will das zumindest suggerieren. Denn schon jetzt kann man seine Wunschkonfiguration im Apple-Store hinterlegen, indem man sich durch die Produktseite klickt, also Farbe, Speicher und Apple-Care-Option auswählt. Zum Stichtag könnt ihr dann im Onlineshop direkt zur Kasse gehen und den Kauf abschließen.
Dass es für Interessierte, die unbedingt zu den Ersten gehören wollen, sinnvoll sein kann, zeigt die Vergangenheit: So war etwa das iPhone X im Oktober 2017 schnell ausverkauft. Andersherum fand das dünne iPhone Air allerdings keinen reißenden Absatz. Wer es ohnehin auf das Duo abgesehen hat, verliert durch das frühe Ausfüllen der Bestellung aber auch nichts.
Brauche ich Apple Care für das iPhone Duo?
Eine Streitfrage bei jedem iPhone-Neukauf: Lohnt sich die Investition in Apple Care Plus? Schließlich kostet die Zusatzversicherung fürs iPhone 20,99 Euro im Monat oder 209,99 Euro im Jahr. Trotz des ohnehin schon hohen Startpreises von 2.299 Euro ist es aber eine Überlegung wert, Apple Care Plus abzuschließen. Denn Foldables gelten nach wie vor als empfindlich und weniger robust als „normale“ Smartphones.
Deswegen solltet ihr zunächst einen Blick auf die Reparaturkosten werfen, die anstehen, wenn das iPhone Duo Schaden nimmt. Der Austausch der Displayschutzfolie des faltbaren Bildschirms ist mit 49 Euro noch einigermaßen erschwinglich. Nimmt das Display aber ernsthaft Schaden, wird es teuer. 1.149 Euro kostet euch die Reparatur ohne Apple Care Plus. Mit dem Zusatzservice sind die Reparaturen zwar nicht gratis, aber wie 9to5Mac berichtet, sinken die Kosten für die Reparatur des inneren Displays auf 99 US-Dollar. Deutsche Preise lassen sich bislang nicht nachvollziehen.
Was ändert sich an der Software?
Auf dem iPhone Duo läuft iOS 27, aber mit ein paar kleineren Änderungen. So befindet sich das Dock nicht mehr unten am Bildschirmrand, sondern rechts an der Seite. Das soll die einhändige Bedienung erleichtern. Außerdem unterstützt das Gerät Multitasking. Wie auf dem iPad ist es möglich, sich auf dem großen Bildschirm zwei Apps im Splitscreen anzeigen zu lassen. Erweiterte Funktionen wie Stage Manager oder den Fenstermodus gibt es allerdings nicht.
Auf der Keynote im September 2027 zeigte das Unternehmen außerdem bereits angepasste Apps wie Netflix oder Slack, die das äußere und das innere Display clever nutzen. Ob das zum Start bei jeder bekannten App so funktionieren wird, bleibt abzuwarten. Entwickler müssen ihre Anwendungen erst an die neuen Formate und dynamischen Größen anpassen. Der Wechsel von der vorherigen auf die neue Liquid-Glass-Designsprache hat gezeigt, dass nicht Anbieter von Tag 1 dabei ist.
Verzichten müsst ihr, wie bei anderen iPhones auch, zunächst auf Siri AI. Apple bringt die KI‑Assistenz vorerst nicht in die EU. Das Duo ist hier kein Sonderfall.
Brauche ich eine Schutzhülle für das iPhone Duo?
Wie gesagt: Foldables sind empfindliche Geräte, auf die es gut achtzugeben gilt. Eine Schutzhülle kann da von Vorteil sein. Es muss ja nicht gleich die 150-Euro-Hülle mit eingebautem Kickstand von Apple sein. Auf den etablierten Plattformen bieten bereits mehrere Hersteller Modelle für um die 30 Euro an.
Wie ihr das Foldable darüber hinaus bestmöglich schützt, könnt ihr zudem in diesem Ratgeber nachlesen.
Was muss ich sonst noch über das iPhone Duo wissen?
Anders als bei anderen Smartphone ist das innere Display beim iPhone nicht glänzend, sondern matt. Das reduziert nicht nur Spiegeleffekte, es soll auch dafür sorgen, dass die Bildschirmfalte nicht so gut sichtbar ist.
Außerdem hat das Gerät keinen Schacht für Sim-Karten. Ihr braucht für die Nutzung im Mobilfunknetz also eine E-Sim. Die sollte euch euer Provider in der Regel kostenlos zur Verfügung stellen.

articles.title: Dacia prépare une 7 places électrique à 30 000 € : la concurrence peut trembler
articles.text:
La gamme des familiales Dacia est aujourd’hui longue comme le bras. Entre le Jogger, le Duster, le Bigster et le Striker, le client lambda a de quoi perdre son latin. Et entre ces quatre modèles, il y a aussi un risque de cannibalisation. Le Jogger, qui est le plus âgé du quatuor, semble maintenant laissé pour compte, même s’il est toujours le seul à proposer 7 places. Bonne nouvelle, la relève approche à grands pas, avec un remplaçant prévu en 2028.
Mieux encore, la seconde génération du Jogger adoptera pour la première fois une motorisation électrique en plus des déclinaisons hybrides déjà existantes. Dans une interview accordée à Auto Express, David Durand, responsable du design chez Dacia, confirme le rôle central du Jogger : « il n’y a pas de marques européennes ou chinoises face à nous ; il n’existe pas de véritable sept places sur le marché à ce prix et avec ce poids ».
Adieu le break rallongé ? Ce détail de design qui changera tout à l’intérieur
Le prochain modèle va donc réitérer la recette de la génération actuelle, avec de légères différences. Durand admet en effet un petit changement de morphologie pour le futur Jogger : « si je devais repartir de zéro, j’avancerais sans hésiter le pare-brise, car cela contribue à accentuer l’impression d’espace à bord ». Le nouveau cru pourrait donc délaisser son habit de break rallongé pour celui de monospace, même si cela demeure une simple hypothèse.
Ce qui est certain, c’est que les fondamentaux subsisteront pour faire des économies d’échelle : « il faut aussi considérer l’avantage de partager la face avant avec la Sandero. Nous réalisons d’importantes économies ; la production peut se faire sur la même chaîne, et le partage de nombreux éléments avec la Sandero représente un gain de coûts considérable ». Le prochain Jogger reprendra donc le visage de la future Sandero, prévue elle aussi en 2028.
Moteurs, autonomie et prix : à quoi faut-il s’attendre sous la barre des 30 000 € ?
L’avant sera donc quasi identique jusqu’au montant B. Ensuite, la familiale proposera certainement une ligne de toit plus rectiligne favorisant l’habitabilité. L’intérieur sera plus moderne en allant toujours à l’essentiel. Les 7 places resteront disponibles en option. Côté technique, le bloc hybride de 155 ch sera fidèle au Jogger aux côtés d’une déclinaison au GPL. La nouveauté viendra de la motorisation électrique permise par la plateforme CMF-B.
À l’heure actuelle, cette dernière embarque au mieux une batterie de 52 kWh permettant environ 400 km d’autonomie. Possible que le Jogger ait droit à une déclinaison rallongée de cette plateforme pour inclure des accumulateurs plus importants. Les prix devraient rester en tout cas maîtrisés, avec une entrée de gamme estimée autour des 23 000 € pour les modèles thermiques et 30 000 € pour les modèles électriques.

articles.title: Staying Evergreen: How we automated secure access and repo hygiene in a shared org
articles.text:
Working with outside collaborators can add more work for a repository owner. You need to confirm who still needs access, change permissions as projects evolve, and archive repositories once they’ve served their purpose.
To keep up, repository owners need to track collaborators, deadlines, and follow-ups for each repository. As a project grows, that manual housekeeping becomes harder to keep up with and easier to defer.
We faced this problem in a shared organization where GitHub employees (“Hubbers”) collaborate with customers and partners on product trials and professional services engagements. Our answer was Evergreen, a GitHub App built with native GitHub features. The workflows below exhibit a pattern you can adapt for your own organization.
Meet Evergreen
Evergreen is a GitHub App that automates organization hygiene through two workflows:
Outside collaborator access reviews. Every quarter, each repo’s outside collaborators are reviewed. Keep who you need, and everyone else is removed.
Stale repository detection and archival. Repos with no human activity past a threshold get flagged, warned, and (if still untouched) archived.
Two design principles shaped everything:
Fail secure. If nobody responds to an access review, we don’t leave access in place and hope for the best. We revoke it. The safe outcome is the default outcome.
Never destroy anything. Evergreen will never delete a repository or its contents. Archived repos are recoverable, and every access change is written into the repo’s tracking issue, so reverting a mistake is as easy as a copy-paste to Copilot.
How it works: One brain, many hands
Under the hood, Evergreen is a small Go webhook server running in a container. But the interesting part is the choreography. Every moving piece is a stock GitHub feature: a GitHub App, scheduled actions, webhooks, issues, custom properties, and plain files in a repo. Nothing exotic to reinvent.
A controller that keeps time
A dedicated controller repo acts as Evergreen’s clock and its memory. Four scheduled GitHub Actions workflows fire repository_dispatch events on a quarterly cadence, and the app wakes up and does the work:
Day
Workflow
What happens
1st
Stale repo review
Flag repos with no recent human activity, open a warning issue
8th
Access review
Snapshot outside collaborators, open a checklist issue per repo
16th
Stale repo cleanup
Archive repos still stale after the grace period
23rd
Access cleanup
Auto‑revoke access for any review left unanswered
Reviews open two weeks before their cleanup runs, and there’s a hard grace period baked in so a stray manual run can never fast‑forward the guillotine. Each workflow also supports workflow_dispatch, so we can trigger any step by hand as needed.
State you can git blame
Evergreen tracks every repo’s status as a JSON file (one per repository) committed to the controller repo under state/repos/<repo_id>.json. The snapshot of who had access, when the review opened, the deadline, who decided, and what happened all lives there. Here’s a completed review where a Hubber kept Alice’s access and let Bob’s lapse:
The best part: because state is just files in git, the commit history is the audit trail. Want to know why someone lost access last spring? git log the state file. There’s no separate database or bespoke audit pipeline to track.
Issue‑ops, everywhere it matters
Evergreen does its talking through issues inside each repository. When an access review kicks off, every repo gets a checklist issue:
The interaction model is delightfully simple: check the boxes for who stays, then close the issue. That’s it. When the issue closes, Evergreen listens for the issues.closed webhook event, reads the checkboxes, retains the checked collaborators, and revokes the rest, then posts a receipt comment listing exactly what it kept and what it removed.
Only the right humans can pull the lever
Closing an access review issue is a privileged action, so Evergreen guards it. If someone who isn’t a Hubber closes an issue, the app quietly reopens it and posts a note explaining why. Decisions only count when they come from the people authorized to make them.
Informing the right people
Here’s a subtle problem: we know the people who need to respond to a review are Hubbers, but we didn’t always know which Hubber(s) owned a given repository.
Evergreen resolves the right people to notify through a fallback chain:
If a repo sets an evergreen_repo_owner custom property (a @user or @org/team), use it.
Otherwise, look at recent issue and commit authors and cc the ones who are on the access review team, i.e., the Hubbers actually working in that repo.
The result: the right owners get pinged automatically, without anyone maintaining a spreadsheet of “who owns what.”
Fail secure, and fail closed
When a review deadline passes with no response, cleanup revokes every collaborator in the snapshot. We were careful about a subtle edge case: what if some removals succeed while others hit a transient API error? Marking the review “done” while a removal is still outstanding would be a quiet inconsistency, and we didn’t want that.
So Evergreen fails closed. If any removal fails, the review stays pending and the issue stays open, and the next run retries the stragglers. It only records “revoked” once every removal actually succeeded. And whatever gets removed is written into the issue, so restoring access is a matter of re‑adding the handles it listed.
The user experience: automation that feels considerate
Automated housekeeping has a reputation for being the office smoke alarm: loud, easy to ignore, and usually going off while you’re cooking something perfectly fine. We worked hard to make Evergreen feel like the opposite:
It comes to you. The work happens as an issue in your repo.
It tags the right people. No “who owns this?” archaeology.
It’s crystal clear about the ask. Every issue states what to do, the exact deadline, and precisely what happens if you ignore it.
It nudges before it acts. A reminder comment lands before the deadline: no surprise revocations.
It has an escape hatch. Org owners (Hubbers) can opt out by setting a custom property (evergreen_exempt_from_access_review or evergreen_exempt_from_archive).
Rolling it out carefully
Automation that manages access and archives repositories deserves a careful rollout, especially into a large, active org (ours has 1,400+ Hubbers, and many more customers and partners). We wanted the very first run to be a complete non‑event. A few practices got us there:
Dry‑run first. Evergreen ships with a DRY_RUN mode that logs every write it would make without touching a single collaborator or repo. We ran it against the real org and read the logs like tea leaves until we trusted the decisions it wanted to make.
Overcommunicate. Before flipping the switch, we broadcast what was coming, when, and what people needed to do, so the first issue anyone saw wasn’t a surprise. We found that when you’re telling a large group the same thing for the seventh time, it’s often when many are still hearing it for the first time.
Watch everything with Splunk. Evergreen emits structured logfmt logs to a dedicated Splunk index. That observability is how we caught edge cases in the wild (empty collaborator lists, unusual permissions, repos with issues disabled) and tightened the logic before they mattered.
Respect the platform’s speed limits. When you open issues and post comments across every repo in a big org, you slam into GitHub’s secondary rate limits for content creation: 80 requests/minute and 500/hour. While this is a thoughtful preventative control to avoid system abuse, it requires a bit of intention when automating IssueOps at large scale.
So Evergreen paces itself by construction. It processes repos in batches, spaces out each content‑creating call by a couple of seconds, and sleeps between batches to let the rolling window clear, and it only counts the repos that actually create content, so a quiet quarter where nothing’s eligible still runs fast. We opted for proactive avoidance over reactive back‑off.
Lessons we’re taking with us
Make the safe path the default path. Fail secure, then make responding easy enough that failing secure rarely triggers.
Use the primitives you already have. Issues, webhooks, custom properties, and git history did the work of a bespoke UI, a job queue, and an audit database.
Meet people where they work. An issue in your repo beats a dashboard you’ll never open.
Logs are a revert button. Writing every change into the issue turned “oops” into “paste these three handles into a Copilot session.”
Respect the limits. At org scale, rate limits aren’t an edge case: they’re the design constraint.
Keep your org evergreen
Routine hygiene is the kind of work that’s easy to defer and perfect to automate. The trick isn’t heroic cleanup sprints: it’s making the boring, safe thing happen on a schedule, with a friendly face and an undo button.
That’s Evergreen. And because it’s built entirely from native GitHub features, you can stand up the same pattern yourself.
Ready to make repository hygiene routine? Start with one recurring access or archival task, then use GitHub Apps, actions, issues, and custom properties to automate the problem away.
Senior Service Delivery Engineer at GitHub, passionate about the intersection of software engineering & security, and helping businesses focus on innovation, growth, and speed to market.
Our new repo star history API now provides trends without returning individual identities or requiring unbounded database work. These are the engineering tradeoffs we made.

articles.title: Ramp reaches $60B valuation as it pushes deeper into AI | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Expense management company Ramp said on Thursday that it had raised $1.85 billion in a new funding round that values it at $60 billion, just four months after raising $750 million at a $44 billion valuation.
The financing was co-led by Dragoneer Investment Group, Thrive Capital, Founders Fund, Sands Capital, and Avenir Growth.
Ramp said its annualized revenue has crossed $2 billion, up from a reported $1.5 billion in June, and that its revenue growth is 25% faster than it was around this time last year. The company claims it now facilitates annualized purchase volume of over $275 billion, up 175% from a year earlier. It also says it has 85,000 customers, up from 70,000 in June, including Visa, Uber, Shopify, Robinhood, Anduril, Notion, Cursor, and Figma.
The funding comes as Ramp has been expanding beyond expense management into payments, fraud detection, procurement, vendor management, and, of late, even accounting.
The startup has also built an AI story around itself, embedding AI agents into its procurement, expense management, accounting, budgeting, and other products. It also launched a corporate credit card specifically designed for AI agents to use, and in August entered the model routing business to tap the booming AI inference market and give existing clients a model routing service that fits neatly with its current products, including AI token usage monitoring and token spend management.
Earlier this month, Ramp launched Glass, a workspace that collects and remembers the AI automations, prompts, and skills that an organization’s employees build so others can take advantage of the company’s collective knowledge and skills.
“In just a few years, Ramp has become a much broader financial operations platform, with AI deeply embedded in how the company builds and operates. We believe Ramp is well on its way to becoming one of the defining companies of this era,” Christian Jensen, partner at Dragoneer, said in a statement.
Other investors in the round include Capital International, Fidelity Management & Research Company, T. Rowe Price, D1 Capital Partners, Greenoaks, ICONIQ, GIC, 8VC, 1789 Capital, Alpha Wave Global, Ontario Teachers’ Pension Plan, Coatue, D.E. Shaw, Definition Capital, FirstMark, General Catalyst, Generation Investment Management, Glade Brook Capital Partners, Khosla Ventures, Lightspeed Venture Partners, Pinegrove Opportunity Partners, Soma Capital, and Stripes.
The company has now raised about $5 billion in funding.
As Ramp has widened its product lineup, it has increasingly run into Rippling, the HR and payroll software company that has pushed into corporate cards, expense management, and bill payments. The overlap puts the two companies in direct competition for the same finance-team budgets.
Early investor Keith Rabois, who has backed Ramp through two firms, Founders Fund and Khosla Ventures, both of which participated in this round, spoke to TechCrunch last month about Ramp’s strategy and his own big ambitions for the company.
“Ramp is not worried about Rippling,” Rabois said. “We’re going to compete with Anthropic,” he continued. “That’s the goal. I want to be larger and more successful and more important than Anthropic. Ramp is going to be the primary way people manage their token spend, how they optimize it, how they measure ROI, and that will lead us to collide probably with Anthropic in many ways.”
— With additional reporting from Connie Loizos

articles.title: Withings now charges $100 per year to sync your data to other apps
articles.text:
If you’re a new user of Withings’ fitness-tracking smartwatches or smart scales and want to sync and access your health data through third party apps like Apple Health or Google Health it’s now going to cost you.
Withings now charges $100 per year to sync your data to other apps
The feature will continue to be free for users who created a Withings account on or before October 12th, 2026.
According to a discussion on Withings’ support forums spotted by MacRumors, new Withings accounts created from October 13th, 2026, and onwards will require a Withings Plus subscription to use the “automatic sync to third-party apps” feature. The subscription costs $9.95 per month or $99.50 per year but Withings’ devices come with a free one month trial that includes the option to sync their data to third-party apps. When the trial is over the syncing is paused but the data in those apps isn’t deleted.
Existing users who already have a Withings account created on or before October 12th, 2026, will continue to have access to automatic third-party app syncing for free, according to official comments shared by a member of Withings’ support team. And because the feature is tied to an existing users’ account and not a specific device, the third-party syncing will continue to be available without a subscription if they buy and register new watches, scales, or other Withings hardware.

articles.title: 436 km sans recharger : Zero prouve qu'une moto électrique peut aller loin, tant qu'on roule doucement
articles.text:
Qui a dit que les motos électriques n’avait pas d’autonomie ? Zero Motorycles vient de prouver le contraire avec un nouveau record officialisé ce mardi 13 octobre 2026 : 436,5 kilomètres sans s’arrêter pour recharger. C’est le journaliste moto belge Jelle Verstaen qui l’a établi fin septembre, en ralliant les Alpes à la Méditerranée.
Le précédent record datait de l’an dernier, quand Sam Clarke et Sara Sloman avaient bouclé 310,689 kilomètres autour de Londres sur une Verge Motorcycles. Zero l’efface de 125,8 kilomètres, soit plus de 40 %. La marque n’en est pas à sa première chasse au record : en 2019, sa SR/F avait échoué à décrocher le meilleur temps à Pikes Peak.
La Zero DS comme modèle de record
Pour homologuer le record, il fallait impérativement une moto actuellement commercialisée et non modifiée. La Zero DS utilisée était donc d’origine, pneus compris, avec une seule option et pas des moindres, le Power Tank. Une batterie d’appoint de 3,6 kWh venant s’ajouter aux 15,6 kWh de l’accumulateur de série qui permet d’augmenter l’autonomie de 40 à 50 km selon les scénario de conduite. Un accessoire non negligeable si l’on prévoit de partir loin, vendu 4 045 € dans le réseau distributeur.
Avant le départ, l’équipe de motards a scellé la prise de recharge avec du ruban adhésif, pour que toute recharge de triche sur la route se remarque. Jelle Verstaen transportait deux traceurs GPS certifiés. À l’arrivée, un arbitre Guinness a passé plus d’une heure à vérifier les données et le carnet de bord.
Le trio est parti vers 19 heures de la station des Claux, à Vars, dans les Hautes-Alpes. Les conditions ont été assez spéciales puisque les trois pilotes ont roulé de nuit, sur des routes départementales, sans autoroute, avec une consigne : tenir environ 52 km/h. La nuit limitait le trafic, donc les freinages et les relances qui vident la batterie. Les 100 derniers kilomètres se sont faits sous une pluie battante, en Camargue.
En plus de celle de Jelle Verstaen, les deux autres motos de l’équipe ont aussi dépassé l’ancien record. Louis Renaud, un client de la marque, s’est arrêté à 350 kilomètres avec sa SR/S, et il lui restait encore 4 % de batterie. Jenny Brookes, responsable de la marque chez Zero, a poussé sa DSR/X jusqu’à 384 kilomètres.
Et à vitesse d’autoroute ?
Si le record est flatteur, il comporte deux gros points qui méritent l’attention. Déjà, le parcours partait des Alpes pour finir au niveau de la mer. Le parcours a donc aidé, grâce au freinage régénératif permettant de récupérer de l’énergie dans les descentes de cols. Mais surtout, la vitesse change tout. En restant à 52 km/h, les motards étaient loin des limites de vitesse et donc de l’allure que peut avoir un client lambda.
Audi avait suivi la même recette en septembre pour son record de 1 338 kilomètres en A6 Sportback e-tron, lui aussi obtenu à vitesse réduite. Le record de Zero prouve surtout que la DS consomme très peu quand on roule doucement. Il ne promet pas 436 kilomètres sur la route des vacances.
Sur un long trajet à allure moyenne (89 km/h), le chiffre à retenir reste donc celui de la fiche officielle : 185 kilomètres sans Power Tank. Pour les arrêts, Zero a annoncé début septembre l’arrivée de la charge rapide en courant continu, en moins de 30 minutes et rétrocompatible jusqu’aux modèles 2022.

articles.title: Recharge en 21 min et 390 km d’autonomie : Leapmotor déballe la B03 pour faire trembler la Renault 5
articles.text:
Leapmotor connaît en France une croissance fulgurante en devenant au mois de septembre le deuxième constructeur chinois. Cette excellente dynamique devrait se poursuivre avec l’arrivée récente de la compacte B05 et du SUV B03X. Et puisque l’on dit jamais deux sans trois, Leapmotor célèbre la présentation d’un troisième modèle au Mondial. Voici la B03, une citadine électrique venant chasser sur les terres des Renault 5 et Peugeot e-208.
Bien que colorée à l’envi avec sa teinte orange citrouille, la petite dernière ne pourra pas compter sur son style, peu mémorable. Son truc à elle, c’est la simplicité d’usage au quotidien. Cela commence ainsi par une fiche technique tout à fait à jour. La batterie de 53 kWh permet en ce sens de parcourir jusqu’à 390 km sur le cycle WLTP. Bien, même si légèrement en deçà de ce que sont capables les françaises.
Recharge en 21 minutes et 197 ch : la fessée technique adressée aux R5 et e-208 ?
Là où la chinoise sort la tête de l’eau, c’est sur la borne, où son chargeur embarqué peut encaisser jusqu’à 133 kW en courant continu DC, contre 100 kW pour les R5 et e-208. Cela se traduit concrètement par un 10 à 80 % de batterie en 21 minutes, ce qui est excellent pour la catégorie. Ce qui est également fort sur le segment est la puissance de la machine électrique. Celle-ci développe en effet 197 ch et 200 Nm de couple aux roues avant.
Avec ses 4,18 mètres de long, 1,79 mètre de large et 1,55 mètre de haut, la B03 est aussi légèrement plus portante que les françaises. De cela résulte une habitabilité optimisée et un volume d’emport de 405 litres. Leapmotor insiste d’autre part sur une présentation soignée avec des « matériaux doux et chaleureux, offrant un aspect et un toucher haut de gamme ». Heureusement, on a envie de dire, car le dessin est banal au possible.
Écran de 14,6 pouces, pompe à chaleur et conduite semi-autonome : la dotation royale
Une planche de bord épurée dominée par un écran central de 14,6 pouces, c’est du déjà-vu. Cela s’accompagne d’une instrumentation numérique de 8,8 pouces permettant une lecture simplifiée des informations essentielles. L’équipement est un point fort, avec des sièges et un volant chauffant, une climatisation automatique, un éclairage d’ambiance multicolore, une pompe à chaleur et la conduite semi-autonome.
La clé sur smartphone est également disponible. Celle-ci permet entre autres de préconditionner l’habitacle, de verrouiller le véhicule, de programmer sa recharge et de le localiser. Les prix de la Leapmotor B03 n’ont pas été communiqués, mais ils devraient être particulièrement agressifs en glissant potentiellement sous les 20 000 €.
