articles.title: iPhone 18 : Apple miserait gros sur son futur modèle
articles.text:
Absent au lancement des nouveaux iPhone cette année, l’iPhone 18 pourrait bien faire une entrée remarquée en 2027. Apple préparerait déjà un stock conséquent pour son prochain smartphone grand public, dont la production doit débuter à la fin du mois de novembre.
L’iPhone 17 aurait-il donné des idées à Apple ? Alors que le marché mondial des smartphones traverse une période difficile, entre pénurie de mémoire et chute des livraisons, la marque à la pomme a réussi à porter sa part de marché à un niveau record pour un troisième trimestre. Et le succès de son dernier modèle pourrait bien pousser Apple à voir grand pour la suite : les premières informations sur la production de l’iPhone 18 laissent entrevoir des stocks particulièrement élevés.
L’iPhone 17 donne des raisons d’être optimiste à Apple
Le succès de l’iPhone 17 pourrait bien peser dans les plans d’Apple. D’après Counterpoint Research, le modèle standard a été le smartphone le plus vendu au monde au premier comme au deuxième trimestre 2026. Il a représenté à lui seul 6 % des ventes mondiales en volume sur chacune de ces périodes, devançant même les iPhone 17 Pro et Pro Max.
Les premiers résultats du téléphone avaient déjà conduit la firme américaine à revoir ses ambitions à la hausse. Selon les informations rapportées par le site MacRumors (via The Information), le constructeur aurait demandé à deux de ses fournisseurs d’augmenter leur production quotidienne d’au moins 30 % après le premier week-end de précommandes de l’iPhone 17.
Apple préparerait désormais le terrain pour son successeur. Le leaker Fixed Focus Digital affirme sur Weibo que la production de l’iPhone 18 standard devrait débuter à la fin du mois de novembre. Les commandes passées dans la chaîne d’approvisionnement laisseraient entrevoir des volumes particulièrement élevés.
Un lancement attendu au printemps 2027
L’iPhone 18 standard devrait être présenté au printemps 2027, aux côtés de l’iPhone 18e et de l’iPhone Air 2. Le géant de Cupertino aurait choisi de décaler son lancement par rapport aux modèles Pro, notamment pour répartir les capacités de production et les composants disponibles, la pénurie de mémoire compliquant quelque peu l’approvisionnement.
Cette organisation laisserait plusieurs mois au fabricant pour constituer ses stocks avant l’arrivée du téléphone en magasin. Le futur modèle devrait conserver un design globalement proche de celui de l’iPhone 17, tout en bénéficiant de plusieurs évolutions possibles, dont une Dynamic Island plus petite, une puce A20 et un modem C2 conçu par Apple.
Reste que les volumes de commandes passées auprès des fournisseurs ne permettent pas de mesurer précisément les quantités qui seront produites. Apple travaille avec plusieurs partenaires pour ses composants, et les informations dont dispose le leaker pourraient ne concerner qu’une partie de la chaîne d’approvisionnement. Nos confrères de 9to5Mac invitent donc, à juste titre, à ne pas tirer de conclusions hâtives de ces premières indications, même si Fixed Focus Digital a souvent vu juste par le passé.

articles.title: Su escuela bloqueó ChatGPT. Ahora esta estudiante de secundaria de 17 años dirige una startup de inteligencia artificial con 1.000 usuarios
articles.text:
Navya Tuteja contacta con sus políticos locales mediante un correo en frío y una idea, y así llegó también a un periodista. Tiene 17 años, cursa el último año de secundaria en un instituto selectivo de las afueras de Washington D. C. y, si su centro nombrara a un mejor alumno, asegura que probablemente optaría por hablar en la graduación.
Lo que proponía en ese correo se llama Raaha: una plataforma gratuita con la que las personas neurodivergentes puntúan una oferta de trabajo antes de postularse. Tuteja asegura que ya reúne más de 1.000 usuarios y 20.000 ofertas. Nació de una pauta que llevaba tiempo viendo: anuncios escritos solo desde el lado del empleador, cargados de requisitos y mudos sobre cómo es el día a día. La financia ella misma y la mantiene gratis mientras suma usuarios; el modelo futuro pasaría por que empresas y organizaciones de empleo paguen por usarla o por mejorar sus ofertas.
El funcionamiento es sencillo: el usuario responde un cuestionario de 12 preguntas sobre cómo trabaja mejor, pega la descripción de un puesto y recibe una puntuación de encaje. El análisis valora factores como el ritmo de trabajo, la comunicación o la previsibilidad del horario, y lo hace Claude, el modelo de Anthropic, con unas instrucciones preparadas con ayuda de especialistas en neurodiversidad.
Quien quiera probarla debe saber que la web de Raaha (raaha.ai) está en inglés, que se nutre de ofertas públicas como las de Adzuna y USAJobs (el portal de empleo del Gobierno federal de Estados Unidos) y que en agosto su aplicación para iOS seguía pendiente de aprobación. Las cifras también han cambiado deprisa: en julio Tuteja hablaba de 150 usuarios, en agosto superaba los 200 y ahora declara más de 1.000. Quiere ir a la universidad, pero se plantea dedicarse a Raaha a tiempo completo si sigue creciendo al ritmo actual.
Un WiFi que no deja entrar a ChatGPT
Su expediente contrasta con el de sus coetáneos. PISA 2025, el Programa para la Evaluación Internacional de Alumnos de la OCDE (Organización para la Cooperación y el Desarrollo Económicos), ha registrado desde 2015 una caída media de 28 puntos en lectura y de 22 en matemáticas en los países de la OCDE, y entre lo que provocan estos datos (siempre según este informe) están las pantallas, la menor atención y la IA generativa. En España, los alumnos de 15 años lograron 451 puntos en lectura y 457 en matemáticas.
Tuteja no discute esa explicación, pero cree que a ella la protegió una medida que no fue idea suya: el WiFi de su instituto bloquea ChatGPT, Claude y herramientas parecidas. “Me hizo usarla mucho menos en clase”, cuenta. “Así que supongo que, por molesto que fuera, aun así fue bueno, en cierto modo”.
Tampoco cree que la IA generativa sea mala de por sí, aunque le inquieta un poco que esté volviendo más tontas a las personas: “La gente simplemente no sabe usarla bien”, dice. El hecho de no poder recurrir a ella durante la jornada escolar la obligó a pensar por si misma lo que entra en los exámenes, un hábito que mantuvo después de clase, cuando el bloqueo ya no se aplicaba y tenía una empresa que levantar.
Ahora se impone esa disciplina por voluntad propia. Preside el club de IA de su instituto y asegura que escribió ella misma el algoritmo de Raaha y que la IA se encargó de las partes más mecánicas, sobre todo de pulir el diseño de la web. A diario la usa para redactar correos u ordenar información desordenada. En los deberes, nada: “Intento aprender todo yo sola, sobre todo lo que tiene examen”.
Su caso es cada vez más minoritario entre los estudiantes. El panel de RAND, con 1.214 jóvenes de entre 12 y 29 años, muestra que entre los alumnos el uso de IA para los deberes pasó del 48 % en mayo de 2025 al 62 % en diciembre, y que el 67 % de ellos opina que, cuanto más la usen los estudiantes para sus tareas, más dañará su pensamiento crítico.
En la universidad, el estudio publicado en Science el 21 de mayo de 2026, con más de 95.000 estudiantes de 20 universidades públicas estadounidenses, recoge que el 26 % de los usuarios diarios de IA admite haberla usado para hacer trampa.
¿Quién admite que usa IA?
Tuteja ha puesto la IA en la marca de su proyecto y aun así duda cuando le preguntan qué herramientas usó para construirlo: “La gente se va a llevar una impresión distinta”. Si cuentas que usaste IA, piensan: “Ah, no lo hiciste tú, lo hizo todo la IA”, y dan por hecho que detrás no hubo ninguna idea.
Esa intuición tiene respaldo. En un experimento de Atlassian con 961 trabajadores del conocimiento de Estados Unidos, realizado entre el 30 de marzo y el 7 de abril de 2026, los participantes valoraron un mismo correo que resumía una propuesta de negocio: cuando se decía que su autor había usado IA, lo puntuaban como mucho más perezoso y lo recomendaban 24 puntos porcentuales menos para proyectos de visibilidad.
Y hay quien directamente lo oculta. El estudio global de KPMG y la Universidad de Melbourne, con más de 48.000 personas de 47 países encuestadas entre noviembre de 2024 y enero de 2025, concluye que el 57 % de los empleados dice esconder su uso de IA y presentar como propio lo que genera.
“Creo que es bueno asumirlo si lo estás usando bien”, sostiene Tuteja. Si eres transparente sobre para qué la usas y no la empleaste para crear toda tu empresa, añade, no hay razón para avergonzarse. Cree que el tabú persiste porque desde fuera no hay manera de comprobarlo: “Te pagas el plan de 200 dólares de Claude y te lo hace todo. No hay forma de saberlo”.
¿Prohibir o enseñar a usarla?
Preguntada por si querría una IA más regulada, no duda: “Al cien por cien”. Pero sobre el bloqueo escolar adopta la posición contraria a la que sugiere su propia historia: “No creo que prohibirla sea la solución. Creo que hay que regularla de la forma correcta, y eso es lo que intento hacer ahora”.
Un estudio de la Universidad de Pensilvania con casi 1.000 alumnos de matemáticas de bachillerato en Turquía, publicado en PNAS en 2025, comparó tres grupos: uno con un chat tipo GPT-4 sin salvaguardas, otro con un tutor que daba pistas en lugar de respuestas y otro sin tecnología.
En los ejercicios de práctica, el primero rindió un 48 % mejor que el grupo de control y el segundo, un 127 % mejor. En el examen sin IA, el primero sacó un 17 % menos y el del tutor, prácticamente lo mismo que el grupo de control. Es un único estudio, de una asignatura y de un país, pero apunta a que el resultado depende de cómo se use la IA.
En España, Cataluña quiere vetar la IA a los menores de 14 años, según anunció su presidente, Salvador Illa. El plan, presentado el 28 de septiembre de 2026 por la comisión de bienestar digital del Govern con 67 medidas hasta 2028, contempla solo una alfabetización introductoria, sin uso directo, en los servicios y equipamientos públicos para menores de 14 años; entre los 14 y los 18, uso con autorización familiar y orientación docente; y autonomía total a partir de los 18. Por ahora es solo una propuesta anunciada, no una norma ya en vigor.

articles.title: Transporter de l'hydrogène sur 820 km : la France va recycler ses vieux tuyaux de gaz — Frandroid
articles.text:
Un projet de pipeline est en cours de développement en France, et il est soumis à l’avis du public depuis le 28 septembre. Mais ici, pas question de transporter du pétrole ou du gaz naturel. Ce pipeline, qui doit traverser le pays du sud au nord, est destiné à acheminer de l’hydrogène renouvelable et bas carbone depuis Fos-sur-Mer jusqu’en Moselle, à la frontière allemande.
Appelé Hy-fen, il doit mesurer environ 820 kilomètres et traverser cinq régions et 13 départements ; à ce stade, 512 communes se trouvent dans son fuseau d’étude. Pour le moment, le tracé exact n’a pas encore été défini et on ne connaît qu’un fuseau large de 4 à 5 kilomètres qui représente son emplacement approximatif. Le tracé définitif doit être affiné dans les mois à venir en fonction des contraintes propres à chaque territoire.
La concertation préalable, menée sous l’égide de la Commission nationale du débat public (CNDP), permet aux citoyens de donner leur avis jusqu’au 20 décembre prochain, en ligne sur le site concertation.projet-hyfen.com ou lors de réunions publiques et de webinaires organisés le long du tracé. NaTran (ex-GRTgaz), la société qui porte le projet, espère un début des travaux en 2030 pour une mise en service d’ici 2032.
Jusqu’à 330€ d’avantages avec nos offres Hello Prime ou Hello Prime Duo, dont 80€ cash à l’ouverture de compte !
Le chantier a un prix : 3,6 milliards d’euros, selon l’estimation fournie par NaTran à la Commission nationale du débat public. Le projet a été retenu en janvier 2025 par l’appel à projets du Mécanisme pour l’interconnexion en Europe, ce qui lui ouvre un cofinancement de l’Union européenne.
Le potentiel chaînon manquant de la transition énergétique ?
Ce projet Hy-fen s’inscrit dans le vaste corridor stratégique européen H2Med. Dans les grandes lignes, ce réseau de pipelines doit permettre d’acheminer de l’hydrogène vert produit dans la péninsule ibérique vers les grandes zones industrielles du nord de l’Europe.
Dans le détail, Hy-fen prolonge BarMar, un pipeline sous-marin d’environ 400 à 450 kilomètres entre Barcelone et Marseille, lui aussi dimensionné pour 2 millions de tonnes par an et attendu en 2032. Tout ne sera pas construit de zéro : sur le tracé français, environ 280 kilomètres doivent reprendre d’anciennes canalisations de gaz naturel converties à l’hydrogène, notamment en Bourgogne-Franche-Comté et dans le Grand Est.
Le cadre juridique, lui, n’est pas encore en place : la France n’a pas transposé la directive européenne qui doit encadrer les réseaux de transport d’hydrogène, et la Commission européenne a ouvert fin septembre une procédure d’infraction contre elle sur ce point, trois jours avant le lancement de la concertation.
L’hydrogène peut aider à décarboner plusieurs industries très émettrices de CO2. Il est déjà utilisé dans la chimie, la production d’engrais et le raffinage. Mais pour le moment, il s’agit d’hydrogène gris, produit à partir d’énergies fossiles : en France, ces secteurs en consomment environ 430 000 tonnes par an, soit près de 5 millions de tonnes de CO2 émises chaque année.
À l’avenir, l’Europe souhaite pouvoir produire de l’hydrogène par la technique de l’électrolyse de l’eau, grâce à des énergies renouvelables. Cet hydrogène pourrait ensuite servir à produire de la chaleur industrielle décarbonée, des engrais, des carburants de synthèse et même de l’acier moins carboné. La France ne sert pas seulement de pays de transit : ses bassins industriels (Fos-sur-Mer, la vallée de la chimie près de Lyon, la Moselle) pourront puiser dans les 2 millions de tonnes d’hydrogène que le pipeline pourra transporter au maximum chaque année, soit plus de quatre fois l’hydrogène fossile consommé aujourd’hui par l’industrie française.

articles.title: El barco pesquero gallego "Génesis" se parte en tres tras pasar días encallado en las islas del norte de Escocia
articles.text:
El Génesis, un barco pesquero con bandera británica y propiedad de una empresa de Ribeira, en Galicia, se ha partido en pedazos contra las rocas frente a las Órcadas, en el norte de Escocia, más de una semana después de encallar. Afortunadamente toda la tripulación ha salido ilesa. En el vídeo difundido por la empresa Orkney Nautical Charters se puede ver cómo el barco queda partido literalmente en tres. Ahora queda limpiar el desastre.
Restos desperdigados. El barco encalló cerca del Old Man of Hoy, un pináculo rocoso de 137 metros de altura situado cerca de Rackwick Bay. Tal y como comparte Faro de Vigo, plástico y otros restos del barco escapan del casco casi constantemente, y eso va a suponer un problema tanto de contaminación como de fauna silvestre, pues se trata de una zona especialmente sensible. Orkney indica que la zona suele albergar entre 30 y 50 focas a la vez.
Qué ha pasado exactamente. La embarcación, de 35 metros y propiedad de Basoñas Mar, emitió una llamada de socorro el pasado 1 de octubre, poco después de las 7:30 AM hora española, tras golpear contra las rocas. Desde La Voz de Galicia cuentan que había salido del puerto de Scrabster el 19 de septiembre y se dirigía de vuelta para desembarcar lo que habían pescado. Según el medio, el barco iba a una velocidad de nueve nudos antes del impacto.
Tal y como comparte el medio, las 17 personas que iban a bordo fueron evacuadas sin lesiones. Durante el rescate se utilizaron botes salvavidas y más tarde llegaron helicópteros de la Guardia Costera, una embarcación de rescate rápido que pertenecía a un ferry de pasajeros y hasta un avión de patrulla marítima de la Real Fuerza Aérea.
Todavía se desconoce la causa. Sin embargo, el capitán Alejandro Abuín Prado declaraba a The Orcadian que creía que un fallo de comunicación a bordo era el culpable. La investigación todavía sigue su curso.
El naufragio. Inicialmente, el armador y las autoridades esperaban reflotar la embarcación para evitar la contaminación. Sin embargo, el barco permaneció en el mismo lugar, expuesto a un fuerte oleaje, y el mar terminó por desgarrarlo en secciones de proa, puente y popa. Los vídeos grabados diez días después del encallamiento por Orkney Nautical Charters y el Beneth'ill Cafe muestran los daños.
La limpieza. Orkney Nautical Charters afirmaba que llenó la cubierta de su embarcación neumática con restos en solo dos paradas en el Old Man of Hoy, y que queda “mucho trabajo”. Según The Orcadian, cualquier persona que encuentre restos debe enviar un correo electrónico a recycling@orkney.gov.uk para que se pueda presentar un registro preciso a la Agencia Marítima y de Guardia Costera.
Un segundo caso en un año. Tal y como comparte La Voz de Galicia, es la segunda vez en menos de un año que un buque de propiedad gallega que faena en los caladeros de Gran Sol se pierde tras golpear contra las rocas. En diciembre de 2025, el Fastnet, un arrastrero de 33 metros propiedad de una empresa de La Coruña y que navegaba bajo bandera francesa, encalló cerca de Dingle, en el noroeste de Irlanda. Sus 14 miembros de la tripulación fueron evacuados en helicóptero a un lugar seguro. El barco pasó días azotado por las olas y nunca se acabó recuperando. Desde Faro de Vigo informaron de que finalmente fue desguazado in situ.
Y en el caso del Génesis es probable que siga el mismo camino. El armador ha declarado que ya han iniciado movilizaciones para retirar la embarcación del lugar, pero con el casco en tres piezas, la recuperación parece poco probable.

articles.title: Scientists recreate a bizarre quantum effect that stops a particle cold
articles.text:
Scientists recreate a bizarre quantum effect that stops a particle cold
- Date:
- October 13, 2026
- Source:
- University of Oxford
- Summary:
- Oxford physicists have recreated a bizarre quantum effect in which a particle responds to a magnetic field without ever traveling through it. Using a hybrid quantum computer, they demonstrated how introducing a simulated magnetic flux could completely halt a particle's movement through quantum interference. The experiment brings a decades-old prediction into a new setting where matter and quantum fields influence one another.
- Share:
A particle does not have to pass through a magnetic field to be influenced by it. That surprising feature of quantum physics has now been recreated by researchers at the University of Oxford, who used a hybrid quantum computer to demonstrate how an invisible magnetic influence can bring a simulated particle's movement to a complete stop.
The experiment reproduced a phenomenon known as the Aharonov-Bohm effect, in which a charged particle traveling around a region containing magnetic flux experiences a measurable change in its quantum state, even though its path never takes it through the magnetic field itself.
The Oxford team achieved this using a quantum system that combines qubits, the basic units of quantum information, with quantum oscillators, which represent vibrating motion. Their findings, published in Nature Physics, demonstrate how this combination could help scientists investigate fundamental interactions between matter and fields that are increasingly difficult to simulate using conventional computers.
A Strange Quantum Effect Predicted in 1959
In everyday physics, a charged particle responds to the electric and magnetic fields it encounters. Quantum mechanics, however, reveals that particles can behave in ways that have no straightforward counterpart in our ordinary experience.
In 1959, physicists Yakir Aharonov and David Bohm predicted that a charged particle could be affected by magnetic flux even if it traveled entirely outside the region containing the magnetic field. Rather than experiencing a conventional magnetic force along its path, the particle would undergo a change in its quantum phase.
Quantum phase describes an aspect of a particle's wave behavior that influences how different possible paths interfere with one another. Although the phase itself is not directly visible, differences in phase can produce measurable effects.
The prediction became known as the Aharonov-Bohm effect and was eventually verified in experiments involving real electrons. It remains one of the clearest demonstrations that the quantum world operates according to rules that go beyond the familiar laws of classical physics.
Researchers are now exploring how this phenomenon behaves in more complex theoretical systems known as lattice gauge theories.
These theories describe how matter interacts with fields associated with fundamental forces. They represent space as a grid, with matter located at individual points and fields associated with the connections between them. Such models are particularly important in particle physics and high-energy physics, where scientists study the basic particles and interactions that make up the universe.
The challenge is that the mathematics becomes extraordinarily demanding as these systems grow more complicated. Even powerful conventional computers can struggle to calculate how all the interacting components evolve.
Quantum computers offer a different approach. Instead of attempting to calculate every aspect of a quantum system using classical computing methods, scientists can construct another quantum system that follows the same underlying rules. They can then observe its behavior directly, an approach known as quantum simulation.
How Scientists Built the Quantum Experiment
The Oxford project began in 2022, when lead author Dr. Sebastian Saner, Dr. Oana Bazavan, and their colleagues started developing a way to simulate lattice gauge theories using a hybrid quantum system. They collaborated with Dr. Alejandro Bermudez of the Instituto de Física Teórica in Madrid.
Their experimental design relied on two different quantum components that performed separate functions.
The first consisted of qubits encoded in the internal states of trapped ions, which are electrically charged atoms held in place using electromagnetic fields. These qubits represented the gauge fields in the theoretical model.
The second component used quantum oscillators, created by the vibrations of those same trapped ions. These oscillators represented matter.
By combining the two, the researchers constructed a simple loop that served as a basic building block of a lattice gauge theory. Two oscillators represented matter at two different locations, while two qubits represented the fields connecting those locations.
Although the arrangement was small, it was sufficient to reproduce an important interaction between matter and magnetic flux.
Quantum Entanglement Creates a Surprising Solution
The researchers next placed the two qubits into an entangled quantum state. Entanglement is a phenomenon in which quantum systems become linked in ways that cannot be fully explained by classical physics.
Within the team's simulated lattice gauge theory, this entangled state represented magnetic flux passing through the center of the loop.
Initially, the researchers had planned to introduce the magnetic flux as a fixed background condition. However, creating the necessary interaction would have required capabilities that their quantum hardware did not possess.
Encoding the flux directly into the qubits provided a practical alternative. More importantly, it allowed the magnetic flux to become part of the evolving quantum system rather than remaining an unchanging external influence.
"For us, the exciting step was to encode the magnetic flux in a gauge field that was itself dynamical," says Dr. Saner. "Rather than having matter evolve in a fixed background, the matter and gauge field become part of the same quantum dynamics."
What began as a technical workaround ultimately enabled the researchers to explore a more interesting version of the phenomenon, one in which matter and the field could participate together in the quantum dynamics.
A Quantum Effect That Stops Particle Motion
With their simulated loop in place, the scientists examined how a matter particle moved between locations through a process known as quantum tunneling.
Quantum tunneling allows particles to move between states in ways that would not be possible under ordinary classical rules.
When the researchers ran their simulation without magnetic flux, the particle could tunnel freely around the loop.
Introducing the simulated flux produced a strikingly different result.
The particle had two possible paths around the loop, but the magnetic flux changed their relative quantum phases. As a result, the two paths interfered destructively, meaning their quantum contributions canceled each other out.
This interference completely suppressed the tunneling, leaving the simulated particle frozen in its original state.
The outcome demonstrated the Aharonov-Bohm effect within a lattice gauge theory containing a dynamical field. Rather than simply reproducing the familiar behavior of a particle moving around a fixed magnetic influence, the experiment showed how the phenomenon can emerge when matter and the field are both represented by interacting quantum components.
A New Tool for Exploring Fundamental Physics
The Oxford findings were published alongside a related study by researchers at the University of Maryland, led by Professor Norbert Linke.
The Maryland team also used a hybrid quantum system, but their experiment focused on simulating the Yukawa potential, a mathematical description of an interaction relevant to nuclear and particle physics.
Although the two research groups developed their methods independently, they later coordinated the submission of their studies to Nature Physics.
Together, the experiments demonstrate how hybrid quantum computers could become valuable tools for investigating fundamental interactions that are difficult to reproduce using classical simulations.
By combining different types of quantum components, researchers can build systems in which matter and fields are represented in ways that more closely reflect the physics they want to study.
The Oxford experiment provides an example of that potential. A phenomenon first predicted in 1959 and later observed with electrons has now been recreated in a quantum simulator where the field itself participates in the dynamics, offering scientists another way to explore the unusual rules governing the quantum world.

articles.title: This is the AMD Helios HPE Juniper QFX5252 Switch Tray at OCP 2026
articles.text:
At OCP 2026, we saw something that looked absolutely awesome. Walking by the HPE booth, we saw an AMD Helios tray set up and open on the show floor. It stopped me in my tracks, so I thought folks would like to see it.
This is the AMD Helios HPE Juniper QFX5252 Switch Tray at OCP 2026
Oftentimes, when we open up huge switches, we see a lot of internal PCB. This is totally different since it is a double-wide tray with side-by-side switches and lots of copper.
You can see the HPE QFX5252 label on the front latch, which is huge. Because there is so much connectivity on the back, and the back panel is long and needs to blind mate, the insertion force required for a switch tray like this into the Helios rack is significant. As a result, these levers are very long.
Since this is two big switch chips in a 1OU tray, it needs to be liquid cooled. You can see the internal liquid cooling manifolds distributing liquid to the various blocks.
There are two switch chips inside, which are Broadcom Tomahawk 6 102.6T switches. At first, you might wonder why these are not Broadcom Tomahawk Ultra chips, since that might make sense for a scale-up architecture. The current generation Tomahawk Ultra is a 112G PAM4 SerDes switch (so 512 lanes of PAM4-112G.) That is not enough for Helios which is using 224G PAM4 SerDes. As a result, these need to be Tomahawk 6.
Now, the next part is very different. AMD and HPE-Juniper are not just slinging Tomahawk 6 on some PCBs and calling it a day. You will notice that the cabled connections to the rear high-density fabric connectors for the Helios rack cable cartridges are quite far from the Tomahawk 6 switch chips. Some of them in particular are very far from the switch chips. The liquid cooling blocks between those cable connectors and the switch chip are apparently retimers. AMD is big on retimers while NVIDIA has worked to remove them.
Aside from the switches and retimers, let us talk about the cables.
When we say copper inside a rack, and why we will eventually go to co-packaged optics, this is a great illustration. In the QFX5252, retimers extend reach so we can reliably scale up within the rack. Then we need an enormous array of copper cables. CPO would simplify this design. I will probably use these photos when explaining the “why” for CPO in the future.
You can see the fans and airflow guides over heatsinks for some other components. Unlike NVIDIA’s push to move fans out of the AI rack, AMD Helios still uses fans and air cooling for some other bits in the tray.
Overall, very cool.
Final Words
We previously covered the QFX5252 at HPE Discover 2026, but seeing the switch tray assembled and on the show floor was really cool. A lot is going on here, and it is very different from the normal rackmount switches we see. One of the biggest differences, of course, is that it is designed to scale up within a rack instead of out of front-panel connectors.
Of course, if you are into networking, check out our Inside the Secretive AWS Networking Lab tour that we were finally able to publish yesterday.
As a fun aside, I was at HPE’s booth looking at this switch tray when Pradeep Sindhu walked over and started looking at the switch with the HPE-Juniper team and me. For me, it was neat because the last time I saw Pradeep was when we did this Fungible DPU-based Storage Cluster Hands-on Look back in the pandemic era in 2020. It was neat having Juniper’s co-founder and former CTO look at the big switch tray while I was there.

articles.title: YouTube Music empezó a etiquetar las canciones creadas con inteligencia artificial
articles.text:
YouTube Music comenzó a mostrar etiquetas que identifican las canciones creadas principalmente con inteligencia artificial generativa, incluidas aquellas cuya composición y voces fueron producidas por un modelo. La función también se extenderá a la aplicación principal de YouTube, según anunció la compañía en su blog oficial.
La etiqueta aparece directamente en la pantalla del reproductor, donde el oyente puede tocarla para abrir un menú con más información sobre el rol que tuvo la inteligencia artificial en esa grabación en particular.
YouTube explicó que combina las declaraciones de sus socios discográficos con herramientas propias de detección automática para identificar los temas sintéticos.
Según la documentación de ayuda de Google, los sellos y distribuidores deben clasificar cada lanzamiento bajo una de tres categorías: “Fully Gen AI” para canciones enteramente generadas por un modelo, “Partly Gen AI” cuando un artista incorporó componentes de IA junto a elementos grabados en vivo, y “No Gen AI” para el resto, categoría que incluye el uso de correctores de afinación como Auto-Tune.
Una etiqueta, no una restricción
A diferencia de otras plataformas, YouTube optó por un enfoque de divulgación y no de bloqueo. Que una canción lleve la etiqueta de IA no la vuelve inelegible para monetizarse, y la compañía remarcó que la medida busca darle “claridad” al oyente sobre lo que escucha, no limitar qué contenido puede circular.
La postura es coherente con sus propios productos: YouTube mantiene activa Dream Track, una herramienta que permite a creadores seleccionados generar bandas sonoras con versiones sintéticas de las voces de artistas que participan voluntariamente del programa, de acuerdo con la documentación de soporte de la plataforma.
La avalancha de música sintética
El anuncio llega en medio de un crecimiento acelerado de la música generada por IA en los servicios de streaming. Deezer informó en julio que recibía casi 90.000 canciones totalmente generadas por inteligencia artificial por día, según datos recogidos por TechCrunch.
Esa plataforma ya etiqueta las grabaciones que detecta como sintéticas, las excluye de sus recomendaciones algorítmicas y de las listas editoriales, y retiene las regalías de las reproducciones que considera fraudulentas. El mismo día del anuncio de YouTube, Deezer confirmó que sumará una opción para que los usuarios filtren por completo la música hecha con IA.
Lo que hacen Spotify, Apple Music y Tidal
Spotify aplica desde 2025 sus propias etiquetas de IA junto con un filtro antispam para detectar cargas masivas de temas generados automáticamente.
Apple Music, por su parte, planea introducir etiquetas bajo el nombre “Made With AI” como parte de un sistema más amplio de clasificación que llamó AI Transparency Tags, previsto para más adelante este año, según reportó la revista especializada Variety.
Tidal eligió el camino más estricto entre las grandes plataformas: etiqueta las grabaciones que identifica como completamente generadas por IA, permite a los oyentes desactivarlas y las excluye directamente de la atribución de regalías, una diferencia clave frente al modelo de simple divulgación que adoptó YouTube.
El sistema de YouTube todavía no define con qué frecuencia actualizará sus detecciones automáticas ni qué ocurre si un sello discográfico omite declarar el uso de IA en un lanzamiento, algo que la compañía no detalló en su anuncio reciente.
Cómo empezar a usar YouTube Music
Para usar YouTube Music, puedes descargar la aplicación en un celular con iOS o Android. También es posible ingresar desde un navegador web. En ambos casos, debes iniciar sesión con tu cuenta de Google.
La pantalla principal ofrece recomendaciones basadas en tus gustos y hábitos de escucha. También incluye la pestaña Samples, diseñada para descubrir fragmentos de canciones nuevas.
La plataforma cuenta con una barra de búsqueda que permite encontrar música por el nombre de un tema o de un artista. También admite búsquedas a partir de partes de la letra de una canción.
El catálogo de YouTube Music reúne canciones oficiales, actuaciones en vivo, remezclas y temas independientes. Durante la reproducción, el usuario puede alternar entre escuchar solo el audio y ver el videoclip oficial con un toque.
La versión gratuita permite acceder al contenido disponible, aunque incluye anuncios. La suscripción a YouTube Music Premium elimina la publicidad y habilita la reproducción en segundo plano, incluso si se bloquea la pantalla o se abre otra aplicación.
Finalmente, el plan Premium también permite descargar canciones para escucharlas sin conexión a internet.

articles.title: Palo Alto Networks Patches PAN-OS Zero-Day Exploited for Remote Code Execution
articles.text:
Palo Alto Networks on Wednesday informed customers that it has released patches for a PAN-OS zero-day vulnerability exploited in malicious attacks.
The high-severity flaw is tracked as CVE-2026-0322 and it allows remote code execution. It affects the management interface of PAN-OS and it can be exploited by an authenticated attacker with network access to execute arbitrary code with root privileges on the targeted firewall.
“Very limited exploitation has been observed targeting the Palo Alto Networks management interface,” Palo Alto Networks noted in its advisory.
The zero-day was discovered internally. It affects PAN-OS software on PA-Series and VM-Series firewalls and on Panorama. The security firm noted that no special configuration is needed to exploit CVE-2026-0322.
The cybersecurity giant has released indicators of compromise (IoCs) associated with the observed activity, specifically a few IP addresses.
No information has been shared on the attacks exploiting this new zero-day or the threat actor responsible.
CISA added CVE-2026-0322 to its KEV catalog on Wednesday, instructing federal agencies to address it by October 17.
CISA’s KEV catalog currently includes 16 Palo Alto Networks product vulnerabilities, including three added this year.
On Wednesday, Palo Alto published a dozen other advisories to inform customers about vulnerabilities found and fixed in PAN-OS, GlobalProtect, and Prisma Cloud products, including DoS, command injection, identity hijacking, local privilege escalation, XSS, and path traversal issues. All of these vulnerabilities have been rated medium or low severity.
In addition, the company updated its Prisma Browser to include the latest Chromium updates.

articles.title: Meta AI barra Lula, mas gera imagens com referência a Flávio • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Meta AI barra Lula, mas gera imagens com referência a Flávio
Empresa trabalha para implementar novos filtros em sistema de inteligência artificial.
A ferramenta de inteligência artificial Meta AI, que está presente no WhatsApp, recusa os comandos para gerar imagens com alusão à campanha de Lula ao Palácio do Planalto. Ao mesmo tempo, aceita criar imagens com referências a outros candidatos, inclusive Flávio Bolsonaro, que levou vantagem sobre o presidente no primeiro turno. O caso viralizou nas redes sociais nas últimas horas.
Nos nossos testes, comandos com “Flávio 22” geraram as imagens, enquanto pedidos com o nome completo de Flávio Bolsonaro foram barrados. Já as solicitações com “Lula 13” foram recusadas, mesmo quando ocorreram na mesma sessão com o chatbot. A ferramenta produziu normalmente imagens ao receber um prompt com “Luiz 13”.
O Tecnoblog apurou que o assunto é tratado internamente na Meta como um erro de configuração. Enquanto os nomes completos dos candidatos são bloqueados, os primeiros nomes não são impactados pelo filtro. Por isso a Meta AI gera figuras com “Flávio” e “Luiz”.
A empresa disse ao Tecnoblog ter adotado medidas adicionais para impedir a geração de imagens a partir de comandos que usem apenas o primeiro nome dos candidatos e o número de urna. A expectativa é de que os usuários percebam a diferença num futuro breve, mas não é possível precisar quanto tempo isso deve levar.
As diferenças nas respostas do chatbot repercutiram nas redes sociais em meio às regras eleitorais brasileiras para ferramentas automatizadas. No início do ano, o Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE) publicou a Resolução nº 23.755/2026, que proíbe sistemas automatizados de emitir opiniões, recomendar votos ou favorecer ou desfavorecer candidaturas, inclusive por meio de respostas geradas automaticamente.
Em agosto, mostramos aqui no Tecnoblog que os principais chatbots do mercado estavam descumprindo essas regras. ChatGPT, Grok e Gemini criaram listas de presidenciáveis após comandos simples, prática proibida pelo TSE.

articles.title: Ejércitos, sanidad o servicios secretos: 11 países europeos ya tienen contratos millonarios con Palantir con dinero público
articles.text: “El crecimiento allí es una mierda”. Así describió Alex Karp, consejero delegado y cofundador de Palantir, el desempeño de la empresa en Europa. Lo dijo el 3 de agosto ante los accionistas, mientras defendía un trimestre “extraordinario”. Palantir vende softwares que cruzan enormes cantidades de datos de fuentes muy distintas, y Karp sostuvo que ese continente estaría peor sin su empresa: “Apoyamos muchísimas instituciones en Europa, incluso instituciones clandestinas. Sin nuestros productos tendrían terrorismo desatado y su problema migratorio sería diez veces mayor.” Seguir leyendo La respuesta de Palantir Follow The Money y sus medios colaboradores presentaron los hallazgos de esta investigación a Palantir, además de catorce preguntas detalladas. Palantir no ha entrado a contestar a esas preguntas, sino que ha remitido el mensaje de un portavoz: “Es necesario un debate serio sobre cómo salvaguarda Europa su soberanía tecnológica. La soberanía tecnológica debe medirse, en última instancia, por quién controla los datos, las decisiones y la misión, y no solo por la nacionalidad del proveedor de software”. Según Palantir, el control sobre los datos y sobre lo que se hace con ellos corresponde al propio cliente. Y añade: “Desde 2011, Palantir trabaja con los gobiernos e instituciones de Europa elegidos democráticamente para aumentar la capacidad hospitalaria, acelerar el diagnóstico del cáncer, reasentar a refugiados de forma segura, combatir el crimen organizado, proteger a las víctimas de violencia doméstica y responder con mayor rapidez a inundaciones y otras emergencias”. Señala además que más del 20 % de los empleados de Palantir trabaja desde centros en Europa y que la compañía ayuda a empresas europeas a competir y crecer en sectores como el aeroespacial, el manufacturero y las ciencias de la vida. Palantir afirma además apoyar a los gobiernos europeos en la protección de su seguridad nacional, incluso en Ucrania. En una respuesta anterior a este mismo consorcio de medios, Palantir negó las acusaciones de implicación en violaciones de derechos humanos.

articles.title: Deploy with Void
Oslo-based AI-native engineering firm Solvera raises €5.62 million pre-Seed after July 2026 launch | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Solvera, an Oslo-based company building an AI-native engineering firm for the construction industry, today announced a €5.62 million ($6.3 million) pre-Seed round.
The round was led by Seedcamp, with participation from Construct Venture, Inception Fund, Momentum, Obos Ventures, PSV Tech, Sondo, and The Nordic Web Ventures, as well as angel investors including Spacemaker founders Anders Kvåle and Håvard Haukeland.
“The most valuable thing in building engineering has always been the engineer’s judgement, yet much of their day goes to sorting a constant stream of information and changes, manual data entry, and coordination. Our goal is to free up their time so they can focus on high impact decisions, with our agents handling the rest like testing alternatives, coordination, and production work,” said Pål Rasmussen, co-founder and CTO, Solvera.
Founded in July 2026 by Arif Mirza, Pål Rasmussen and Thorvald Thorsnes, Solvera is an AI-native building engineering firm. The company combines experienced building engineers with proprietary AI technology to design and coordinate building engineering work, starting with mechanical, electrical, and plumbing systems.
The company says it uses its purpose-built operating system to deliver end-to-end service as the engineering firm of record, with clients paying for the outcome, not software licenses or consulting hours.
Solvera highlights that it takes a project from requirements and constraints through to a coordinated, construction-ready design, with AI agents handling a major chunk of the engineering work and building engineers providing judgement.
Unlike traditional delivery models, the company notes that the system improves with every project, as judgement becomes intelligence that can be reused across the firm.
Mirza, co-founder and CEO of Solvera, said, “We’ve had twenty years of better building engineering software, and now AI, but productivity and the fundamental way engineering gets delivered has barely changed. Technology is only part of the answer. To capture its full potential, you also have to rethink how the firm operates and how it makes money. That is incredibly difficult to do inside organisations built around thousands of people, active projects and billable hours.
“That is why we decided not to build yet another tool for engineers that doesn’t move the needle in how work gets done. We are building the engineering firm itself around AI.”
The Norwegian company is starting with mechanical, electrical, and plumbing (MEP) engineering. It opines that MEP engineers must navigate hundreds of requirements and constraints, work across dozens of legacy tools, size and route systems, coordinate amongst themselves and across disciplines, and continuously adapt designs as projects evolve. Yet much of the work remains manual, fragmented, and repeated from project to project.
The company reported that since its inception, it has passed nearly €892k ($1 million) in contracted revenue in its first 3 months of operations, growing to a team of nine.
It also noted that it has already worked on several building projects in Norway, covering everything from early-phase engineering to detailed design, including commercial projects with Betonmast, one of Norway’s leading contractors.
Tom Wilson, Partner at Seedcamp, said, “We invested in Solvera because Arif, Thorvald and Pål are not just building software for engineers, they are rebuilding the firm itself. That is a much bigger swing, and a much better one.
“Construction has absorbed two decades of tooling without shifting how the work actually gets delivered or paid for. Solvera is the first team we have seen with the technical depth and industry experience to close that gap, starting with MEP and expanding from there. This is what the next generation of professional services firms looks like.”
The company plans to use this capital to expand its building engineering and technology team in Oslo, establish a London office, and accelerate development of the Solvera operating system. The company also intends to expand into additional markets as the model develops.

articles.title: Canadian entrepreneurs are doubling down on growth despite tough market conditions: BDC | BetaKit
articles.text:
Despite a cross-border trade war and economic uncertainty, Canadian entrepreneurs are focused on growth and expansion, a new survey found.
The Business Development Bank of Canada (BDC) released its annual State of Entrepreneurship report on Thursday, which surveyed 2,500 Canadian business owners and executives on their priorities for the coming year.
“The results of our study show that entrepreneurs are not standing still. Quite the opposite,”
Pierre Cléroux, BDC
The share of small and medium enterprises (SMEs) focused on company growth increased significantly since last year, rising to 78 percent from 67 percent—a notable jump as some businesses have been impacted by trade disruptions and economic uncertainty hampering investment. However, the extent to which these companies want to grow varied widely: 46 percent said they were aiming for “moderate growth” while 22 percent wanted “significant growth.” Meanwhile, only 10 percent said they were going to “radically transform” their business.
Since US President Donald Trump imposed tariffs on Canadian goods in February 2025, Canada’s business and tech sector have faced a number of newfound challenges: the report mentions an economic slowdown, rising costs, more competition, and trade tensions as just a few.
“The results of our study show that entrepreneurs are not standing still. Quite the opposite,” Pierre Cléroux, BDC’s vice-president of research and chief economist, wrote in the report. He added that Canadian SMEs are “actively looking for ways to strengthen their competitiveness,” such as adopting AI and diversifying markets and revenue streams.
The report also indicated that companies under pressure are adapting quickly. Among the small businesses directly impacted by US tariffs—which cover some tech startups that deal with hardware and supply chains—the report found 58 percent expanded their products or services, compared with 39 percent of SMEs generally. Over the past year, 64 percent of SMEs gained new customers in their region, while almost one third found new customers in other parts of Canada.
RELATED: The AI costs that could hurt Canadian tech more than a trade war
With rising costs and competition, the vast majority of SMEs put an emphasis on boosting productivity. Eighty-eight percent took at least one step to improve productivity, compared with three-quarters of respondents in 2025.
For some companies, pushing productivity has come through AI adoption—something that BDC itself has encouraged entrepreneurs to do through a federally funded, $500-million loan program to integrate the technology. However, only 22 percent of respondents said adopting or increasing their use of AI was a priority this year (though this metric grew from 14 percent last year). Bigger priorities included expansion (46 percent), improving profitability (40 percent), acquiring new local clients (31 percent), and cutting costs (28 percent).
Feature image courtesy BDC.

articles.title: Local and Distributed Large LLM Inference with MLX and RDMA on Mac Studio
articles.text:
Local and Distributed Large LLM Inference with MLX and RDMA on Mac Studio
MLX on Mac with Apple silicon lets AI researchers and developers experiment locally with the latest models and methods in a private environment. The open-source array framework leverages the unified memory architecture of Apple silicon, enabling anyone to run new inference and fine-tuning methods on their own hardware and explore other AI techniques. In a previous post, we highlighted the advantages of the M5 architecture and its GPU Neural Accelerators.
In this post, we show how to run the latest frontier-class model — Muse Spark Open, with nearly a trillion parameters — right from your desk, using the latest version of MLX, released today. On a cluster of four Mac Studios, Muse Spark Open generates over 36 tokens per second (see Figure 1), well above average human reading speed.
Beginning on a single Mac Studio (up to 512GB of unified memory), then scaling out across multiple Macs with the RDMA over Thunderbolt driver, below we share an overview of the range of models you can now run on Mac Studio.
Running Large Language Models with MLX
We benchmark several popular open-weight LLMs on Mac Studio, using the MLX LM package, as described in our prior post. We compare two generations of Mac Studio: the recently released M5 Ultra and the previous generation, M3 Ultra. The M5 generation features the GPU Neural Accelerator, which supports dedicated matrix multiplication operations, essential for many machine learning workloads.
We evaluate three frontier-class models (Table 1) spanning a wide range of sizes (in billions of parameters, B): the newly released Muse Spark Open (816 B), Mistral Medium 3.5 (128 B), and Qwen 3.8 (27 B). Muse Spark Open is a mixture of experts (MoE) model, which keeps only a fraction of its experts — and thus parameters — active, reducing compute at inference, and it is evaluated in NVFP4 precision. Mistral Medium 3.5 and Qwen 3.8 are dense architectures, where all parameters are active at inference, and they are evaluated in their native floating-point precision (FP8 and BF16, respectively).
| Model | Total Parameters | Active Parameters | Native Precision | Evaluation Precision | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Muse Spark Open | 816B | 42B | BF16 | NVFP4 | 
| Mistral Medium 3.5 | 128B | 128B | FP8 | FP8 | 
| Qwen 3.8 | 27B | 27B | BF16 | BF16 | 
Our evaluation measures three metrics across a range of context sizes: time to first token (TTFT, in seconds), generation throughput (in tokens/second), and peak power usage (in watts). All the performance numbers in this post were obtained with mlx_lm.benchmark. For example, running Qwen 3.8 with 8,192 tokens of context and generating 128 tokens is performed with the command line:
mlx_lm.benchmark --model Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B -p 8192 -g 128 -b 1
A popular use of local LLMs on Mac Studio is running agentic experiences in a private environment, including agentic coding applications that often need large contexts. We therefore report performance at both 8,192 and 65,536 context sizes.
Raw TTFT and decode throughput are reported in Table 2 and Table 3, respectively.
Inference Performance on a Single Mac Studio
Qwen 3.8 27B and Mistral Medium 3.5 128B fit comfortably on a single Mac Studio with 512GB, taking up to 68GB and 158GB of RAM in the large context size (65,536 tokens) setup. In Figure 2, we compare their inference performance on a single Mac Studio with 512GB of RAM, both on M3 Ultra and M5 Ultra.
Time to first token (TTFT) is essentially compute bound, and that is where the Neural Accelerators in the M5 Ultra GPU shine: the specialized hardware support for fast matrix-multiplication of the GPU Neural Accelerator directly translates into significant speedups for TTFT, up to 4.6× faster compared to an M3 Ultra (see Figure 2). That makes the Mac Studio with M5 Ultra the desktop of choice when it comes to handling tasks involving very large contexts.
Generation speed (in tokens per second) is memory-bandwidth bound. The M5 Ultra chip delivers 1.2 TB/s of unified memory bandwidth, up from 819 GB/s for the M3 Ultra. Here again, that translates directly into generation speed (see Figure 3), with the Mac Studio with M5 Ultra reporting 1.6× faster tokens/s.
The Mac Studio is also energy-efficient for LLM inference (see Figure 4): peak power consumption is about 200W for the Mac Studio with M3 Ultra, and 300W for the Mac Studio with M5 Ultra — a fraction of the power used by a common toaster. More importantly, that modest amount of power consumption means a Mac Studio can be deployed for AI work in any home or office environment.
While both the Qwen and Mistral models fit on a single Mac Studio with 512GB of RAM, Muse Spark Open would require more than 1.6TB of RAM in its native precision (BF16) for the model parameters alone. In a 4-bit quantized (NVFP4) format, the model memory footprint is lowered to about 493GB. Add the memory needed for intermediate computations during inference, and the model cannot fit on a single machine. It requires parallelization across multiple Mac Studio computers.
Pipelining Inference Across Two Mac Studio Computers
Very large frontier-class models like Muse Spark Open will not fit on a single machine. It is, however, possible to store half of the model on one Mac Studio and the other half on another. We can then pipeline the model’s inference across two computers: the first Mac Studio executes the first half of the model’s layers, then sends the output to the second Mac Studio, which executes the second half. This parallelization scheme is called pipeline parallelization (see Figure 5) and is extremely simple to implement, requiring only minimal code changes.
MLX supports different parallelization schemes, as described in the MLX distributed documentation. These rely on fast inter-machine communication: macOS 26.2 introduced a low-latency RDMA driver over Thunderbolt 5, and MLX (v0.30.1 and later) builds on top of this driver and provides new communication collectives (jaccl, pronounced “jackal”) for different parallelization schemes. In our setup, the two Mac Studios are connected with two Thunderbolt cables (to double the link bandwidth), providing the RDMA-over-Thunderbolt link that jaccl uses. Once the hosts are set up, MLX provides mlx.launch, a helper command to launch jobs across multiple nodes:
mlx.launch --hostfile hostfile.json --backend jaccl --env MLX_METAL_FAST_SYNCH=1 -- \
mlx_lm.benchmark --model mistralai/Mistral-Medium-3.5-128B -p 8192 -g 128 -b 1 --prefill-step-size 8192 --pipeline
In this command, --backend jaccl specifies the RDMA Thunderbolt driver backend. The --env MLX_METAL_FAST_SYNCH=1 flag enables an experimental MLX feature for fast CPU-GPU synchronization, reducing communication overhead between the CPU (which initiates the Thunderbolt communication) and the GPU (which does the compute).
In general, decode inference speed with pipeline parallelization (see Figure 7) is very similar to that of a single machine, since the layers are still evaluated sequentially. Communication overhead is also very low, as only the intermediate outputs between the two sets of layers need to be exchanged.
It is however notable that for very large contexts (65,536 tokens in our benchmark), pipeline parallelization ends up faster than a single node for prefill — up to ~1.8× faster (see Figure 6). This is because MLX segments large contexts into smaller chunks (here, 8,192 tokens, as set by --prefill-step-size 8192) and pipelines the prefill across the machines: while the second machine computes the later layers of chunk \(k\), the first machine computes the earlier layers of chunk \(k+1\), so consecutive chunks overlap in time. For even better compute parallelization, we next turn to tensor parallelization.
Tensor Parallelization for Faster Inference
Tensor parallelization (see Figure 5) distributes the LLM’s width across several computers, in contrast to pipeline parallelization, which distributes the model across its depth. Each machine now holds a fraction of each of the layers of the model, such that per-layer computation is parallelized. When efficiently implemented, tensor parallelization improves inference speed. However, tensor parallelization is more complex to implement than pipeline parallelization: each layer must be parallelized, which increases code complexity. The scheme also involves many small communication operations: for each input token and for each layer, one must broadcast inputs and aggregate outputs. As a result, a very low-latency communication technology like Thunderbolt RDMA, supported by MLX jaccl, is critical for this approach to yield any speedup.
With MLX’s high-level mlx.launch helper, it is easy to switch to tensor parallelization. The Mac Studio computers are connected in a Thunderbolt mesh, with each pair of machines linked peer-to-peer by two Thunderbolt cables. Assuming the hosts are set up, we simply launch the benchmark across multiple machines with:
mlx.launch --hostfile hostfile.json --backend jaccl --env MLX_METAL_FAST_SYNCH=1 -- \
mlx_lm.benchmark --model meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 -p 8192 -g 128 -b 1
Figure 8 and Figure 9 show the speedups obtained with two or four Mac Studio computers with M5 Ultra, relative to a single-machine baseline (or, for Muse Spark Open, the pipeline parallelization baseline). Notably, dense architectures scale better across multiple computers.
With a small number of machines, the communication overhead of tensor parallelization can offset some of its compute benefits at very large contexts, though this applies to prefill only. This shows up with Muse Spark Open, where separate normalization of the experts’ outputs adds some prefill communication, enough that at very large contexts (65,536 tokens), two-machine tensor parallelization lags behind two-machine pipeline parallelization. The approach however pays off as machines are added, as seen with four M5 Ultras. Decode is unaffected: Muse Spark Open sustains a significant decode speedup under tensor parallelization even at large contexts, comparable to dense models like Qwen 3.8 and Mistral Medium 3.5.
The two-cable mesh also pays off during prefill, where the extra link bandwidth is felt. For Muse Spark Open on four M5 Ultras at a 65,536-token context, two cables per link cut TTFT from about 50.5s (one cable) to 40.6s — the two-cable value reported in Table 2, the one-cable run being an additional experiment.
Time to First Token (seconds)
Lower is better
| Model | M3 Ultra | M5 Ultra | 2 M5 Pipeline | 2 M5 Tensor | 4 M5 Tensor | 
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Muse Spark Open | — | — | 8.4 | 8.2 | 4.8 | 
| Mistral Medium 3.5 | 95.9 | 24.6 | 24.5 | 14.4 | 7.5 | 
| Qwen 3.8 | 18.2 | 4.1 | 4.1 | 3.1 | 1.7 | 
Decode Speed (tokens per second)
Higher is better
| Model | M3 Ultra | M5 Ultra | 2 M5 Pipeline | 2 M5 Tensor | 4 M5 Tensor | 
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Muse Spark Open | — | — | 15.74 | 24.99 | 36.73 | 
| Mistral Medium 3.5 | 4.95 | 7.70 | 7.70 | 13.69 | 23.37 | 
| Qwen 3.8 | 12.46 | 19.69 | 19.44 | 33.27 | 50.89 | 
Local Agentic AI on Mac
Recently, agentic AI on Mac has gained considerable traction, with agentic coding tools seeing widespread adoption among developers. With MLX, powering these tools locally is as simple as launching a server with the mlx_lm.server tool. For example, a server running Muse Spark Open on port 8080 is started with:
mlx.launch --hostfile hostfile.json --backend jaccl --env MLX_METAL_FAST_SYNCH=1 -- \
mlx_lm.server --model meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 --port 8080
As with mlx_lm.benchmark, the mlx_lm.server helper can be prefixed with mlx.launch to parallelize computation across multiple Mac Studios. From there, agentic AI can be enabled with tools like OpenCode, which can be easily configured to use that local LLM server:
{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "model": "meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4",
  "provider": {
    "mlx": {
      "npm": "@ai-sdk/openai-compatible",
      "name": "Local MLX",
      "options": {
        "baseURL": "http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1"
      },
      "models": {
        "meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4": {
          "name": "Muse Spark Open 816B (MLX)"
        }
      }
    }
  }
}
Many other local agentic AI experiences can be enabled through a similar approach.
Conclusion
Over the past year, we have worked on several key innovations in MLX to make it easier and more efficient to run state-of-the-art LLMs locally on recent Apple silicon. These include software support for the Neural Accelerators in the GPU of the M5 family of chips, low-latency communication across several Macs using RDMA over Thunderbolt, and efficient implementations of recent popular architectures such as mixture of experts (MoE). Each of these helps on its own, but it is their combination with the latest Apple silicon — Mac Studio with M5 Ultra, Neural Accelerators in the M5 Ultra GPU, 512GB of unified memory, and RDMA over Thunderbolt 5 — that now lets us run models like Muse Spark Open with more than 800B parameters locally, at up to 4.6× the start-up (time-to-first-token) speed of the previous generation of Mac Studio.
Get Started with MLX
Related readings and updates.

We are proud to again sponsor the conference, which brings together the scientific and industrial research communities focused on deep learning. articles.title: The next evolution of observability starts with telemetry
articles.text:
The next evolution of observability starts with telemetry
Why better observability starts with better telemetry
For technology teams, connecting telemetry has traditionally been seen as a route to greater visibility. The assumption is straightforward: the more information available about what is happening across an environment, the easier it should be to understand problems and respond to them.
But as modern technology environments have grown in scale and complexity, that equation no longer looks quite so simple and teams have found themselves dealing with fragmented telemetry and unclear signals. It now takes longer to understand what’s gone wrong, and even longer to fix it. And to add to the challenge further, the cost of storing and processing all this telemetry and data continues to be on the rise.
Vice President of Sales for Log Management at Dynatrace.
This is prompting organizations to reconsider where the problem should be addressed. Rather than collecting everything and attempting to make sense of it later, attention is shifting towards improving telemetry earlier in its lifecycle. Filtering, enriching and directing it from the outset can make the information reaching teams more relevant and ultimately easier to act on.
More data doesn’t always mean better insight
The volume of telemetry available isn’t the fundamental issue. Its quality is. As AI-driven capabilities become deeply embedded in software delivery and operations, the quality of observability telemetry becomes even more important. Collecting telemetry without filtering out what isn’t needed can leave employees spending more time managing information than extracting value from it.
Fragmentation makes this even more challenging. With data sitting across several tools and agents, each of which generates varied forms of signal and alert. When an outage occurs, teams may then need to piece together inconsistent information from across those tools before they can understand the root-cause of the problem. Consuming valuable time while the impact on the business continues to grow.
There is also a significant financial cost attached to this approach. Processing and storing telemetry and data at scale requires considerable resources, particularly when organizations are retaining information that contributes more noise than insight. In the traditional sense, this isn’t a technology problem. It’s a telemetry and data quality concern, and the longer it’s ignored, the worse it usually gets.
Rethinking where telemetry is processed
One way organizations are responding is by moving intelligence further upstream in the technology stack. In practice, that means making decisions about telemetry earlier – filtering out what isn’t useful, enriching important information and routing meaningful telemetry before it reaches downstream systems.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
Teams are beginning to collect, process and route relevant observability telemetry in real-time before it is ingested into downstream systems. As a result, there is a less volume to handle, reduced expenses and cleaner telemetry to deal with since only the relevant signals are sent downstream.
Open standards such as OpenTelemtry are making it increasingly possible to take this approach across complex environments. They allow teams to gather telemetry consistently without being dependent on a particular vendor or set of tools. That flexibility is particularly valuable when working with intricate, distributed systems that span several clouds, security and storage platforms.
Furthermore, as environments continue to evolve, it makes adapting to them that much easier.
AI needs reliable information to make reliable decisions
The implications become particularly important as organizations introduce more AI-powered capabilities into their operations. AI systems depend on accurate, contextualized telemetry and data to produce insights and automate decisions.
Teams are not only slowed down by incomplete or cluttered telemetry, but it’s this simple: poor quality telemetry leads to poor quality insights. When those insights are applied to large-scale automated decision-making, the margin for error drastically lowers.
The same principle applies to trust. Teams responsible for automated systems need to understand what has happened and explain why decisions about performance or security have been made. Doing so becomes much more difficult when those decisions are based on inconsistent information.
And this requirement for confidence matters far beyond just the technical teams. As senior management and board members are being increasingly asked to support AI-driven decision making, they need to trust the information those decisions are built upon. Credible, consistent telemetry and data can make that conversation much simpler.
The operational advantages are also evident. Teams can work quicker if they aren’t continuously battling erratic telemetry and data. They spend less time on manual research, detect issues early, and automate with greater confidence.
A strong telemetry and data foundation and a unified, context-driven platform not only enhance daily operations but also increases the successes of the AI-powered capabilities the organization invests in over time.
Quality has to be built in from the beginning
Ultimately, faster innovation and better customer outcomes depend on organizations having useful telemetry and signals available when they are needed. The good news is that it doesn't require starting from scratch, it's about making choices early in the telemetry lifecycle.
By introducing intelligence at that stage, teams can improve the quality of what ultimately reaches their observability platforms and ensure it can scale as their environments grow. The advantage will not come from simply collecting more. It will come from ensuring the telemetry an organization does collect is relevant, trustworthy and ready to support action.

articles.title: Meta lança IA de peso aberto que roda em Macs; veja como funciona
articles.text:
A Meta lançou, nesta quinta-feira (15), o Muse Spark Open, modelo de inteligência artificial (IA) de peso aberto voltado a tarefas complexas de programação, raciocínio e execução de atividades por agentes de IA. A novidade chama a atenção por ter sido otimizada para funcionar diretamente em computadores da Apple, em colaboração entre duas empresas que historicamente disputam espaço no setor de tecnologia.
De acordo com a Meta, o modelo reúne 816 bilhões de parâmetros e conta com janela de contexto de até um milhão de tokens. Os pesos estão disponíveis para download, permitindo que desenvolvedores executem e adaptem a tecnologia em suas próprias infraestruturas, dentro das condições estabelecidas pela licença.
A iniciativa também representa aposta na execução local de modelos avançados, reduzindo a dependência de serviços de IA hospedados exclusivamente na nuvem.
Como funciona o Muse Spark Open?
O Muse Spark Open foi desenvolvido para lidar com tarefas que exigem várias etapas de raciocínio, projetos complexos de software e atividades executadas por agentes de IA. Diferentemente de assistentes que apenas respondem a perguntas, esses agentes podem trabalhar em sequências de ações para atingir um objetivo.
O modelo é multimodal: consegue receber informações em texto, imagens, áudio e vídeo, embora sua saída seja textual. Segundo a documentação técnica da Meta, ele utiliza arquitetura chamada mixture of experts (mistura de especialistas).
Embora tenha 816 bilhões de parâmetros no total, cerca de 42 bilhões ficam ativos para cada token processado. Isso permite concentrar o processamento em partes específicas da rede neural, sem dispensar a memória necessária para manter o modelo completo carregado.
A Meta afirma que a tecnologia foi projetada para trabalhos prolongados de programação, engenharia de software e raciocínio em múltiplas etapas. O modelo também pode ser personalizado por desenvolvedores.
Por que são necessários dois Macs potentes?
- A empresa trabalhou com a Apple para otimizar a execução do modelo por meio do MLX, estrutura de aprendizado de máquina desenvolvida para os chips da companhia;
- A configuração destacada pelas empresas utiliza dois computadores Mac Studio equipados com chips M5 Ultra, cada um com até 512 GB de memória unificada. Juntos, os equipamentos podem oferecer até 1 TB de memória para manter o modelo disponível durante a execução;
- A arquitetura dos chips da Apple permite que a GPU integrada acesse a memória unificada. Segundo a Meta, a largura de banda de memória do M5 Ultra chega a 1,2 TB/s, característica importante para alimentar o processamento de modelos dessa dimensão;
- Na prática, isso significa que executar o Muse Spark Open localmente exige equipamentos de alto desempenho e não é opção viável para qualquer Mac. A configuração apresentada é voltada principalmente a desenvolvedores e equipes com recursos para montar infraestrutura robusta;
- A empresa demonstrou o modelo em tarefas que incluem alterações em aplicativo de peso aberto para Mastodon, com correções de erros, novos recursos e compilação do projeto. Também mostrou o sistema trabalhando com o DaVinci Resolve, software de edição de vídeo, para analisar imagens e selecionar trechos que poderiam ser recortados em formato vertical.
Leia mais:
- Multa de R$ 138 milhões faz Meta acionar Suprema Corte em Londres
- MPF investiga Meta e X por bloqueios e remoções de conteúdo nas eleições 2026
- PT denuncia Meta à OEA por suposta interferência nas eleições de 2026
Modelo pode ser usado fora dos computadores da Apple
Apesar da parceria com a Apple, o Muse Spark Open não está restrito aos Macs. A Meta disponibilizou os pesos para download e anunciou acesso por plataformas de API, incluindo Baseten, Fireworks AI, Groq, Modal, Nebius, OpenRouter e Together AI.
O modelo também é compatível com diferentes ferramentas de execução, entre elas SGLang, vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, Hugging Face Transformers, MLX e llama.cpp. Há configurações voltadas a diferentes tipos de hardware, incluindo aceleradores de empresas, como AMD, Intel e Nvidia.
A documentação técnica descreve versões com diferentes formatos de precisão. O formato BF16 ocupa aproximadamente 1,65 TB em pesos, enquanto a versão compactada NVFP4 tem cerca de 537 GB. Mesmo a versão menor exige infraestrutura de memória considerável para funcionar, além do espaço necessário para os próprios pesos.
O que significa ter pesos abertos?
Modelos de pesos abertos disponibilizam os parâmetros treinados para que outras pessoas possam baixar, executar e, conforme as condições da licença, adaptar a tecnologia. Isso oferece mais flexibilidade do que sistemas proprietários, cujo funcionamento depende exclusivamente dos serviços controlados pela empresa desenvolvedora.
A abordagem também pode facilitar a execução de tarefas dentro da infraestrutura de uma organização, ampliando o controle sobre dados e processos. Por outro lado, rodar modelos grandes localmente exige hardware, conhecimento técnico e recursos para manutenção.
A disponibilização dos pesos do Muse Spark Open não significa, porém, que o modelo seja inteiramente de código aberto ou que não existam restrições. A Meta utiliza a Muse Model License, que prevê condições específicas para o uso comercial.
Com o lançamento, a companhia amplia sua aposta em modelos que desenvolvedores podem executar e adaptar, enquanto a parceria com a Apple demonstra como computadores pessoais de alto desempenho podem ser usados para tarefas de IA que, até então, eram frequentemente associadas a grandes infraestruturas de servidores.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: Am Finger, im Ohr oder auf der Nase: 9 Gadgets um eure Fitness zu optimieren
articles.text:
Am Finger, im Ohr oder auf der Nase: 9 Gadgets, um eure Fitness zu optimieren
Natürlich kann man jeden Sport auch ganz ohne teure Zusatzkäufe machen. Manchmal lohnt es sich sogar, genau das zu tun: die Joggingschuhe anziehen und einfach nur loslaufen. Ohne dabei immer an Optimierung und die Überwachung des eigenen Körpers zu denken.
Aber manchmal lohnt es sich eben doch, mit funktionalen Gadgets in den Ohren, am Handgelenk oder auf der Nase die eigene Fitness etwas genauer in den Fokus zu nehmen. Sei es, um das Maximum beim Sport herauszuholen. Oder einfach nur, um eine Motivation zu haben, sich doch etwas mehr zu bewegen. articles.title: Meta and Apple team up to make Muse AI models run better on Macs
articles.text:
Meta announced the Muse Spark Open AI model today, claiming that it’s the “most capable US open-weight model to date.” But the company also says that it’s the “the first model in its class” that can “run on your desktop using two Apple M5 Ultra Mac Studios with the latest MLX framework.”
Meta and Apple team up to make Muse AI models run better on Macs
Meta and Apple’s CEOs are publicly supporting each company’s work on Muse Spark Open.
Meta and Apple, typically rivals, worked together on the launch and are publicly supporting each other.
“Muse Spark Open -- weights releasing today -- runs great on new Mac Studios thanks to work with @johnternus and Apple,” Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said on X.
“Congrats to the team!” new Apple CEO John Ternus said in a reply. “Amazing to run a model of Muse Spark Open’s caliber and scale this efficiently, right from your desk. Mac Studio keeps pushing the boundaries of on-device AI!”
“We’re excited for mommy and daddy to be playing nice again,” Meta chief AI officer Alexandr Wang said to Axios, who also noted that the companies have been collaborating over several months.
The new model is a “natively multimodal model” with 816 billion total parameters that “excels at long-horizon tasks, complex software engineering, and multi-step reasoning,” according to Meta. Apple also published a new technical post about MLX, an “array framework” for ML tasks on Apple Silicon, Muse Spark Open, and two other open models.

articles.title: Google’s Universal Cart shopping tool launches in the US | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Google on Thursday said “Universal Cart,” a tool that lets users collect and monitor products they find across search and in the Gemini app, is now available to U.S. users. The company first previewed the tool at Google I/O in May.
The idea is to make online shopping easier to manage. Find something you like, save it to your cart, and move on. When you return later, your items and shopping progress are still there, so you don’t have to hunt down the same products or start over. Universal Cart can collect items from multiple retailers, turning it into a central hub for browsing and keeping track of potential purchases.
Google says the cart can also help shoppers stay on top of deals and availability. The tool can send notifications when a saved product’s price drops or when an out-of-stock item becomes available again.
The tool is also designed to offer more tailored help during the shopping process. Google says it can take credit card perks into account when helping users choose how to pay, and also surface relevant promo codes.
Checkout is tied to Google’s Universal Commerce Protocol, or UCP, an open standard the company introduced earlier this year. UCP is designed to help AI agents and retailers work together across different parts of the shopping journey, including checkout.
Google is already deeply invested in AI-powered shopping, and Universal Cart is its latest effort to make the experience more convenient. It joins features such as conversational product discovery in Search’s AI Mode and Google’s “Let Google Call” tool, which uses an AI agent to contact nearby stores and check whether an item is in stock.
Google isn’t the only company bringing AI into e-commerce. Amazon, OpenAI, and other rivals have added agentic commerce features as companies look for ways to make chatbots useful beyond answering questions.
