articles.title: Magnetar brings faster, simpler, quantum-ready zero-knowledge proofs
articles.text:
At a glance
- A new form of computing. Zero-knowledge proofs let you run a workload and receive, alongside the result, a short proof that the program ran correctly. Anyone can check the proof in milliseconds, without rerunning the program, without trusting whoever ran it, and without needing data on which the program was run.
- Three grand challenges have stood in the way of broad adoption: making proofs fast enough to produce, making them available to normal programs without cryptographic expertise, and resting them on cryptography that will still be trusted many decades from now.
- Magnetar makes major progress on all three challenges. It proves programs written in Rust, Go, or C, runs 10 to 39 times faster on average than the prior fastest comparable systems, and rests its security only on standard hash functions. It is the latest result of more than a decade of research at Microsoft Research on making zero-knowledge proofs practical.
A new form of computing
Every result a computer produces comes with an implicit question: did the program run as claimed and produce correct outputs? Today, answering that question often requires a degree of trust alongside verification. We trust the operator, the vendor, the counterparty, or the agent, and we rely on contracts, audits, and logs to establish that trust.
Zero-knowledge proofs offer a fundamentally different approach to establishing trust. A program runs, and along with its output it produces a short proof, a cryptographic certificate that this program, on these inputs, produced this output. The proof is small and fast to check. Whoever receives it can confirm the result in milliseconds without rerunning the program, and can pass the proof on to anyone else who needs the same assurance. With the zero-knowledge property, the proof also reveals nothing about inputs that should stay private.
This changes what correctness means in the real world. A result no longer has to be trusted because of who produced it. It can be checked because of what accompanies it. An AI agent acting on someone’s behalf could attach a proof that each action complied with the policy it was given. Regulated financial institutions could prove that transactions were processed correctly without making their transactions public. These become possible once producing a proof is as routine as running the program.
Three grand challenges
Zero-knowledge proofs were invented in the 1980s, and the ideas behind proving program execution have been around nearly as long. What has kept them from becoming a general tool is three challenges that have resisted being solved at the same time.
Efficiency. Producing a proof has historically taken millions of times more computation than running the program itself. Years of research have brought that overhead down, but the fastest systems have achieved their speed by making compromises elsewhere.
Generality and usability. Many proof systems require developers to manually rewrite their program as a cryptographic circuit, which is a fixed arithmetic description of that exact computation. This takes months. Every change to the application means a new circuit, and the translation is itself a frequent source of security bugs. A general-purpose alternative is to prove the execution of an ordinary processor, so that any compiled program can be proven as written. Until recently, that generality came at a steep cost in speed or security.
Security. A proof is only as strong as the cryptography beneath it. Many proof systems rest on elliptic curves, which can be broken by a sufficiently powerful quantum computer. Microsoft is addressing this problem with its Quantum Safe Program, which will move its products and services to post-quantum cryptography, a goal it recently accelerated to 2029. Post-quantum proof systems already exist, but some rest on lattice assumptions, and most rest on new cryptographic functions invented to reduce the cost of proving. These new cryptographic functions have not faced the decades of scrutiny given to the cryptography protecting today’s internet, and some rest on mathematical conjectures about error-correcting codes that have not been proven. They have bought their speed with strong assumptions.
PODCAST SERIES
More than a decade of work
For more than a decade, Microsoft Research has worked on making zero-knowledge proofs and verifiable computing practical. Early research followed two approaches, both practical only for small programs. The first (opens in new tab) (opens in new tab)lets a verifier check a long computation through a short conversation with the prover using a technique called the sum-check protocol (opens in new tab), but this applied only to computations with a particular layered structure. The second (opens in new tab) (opens in new tab)used elliptic-curve cryptography to create very small proofs for almost any computation. But this requires a one-time trusted setup involving secret information which, if leaked, could allow anyone to forge proofs. This approach is also vulnerable to quantum computers.
In 2019, a new zero-knowledge proof system called Spartan returned to the sum-check approach and made it work for general-purpose programs without a trusted setup. Spartan can also be instantiated with different cryptographic building blocks. That flexibility is what later allowed the proof system to be built on hash functions alone. A sequence of results then filled in the remaining pieces:
- Phalanx (opens in new tab), in 2021, showed how to exploit repetition, such as a processor running the same instruction cycle on every step, to prove computations an order of magnitude faster than Spartan. Magnetar’s processor description is built on this idea.
- Nova (opens in new tab), HyperNova (opens in new tab), NeutronNova (opens in new tab), Neo and SuperNeo (opens in new tab) showed that stopping Spartan’s proving early, and folding the partial results together, makes it practical to prove computations of any size at far lower cost.
- Brakedown (opens in new tab), in 2021, introduced a fast hash-based commitment scheme and combined it with Spartan, giving the first Spartan variant whose security rests on standard hash functions.
- Spice (opens in new tab), Lasso (opens in new tab), Nebula (opens in new tab), and then Twist and Shout (opens in new tab) made the memory operations at the heart of a general-purpose processor inexpensive to prove, and Jolt (opens in new tab) showed that combining them with Spartan can efficiently prove the execution of a complete processor.
- Earlier this year, Vega (opens in new tab) applied this line of work to digital identity, proving facts from a government credential in under a tenth of a second.
- More recently, BinarySpartan (opens in new tab) brought Spartan to binary fields, where a processor’s logic and standard hash functions can be efficiently expressed. BinarySpartan also relies on Ligerito (opens in new tab), a Brakedown-style commitment scheme with much shorter proofs, and on ring switching (opens in new tab), which makes it efficient to commit to vectors of bits.
Each of these solved a piece of the problem. Magnetar is where the pieces come together.
Magnetar
Magnetar is a zero-knowledge virtual machine, or zkVM, and it makes major progress on all three challenges at once.
It is general-purpose. Magnetar proves the execution of RISC-V, an open processor architecture with mature compilers for every mainstream language. A developer writes a program in Rust, Go, or C, compiles it as usual, and Magnetar proves it as written. Consider what this means in practice. A business policy, a data pipeline, or an interpreter for the Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM) is just a program, and the engineers who already maintain it can prove their executions exactly as written. As a result, proving stops being a specialist activity.
It is faster than prior systems in the same class. Magnetar proves 7.2 to 8.7 million processor instructions per second on a laptop. Across 15 benchmark programs, from cryptographic hashing to token transfers inside a small EVM interpreter, it is 10 to 39 times faster on average than the fastest existing zkVMs on the same machine, and more than 300 times faster than two others on a token-transfer benchmark. An optimized Magnetar proves 9.5–12.8 million cycles per second, which increases each speedup reported here by about 1.3×. Its proofs verify in about 12 milliseconds.
Its security rests on standard cryptography. Magnetar depends on a standard hash function such as SHA-256 or SHA-3, the same primitives that already protect every organization’s systems. It requires no elliptic curves, no lattices, no special-purpose hash functions, no trusted setup, and no unproven conjecture about error-correcting codes. Hash functions are the most thoroughly studied primitives in the cryptographic toolkit, and they are the basis of the stateless hash-based signatures that NIST standardized as its own conservative post-quantum option. For a system that must still be trustworthy in many decades to come, relying only on standard hash functions removes a cryptographic migration from the roadmap.
The same design decision pays a second dividend. Checking a Magnetar proof consists mostly of evaluating standard hash functions and binary-field arithmetic, which are exactly the operations Magnetar proves efficiently. Verifying a proof is therefore an ordinary workload for it. This is what allows Magnetar to prove computations of any size, by proving them in pieces and then combining the pieces. This also allows Magnetar to prove a long-running system such as a ledger or a blockchain.
The technical paper gives the full design, security analysis, and measurements.
Looking ahead
Magnetar advances zero-knowledge proofs and verifiable computing to a stage where they can be built on the cryptography that organizations already trust, at speeds that make it usable, by engineers who write normal code. Magnetar enables a future where cryptographic proofs are a routine output of computation. We expect that technology leaders will stop asking whether proofs of execution are practical and focus instead on which results would they prefer to verify rather than taking on trust.
If you’re interested in exploring how zero-knowledge proofs can support your use case, we’d love to hear from you (opens in new tab).

articles.title: À court de cartes graphiques, Apple réquisitionne les Mac de ses employés
articles.text:
Les ingénieurs d’Apple viennent de documenter Minions, un système interne qui met au travail les GPU inutilisés des Mac de l’entreprise. Le principe tient en une phrase des auteurs : « un nuage GPU virtuel, dynamique et distribué, qui agrège les GPU Apple Silicon inactifs des machines macOS pour exécuter des charges d’inférence d’apprentissage automatique à grande échelle ». Avant son déploiement, certaines tâches attendaient plus de dix heures en file, faute de GPU disponibles dans le parc centralisé ; elles démarrent désormais, le plus souvent, en quelques minutes.
Quatre rouages et un chien de garde
Le dispositif repose sur quatre composants. Un serveur central, le Minion Server, reçoit les requêtes des équipes et les découpe en sous-tâches, dont l’état est consigné dans une base PostgreSQL. Sur chaque Mac enrôlé, un Minion Executor exécute sa part du calcul sur le GPU local, téléverse le résultat vers un stockage S3 et rend compte au serveur.
Un chien de garde, le Minion Watchdog, surveille l’ensemble : si une machine cesse de répondre, ses tâches sont réattribuées ailleurs. Des tableaux de bord offrent une visibilité en temps réel sur l’état du troupeau.
Les Mac mini et Mac Studio récents savent par ailleurs s’associer via RDMA sur Thunderbolt 5, en combinant mémoire et puissance de calcul pour charger un modèle trop volumineux pour une seule machine.
La disponibilité plutôt que la puissance brute
L’objectif tranche avec les grappes de GPU Nvidia, optimisées pour le débit et la latence sur de très grands modèles. Minions vise d’abord le taux d’occupation et récupère des ressources laissées en jachère sur les bureaux. Le système redistribue la puissance déjà présente sur le réseau interne, au profit des équipes qui en manquent, sans viser les modèles géants du marché.
Hors de Cupertino, des services proposent déjà aux particuliers de louer la puissance de leur Mac à des entreprises d’IA, parfois jusqu’à 200 dollars par mois. Apple vient d’appliquer la recette à l’intérieur, sur des machines qui lui appartiennent. Drôle de situation pour l’entreprise qui conçoit l’un des meilleurs hardware d’inférence au monde.

articles.title: The Batman 2 pourrait t-il ne jamais reprendre son tournage ? Le président de DC répond
articles.text:
Warner Bros. et DC Studios ont suspendu le tournage de The Batman: Part II le 5 octobre, à Londres, le temps que Matt Reeves se consacre à « une affaire familiale ». Aucune date de reprise n’a été donnée. Le lendemain, Paramount Skydance finalisait le rachat de Warner Bros. Discovery pour 110 milliards de dollars (environ 95 milliards d’euros), sous le nom de Skydance. Ces deux annonces coup sur coup ont fait craindre aux fans un abandon du film.
Beaucoup s’interrogeaient : le blockbuster porté par Robert Pattinson risquait-il de faire les frais des réorganisations internes ou d’être enterré avant même la fin de ses prises de vues ?
« Est-il possible que le tournage ne reprenne jamais ? »
À l’approche de la sortie de Clayface, Peter Safran, qui codirige DC Studios avec James Gunn, a répondu aux questions d’IGN ce 14 octobre. Ce film d’horreur, classé R aux États-Unis (interdit aux moins de 17 ans non accompagnés), est réalisé par James Watkins, sur un scénario de Mike Flanagan et Hossein Amini. Le journaliste lui a demandé, en pesant ses mots, s’il existait un scénario dans lequel le tournage de The Batman: Part II ne reprendrait pas. Peter Safran a répondu d’un mot : « Non. »
Tout en reconnaissant à demi-mot les embûches actuelles (« Tout le monde est conscient des difficultés que nous traversons en ce moment »), le bras droit de James Gunn s’est voulu particulièrement rassurant sur la qualité du matériel déjà mis en boîte. Selon lui, les premières images du tournage sont « absolument fantastiques » et la confiance envers le réalisateur Matt Reeves reste totale.
Le maintien de cette suite pose néanmoins la question de la cohabitation entre deux incarnations différentes du protecteur de Gotham. Le Batman de Matt Reeves évolue hors du DCU, l’univers partagé piloté par James Gunn et Peter Safran, et ne sortira qu’en 2028, après plusieurs reports. Le DCU prépare sa propre version du héros, qui doit apparaître dans Batman: The Brave and the Bold, prévu pour 2028.
Sur ce point, Peter Safran martèle que le public saura faire la différence et refuse de standardiser les visions artistiques. L’objectif affiché reste de laisser chaque cinéaste imprimer sa propre patte visuelle sur Gotham, tout en conservant l’ADN poisseux et dangereux de la ville, sans pour autant saturer le marché avec deux Batman qui se tireraient dans les pattes.

articles.title: Vaonis annonce Atlas, un télescope connecté modulaire qui peut changer d'optique comme un appareil photo, mais il coûte une fortune
articles.text:
Dix ans après Stellina, son tout premier télescope connecté, la start-up montpelliéraine Vaonis veut aller encore plus loin. Elle a présenté ce jeudi 15 octobre Atlas, un télescope qui a la particularité d’être modulaire. Le principe : on achète une monture motorisée, puis on y fixe un ou deux tubes optiques, comme on change d’objectif sur un appareil photo.
En astronomie, il ne faut pas le même type de matériel pour faire du planétaire et du ciel profond. Vaonis tente donc d’apporter une solution à ce problème, aussi onéreuse soit-elle. Atlas coûtera 4 990 euros dans sa version de base une fois l’offre de lancement terminée, soit 2 000 euros de plus que le Vespera Pro 2, le dernier télescope haut de la gamme de la marque.
Vaonis n’a évidemment jamais été la marque la moins chère du marché, surtout en face d’un ZWO qui tire fortement les prix vers le bas, notamment avec son récent Seestar S50 Pro vendu à 999 euros et son Seestar S30 Pro encore moins cher. Avec Atlas, Vaonis sort carrément de cette bataille.
Jusqu’à 330€ d’avantages avec nos offres Hello Prime ou Hello Prime Duo, dont 80€ cash à l’ouverture de compte !
Plus de lumière, mais moins d’autonomie
Pour l’instant, un seul tube existe, l’Atlas 80. Il associe une optique de 80 mm de diamètre (un quadruplet apochromatique, c’est-à-dire quatre lentilles qui limitent les franges colorées autour des étoiles) à une focale de 360 mm et à un capteur Sony IMX585 de 8,3 mégapixels. D’après Vaonis, le système SkyDock permet de retirer ou de changer ce module en quelques secondes, sans outil.
Face au Vespera 3, l’écart vient surtout de l’optique, puisque le capteur est le même IMX585. Avec 80 mm de diamètre contre 50 mm, Atlas offre environ 2,5 fois plus de surface pour capter la lumière. En contrepartie, le champ se resserre. Avec le même capteur et une focale environ 1,5 fois plus longue, Atlas devrait cadrer une portion du ciel d’environ 1,8 x 1 degré, contre 2,6 x 1,4 degrés pour le Vespera 3. Les plus grandes nébuleuses comme Orion ne tiendront donc pas toujours dans une seule image.
Atlas pèse 6,5 kg avec un seul module et sans le trépied, contre 5 kg pour un Vespera 3 ou un Vespera Pro 2. On est donc loin d’un modèle compact et facile à transporter. Et il annonce jusqu’à 6 heures d’autonomie, contre 11 heures pour ces derniers Vespera.
La version Twin, elle, embarque deux Atlas 80 pointés vers la même cible. Selon Vaonis, ce mode SkyTwin capte deux fois plus de lumière, ce qui réduit le temps nécessaire pour faire ressortir les fins détails des nébuleuses et galaxies.
Dans tous les cas, une caméra grand-angle, SkyGuard, filme le ciel en continu. Elle sert à choisir ses cibles en réalité augmentée dans l’application Gaia, et même à monter un timelapse de la nuit.
Une modularité encore à construire
Une bonne partie de l’écosystème reste à l’état de promesse. Un tube consacré aux planètes, une table équatoriale, des filtres et un sac à dos sont annoncés, sans date ni prix. Vaonis compense ce flou avec une garantie de 10 ans sur la monture et de 5 ans sur le module.
Sur le papier, Atlas peut séduire un astronome amateur qui a fait le tour de son matériel et qui veut évoluer. Mais pour débuter, un Vespera 2, 3 ou même un Seestar S50 Pro ou S30 Pro coûtent de deux à sept fois moins cher qu’Atlas à son prix public, et ils font déjà amplement le travail sur les nébuleuses et les galaxies.
Les précommandes pour Atlas sont ouvertes depuis ce jeudi 15 octobre, au prix de lancement de 3 990 euros pour un seul tube et 5 490 euros pour deux tubes, jusqu’au 15 novembre 2026. Après cette date, le prix passera à 4 990 euros pour un tube et 6 990 euros pour deux tubes. Les premières livraisons se feront à partir de mars 2027.

articles.title: Sam Altman rechaza que la IA sea una nueva Revolución Industrial: “Debe dar más poder a las personas”
articles.text:
Sam Altman subió al escenario del DevDay para presentar un agente de IA que trabaja las 24 horas, y acabó hablando de engranajes. “La mejor versión de la IA no consiste en convertir a las personas en engranajes de una máquina gigantesca que gira cada vez más deprisa”, dijo el consejero delegado de OpenAI. Y añadió que “hay partes de la vida que no podemos ni debemos automatizar” y que la IA “debería consistir en dar a las personas más poder sobre sus propias vidas”.
La metáfora tiene año y medio. El 18 de abril de 2025, Altman escribió en X que la IA iba a parecerse más al Renacimiento que a la Revolución Industrial. En San Francisco la desarrolló un poco más.
¿Rechaza Altman la Revolución Industrial o la quiere corregida?
Ninguna de las dos cosas del todo. Altman dijo que cree que la IA tendrá un impacto mayor que el de la Revolución Industrial, así que la escala no la discute. Lo que discute es el modelo. “No creo que el propósito de esta tecnología sea simplemente hacer girar la manivela económica cada vez más deprisa en beneficio de las propias IA”, afirmó, y añadió: “Creo que deberíamos aprender de los errores de la Revolución Industrial, y pienso que deberíamos parecernos más al Renacimiento”.
Dicho de otro modo, no se discute cuánto pesa la máquina. Se discute para qué gira.
En la ONU pidió contar los fallos “antes de que se conviertan en catástrofes”
Seis días antes del DevDay, el 23 de septiembre, Altman había hablado en persona ante el Consejo de Seguridad de la ONU. Allí defendió un camino pragmático entre el optimismo ciego y el pesimismo, con tres principios: que, “a medida que la IA se vuelve más capaz, las personas deben seguir en el centro de las decisiones sobre IA”; que los beneficios del progreso científico y del crecimiento económico “deben ser por y para las personas”; y que “esta tecnología debe empoderar a las personas individualmente”.
Y una frase que resume el tono: “La historia continua del progreso humano no es que las herramientas sustituyan la capacidad de acción humana. Es que las herramientas adecuadas hacen a las personas más capaces”.
Llevó además peticiones concretas. Un mecanismo de estándares nacionales e internacionales para la IA de frontera (cómo medir capacidades, evaluar riesgos y decidir si las salvaguardas bastan). Protocolos “precisos y rápidos” para notificar y clasificar incidentes, “para que el mundo aprenda de los fallos antes de que se conviertan en catástrofes”. Y canales seguros entre gobiernos, operadores de infraestructuras críticas y expertos técnicos para compartir vulnerabilidades.
Eso sí, con una condición: que esos estándares no “blinden a los actores establecidos ni favorezcan un modelo de negocio frente a otro”, y que cada gobierno decida cómo incorporarlos a su ordenamiento.
Entre la ONU y el DevDay, OpenAI avisó a decenas de instituciones y canceló un modelo
La secuencia, con fechas: el miércoles 23, el discurso de la ONU. El viernes 25, OpenAI dijo haber avisado a decenas de instituciones por casos de comportamiento desalineado de sus agentes. El lunes 28, anunció que no lanzará GPT-6.1 Astra porque, en pruebas internas, no cumplía sus estándares.
Saachi Jain, responsable de sistemas de seguridad de la empresa, dijo que el modelo no alcanzaba el listón en alcance y autorización de las tareas ni en cómo informa al usuario del trabajo hecho. En julio, OpenAI ya había reconocido que modelos de prueba salieron de un entorno controlado y atacaron a Hugging Face. El martes 29, el DevDay.
Altman no se refirió a esas preocupaciones en el discurso principal. En el turno de preguntas dijo que la empresa invierte más en seguridad, protección y supervisión de los agentes de IA. A los pocos días, OpenAI elevó a más de 100 las organizaciones notificadas por esos casos.
Dots, el agente “siempre activo”, no está disponible en España con el plan Pro
Lo que presentó se llama Dots: agentes que siguen trabajando en proyectos y tareas cotidianas en tu nombre, tienen su propio ordenador en la nube y se conectan mediante plugins a más de 4.000 aplicaciones. Llega, además, junto a otros productos que se solapan, como los espacios de trabajo compartidos y las tareas programadas.
Funcionan con GPT-6 Astra, el modelo que el Instituto de Seguridad de IA del Reino Unido evaluó antes de su lanzamiento. El 28 de septiembre publicó que, en una simulación y con los clasificadores de ciberseguridad de OpenAI desactivados, GPT-6 Astra completó ataques no autorizados a la cadena de suministro, fuera del alcance de la tarea, el 29,2 % de las veces. Todas las acciones fueron simuladas, y las salvaguardas estándar de OpenAI, que no se usaron en la prueba, están diseñadas para bloquear ese comportamiento.
El primer dot va incluido sin coste extra en los planes Pro y Business Premium, y Enterprise puede probar la beta si su administrador la activa. Pero según la ayuda de OpenAI, el despliegue a usuarios Pro, en cualquiera de sus niveles, excluye el Espacio Económico Europeo, Suiza y el Reino Unido.
Business Premium y Enterprise, en cambio, se despliegan en todo el mundo. Traducido: desde España, de momento, solo se puede probar con un plan de empresa y no con un Pro personal. Y el acceso puede tardar varios días en llegar a la cuenta, incluso donde ya se ofrece.
OpenAI no da fecha para Europa. En su anuncio solo dice que planea ampliar los dots a más usuarios “pronto”.

articles.title: Physicists discover “astonishing” property of light that defies expectations
articles.text:
Physicists discover “astonishing” property of light that defies expectations
- Date:
- October 13, 2026
- Source:
- University of East Anglia
- Summary:
- Scientists have uncovered a surprising hidden ability of light that allows it to develop spinning, twisting behavior as it travels through empty space, without special lenses, mirrors, or materials. Researchers discovered that light’s internal geometry can naturally produce left- and right-handed patterns, challenging long-standing assumptions about how light behaves. By carefully arranging a beam’s structure, scientists can control where and how these spinning patterns emerge, unlocking a new way to manipulate light.
- Share:
Scientists have discovered a surprising ability of light that allows it to develop spinning patterns as it moves through empty space, without relying on special lenses, mirrors, or materials. The finding reveals that light possesses a hidden geometric structure that can influence its behavior in ways researchers previously thought were difficult to achieve.
The discovery comes from an international team led by researchers at the University of East Anglia (UEA) in the United Kingdom, working with scientists in South Africa. Their experiments demonstrate that carefully prepared light can be controlled through its own internal geometry, offering a new approach to manipulating how light spins and twists.
The findings challenge long-standing assumptions about how different properties of light interact. They could eventually lead to more sensitive medical tests, faster and more secure communications, and advanced quantum technologies that use light to transmit and protect information.
Why the Direction of Light's Spin Matters
One of the most intriguing aspects of the discovery involves chirality, a scientific term describing the difference between left-handed and right-handed structures.
Human hands provide a familiar example. Although they are mirror images of each other, a left hand cannot be perfectly superimposed on a right hand. Many molecules have a similar property, including compounds used in medicines. Two versions of the same molecule can have nearly identical chemical structures yet produce very different effects in the body.
Scientists can distinguish these molecular forms by studying how they interact with light that has a particular rotational behavior. Traditionally, producing and controlling such light has often involved specialized materials, carefully designed surfaces, or powerful lenses that focus beams extremely tightly.
The research demonstrates that appropriately prepared light can develop this behavior naturally as it travels, without requiring those additional optical components.
"Our work shows that light can naturally develop this handed behavior all on its own," said Dr. Kayn Forbes from UEA's School of Chemistry, Pharmacy and Pharmacology.
"You just have to prepare it in the right way.
"Most people think of light as traveling in straight lines. But scientists can also create structured light -- light whose brightness, shape, and direction are carefully arranged.
"One extreme example is light that twists as it travels, forming a corkscrew shape known as an optical vortex. Each twist can carry information, making this kind of light valuable for high-speed internet, secure communications, and advanced sensors.
"Light can also spin as it travels, depending on how it is polarized. This spin can be left-handed or right-handed -- another form of chirality."
Scientists Discover How Light Develops a Hidden Spin
Light can exhibit different kinds of rotational behavior. An optical vortex, for example, has a wave pattern that twists around its direction of travel, much like a corkscrew. Light also has a property known as polarization, which describes how its electric field oscillates. Certain polarization patterns produce a form of rotation called spin.
Physicists have long studied the relationship between these two properties. However, the interactions responsible for the newly observed effect were generally considered extremely weak and difficult to detect without specialized experimental conditions.
The researchers found that the situation changes when a beam of light is prepared in a particular balanced configuration.
Under those conditions, the beam can initially have no spin, yet distinct regions with spinning behavior emerge as it travels through free space. The effect does not require the light to pass through engineered materials or additional optical devices.
"It starts off with no spin at all," explained MSc student Light Mkhumbuza, who carried out key experiments. "But as the beam travels forward, spinning regions appear and separate out -- almost as if the spin was hiding and then revealed itself."
Rather than creating spin through an external optical component, the researchers demonstrated how the beam's existing internal structure can determine where spinning regions develop during propagation.
The Hidden Geometry That Controls Light
To explain this unexpected behavior, the researchers turned to topology, a mathematical field concerned with properties that remain unchanged when objects are continuously stretched, bent, or reshaped.
Dr. Isaac Nape, from the University of the Witwatersrand in Johannesburg, South Africa, offered a simple way to understand the concept.
"To explain it, imagine a mug and a doughnut," he said. "You can morph one into the other without tearing it, because they both have one hole. That hole is a topological feature."
The researchers found that structured light possesses its own topological characteristics, encoded in the arrangement of its polarization.
This underlying pattern acts like a mathematical fingerprint. Even as the light beam changes shape while traveling, its topological structure remains, influencing how different regions of the beam evolve.
As a result, the arrangement of the light itself can determine where its left-handed and right-handed spinning patterns become visible.
The discovery gives scientists a way to guide this behavior by designing the beam's initial structure, rather than depending on specialized materials to produce the desired effect.
"This gives us a completely new tuning knob for light. By adjusting its topology, we can decide how and where chirality appears," said Dr. Nape.
Potential Breakthroughs in Medicine and Communications
The ability to control light through its geometry could eventually make several important optical technologies simpler, more affordable, and more versatile.
One particularly promising application involves medical diagnostics and pharmaceutical research. Because many biologically important molecules have left-handed and right-handed forms, carefully structured light could help scientists identify these differences with greater sensitivity. Such tools could be valuable for evaluating drug safety and detecting biological markers associated with disease.
The same principles could support smaller optical sensors capable of identifying chemicals or biological substances without requiring large, sophisticated laboratory instruments.
Communications technology could also benefit. By encoding information into different twisting and spinning patterns, researchers may be able to increase the amount of data carried by individual light beams. This could contribute to faster optical communications, improved information security, and future quantum networks.
Other potential uses include manipulating microscopic particles, cells, and molecules with light, as well as developing more resilient quantum systems. Topological properties may help protect delicate quantum information against certain forms of noise and interference.
"The implications are wide-ranging," said Dr. Forbes. "This work could lead to simpler and more sensitive medical tests, especially in drug development.
"It could also be used to pack more information into laser beams -- boosting data capacity for communications, including future quantum networks.
"And because the effect doesn't rely on fragile materials or precision-engineered surfaces, it could be easier and cheaper to use in real-world technologies.
"This research could lay the foundations for a new generation of light-based technologies, by showing that light's behavior can be controlled using its own internal geometry," he added.
These applications remain possibilities for future development, but the underlying discovery provides researchers with another way to design and control the behavior of light.
A Hidden Property of Light Finally Revealed
For decades, scientists have relied on increasingly sophisticated optical equipment to produce and manipulate unusual forms of light. The findings suggest that some of these behaviors can instead arise from carefully designed structures already encoded within a light beam.
By showing how topology governs the emergence of spinning regions during propagation, the team has revealed a previously underappreciated connection between light's geometry and its physical behavior.
The discovery also illustrates how much remains to be learned about something as familiar and extensively studied as light.
"For something so familiar, light is proving to be far richer, stranger and more powerful than anyone imagined," said Dr. Forbes.
"And astonishingly, this new behavior has been there all along -- just waiting to be seen."
The research, 'Topological Control of Chirality and Spin with Structured Light', was published in the journal Light: Science & Applications.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of East Anglia. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Light Mkhumbuza, Pedro Ornelas, Angela Dudley, Isaac Nape, Kayn A. Forbes. Topological control of chirality and spin with structured light. Light: Science, 2026; 15 (1) DOI: 10.1038/s41377-026-02278-6

articles.title: Profitable French accounting company Dougs raises €50 million to accelerate AI automation | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Dougs, a Lyon-based technology company delivering regulated accounting and financial management services to small businesses, has raised €50 million in funding.
The funding came from Expedition Growth Capital, a growth equity firm with offices in London and Boston, backing rapidly growing, founder-owned software and AI companies on their path to market leadership. It manages more than €900 million ($1 billion) in assets and raised €323 million for Fund III in December 2025.
“Artificial intelligence is radically transforming the services sector, but its impact is all the greater when underpinned by deep domain expertise. Dougs is a rare example of this fusion in the accountancy industry. The company is mastering the optimal mix of deterministic code, frontier AI and certified professionals to deliver industry leading service and value to a rapidly growing base of 50,000 customers. We are convinced that this combination makes it one of the best-positioned players to shape the next generation of accountancy in Europe,” said Oliver Thomas, founder and Managing Partner at Expedition Growth.
Founded by chartered accountants and registered with the French Order of Chartered Accountants, Dougs has been profitable since its founding in 2015 and self-funded until its first funding round in 2023. Rather than selling software services or tools to accountants, Dougs owns the client relationship directly.
Its platform covers company formation, accounting, legal, payroll, invoicing through a certified e-invoicing platform, a business account, and wealth management via a dedicated subsidiary. It now serves more than 50,000 businesses and generates over €50 million in annual recurring revenue (ARR), with a growth rate of 50% or more annually for a decade.
Dougs says it has built the entire technology stack in-house and employs over 100 engineers. Since being founded in 2014, the company has filed hundreds of thousands of tax returns and financial statements, building a proprietary record of accounting workflows, customer context, exceptions, and professional decisions.
“We are chartered accountants who happen to write our own software. That is the whole point,” said Patrick Maurice, CEO and co-founder of Dougs.
The combination of technology and human expertise, Dougs argues, has driven gross margins above 80%, well above the industry norm of below 50%. The company says a single Dougs accountant is able to handle many times more clients than a typical accountant.
“We can automate accounting production because we have done the work ourselves for ten years and know what good looks like. Every improvement in AI models makes our service faster and cheaper, while our regulatory licence and the scale of our client base are very hard to copy. With this round, we will finish automating production and use the time it frees up to get closer to our clients,” added Maurice.
Dougs has already embedded AI into its accounting production, completing bookkeeping workflows autonomously, and is now pushing toward agentic accounting services, where financial systems are generated entirely by agentic systems, reviewed and signed off by a chartered accountant.
“Automating most of the bookkeeping was only the starting point. AI lets us go much further and rethink how accounting is actually produced. We built our own agentic platform, with a harness that plugs straight into our tools and encodes our accounting expertise. Our accountants work with it every day, and it’s already running entire stages of production end to end. The next milestone is financial statements generated autonomously, then reviewed and signed off by an accountant. AI does the heavy lifting while our accountants bring the judgement,” said Florent Galland, COO and co-founder of Dougs.
Dougs says the new capital will be used to accelerate its proprietary AI and automation technology, broaden its platform across accounting, legal, and financial management, while strengthening its presence in France through a network of local partners.
In a statement, the company said France represents a market of over €20 billion across accounting and adjacent services, and Dougs’ core segment alone accounts for approximately €1.5 billion today. The company is targeting €100 million in ARR and 100,000 customers in the coming years, with the goal of becoming France’s largest chartered accounting business.

articles.title: Apple Homeview-Hub, Homepod Mini 2 & mehr: Das ist die neue Smarthome-Offensive
articles.text:
Apple Homeview-Hub: Alle Infos zu den neuen Smarthome-Gadgets
Das „Welcome Home“-Event von Apple hat es mit seinem Namen schon verraten: Der iPhone-Konzern plante geraume Zeit eine neue Offensive im Smarthome-Sektor. Jetzt hat Apple sein Portfolio deutlich aufgestockt. Im Zentrum des neuen Smarthomes steht dabei ganz klar der neue Homeview-Hub, der vom Homepod Mini und zahlreichen anderen smarten Gadgets unterstützt wird. Doch für deutsche Apple-Fans gibt es einen großen Haken.
Homeview-Hub: Deutsche Apple-Fans gehen leer aus
Beim Homeview-Hub handelt es sich um ein 7‑Zoll-großes Display, das auf einer stationären Halterung samt integriertem Lautsprecher befestigt ist. Wer will, kann das Display aber auch in einer Wall-Mounted-Version kaufen und es stattdessen an der Wand anbringen. Mit an Bord sind Mikrofone, eine Kamera sowie Siri AI. Über die Kamera kann der Homeview-Hub verschiedene User:innen im Haushalt erkennen und ihnen personalisierte Homescreens anzeigen lassen. Bis zu sechs Personen kann sich der smarte Hub dabei merken.
Wie bei vielen anderen smarten Hubs mit Display können über das Gadget auch Videoanrufe per Facetime geführt, Musik abgespielt und eben dein Smarthome gesteuert werden. Die Steuerung erfolgt dabei über Touch-Eingaben oder per Sprachsteuerung und Siri. Smarthome-Dashboards werden dabei in neun Kacheln auf dem viereckigen Display unterteilt. Mit ausreichend kompatiblen Geräten können sich User:innen also auch neun Videofeeds von Überwachungskameras gleichzeitig auf dem Homeview-Hub anschauen.
Gerade in Verbindung mit einem iPhone, auf dem Apple Intelligence aktiviert ist, soll Siri AI auf dem Homeview-Hub ihre Stärke demonstrieren. Dann kann die KI das Smartphone nach Nachrichten und Kalendereinträgen oder etwa Playlists bei Apple Music durchsuchen, um personalisierten Kontext über die Nutzer:innen zu erfahren. Wer kein iPhone mit Apple Intelligence nutzt, soll dennoch von Siris neuem Wissen, Konversationsfertigkeiten und „verbesserter Musiksuche“ profitieren.
Siri AI ist auch der Grund, warum deutsche und europäische Apple-Fans im Allgemeinen einen Dämpfer hinnehmen müssen. Im Kleingedruckten der Ankündigung des Smarthome-Hubs steht, dass das Gadget vorerst nicht in der EU erscheinen wird. Da Siri AI nicht in iOS in der EU verfügbar ist, bleibt auch das Gadget vorerst vom Markt fern. Wann sich das ändern wird, ist nicht klar. In anderen Märkten startet der Homeview-Hub zum Preis von 299 US-Dollar.
Homepod Mini mit integrierter Siri
Der neue Homepod Mini der zweiten Generation lässt sich aber hierzulande problemlos vorbestellen. Apple bietet den smarten Speaker für 169 Euro in Grün, Weiß, Blau, Pink und Schwarz an. Die Auslieferungen sollen ab dem 30. Oktober 2026 starten. Wie schon der Homeview-Hub unterstützt auch der Homepod Mini 2 Siri AI.
So kann ebenfalls ein iPhone mit Apple Intelligence verknüpft werden, um personalisiertere Antworten zu bekommen. Allerdings wird die KI erst per Update nachgereicht. Selbiges wird hierzulande dann wohl ausgesetzt. Wer den Homepod Mini 2 kauft, muss also auf die intelligentere Version von Siri verzichten und stattdessen mit dem regulären KI-gestützten Sprachassistenten vorliebnehmen.
Abgesehen von den KI-Neuerungen liefert der Homepod Mini der zweiten Generation jetzt nicht nur allein 360-Grad-Sound, sondern kann auch als Stereopaar und an einem Mac genutzt werden. In Verbindung mit dem neuen Apple TV 4K sind sogar vier Speaker gleichzeitig möglich, die einander im Raum erkennen und so den Sound der TV-Wiedergabe optimieren.
Neu ist auch das sogenannte „Sound Glow“. Auf der Oberseite des Homepod Mini 2 zeigt das Gerät eine Visualisierung des wiedergegebenen Sounds. Der smarte Speaker reagiert in Echtzeit auf Bässe und Höhen und nutzt für die farbliche Abstimmung die Cover-Farben von den gespielten Alben. Zu guter Letzt kann der Homepod Mini 2 natürlich auch ins Smarthome integriert werden, um Geräte per Spracheingabe zu steuern und Benachrichtigungen laut im Raum abzuspielen.
Neues Apple TV 4K mit alter Siri
Ebenso sieht es beim neuen Apple TV 4K aus. Das Gerät funktioniert dank Matter-Untertützung ebenfalls als Smarthome-Zentrale. Das war aber schon beim Vorgänger der Fall. Neu sind ein schnellerer Prozessor, der mehr Rechenleistung und dank eines Decoders qualitativ hochwertiges Streaming bei niedriger Bandbreite ermöglichen soll. In der Theorie war das neue Apple TV 4K damit auch fit für Apple Intelligence oder vorrangig Siri AI. Dass die Box darauf ausgelegt ist, zeigen die drei integrierten Fernfeldmikrofone, mit der man das Apple TV freihändig bedienen können soll.
In der Praxis schaltet Apple die neue Version von Siri in tvOS 27.2 jedoch nur in sieben Ländern frei. Deutschland gehört nicht dazu. Die Mikrofone lassen sich zwar nutzen, allerdings nur mit der alten Version von Siri. Vorbestellen lässt sich die Streaming-Box ab sofort. Ausgeliefert wird ab dem 13. November. Der Preis liegt bei 349 Euro.
Smarte Türschlösser, Klingeln und Thermostate von Apple und LG
Zu guter Letzt hat Apple die Home Collection vorgestellt. Dabei handelt es sich um eine Reihe von Gadgets von Thermostaten über Temperatursensoren bis zu smarten Türschlössern. Diese sind in Zusammenarbeit mit LG Electronics und Schneider Electric entstanden. Apple verspricht, dass sie sich allesamt mit nur einem Fingertippen mit Apple Home verbinden und nutzen lassen. Die Steuerung erfolgt über die Home-App und benötigt keinerlei Anwendung von Dritten. Neben Apple Home unterstützen die Geräte auch Matter, um sie in andere Systeme wie Home Assistant integrieren und vernetzen zu können.
Im Bereich der Eigenheimüberwachung bietet Apple eine LG‑Videotürklingel mit 2,5-K-Auflösung (250 Dollar), eine Flutlichtkamera mit Bewegungsmelder (400 Dollar) sowie eine Outdoor-Kamera mit Nachtsicht (300 Dollar) und eine Indoor-Kamera (200 Dollar) an. Alle Kameras funktionieren mit iCloud Plus, wodurch User:innen auf die Aufzeichnungen der vergangenen zehn Tage zugreifen können. Apple Intelligence kann dabei sogar die Aufnahmen durchsuchen und zusammenfassen, was darin passiert.
Daneben gibt es noch ein smartes Türschloss, für 350 Dollar, das Nutzer:innen und deren Apple-Produkte über Ultra-Breitband erkennt und automatisch die Tür öffnen kann. Wer die automatische Erkennung nicht nutzen will, kann iPhone oder Apple Watch aber auch an den integrierten Scanner halten oder einen PIN‑Code eingeben. Zudem bietet das Türschloss ein „verstecktes Backup-Schlüsselloch“.
Zu guter Letzt gibt es zwei Thermostate für je 200 Dollar, eins von LG, eins von Schneider Electric. So sollen Apple-User:innen die Wahl haben, welches Gerät mehr zu ihrem Smarthome-Ökosystem passt. Die Thermostate können dabei mit separat erhältlichen Temperatursensoren (je 40 Dollar) gekoppelt werden oder die Temperaturfühler nutzen, die im Homeview-Hub, dem Homepod oder Homepod Mini enthalten sind. Sämtliche Produkte der Collection sollen ab Dezember 2026 bei Apple verfügbar sein.

articles.title: What a Radioactive Lake In China Can Teach the World About Rare Earths
articles.text:
One of the singular features of Baotou, an industrial city of 2 million people in Inner Mongolia, is a 10-square-kilometer (4-square-mile) lake that is among the most polluted in the world. The artificial lake, referred to by the name of the dam associated with it, Weikuang Dam (or Baogang Tailings Dam), has for decades collected the effluent from minerals processing for China’s globally dominant iron, steel, and rare-earths industries.
Built in the late 1950s, the lake contains a highly toxic stew of industrial chemicals with substantial amounts of radioactive thorium, the latter resulting primarily from the processing of monazite ores for rare-earths. China has since greatly tightened its environmental regulations and restrictions on mining and minerals processing. For example, largely because of the environmental disaster that is Weikuang Dam, the country doesn’t permit the development or operation of stand-alone monazite mines—that is, mines where nothing is mined except monazite ore.
Now, with industrialized nations in North America, Asia, and Europe spending billions to shore up their rare-earths supply chains, and counting on monazite to help them do it, China’s history and experiences with monazite offer important lessons.
This article is a collaboration between Foreign Policy, the global magazine of politics and ideas, and IEEE Spectrum, the flagship magazine of the IEEE.
Monazite ore is a pillar of China’s rare-earths industry because it is a prime source of some less common but extremely important rare-earth elements, notably dysprosium, terbium, yttrium, and erbium. The country mines and processes vast quantities of monazite ore; it also imports huge amounts of monazite ore for processing.
Most of the domestically mined monazite ore comes from a single mine: the mammoth Bayan Obo complex, 150 kilometers north of Baotou, in Inner Mongolia. Bayan Obo, which is primarily an iron-ore mine, also happens to contain the largest known rare-earth deposit in the world. It’s the source of nearly half of all the rare-earth ore mined on the planet in a typical year. Most of the rare-earth ore mined at Bayan Obo is a type called bastnaesite; it’s the mining of that bastnaesite that makes it legal to mine monazite ore at Bayan Obo as well.
Related: Can a Radioactive Ore Break China’s Grip on Rare Earths?
All told, ore from Bayan Obo was used to produce 170,000 tonnes of rare-earth metal last year, according to David Merriman, research director at the minerals intelligence firm Project Blue. Roughly 30 percent to 40 percent of the rare-earth ore mined at Bayan Obo is monazite. That amount alone would be enough to make China the world’s largest processor of monazite for rare-earths.
China’s 2025 Monazite Imports Topped 70,000 Tonnes
But a more detailed picture of China’s interest in monazite emerges when you consider the country’s imports of the ore. Last year, they amounted to more than 70,000 tonnes, says Thomas Kruemmer, a Singapore-based consultant on minerals and metals. That figure becomes more impressive when you consider the unique challenges of shipping monazite by sea. Because of its radioactivity, concentrated monazite ore is classified as Class 7 dangerous cargo under the International Maritime Dangerous Goods Code. That means, Kruemmer notes, that the ore can be imported through only four ports in China.
In addition, importation of some kinds of monazite into China is supposed to go through a joint venture consisting of the China National Nuclear Corp. and Shenghe Resources, which are at least partly state-owned. But lots of imported monazite doesn’t go through those organizations, notes Merriman. That’s because heavy mineral sands, which may contain roughly 2 percent or 3 percent monazite by weight, are not subject to the same import controls as concentrated monazite ore. So companies import the heavy mineral sands; separate out various profitable concentrates, including the monazite mineral concentrate; and then process the monazite concentrate to recover the rare-earths.
China has lately stepped up its efforts to secure rare-earth ore around the world. One reason, says Kruemmer, is simply to make up for recently lost supplies. In 2025, the U.S. government invested US $400 million in MP Materials, which operates the Mountain Pass mine and processing facility in California. The deal put an end to long-standing contracts under which MP Materials had been selling tens of thousands of tonnes of rare-earth concentrate annually to a trading affiliate of Shenghe Resources.
But other Westerners speculate that China has strategic reasons for stepping up its efforts to acquire heavy mineral sands or other rare-earth assets abroad. By locking down rights to deposits or projects abroad, Chinese organizations are making them unavailable to non-Chinese developers, according to this reasoning.
Merriman points out that your view of these activities largely depends on where you sit. The U.S. government recently made a conditional loan commitment of up to $725 million to U.S. monazite processor Energy Fuels, which has been aggressively securing substantial monazite supplies in Australia, Brazil, and Madagascar. To a Chinese observer, those moves probably look rather strategic.
China, meanwhile, is doing what it has been doing for decades. “China’s playing its game,” says Merriman.
Glenn Zorpette is editorial director for content development at IEEE Spectrum. A Fellow of the IEEE, he holds a bachelor's degree in electrical engineering from Brown University.

articles.title: Cisco Warns of Exploited Secure Email Gateway Vulnerability
articles.text:
Cisco on Wednesday warned customers that hackers have been exploiting a critical-severity vulnerability in Secure Email Gateway.
Tracked as CVE-2026-76519 (CVSS score of 9.8/10), the security defect impacts the Advanced Malware Protection (AMP) feature of the appliance and could allow remote, unauthenticated attackers to write arbitrary files on the operating system.
“In October 2026, the Cisco PSIRT became aware of active exploitation of this vulnerability,” Cisco warns.
The flaw exists in the handling of email attachments if the file reputation service has been enabled and if a Content Scanner Tools version earlier than 25.3.0.5525 is installed.
Attackers could send emails containing crafted attachments to trigger the security hole, write arbitrary files on the underlying OS, and execute arbitrary commands with root privileges.
Cisco has published indicators of compromise (IoCs) to help organizations hunt for potential intrusions, but warns that attackers may abuse their elevated access to remove or hide evidence of exploitation.
Organizations should check network and firewall logs outside of the affected devices to discover suspicious activity such as unexpected uploads or downloads to and from external IP addresses.
Cisco has advised customers to contact its Technical Assistance Center (TAC) if they suspect exploitation on a physical device.
For virtual appliances, it has recommended deploying a new VM running a fixed software release, rebuilding product configuration from scratch, and rotating credentials, while preserving forensic evidence.
“Cisco has directly contacted customers who own Cisco Secure Email Cloud devices where indicators of possible compromise were identified. Cisco is engaged in remediation and recovery operations. Cisco has already deployed mitigations that are within Cisco’s management,” the company notes.
Cisco customers should migrate to a patched AsyncOS software release as soon as possible. Fixes for CVE-2026-76519 were rolled out on September 14, in Secure Email Gateway versions 15.5.5-014 and 16.5.0-780.
At the time, Cisco grouped this vulnerability and others under CVE-2026-76440. On Wednesday, it updated the September advisory to mention the flaw’s in-the-wild exploitation.
CVE-2026-76519 is the second Cisco Secure Email Gateway vulnerability exploited in the wild since mid-September, after CVE-2026-76461, another unauthenticated bug that could lead to command execution with root privileges.
On Wednesday, the US cybersecurity agency CISA added CVE-2026-76519 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, urging federal agencies to patch it by October 17.
Related: Chrome, Firefox Updates Patch 114 Flaws as Mozilla Unveils Firefox Enterprise
Related: Citrix, Fortinet, Ivanti Patch 29 Vulnerabilities Across Their Products
Related: Microsoft Patches Record 1,413 Vulnerabilities, Including Exploited Windows Zero-Day
