articles.title: Demandan a OpenAI porque ChatGPT habría incitado a adolescentes a autolesionarse en Estados Unidos
articles.text:
Ocho fiscales generales de Estados Unidos demandaron a OpenAI en tribunales estatales, acusando a la empresa de diseñar ChatGPT para enganchar a menores mientras ocultaba riesgos que, según las demandas, llevaron a chicos a autolesionarse.
Los estados que presentaron acciones independientes son Arkansas, Arizona, Idaho, Iowa, Kansas, Montana, Nebraska y Virginia Occidental, en lo que la agencia Reuters calificó como la acción coordinada más significativa de gobiernos estatales contra una empresa de inteligencia artificial.
Cada fiscalía presentó su propia demanda en su corte estatal, pero todas comparten el mismo reclamo central: OpenAI habría promocionado a ChatGPT como seguro para usuarios de 13 años en adelante mientras conocía fallas que ponían en riesgo a menores y a otros usuarios vulnerables.
El fiscal general de Kansas, Kris Kobach, precisó que las ocho demandas son acciones paralelas e independientes, presentadas cada una en la corte de su propio estado y no como un litigio conjunto, según reprodujo el canal local WDTV.
Los casos que citan las demandas
La fiscal general de Iowa, Brenna Bird, dijo que OpenAI “le dijo a los usuarios de todo el país que ChatGPT es seguro, cuando no lo es”, según la citó Bloomberg Law. Bird agregó que el chatbot refuerza delirios y brinda consejos médicos peligrosos.
El fiscal general de Virginia Occidental, JB McCuskey, presentó su demanda junto a sus pares de Iowa, Kansas y Nebraska en una conferencia de prensa. Según su oficina, el reclamo describe un caso en el que ChatGPT incitó a un adolescente para que se quitara la vida.
Los fiscales también citaron el caso de un adolescente de Texas al que, según la demanda de Iowa, ChatGPT le dio información médica peligrosa sobre la combinación de Xanax y kratom que terminó en su muerte.
La fiscal general de Arizona, Kris Mayes, presentó su demanda en la Corte Superior del condado de Maricopa. Según el texto difundido por su oficina, OpenAI “diseñó un producto para atraer a usuarios jóvenes y mantenerlos enganchados el mayor tiempo posible” con el fin de capturar sus datos personales.
El fiscal general de Nebraska, Mike Hilgers, sostuvo en la misma conferencia que Estados Unidos “debe ganar la carrera de la inteligencia artificial”, pero que las empresas del sector “no pueden engañar o desinformar a los consumidores sobre su tecnología” en el proceso.
Qué piden los fiscales
Las demandas invocan leyes estatales de protección al consumidor y, en algunos casos, normas específicas sobre privacidad infantil en línea. Los estados acusan a OpenAI de generar una molestia pública al poner en riesgo la salud de sus residentes.
Entre los pedidos figuran órdenes judiciales que obliguen a la empresa a modificar el funcionamiento de ChatGPT, divulgar de forma clara los riesgos del producto y entregar las ganancias obtenidas a partir del uso de menores. También reclaman sanciones civiles e indemnizaciones.
Arkansas fue más allá: su demanda pide que se frene el desarrollo de modelos de inteligencia artificial capaces de mejorarse a sí mismos hasta que existan garantías de que esos sistemas están alineados con los valores humanos.
El fiscal general de Arkansas, Tim Griffin, detalló que su demanda incluye reclamos por violaciones a la ley estatal de prácticas comerciales engañosas y a la normativa de protección de datos de chicos y adolescentes, además de cargos de negligencia y defecto de diseño del producto.
Según Griffin, su oficina documentó casos de usuarios, incluidos menores, que obtuvieron de ChatGPT instrucciones para autolesionarse y lograron sortear los filtros de seguridad que la empresa aseguraba tener implementados.
Varias fiscalías mencionaron además episodios en los que agentes de IA de OpenAI, asistentes capaces de ejecutar tareas por su cuenta, habrían actuado de forma autónoma e irrumpido en sistemas de otras compañías, un antecedente que usan para cuestionar los controles internos de la empresa.
La respuesta de OpenAI
Un vocero de OpenAI, Drew Pusateri, defendió las medidas de la compañía ante el canal local KVOA, en Arizona. “Construimos protecciones específicas por edad que muchas otras empresas de IA no tienen”, afirmó, y agregó que la empresa seguirá trabajando con especialistas para sumar salvaguardas.
Pusateri señaló que ChatGPT está pensado para usuarios de 13 años en adelante, que los menores de 18 necesitan permiso de un adulto y que los usuarios adolescentes pasan, en promedio, menos de quince minutos por día en la plataforma.
OpenAI no respondió de inmediato a los pedidos de comentario de otras agencias, entre ellas Reuters. La empresa enfrenta además decenas de demandas de particulares que la acusan de haber contribuido a planificar actos de violencia o episodios de autolesión.
Florida había presentado en junio una demanda similar y abrió una investigación penal sobre el rol de ChatGPT en la planificación de un tiroteo, según consignó The Guardian. Los fiscales de los ocho estados advirtieron que podrían sumarse más demandas estatales en las próximas semanas.
Las acciones legales llegan mientras OpenAI se prepara para una eventual salida a bolsa y mientras ChatGPT, lanzado en 2022, se mantiene como el chatbot más usado del mundo, con cerca de la mitad del mercado estadounidense de asistentes conversacionales, según los propios fiscales.
Líneas de ayuda y prevención
En Estados Unidos, existe la Red Nacional de Prevención del Suicidio para pedir ayuda, puedes llamar al 1-888-628-9454 o al 1-800-273-8255, la línea del Servicio Nacional de Prevención del Suicidio, para hablar con alguien que te brindará apoyo gratuito y confidencial las 24 horas del día, los siete días de la semana. Los CDC también recomienda sus propias políticas, programas y prácticas de prevención.
Línea de prevención del suicidio en Argentina: el Centro de Asistencia al Suicida ofrece orientación y apoyo. Tienen una línea de prevención del suicidio disponible al teléfono 135 (línea gratuita) o al (011)5275-1135 y 0800 345 1435 para llamadas desde todo el país.
En México, para aquellos que buscan ayuda o asistencia en relación al suicidio, existe la Línea de la Vida: 800-911-2000, este servicio es gratuito y está disponible las 24 horas del día, los 7 días de la semana.
En Colombia, la Línea de la Vida brinda apoyo emocional a individuos que enfrentan crisis de suicidio o angustia. Este servicio está disponible en varias ciudades del país. En Bogotá, se puede contactar a través de la línea 106 o vía WhatsApp al 3007548933. Barranquilla cuenta con la línea 339 99 99, mientras que en Medellín se dispone de la Línea Amiga al 444 44 48. En Cali, al igual que en Bogotá, la línea de atención es el 106. Estas líneas ofrecen una respuesta inmediata a quienes necesitan ayuda en momentos críticos.
En Perú, el Ministerio de Salud (Minsa) ofrece apoyo emocional a través de la Línea 113 Salud, accesible nacionalmente por teléfono, WhatsApp o Telegram en los números 955557000 y 952842623.
En España, el Ministerio de Sanidad ha establecido la Línea 024 para la atención a la conducta suicida.

articles.title: Cloudflare and OpenAI: making AI discovery better for everyone
articles.text:
Cloudflare and OpenAI: Making AI discovery better for everyone
Optimizing your site for AI is of little use if AI can't find it. The answer to someone's question may already be on your website: the installation guide you spent a week writing, or a first-hand account of using a product, with the details that make the difference for whether they buy it. As more people turn to AI for help, you want those systems to find your work, represent it accurately, and send interested people your way. You also want control over how they access your site.
Cloudflare and OpenAI launched a research pilot in July 2026 with those interests in mind. We wanted to find out whether signals from Cloudflare’s network could help ChatGPT users discover new content more efficiently.
Today, we’re sharing early results. So far, the answer is a resounding yes: the pilot has brought previously unknown pages into OpenAI’s search index, giving ChatGPT more sources to draw on to help people find relevant, timely information. Along the way, we’ve learned more about what makes a page worth discovering and how AI systems use the web.
Finding more of the web
The web is full of specifics. Someone fixing a washing machine needs the manual for their exact model. Someone applying for a passport needs the current requirements and fees. Someone choosing a local restaurant needs its latest menu and opening hours. Finding the right page can be the difference between a wrong answer and one that actually helps. These pages can be valuable even if few other sites link to them.
In the previous version of the web, discoverability was getting to the top of a search result page. It was then up to the human who visited your page to determine the value of the information, book that table, apply for that passport. As people increasingly rely on AI to find information and complete tasks, discoverability matters in new ways. AI systems need to find the right sources, understand what's useful, and connect people with relevant information – whether that's through an answer, a citation, or a visit to the website itself.
Cloudflare's network provides signals that can help OpenAI’s search crawler discover more useful pages across the web to surface to ChatGPT users. OpenAI then independently evaluates and ranks how those pages appear based on how relevant and helpful they are. Together, this creates a feedback loop that can improve both discovery and the quality of information people find.
This joint pilot, which used a participating cohort of ~1% of Cloudflare’s total network, has enabled OpenAI to discover and index hundreds of millions of new web pages, helping people discover more useful content and get more questions answered through ChatGPT. By linking back to relevant sources, ChatGPT Search also gives people a way to explore the original content and discover the websites and publishers behind it.
With GPT-6 and Intelligent UI, OpenAI is also making ChatGPT an even better place to shop, learn, and find answers, with more visual, interactive experiences tailored to what people need. This work complements these advances by helping ChatGPT discover more useful, up-to-date information from across the web.
From discovery to useful answers
Finding a URL is only the start. We need to know whether it leads to a page someone can access, whether that page offers anything distinct, and what it might help someone do.
We’ve learned, for example, how easily automated traffic can make a nonexistent page look interesting. Bots repeatedly ask for files that aren’t there. Some sites redirect almost any address to their homepage. Other addresses lead to copies of the same content. Recognizing these patterns gives us a way to cut wasted work before a crawler fetches the page, and improve efficiency in a way that benefits site owners.
We're also testing signals that identify and flag potentially harmful pages, adding another layer of information to support safer, more reliable discovery. A legitimate site can have a single compromised page, such as a fake login form planted by an attacker. Flagging that one page, rather than the whole domain, keeps people safe without penalizing the site owner. Early results suggest these signals can help identify pages that should be kept out of an index.
Making discovery easier
As more people use AI to discover information, website owners have new opportunities to reach interested audiences. For those who choose to make their content available to AI systems, these improvements make discovery easier and more efficient.
Keeping up by fetching every page more often would be expensive for everyone. For a website owner, a crawler that repeatedly downloads an unchanged page adds load without bringing any benefit.
The signals above are how we avoid that. Filtering keeps crawlers away from pages that don't exist or that redirect elsewhere. Change signals tell them when a page is worth another visit, and when it isn't.
There's a balance to get right. Finding new pages can initially increase crawling as those pages are evaluated and indexed. The goal is to keep discovering and stay current while reducing the work that takes. For Cloudflare customers, that means less unnecessary load. For OpenAI, it means more of its search resources are spent on information that helps people.
Making it worthwhile to participate
The next phase will build on what we’ve learned: improve the selection of pages, test faster and more reliable change signals, and measure what happens after content is discovered.
We’re continuing to work with OpenAI to understand how better site discovery can translate into real business outcomes, and we’ll keep sharing what we learn along the way.
Domain owners’ choices matter throughout. A signal about a page doesn’t grant permission to access it. This research uses metadata about the web for search and discovery, rather than sharing page content for model training.
You can use Cloudflare’s AI Crawl Control to understand and manage how AI systems access your website.

articles.title: ChatGPT ganha vozes mais naturais e melhora reconhecimento de sotaques; veja novidades
articles.text:
A OpenAI anunciou, nesta quinta-feira (15), uma atualização do modo Voz do ChatGPT, com melhorias no reconhecimento da fala, na compreensão de diferentes sotaques e na naturalidade das conversas. A novidade inclui os modelos GPT-Live-1.1 e GPT-Live-1.1 Quip, versão menor da tecnologia, além de novas opções de vozes em diferentes idiomas.
No Brasil, a atualização chega em momento de expansão do uso de recursos de voz e ditado na plataforma. Segundo informações divulgadas pela OpenAI, o país está entre os cinco maiores mercados do ChatGPT nesse tipo de interação, e o número de usuários semanais do modo Voz dobrou ao longo do último ano.
A empresa também destaca que a experiência foi aprimorada para situações cotidianas, como fazer perguntas, desenvolver ideias em voz alta e pedir ajuda para organizar tarefas. A proposta é tornar as conversas mais fluidas, inclusive quando o usuário mistura idiomas ou precisa transmitir informações que combinam letras e números.
O que muda no modo Voz do ChatGPT?
A atualização reúne três melhorias principais: compreensão da fala, fluidez das respostas e ampliação das opções de vozes.
- Reconhecimento de sotaques: os modelos receberam melhorias para compreender diferentes formas de pronúncia em vários idiomas, inclusive em conversas que misturam línguas;
- Conversas mais naturais: o ChatGPT passa a variar melhor as expressões curtas usadas durante a execução de uma solicitação, evitando repetições, como “Estou verificando isso…” enquanto realiza uma tarefa;
- Novas vozes: foram adicionadas opções em francês, alemão, hindi, espanhol do México, coreano e japonês, além da voz Bubbie, em inglês, inspirada na maneira de falar de avós.
A atualização também busca melhorar a compreensão de informações que combinam letras e números, algo útil para transmitir códigos, nomes, identificadores e outros dados durante uma conversa.
GPT-Live-1.1 e Quip: qual é a diferença?
A OpenAI está disponibilizando duas versões atualizadas dos modelos que alimentam o modo Voz do ChatGPT.
O GPT-Live-1.1 é o sucessor do GPT-Live-1, enquanto o GPT-Live-1.1 Quip substitui o GPT-Live-1 mini. Segundo a documentação técnica da empresa, o primeiro será o modelo padrão de voz para usuários Plus e planos superiores. O Quip será utilizado por padrão pelos demais usuários.
Os dois modelos foram desenvolvidos para permitir interações contínuas, nas quais o ChatGPT pode ouvir e responder sem esperar que cada fala termine de maneira perfeitamente definida. Isso ajuda a tornar as interrupções e as mudanças de ritmo mais naturais.
A atualização também se estende ao Codex e ao Dots, produtos da OpenAI que utilizam recursos de inteligência artificial (IA) para auxiliar em tarefas e fluxos de trabalho.
A disponibilização é gradual, e os recursos disponíveis podem variar de acordo com o plano e a conta.
Leia mais:
- O que a inteligência artificial sabe sobre você?
- 8 estados dos EUA processam OpenAI e acusam ChatGPT de colocar jovens em risco
- OpenAI alerta Polícia Federal sobre ameaças contra Lula feitas no ChatGPT
Como ficam as vozes em português brasileiro?
Embora a atualização apresente novas vozes para outros idiomas, a OpenAI já oferece opções desenvolvidas para o português brasileiro: Viola e Rio. A Viola tem uma personalidade leve, espontânea e curiosa. Já a Rio foi concebida com um estilo caloroso, acolhedor e prestativo.
Essas opções fazem parte da estratégia de adaptar a experiência de voz às características de diferentes idiomas e públicos. A empresa não anunciou a Viola e a Rio como novidades desta atualização específica, mas destacou que o Brasil é um mercado importante para o uso de voz e ditado no ChatGPT.
Para conferir as opções disponíveis, o usuário pode abrir as configurações do ChatGPT, acessar a seção “Voz” e selecionar a opção desejada. A lista pode variar conforme a região e a conta.
Voz ganha espaço nas tarefas do dia a dia
A OpenAI também quer ampliar o uso do modo Voz para além de perguntas rápidas. A ferramenta pode servir para explorar ideias, organizar atividades e desenvolver planos por meio de uma conversa.
Um exemplo apresentado pela empresa é o planejamento de um almoço em família. O usuário pode informar quais ingredientes tem na geladeira, quantas pessoas participarão da refeição e quais são suas preferências alimentares. A partir dessas informações, o ChatGPT pode sugerir pratos, alternativas de ingredientes e listas de compras.
A vantagem desse formato é permitir que o usuário acrescente informações e ajuste o pedido naturalmente, sem precisar formular uma nova solicitação completa a cada mudança.
O modo Voz também pode ser usado em conjunto com texto e imagens no mesmo chat, conforme os recursos disponíveis para a conta. Assim, a interação não fica restrita à fala: o usuário pode complementar a conversa digitando ou enviando imagens.
OpenAI divulga avaliações de segurança dos novos modelos
Junto à atualização, a OpenAI publicou documentação técnica sobre o GPT-Live-1.1 e o GPT-Live-1.1 Quip, com informações sobre treinamento, avaliações e mecanismos de segurança.
Segundo a empresa, os modelos mantêm, em geral, desempenho semelhante ao de seus antecessores nas avaliações de segurança. A documentação, porém, registra pioras estatisticamente significativas do GPT-Live-1.1 em algumas categorias de testes sintéticos, incluindo conteúdo sexual, saúde mental, dependência emocional e violência gráfica. A OpenAI afirma que são necessárias mais pesquisas para compreender essas diferenças e que pretende melhorar esses aspectos em versões futuras.
A empresa ressalta que esses testes são construídos para avaliar situações específicas e difíceis; portanto, não representam diretamente a frequência com que problemas desse tipo ocorrem no uso cotidiano.
A publicação das avaliações acompanha a evolução dos recursos de voz, que passam a ocupar um papel mais importante nas interações com o ChatGPT. O objetivo anunciado é tornar as conversas mais naturais em diferentes idiomas e ampliar a utilidade da ferramenta em atividades do dia a dia.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: Sony made a $5,900 gold-plated Walkman MP3 player
articles.text:
Sony has announced a trio of new Walkman portable media players that start at an already absurd $1,899.99 for the NW-ZX900 and climb all the way up to $5,899 for the gold-plated NW-WM1ZM3. Sandwiched in between is the $2,999.99 Walkman NW-WM1AM3, which is nearly identical to the WM1ZM3, just minus the gaudy gold shell.
Sony made a $5,900 gold-plated Walkman MP3 player
A $6,000 media player slathered is gold is the perfect gift for the millionaire audiophile in your life.
All three devices are aimed squarely at the audiophile market, if the price tag didn’t make that clear. All three feature Sony’s DSD (Direct Stream Digital) Remastering Engine, which upsamples standard PCM audio to an 11.2MHz DSD stream, which it claims delivers a more analog-like sound. They also all feature gold-plating on the rear chassis that’s meant to reduce interference and lower noise.
The higher-end Walkman NW-WM1ZM3 and NW-WM1AM3 add hand-soldered oxygen-free copper (OFC) wiring and upgraded power circuitry to lower noise even further. A milled OFC block isolates the digital circuits from the analog ones to limit potential interference.
What sets the WM1ZM3 apart is that the entire chassis is made of OFC and then gold-plated.
This is not the first time Sony has gone all out on a gold media player. In fact, you can pick up the previous model — the NW-WM1ZM2 — on sale now for just $2,599.99. A veritable steal. Though, an old iPod bought off eBay is still probably the better bargain.

articles.title: Amazon's Bee launches two new personal AI devices, starting at $75 | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Amazon’s personal AI wearable maker, Bee, is announcing its first new products since being acquired by the retail giant last year. The tech company on Thursday introduced the Bee Frontier, the next generation of its device that can be worn on the wrist or pinned to clothes, along with Bee Eclipse, a credit-card-sized device that magnetically attaches to the back of your smartphone.
The latter puts Bee into more direct competition with AI devices like the Plaud Note or Pocket, but at a lower price point — the Bee Frontier is $74.99, compared with $159 for the Plaud Note (or $189 for the Note Pro), or $129 for the Pocket AI device.
The Bee Frontier will come in Onyx, Lavender, and Sage, while the $99.99 Bee Eclipse will be offered in Silver, Midnight, Honey, and Blush.
Like the original Bee, the idea with the new devices is to leverage AI to take notes from your everyday conversations, allowing you to remember the important things that were said, and then turn those into actionable to-dos, summaries, and insights.
For instance, if you discussed making plans with friends, the Bee would remember the date and time you agreed on, then create a calendar invite. You could also use the Bee to take lecture notes in class, or to jot down the care plan you discussed with a doctor, among other things.
All Bee devices can create conversation summaries and recaps for free, and offer 14 days of memory. With an $11.99 per month Bee Pro subscription, users receive unlimited conversation summaries and integrations with Amazon.com, Alexa+, and third-party applications. Pro users also get suggested to-dos, daily memories, a personal chat assistant, and conversation templates.
To make all this possible, Bee devices use a private computing security architecture, which doesn’t store the raw audio from your conversations. Instead, audio is processed in real time and then deleted. Transcripts of the conversation are encrypted using keys that your device creates and controls, which means no one else, including Amazon employees, can access those files unless you manually and intentionally share them.
In addition, you can opt to connect the Bee to Alexa, allowing your Echo device to use its ability to identify your voice, a feature called Voice ID, to recognize when you’re speaking. It can then record your conversations to provide Bee’s insights. (This aspect of Bee is optional, and Amazon notes you can delete transcripts and summaries at any time.)
With its new connections to Amazon.com and Alexa, Bee users can make purchases from Amazon or ask Alexa for their Bee insights, summaries, or to-dos hands-free.
Bee also works with your existing productivity software, like Gmail, Google Calendar, and Microsoft Outlook, so it can draft emails, set up meetings, surface action items, and more.
Plus, you can upload photos to Bee or connect it with Apple’s HealthKit to add a picture of your overall wellness to be integrated into your provided insights.
The Bee Frontier and Bee Eclipse both have just one button that turns the device off and on, and include an indicator light when it’s summarizing a conversation. The Frontier also offers IP67 water resistance, up to seven days of battery life, USB-C charging, and dual microphones with advanced noise filtering.
All Bee devices come with a companion mobile app, which has also been newly redesigned, plus a new desktop app.
The Bee Frontier is available now on Amazon, and the Eclipse will be available soon thereafter.

articles.title: Open From Data Center to Desktop: NVIDIA Expands Nemotron Family With Highest Efficiency Super VL and Bolt Models
articles.text:
NVIDIA today released Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, an open 120-billion-parameter model that delivers the fastest task completion and highest accuracy for specialized always-on agents.
Joining it are two new edge models: Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB, optimized to balance intelligence and speed per GB for local agentic workloads, and Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB, optimized for intelligence per GB for fast conversational agents.
Super VL and Bolt 74B-A9B are available now, with Bolt E4B coming Oct. 23.
The three open models together cover the full range of agent deployments, from large enterprise servers down to edge devices and local hardware. 
Any organization that wants to run agents on NVIDIA infrastructure now has an open, optimized model for their tier, without having to choose between capability and deployability.
Super VL and Bolt join the Nemotron family alongside Lightning and Ultra.
Lightning, released in August, handles high-throughput workloads; Ultra handles the hardest reasoning tasks; and Bolt brings intelligence to the edge.
Nemotron 3.5 Super VL: Frontier Accuracy at One-Fifth the Size
Super VL, built in collaboration with the Nemotron Coalition, delivers leading accuracy on multimodal agentic tasks — instruction following, tool use, multistep business workflows, and visual understanding — comparable with NVIDIA’s largest reasoning model at roughly one-fifth the parameter count.
As the fastest open agentic model in its class — 5x faster than the next best — it helps enterprise agents complete high-volume tasks faster across workflows that span days or weeks.
Unlike closed frontier models, organizations can post-train Super VL on their own data, deploy it on their own infrastructure and oversee what they build.
Nemotron 3.5 Bolt: Agentic Intelligence at the Edge
Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB is designed to run everyday agentic tasks locally on NVIDIA RTX/DGX Spark, using a native 2-bit quantization to fit in 24GB of memory and run alongside other applications.
Relative to other models with a similar memory footprint, it provides a good balance of intelligence and speed: smart enough to get most jobs done, yet much faster than the smartest models.
With Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB, users can delegate their projects to popular local agent harnesses — from researching the web to writing to debugging code — all without sending those workloads to the cloud. It is the #1 open model in its class on PinchBench, and the #2 open model for BrowseComp.
Bolt E4B 4GB is built for physical and conversational agents on GeForce RTX, Jetson, and RTX/DGX Spark. It combines natural conversation with multi-turn agentic capabilities to power fast local voice assistants, interactive characters and embedded interfaces. 
Adoption of Custom Super Intelligence
Dozens of organizations across industries are post-training Super VL on their own data, tools, policies and workflows to push accuracy higher on the specialized tasks that define their agent deployments.
Super VL is being post-trained and customized by organizations across industries. Scale AI post-trained the model for Skydance’s vendor credit finance agent and for EY’s M&A due diligence agent. AfterQuery customized the model for Hebbia for credit agreement analysis. AI21 and Alice post-trained the model for cybersecurity attack resilience. Mercor post-trained the model on APEX-SWE coding benchmark, for coding agents that plan, write and debug code. ModelScope enables developers to fine-tune the model through its ms-swift framework for specialized multimodal applications.
Additional organizations customizing Nemotron 3.5 Super VL include Ramp for financial document intelligence; Dream, sovereign AI-powered cybersecurity research and vulnerability analysis; Lila Sciences for scientific discovery and search, and R1 for medical claims analysis and revenue cycle management. TrainLoop post-trained the model with dermatology data from Nolla, which just became the first company approved for AI to write initial patient prescriptions.
Software platform companies integrating Nemotron 3.5 Super VL include: 
- Atlassian, for tasks like agentic search across apps such as Jira and Confluence.
- CrowdStrike, which is customizing the model for agentic blue teaming in enterprise security.
- Dassault Systèmes, powering engineering design and simulation.
- Perplexity, for search and agentic tasks in Perplexity Search and Computer.
- Salesforce, which is customizing Nemotron to power AI agents that digitize and automate complex government workflows in secure customer environments through Missionforce Operations.
- Synopsys software for semiconductor design verification interoperates with the model.
What Nemotron 3.5 Super VL Actually Sees
Nemotron 3.5 Super VL’s vision language strengths are targeted at what agents encounter in practice: optical character recognition, tables, charts and structured information in visual documents.
It processes a web page, extracts text, reads graphs and charts, and returns insights from what it finds. The same applies to PDFs and other documents agents commonly work with.
Nemotron 3.5 Super VL understands images, webpages and PDFs and acts on that understanding. Combining text and visual understanding in one model means agents don’t need to route tasks between separate systems — context carries through as work moves from document to data to decision.
Open for Maximum Control, Security, and Privacy
Openness and customizability reinforce each other. The model ships with open weights, open datasets and training recipes.
Control runs in two directions. Organizations can run the model wherever their security and data-residency requirements dictate. They also choose to adopt a model they can adapt, rather than one subject to a provider’s restrictions.
In insurance, for example, a customized agent can scan claims for fraud markers on repeat. In financial services, an agent can review credit scores and flag activity against an organization’s own lending criteria. The model stays on premises. The data stays private.
Customization is supported through NVIDIA NeMo, Python-based pipelines and open datasets.
Nemotron 3.5 Super VL was trained on about 26 trillion tokens across pretraining and continued pretraining, then post-trained with roughly 3.8 million samples and reinforcement learning across dozens of environments.
NVIDIA is also releasing open datasets on Hugging Face spanning agentic tool use, finance, instruction following, long context, fairness and vision-language understanding, along with the reinforcement learning environments in NeMo Gym.
NVIDIA NIM packages the model as a production-ready microservice with performance-optimized, validated configurations and enterprise-grade support, refreshed every two weeks with security patches and performance improvements.
And with the model running on NVIDIA Dynamo, organizations can serve up to 8x more users with 85% lower latency.
Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is available now on Hugging Face, Open Router, ModelScope community and as NVIDIA NIM.
Runs on DGX Spark, DGX Station, and RTX
Nemotron 3.5 Super VL runs across NVIDIA’s full hardware stack: on DGX Spark, DGX Station, RTX PRO and RTX systems for local intelligence at the desktop, on NVIDIA Jetson at the edge, and across data center and cloud environments.
Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB is available now on Hugging Face, with support for llama.cpp, Ollama, LM Studio, Unsloth, and vLLM. Built for NVIDIA RTX Spark laptops arriving Oct. 16, it also runs on GeForce RTX PCs, DGX Spark, DGX Station and RTX PRO workstations.
Download the open weights, explore customization resources with NVIDIA NeMo, or read the technical blog for the full architecture breakdown.
Stay up to date on agents, NVIDIA Nemotron and more by subscribing to NVIDIA news, joining the community, and following NVIDIA AI on LinkedIn, Instagram, X and Facebook.
Explore self-paced video tutorials and livestreams.

articles.title: Dial Up the Cloud: NVIDIA DLSS 4.5 Controls Arrive on GeForce NOW
articles.text:
Dial in the next gaming session this GFN Thursday. New NVIDIA DLSS 4.5 controls give GeForce NOW members more choice over how supported games look and perform in the cloud, even without the latest hardware.
Then, step into the Shroud as Keen Games’ Enshrouded leaves early access with its 1.0 release, or let the bolts fly in Warhammer 40,000: Boltgun 2. Both are streaming on GeForce NOW at launch.
With 10 new games joining the cloud this week, members can put the new controls to work in supported titles and keep playing across supported devices without downloads, installs or expensive hardware upgrades.
Fine-Tune the Cloud With DLSS 4.5 Controls
NVIDIA DLSS 4.5 controls are now available on GeForce NOW, giving members more choice over how supported games look and perform in the cloud, even without the latest hardware. DLSS Super Resolution sharpens image quality, while Dynamic Multi Frame Generation delivers lower latency and reduces stutter for smoother streaming, and Ray Reconstruction enhances ray-traced visuals. In addition, Ultimate members streaming on GeForce RTX 5080-powered cloud rigs benefit from the maximum available options, including Dynamic Multi Frame Generation up to 4X.
From James Bond’s globe-trotting missions in 007 First Light — now with path tracing support — to CONTROL Resonant’s reality-bending Manhattan and the shadowy scares of Resident Evil Requiem, the controls help fine-tune supported games for image quality, responsiveness or a preferred balance between the two.
These new settings are available in the GeForce NOW app under settings, for Windows, macOS, Chrome OS and Steam OS platforms. Members can read here for more details on using the feature with their membership tier, and more information on how to get the smoothest cloud game streaming for some games on GeForce NOW.
Rise, Flameborn
Enshrouded 1.0 brings the co-op survival action role-playing game out of early access and into its full release. Rise as a Flameborn, the last ember of hope of a dying race, and venture into a vast world of survival, action and role-playing, where a corrupting fog has consumed a once-beautiful kingdom.
The title brings improvements to existing systems, alongside expansions in combat with nine new spells, new mage and archer skills, reworked wands and upgradeable Eternal spells and arrows. New enemy variants keep encounters fresh, while a new biome raises the player level cap to 50 and equipment cap to 55.
GeForce NOW offers Enshrouded 1.0 ready to play in the cloud at launch across supported devices. Skip the 60GB local install to save precious storage space, then step into the Shroud without waiting for downloads or needing to make room for the update.
Let the Bolts Fly
Warhammer 40,000: Boltgun 2 is now streaming on GeForce NOW. The brutal, fast-paced sequel to the retro first-person shooter brings more enemies, more weapons and new ways to purge.
Picking up directly after the original game, a branching single-player campaign sends the fight to grimdark new worlds.
Choose between the formidable Sternguard Veteran Malum Caedo and the swift Sister of Battle Nyra Veyrath, each with distinct abilities, weapons and play styles. From towering hive cities to jungle mangrove swamps, new enemy types await in every biome.
GeForce NOW keeps the campaign ready in the cloud. No local rig upgrades or game installs stand between members and the fight — the Emperor’s work waits for no loading bar.
In addition, members can look for the following joining the GeForce NOW library:
- Deep Dish Dungeon (New release on Steam, Oct. 13)
- Planet Zoo 2 (New release on Steam, Oct. 13)
- Total War: SHOGUN 2 – Complete Edition (New release on Steam, Oct. 13)
- Valor Mortis (New release on Steam, Oct. 13)

- Beyond These Stars (New release on Steam and Xbox, Oct. 15), available on Game Pass
- Tenebris Somnia (New release on Steam, Oct. 16)
- The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt – Remastered (Xbox), available on Microsoft Store
Also this week, the performance of DLSS 5’s 3D-Guided Neural Rendering model is improving by 2X, enabling even more gamers to enjoy DLSS 5’s transformative uplift in lighting and materials at high frame rates and settings. The new, more performant DLSS 5 model will debut in NBA 2K27 on Oct. 16 on GeForce NOW, GeForce RTX 50 Series GPUs and RTX Spark laptops.
Dates listed above reflect when games are released on their respective stores. GeForce NOW availability may vary, as games are onboarded after they’re released and added throughout the week. Keep an eye on GeForce NOW channels and GFN Thursdays for availability updates to announced titles.
Gamers who want to test out the new 4.5 controls and high-performance GeForce NOW cloud gaming can start with a day pass to try premium cloud gaming before committing to a membership. Better yet, the cost of the day pass can be applied toward a first monthly membership — making it easy to try GeForce RTX-powered cloud gaming with the latest releases, then level up for more.

articles.title: Heavy Mineral Sands Are Quietly Rewriting Rare Earth Supply Chains
articles.text:
Can a Radioactive Ore Break China’s Grip on Rare Earths?
Monazite ore holds the key to powerful motor magnets—if we can handle it
The global campaigns to break China’s dominance of vital rare-earth markets are shaping up into one of the signature geostrategic struggles of the early 21st century. Hundreds of mining companies, government agencies, and industrial facilities scattered across North America, Australasia, and Europe are striving to wrest share from Chinese firms, which control roughly 90 percent of the markets for rare-earth oxides and rare-earth metals.
Rare earths are the ingredients on which vast and crucial manufacturing categories depend: semiconductors, LEDs, lasers, displays, metal alloys, optical lenses, and catalysts for petroleum and chemical processing. Most important, though, are permanent magnets. Essentially all powerful electric motors are based on rare-earth permanent magnets. These motors are the heart of electric vehicles, heating and cooling systems, robots, appliances, and tools. Rare-earth magnets are also in the motors for military systems ranging from tactical drones to ballistic-missile submarines.
This article is a collaboration between Foreign Policy, the global magazine of politics and ideas, and IEEE Spectrum, the flagship magazine of the IEEE.
Succinctly put, any industrial power that wants to remain competitive in vital, high-tech industries must have access to a steady supply of rare-earth elements or products based on them. The traditional supply chain for these elements, originating in China, is increasingly fraught—so much so that some analysts are beginning to use the term “mineral war.” The countries that are now scrambling to piece together alternative supply chains, whether by themselves or in cooperation with each other, face daunting odds. Never mind the sheer momentum of the Chinese rare earths juggernaut. Few industries can match the rare earths business for instability, risk, intrigue, and sheer frustration.
And yet, many rare-earth experts see a way forward, and it depends on a specific kind of ore, called monazite. The ore contains huge amounts of valuable rare earths, including neodymium, praseodymium, and dysprosium.
“The future is monazite,” declares Jack Lifton, an analyst, consultant, and author. Lifton, who has been studying the rare earths industry since 1962, has seen countless trends, companies, and technologies come and go, and he isn’t given to sweeping statements. But on the subject of monazites, he’s bullish. “Right now, in my opinion, monazite is the most important rare-earth ore,” says Lifton, who is also cochairman of the Critical Minerals Institute, an organization that’s promoting the creation of a North American supply chain.
Related: Chasing China’s Monazite Monopoly
That path forward isn’t going to be smooth or straight, Lifton and others are quick to acknowledge. Monazite typically contains radioactive thorium and uranium, which means its handling, storage, and processing are tightly regulated by government agencies. It can be processed only with special techniques and procedures, and the mildly radioactive wastes generated by processing must be stored in isolation indefinitely.
Nevertheless, major investment is now flowing to monazite mines and processing technologies. In the United States, Energy Fuels, which operates the country’s only conventional uranium mill, has developed its own extraction process and is producing mixed oxides of neodymium and praseodymium—and also pilot-scale quantities of dysprosium and terbium oxides, key heavy rare earths that are otherwise produced almost exclusively in China.
Energy Fuels is processing monazite into rare-earth oxides at its White Mesa Mill in southeastern Utah. The body of water at left in the image is a tailings impoundment, where radioactive waste from processing is stored.Energy Fuels
The company has spent more than US $200 million to secure monazite assets in Brazil and Madagascar, and plans to scale its rare-earth production to higher commercial levels, at an estimated cost of $410 million. Energy Fuels’ rare-earth ambitions received a significant boost in June, when the Trump administration announced that it had signed a $725 million conditional loan commitment with the company.
Meanwhile, though, a government-backed project in Saskatchewan, Canada, stands as a cautionary tale for monazite backers. After six years of construction and expenditures of more than CA $100 million (US $72 million), a processing plant there has produced only minuscule quantities of rare earths. The processing plant, built by the Saskatchewan Research Council, was supposed to be producing 40 tonnes of rare earths per month by the end of 2024. That didn’t happen. “Full operation,” with production of 400 tonnes of metal per year was planned for “early 2025.” That didn’t happen, either. The organization is now targeting late 2027—by which time the project will have cost more than CA $216 million, according to the Saskatchewan Research Council’s CEO, Mike Crabtree.
Outside of North America, major monazite projects are also planned by Astron Limited, Hastings Technology Metals, Iluka Resources, Mkango Resources, Sovereign Metals, Steenkampskraal Holdings, and Tronox, among others. Perth, Australia–based Lynas Rare Earths, the largest rare-earths company outside of China, is expanding its monazite mining and processing operations. Most notable is the Lynas mine at Mount Weld, Australia, one of the world’s top monazite resources; the ore is processed at a sprawling facility in Malaysia.
Of course, for countries outside of China, all this surging activity doesn’t guarantee a route to rare earths independence. It’s not even close. So the vital questions now are, What else has to happen to broaden and diversify the rare-earths supply chains? And can all of this be done safely?
What Are the Advantages of Monazite Ore?
Planet Earth has enormous quantities of monazite ore, in two different forms. In Australia, Canada, China, and South Africa, massive deposits of monazite take the form of veins of hard rock that run through mountains and calderas. Much of the new interest in monazite, though, is focused on a second type, called heavy mineral sands. The sands are the result of tens of millions of years of exposure to wind, water, and gravity crumbling mineral-rich rocks into grains, which then accumulated in coastal areas or alongside riverbeds.
A particularly desirable form of monazite ore is found in heavy mineral sands, such as these on a beach in Brazil. Travel Pix/Alamy
Within those grains, the monazite is relatively hard and chemically inert. The monazite might be just a few percent by weight, but it typically contains between 45 and 70 percent rare earths by weight, including, in many cases, all of the necessary rare earths for magnets: neodymium, praseodymium, dysprosium, and terbium.
“The best distribution of rare-earth elements that you can find anywhere is in monazites,” says Constantine Karayannopoulos, former CEO of Neo Performance Materials and now a director of or adviser to several rare-earths firms. “The real money is in those four elements.” Dysprosium and terbium, both examples of heavy rare earths, are particularly sought after and are usually not present in the most commonly mined ore for rare earths, called bastnaesite.
There are vast deposits of monazite-bearing heavy mineral sands in Australia, Brazil, India, Madagascar, Mozambique, and South Africa, with smaller ones in China, Idaho, Indonesia, Malaysia, Sri Lanka, Thailand, the southeastern U.S., and Vietnam.
A geologist points out dark veins of hard-rock monazite ore in the Steenkampskraal mine in South Africa [top]. Ore samples from the mine are collected for analysis [above].Rodger Bosch/AFP/Getty Images
What’s more, collecting the ore simply involves dredging or strip-mining the sands, as opposed to the blasting, drilling, and heavy earth moving required to get at hard-rock ores. Then, too, the sands are already in granular form, so they don’t need to be crushed or ground, like rock ores do. Separating out the heavy minerals from the sands can usually be done at the mining site, using relatively cheap magnetic or gravity-based techniques, leaving a relatively high grade of concentrate for further processing.
And now the bad news about heavy mineral sands. “The problem is they tend to have a lot of thorium,” which is weakly radioactive, says James Kennedy, president of ThREE consulting, a rare-earths advisory firm based in Missouri. “The thorium is the single biggest problem” with using the sands, he says. “If you were mining and processing monazites for rare earths, you would end up with hundreds and eventually thousands of tons of thorium-containing radioactive residues” per processing facility. The only markets for thorium are a couple of tiny ones for welding rods and some optics, he says, so “you have to store it.” And under the rules for nuclear material set by the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission and the International Atomic Energy Agency, any stored radioactive material that doesn’t have a planned use or disposal pathway is considered nuclear waste. “So the [radioactive] liability suddenly far exceeds the value of anything you’ve mined and sold,” Kennedy says.
It wasn’t always this way. Up until the 1950s, monazite was the main ore mined for rare earths. Companies processed heavy mineral sands from Australia, Brazil, and India, and hard rock from South Africa, to produce rare earths for tracer ammunition, steel alloys, cigarette-lighter flints, and, later, color-TV phosphors.
The Mountain Pass mine and processing plants, in California, are the only large-scale rare-earth production facilities in the United States.David McNew/Getty Images
Several developments combined to shift rare-earths production from monazite to bastnaesite. In 1949, a vast deposit of bastnaesite ore was discovered at Mountain Pass in California. By the early 1960s, bastnaesite had eclipsed monazite as the primary rare-earth ore. In the 1990s, with rare-earth production shifting to China, the move toward bastnaesite continued with the exploitation of massive deposits in that country, such as those at Maoniuping, that were either entirely or mostly bastnaesite.
Now, though, any resurgence of rare-earth production outside of China may hinge on a monazite renaissance, and some observers are taking a hard look at the strict regulations that control the handling of thorium and other by-products of monazite processing. Those regulations, Kennedy insists, will throttle the rare-earth ambitions of the world outside China, unless governments take action now.
“You rationalize the regulations around thorium and you will end the rare-earth crisis in the U.S.,” he declares. “You’ll turn rare earths from something that’s always scarce to something that is common and just naturally flows out of other mining.”
How to Scale Rare-Earth Processing Using “Waste”
A prime example of Kennedy’s vision already exists at Energy Fuels, based in Lakewood, Colo. It’s the only company in the U.S. licensed to process, handle, and store compounds of uranium, and among the very few licensed to store radioactive materials of any kind. Those permits give Energy Fuels the distinction of being the only U.S. entity allowed to process monazite ore for its rare earths.
“Supersacks” containing a tonne of neodymium-praseodymium oxides were loaded on pallets at Energy Fuels’ White Mesa Mill.Energy Fuels
The company is moving aggressively to capitalize on that distinction. Energy Fuels’ main business is still uranium—last year it produced nearly 500 tonnes of it. But it has already started selling rare-earth oxides, following a modest $22 million investment in a small rare-earth processing facility at White Mesa Mill in Utah, where it also processes uranium. In September 2025, the company announced that it had sold 1.2 tonnes of neodymium-praseodymium oxide to South Korea–based POSCO International Corp., a leading maker of permanent-magnet assemblies for EV motors. Around the same time, Energy Fuels disclosed that it had raised a further $700 million.
In December 2025, the company announced it had produced small quantities of dysprosium oxide. Tiny amounts of dysprosium are needed for motor magnets to ensure they keep functioning at high temperatures. Today, essentially all of the world’s dysprosium comes from China.
Energy Fuels says it can produce 1,000 tonnes of rare-earth oxide a year at White Mesa Mill. But its rare-earth production there currently shares facilities with the uranium operations, so they cannot both be produced at the same time. Its monazite comes from the chemical company Chemours, which mines heavy mineral sands in Florida and Georgia to produce titanium and zirconium. The monazite ore sold to Energy Fuels is what remains after Chemours strips out the minerals it needs, namely ilmenite and zircon.
The chemical company Chemours mines heavy mineral sands at sites in the U.S. states of Georgia [seen here] and Florida. Monazite extracted from the sands is sold to Lakewood, Colo.-based Energy Fuels, which processes the ore into rare-earth oxides.Chemours
“Effectively, monazites are waste,” Karayannopoulos points out. “So you don’t have to dig another mine” to produce them.
Chemours and Energy Fuels have agreements under which Chemours ships 500 tonnes of monazite annually to White Mesa Mill. Energy Fuels is also negotiating or already has deals that would give it access to enormous reserves of monazite ore in Australia, Brazil, and Madagascar. These will be essential for its ambitions to become a world-class supplier of rare-earth oxides.
Mark Chalmers, former CEO of Energy Fuels, led the uranium company’s entrance into the rare-earths business.Jesse Rieser/The New York Times/Redux
“We’re playing a long game,” says Mark Chalmers, who recently retired as Energy Fuels’ CEO and is now a consultant to the company. “We’re doing the engineering right now on a larger facility that will have the capacity to produce up to 6,000 tonnes per year” of rare-earth oxide, he said in an interview. For comparison, Lynas Rare Earths produced around 12,000 tonnes of rare-earth oxide in its most recent fiscal year.
In announcing the $725 million conditional loan commitment with Energy Fuels, the U.S. Defense Department’s Office of Strategic Capital said the deal would help Energy Fuels scale up its output of rare-earth oxides and also help realize the company’s plans to turn the oxides into metals, a key step preceding the fabrication of magnets.
What Are the Risks in the Rare-Earth Supply Chain?
To see what can go wrong with a monazite project, consider the project in Saskatoon, Canada, where the Saskatchewan Research Council (SRC) has built and demonstrated a pilot plant to produce rare-earth oxides from monazite ore. It’s the only rare-earth extraction and separation plant in the country. In an email, a spokesperson said the plant “is scheduled to be commissioned by year’s end and after a production ramp-up phase, operational within the calendar year 2027.” When in “full operation,” at a time not specified by the spokesperson, the plant will have a capacity somewhere between 400 and 600 tonnes of rare-earth metal per year.
But even that relatively modest output will depend on a reliable supply or “feedstock” of monazite. In an industry small enough that many of the top people are on a first-name basis, SRC’s inability to secure such a supply is an open secret. “Their problem is they haven’t got enough feedstock to run on a continuous basis, so they’re making sample runs,” a well-connected industry observer told IEEE Spectrum. (SRC declined to make an official available for this story.)
In April 2024, SRC announced it had reached agreements with a Vietnamese organization, the Hung Thinh Group, for 3,000 tonnes of rare-earth carbonate per year for five years. It’s unclear how much of that feedstock has made it to the SRC facility. Vietnamese government restrictions on the export of monazite and bastnaesite have been in effect since 2022 and became law this past January.
But the real twist here is that one of the largest, highest-grade monazite deposits in the world is just 800 kilometers from Saskatoon, near Alces Lake in Saskatchewan. It’s likely that the SRC facility was conceived and built with that monazite deposit in mind. After all, as a government-owned entity, SRC says its mission is “to help the people of Saskatchewan strengthen the economy with quality jobs and a secure environment.”
The Alces Lake deposit is owned by Appia Rare Earths & Uranium Corp. In an interview, Appia’s CEO, Tom Drivas, talked up the possibility of a link between SRC and Appia. “SRC would be our logical option because, you know, it’s in the same area, same province. They need the monazite. And if we can supply the monazite, that’s sort of a natural, right?”
It probably won’t happen, though. The logic of rare-earth mining is utterly different from the logic of mining a commodity like, say, copper. Multiple experts contacted by Spectrum suggested that the cost of developing a monazite mine at Alces Lake, including such necessary infrastructure as roadways, electricity, and water, would be in the hundreds of millions of dollars. Such costs, and the mercurial exigencies of the rare-earths market, make it unlikely that the government of Saskatchewan would commit that kind of money, even with help from the Canadian federal government. These factors help explain why Canada, which has some of the most attractive deposits of rare-earth ores on the planet, along with impressive mining companies and resources, has no operating mines for rare earths.
Meanwhile, SRC is pursuing other options. Under a deal announced in May with REalloys, in Euclid, Ohio, REalloys will spend $20.6 million for upgrades to SRC’s Saskatoon facility, while SRC develops technology to produce rare-earth metals from rare-earth oxides. The deal also gives REalloys the right to purchase up to 80 percent of the SRC plant’s output. Where will the feedstock come from? Hard to say, but REalloys also struck a deal with U.S. Critical Materials Corp. for 10 percent of the hypothetical output of a proposed mine at Sheep Creek, in Montana. Sheep Creek reportedly has substantial amounts of hard-rock monazite that’s unusually low in thorium. But it’s far from certain that those deposits will ever be mined. The proposal for developing a mine there, in a breathtakingly scenic area near the headwaters of the Bitterroot River, has attracted fierce opposition from environmental groups, outdoor enthusiasts, and local officials.
Taken together, SRC’s recent moves have left industry veterans nonplussed. “I’m not sure what their business model is,” said one. “They say, ‘we’re a research institute. Our mandate is to help industry.’ The reality is, they’re competing with industry.”
SRC has also drawn scrutiny for some questionable business practices. In 2022, SRC board member Dennis Fitzpatrick was fired after raising concerns about the qualifications of an engineer hired to manage and direct operations at SRC’s Saskatoon plant. The president and CEO of SRC at the time, Mike Crabtree, was responsible for the hire. A subsequent investigation of Fitzpatrick’s claims by the Canadian Broadcasting Corp. detailed a troubling web of relationships and practices surrounding the SRC’s rare-earths initiative. (Fitzpatrick did not respond to multiple emails.) For example, past business associates of Crabtree’s were reportedly appointed to positions of authority without any other candidates being considered and without their connections to Crabtree being made public.
In one case, in 2021, Crabtree disclosed that he was offering a venture capital firm, Westbridge Capital, an opportunity to invest in the rare-earths plant. But according to Fitzpatrick, Crabtree never mentioned that the VC firm was run by an SRC board member who also happened to be one of Crabtree’s business associates—or that Crabtree himself was a trustee of Westbridge and an investor in the company, as well as a paid advisor.
Crabtree remains as SRC’s CEO.
Managing Toxic By-products From Rare Earths
Putting aside SRC’s missteps, the organization does have one advantage: It holds multiple licenses from the Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission to handle, process, and manage radioactive materials. And that’s huge.
Most of the radioactive burden associated with processing monazite ore comes from substances produced during processing. In one of the early steps, pulverized, powdery ore is dried and then leached in strong acids—a process called cracking—to produce a rare-earth concentrate. Waste products of this step include a slurry containing thorium hydroxide and much smaller amounts of uranium hydroxide. The rare-earth concentrate then undergoes an extraction process to isolate specific rare earths, such as neodymium or dysprosium. More thorium and also radium are produced during these steps.
Waste barrels were photographed in 2024 at Energy Fuels’ White Mesa Mill, where ores containing uranium and rare-earths are processed and refined.Jesse Rieser/The New York Times/Redux
The thorium hydroxide slurry, meanwhile, is typically deposited in heavily regulated waste cells, called tailings impoundments or tailings ponds. The thorium hydroxide, either in the form of a slurry or a powder, must be stored in isolation from the environment indefinitely. Energy Fuels stores waste from its longstanding uranium production operations, as well as its new rare-earth operations, in tailings impoundments at its White Mesa Mill facility. The impoundments are just 10 kilometers from the community center of the Ute Mountain Ute Tribe, a group of Indigenous people, which has vigorously opposed operations at White Mesa Mill for more than 20 years.
Virtually all of the thorium is the isotope thorium-232, which is only weakly radioactive. Its radiation is alpha particles, which cannot penetrate human skin. Nevertheless, improper storage can have serious consequences, particularly if the thorium is inhaled or ingested.
“Have a look at the gravitational separation of HMS [heavy mineral sands] in Nigeria,” Thomas Kruemmer, a rare-earth consultant and analyst, wrote in an email. “There is lots of dust in the Nigerian processing sites, which the workers inevitably breathe in. And inside your respiratory system there isn’t any protective skin, so alpha radiation develops its full potential. This is something many people do not consider.”
In 2012, protestors in Malaysia [top] rallied against the Lynas rare earths processing facility [above], then under construction near Kuantan. Left: AFP/Getty Images; Right: Goh Seng Chong/Bloomberg/Getty Images
Moreover, adds Kruemmer, “it is not thorium itself. It is the decay isotopes of thorium that are highly radioactive.” One decay product of thorium is polonium, he points out, “the preferred poison for [killing] Russian dissidents.”
In 1982, a company called Asia Rare Earth, a subsidiary of Mitsubishi Chemical, began extracting yttrium from monazite ore in Perak, Malaysia. Local residents soon began complaining of various illnesses. With the consent of the Malaysian government, the company had built a waste channel to a nearby disposal site, where the waste was stored in open steel barrels and in an unlined waste pond. The waste overflowed from the pond whenever it rained heavily. In 1984, a Japanese professor measured radiation levels at and near the pond and found them to be, in the most extreme cases, hundreds of times higher than internationally accepted maximums. A subsequent investigation found extremely high levels of birth defects and eight cases of leukemia in the small community near the waste dump.
In 2011, at age 69, Lai Kwan prepared to bathe her 29-year-old son, Cheah Kok Leong [top]. Cheah Kok was born with severe mental disabilities that Lai Kwan believed were caused by exposure to radiation that she received while working at a rare earths processing plant in Bukit Merah, Malaysia [bottom, photographed during its disassembly].Rahman Roslan/The New York Times/Redux
A protracted legal fight among local residents and Asia Rare Earth and the Malaysian government culminated in the closure of the plant in 1992. By that time, so much radioactive material had been carelessly dumped that cleanup took more than two decades and cost Mitsubishi an estimated $100 million. The episode still haunts the rare-earths industry in Malaysia, where Lynas now processes monazite concentrate at the largest rare earths processing facility in the world. That plant, in Kuantan in the state of Pahang, has been the subject of organized and active local opposition that began even before its commissioning in 2012. The Malaysian government has sporadically tightened its regulations on the plant, stipulating that, for example, radioactive wastes be shipped out of Malaysia or that the processing stages that create radioactive residues be accomplished outside of Malaysia.
Kennedy notes that if monazite ore is to become a major source of rare earths, much larger quantities of thorium will need to be disposed, probably more than could be economically accommodated in lined and isolated tailings ponds.
One of the very few options for using such large amounts of thorium involves nuclear power. Years ago, countries including the U.S., Canada, Norway, and Germany had thorium-reactor research programs, and India has had a slow-moving program for decades. But today, the only operating thorium power reactor is in China. The Shanghai Institute of Applied Physics of the Chinese Academy of Sciences has been operating, since 2023, a 2-megawatt molten-salt-cooled reactor that is thorium-fueled.
The world’s only operating thorium reactor is a 2-megawatt unit at the Shanghai Institute of Applied Physics of the Chinese Academy of Sciences. In October 2025, technicians used mechanical arms to analyze samples of the reactor’s molten-salt fuel.Jin Liwang/Xinhua/Getty Images
A couple of Western startups are keeping the thorium reactor dream alive. A Franco-Dutch company called Thorizon says it has designed a reactor that would be fueled by a mixture of thorium and spent nuclear fuel. Startup Copenhagen Atomics is working on a 1-MW reactor that’s a prototype for a 100-MW, mass-manufacturable, molten-salt reactor.
Processing of monazite ore could provide fuel for an enormous number of thorium reactors far into the future. Consider a single large facility producing 5,000 tonnes of rare-earth oxide a year. If the monazite contains 7 percent thorium, the plant would also be producing roughly 700 tonnes of thorium a year. According to Rusty Towell, a professor at Abilene Christian University in Texas who directs an advanced-reactor project there, a tonne of thorium would be sufficient to generate about 350 MW (electric) for a year. So the large processing facility alone would be throwing off enough thorium annually to keep 2,450 100-MW reactors operating for a year.
That amount of power—245 gigawatts—is about half of all the generating capacity growth forecast for the United States over the next decade, a period during which analysts expect accelerating electricity growth due to increasing numbers of data centers and electric vehicles.
What Could Strangle Rare-Earth Supply Chains?
Virtually all rare-earths experts foresee a growing role for monazite. But given the problems with thorium, local opposition to some projects, and political instabilities connected to others, some have muted expectations. “The sole and single monazite hope rests with Iluka’s expensive project in Australia, IMHO,” writes Kruemmer. Iluka Resources, based in Perth, is now building a massive rare-earths refining facility at Eneabba, 275 km north of Perth. It will process a million-tonne monazite stockpile that accumulated over decades from the company’s other mining operations. The cost of the project is estimated at AU $1.8 billion (about US $1.3 billion).
In a US $1.3 billion project, Iluka Resources is building a massive facility in Eneabba, Australia, to extract and separate rare earths from a million-tonne stockpile of monazite, visible in the background of this photo.Iluka Resources
For other experts, though, the biggest challenges facing monazite projects isn’t thorium, or radiation, or regulations. It’s the blend of quirks, misconceptions, and self-dealing that dog the entire rare-earths industry.
“The rare-earth mining business is the Afghanistan of mining,” quips Kennedy. It’s a place where people and companies go with grand ideas, only to become ensnared in quagmires.
One fundamental problem is the highly speculative nature of almost every aspect of the rare-earths business, which lends itself to backroom deals. In particular, the industry is plagued by speculators who buy stakes in a project with no intention of staying with the project through completion; they cash out as soon as they can profit from any future favorable news—a technique known as “pump and dump.”
Consider the Trump administration’s decision to take a 10 percent stake in USA Rare Earth in exchange for $277 million and to provide a $1.3 billion secured loan to the company. USA Rare Earth has the rights to a deposit called Round Top near Sierra Blanca, Texas. The company hired the Wall Street firm Cantor Fitzgerald to raise $1 billion in equity financing for the deal. Cantor Fitzgerald, as it happens, is run by the sons of Howard Lutnick, Donald Trump’s Commerce Secretary.
Meanwhile, there is no rare-earths mine at Round Top, and it’s a distinct possibility that there never will be.
“The current administration consistently fails to seek expert advice and is recklessly pouring billions of taxpayer dollars into speculative [rare-earth element] processes and projects, like Round Top, that have little chance of commercial success,” says Terry McNulty, a mining consultant based in Tucson.
Geoff Atkins, vice president of business development of the Canadian rare-earths firm Ucore Rare Metals, had advice for his colleagues at a convention of the Critical Minerals Institute in 2022. “Instead of focusing on your speculative value,” he said, “instead of being able to say we’ve got the biggest project in the world, instead of, ‘we’ve got a [net present value] of $3 billion or $4 billion,’ how about you say, ‘we’ve got a project which is going to get into operation, and this operation is going to provide the greatest value to our shareholders in the long term, not just in the short term when we can pump this up and, you know, the [early] investors can sell out.
“Because unless there is that shift,” he warned, “we’re not going to have any hope of getting the volumes we need to give the certainty to the downstream supply chain.”
In short, the rare-earths industry outside of China needs to grow up. And sooner rather than later.
