articles.title: Governments are hacking people with 'zero-click' spyware by showing them online ads | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Security researchers at digital rights unit The Citizen Lab say government spyware makers are abusing global advertising networks to target and hack devices by serving malicious online adverts.
A new report published Thursday by the University of Toronto lab, which investigates surveillance and digital rights abuses, said an Israeli company called Discover-Tech allows spyware makers to use its advertising platform to target specific people or devices almost anywhere in the world with spyware capable of invisibly stealing their data.
The researchers say Discover-Tech presents itself as a legitimate advertising firm, but instead serves as a “bridge between ad vendors and the mercenary spyware ecosystem.”
Citizen Lab said at least two makers of zero-click spyware, Candiru and Bindecy, used Discover-Tech’s platform to target people. Both of these spyware makers provide surveillance products that can infect devices without the victim having to open a message or click on a link.
The researchers found that one attack affected at least 45 Windows computers at media organization Al Jazeera. The devices were apparently hacked in 2024 and 2025 via Candiru’s spyware after being exposed to online ads packed with malicious code.
Citizen Lab said it wasn’t clear which governments were behind the attacks, but said this is the first confirmation of zero-click government-backed spyware attacks being delivered through online ads, potentially putting a vast number of devices around the world at risk of being targeted and hacked.
“There has been a lot of buzz that online ads can be used to identify and automatically hack targets with pinpoint precision, but now for the first time, we have concrete technical evidence showing this process in action,” said Bill Marczak, a Citizen Lab senior researcher, ahead of the report’s release.
Hackers have long sought ways to abuse access to advertising networks, in part because of their ability to reach almost any internet-connected device in the world. Ad networks are designed to help advertisers target certain kinds of people, devices, and organizations with specific ads, but they can also be abused to target specific individuals or devices with malicious code.
While such so-called “malvertising” attacks are not new, using online ads to allow powerful government spyware to silently hack into devices is a notable escalation.
Security and privacy experts have for years encouraged people to install ad-blockers to prevent ads from being displayed on desktop and mobile screens, including within apps. But the ubiquity of online advertising makes it difficult to escape the industry’s clutches entirely.
The researchers said Discover-Tech’s platform, which the company calls Controlium, left some of its source code exposed on its login pages, allowing the researchers to recreate its web-based control panel dashboard without needing to log in. The researchers say the web dashboard “appears to be specifically designed to allow them to push malicious content to individual targeted users alongside advertisements.”
Citizen Lab also found that Discover-Tech’s site had a publicly accessible portion that allowed the researchers to download reams of user login records for the Controlium dashboard without needing a password. Some login details belonged to at least two employees of spyware maker Candiru, as well as some from Bindecy.
The researchers also found billions of ad bidding records left exposed on Discover-Tech’s website, which showed that its ads had ultimately been displayed across tens of thousands of mobile apps and websites between March and June 2026.
The bidding records show that the ads were shown on devices used by militaries, governments, critical infrastructure, and national cyber agencies. However, it’s unclear if the displayed ads resulted in a compromise or infection.
Security researchers with ad quality platform Confiant, which worked with Citizen Lab to investigate, said they found evidence that potentially malicious ads were similarly shown on devices on the networks of the International Atomic Energy Agency and the International Criminal Court.
Citizen Lab’s Marczak said Discover-Tech is “surely just the tip of the iceberg,” and urged people to take defensive action.
“If you might be targeted based on who you are or what you do, it’s time to disable ad tracking on your devices or even block ads altogether,” said Marczak.
Al Jazeera did not respond to a request for comment about the hacks. Neither did Discover-Tech, and Candiru maker Integrity Labs could not be reached for comment.

articles.title: 16,8 Milliarden Dollar Umsatz: Anthropic nimmt den IPO ins Visier
articles.text:
Vor dem Börsengang: Anthropic steigert Umsatz auf 16,8 Milliarden Dollar
Anthropic meldet vor dem erwarteten Börsengang einen Umsatzsprung auf 16,8 Milliarden Dollar im dritten Quartal. Das berichtet die Nachrichtenagentur Bloomberg unter Berufung auf mit der Angelegenheit vertraute Personen.
Das ist eine deutliche Steigerung: Im ersten Quartal hatte der Umsatz noch bei 4,7 Milliarden Dollar gelegen, im zweiten Quartal stieg er auf 11,6 Milliarden US-Dollar.
Laut dem Bericht soll der Claude-Entwickler Investoren bei einer Präsentation am Mittwoch in seiner Zentrale in San Francisco entsprechende Zahlen vorgelegt haben, die außerdem zeigen, dass Anthropic im vergangenen Quartal auf bereinigter Basis profitabel gewesen ist.
Im vergangenen Jahr hatte Anthropic noch einen Nettoverlust von fast 42 Milliarden Dollar verzeichnet – rund fünfmal so viel wie im Vorjahr. Der operative Verlust stieg auf mehr als acht Milliarden Dollar. Gleichzeitig lag der Jahresumsatz 2025 bei rund 4,6 Milliarden Dollar und damit deutlich über den 386 Millionen Dollar des Vorjahres.
Allerdings machte das KI-Unternehmen zuletzt laut einem Bericht der Financial Times fast ein Viertel des Umsatzes mit lediglich zwei Kunden. Außerdem sollen viele der größten Kunden nicht durch langfristige Verträge an Anthropic gebunden sein, könnten also jederzeit zur günstigeren Konkurrenz wechseln.
Das wirft die Frage auf, ob das von früheren OpenAI-Führungskräften gegründete Unternehmen langfristig den hohen Kosten für die Entwicklung und den Betrieb seiner KI-Systeme entsprechende Umsätze entgegensetzen kann.
Bislang wurde das Wachstum von Anthropic auch durch Amazon und Google gestützt, die bei dem KI-Startup zugleich Großinvestoren, Lieferanten von Rechenleistung und Vertriebspartner sind. Gleichzeitig entwickelt die Google-Mutter Alphabet mit Gemini ein eigenes KI-System, und auch Amazon arbeitet mit Amazon Nova an einem eigenen Sprachmodell.
Börsengang im Herbst
Die Börsennotierung soll noch in diesem Jahr erfolgen. Laut dem Bloomberg-Bericht könnte Anthropic bereits ab dem 9. November offiziell mit der Vermarktung des Börsengangs beginnen. Der IPO selbst könnte dann noch vor dem US-amerikanischen Thanksgiving-Feiertag erfolgen. Anthropic strebt dabei eine Rekordbewertung von mehr als zwei Billionen Dollar an. Zuletzt hatten Investoren eine Bewertung zwischen 1,8 und 2 Billionen Dollar für realistisch gehalten.
Damit könnte Anthropic den jüngst von SpaceX aufgestellten Rekord-Börsengang vielleicht sogar in den Schatten stellen. Die Firma von Elon Musk ist im Juni mit einer Bewertung von rund 1,8 Billionen Dollar an die Börse gegangen.
Außerdem sieht es so aus, als würde Anthropic das Rennen gegen OpenAI gewinnen. Auch der ChatGPT-Entwickler strebt an die Börse, hat aber zuletzt das Tempo gedrosselt. Firmenchef Sam Altman sagt in Interviews, er gehe nicht mehr von einem Börsengang im Jahr 2026 aus. Dabei hatte auch OpenAI im Juni dieses Jahres, kurz nach Anthropic, einen vertraulichen Antrag für den IPO bei der US-Börsenaufsicht SEC eingereicht. Der erste Schritt zur Einleitung des Börsengangs.
Im Gegensatz zu OpenAI setzt Anthropic von Beginn an stärker auf Firmenkunden und versucht, sich über das Thema KI-Sicherheit von der Konkurrenz abzuheben. Das Unternehmen warnt etwa vor den Gefahren immer leistungsfähigerer Systeme.
Gleichzeitig bewerten Anleger die hohen Investitionen der KI-Unternehmen zunehmend kritisch und verlangen Belege dafür, dass sich die hohen Ausgaben in Gewinne umwandeln lassen.

articles.title: NVIDIA Expands Advanced Technology Access for Europe’s Scientific Community Through Open Learning Resources, Collaborations and Compute
articles.text:
Much of today’s scientific progress begins with computation.
But turning accelerated computing’s potential into scientific progress — modeling climate systems, designing molecules, simulating materials and more — depends on more than breakthrough technology. Especially for smaller labs, early-career scientists or science-based startups, the hardest part of research can be everything that comes before the science: assembling tools, finding compute and building the expertise to use both.
At the AI in Science Summit in Dublin today, the European Commission launched the AI in Science Enablers Initiative, a shared framework connected to RAISE — the Resource for AI Science in Europe — that brings private-sector support closer to Europe’s research community.
NVIDIA is joining the campaign, providing:
- Access to accelerated tools, models and platforms
- Compute, cloud resources, data and scientific resources
- Skills, training and technical support
- Collaborative projects and pilots along with support for researchers and talent
- Support for startups and ecosystem development
“Europe’s ambition in AI in science can only become reality if we bring together the strengths of our research community, industry and other partners,” Ekaterina Zaharieva, European Commissioner for Startups, Research and Innovation. “Through the AI in Science Enablers campaign, we are turning this ambition into concrete commitments that give researchers access to the tools, expertise and resources they need to innovate.”
Open Models
NVIDIA’s pledge begins with open source technology.
NVIDIA has released more than 250 open models, 250 open datasets and over 1,400 open source software projects spanning large language models, healthcare, robotics, climate science, physical AI, autonomous vehicles and scientific research. The models and datasets are available on Hugging Face and GitHub.
Building on this open ecosystem, researchers can build agentic reasoning capabilities with NVIDIA Nemotron — a family of architectures, open weights, open source models, training data and recipes — and scientific software including NVIDIA BioNeMo Agent Toolkit, NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo libraries, NVIDIA Earth-2 models and NVIDIA ALCHEMI NIM microservices to accelerate research across biology, chemistry, molecular design, weather and climate, energy, engineering, physics and material sciences.
Skills and Training
Building advanced intelligence capability across Europe requires knowledge that travels as freely as compute.
The NVIDIA Deep Learning Institute has launched a new open source courseware hub with hands-on course materials covering accelerated computing and deep learning — freely downloadable and openly licensed, with no enrollment, fees or deadline.
Modular by design, the courses can be adapted for university curricula, supercomputing center bootcamps or developer community events, and serve as a direct bridge to NVIDIA’s broader training and certification programs.
Access to Compute
NVIDIA is collaborating with cloud infrastructure partners and European national AI factories — including in France, Spain and Sweden — to open new routes for startups and small- and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) to access sovereign European compute and services.
The NVIDIA Inception program for startups provides access to compute resources and technical support, lowering the barrier to entry for startups seeking high-performance infrastructure and technological education.
AI2F in France is the first AI factory to have collaborated with the Inception program for four months, demonstrating strong results.
The BSC AI Factory ran a pilot initiative and is now rolling out its first full accelerator program, with growing interest from other European national AI factories in replicating the model in 2027. Beyond startup support, this program is designed to contribute to a broader strategic objective: building self-sustaining AI ventures in Spain and Europe.
Sweden AI Factory, one of Europe’s 19 EuroHPC-funded AI factories, announced a collaboration with NVIDIA to open its infrastructure and expertise to Inception startups and SMEs enterprises across sectors including life and material sciences, autonomous systems and gaming.
Finally, EuroHPC supercomputing centers such as CINECA and JSC provide academia and startups with free access to NVIDIA GPU infrastructure and services for open research. NVIDIA complements this access with office hours, bootcamps and hackathons that help researchers fine-tune models on their own datasets.
As an example, NVIDIA is co-organizing an European AI hackathon this month alongside Austrian Scientific Computing, the Leibniz Supercomputing Centre, the High-Performance Computing Center Stuttgart and The Cyprus Institute, for Pharos-CY.
AI Infrastructure Expansion

articles.title: NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL Powers Specialized Agents with Multimodal Reasoning | NVIDIA Technical Blog
articles.text:
Always-on agents are taking on longer, more complex enterprise workflows. A single request can involve reading a document, checking information across sources, following company policy, and calling several tools.
NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is an open, customizable multimodal model for these specialized workflows. Its 120B-parameter mixture-of-experts (MoE) architecture activates 12B parameters per token, balancing model capacity with inference efficiency.
On a single GPU, this model delivers up to 5x higher throughput for agentic tasks compared to other open models in its size category.
The model combines reasoning, instruction following, and tool use with text, image, document, and video understanding. By combining these capabilities into one model, teams can handle text and visual tasks without deploying separate text and vision-language models or passing task context between them.
Developers can post-train Nemotron 3.5 Super VL with NVIDIA NeMo using their own data, tools, policies, and workflows. This post explains how to use that foundation to build specialized enterprise agents and describes the training and inference techniques that power it.
Why Nemotron 3.5 Super VL for specialized agents?
Agents need to understand both their tasks and operating environments. A customer-service agent must follow company return policies. Research agents connect evidence across sources, while document agents interpret tables, charts, and page layouts.
Nemotron 3.5 Super VL combines reasoning and visual understanding across a range of agent workflows, including:
- Coding: Test and validate code, analyze errors, and recommend fixes.
- Web research: Search across websites, connect information, and verify answers.
- Document intelligence: Extract information from tables, charts, and page layouts to produce summaries and reports.
- Cybersecurity: Identify security vulnerabilities and triage threats to prioritize remediation.
- Video understanding: Extract information for search, content review, and incident analysis.
Within a system of models, Nemotron 3.5 Super VL handles specialized, multistep work that needs reasoning, tool use, and text and visual understanding together. Smaller models, such as NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, handle high-volume text tasks, while frontier models such as NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Ultra tackle complex planning and orchestration.
Customize Nemotron 3.5 Super VL for domain data, tools, and policies
Specialized agents must learn how an organization works. Domain terminology, tool interfaces, operating procedures, and policy requirements shape how agents complete tasks successfully.
Organizations in industries ranging from cybersecurity and finance to healthcare are post-training Nemotron 3.5 Super VL to outperform frontier models in accuracy and efficiency across their production workflows. For example:
- Scale AI, an AI data and technology provider, post-trained Nemotron 3.5 Super VL for automated vendor credit processing at Skydance Corporation, a media and entertainment company. Inference cost for this workload will decrease by 40x and latency by 5x.
- Ramp, a financial operations platform provider, is converting receipt images into structured JSON containing merchant information, dates, and payment data. Ramp expects up to 50% higher throughput and 10x lower latency.
- AI21 and Alice post-trained Nemotron 3.5 Super VL for threat intelligence and vulnerability analysis, improving accuracy by 41%.
Teams can use NVIDIA NeMo open libraries to post-train models to meet these requirements. Developers can use NVIDIA NeMo AutoModel for supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and low-rank adaptation (LoRA) to teach domain-specific behavior. Reinforcement learning (RL) improves performance in agentic environments that reflect organizational workflows.
Alongside Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, NVIDIA is releasing open datasets on Hugging Face. These include agentic tool-use and conversational data, finance reasoning and tool-calling datasets, instruction-following and chat data, long-context transduction and translation data, fairness data, and 40 vision-language datasets. These datasets can supplement proprietary data for SFT and RL.
For multimodal data, start with NeMo Data Designer resources for chart question answering and long-document understanding. Explore NVIDIA NeMo RL and NVIDIA NeMo Gym for RL and environment-based evaluation.
Organizations can adapt and deploy the model’s open weights in supported local, data center, or cloud environments to meet their infrastructure and data requirements. For customization resources, see the Nemotron 3.5 Super VL usage cookbook on GitHub.
Combine text and visual understanding in one workflow
Nemotron 3.5 Super VL combines text, image, document, and video understanding with reasoning and instruction following to answer questions across these inputs.
Its visual training covers charts, tables, optical character recognition (OCR), multipage documents, and video understanding. A two-stage SFT pipeline trains the language and vision components, combining visual evidence with reasoning, chat, safety, long-context data, and agent trajectories.
For document intelligence, the same model can interpret a chart, connect it with a table elsewhere in a document, and summarize both. Developers can tailor the workflow to their own documents and evaluation criteria.
Diverse training data generated with NeMo Data Designer helped the model better understand complex charts. On CharXiv, a chart-reasoning benchmark, the model scored 80.8%, compared with 63% for Nemotron 3 Nano Omni. With Python code interpretation, it reached 84%. For the approach and lessons learned, read the chart-understanding deep dive and the open-source chart question-answering pipeline.
This model was built with support and expertise from Nemotron Coalition organizations. For instance, high-quality datasets from Perplexity helped improve and streamline the model’s mid-training. Environments from Prime Intellect enabled building better teacher models.
Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is also one of the top open models on the OCRBench v2 leaderboard.
Accuracy and efficiency across agent tasks
Evaluations of Nemotron 3.5 Super VL span Hermes, LangChain, OpenClaw, OpenCode, Pi, Codex, and Claude. In addition to coding tasks, agent harness providers use their own evaluations to test a wide range of agent tasks. On Hermes Bench and LangChain behavioral evaluations, Nemotron 3.5 Super VL scores higher than Nemotron 3 Ultra.
| Model | Hermes Bench | LangChain Evals | 
|---|---|---|
| Nemotron 3 Ultra | 56.33% | 84.3% | 
| Nemotron 3.5 Super VL | 63.44% | 87.05% | 
For always-on agents, efficiency determines how much work a deployment can complete. Throughput, token usage, tool calls, and the steps needed to reach a correct result all affect task completion time.
This model was also optimized to run locally on NVIDIA DGX Spark. An independent evaluation by EXO Labs placed Nemotron 3.5 Super VL on the Pareto frontier for accuracy and task completion time.
Nemotron 3.5 Super VL under the hood
The model builds on a strong foundation and uses a hybrid architecture, speculative decoding, context reuse, and mixed precision to reduce inference work across repeated agent calls.
Building a strong base model
Nemotron 3.5 Super VL was distilled from Nemotron 3 Ultra. Ultra’s coding capabilities, combined with the SkewReverse loss used during distillation, helped improve coding accuracy.
During post-training, multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) combines guidance from specialized teachers across text and vision. The model generates responses, and the teachers score them for video reasoning and tracking, vision tool use, and alignment.
Additional training on examples of agent actions, code repositories, and software engineering tasks improved the model’s performance on agent tasks. Nemotron 3.5 Super VL outperforms Nemotron 3 Super on SWE-bench and Terminal-Bench across multiple evaluation setups.
Continued pretraining with high-quality natural and synthetic data improved Indic-language capabilities and contributed to higher overall scores after post-training. This stage added 10B Indic tokens, drawn from a 12-language subset of Nemotron-pretraining-Indic-v1 and natural Indic text.
NVIDIA is releasing the full dataset, which contains about 2.8T tokens across 22 Indian languages and was developed with IIT Madras and its AI4Bharat lab. The following results are based on the post-trained Nemotron 3.5 Super VL.
Developers can use NeMo to build on this foundation and customize Nemotron 3.5 Super VL for their applications, adapting its reasoning and agentic capabilities to their data, tools, and workflows.
LiLiCorr: An open speculative decoding technique
LiLiCorr improves parallel speculative decoding by jointly evaluating token candidates across an entire draft, capturing dependencies that independent token predictions miss. A lightweight network computes compatibility scores in a single pass to produce more coherent drafts, leaving only a low-cost, sequential final selection step.
On DGX Spark, LiLiCorr is the recommended drafter for low-latency inference with Nemotron 3.5 Super VL. It delivers up to 2.3x faster token generation than decoding without speculation.
NVFP4 and mixed precision
The model uses NVIDIA Model Optimizer for post-training quantization and quantization-aware distillation (QAD). The NVFP4 recipe uses 4-bit weights and activations on the NVIDIA Blackwell architecture. The same checkpoint runs on non-Blackwell platforms with 4-bit weights and 16-bit activations. Precision is selected separately for sensitive components.
NVFP4 makes the model smaller, and QAD helps it retain its accuracy at lower precision. During QAD, the quantized model learns to match the outputs of the original BF16 model, which closes the accuracy gap that quantization introduces. QAD also supports storing the key-value (KV) cache in NVFP4 instead of FP8 while still meeting accuracy targets. Because QAD happens during training, it adds no inference overhead.
Multi-token prediction
Multi-token prediction (MTP) gives Nemotron 3.5 Super VL an internal drafter that proposes several tokens for the main model to verify in one forward pass. Accepting multiple tokens at once reduces the number of compute-intensive verification steps needed to generate a response.
A dedicated MTP-boosting training phase further aligned the drafter with the final model.
Context reuse across agent turns
Agents repeatedly pass system instructions, tool definitions, and conversation history back to the model. Prefix caching reuses computation from those shared inputs.
The model’s serving optimizations preserve both attention caches and Mamba recurrent states. Additional Mamba checkpoints reduce the replay needed to recover inputs for speculative decoding, while internal checkpointing avoids extra model passes during prompt processing.
Simplify production deployment with NVIDIA NIM and NVIDIA Dynamo
NVIDIA NIM packages models with optimized inference engines, validated configurations, and standard APIs for cloud and data center deployment. NIM receives ongoing security, feature, and performance updates. Enterprise support is available through NVIDIA AI Enterprise. Get started with NIM.
NVIDIA Dynamo supports distributed inference optimizations to increase throughput and reduce latency, including KV-cache-aware routing, KV cache management, and disaggregated serving.
On 16 NVIDIA B200 GPUs at 50 tokens per second per user, KV-aware routing with session affinity and KV cache offload serves up to 8x as many users while reducing first-token latency by 85%. Get started with the Dynamo deployment recipes.
Get started with Nemotron 3.5 Super VL
Build specialized agents with multimodal reasoning and tool use. Customize the model for specialized workflows, then deploy it in a supported environment.
The release includes base, post-trained, and NVFP4-quantized checkpoints with training recipes, data, and reinforcement-learning environments.
See the Nemotron 3.5 technical report for model details and Hugging Face or ModelScope for deployment instructions. For hosted model access, see OpenRouter.

articles.title: Meta’s Muse Spark Open now available in Amazon SageMaker JumpStart | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Meta’s Muse Spark Open now available in Amazon SageMaker JumpStart
Muse Spark Open, Meta’s coding-optimized open-weight model, is now available in Amazon SageMaker JumpStart, the machine learning (ML) hub of Amazon SageMaker AI. The model was trained on real developer workflows, such as multi-file refactors and long debugging sessions, and it supports a context window of 1 million tokens. You can deploy it to a SageMaker AI endpoint in your own AWS account in a few steps, without managing the serving infrastructure yourself. SageMaker JumpStart offers two variants: BF16 (Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B) and NVFP4 quantized (Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4).
In this post, we introduce Muse Spark Open and show you how to deploy the model with Amazon SageMaker Studio and the SageMaker Python SDK, send it a first inference request, and clean up.
Overview of Muse Spark Open
Meta describes Muse Spark Open as a coding-optimized model trained for agentic coding workflows, with a focus on first-attempt accuracy, tool calling, and understanding of large codebases. It’s a reasoning model, and it accepts text, images, documents, audio, and audio-video as input and returns text.
Muse Spark Open uses a mixture-of-experts (MoE) architecture with 816 billion total parameters, of which 42 billion are active for each token. The model holds the capacity of a very large network, while the compute it spends on each token is closer to that of a much smaller dense model. Meta releases the weights under the Muse Model License, which includes the Muse Spark Usage Policy.
The following table summarizes the model.
| Attribute | Muse Spark Open | 
| Provider | Meta | 
| Architecture | Mixture of experts (MoE), reasoning model | 
| Parameters | 816B total, 42B active | 
| Context length | 1M tokens | 
| Input modalities | Text, image, document, audio, audio-video | 
| Output modalities | Text | 
| Variants in SageMaker JumpStart | BF16 and NVFP4 | 
| License | Muse Model License, including the Muse Spark Usage Policy | 
Built for long-running coding agents
Meta trained Muse Spark Open on the way developers work in real repositories: code generation, debugging, multi-file refactors, and tasks that run for a long time. With the 1 million-token context window, the model can take in a whole project, including its dependencies, legacy code, and thousands of files. You don’t need to split a task into smaller pieces to fit the context.
Meta also designed Muse Spark Open as an agentic model from the start. Meta says the model plans, acts, observes the result, and corrects itself over long horizons, rather than making single tool calls. As a reasoning model, it works through a task before it acts, and the SageMaker AI endpoint returns that reasoning alongside the answer, so you can follow what an agent is doing and why. Meta trained the model to browse the web, coordinate subagents for work that can be split up, and operate computers across desktop, mobile, and browser environments. These are capabilities of the model. On SageMaker AI, your application or agent framework provides the tools, browser, and computer-use environment that the model calls. Beyond code, Meta reports that Muse Spark Open reasons across images, documents, audio, and video.
Two properties of the model shape how you serve it. First, sparse activation keeps per-token compute low, but serving still requires enough GPU memory to hold all 816 billion parameters, so the instance choice comes down to memory capacity. Second, the NVFP4 variant stores weights in NVIDIA’s 4-bit floating point format, which needs roughly a quarter of the memory of the BF16 weights. On SageMaker AI, that difference decides the instance: the NVFP4 variant runs on ml.p5e.48xlarge, and the BF16 variant runs on ml.p6-b300.48xlarge. That makes NVFP4 the variant to try first when you size for cost. Evaluate it on your own workloads to confirm the quality fits your use case.
With open weights on SageMaker AI, you also control the deployment. The endpoint runs in your AWS account, so your source code and prompts are processed on infrastructure that you configure and control. You can attach the endpoint to your own Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC), encrypt its storage volume with a key from AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS), and turn on network isolation for the container. You also choose the instance type and scaling limits, and you pin the model version, so the model only changes when you redeploy.
Use cases
You can use Muse Spark Open for a wide range of applications. Meta’s focus on coding and agentic workflows suits it to the following use cases:
- Coding assistants over private repositories: Answer questions about large codebases, refactor them, and debug them with the full project in context, while the code is processed on an endpoint in your account.
- Long-running coding agents: Run agents that plan a change, edit across multiple files, run tests in your own sandbox, and correct course based on the results.
- Multimodal engineering workflows: Turn screenshots, design documents, or a recorded bug report with audio and video into a reproduction plan or a draft fix.
Getting started with SageMaker JumpStart
You can deploy Muse Spark Open from SageMaker Studio or with the SageMaker Python SDK. Each path creates a real-time SageMaker AI endpoint in your account.
Prerequisites
Before you start, make sure that you have the following:
- An AWS account with permissions to create SageMaker AI models and endpoints.
- An AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) execution role for SageMaker AI. For this walkthrough, the AmazonSageMakerFullAccess managed policy is sufficient. For production, scope the role to the actions and resources that your deployment needs. For details, refer to How to use SageMaker AI execution roles.
- A SageMaker AI domain with access to SageMaker Studio, for the Studio path. For setup instructions, refer to Use quick setup for Amazon SageMaker AI.
- Service quota for the endpoint instance type: ml.p5e.48xlarge for endpoint usage for the NVFP4 variant, or ml.p6-b300.48xlarge for endpoint usage for the BF16 variant. To raise a quota, refer to Requesting a quota increase.
- For the SDK path: Python 3.10 or later and SageMaker Python SDK v3 (pip install --upgrade sagemaker).
- An AWS Region where Muse Spark Open is available in SageMaker JumpStart. At launch, Muse Spark Open is available in US East (N. Virginia) and US East (Ohio). To check availability in other Regions, open SageMaker JumpStart in your Region.
The instances that host Muse Spark Open are multi-GPU instances, and you pay for an endpoint for as long as it runs, whether or not it serves requests. Delete the endpoint when you finish, as described in the clean-up section of this post. For rates, refer to Amazon SageMaker AI pricing.
Deploy using SageMaker Studio
The SageMaker Studio path suits a first evaluation: you find the model, review its license, and deploy it from one model detail card.
To find Muse Spark Open in SageMaker JumpStart
- Open SageMaker Studio.
- In the navigation pane, choose JumpStart.
- In the search box, enter Muse Spark Open.
- Choose Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B for the BF16 variant or Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 for the NVFP4 variant to open its model detail card.
Figure 1 shows the model detail card, which lists the model description, license, and the Deploy option.
To deploy the model
- On the model detail card, choose Deploy.
- Muse Spark Open is a gated model, so SageMaker Studio shows its end-user license agreement (EULA). Review the agreement and accept it to continue.
- For Endpoint name, keep the generated name or enter your own.
- For Instance type, select ml.p5e.48xlarge for NVFP4 or ml.p6-b300.48xlarge for BF16. SageMaker Studio lists only the instance types that the model supports.
- For Initial instance count, enter 1.
- (Optional) Under Advanced options, select a VPC and an AWS KMS key, or turn on network isolation.
- Choose Deploy.
Figure 2 shows the deployment settings for the NVFP4 variant.
Deployment typically takes 15–20 minutes while SageMaker AI provisions the instance and loads the weights. When the endpoint status changes to InService, the endpoint is ready for requests, as shown in Figure 3.
Deploy using the SageMaker Python SDK
SageMaker JumpStart identifies each variant by a model ID:
- BF16: meta-vlm-muse-spark-open-816b-a42b.
- NVFP4: meta-vlm-muse-spark-open-816b-a42b-nvfp4.
The following code deploys the NVFP4 variant with SageMaker Python SDK v3. You can run it in a SageMaker Studio notebook, which uses your domain’s execution role. In any other Python environment with AWS credentials, pass your SageMaker AI execution role with the role_arn parameter. Muse Spark Open is a gated model, so you must set accept_eula=True to deploy it. To pin a specific model version, add model_version to JumpStartConfig.
Run inference
When the endpoint is in service, send it a request with the invoke method. The endpoint accepts an OpenAI-compatible chat payload with a messages list and returns a chat completion. The final answer is in message.content, the model’s reasoning is in message.reasoning_content, and usage.reasoning_tokens reports how many tokens the reasoning used. Because Muse Spark Open is a reasoning model, leave enough room in max_tokens for its reasoning and the final answer.
The endpoint also supports streaming. To receive tokens as they’re generated, add "stream": true to the request body and call endpoint.invoke_with_response_stream instead of invoke.
Clean up
To stop incurring charges, delete the endpoint when you no longer need it. If you deployed with the SDK, delete the model, the endpoint, and the endpoint configuration:
If you deployed from SageMaker Studio, delete the endpoint in the SageMaker AI console: choose Inference, then Endpoints, select the endpoint, and choose Actions, Delete.
Conclusion
In this post, we showed how to deploy Muse Spark Open, Meta’s coding-optimized open-weight model, from SageMaker JumpStart to an endpoint in your own AWS account. You used SageMaker Studio or the SageMaker Python SDK and sent the model a first inference request. Benchmark both variants on your own repositories before you choose an instance for production.
To get started, search for Muse Spark Open in SageMaker JumpStart in SageMaker Studio. For more deployment options, such as inference components and optimized deployment configurations, refer to JumpStart foundation model usage in the Amazon SageMaker AI Developer Guide. Before you deploy, review the Muse Model License, which SageMaker JumpStart shows when you deploy the model. For help planning a production deployment, contact AWS.

articles.title: Starlink bridé en Ukraine : Elon Musk se défausse sur Donald Trump
articles.text:
L’affaire Starlink en Ukraine connaît un rebondissement, provoqué par Elon Musk. Dans une réponse adressée ce mercredi 14 octobre à Mykhailo Fedorov, ex-ministre ukrainien de la Défense, le patron de SpaceX renvoie la responsabilité à la Maison-Blanche.
Dans sa réponse, Elon Musk explique que Starshield, la version militarisée de Starlink, appartient au gouvernement américain. Toute limite est décidée « par l’armée américaine et, au final, par le président des États-Unis », c’est-à-dire Donald Trump. Elon Musk laisse ainsi entendre que les réclamations doivent être adressées au président américain.
Pour rappel, les drones ukrainiens équipés de terminaux Starlink ont perdu leur connexion dès que leur vitesse dépassait les 160 km/h. Les forces ukrainiennes s’en sont aperçues dans la nuit du 13 au 14 octobre. La coupure a suscité un vif émoi en Ukraine, mais aussi en Europe. Kiev, en effet, mise beaucoup sur ce réseau satellitaire pour communiquer avec ses troupes et diriger ses drones.
À 160 km/h, ce sont surtout les drones intercepteurs ukrainiens qui ne peuvent plus utiliser ce réseau. Serhii Beskrestnov, conseiller de Volodymyr Zelensky pour les technologies de défense, a rappelé au passage sur Telegram que ces drones, guidés par Starlink, sont aujourd’hui la parade la plus efficace contre les Shahed à réaction.
« Starlink est utilisé dans la solution la plus efficace à l’heure actuelle (les intercepteurs) pour protéger notre espace aérien contre les Shahed à réaction. En réalité, par leurs actions, nos partenaires nous privent de l’une des rares chances dont nous disposons pour protéger le pays contre les Shahed à réaction », a-t-il écrit.
Selon Mykhailo Fedorov, le problème serait résolu ou en passe de l’être. « La connectivité Starlink à des vitesses pouvant atteindre 160 km/h est en train d’être rétablie. La suppression totale de la limite de vitesse imposée par Starshield est désormais essentielle pour la défense de l’Ukraine. Merci, Elon Musk. Nous espérons pouvoir compter sur votre soutien continu. »
Cela étant, mercredi soir, le ministère ukrainien de la Défense a fait état d’une meilleure qualité de connexion, tout en précisant que la limite de 160 km/h restait en place.
Musk ne dit rien du Starlink civil
Dans son message, Elon Musk distingue deux réseaux. Starlink reste selon lui un service commercial contrôlé par SpaceX, réservé aux usages civils ou défensifs. Pourtant, Kiev a affirmé que les deux systèmes ont été bridés. Sur ce réseau, qu’il contrôle, le patron de SpaceX n’a rien dit.
À Kiev, on doute du hasard. Serhii Beskrestnov, toujours sur sa chaîne Telegram, a relié la mesure à « la situation politique actuelle ». Donald Trump reproche aux frappes ukrainiennes sur les raffineries russes la hausse des prix à la pompe, à moins de trois semaines des élections de mi-mandat du 3 novembre, passant sous silence son expédition militaire en Iran.
Sur X, la réponse d’Elon Musk a circulé très vite. L’économiste ukrainien Tymofiy Mylovanov l’a relayée avec une réaction de Volodymyr Zelensky. Yaroslav Trofimov, correspondant du Wall Street Journal, a relevé que cela montre tout l’intérêt d’une solution rivale européenne.
Plus tôt dans la journée, le ministre polonais des Affaires étrangères, Radosław Sikorski, avait déjà reproché à Musk de faire de la politique avec ses produits.

articles.title: Scale Agentic Coding Workflows with Meta’s Muse Spark Open on NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 | NVIDIA Technical Blog
articles.text:
Meta launches Muse Spark Open, a coding-optimized 816B mixture-of-experts (MoE) model with 42B active parameters and a 1M token context window. Trained on NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 Blackwell Ultra specifically for agentic coding workflows, it delivers higher first attempt accuracy, reliable tool calling, and deep codebase understanding across repositories. The 1M token context window holds an entire project, including complex dependencies, legacy code, and thousands of files without breaking a task into pieces.
As a reasoning model, Muse Spark Open adds audio and video perception alongside image and document understanding, working natively and reliably across what it sees, hears, and reads. NVFP4 checkpoints generated by Meta and optimized for NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra shrink the memory footprint of all 816B parameters with native FP4 Tensor Core acceleration. Fewer bytes moved per token to increase tokens per second per user, and the freed-up memory supports larger KV cache for concurrent long context sessions, delivering higher throughput, a lower cost per token.
Custom-built for agentic coding multimodal understanding across text, image, video, and audio
General coding models are optimized for single-shot completions such as generating a function, writing a unit test, or suggesting an inline fix. They excel at discrete, well-scoped tasks where the context is small, and the answer is immediate. Agentic coding demands something fundamentally different. Planning a multifile refactor, navigating thousands of files, recovering from failing tests, and coordinating subagents over long horizons requires a model built for sustained, multistep work.
Muse Spark Open is built for exactly these workloads, delivering higher first-attempt accuracy, reliable tool calling, and deep codebase understanding across repositories. It plans, acts, observes, and self corrects. It supports multistep task execution with tool use, output evaluation, and iterative refinement. The model uses goal conditioning to hold direction and context compaction to retain the knowledge needed to sustain progress across long-running sessions. With a 1M token context window, it holds an entire project, including complex dependencies, legacy code, and thousands of files without breaking tasks into pieces.
Beyond coding, it searches the web (including multimodal browsing), spawns and coordinates subagents for decomposable tasks, and leverages computer use capabilities unified across desktop, mobile, and browser. It generates separate commentary before each action, so developers know what the agent is doing and why.
The model’s 1.8B perception encoder natively processes interleaved text, images, video frames, and audio without separate pipelines per modality. This means that the model reasons over what it sees, hears, and reads in a single unified pass. This suits developer workflows spanning screenshots, diagrams, error logs, and video walkthroughs within the same agent session. Sparse MoE routing activates only 42B of 816B total parameters per token, delivering frontier agentic capability at a fraction of the serving cost of dense models at equivalent scale.
Muse Spark Open optimized performance on GB300 NVL72
The NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 features a rack scale architecture that integrates 72 NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra GPUs into a single platform. Its large, 72-GPU NVIDIA NVLink domain enables efficient communication at 130 TB/s, eliminating bottlenecks that appear when expert traffic must cross traditional off-the-shelf networks. For a sparse MoE model like Muse Spark Open, which routes each token to eight of 256 experts, that bandwidth directly determines how much of the theoretical throughput a deployment realizes.
Agentic workloads turn static single-turn interactions into multistep workflows that reason, invoke tools, coordinate subagents, and carry growing context from one turn to the next. Out of the box, Muse Spark Open running agentic workloads on NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 delivers up to 50K per second per GPU and up to 600 tokens per second per user, enabling AI factories to run large parameter models in production at high throughput and low latency.
Flexible deployment options for Muse Spark Open
NVIDIA supports multiple inference stacks to meet a variety of developer needs. SGLang, vLLM, and TensorRT LLM give developers direct control over serving configuration, parallelism, and batching on the NVIDIA accelerated computing platform. TensorRT LLM adds compiled engines tuned for NVIDIA GPUs. NVIDIA Dynamo publishes deployment recipes for all three, and separates prefill from decode across dedicated GPU pools, so compute bound prompt processing doesn’t slow token generation. Its KV cache-aware routing sends each request to the worker already holding the relevant prefix, avoiding precomputation as context accumulates across long agentic sessions.
Post-train Muse Spark Open with NeMo AutoModel and Megatron Bridge
Developers can post-train Muse Spark Open on domain specific datasets using NVIDIA NeMo AutoModel, a PyTorch native training library with native Hugging Face checkpoint support and no model conversion required. It enables full SFT and LoRA fine tuning out of the box, optimized for rapid experimentation over a wide variety of industry specific cases.
Developers can also leverage NVIDIA Megatron Bridge to convert Hugging Face checkpoints to Megatron format when they are ready for large production-scale training to take advantage of the optimizations.
Get started with GPU-accelerated Muse Spark Open
To get started, download Muse Spark Open NVFP4 weights from Hugging Face. For production deployments, try the downloadable NVIDIA NIM. The NIM reduces setup to a single command, replacing benchmarking and tuning cycles with a container that automatically selects the best serving backend and precision for the detected hardware.

articles.title: Android Earthquake Alerts : votre smartphone Android sert de sismomètre, et Google l'active maintenant dans plus de 200 pays et régions — Frandroid
articles.text:
Google étend son détecteur de séismes à beaucoup plus de pays. Dans un billet de blog publié ce jeudi 15 octobre, Boone Spooner, Group Product Manager chargé des alertes sismiques chez Google, annonce que l’Android Earthquake Alerts System passe de 98 pays et régions à plus de 200.
Le Panama et le Guatemala font partie des nouveaux pays couverts. Pour leurs habitants, ça peut représenter quelques secondes de préavis avant les secousses, assez pour se mettre à l’abri sous une table.
Google avait d’abord lancé ce système hors des États-Unis en avril 2021, en Grèce et en Nouvelle-Zélande. Depuis, il a envoyé plus d’un milliard d’alertes. L’entreprise le présente comme « le plus grand réseau de détection de séismes basé sur le mobile au monde » (la modestie, ce sera pour une autre fois).
Google ne cite que deux nouveaux pays. Ce jeudi, sa page d’aide, qui liste les zones couvertes, n’avait pas encore été mise à jour. La France y figure déjà, tout comme la Guadeloupe, Saint-Martin et Saint-Barthélemy. Les utilisateurs d’Android sur ces territoires peuvent donc déjà recevoir ces alertes.
Des smartphones qui jouent les sismomètres
Tout repose sur un composant, l’accéléromètre. Ce capteur de mouvement, présent dans la plupart des smartphones Android, sert d’habitude à faire pivoter l’écran. Google s’en sert pour repérer les ondes sismiques, ce qui revient à transformer chaque téléphone en détecteur de séismes collaboratif.
Quand un smartphone détecte une secousse qui ressemble à un séisme, il envoie un signal aux serveurs de Google avec sa position approximative. Les serveurs croisent ensuite les signaux de nombreux appareils pour confirmer le tremblement de terre, le localiser et estimer sa magnitude. Les données circulent plus vite que les ondes sismiques, ce qui permet de prévenir les zones que les secousses n’ont pas encore atteintes.
Ces mini-sismomètres de poche ont déjà servi. Au Venezuela, par exemple, les smartphones Android ont alerté leurs utilisateurs avant les secousses.
Selon l’intensité estimée des secousses à l’endroit où l’on se trouve, le téléphone affiche l’un des trois niveaux d’alerte :
- « Be Aware » (soyez attentif), une alerte simple pour des secousses légères, qui signale qu’un séisme a été détecté à proximité.
- « Be Ready » (soyez prêt), une alerte plus détaillée pour des secousses plus fortes, qui invite à se préparer à agir.
- « Take Action » (agissez), une alerte en plein écran pour des secousses modérées à fortes, avec des consignes immédiates pour se protéger.
Une alerte « Be Ready » plus complète, mais sans date
Google va aussi enrichir l’alerte intermédiaire. Dans les prochains mois, « Be Ready » affichera une carte du rayon dans lequel des secousses ont été détectées, la magnitude estimée du séisme et les gestes à faire. Un bouton permettra aussi de suivre les informations sur le séisme à mesure qu’elles arrivent. Google ne donne pas de calendrier plus précis.
Le système a ses limites, et Google les affiche lui-même sur sa page d’aide. Les alertes ne concernent que les séismes de magnitude 4,5 et plus, et tous ne sont pas détectés. Les estimations de magnitude peuvent se tromper. Surtout, l’alerte peut arriver avant, pendant ou même après le début des secousses, et le téléphone doit être connecté en Wi-Fi ou en données mobiles.
Pourquoi se battre pour quelques secondes ? Dans son billet de 2021, Google citait une étude sur les coûts et bénéfices de l’alerte précoce. D’après celle-ci, plus de la moitié des blessures pourraient être évitées si les gens étaient prévenus à temps.
Ces alertes font partie d’un programme plus large, que Google appelle « résilience face aux crises ». En juin 2026, Yossi Matias, à la tête de Google Research, présentait les autres outils du groupe. On y trouve des prévisions de crues jusqu’à sept jours à l’avance, pour 2 milliards de personnes dans plus de 150 pays, ou encore le suivi des incendies dans 34 pays.
Ce jeudi, Google a aussi publié un livre blanc baptisé « Crisis Resilience » qui fait le point sur ces travaux. La date n’a pas été choisie au hasard. Le 15 octobre, c’est l’International ShakeOut Day, la journée où des millions de personnes s’entraînent aux gestes à faire en cas de séisme.
Android prépare d’autres fonctions d’urgence, comme une option pour appeler les secours en disant trois fois « à l’aide ».
Les alertes sismiques sont activées par défaut. On peut les couper dans les paramètres du téléphone, rubrique « Sécurité et urgences ». Si on ne veut plus que son téléphone serve de capteur au réseau, il faut désactiver la « Précision de la localisation Google ».
Envie de retrouver les meilleurs articles de Frandroid sur Google News ? Vous pouvez suivre Frandroid sur Google News en un clic.
Pour nous soutenir gratuitement, dites simplement à Google d’ajouter Frandroid à vos sources préférées en cliquant ici.
