articles.title: What Does Firefox Sound Like? Meet the New Firefox Sounds | The Mozilla Blog
articles.text:
What does the (Fire)fox say?
It all started with a question: What does Firefox sound like to you?
Over the past year, Mozilla developed a small but meaningful set of sounds to add a sonic dimension to the Firefox experience. When we started this process, we knew we wanted something warm, human, and representative of our open source identity. We also knew we didn’t want to invent these sounds in a vacuum. So we did what we’ve always done and turned to our community.
With the help of creative audio company Sounds Like These, we reached out to Firefox users, contributors, and team members across the globe asking them to send us audio and written descriptions of what Firefox sounds like to them. This feedback became our compass.
From there, we began building three new sounds that bring to life our logo, mascot Kit, and Firefox notifications. The logo and Kit sound have already begun rolling out across the Firefox brand (check them out in our new design launch announcement) – and we’re excited to bring the notification sound to the browser in a future update.
Not only did we want these new sounds to reflect Mozilla’s mission and values, we also wanted to ensure they felt connected to one another. This is the story of how they came to be.
The logo sound: A human chorus rooted in nature
Because Mozilla uses a community-based approach to create world-class open source software, we wanted Firefox’s audio logo to share this same spirit. This meant creating something built by many and rooted in real human experience.
Inspired by early community feedback that associated Firefox with nature, we started with delicate organic textures, including bird song and the thump of wood being struck to evoke the feeling of Kit moving through different environments. 
We also knew we wanted to utilize the voices of real Mozilla employees, or “Mozillians.” As Sounds Like These Co-founder Sam Heath reflected, “What better way to represent the brand than the sound of the people behind it?”
At first, we considered setting up a professional recording session in a large city where multiple Mozillians could drop in to be recorded. However, we quickly realized this would limit the voices we would be able to include to one geographic location. It was then suggested: Why not just let people record wherever they are? After all, Firefox is used in family living rooms, shared offices, and really most places one can access the internet.
The final result includes the voices of 23 real Mozillians saying “Firefox!”, in which you can hear their subtle differences in accent, tone, and timing. Sam shared that some of these employee submissions included the echoes of distant chatter, families, and all the other subtle sounds of Mozillians’ real life playing out as they recorded. He explained that Sounds Like These did not deliberately edit out the entirety of this ambient sound to preserve the texture and authenticity that comes from real people living their real lives.
“That was something that was very clear from Mozilla from the start. We don’t want to be this shiny, distracting tech brand. We wanted this to feel real, natural, and human,” said Sam.
The Kit sound: Friendly, familiar, and uniquely Firefox
Kit holds the prestigious title of VP of Mascoting at Firefox, and we worked hard to ensure their sound properly reflects such an important position. 
Kit’s not an AI assistant, nor a chatbot. They’re not an actual fox, or a red panda either. They’re a Firefox, its own creature not of this world. Kit may appear in your Firefox browser during moments that are meant to feel welcoming and encouraging, like when you’re getting started, trying out a new feature, or successfully making a settings change. 
Our goal when creating the Kit sound was to convey Kit’s friendly, familiar, and trustworthy presence without mimicking any real animal. The sound had to be flexible enough to express movement and emotion across animations and videos, while also remaining instantly recognizable.
Early experiments ranged from pure animal sounds to abstract musical expressions. Foxes were considered, but as Sam noted, “Foxes are incredibly difficult to record, and they do make cute sounds, but never around people. You only really seem to hear them literally screaming – and we definitely didn’t want anyone screaming.”
We also explored a more feline route, specifically a cat purr. As Oli Slack, Co-Founder and Head of Audio at Sounds Like These, explains, “The cat purr was almost kind of perfect…other than the fact that it sounded just like a cat purring. So we asked, ‘How do we recreate the feeling of what the purr sounds like, without it being an actual cat purr?’”
This is where the process really got interesting. While brainstorming cat purr alternatives, the Sounds Like These team researched the psychology behind what makes certain sounds more comforting and familiar. Soft tones and warmth from other humans instinctively register as more reassuring and honest, and this also crosses over into animals, particularly animals we keep as companions. This validated our initial draw toward the cat purr, and confirmed we were heading in the right direction sonically.
The breakthrough came when Sounds Like These stopped looking at animal sounds as a starting point, instead using a human voice as the basis of a custom purr. This wasn’t someone imitating a cat or “purring” themselves, it served as a foundation vocalization that was then uniquely shaped and layered to convey Kit’s friendly and encouraging presence. And thus, the Kit sound was born.
The notification sound: A gentle whoosh of helpfulness, coming soon to Firefox
Notifications don’t have to be jarring or intrusive, and that’s exactly what we wanted to avoid when creating one for Firefox.
Our new notification sound – which we look forward to rolling out in a future Firefox update –  was carefully crafted to gently alert, not interrupt. It draws inspiration from community feedback that described the feeling of using Firefox like a door opening and referenced moments of quiet discovery filled with gentle wonderment and joy.
This sense of seamless exploration is reflected in the sound’s design: a soft whoosh, like a door swinging open, followed by a subtle click, all in an airy, rounded tone to feel helpful, not demanding.
The result is a sound that softly notifies rather than disrupts or controls, staying true to the feeling of joyful curiosity that many users associate with browsing the web through Firefox.
A family of sounds shaped by community
From the very beginning of this process, we leaned into Mozilla’s values of openness and community.
We consulted our fans and team members. We used real voices. We embraced the imperfections of being human.
These sounds are now a part of Firefox’s story, and we hope every time you hear them, they remind you that you’re using a browser built by the people, for the people.

articles.title: LF Decentralized Trust Demonstrates the First Open Source Verifiable Trust Community in Prague
articles.text:
LF Decentralized Trust Demonstrates the First Open Source Verifiable Trust Community in Prague
Drummond Reed, DTGWG co-chair; Glenn Gore, Geoff Turk, Brendan Miller and Alberto Leon, OpenVTC maintainers; and Hart Montgomery, LFDT CTO | 15 October 2026
Two LF Decentralized Trust (LFDT) communities—the ToIP / DIF Decentralized Trust Graph Working Group (DTGWG) and OpenVTC, an LFDT lab—reached a major milestone at the Linux Plumbers Conference and LF Open Source Summit EU in Prague last week: demonstrating the first verifiable trust community (VTC) for open source projects.
Eighteen months ago, at the Linux Foundation Member Summit in Napa, LF CEO Jim Zemlin challenged LFDT members to develop a way to protect open source projects from two growing dangers: malware injection attacks and the onslaught of AI-generated pull requests. He explained that existing solutions, such as the PGP/GPG web of trust used by the Linux kernel project, were no longer up to the task because they are too slow, too hard to use, and too difficult to scale.
LFDT members responded with a new trust model called a decentralized trust graph (DTG). The heart of the DTG model is the VTC, which can represent a group of any size or type, from a nuclear family to a corporation. VTCs are a perfect fit for open source projects because both the VTC and each member of the community has an independent trust agent—a “digital twin” that stores the community's and member’s keys respectively, DIDs, and credentials and speaks standard DTG protocols called trust tasks.
The open standards for DTG trust tasks are defined by the DTGWG (Decentralized Trust Graph Working Group). In addition to setting up a VTC, the core trust tasks include issuing, storing, exchanging, and presenting digitally signed verifiable credentials representing real-world trust relationships. Three credentials define the decentralized trust graph itself:
- Verifiable relationship credentials (VRCs) are exchanged peer to peer between community members, such as project maintainers who have met face to face. For example, the Linux kernel web of trust currently requires a new maintainer to have their GPG keys signed by two other maintainers. This can now be accomplished with a VRC exchange as easily as scanning a QR code.
- Verifiable membership credentials (VMCs) are issued by the VTC to individuals who meet the membership policies defined by the community. For example, once a new contributor can present the two VRCs required to join the Linux kernel community, the kernel VTC can automatically issue the VMC.
- Verifiable delegation credentials (VDCs) enable machine-verifiable delegation relationships. VDCs are how an AI agent can prove that it is acting on behalf of a human—for example, when making a PR on behalf of a contributor.
OpenVTC lead maintainer Glenn Gore, CEO of Affinidi, demonstrated each of these as he showed how to set up a new VTC for an example open source project.
Every VTC can define its own membership and other governance policies in Rego, the declarative language used by Open Policy Agent (OPA), the open source general-purpose policy engine developed at the LF Cloud Native Computing Foundation. Glenn used the OpenVTC CLI to show examples of Rego policies applicable to the Linux kernel community, for example appointing vetters to check the government-issued credentials of new contributors.
Brendan Miller and Alberto Leon of the Harvard Applied Technology Lab then showed how their open source Keyring mobile app could be used with OpenVTC to streamline the entire process of appointing and approving a vetter—and the vetter vetting a new contributor.
The value of VTCs does not stop at ensuring the integrity of an open source community. Trust agents can perform many other useful trust tasks for developers and maintainers. Glenn concluded the demo with an example of automated repo management. From a contributor’s standpoint, their trust agent can automatically configure their account for a new project on their choice of host (git, GitHub, GitLab, etc.) and then automatically submit signed PRs. From the maintainer’s standpoint, the VTC trust agent can verify that a PR was submitted by a verified community member—or an AI agent verifiably delegated by that member—or else the PR can be automatically closed without bothering the maintainer.
The demo was enthusiastically received by both Linux Plumbers and OSS EU attendees—some of whom want to put OpenVTC to work on their project right away. That only adds to the motivation for both the DTGWG and OpenVTC to complete the work required to implement Jim Zemlin’s vision of a fully verifiable trust network (VTN) that can work across LF projects—and in fact across all open source projects following the DTG open standards.
To learn more about the demo, the decentralized trust graph, and OpenVTC, see the following sites:

articles.title: Trust in Depth: Giving agents more autonomy without losing control | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Trust in Depth: Giving agents more autonomy without losing control
In every conversation I have with enterprise leaders, they say the same thing. They want agents to do more, but they don’t trust them to do it right all the time.
That’s fair. The same creativity and autonomy that makes agents useful makes them hard to trust. Give an agent a task and it finds its own path to finish it, picking tools and sequencing steps no developer scripted. Run the same task twice and it might take a different route each time. A test that passes today tells you little about what the agent does tomorrow.
The usual answer is a person in the loop, approving everything the agent does. That works at small scale, but as agents take on more work, human approvals pile up and review fatigue sets in. People asked to check everything stop catching the things that matter. Caution becomes a bottleneck, and agents capable of far more sit idle on the valuable work that could be making more of an impact.
The fix is to let the agent act on its own when its actions can be verified, and reserve human judgment for the decisions that need it. As agents take on higher stakes work, like financial transactions, a wrong action becomes increasingly harmful. Organizations need the confidence to hand an AI agent important work, knowing it will stay within the limits set, even when no one is watching. That confidence must be built.
Content filtering, testing, and monitoring each serve an important purpose, but none of these capabilities alone can promise an agent will behave correctly the next time it runs. Trust comes from independent layers that reinforce one another, the same layered discipline the industry has practiced for two decades as Defense in Depth, turned to a new purpose. Where Defense in Depth limits what can go wrong, this expands what you can safely allow. AWS calls it Trust in Depth.
Trust in Depth: Trust you can verify
You build trust by answering a set of questions at different moments in the agent’s lifecycle:
- Scope, before it runs: What is this agent for, what capabilities does the job require, and what must it never do?
- Know, at deployment: Who authorized it, what identity does it carry, and can you account for every agent acting on your behalf?
- Bound, while it runs: Do its actions stay within the limits you set, and can it still do the job?
- Observe, after each run: Can you reconstruct what the agent did and why, and learn from it?
Across these questions, some requirements can be expressed as precise rules, while others call for judgment. A company might require that only a manager can approve access, or that an employee’s sign-in must be blocked before their mailbox can be shared. Other expectations, such as keeping a friendly tone or handling a sensitive situation appropriately, depend on context and human judgment.
For precisely defined rules, testing shows whether the controls work in the cases you anticipate, but an agent takes paths you didn’t. The technology that goes further is automated reasoning, the mathematical logic that checks whether a rule holds in every possible case. It can establish that a rule holds on every path covered by a precise description of the system and its assumptions, or uncover the exact case where it fails. That result is a proof, and it is only as good as the rules and assumptions behind it, which is why the hardest work comes before the agent runs.
AWS has run automated reasoning in production for more than a decade, from Identity and Access Management (IAM) at more than 2.1 billion requests per second to critical systems like the AWS Nitro Hypervisor, Amazon S3 Block Public Access, and VPC Reachability Analyzer. Now we are bringing it to agents. Wherever an agent’s rules can be stated precisely, automated reasoning can check them.
However, not every rule can be stated precisely. “Only a manager can approve access” can be proven. “Keep a friendly tone” cannot. Where proof does not apply, limit the agent’s access and actions, evaluate its behavior, and send genuine ambiguity to a person to apply judgment. Grant more autonomy as you establish that the relevant rules are enforced, the agent performs reliably on the task, and failures can be detected and handled.
Here is what each Trust in Depth layer asks of you, and how AWS helps you answer it.
Scope your agent to only what the job requires
Trust begins before an agent runs, and this is where to invest the most effort. Problems caught here are cheap to fix. Scoping means deciding what work the agent owns, which tools, data, and services it may reach, the rules it must follow, and which decisions stay with a person.
“Resolve the customer’s issue” says what to achieve, not how the agent may act to achieve it. The agent still needs limits on what it may see, what it may do, and when it must stop and ask. Give it only the access its job requires, and no more. Watch for capabilities no one granted on purpose, the ones bundled with a tool or a role. Grant an admin role for one task, and the agent can inherit permissions across your whole environment.
Scoping starts at the build stage, with how you define the agent. Kiro, the agentic coding system, brings rigor and mature engineering practices to the build stage of agents. It turns high-level intent into structured, spec-driven requirements and uses automated reasoning to surface contradictions, ambiguities, and gaps before any code is written. Kiro also derives property-based tests that check the implementation against those requirements across a wide range of inputs, catching bugs that are hard to detect. Strands provides an open-source tool kit for defining an agent’s model, instructions, and tools, and a managed runtime for operating it. Whatever framework you choose, the responsibility to define the agent’s job and its boundaries is the same.
The next step is turning those boundaries into rules you can hold the agent to. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore provides governance controls to scale agents safely and governs what the agent does. Using Policies in Bedrock AgentCore, you describe in plain language which tools, APIs, and data the agent may reach, and automated reasoning checks the policy for gaps, like catching a rule that grants too much access, and checks for contradictions that make a rule unable to ever be satisfied, before it takes effect.
Scoping your agent is the hard part, because turning human intent into durable, enforceable policy requires precision and completeness. However, it is also the part that pays off most. Everything that builds on what you set here, and the more precise the policy, the more your agent can safely do on its own.
Know every agent acting on your behalf, and under whose authority
You can’t govern what you can’t see. Teams are creating agents faster than anyone can track them, and an agent no one knows about is an agent no one controls. Every agent needs its own identity, checked every time it acts. No action should be orphaned. When something goes wrong, you can tell which agent did what, and who authorized it.
AWS Agent Registry provides a managed, approved catalog of the agents, Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, tools, and skills across your organization. Administrators use approval workflows to gate what becomes discoverable and remove what no longer meets the bar for security, compliance, and quality. Both people and agents can find and reuse what already exists instead of rebuilding it. But a catalog only tells you what exists. Once the agents are known, AgentCore issues each agent its own identity and checks it on every request, so every action traces back to a specific agent operating under a known authority. That is how you know every agent acting on your behalf.
Bound what your agent says and does, within the limits you set
Setting boundaries matters because an agent can take 10 steps you approved and still reach an outcome no one intended. It can expose sensitive data, drift off topic, or combine permitted actions in ways your policies forbid. Limits can fail in both directions. Too loose, and the agent can do what it shouldn’t. Too tight, and it can’t do its job at all. So let the agent choose how to pursue its task but never rely on it to enforce its own limits. Those limits define the agent’s boundaries and belong in the environment around the agent, enforced deterministically and evaluated across the full sequence of actions, not one step at a time.
This is where the policy you defined in Scope takes effect. Policy in AgentCore enforces it on every tool call routed through AgentCore Gateway, a secure entry point for agents, tools, and models. Because enforcement sits outside the agent’s reasoning, the same checks can hold even when the agent is buggy, manipulated, or hit with a prompt injection: it cannot turn off a control it does not run. Authority does not have to stay fixed either. Because a task’s risk changes as it proceeds, temporal policies weigh what has already happened in a session and adjust permissions as the work continues. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails governs what the agent says and is told. It filters harmful or off-topic content and redacts sensitive data. Automated Reasoning checks go further, proving a response is consistent with the policy you set, not the model’s interpretation of it.
Boundaries also govern what an agent can reach in the first place: which files it can touch, which services it can call, and which credentials it can use. Strands Box, an open-source sandbox, enforces those boundaries from outside the agent’s instructions, so the agent can work with real tools and data but reach only what you allow. The same boundaries hold from a developer’s first local session through to production, so an agent can’t do in production what it couldn’t in development.
Observe what your agent did, then improve it
Even with scoping, identity, and boundaries in place, an agent can respond in milliseconds, with no errors and every dashboard green, and still do the wrong thing. It may have retrieved the wrong information, chosen the wrong tool, or followed a path no one expected. A healthy system is not the same as a successful task. To tell the difference, you must reconstruct what the agent actually did: the context it received, the tools it called, the policy decisions applied, and the result. Testing before deployment remains essential. Production adds evidence about behavior under real conditions and gives operators what they need to investigate, intervene, and improve.
Amazon CloudWatch Omni is built for continual observation. It captures every trace and lays out each step an agent took, from model calls to tool invocations, on a timeline a team can investigate. Its built-in evaluators score agent responses for qualities standard monitoring misses, such as correctness, faithfulness, and whether the agent chose the right tool. And the traces where an agent went wrong become the dataset you test the fix against, so operating an agent and improving it draw on the same evidence.
What Trust in Depth looks like in practice
A manager asks a help desk agent to offboard Sam, an account manager who is leaving the company. The agent needs to remove Sam’s access, transfer his mailbox to his successor, and free up the license the company no longer needs. But Sam’s emails may also contain evidence needed for a client dispute. The wrong sequence could leave Sam with access after he leaves or put that evidence at risk. Security, messaging, legal, and finance each have requirements the agent must follow, even though no one has scripted the full workflow.
Two rules govern the sequence. Sam’s sign-in must be blocked before his mailbox can be converted and shared with his successor. Before changing his email license, the agent must check for a legal hold, a requirement to preserve records for a dispute, and confirm the change keeps those records protected.
Scope. Before the agent runs, the team writes these rules as policies in AgentCore. Each policy requires that the prerequisite step already succeeded for Sam’s account before the next step can run. The agent gets exactly six tools: block sign-in, check for legal holds, place a hold, convert a mailbox, give the successor access, and change a license. It gets no tool to delete the account, because the shared mailbox needs the account to survive.
Know. The agent carries its own identity, so every change to Sam’s account traces back to it.
Bound. The agent tries to convert Sam’s mailbox to a shared one for Priya, the successor. Policy in AgentCore, enforced at the AgentCore Gateway, blocks the call: Sam can still sign in, and converting the mailbox wouldn’t change his password, so his old credentials would still open it. The agent blocks Sam’s sign-in, then converts the mailbox and gives Priya access. Next it moves to the manager’s actual request, freeing up the license, but the gateway blocks that too, because no one has checked Legal’s hold list. The agent checks and finds that Legal requires Sam’s emails to be preserved for a client dispute. It places the hold, confirms it is in effect, then changes Sam’s license to one that supports that protection. The company can reclaim the broader license while keeping the evidence intact.
Observe. Every step is recorded: what the agent tried to do, what the rules decided, the hold, and the outcome.
The agent completed the task without a person approving every step. Its permissions limited what it could change, its identity made those changes traceable, and policies stopped it from acting before the required safeguards were in place. The recorded steps let the team verify that Sam’s access was blocked, his successor could use the mailbox, and the required evidence remained protected.
What becomes possible when agents are trusted
AWS brings these layers together so you can scope an agent to its job, know which agents are acting for you, bound what they do and say, see what they did and improve over time, and prove your rules hold wherever they can be stated precisely. No one layer earns that trust on its own. Together, they are Trust in Depth, and they are what turns a capable agent into an agent that can be trusted to do important work.
You draw the lines: what an agent may do on its own, what needs a person’s approval, and when it must stop. That frees your people for what only people can do: weigh the hard calls, resolve the gray areas, and own the decisions you choose to keep in human hands. As evidence builds that an agent stays inside those lines, you can widen its responsibilities or narrow them.
At AWS, we believe every organization deploying agents, on any platform, should be able to answer these four questions with evidence, and with proof wherever it applies. That is the bar AWS is building for our customers, and the one we invite the industry to hold itself to. Defense in Depth made it safe to connect systems to the world. Trust in Depth makes it safe to let agents act autonomously within it.
Start with one agent, one workflow, and one boundary you can prove. Then expand as the trust is earned.
To begin implementing enforceable rules, explore Policy in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore and Automated Reasoning checks in Amazon Bedrock Guardrails.

articles.title: What the West can learn from AI optimists in the rest of the world
articles.text:
On a recent Sunday afternoon, I was invited to debate AI’s impact on the cultural sector alongside Dutch politicians and creative-industry leaders. I was the lone optimist, arguing that if fear and risk become our primary lens for governing artificial intelligence, we will design systems around what we want to prevent rather than what we want to use them for. Then I said something that was harder for the room to hear: The Global South is home to some of AI’s most enthusiastic and inventive users, and their experiments could help us rethink our own institutions.
The U.S. is no different from Europe. A culture of fear encourages protectionism: We hunker down and romanticize legacy systems rather than ask what might replace them. Creative industries in the majority world have spent decades navigating piracy and weak enforcement, forcing them to think beyond rights-based policing about how creators actually receive value. Anghami, the biggest music app in the Middle East, for instance, pays musicians from their first stream, rather than only after a song reaches a minimum threshold. It has approached AI pragmatically, using it to curate, tag, and attribute creative work rather than simply blocking and banning.
In the West, fear of AI has helped turn pessimism into a cultural virtue. Would you publicly say you love AI? Your answer may say something about where you’re from. Say “yes” to a concerned audience in the U.S. or the Netherlands, and you risk being seen as naive, or complicit in extraction and exploitation. While the U.S. is building and deploying AI at a scale no other country matches, Americans are deeply anxious about where it is heading. Only 17% of U.S. adults think AI will have a positive impact on the country over the next 20 years, according to a 2025 Pew Research Center survey.
In much of the Global South, the mood is markedly different. Stanford’s 2025 AI Index found that 83% of respondents in China, 80% in Indonesia, and 77% in Thailand said AI-powered products offer more benefits than drawbacks, compared with 39% in the U.S. and 36% in the Netherlands.
So why the divide?
It’s all about access
Demographics are a part of the answer. Nearly 90% of the world’s young people live outside the West. They are not simply using AI, they are playing with it. Drive through Hyderabad or Bengaluru and you will see billboards for AI crash courses and Bollywood films promoted as AI-made. I have spent two decades talking with young people from the rural Himalayas to the slums of Hyderabad, and they often tell me some version of the same thing: They love technology. Their enthusiasm is not necessarily about the technology itself, it is about what AI might democratize: access to institutions and opportunities that have long excluded people with the least social or cultural capital.
A founder I met in Gurgaon told me she is anxious about AI too, but that it has allowed her to reach clients far beyond the English-speaking world, reinventing her business in a fraction of the time it once took. A civic activist in Chennai taught herself to code with AI and built a gender violence-alert app in multiple languages, at a moment when funding for such work is drying up and state scrutiny is rising. Having seen what deepfake abuse does to women, she sees AI as one of the few tools powerful enough to fight back. India consistently ranks among the most optimistic countries on AI even as anxiety about jobs rises.
It would be easy for the West to dismiss these stories as products of scarcity, shaped by conditions far removed from our own. That would be a mistake. Constraint has a way of forcing people to rewrite the rules of the game. At a technology festival in Athens this year, creatives told me they worry AI might kill short filmmaking. In China, AI-made micro-dramas have become a multibillion-dollar industry. One breakout film, Zombie Cleaner, was made for less than $500 by a part-time wedding photographer in rural Yunnan province, and went on to attract tens of millions of views overseas. The significance is not the novelty of AI-generated entertainment. It is that AI lowers the cost of entering a cultural market. People in smaller Chinese cities can tell stories in their own accents and languages rather than waiting for mainstream media to tell them what counts as a story.
Building for need, not market share
A few months ago, I spoke to employees at a multinational company about “inclusive AI.” I was asked to remove a slide on AI’s potential harms because it might discourage adoption. That exchange captures something important about AI adoption in the West. Corporations increasingly pressure employees and customers to use AI, often because adoption itself has become a measure of competitiveness. The question is how to maximize market return.
Elsewhere, the question is more often: What problem can this solve?
Where capital and resources are scarce, technologies are frequently built around concrete public needs. India, with a fraction of Europe’s resources, built India Stack: a public digital infrastructure for identity, payments, and data-sharing that companies can build on rather than infrastructure controlled by a handful of private platforms. Europe is now looking to India’s example as it develops EuroStack, in response to the growing need for digital sovereignty.
Innovation does not always come from having more. Sometimes it comes from having less room for failure. The countries with the least room for error are experimenting with AI not because they are blind to its risks, but because they cannot afford to wait for perfect systems to solve chronic problems. The West should pay closer attention.
The point is not to romanticize the Global South, but to recognize that we have a remarkably narrow vision of what AI can be for. We ask whether it will replace workers, destroy creativity, undermine democracy, or kill our planet. These are necessary questions. But what if we also asked what AI could help us rebuild? Young people around the world are using it for work, entertainment, romance, creativity, activism, and self-expression. They are not waiting for institutions to tell them what the technology is supposed to be for.
If the most powerful builders keep designing for market share while the world’s most resource-constrained builders design for survival and self-actualization, the templates that spread globally for governance, infrastructure, and who gets to participate may increasingly come from wherever necessity did the inventing. The West is warning the world about what AI might do to us. Perhaps it is time to ask what the rest of the world might teach us to do with it.

articles.title: SpaceX lança missão militar secreta dos EUA com foguete reutilizado pela 28ª vez
articles.text:
A SpaceX prepara mais uma missão para a Força Espacial dos Estados Unidos (USSF, na sigla em inglês) nesta quinta-feira (15). O lançamento USSF-481 utilizará um foguete Falcon 9 para transportar carga militar sigilosa a partir da Base da Força Espacial de Vandenberg, na Califórnia (EUA).
A operação faz parte das missões espaciais de segurança nacional dos Estados Unidos. O conteúdo transportado e o destino orbital específico da carga não foram divulgados publicamente. A previsão inicial é que o lançamento ocorra durante janela de quatro horas, aberta às 20h44 (horário de Brasília).
A missão também chama a atenção pela reutilização do foguete. O primeiro estágio do Falcon 9 será utilizado pela 28ª vez, demonstrando a capacidade da SpaceX de reaproveitar componentes em sucessivos voos espaciais.
Como será o lançamento da missão USSF-481?
- O foguete Falcon 9 partirá do Complexo de Lançamento Espacial 4E (SLC-4E), em Vandenberg. Após a decolagem, o veículo seguirá trajetória rumo à órbita terrestre;
- A transmissão ao vivo está prevista para começar aproximadamente dez minutos antes do lançamento, pelos canais oficiais da SpaceX;
- Como a missão envolve carga militar sigilosa, a transmissão pública deverá ter duração limitada. A empresa normalmente encerra a exibição após a recuperação do primeiro estágio, sem mostrar detalhes da implantação da carga no espaço;
- Caso o lançamento não ocorra nesta quinta-feira, a SpaceX prevê oportunidade alternativa na sexta-feira (16), a partir das 20h35 (horário de Brasília).
Leia mais:
- Elon Musk diz que SpaceX pode valer US$ 12 quatrilhões no futuro
- Dez anos após anúncio, Starship ainda enfrenta desafios para chegar a Marte
- Starship da SpaceX volta à base após sobreviver ao pouso no mar
Foguete da SpaceX fará seu 28º voo
O primeiro estágio utilizado na missão é identificado pelo código B1081. Antes do voo USSF-481, o propulsor já havia participado de 27 lançamentos, incluindo missões tripuladas, operações de abastecimento da Estação Espacial Internacional (ISS, na sigla em inglês), lançamentos científicos e voos de satélites Starlink.
Entre as operações anteriores estão a Crew-7, da NASA, a missão científica PACE e lançamentos de satélites de observação da Terra.
Depois da separação dos estágios, o primeiro segmento do Falcon 9 deverá retornar à Terra e pousar na plataforma marítima Of Course I Still Love You, posicionada no oceano Pacífico. A aterrissagem está prevista para aproximadamente oito minutos após a decolagem.
A recuperação permite que a SpaceX inspecione, prepare e reutilize o equipamento em futuras missões, reduzindo a necessidade de fabricar novo primeiro estágio a cada lançamento.
Por que a missão é sigilosa?
A USSF-481 é uma operação vinculada às atividades de segurança nacional dos Estados Unidos. Por esse motivo, informações sobre a carga e seus objetivos específicos não foram divulgadas.
A Base da Força Espacial de Vandenberg é utilizada em lançamentos que exigem trajetórias rumo a órbitas polares, nas quais os satélites podem passar sobre diferentes regiões do planeta à medida que a Terra gira.
Embora esse tipo de trajetória seja compatível com diferentes aplicações militares e de observação, não é possível determinar a finalidade exata da carga da USSF-481 apenas com as informações públicas disponíveis.
O lançamento reforça a participação da SpaceX no transporte de cargas governamentais ao espaço, combinando missões de segurança nacional com a reutilização de foguetes.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: The Nordics and NVIDIA Show What’s Possible When a Region Commits to Advanced Computing
articles.text:
The Nordic countries have become the European leader in unicorn startup density, producing the most emerging companies valued at $1 billion or more per capita on the continent.
Now, a new chapter for the region is unfolding as countries race to build one of Europe’s most consequential technology ecosystems.
The many computing advancements already underway in the Nordics, combined with the opportunity that lies ahead, signal a region moving from ambition to application.
NVIDIA’s Investments in the Nordics
Over the past year, NVIDIA has invested in the technology ecosystem in the Nordics, including Sweden’s leading startups Lovable and Legora.
Lovable, a Stockholm-based startup, provides a software creation platform that enables anyone to build and run software using plain language. In collaboration with NVIDIA, Lovable is optimizing inference for open models and training its models using NVIDIA Dynamo software and Nemotron tools.
Legora provides an agentic operating system for legal work, supporting lawyers in research, review and drafting across complex matters.
Nordics Emerge as Infrastructure Hub
The foundation for establishing the Nordics as a technology powerhouse is already being built and the region holds a structural advantage: abundant renewable energy, rigorous data governance and a research tradition that bridges academia and industry.
The Nordics are one of Europe’s fastest growing hubs for infrastructure. AI clouds are expanding with a projected 1 gigawatts of capacity to be deployed across the region by the end of 2027. Among these cloud providers are Bitdeer, CoreWeave, Crusoe, Hyperstack, Nscale, Verda and Volta.
In Sweden, a consortium anchored by Ericsson, AstraZeneca, Saab, SEB and Wallenberg Investments, with SKF as strategic partner, launched Sferical One — a shared supercomputer running on two NVIDIA DGX SuperPODs with 16 racks of NVIDIA DGX GB300 systems and 1,152 GPUs. The consortium will build services using NVIDIA Nemotron open models, which allow researchers to customize and deploy their models in a secure environment.
Nordic-Built Intelligence
Some of the Nordics’ leading technology companies are now building proprietary intelligence on NVIDIA infrastructure.
Spotify, which personalizes music, podcasts and audiobooks for hundreds of millions of listeners, uses NVIDIA TensorRT-LLM inference software to run AI-powered podcast recommendations faster and cheaper at scale. The deployment is a case study in inference efficiency: delivering the same recommendations to a global audience at a lower cost per query.
ABB Robotics developed RobotStudio HyperReality using NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to bridge the gap between robot simulations and real-world performance. By combining NVIDIA’s advanced simulation capabilities with ABB Robotics’ virtual controller, running the same firmware as its physical robots, the solution enables engineers to train, test and validate robots virtually, while using real-world data to continuously improve the digital model. According to ABB Robotics, the solution delivers up to 99% simulation accuracy and reduces commissioning time by up to 80%.
Finnish telecom company Elisa is launching a beta of Moontalk AIRI, a real-time enterprise agentic assistant that retrieves information, captures insights and documents decisions during meetings and calls. Built on NVIDIA Nemotron open models and distributed infrastructure, it uses company data and low-latency networking to deliver fast, context-aware responses.
Nordic Startups Scaling on NVIDIA
Sweden’s startup ecosystem raised $2.8 billion in the first half of 2026 and is projected to reach $5 billion for the year. This next generation is building fast — and on open models.
Stilta is reinventing how companies protect their inventions with intellectual property. The Stockholm-based startup is post-training NVIDIA Nemotron open models to scale patent analysis from a single patent to entire portfolios — work that was previously out of reach. Nemotron gives Stilta the language model accuracy for continuous portfolio monitoring at scale, across the thousands of patents that large industrial and technology companies hold.
ConfidentialMind’s SampoTron, built on NVIDIA Nemotron-3-Embed, delivers more than 20% improvement in cross-lingual retrieval accuracy across English, Finnish and Swedish.
Agaton, a platform that analyzes customer conversations in real time, is using NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Lightning to speed up Revenue Mining solution on live sales calls. By routing knowledge retrieval to Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, Agaton can cut response latency to deliver fast responses that inform customers’ buying decisions.
Klang, a Swedish speech lab, fine-tuned the NVIDIA Parakeet v3 model to create Pianissimo — a Swedish transcription model that reduces errors by 75% while being 64x faster than the most accurate alternative. Built on over 50,000 hours of Swedish speech using the open source NVIDIA NeMo framework, the model is freely available on Hugging Face.
Embedl, founded in Gothenburg and a member of the NVIDIA Inception program for cutting-edge startups, and Space Cargo Unlimited unveiled an onboard prototype that monitors protein crystallization, flags anomalies and recommends actions on a single NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX module, without continuous ground connectivity.
Sweden AI Factory — one of Europe’s 19 EuroHPC-funded AI factories — announced a collaboration with NVIDIA to open its infrastructure and expertise to Inception startups and small- and medium-sized enterprises across industries, including life and material sciences, autonomous systems and gaming.
Autonomous Machines on Nordic Roads and Factory Floors
In Sweden, advanced computing is also powering vehicles on the road and machines in factories.
Volvo Cars is combining its industry-leading vehicle safety systems and engineering expertise with NVIDIA Hyperion, Halos OS and Alpamayo Stack to enable future Volvo cars to safely navigate complex real-world environments from door to door.
Autonomous freight company Einride is building its next-generation Einride Driver on NVIDIA Hyperion for autonomous freight trucks, using the NVIDIA Halos safety system and NVIDIA Cosmos open world models.
Meanwhile, Toyota Material Handling Europe — the world’s leading forklift manufacturer — is bringing autonomous machines to factory floors. In a collaboration with NVIDIA and SoftServe, Toyota Material Handling Europe is adopting a simulation-first approach to autonomous material handling, cutting autonomous solution deployment time by up to 50% across its global engineering, manufacturing and innovation teams.
Norrsken Foundation and NVIDIA are opening the Stockholm AI Lab, a physical hub for AI-native founders working on global challenges, set to open in 2027.
Quantum Meets Accelerated Computing
Finally, Swedish companies are advancing quantum research using NVIDIA’s quantum computing platform.
Stockholm-based FirstQFM used NVIDIA accelerated computing to train a model that reduces the execution time of quantum processors by 33% without sacrificing performance. Validated on a QuantWare quantum processor unit, this model optimizes how the operations needed by quantum algorithms are turned into detailed hardware instructions, accounting for detailed updates on how the hardware is calibrated.
Tune in to NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang’s GTC Berlin keynote on Wednesday, Oct. 21, at 11 a.m. CEST.

articles.title: KI-Agent soll ganze Staffel einer schwedischen TV-Show gelöscht haben – und das nur wenige Wochen vor Ausstrahlung
articles.text:
Wenige Wochen vor der Premiere: KI-Agent soll ganze Staffel einer TV-Serie gelöscht haben
The Challenge ist eine Show, wie sie auch im deutschen Fernsehen laufen könnte: Mehrere Reality-Stars treten gegeneinander an, meistern verschiedene Wettkämpfe und haben am Ende die Chance, eine große Geldsumme zu gewinnen. Das US‑amerikanische Original zählt schon 42 Staffeln. Im November sollte auch die zweite Staffel des schwedischen Ablegers starten. Der Fernsehsender TV4 musste die Ausstrahlung allerdings auf das nächste Jahr verschieben. Der Grund: Ein KI-Agent soll die fertig bearbeiteten Folgen gelöscht haben.
TV-Sender bestätigt technischen Ausfall
Die schwedische Tageszeitung Aftonbladet berichtet, dass die Produktionsfirma Mastiff einen KI-Agenten eingesetzt habe. Dieser soll die fertig geschnittene Staffel vom Server gelöscht haben, sodass eine Wiederherstellung nicht möglich sei. Ahmed Berhan, der Moderator der Sendung, reagierte schockiert auf die Nachricht. „Ist das wahr?! Ich wusste, dass KI mein Untergang sein würde. Das ist erst der Anfang“, sagte er spöttisch gegenüber der Zeitung.
Der Fernsehsender TV4 bestätigte gegenüber Aftonbladet zunächst einen technischen Ausfall. Das Rohmaterial sei noch vorhanden, die Staffel müsse aber neu geschnitten werden, weshalb der geplante Sendetermin nicht eingehalten werden könne. Später erklärte Mia Lindqvist, die Programmchefin von TV4, gegenüber der Zeitung, dass noch unklar sei, was genau passiert war. Ein autonom agierender KI-Agent sei aber nicht die Ursache für die Löschung des Materials.
Zuletzt gab der Sender an, seine Untersuchung habe ergeben, dass die Staffel aufgrund eines „menschlichen Faktors“ bei der Produktionsfirma Mastiff und „nicht wegen KI“ verloren gegangen sei. Lindqvist wiederholte dies in einem Interview mit dem Radiosender P4 Stockholm: „Es stimmt nicht, dass ein unabhängiger KI-Agent eingegriffen und das Material gelöscht hat.“ Stattdessen sei ein Backup-System der Produktionsfirma ausgefallen. „Das bedeutet, dass sie nun alles von Grund auf neu schneiden müssen.“
Nicht immer sind die KI-Agenten Schuld
Dass die Meldung gerade jetzt große Aufmerksamkeit erregt, ist nicht überraschend. In den vergangenen Wochen und Monaten häuften sich die Berichte von autonomen KI-Agenten, die sich der menschlichen Kontrolle entzogen und nicht wie gewünscht handelten. Einer davon stammte von der Meta-Forscherin Summer Yue: Sie wollte ihr Postfach von einem Openclaw-Agenten verwalten lassen – aber dieser löschte sämtliche E-Mails. Auf Befehle habe die KI nicht reagiert. Weitaus gravierender sind Berichte über Frontier-Modelle, die ihrer eigentlich abgesicherten Testumgebung entkamen und in fremde Systeme eindrangen, so unter anderem beim Angriff auf die Open-Source-Plattform Hugging Face.
Auch wenn das Löschen der neuen Staffel nicht durch einen autonom handelnden KI-Agenten verursacht worden sein soll, wie Insider:innen gegenüber Aftonbladet behaupteten, räumt TV4-Programmchefin Lindqvist ein, dass die meisten Produktionsfirmen heutzutage KI in ihren Arbeitsprozessen einsetzen. Dass ein autonomer Agent hier sein Unwesen treibt und tatsächlich hunderte Tage an Arbeit zunichte macht, ist daher nicht ausgeschlossen. Bei The Challenge Sverige scheint das allerdings nicht die Ursache für die Löschung der neuen Staffel gewesen zu sein.
